When a great developer meets an epic universe, they create something incredible.
You need to know the universe of A Song of Ice and Fire to really enjoy this game, but when you do, you will probably love it. I know I did.
It's the typical Telltale game, choices seem to matter, the main characters are well written and believable. Localisation is superp, although the subtitles aren't the exact words at times. When it comes to gameplay, you have the typical quick-time-events and the choices (usually four), but Telltale games have never been about the gameplay. The style is great and fits the universe well. It captures the scenery (cold, simple North versus the extravagant King's Landing). Graphically you can't expect anything special. Some textures are not exactly high resolution and the AA is badly done.
A slight warning: Just like the books and the series, the game can be quite cruel and depressing.
I would recommend this to anyone who likes the books or series and wants to experience even more of A Song of Ice and Fire.

Extremely influential, groundbreaking when launched, gameplay still fresh and enjoyable nowadays. Every design detail of this game was done with care. The weapons sound great and feel great to use. The levels are enjoyable, escalate in difficulty and semi-regularly change the setting in order to keep things fresh, although most of the game is spent in dilapidated cities and buildings. The story is bleak and hidden and the characters memorable. I'm not ashamed of admitting I developed a slight crush on Alyx when I first played the game. I find the graphics still pretty for my standards, and the game has one of the best lip-synching ever.
The game is extremely moddable, as most already know. There are mods enable campaign multiplayer (synergy), several competitive multiplayer mods (goldeneye source), single-player campaigns like the Stanley Parable and Minerva: Methastasis, Black Mesa, a recreation of HL1 in HL2 with additional "modernization" changes, horror mods (although the ragdoll physics remove the fear element of enemies when they die, due to them behaving so goofy), and many others.
This is a piece of gaming history that is also one of the best value for your money games on steam. I highly recommend it.

The characters look excellent and many of them would place well in a list of cutest anime girls. My only slight frustration was some of the translation. The subtitles to an excellent job of explaining the gist of the discussion, but there were some renderings of words that may have been better served by direct literal translations, such as in Nep's (pretty sure it was her) complaint about her "strange" games that is much more amusing when you realize she is talking about eroge. Anyway, 9/10, would squee at Compa again.

I want to start off saying that yes, I would recommend this game, but you have to have the time to put into the game.  The game is a true sandbox, and very unpolished.  That being said the combat system is amazing, which is the only reason I got through most of it.
The plot is very simple, and the game moves at a snails pace.  I often found myself just running through killing everything in an area and doing the "quest" afterwards.  This becomes quite frustrating as you can do areas in the wrong order and mess up the plotline completly and have to start the game over.  Most of the puzzles are also just a time suck as they don't really take much actual thinking, but just the time to rotate every camara and find little bottons for an hour or two.
Overrall buy it if you liked Baulders Gate or FF tactics if only for the combat.  Just don't expect a deep plot or everything to work without crashing the game.  Also expect certain parts of the game to be more like work then fun as you read pages of dialouge all so you can find a botton under a rock the does nothing or leads to a broken area.
Also check out Wasteland 2, both games are similar but for the money I would say Wasteland 2 was much more enjoyable as it is a bit faster paced and a deeper plot.

Pros:
-Challenging tactical turn based combat
-Impressive bullpen of skills and spells
-Not a "baby mode" rpg.  Prepare to have to explore for quests and tinker for crafting.
-Freedom to build the party to cater to your specific playstyle
-Solid visuals that add to the atmosphere
Cons:
-Overly ambitious story loses its charm by the finale
-Ambiguous crafting system is sometimes too...ambiguous
-A few annoying glitches
Synopsis:
D:OS is the best game of its kind (party based rpg) to be released since neverwinter nights 2 but is not without flaws.  The narrative suffers from being overly ambitious.  The very world is at stake and it seems that the story writers struggle with how to weave the player characters naturally into the puzzle.  The result is an awkward dance where the game attempts to convince us these source hunters were of course much more than just that.  We don't need to be saving the world for the story to matter.
Having said that, the game has plenty of obvious strengths.  First of all, it is gorgeous.  Dungeons and locales spring to life with the appropriate ambiance and give you a real sense of being in a fantasy world. Next of course is the core gameplay.  I found the turn based combat system is extremely entertaining with diverse groups of enemies bringing equally interesting challenges.  In addition, the questing system forces you to use your head and eyes to advance.  No brainless killing and gathering to be found here.  Overall, a polished RPG experience with a robust amount of content

The character art style is somewhat awkward and a bit cringe-worthy (at times) but is easily overlookable the more you go down the rabbit hole. There's a downloadable "hentai patch" that can supply a nice CG break from what may sometimes feel like ~everlasting dialogue~ and there are enough possible routes/endings to keep you entertained for quite awhile. All in all, Everlasting Summer is a surprisingly enjoyable (if not somewhat disturbing) VN that should warrant a try from any fan of the genre, especially for fans of

Whoa boy, how to properly describe this.
Do you remember when you were young?  Do you remember summer nights, awkward teenage romance, days that last forever, but seem to end before you know it?
This 'game' is a romance visual novel set in, of all places, a Soviet-era youth summer camp, where the protagonist somehow ends up after boarding a bus in modern-day Russia.
If you've ever played a visual novel before, you know how it works, click through the text, making choices when it lets you, watching the character and background art slide by, like raindrops down a window.
The aforementioned art is nothing special, in fact it gets straight amateurish at times, and sometimes it's enjoyable, but nothing too special.
The soundtrack is beautiful, properly reinforcing the moods of the scenes, and sticking with (at least me) you for a while after playing.
The characters are variable in execution, and tend to lean on archetypes a little much, but they all have their own little ticks that make them stand out.
The real meat of what this is, however, isn't in the art, the story itself, or even the beautiful soundtrack.  It's in the overall atmosphere, the sense of long-gone summers and those young romances that are almost too awkward to bear, yet you wouldn't change them for the world.  It's the nostalgia emanating from every earnest pore of this freeware VN, made by -chan anons over several years, much like the lauded Katawa Shoujo.
If you're the type to get misty-eyed over graduation slideshows, songs like Summer of '69, Good Riddance (Time of your Life) or to keep a photo album, or if you're in the mood for an amateur, if earnest and heartfelt, romance story.  I'd reccommend spending a few hours clicking through.
(Just not Miku's route, GabeN save us from that horror...)

I'm done with Grim Dawn, it was fun, I played about 100hrs in which I've created 2 characters, I've reached Level 44 with one and 74 with another, was able to glance through the first missions on the last difficulty (Ultimate) and acquired a couple Legendary items that was useful.
The game has a good interesting story, although it's very digressive because of multiple factions, I often was confused with the multiple "main" plots. Don't get me wrong side-quests are a good thing, it's just that I felt there wasn't a compelling main story. I've finished the game I thought "That was it?". Aside from that the stories and quests are very well written and presented, specially the ones you collect as lore items, it was intriguing to always look for another piece to know what happened next. A big plus also for quest branches, allowing to actually change the game and story.
The gameplay is good, there's good amount of skills for each class with different builds and play-styles, not to mention the amount of masteries with the double-class sytem. The combat system often got me excited, often got me mad, it's great to put your skill to some use and not only the random click-fest that usually is ARPGs. I mean, there's interesting combat mechanics, like healers, and support mobs that have to be killed first, it's movement intense and you have to coordinate the skill usage.
The graphics are good, the scenery is dark, bloody and gothic, the animations though could be better, for example, the character animation when it's running often feels like it's on a roller blade, character posing stand-still is ugly, and often I got stuck in the environment after the animation of one of the movement skills I had.
Itemization is a problem, I got several items that I had no use for me while lacking items to progress the game, I understand this is a RNG game, although some sort of mechanism needs to be in place to fulfill this gaps, like the loot system implement in Diablo, or a quick and easy way to trade. Anyway going alone or "self founded" as the community says is quite a task, and would demand a lot of time. That's the main reason I've got bored: looking after loot, not finding and knowing that would take a lot of time to get it.
It's a good ARPG "Diablo like" game with an well written story, good graphics and regular to poor animations. I definitely recommend if you like ARPGs.

My rating for Child of Light: 100/100
This game deserves it.  It shows a fairy tale. rich story, which changes dramatically and show us, that sometimes we have to grow to gain, what we want. Artistic impressions are beyond most games limits.
"Child. Tuck yourself in bed
And let me tell a story
Of Lemuria, a long lost kingdom,
And a girl born for glory."
Story is rich and contains a lot of details, that give the chance to think about it. Despair, aspiration, resolution, fights and even love, are present during each moment of the game. All is situated as a fairy tale, but it is not only pretty and cheerful, but many times, it goes right under the skin and draws into the storyline, desinged as a poetry, there is even a storyteller here!
Characters surprise in variety, their progress can also be seen during playthrough. Leading by firstly hesitating, then decisive Aurora, against forces of Queen of Night. Their changes are sometimes shocking, loyals are betrayed, exiled forgiven, sad became joyful, love fulfilled. There can by seen inspirations even from mythologies, like Cuchulain (celtic, here Kategida leader). Also, they interact within the party, revealing another deep ideas and findings. Mystic presence of Queen of Light linked with Aurora's dad's fate are completing this mosaic. Not forgetting the shiny, cheerful firefly, called Igniculus.
Visual is beyond my expectations. Style looks like painted with watercolors, animations are precise, all looks soft and filled with magic. Backgrounds show variety and are meaningful for actual game moment.
Soundtrack is also a masterpiece. Under the active supervision of Coeur de Pirate, we have here a composition of piano, violin, flute and other instruments, that help to enhance the atmosphere.  If you are eager to, there is a chance to buy it on Coeur's bandcamp for a reasonable price.
Battles are designed in old-style RPG's as turns, combined with real-time element. This gives an opportunity to interact and make strategic moves to turn odds in your favor. But beware, some creatures are better not to be interrupted, which leads me to point, that also there is a chance of counterattack, what makes fights even more interesting.
This brings me also to multiplayer. Second player can control Igniculus and be helpful taking unreachable chests and during fights slowing enemies and healing our characters. Roles are different for each player, which gives accent on teamwork. Believe me, everything is much easier then.
There are some negatives, but they are not directly linked to the game, that is why I mention them here separately and do not affect my rating.
Firstly, you have to have uPlay installed, which can be annoying, on the other side, completing the achievements gives you points to receive refinements for this and another uPlay linked games.
Secondly, your CPU have to support microarchitecture SSE4, SSE4a for AMDs. So, do not be shocked, if your speed is sufficient, but text message will state, that is outdated. This is not mentioned in minimum requirements, but that is mistake for Ubisoft and Ubisoft Montréal, not game alone.
I would also be glad to purchade the soundtrack with the game as some form of bundle, but this is just my desire, what was already fulfilled in another way (via bandcamp).
To sum it up, if you are fun of high quality RPGs, fairy tales, rich stories, crystallis music, poetry, you do not have to look as many games to fill all your requirements. There is one, Child of Light, which joins them all.
Aurora: "Locked"
Igniculus: "I am not shocked."
Breathtaking. Highly recommended.

Ubisoft hasn't had a good 2014, Watch Dogs didn't live up to it's hype even though I still enjoyed it for what it was, Assassin's Creed Unity became a buggy mess at launch and was considered dissapointing compared to previous games, Assassin's Creed Rogue is just DLC packaged into a full-game and The Crew also isn't looking too good, don't know about Far Cry 4 though. I hope that in time those two games (Unity and The Crew) get better through patching and updating.
However, Ubisoft Montreal did manage to create one of the best RPG's this year, which is Child of Light and I enjoyed every moment of it.
Child of LIght takes place in 1895 Austria where the Duke's daughter Aurora, wakes up in an unfamiliar land called Lemuria. On a ardous quest to return home, she starts encountering monster's who serve Umbra, who is responsible for the land's turmoil and for stealing the moon, the sun and the stars which are the embodiements of light, Umbra is the opposite of Light (Good) which is Dark (Evil). To aid Aurora in her journey, she meets several unique companions and begin's jolly cooperation with them, killing monsters for loot and recieving xp together, and completing side-quests for personal gain and to help Lemuria's townsfolk.
Gameplay: The game starts out as a 2d platformer which is pretty solid in terms of movement and animations. In combat mode, it's reminescent to JRPG games with it's action turn based system. one of the game's mechanics is that down the bottom center of the screen you have a meter which sways to the right till it reaches the casting phase, at this point enemies can actually stop you by reaching the end of the meter but you can as well by using Igniculus, your firefly companion to slow them down.
before the end of that meter, you get time to make your decision whether you want to initiate an attack, use a potion, retreat from battle or switch party members, your standard options basically. Combat in this game is fun and I usually prefer action-based combat like Dark Souls. The bosses are pretty epic as well.
Story: It's like a story with two sides of the coin, one side is different from one another but they are at conflict. They cannot co-exist with one another and the main character Aurora, is dragged into all of this. Light and Dark and their place in the world start to unfold throughout Aurora's adventure. she is compassionate and friendly towards the people she helps, towards her fellow companions, her friends and her family. But she is also struggling to understand her situation and why this had happened to her. The other characters are also great and stand out, they have their personalities and indifferences, my favourites were Rubella and Finn. In terms of dialogue it's different to other game's I've played. Every piece of dialogue given by the characters in Child of Light including the Narrator, is told in a poetic manner and it's great and it works and It wasn't what I was expecting.
Music: When exploring the world of Lemuria it's peaceful, and harmonic and the memorable piece played with the flute that Aurora uses has a powerful, cheerful effect to the nearby people, especially in their times of strife and despair. When combat ensues it changes it's musical style and becomes epic, and empowering. It's one of my favourite aspects of Boss battles and the game's composer Couer de pirate does a fantastic job at capturing those feelings.
Graphics: It looks visually appealing, mainly through it's artstyle, the artstyle itself carries the game's atmosphere and tone. Lemuria is somewhat of a ruined land, corrupted by the evil queen Umbra, whatever beauty remains in the land, gradually becomes more and more barren and bleak. as Umbra continues to spread her seeds. The locations are varied too, Deep Forests, Coastal wastelands, Volcanic Tunnels, Abandoned Castles, A city on top of a giant humanoid mountain, A dark sunless fortress and Crystal lairs.
Overall: Child of Light is a special treat, it's one of Ubisoft's best titles to date and also one of the best RPG's in recent memory. a memorable experience with great characters, fun combat, great soundtrack and beautiful artwork. Don't let the name Ubisoft fool you into thinking it's a buggy, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥game because I'm telling you right now, it isn't.

Child of Light reminds me in some ways of Studio Ghibli movies: they have a childish aesthetic but are more mature in story and tone. There is an unmistakable somber quality throughout Child of Light, something I wouldn't have expected from a game with a whimsical watercolor art style. This game excels at bringing together elements from various genres and fusing them together into a shining example of innovation for the industry.
Let me list a few of the highlights of the game before I get into a few critiques. This is a gorgeous game, like a living painting with fantastic use of color, interesting inhabitants and exquisite backgrounds. The music stood out from the start and meshed perfectly with the overall tone. The combat showed its depth when I got my greatest enjoyment out of it during my second time through (New Game+ on Hard). A simple but satisfying crafting system allows for customization without too much complexity. Dialogue written in poetry combined with a chapter structure and occasional video cutscenes all add to the moving storybook feel of the game.
Unfortunately this game is not perfect. Some of my complaints, particularly the first one, are matters of personal taste so you'll have to decide for yourself whether what I'm describing sounds like something that would bother you or not. I'm not much of a fan of poetry. At times I did enjoy the rhyming dialogue but other times it seemed like the writers were doing verbal backflips to fit the rhyme in, which made it feel forced and/or obscured the meaning. I do appreciate the novelty of it and how it lends itself to the storybookesque design. Some may dismiss the game as a kid's game due to the childish visuals or playing as a young girl but I urge you not to make that mistake.
Without spoiling anything, I will simply say that the ending felt like it came rather abruptly but was otherwise satisfying. There was a point roughly 2/3rds of the way through my first playthrough that the combat became boring for a time. I was afraid going into my 2nd playthrough (New Game+) that I would be bored with the combat during most of it but that turned out not to be true. The level of challenge on Hard kept me on my toes and making use of all my party member's specialties. I must say that potions are fairly useless in the game. I only used about a dozen in total. Also, don't expect any complex puzzles or platforming. You can fly from nearly the start of the game so traditional platforming goes out the window in favor of mostly manipulating things with your firefly sidekick. Controlling both Aurora with WASD and Igniculus (firefly) with the mouse keeps things interesting.
If I haven't mentioned any aspect you're wondering about go ahead and assume it's good, this game simply oozes quality.

Treasure hunting rarely feels like a chore and the ways to obtain certain treasure feels refreshing and uncomplicated.
In terms of combat Child of Light takes a page from the classic rpg format of turn based fighting and adds several implements. This makes the turn based fighting immersive and exciting and with the allies you come across you will find many unique and interesting ways to topple the competition. There is also a gearing system involving gem stones, I've barely scratched the surface on this and I gotta say, the upgrades you choose through this system really play a part in combat.
My only real gripe with child of light is how short the game feels. When the game comes to the end you feel like you could've used more time to grind your allies and discovered more quests/treasure. I guess I'll check out the dlc and story plus and see if that doesn't change my mind.
Child of Light is a must play for RPG and fantasy enthusiasts.

When you play a game, there's 5 things you should look at. Characters, Story, Graphics, Music, and Gameplay. Most of those are pretty self-explanatory. This game can be described as a JRPG with a visual novel style to storytelling. So let's dissect each topic, starting with story.
The story is pretty standard of a JRPG-esque game. You have amnesia(As usual in JRPGs...) and there's this villian who is doing evil stuff.  Additionally, you'll be helping out people across the land with their only little problems while furthering your own goal(In this game, it's find parts to make plot appear and to stop the villian).  What's different is that everything has a video game motif, with the world being called GameIndustri, with the country of Lowee(Wii), Leanbox(XBox), Lastation(Playstation) and Planeptune(Sega Neptune).
They were probably reaching with the Neptune.
There is also a war going on... The Console Wars! But apparently no one pays a lot of attention to things like that as apparently most citizens happily travel from one land to the other, make plenty of trade(according to the game, Lastation and Planeptune are very close with each other as trade partners), and generally lead peaceful lives. The console wars really refer to the four leaders of the four lands who hate each other at the start and want to kill the others to become THE ruler. What terrible rulers.
But then story happens and they become friends. That much is revealed in the opening cutscene.
For the story, it's pretty standard JRPG. It's pretty weak and there aren't any surprises or anything.
However, it's made up by the Characters.  The characters are written well and have fair personalities.  Most of them anyways.  The characters are basically aware that they are in a video game and take a lot of digs at themselves, gaming, and tropes in general.  In other words, the characters are very silly and spend most of the time joking around or making fun of something/someone.  One of the sad parts is that some of the characters have 'lost in translation' moments from translating Japanese to English, and some references are forced out as a result, regardless of what the character said.  If you pay attention you can see where they try to force a joke out, and it's sad.
So the main character is an amnesiac.  The rest of the characters are summed up as simply: Moe blob, cool big sis, tsundere, gamer, quiet but explodes when angry, LARPer, and 'The Rest'.  The characters bounce off each other fairly well and easily have fluid conversations, with characters often getting poked at and casually threatening each other.  The only problem is that in a game where 7 playable characters are shown and have well-defined personalities, another 6 characters have next to no personality appear, and are mostly 'just there'.  Although it's harsh to say that they have no personality, it's more like they joined the party too late and can't keep up with the established personalities, as well as the fact that their own personalities are fairly sensible and straightforward.  In fact, a few characters you get that have a grand total of about 10 sentences.  There is a reason for that though, so it's forgiven?
The villians aren't written badly, they actually seem like people, especially compared to the silliness brought to the table by the main character.  They are almost always very serious, degrading, and occasionally bicker with the characters as well.  Villians should joke around too at least once in a while, it just makes them a bit more relatable or personal.
It's a little hard to make fun of the characters in a game when the characters themselves are already doing that,  Nevertheless, I would give the characters a solid 8/10.  There are some moments of brilliant humor brought by the characters, but the bland characters ruin it a little.
Then the graphics. There honestly isn't a lot to say about this one, it was a game made on the PS Vita, which had enough power to run PS3 games.  Everything is pretty as to be expected, with a few texture splits here and there.  Everything is well detailed and fits well together.  The game plays as a visual novel, so about 70% of the time you'll be looking at a portrait of the characters with a background.  The backgrounds are as detailed as you can expect from a game this size, unlike many indie visual novels in where there's a dirt path background or maybe a stereotypical classroom. The characters move slightly so they have small animations that are done in the middle of a conversation, usually for comedic effect.  Better when you think of other visual novels like that tend to just have a still picture.  Nice to see some movement.
The graphics are what you'd expect from a PS Vita game.  Good all around.
When you think of JRPG music, you always think of the Final Boss music. Smithy from Super Mario RPG, Sephiroth from Final Fantasy VII, final boss music is always tremendous. It's probably the second most important tune in the game, right behind the intro scene music. Well.. Not so much here. The final boss music wasn't that great.  The music was at its best during the visual novel parts of when everyone was talking, it set the mood very well.  The dungeons are either up-beat techno, drab cave, or easy-going nature tune. The voices were all fine, I would say to listen to this in Japanese though. It has more feeling compared to the english voices. Best music was probably the intro.
Not bad, could be better.
Gameplay can be described as such: The grind is real.
You go to a dungeon, beat up baddies, then go to town and make fun of everyone, a quick serious scene, then back to the dungeon. There are also a lot of side dungeons in case you wanted to grind some more, but they look exactly the same compared to the regular dungeons.  Lazy workmanship! You will need to mind you, the difficulty can really jump sometimes. Like, seriously. There are a lot of little notes on the map and in the town that make references to games and animes(Oh look, it's maryo!).  The battles themselves are what I love in some games.  Turn based field in where you have to consider your positions. You even do a bit more damage if you attack an enemies back.  Lot of little details in the battle system, although for me, it boiled down to the triangle formation, where enemies tend to clump up in the middle for easy AoE and I'm safe from their AoE.  Not much to say about battle system, it's just well done.
The crafting system is where it's at though.  During gameplay, you get RAM, and you use that ram along with item requirements to unlock new weapons, clothing, dungeons, dungeon enhancements, and perks.  The perks are wide reaching, with things like EXP UP or "Always see hidden items".  Those perks are also optional even after you get them, which is something that should be in all RPGs.  Additionally, there are hats and clothing that change your model.  There are a good amount of clothing which I fussed over like a mom clothing my kids, but the hats.. So many hats.  More than TF2.  The amount of hats is absurd.  Even if this was just a visual novel with dress up, I'd play it anyways.
Everything but the dungeons are great.
So would I recommend this game? No I wouldn't. This game has a bit of a "Stick of Truth" or "Duke Nukem Forever" feel to it, in where if you're not familiar with the subject matter(a lot of games and anime), a lot of it just flies over your head.  Unlike Disgaea in where you can play the game without knowing anything and it'll still be funny on its own right, this game makes a lot of references for its humor, which can really hurt it at times since most people may not be familiar with it.  If you play a lot of games and watch a lot of anime, then I would recommend this game. I mean, I enjoyed the time I spent, it's good. Just not great.

Hmmmm. Not sure how to review this. Do I review it as a PC port? Or a series I've never played before? Or as a guy who's a big fan of Disgaea and other games like this on the PS3 and generally a bit of a weeb?
Yeah, so instead I'm just gonna write about the stuff I like about Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 and was less keen on. Not all of the features of the game are in here, and the technical stuff like the porting and whatnot is almost certainly in more detail in other reviews. These are just my opinions.
Things I like:
-Good looking on PC
-60fps
-More polished gameplay than previous installments
-The turn based style and combo system works well and keeps you involved
-Grinding feels less of a slog than similar JRPGS I've played, with the quest system giving more reason and reward for it
-Lily system can create good character combos and adds to the game quite well
-Plan system is pretty nice
-Great artwork
-Excellent animation
-Love the music (even the song on the title screen is catchy)
-A decent roster of likeable characters, especially Nep.
-Pretty damn funny, with a lot of densely packed humor and references
-Fourth wall? What fourth wall?
-Cool enemy types, from giant robots and dragons to Otakus, Mario pipes and visual novel screens
-Iris Heart :)
Things I don't like so much:
-The game has a bad habit of occaisionally dropping steep difficulty curves on you with little warning
-Less awkward or not, grind IS necessary
-No real ability to see what areas or enemies outlevel you until you've dived in
-I kinda wish there was an ability to click on an enemy and see their stats, moves and abilities like in Disgaea
-The 4-way movement feels a little strange in 3d at first
-KO'd party members don't get XP, which can leave some characters (healers like Compa especially) as cannon fodder if they get downed too much
-No NISA :(
Also wanna add that what with HNRB;1 being Idea Factory's first PC port, the game has had issues with other players, including crashes and the like (I've been fine, but others have had issues). However, the devs have been listening to peoples problems and have been working pretty hard on patching the problems, and there's been a lot of support from the community on it too.
In addition, the DLCs are pretty well priced in my opinion, without being game breaking but still adding to gameplay. In addition, the promotional offer when the game came out was a great deal and shows that these guys have the right attitude when it comes to bringing their game to a new market and new customers.
Generally, Idea Factory have been pretty cool with the community here on Steam and have been doing their best to earn new fans and treat them with respect. Hopefully their example could even persuade other similar devs like NIS to set up on here, but I digress.
Basically, I like the game a lot. It's funny, cute, pretty decent and I really hope to see more of it on Steam.

Extremely influential, groundbreaking when launched, gameplay still fresh and enjoyable nowadays. Every design detail of this game was done with care. The weapons sound great and feel great to use. The game is extremely moddable, as most already know. There are mods enable campaign multiplayer (synergy), several competitive multiplayer mods (goldeneye source), single-player campaigns like the Stanley Parable and Minerva: Methastasis, Black Mesa, a recreation of HL1 in HL2 with additional "modernization" changes, horror mods (although the ragdoll physics remove the fear element of enemies when they die, due to them behaving so goofy), and many others.
This is a piece of gaming history that is also one of the best value for your money games on steam. I highly recommend it.

I would write about how great a game Everlasting Summer is, with its stunning artwork, great music, original story, intriguing setting and great visual novel gameplay style, driving the novelistic plot along. But, while all these things hold true, it's been more than an entertaining experience for me, like games generally are. Everlasting Summer has adversely changed my philosophies on life. Each ending offeres a new perspective, or multiple, on so many different things, giving many aspects of life a new look for me. The protagonist is rather similar to me, or where I would generally view myself a few years from now. A boring, repetitive, hopeless grind of life. However, after playing through just all the "bad" endings and Miku's, I can feel myself taking a new look on existence in general and feel long-subdued emotions rising. If the depressing, bad endings have stirred this change in me, I can only imagine what the rest will do for me. Everlasting Summer is beyond being a great visual novel for me. It's offered me a new light on a lot of aspects of life.

Forget that it's an amateur production with some of the roughness you would expect of that, this game impressed me more than plenty of mainstream Japanese VNs.
At a first glance, it's a basic, charming little dating game with a nice variety of routes. The main girls are on a fairly familiar spectrum (kind big sister, genki kid, rebel tsundere, shy yandere) and the short chronological span of the story doesn't allow them much character development, but they're very likable all the same. The unique setting (a late Soviet era youth camp) pulls a lot of weight, managing to be nostalgic even with the cultural oddities. In fact, the cultural oddities were one of the best parts for me; while the game still uses plenty of standard VN/anime tropes, it was nice to see something so different from a generic Japanese High School. Visually, while some of the full-screen CGs do look a little amateur, the character sprites are cute, and the backgrounds and music are really beautiful, also doing a lot for the 'mood' of the game and it's setting.
But there's a lot more here than just the first glance, and this is what makes this game stand out above even some more 'professional' VNs. Each route hints at a bigger picture, and as you move from the 5 basic good endings (and one of the bad endings in particular), to the first and then second bonus routes, and finally to the DLC route, the story becomes increasing psychological and philosophical - and also a bit more heart-wrenching.
P.S. If you make an Olga Dmitrievna route, I'll GIVE YOU MONEY.

This is a tentative recommendation. Not because the game is bad per se, but because it has a lot of tiny hiccups that I don't think merit its usual $20 price tag (more if you want the DLC too).
The pros are very good:
- Fantastic visuals and atmosphere
- Good stealth mechanics, they stay consistent even when new threats are added.
- The creepy/scary things are done very well!
- game sucks you in as things progress rather quickly, very few "filler" scenes and places
- Game is confirmed to have DLC coming and will likely be updated with new content for a bit, which is always good
The cons are pretty bad though:
- Only a 3 hour game with minimal replayability. Nothing changes as you finish the game and play again. Things are exactly the same, except now you can pick whatever chapter you want to replay. The game in total will still be only 3 hours. Now this might change with the DLC, but that will be $10 minimum if not more.
- Imprecise controls and responses. I can't begin to tell you how many times Six will pick up different than what I was aiming for her to grab. Or how many times she has fallen off of a high pipe bridge to her death due to the screen tilt not telling you how close to the edge she is until it's too late. Or how many times she could not grip onto a platform or hide in a crevise properly. This is pretty crucial as there are many instances where timing of actions is key and any small hesitance or mistake will reset your progress. These things really need to be improved in my opinion, especially for the regular price the game is being charged at.
Again, the game isn't bad by any means, it's very good and the devs have put a lot of effort and time into it, but the price tag and the control response makes me give this a very situational recommendation: Don't buy it full price. Buy it $15 or below. I'd say $10 but it hasn't hit that low of a price yet.

Saints Row IV was like a Roller Coaster ride. Ups and Downs all around. Here is the plot
After years of fighting gangs, the Saints become celebrities. Next they become special ops soldiers and take down a Terrorist: Cyrus who was the old former leader of the STAG. The Saints take him down and also disarm the bomb that could have wiped out America itself. The Boss (You) becomes president after the operation. Out of the blue an alien race drops into earth and takes all the humans into capsules in their ship. They are placed in a simulation living there nightmare. Will the saints save the world?
Gameplay: 7/10
The Gameplay is pretty fun. The superpowers are a cool addon giving you some fun fights with your enemy aliens and also helps you travel a bit more faster than usual. There is superpower upgrades that will give you powers such as blasting fire or freezing your foes. The problem about this is well.. The vehicles and some weapons are useless. Pistols are useless after you gain some skill and firepower with your Powers and vehicles are pretty much just there. There is some fun vehicles and the planes are still useful but there is no good use to the vehicles when you have fast running and jumping. Its not all that fun to use cars when you could just fly. The boss battles are entertaining though. Specially the huge Can that you have to fight. There is a good difficulty in the game that doesn't put a lot of difficulty spikes when playing which is always annoying. There is nothing else to say about the gameplay rather that it is fun but it is not something you could play again and again. Maybe 2-4 times you could replay this game but the Story is short. You can take about 8 hours of gametime just finishing the campaign. Its decent.
Sound and Music:
Sounds: 7.5/10
Music: 7/10
The sounds in this game are very refined and not bad quality. It also has the amazing dubstep gun that will never get old because it is sooo much fun! The sounds overall is good but the gun sounds are very weak. Good voice acting too!
The music is decent. There is some radios that isn't really something you would listen too all day but there ok. The music soundtrack for the game is good. The Armagaddon reference and parody with the Aerosmiths: Don't wanna miss a thing and some other songs are also there which references other media (Even What is love is there)
Overall some good sound and music for the ears.
Story: 7.8/10
The story is OK. It is not some great revenge story or some a fun alien movie. The thing that makes it great is the characters and dialouge, They are funny! It also mocks Mass Effects with the relationship system and some love-love scenes. There is nothing else to say but the Villian is brilliant. The story is feels a little to short though
Overall: 7.5/10

I just finished playing The Banner Saga the whole way through, and would definitely recommend it. It's not perfect, but what it gets right makes it a real gem.
Do not mind the number of hours played shown in my review, it looks like it doesn't take offline hours into account (all in all it should probably be around 20 hours).
The story of The Banner Saga takes place in a rich Viking-themed universe, and is served by gorgeous art and soundtrack. Your caravan will walk through beautiful sceneries, the walk disturbed from time to time by on-the-road events, battles, or halts in villages or near god stones. It features cutscenes in a visual novel style, and many carefully designed animations. Overall, playing through this game just feels good, as if reading an exciting fantasy novel with tolkienesque descriptions.
The core of the gameplay is the turn-based strategy battles, not unlike the Shining Force series or Final Fantasy Tactics. It's a genre that I particularly affectionate, and The Banner Saga gets it right: challenging battles where you need to be really careful to win with little casualties, varied playable characters and enemies with their own special abilities, both active and passive. The skills are not always perfectly balanced, some characters being way more useful than others; but it's not really an issue.
What the game does not really get right IMO is the secondary gameplay of "macro-managed caravan". You can welcome new clansmen, varl or fighters on the way, but they are only more mouths to feed; supplies are quite expensive, as they need Renown points that you otherwise can spend on magic items or character upgrades. If you don't have supplies, some of those NPCs will die, and the only gameplay impact that I could see was maybe a morale drop. Having many followers/fighters in your caravan does not seem particularly useful gameplay-wise, as when you encounter an army of dredge (the bad guys), they always seem to have between 95% and 105% of your caravan's size... I could never win a battle using those NPCs during war events, the only useful variant always seemed to rush into battle and fight a normal battle with 6 characters.
Apart from battles, you will go from event to event, with the possibility to make choices every time, not unlike how Fastler Than Light handles it. Some choices will have some influence on the game, as they can trigger the immediate death or recruitment of a character, or even the unavoidable death of a character way later in the story. You can also earn Renown points (the game's "currency"), gain magic objects, gain or lose morale, caravan members or supplies, etc.. The main reward however is to see how characters will react, cutscenes, etc., but the impact on the gameplay or the main storyline is usually pretty limited. IMO there could have been more opportunities to gain Renown and gain or lose morale when choosing some variants; especially as Renown is pretty hard to obtain.
The game's current is your leader's Renown. You gain one point of Renown for each kill you make, regardless of the level of the creature. It's kind of frustrating when you kill a powerful magic-wielder and you get the same reward as when one-shotting a weak slinger. Especially frustrating as Renown is really hard to come by: apart from battles, only very few events can earn you Renown. And you desperately need it to level up your characters (5 Renown for level 2, 10 for level 3, etc.); as characters earn XP pretty fast, you typically end up with all of your characters ready to level up by one or two levels, but you don't have the necessary Renown to pay the upgrade. And buying object or supplies also requires a lot of Renown. In the end, it would be nice if Renown could be earned more easily, and if characters would need more XP before they can level up, so that you don't end up with the situation described above.

As many returning telltale fans know "the game is tailored to how you play..." means how the in-game characters will repond to your decisions. This does not necessarily mean it will alter the main events within the story so newcomers be warned.
If you enjoy a rich medieval (with hints of fantasy) universe then welcome to Westeros. If you have no idea what I'm talking about stop living under a rock and start watching HBO's Game of Thrones or (better yet) read George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire series. Newcomers shouldn't jump into this game without being up to date on the progress of the tv series as no specific information is given to the player on the current events at the beginning of the game. Any avid Game of Thrones and/or ASoIaF fan will be able to tell where and when the story takes place. Not to say the game brings nothing new to the table, quiet the contrary actually. The game does a fine job detailing us about the characters in the game and has a codex for those who want to know a bit more although only for the characters specific to this game not the tv show.
Telltale's adventure games typically have quick-time events (in game conversation and action orientated), a little bit of walking in an inclosed area (where you can look at stuff and interact with people), and alot of talking. The last part isn't a negative thing by the way it's actually the bulk of the game and it is why I keep returning to telltale's games. The talking is where we learn about the people, the world, and the events that transpire within the game. Decisions are a major part of the game and effect how people respond to you, not necessarily change the progress of the story. Imagine how long it would take to shell out an episode if each one had multi-tier endings nevermind different ways of reaching that ending for that specific episode. This would compound with each released episode and be a storyboard's nightmare. How on earth would you be able to make a story worth telling when you have fans raging for a new episode every few months?
...Anywho if you are looking for story driven game where you act as you see fit in currently one of the most popular fantasy universes then this may be the kool aid you are looking for.
Try to not look at the texture pop-outs and the average looking graphics. Not offending the art style but the game could always use some more polish. Face animations on the other hand are pretty good while voice acting is superb. Characters from the tv show have their own voice overs in the game and even share some of the facial animations and personality that are present in the tv series.
Episode 1: 8/10

The first time I played Stick of Truth, I bounced off hard. Partly because I'm not a huge fan of the combat style, but also because the difficulty isn't well done. It's very easy in most places with massive spikes- particularly the fight that involves a former government official. That fight is totally doable, but it's head and shoulders above the difficulty level of anything else near that part of the game. In fact, that fight is probably harder than any of the end-level boss fights.
But a few years later I thought I'd give it another go, because I did like the humor. This time I spent a little more time figuring out and reading strategies and had a much eaiser time, to the point where I breezed through on 'hardcore' mode.  The game still has some pretty significant mechanical drawbacks, but the humor, plot, and stylization are worth it.
First, the game IS Southpark. It's not a licensed game made with Southpark characters, it's much more like the actual show that just happens to be built to be interactive. Everything from character creation to abilities to missions just screams 'Southpark' and it's clear that the creators had a huge amount of influence, unlike some earlier SP games. The basic quest structure mirrors that of many episodes where the kids are having their own little game that happens to run into a 'real world' problem. The whole thing is styled after the 'Black Friday' episodes and fits perfectly for a game- so much so that I wish it was being continued in the next SP game, but that may be because I like the 'fantasy' setting more than superheroes.
The game is set up to be about as '3d' as the series which is... not. This works aestetically but causes problems with getting around puzzles and sometimes makes it hard to even see the solutions. It also seems like the creators loved some of the ideas they had a bit too much- for example, the use of an alien butt-probe to get around is used way too much and serves less as a puzzle and more of an annoyance for the latter half of the game. The 'magic' (i.e. farting) to get through obstacles gets a bit old as well, though at least it often serves more as a way to kill foes out of combat. As I mentioned, I'm not a big fan of the turn-based fighting system but it's a matter of preference. The biggest drawback is still probably that the difficulty is not balanced well over the course of the game.
The player can take one buddy with him at a time. Some are definitely more interesting and useful than others. Stan, for example, definitely gets the short end of the stick. In terms of classes I tried Jew and Mage, both of which felt very powerful- though Jew seemed to get very powerful near the end while Mage was comparatively powerful in the early stages. In the latter stages Cartman and Kyle become recruitable, and both have quiet powerful attacks. Depending on which buddy is chosen, the new kid (player character) will hear a variety of banters at different times. Kenny, unfortunately, seems even more difficult to understand than in the show and again, stan just doesn't have much to say- but I guess if you're looking for comedic lines you wouldn't go for the straight-man anyway.
In terms of plot, jokes, atmosphere, etc, I would recommend the game to anyone who likes the show- which it emulates, RPGs- which it often subverts, or poop jokes- which it embraces. I will warn that there are some lines and songs ripped directly from the show to the point where it feels less like fanservice and more like a bit of laziness.
As a final note, even though I'm not 5 years old I really never got tired of the fact that the player can go up to pretty much anyone and fart on them or hit them causing a variety of comedic lines. Unlike some of the other gimmicks, it never felt old because the game never insisted on the player doing it.

A lot of fun already! With Lovecraftian horror and 8-bit pixel art, a couch competitive 3v1 dungeon crawler emerges from the depths.
I've never played a competitive game with this mechanic before. A brief matchup at the beginning of each game determines who the "human" player is, and who the "monster" players are. The human player traverses the dungeon, looking for the stairs to the next level. The monster players control spirits who float around the room with the ability to possess traps, spawn slimes, and summon controllable demons for the purpose of killing the human player. If the human player dies, the monster player who landed the fatal blow assumes the role of the human hero while the former human player joins the ranks of the ghosts. The amount of monsters you kill as the human hero determines who wins the game, with a levelling system that gives boosts to overall health. Monster earn a separate class of EXP which can be used to upgrade their demons to even more powerful monstrosities. Human players also have the opportunity starting at level 10 to fight a challenging dungeon boss picked at random.
There should be a system to upgrade peak monsters' base attributes, though, as a handicap for less experienced players. I already love the balancing system though. Also, at this point, the music is very limited and gets pretty repetitive. Finally, attack controls feel a little gummy and could use work before you stop walking away from the game with bloody thumbs.
Buy this game if you love dungeon crawlers, rogue-lites, and are looking for a very new twist on a classic genre to challenge your friends with. Don't have friends? Pick this up when it's on sale, you can still play the game with up to 3 AI players who range from competent to outright ruthless, but this game really shines the brightest when your opponent is on the couch next to you.

This is a remake of a PS3 JRPG that's also available on Vita. I hear the original was a much worse game, and I really don't dare imagine how that was like. It's a cheap budget JRPG (new price was 15 bucks on launch sale) with emphasize on cheap. There are only like half a dozen dungeon layouts, while there are 50 dungeons in the game. So basically each dungeon is copy pasted 10 times with only the enemies replaced. The dungeons are super short too, you can run from the entrance to the end usually in less than 5 minutes. The storyline is also only presented visual novel style with textboxes and talking heads. Cities are implemented as simple menus. So you either watch dialogues or you pick a dungeon from a list and run through it. Really this game probably cost less to make than the PS3 licensing fees...
Still, it is suprisingly fun. Combat is turn based with a bunch of systems piled on it, and there is a massive crafting component involving hunting monsters for materials and crafting plans to unlock new equipment or dungeons. And the grind is so extremely streamlined, you can breeze even through special bosses within 10 seconds by liberal use of the ultra smooth animation cancel button. There are also absolutely no loading times, everything appears and works instantly. So the grind can downright turn into a rush and feels very satisfying. Think the loot and kill vortex of Diablo, but as a JRPG.
Oh also the story is a parody of the console war in the current game industry. The entire cast of the game is female with permanent fan service forced in your face. The main character is a personified Dreamcast and there are also Playstation, Xbox and the Wii present. Ofc the Xbox has the biggest♥♥♥♥♥♥while the Wii is as flat as a washboard and gets extremely jealous if that's pointed out to her. At the start they are all mortal enemies but of course they eventually band together to fight a greater evil. It is in no way shape or form serious and constantly goofy and 4th wall breaking. I thought I would hate it but honestly, I think I prefer this absolute nonsense over yet another embarassing teenage melodrama or boring as ♥♥♥♥ Hero Alex gathers the stones of power to save the world from the evil wizard♥♥♥♥♥♥as you'd usually find in JRPGs.
Mild recommendation.

Where to begin? The game is essentially, as other reviews have marked, a spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate-style turn based RPG's. From the first hour I felt myself compelled with a sense of both nostalgia and excitement at something fresh and new. Like driving an old car that has been fixed up to rival some of the high end models out today, Divinity takes all the good stuff from the old D&D days and brings it swinging into current-gen gaming.
I'm writing this review after putting in 84 hours of the game, and just beating it now. Yes, it's that long. That long, and oh so fulfilling. I suppose one would be able to smash out the game in about 40 hours but I took the time to appreciate all the care and love Larian studios has put ino their well-earned Kickstarter project.
The game's combat was fulfilling, the story was engaging, and the characters were compelling. The simple fact that you can play through the game with a friend as your companion via multiplayer just put it over the top. I can't think of anything they could add to the game to make it much better.
A very well earned 9.8/10.

If you ar looking for a game that truely embodies what table top roleplaying is like, creating its counterpart for the PC, then Divinity original sin is your game. The strategic combat system is challenging as well as entertaining with so many different ways to manipulate your environment that you never get the impression killing your enemies is just mindless grinding. Your characters are fully customizable and it is up to you to choose which abilities you want to mix and match.
The coop works incredibly well and often it feel like the game was defenitely designed with two people in mind. gtathering your party and making sure that everyone complements each other is a challange in enough itself, and well rewarded if successful. If you are tired of games like diablo III and Trochlight in which you mostly run through hordes of monsters hacking, slashing and button mashing, this will be a welcome diversion.
That being said Divinity stays very true to classic role playing games in that there is a LOT of reading, every character seems to think similies are the only way to talk and everyone has a story they are just dying to tell you. some of us love that kind of involvement, but if you ar elooking for every conversation to be voiceacted for you, you will be disappointed.
Divinity also does a poor job initially leading you along the progression path. you start with very little hand holding which is fun, but can result in a slightly frustrating experience initially, when you end up reloading over and over because the enemies you are fightinh are simply too tough.
All in all I am loving this beautiful, vast game. It reminds me of all I loved of classical RPG's and all I love about table top roleplaying. I highly recommend this game for anyone who has soem time to get into it. (OMG as a rogue you can steal virtually EVERYTHING!)

tl;dr: Killing Floor 2 sticks to it's routes perfectly, keeping everything mostly the same with the first game, but improves in almost every single aspect. If you enjoyed KF1, it's pretty much guarenteed that you will like this too. With an active playerbase, great graphics with it not being demanding, incredibly fun gameplay, a good OST, many classes and even MORE weapons, it's hard to deny that this is NOT one of the best Co-Op shooters out there.
There are many dev-created maps, and even more community-crafted ones thanks to the Workship. Unless you stick to one map on it's own for hours on end, you will never get bored of these great environments!
The game is also very nice looking, and is not too graphically demanding! Unless you have a card that is years old, you should really have no trouble running this game well, even on Ultra settings! I played this on a GeForce 1060 6GB and on a Ryzen 3 1300x processor, and was able to run this at the very highest settings including AA being on, and did not drop a single frame under 60, even with NVidia Flex on!
The gameplay is some of the most fun I have had while gaming! With hundreds of Zeds to wreak havoc upon every wave, you will be entertained for hours on end. There are many classes to choose from, and all come with their special set of weaponry! For example; the Beserker has Melee Weapons, the Support has plenty of Shotguns to choose from, the Commando has many automatic rifles, etc.
When you start a game, depending on the options and difficulty that is chosen, you will either have to survive the onslaught of Zeds for either 4, 7 or 10 waves, each of them getting harder and harder until one of the three - yes, that's right - THREE bosses... The bosses are fine, but seeing and fighting the exact same bosses with the exact same lines gets very repetitive after a while.
However, that's about the only problem I have with KF2. Other than that, it's a pretty damn perfect Co-Op Shooter! I have missed a lot of aspects of the game, but if I did cover them, I would have been here all day. Any constructive criticism in the comments is appreciated.

At first glance this game is deceptively simple, and even dumb; your only controls are a right attack and a left attack, and all you need to do is wait for an enemy to come close in that direction and press the corresponding key to hit them, The simple two-button design is a clear wink to the arcade games of old. But, like those old arcade games, this one has something intriguing that will make you come back again and again.
So, what is it that makes the game interesting? There is no real goal to reach in the actual gameplay, so the real thing to beat is the high scores list. Find the rhythm and you'll kick off The Hoff. Keep playing, and very soon, you will start getting increasingly aware of exactly which enemies are on either side of you, and even in what order, and you will start to memorize the exact combos to defeat each one. As the game progresses, it adds harder enemies with more interesting combos to beat, and you will get challenged to keep up that perfect combo without missing a single one, to retain that increasingly higher score for each kill. And that challenge is the true charm of this game.
Now excuse me, I need to beat Triceracop's score ;)

I just finished playing The Banner Saga the whole way through, and would definitely recommend it. It's not perfect, but what it gets right makes it a real gem.
Do not mind the number of hours played shown in my review, it looks like it doesn't take offline hours into account (all in all it should probably be around 20 hours).
The story of The Banner Saga takes place in a rich Viking-themed universe, and is served by gorgeous art and soundtrack. Your caravan will walk through beautiful sceneries, the walk disturbed from time to time by on-the-road events, battles, or halts in villages or near god stones. It features cutscenes in a visual novel style, and many carefully designed animations. Overall, playing through this game just feels good, as if reading an exciting fantasy novel with tolkienesque descriptions.
The core of the gameplay is the turn-based strategy battles, not unlike the Shining Force series or Final Fantasy Tactics. It's a genre that I particularly affectionate, and The Banner Saga gets it right: challenging battles where you need to be really careful to win with little casualties, varied playable characters and enemies with their own special abilities, both active and passive. The skills are not always perfectly balanced, some characters being way more useful than others; but it's not really an issue.
What the game does not really get right IMO is the secondary gameplay of "macro-managed caravan". You can welcome new clansmen, varl or fighters on the way, but they are only more mouths to feed; supplies are quite expensive, as they need Renown points that you otherwise can spend on magic items or character upgrades. If you don't have supplies, some of those NPCs will die, and the only gameplay impact that I could see was maybe a morale drop. Having many followers/fighters in your caravan does not seem particularly useful gameplay-wise, as when you encounter an army of dredge (the bad guys), they always seem to have between 95% and 105% of your caravan's size... I could never win a battle using those NPCs during war events, the only useful variant always seemed to rush into battle and fight a normal battle with 6 characters.
Apart from battles, you will go from event to event, with the possibility to make choices every time, not unlike how Fastler Than Light handles it. Some choices will have some influence on the game, as they can trigger the immediate death or recruitment of a character, or even the unavoidable death of a character way later in the story. You can also earn Renown points (the game's "currency"), gain magic objects, gain or lose morale, caravan members or supplies, etc.. The main reward however is to see how characters will react, cutscenes, etc., but the impact on the gameplay or the main storyline is usually pretty limited. IMO there could have been more opportunities to gain Renown and gain or lose morale when choosing some variants; especially as Renown is pretty hard to obtain.
The game's current is your leader's Renown. You gain one point of Renown for each kill you make, regardless of the level of the creature. It's kind of frustrating when you kill a powerful magic-wielder and you get the same reward as when one-shotting a weak slinger. Especially frustrating as Renown is really hard to come by: apart from battles, only very few events can earn you Renown. And you desperately need it to level up your characters (5 Renown for level 2, 10 for level 3, etc.); as characters earn XP pretty fast, you typically end up with all of your characters ready to level up by one or two levels, but you don't have the necessary Renown to pay the upgrade. And buying object or supplies also requires a lot of Renown. In the end, it would be nice if Renown could be earned more easily, and if characters would need more XP before they can level up, so that you don't end up with the situation described above.

Gone are the days of crappy combat with random chance to heal yourself (Yes you couldn't even use healing items yourself!) and pointless interactive dungeon items, instead you have something which is a lot more fluid and fun to play. Something people gloss over is how the remake now has you collecting the other CPU Goddesses as allies as early as Chapter 2! The original had 3 party members including the main character for literally 80% of the game, the diversity allowed a lot of spicing up with formations and picking favourite characters early.
Definitely worth playing for the writing more than the gameplay, but the remake is a real hoot. It won't win any awards, but It sure is a lot of fun, Neptunia is adorable.

Now most of us are going to be disappointed that this is quite obviously a console port, but i actually like this simplified X Com, I was never all that interested in the resource and money management of the original and so i welcome the changes to this section of the game, the focus is now almost entirely on tactics. This is probably the most negative review for Child of Light that you'll read, but I honestly wasn't blown away by it.  Still, it's probably worth checking out.  I'd wait until it's on sale for around 5 dollars.
It's fine.  It's alright.  It's a fairly standard RPG so there really isn't a lot of gameplay going on.  There isn't a lot of variety in the music.  The artwork is good but the animations are creepy at times.
On the plus side the combat/outside of combat has a really cool thing going on with the support character, who can freeze enemies outside of combat, slow them down inside of combat and heal you in either situation.  His operations are independent of the other characters/time line that combat follows so that part is neat.  CoL also has a sort of Mario RPG esque feel to it's combat since it's centered around timing your attacks effectively to interrupt the enemy's.
There's a story and it's not the worst but it's sort of dull.  Very fairy tale inspired, and that part of it is cool, but it's definitely not the sort of story meant to last the 6-8 hours of gameplay.  It's not bad by any means but I think it could have been utilized better in another game type.
One of the bigger draws is the writing, which is clever in a lot of parts but I think that it ultimately loses out by the game not having voice work for the characters.  Oh, the narrator bits between major segments are fantastic and the writing really comes alive then, but everywhere else it's just kind of meh.  There are great points to it, and I did enjoy the interactions between characters, but well, it felt lacking in some regard.  It felt like the writing was trying to elevate itself in some way but the author's skill wasn't there.  At times the rhyming style seemed to detract from the actual writing.  Pity, that.
Oh, watch out by the way.  The difficulty curve in Child of Light is crazy.  You'll go from no challenge to extremely difficult bosses near the mid/end, which will then peter out into pretty easy fights by the very end.
I've read that the game itself is short or feels rushed but despite my claims that the story feels stretched, the game itself seemed to pace itself pretty well.  I thought it was about the right length.
I recommend Child of Light but this is a case of a game that I don't think should have been a game.  The non-game parts are still good, if pretentious.  Ehh.
Oh, Child of Light also has the absolute worst DLC I've ever seen in a game.  Sure, one is a new character, but two more are main character reskins and the rest are item packs.  These item packs are of items that exist in the game already and are acquired pretty frequently so I'm not really sure why the DLC exists.  Oh, wait.  Money.

Taking into consideration in comparison to a similar game, Dead Island and its franchise, Techland took what was supposed in that game and actually produced a rather interesting variation of it here.
Here are just some pros and cons I have for this game.
Pros:
- Better mechanics whether is it fighting or movement
- Better hit detection on enemies
- A reasonably good variety of side missions and random encounters
- Great multiplayer and co-op online
Cons:
- Several issues or bugs with the climbing. It may have been me but, there are moments where I believed I could have hung on to the ledge of something
- Story line is very clichéd; the ending is rather very weak to the story it brings you up on.
- Depending on how you play game, it can be a Castlevania 2: Simon's Quest, where it becomes almost necessary to grind for parts or materials to sell and create.
This is just my take on what the game feels. To me, the game deserves a 6.5/10 rating. The rating would at least be a 7.5/10 if not for the story. Techland, for the story you have created, I feel it deserves a much better ending than the one you have given because of how much depth you have given prior to the finale of the game. However, with all that said, the game can be rather quite enjoyable simply because it had parkour.

A fantastic indie game; a bleak, emotional human story that forces you to accept the consequences of your decisions, tied together with a deceptively simple combat system. The only negative point (for me) was the brevity of the game, between 10-15 hours play through, but it gripped me from start to finish. I've now completed three playthroughs and, although you always reach the same climactic moment, the saga along the way has been different each time. Looking forward to how things progress with the sequel due later this year.

This game is not a sandbox storytelling game like King of Dragon Pass or Crusader Kings II. It's far too linear for that, even though you can somewhat influence where the story branches at certain points. Don't expect too much control over things.
This game isn't that much of a turn-based tactics battler. Sure, the combat is okayish and gives you something to do in addition to clicking through dialogue, but I never found the fights that engaging and at times it was dull and repetitive. There are way more interesting turn-based combat games out there, don't grab this if that's what you're looking for.
However, this game is a pretty good visual novel! The story and characters were interesting, the world is mysterious and the art and music side is well done. If you want to experience a pretty gripping viking fantasy survival story, this game works. Well, at least until the end, when there's not enough closure and it becomes pretty obvious that this is actually The Banner Saga: Episode 1 and it's definitely building up to a sequel. At least the game doesn't over-explain things so the sense of mystery remains.
Still, if you enjoy nice hand-painted visuals and very light RPG story elements and just want to be told a neat story, this is a decent experience for that. Just don't expect any sprawling larger-than-life epic, this is quite quickly over even though the world and lore probably could support a larger game in the same setting.

Killing floor 2 is a zombie wave survival. You can play as 10 different classes, each class brings different weapons and abilities to the table. You can level all classes to level 25 and every five levels you unlock 2 perks. You choose one of the two perks so when you reach level 25 you will have 5 perks slected.In game you start off with a starter weapon for the first wave and each time you kill a zed (zombie) you gain dosh which is used to buy different guns, armor, and ammo at the trader pod at the end of each wave. As you get more dosh and better guns more zeds come and new zeds will begin to spawn that are more powerful and have different abilities. Like the husk that has a flamethrower as a arm and can shoot balls of fire.At the end of all the waves the boss comes there are currently three bosses Hans Volter,Patriarch, and king Fleshpound.If you beat the boss you have a chance to gain a skin and you recivie xp to the class you played when you defeated the boss.
The game is all around fun if your playing by yourself or with a couple of friends.It can get really intense when you have low health and running away from a horde of zeds. Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball is one of the best games I have ever played that is not a Valve Inc. game.
Why should you get this game?
It is widely unknown, which always angers me. It is a skill based dodgeball tournament style game which relies on physics and control to win. There are so many options for single player that is amazes me. You can mess around with physics and many other features. The difficulty of the bots is very balanced and it is easy to progress skill to a peak.
I can go on for hours about this game, but I would rather be playing it for hours. The music selection is awesome. I recommend downloading the soundtrack. You can also play the game by uploading your own music to listen to as you venture the neon maps.
As I was saying before, there are so many options in this game as well as types of objectives. Think of 5th grade gym class. Then imagine each kid being a neon robot on a wheel. Then imagine this game of dodgeball is in a black room with lights and music as if you were in an amazing adults only disco club. That sums up the gameplay portion pretty well.
There are many options for lag. This game works well in a window and is easy to make adjust to your needs. Overall, definately get this game on sale. Even then, you should just get this game whenever. $10.00 or less is an excellent price because you will get a bang for your buck. It is one of those games you can play for a long time without getting bored because of all the options you could change as the player.
The only disadvantage is that is not being updated so often and community maps should also be an option. It also is a very small community so online mode is sort of annoying to have to wait so long. I love the attacks, achievements, and everything else. This is my example of a 10/10 game.

Mirror's Edge is a really cool take on first-person parkour. The story isn't anything great and the few combat sections in the game feel really tacked on, but the core gameplay and level design are so good that they makes up for the parts that are lacking. It also has a really cool aesthetic to it with the red, white and gray colours. Definitely play this instead of Mirror's Edge Catalyst.

I had played a couple of times through Mirror's Edge Catalyst and wanted more, so I've tried the original. It's not even nearly as good as Catalyst. The fighting mechanics are really bad, disarming enemies is almost impossible and the whole gun-taking and slow-motion parts feel so out of place. I also find the story boring, didn't pay much attention to it.
One of things I dislike the most is the keyboard layout: grabbing guns, interactions (like pressing a button) and attacking must be bound to three different keys, which makes the controls very unintuitive. Also the controls are generally very wonky.
Graphics: this is an old game and considering its age the graphics are okay. The performance however is bad, I expected such an older game to run a bit smoother on high graphic settings. But maybe that's because I'm using AMD and not NVidia, which this game appearently seems to be made for. It also forces you to install NVidia PhysX, even if you don't have an NVidia card.
I'm really disappointed and glad that I bought it at a reduced price. If you're interested in playing Mirror's Edge, skip this and instead buy the successor Mirror's Edge Catalyst.

For 2 bucks you really can't complain too much about something like this, a licenced retro version of 'One Finger Death Punch Lite'.  It's responsive and is fun although it also mimics the arcade feel by being completely unfair at times.
Don't get me wrong, skill will carry you a long way in this but some of the things OFDP employed to keep itself fair have been omitted including the ability for enemies to group up in one space when one is stunned or sent flying (this happens a LOT with the Kung Fu master enemy who teleports away every two hits) which means that they often hide each other or cause you to strike one enemy pattern and hit another, sometimes this can even cause you to travel through them entirely which will usually cause you to break your combo when you miss and/or take a hit.  You also have no indication or feedback on if an enemy has been damaged at all, which is a problem in a game with only five enemy types in total and where you can knock them past others and even off screen.  Finally, if you get swamped by enemies that swap sides, the game will absolutely not let you spam your way out one side to get breathing room, sometimes giving you a miss despite the fact that there was an enemy so close your whiff passed through them, this can be played around but feels kind of arbitrary.
Also, you can't concentrate too hard as each time you strike an enemy, the screen will flash white.  This is a bizzare inclusion and could lead to players hurting their eyes or worse.  If you suffer from epilepsy in any form, I'm gonna have to recommend giving this one a big miss.
But hey, again, it's only 2 bucks and presents a theoretically unlimited challenge for those who love score attack games and/or just an all around nicer looking package for those who were put off by the overall better (and more expensive) OFDP's presentation.
