A lovely game, overall, though it took me a while to get into it. I'm not a fan of the Final Fantasy style fights, but, eh... The game itself is simple enough, with Aurora an exiled girl running and flying around, collecting a band of warriors drawn from the various fantasy races, fighting random evil and exorcising the big baddies. The narrative is fine, and would do better were it not for the horrible doggerel it is written in. It is a problem of good narrative made bad to fit into cramped and unwieldy rhyme: it would have been better to keep a bedtime story style with prose and some couplets at the end of each scene. Dialogue appears between companions at the end of fights (by the end, that is), which was unwelcome, since by that point the various interruptions the game presents tend to add up to a nuisance.
For as bad as the rhymes were, though, the graphics were outstanding. Watching Aurora grow and transform is very well done: she is a good character design, and the animations overall (especially of her) are very good. The scenes appear to be hand-drawn, and the addition of Igniculus (the sprite/elemental) creates nice shadow/lighting effects (as well as very important strategies in the fight sequences). The graphics are really what make this game worth playing. The soundtrack, also, is very well produced (I can't confirm, but it seemed to me to be actual orchestral tracks for some of the key melodies). If you can get over the bad verse, you should find this game to be quite enjoyable. 7/10.

Basically it's aliens attacking Earth and it's a remake of a classic turn-based squad strategy game. I did not play that however. XCOM: EU and it's expansion is one of the most addicting games I've ever played and it lures me back into playing even after month. That usually never happens!
But what HAPPENS in the game? First of all you build an underground base with all sorts of facilities that are designed to research and create equipment for the soldiers you sent on missions in order to defeat the alien threat. What makes this so special, is the fact that you are constantly required to make decisive choices that will heavily influence the success or failure of your campaign. For instance you can only send your squad (that contains up to 6 characters) on one mission at a time although there are always three popping up. The two others you discard will cause panic to spread within the continent they occur and if a country has reached a certain panic level it will withdraw from the XCOM project. If that happens too often you lose the game.
But as if that was not challenging enough, the turn-based missions are as hard as can be. Depending on the difficulty setting of course. Easy and normal are pretty much a piece of cake but "classic" and "impossible" will really have you on your toes and not only once will you mourn over the death of soldiers you've grown onto. And once you finished the game you will be able to activate "Second Wave" options that can alter a lot of settings of the game and you could find yourself in a very different style of playing.
This game is really something for gamers with a passion for turn-based games who like to get challenged a LOT.
Plus the graphics are solid and the story is presented very well although it's not very original.
I promise you'll get a ton of hours of fun gameplay out of this game!

Grim Dawn takes the best of a lot of other action RPGs and creates well thought out and yet original hack & slash adventure. If you are a fan of action role playing games (ARPG) then I highly recommended it. The games does allot of things right. Biggest one, not constantly online like Diablo 3 or Path to Exile. The game gives you base classes, a tragic world inhabited by monsters in a wide variety of flavors, nearly constant loot drops, action-oriented combat, an interesting story line, player choices that matter, online play and hardcore mode. This game almost reminds me of an updated and better version of Dungeon Siege or Diablo. Here are my gribes with the game though. All can easily be fixed in a patch, maybe one day. I don't like that not every character is voiced acted. Not being able to save when I want is annoying. Can only have 4 players in your online world, with an option for PVP there should be no limit to players. When you sell stuff to the vendor, after you return, the items are not listed for resale for buyback or for other players to purchase, needs more story and choices that matters, no mod support or tools, the ending was a let down and you can't swap chars to harder difficulty without completeing the game first with each character, even if your characters are the same level,  Overall, it's a fun ARPG, nothing great but fun. It does have the potential of being allot better.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a game that, while flawed in some critical areas, can still manage to win over players with its sheer amount of charm and character, videogame reference-based humor, and a solid set of combat mechanics.
The story is loosely based on the Console War, with cute anime girls playing the roles of goddesses to landmasses that are based on Sega, Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony. The idea is neat, but the environments never really truly capture the "spirit" of any of the companies being represented and there's a real lack of creativity in bringing these lands alive in that respect. Which brings me to the game's biggest issue: Its lack of variety in locales and recycled dungeon designs. You'll see nearly every type of environment in the first 5 or so hours of the game, and from there, almost nothing but repeats, which will also be the case for most enemies and bosses as well.
Combat is turn-based and fast, and you're given a myriad of options on how you want to outfit your characters' equipment and combo loadouts. Boss battles can be long, drawn-out, and at times strategy intensive ordeals that rarely, if ever, require grinding to overcome.
The progression in terms of the game's difficulty is a fairly balanced curve most of the way, with the player given many opportunities to tip the balance into their favor by either gaining a few extra levels, or utilizing the game's "Remake" system which can allow you to craft new items to buy, add more powerful enemies to duneons, and change what items appear. Again, there's not much grinding involved at all in order to complete the story, and most sidequests can be ignored if you so choose.
The only real grinding in the game involves needing to run back through areas to collect items which may be necessary to craft new Plans you've come across. The game leans a bit hard into this system and it at times can drag things to a screeching halt, but again, beyond the basics and a few nice things here and there, you don't necessarily HAVE to engage with it.
While flawed, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a solid JRPG and will more than please those looking for something a little different in the genre.

To the people who are interested in purchasing this game, these are some thing that you should know:
It is a platform RPG with a unique battle system
Although the battle system is not what i'd call "super fun", but it is interesting enough to not be boring or tedious, unlike other RPGs, the battle system in COL focuses a lot on timing. However, what you should also know is that if you're playing the game on normal mode, you won't have to worry too much about being defeated, the game is not very difficult because it heavily focuses on the story and fantasy aspect.
Adding stats is fun, it isn't super complex but there are decisions that will affect how you play in battle. Plus, there are a lot of different characters to play and they all excel in different fields like defense, attack, magic, heal, etc.
There really isn't much of a platform aspect in this game since you fly, all the platforms and traps are very easy to go through. Also, the puzzles are pretty easy as well.
The mood and the scenery of the game is the selling point, the game is undisputibly beautiful, the storyline is not exciting but it adds a melancholy and passive mood that adds to the overall atmosphere of the game.
I wouldn't exactly call this an exploration game, partially because its 2D, but also because it is quite linear. There are some side quests that are fun but the game is based on a linear storyline.
Final impression:
Buy this game if you're mainly interested in storyline and scenery, I don't sense high replay value because there isn't much to do in the very linear storyline. But it is definitely worth the money.

A beautiful game from beginning to end this is one of the brightest gems among indie games. Like a fairy tale told with perfect pace forward combined with battles to break of the rhyming dialogue.

First and most importantly, the game is absolutely amazing to look at. The visuals, along with the soundtrack, are what make the game so enjoyable for me and the main reason I have replayed it a few times. The art style reminds me of a pop-up book with a hand drawn feel to it, all the characters minus Aurora and a few others (who are 3D models) matching this 2D storybook art style. Everything about the art is gorgeous and the 3D models contrast really well with the 2D, clearly showing the difference between the inhabitants Lemuria and the real world.
The story of the game itself is incredibly short and ends rather abruptly, which makes the ending seem disjointed, rushed, and almost as if the game itself was not finished. A girl, named Aurora, is the daughter of a Duke who loves her very much and her mother has passed away before the start of the story. Eventually the Duke remarries and one night when Aurora goes to bed she falls ill then dies in her sleep, yet awake in a strange land called Lemuria rather than being truly dead. The plot is rather simplistic though the narrator does a great job of conveying it to the player through poetry, much like most of the game's dialogue.
The combat system is your typically turn based rpg with the added twist that if you or the enemy take a hit while in the red "casting" portion of the action bar, you effecively lose your turn and are send back to the beginning (or 30% for the enemy) of the action bar. Battle effects are cute but not in large variety and later I found that some battles required either a little bit of grinding or some item tossing every few turns. Characters themselves have mostly defined roles in combat (buffer, healer, critical hitter, magic user, etc) minus the main character Aurora who is able to deal decent physical and magical damage (healing as well if you got her DLC).
Child of Light also has a very good musical score with almost every piece of music being good to great in quality and fitting the atmosphere of the scene it is used in. However, there are not too many different tunes in the game and you will quickly realise that the game reuses the same tunes constantly. For me this was not a huge issue as I enjoyed the music a lot but later on I did eventually start to tune the music out unconciously.
Gameplay is alright as well though nothing too new for anyone who has played a platformer. As Aurora you travel the land of Lemuria on your quest to get back home, finding various chests with loot, fighting enemies, and picking up some sidequests as well. The controls were responsive for me and I do recommend using a controller when you play as I found the keyboard a bit awkward to use for this kind of game. You also get to control a little blue "firefly" that can be used to open far away chests, activate switches, slow enemies, heal your party, and provide light in dark rooms. A second person can use the mouse to control the firefly as well, adding what is kind of two player experience to the game. You are also able to craft and equip Oculi, gem stones which grant various buffs to the player depending on the type and slot it is equip to. If you know what colours make what when mixed, you will handle the crafting system just fine.
For me the game was basically glitch free as well minus one glitch that has appeared a total of three times, one for each play through. While not game breaking or altering, the glitch many happens when I fight an enemy midjump, which sometimes seems to cause the game to not render Aurora's hair, effectively making her bald for the duration of the battle. Other than that the game gives me stable frame rate the entire time with no other glitches so you should not have to worry about any of that.
Lastly, and most disappointing of all, is the fact that the game requires the use of uPlay. Yes, it requires it. If you do not have uPlay you will have to download it to play this game for what I can only conceive as double DRM. If you launch the game through Steam it will automatically open up the uPlay service and have you register the game if you have not yet. Please note that this registration only apply to one uPlay account and cannot be moved so once it's registered you cannot use it with any other account. Should you delete your account or anything the game is effectively gone. After uPlay launches you will have to hit play, at which point uPlay will then launch Steam and then the game itself. This is by far the biggest draw back to the game as uPlay itself is not all that great and it may be a deal breaker for some people who do not already have uPlay on their computers. This also means that you will want to make sure your specs are above the recommended level as your computer will, as far as I know, run both Steam and uPlay at the same time which can heavily drain resources over time.
All in all Child of Light is an incredible game, though very short for the price tag given (at full price.) If you like artsy games, turn based rpgs, witty poetry, and a cute story the game may be for you, but just be warned that uPlay will try to impede your progress the first time you boot it up and then less so every time afterwards.

This is a great update of the original XCOM. It doesn't go for copying the original, but for getting the feel and many of the general aspects the same, while having it's own style. If you just want to play the original XCOM, build multiple bases, have more than a dozen soldiers on a mission, and have a bit more in depth interceptions and engineering mechanics, and absolutely broken psionics, the original is still out there. But this game will have you crying over your top soldiers being turned into paste, cheering after you take a huge risk to save the mission and succeed, having to make tough decisions as to your next research and what to do with your limited cash reserve. And that, I feel, is what makes it a good XCOM game, as well as a good game in general. The addition of named characters is kinda just meh for me, it's nice to have officer bradley relaying important mission info, but the escort NPCs are just grating on the ears. The best part of the voice acting is the different languages spoken by your soldiers based on their nationalities (might be the expansion that enabled this feature, or a patch, can't remember, but it wasn't in the game when it launched).
The expansion, enemy within, is a must if you like the base game. More options, more tough decisions, more maps and mission types (and one particularly nefarious one in Newfoundland), and they beefed up the sectopods (which really didn't have as big of an impact in the base game, due to it being common to just gang up and slaughter them in one turn before they become an issue).
Multiplayer is fun, but for me, I've rarely played it. The single player is where it's at for me. Short death matches with my squad isn't really the XCOM experience for me. If they added coop where'd you'd have to work with other xcom bases around the globe, that would be fantastic. But they don't have that.

This game is beautiful and intelligent.
Aesthetically, it is a lovingly rendered ode to classic fantasy archetypes and norse mythology.  You can tell the developers invested a lot of creative energy, crafting a compelling and mysterious world.
The dialogue and narrative are simple, but fascinating.  The sparseness of the story and dialogue only helps fuel the mysterious aesthetic of the game.
Perhaps most importantly, it is fun.  The gameplay is inspired by classic rpg elements.  The turn-based party combat seems to borrow as much from XCOM or the Games Workshop table top games as from Baldur's Gate, while the journey aspect evokes fond memories of Oregon Trail.
Your choices in the narrative really matter and are refreshingly subtle.  There is no obvious light side/dark side or paragon/renegade dichotomy to your decisions.  There are hard choices with no obvious right answer, that really make you feel the burden of command.
This is a back to the basics rpg that trims away some of the bloated and distracting features of recent games.  It is raw, gritty, and wondrous.  I expect I will play this game through many times before The Banner Saga 2 is realeased.

Long Review  Inc.
I have a lot of nostalgia attacked to games I grew up playing, and I often have trouble finding new ones.  In the ARPG genre, I grew up on Diablo II, and spent hundreds, if not thousands, of hours in that game.
Since then, few have held my interest the same way: Torchlight, Torchlight 2, Titan Quest being the exceptions.
Until now.
Grim Dawn may be my favorite game in the genre now.  I cannot say enough about it.
Grim Dawn was made by the makers of Titan Quest, and many of the game systems share many of the same features.  The game offers a playthrough style identical  to Diablo 2, where the player plays through the narrative three times.  The first playthrough can be played on either Normal or Veteran (harder, yet better loot) offering a better play experience for new and experienced  players alike.
Priced at $25, this game is a steal.  Half the price of a Triple-A game, yet all the quality.
The classes allow a lot of variety and experimentation.  The player picks two "classes" each with several  different possible playstyles, combining them into  the player's final "class."  While it could use a few more skills in each class, the mix of actives and passives, and  the accompanying devotion system, leave countless ways to play your character.  Even  in the same class, one could playthrough several different ways.  Combine this with skills granted by items and the  player is presented  a deep class system with enough variety for playthrough after playthrough.
On the subject of items, the game offers quite a few affixes on items, giving a lot of depth to gearing.  A player new to the genre may be intimidated by the number of possible stats on any piece of gear, but the game difficulty is such that a player should have no trouble absorbing what each one does by the time that knowledge is necessary.
The aforementioned devotion system  is a large array of passives, allowing a character multiple ways of augmenting needed stats and acquiring new abilities.
The tone is dark and gritty, yet as the narrative progresses, the aesthetics and the mob types change, so as to offer the player a variety of visuals and combat scenarios. The UI is unobtrusive, and yet presents enough information to allow smooth gameplay.
The one drawback for me is bagspace and stash size.  They are too small.  That is the case in EVERY loot-based game, so here I do not dwell.  However, the extra bag space you get is separated from the main bag, leaving you with several  smaller containers, rather than one large one.   A minor complaint, but one I feel worth mentioning.
Overall, this is one of the best games I have played in a long time.  If you loved Titan Quest, or any other classic ARPG, this game is for you.  The price is a steal.  Seriously.  Buy it.
Update: The expansion, Ashes of Malmouth has continued this game's tradition of exceeding my expectations.  There are more monsters.  More  items.  More class masteries.  More skills.  This game is thoroughly worth its price and more.

Beyond that, I discovered through this game what I'd been missing in ARPGs all these years.

Grim Dawn is one of a handful of games in which I'm happy to see a rotting corpse. Nowhere in life are we supposed to be thrilled to see rotting corpses. Even in other video games, rotting corpses are often doing their best to turn you into a rotting corpse. Last time I checked, being a rotting corpse was a downgrade.
Like in Diablo 3, Van Helsing and Victor Vran, Grim Dawn peppers the landscape with lootbags, often in the form of rotting corpses, interspersed with herds of bad guys for you to slice, electrocute, burn, freeze and magically blast into flopping corpses (totally different from the rotting corpses) or even simply reduce to red smears when overkilled. All these RPGs, steam-punky, bloody and dark, are loaded with gore. Grim Dawn is no exception.
Level after level adds skill points to invest in broad and deep class skill trees. In additon, special devotion points can be acquired that allow any character to acquire sets of bonuses and procs that can be added to other abilities to make even more glorious, broken mayhem. While the game only has three base stats: Physique, Cunning and Spirit; but, it boasts a host of bonuses and modifiers that can be stacked through gear, skills and devotions to create all sorts of perverse creations.
If you like Diablo, Van Helsing, Torchlight or just action RPGs in general, then Grim Dawn is a fine representative. It'll certainly scratch the clicking itch for many hours. The game allows for a great deal of flexibility in character build (even if it is shockingly bare in terms of appearance customization.). The controls and the conventions are mostly familiar, with little flourishes that  mostly add to the experience.
On the other hand, I can't comment on the story at all because the first cinematic began with a mediocre voice-over of equally tepid expositional writing that had me fighting off a coma. I turned off the voices immediately and clicked through the sad stories from all the sad characters who live in a sad world, not just of rotting corpses, but people like me who are ecstatic to find and loot said rotting corpses: sad, right?
If you've never played an action RPG, however, this is a fine candidate (at a good price) with which to dip your toe in the water; though, with all the mayhem, pretty graphics and loads of loot, it's likely that you'll find yourself completely sucked in. Fortunately, the game offers a relatively inexpensive respec system to enable reallocation of some misspent skill points, so not every choice is indelible.
Though the rotting corpse has proven a faithful provider of health and mana potions, pocket change and occassional items, just once I'd like to flip a rotting corpse over in Grim Dawn and have the guy wipe at his eyes and demand to know why I was interrupting his nice nap in a pool of his own blood.
Just once, I'd like that.

Review: Crawl is one of the most addicting local multiplayer games that I've ever had the pleasure to play. I love the pixel art style and the dreadful vibe. The music fits the game's style perfectly. In the game, you can choose to worship different gods, each of which correlating with a different set of monsters that you can spawn as, when playing as a villain. Throughout the game, you can earn XP in order to evolve your monsters. The more you play the game, the more gods, creatures, and evolutions you unlock, in addition to weapons and powerups.
I also love the combination of co-op and competition that you get through this game. No matter how many people you have playing the game, there will always be one human, with all of the other players playing as monsters. As soon as a monster making the killing blow against the human character, that player takes the place of the human. With players constantly shifting between human and monster characters, so do their goals. As a human, you want to survive as long as possible, earning enough XP to level up and beat the boss. As a monster, your goal is to destroy the human, earning XP that will help you evolve your monster selections along the way.
The only thing that I'm currently disappointed with is the lack of variety in final bosses. I love the way that the bosses are set up (with one character fighting the boss and the other characters controlling different parts of the boss), but so far I've only come across two bosses. I hope and trust that the developers will add more variety to the final boss feature in time.
The gameplay is difficult to explain, and it's absolutely best experienced first hand. Crawl seems so perfected that I'm honestly surprised that it's still an Early Access game. Overall, I absolutely recommend this game, and the $10 is definitely worth the countless hours that you and your friends will spend battling it out in dungeons.

This game is a refreshing entrant into the couch-multiplayer games genre.
As much as these types of games are appreciated within the gaming community, Crawl offers something more unique that I personally had never seen before in a dungeon crawler. That is saying a lot, given how many of those types of games are on Steam alone.
Unlike many of those games, Crawl is played out in a king of the hill style, with one player controlling the hero, and the other three controlling monsters and traps. Kill the hero: become him. This is a mechanic I had never seen before and am thouroughly impressed with how well it was implemented. It draws you in. The fights and tension between players is genuine, and when you find yourself shouting with excitement... or resentment, without even realizing it, that is a very good thing.
The art is amazing. As someone who appreciates pixel art style, especially the retro, arcade-type pixelation, the art and animation immediately stood out to me. Very fluid and well done but at the same time still able to hold that nostalgic factor.
The soundtrack, while limited, shines where it is implemented. A very omnious feeling throughout, and the tracks change appropriately depending on certain events such as a player approaching victory or entering a boss fight.
The gameplay is well balanced and thought out, characters and monsters can be upgraded, and the rubber-banding is appropriate. Players can come back from any defecit at any point in the game.
The game is a must buy in my opinion. It is best played with friends, but I have enjoyed several hours of playtime with the AI, which can give you a run for your money. Updates are still on the horizon at the time of this review, showing the devs really care about this game and its success. Their forum on their website posts upcoming updates for the game and gives players the oppurtunity to give feedback, which is a welcome stand-out from a lot of other developers.
With more content on the horizon, Crawl is shaping up to be a very promising game. As of now even, it is definitely a complete, polished game worthy of many hours of playtime.

This game is probably the best bang-for-buck game purchase I have ever made. It is deeply challenging, imensely fun, highly addictive, and infinitly replayable. The music is fantastic, giving the down moments between battles a calm, soothing feeling, which is then shattered by the rush of the next battle - dodging missiles, thwarting boarding parties, putting out fires, and frantically trying to coordinate your weapons to rip through your opponents shields and destroy their ship. The challenge is amplified by the decisions that must be made at each new location; the events are varied enough that you are consistently surprised and terrified, and the choices have a great balance of transparency without it being obvious which should be picked. Do you give these stranded travelers some of your precious fuel in the hope that they will reward you with an epic new weapon? Do you engage these pirates who are beseiging these refugees knowing that they are more well armed than you? Do you have time to visit the store to repair your hull before the rebels seal off your only exit? Most likely, it won't matter - in the end, you're still gonna die, but that will just give you a chance to start a new game and make new choices and face new trials. It's all exhilirating, all fun, and totally worth your money.

Mirror's Edge is visually beautiful game with excellent sound design and a lovely background score. The pastel colours used in the game would make the player spend hours staring at the surroundings in the game. There is an amazing level of detail to which the developers have gone to make the game feel as realistic as possible. For instance, when the protagonist, Faith, plants her hand on the wall, the user can listen to the distinct clap the hands make when they touch the wall. Also, when the player wields a weapon, the speed of the character reduces, depending upon the weight of the gun she is wielding. This makes for some interesting strategies where the user has to decide between yielding a weapon or choosing speed. This is one of the rare games where the player can see the feet of the character in the game, and can hence move to ledges with a higher level of precision that in other games where one cannot see the feet of the character.
The main criticisms for me are that the story of the game seemed a little forced (the reason why the runners were being hunted did not make sense to me), the unavailability of quick save, which meant that if you happen to die between two auto save points, you would have to play a long section of the game over and over again till you get to the next auto save point, which could lead to a lot of frustration. The combat in the system relies of the character snatching weapons from the enemies using a feature similar to the bullet time feature in Max Payne, which is innovative, but the absence of being able to block blows from enemies in melee combat made the fights a little cumbersome.
Overall, the game has a beautiful enviroment, some innovative gameplay, excellent design and background music, and is worth investing eight hours to play it.

I'm on the fence about this one. If you're just a fan of the series, by all means, pick it up; especially if it's on sale. But if you're more a fan of gameplay and mechanics from the previous games, you might want to stay away. The third installment was by far my favorite: Just enough whacky to keep me interested, and just open world enough to keep me wanting to play for hours on end. This game takes the whacky portion to a whole new extreme. So much so that the whacky takes over and leaves you wishing for a more down-to-earth (pun not intended) game with less insanely weird missions.
The superpowers are fun for a time, but after a while they make you just wish it was feasible to hop in a car and cruise around to good music. It's because of the over-the-top whacky factor that I'm finding the game difficult to finish.

A lot of games claim to be “unique.” Few are. Games just take too much money to make these days for people to produce something that might not sell. So developers generally stick to tried-and-true formulas. Mirror’s Edge is the rare game that not only breaks that trend, but delivers a fun, memorable, experience.

Mirror’s Edge is a lot of fun and delivers a slick, action-packed experience. The gameplay revolves around running and traversing obstacles, often at high speeds. The closest thing I can compare it to is a cyberpunk Sonic the Hedgehog, but that’s a bit of a stretch. While you occasionally “fight,” those instances are few and far between.

The graphics are also presented in a different way than anything else I’ve seen before or since. While the plot isn’t as good as, say, BioShock, it’s certainly above average and is more than enough to keep you engaged in the game.

My one “negative” comment would be to encourage you to buy the game on sale as it’s extremely short (it only took me about 8 hours to complete). At least for me, even $20 seems a bit steep for that amount of playtime.

First and most importantly, the game is absolutely amazing to look at. The visuals, along with the soundtrack, are what make the game so enjoyable for me and the main reason I have replayed it a few times. The art style reminds me of a pop-up book with a hand drawn feel to it, all the characters minus Aurora and a few others (who are 3D models) matching this 2D storybook art style. Everything about the art is gorgeous and the 3D models contrast really well with the 2D, clearly showing the difference between the inhabitants Lemuria and the real world.
The story of the game itself is incredibly short and ends rather abruptly, which makes the ending seem disjointed, rushed, and almost as if the game itself was not finished. A girl, named Aurora, is the daughter of a Duke who loves her very much and her mother has passed away before the start of the story. Eventually the Duke remarries and one night when Aurora goes to bed she falls ill then dies in her sleep, yet awake in a strange land called Lemuria rather than being truly dead. The plot is rather simplistic though the narrator does a great job of conveying it to the player through poetry, much like most of the game's dialogue.
The combat system is your typically turn based rpg with the added twist that if you or the enemy take a hit while in the red "casting" portion of the action bar, you effecively lose your turn and are send back to the beginning (or 30% for the enemy) of the action bar. Battle effects are cute but not in large variety and later I found that some battles required either a little bit of grinding or some item tossing every few turns. Characters themselves have mostly defined roles in combat (buffer, healer, critical hitter, magic user, etc) minus the main character Aurora who is able to deal decent physical and magical damage (healing as well if you got her DLC).
Child of Light also has a very good musical score with almost every piece of music being good to great in quality and fitting the atmosphere of the scene it is used in. However, there are not too many different tunes in the game and you will quickly realise that the game reuses the same tunes constantly. For me this was not a huge issue as I enjoyed the music a lot but later on I did eventually start to tune the music out unconciously.
Gameplay is alright as well though nothing too new for anyone who has played a platformer. As Aurora you travel the land of Lemuria on your quest to get back home, finding various chests with loot, fighting enemies, and picking up some sidequests as well. The controls were responsive for me and I do recommend using a controller when you play as I found the keyboard a bit awkward to use for this kind of game. You also get to control a little blue "firefly" that can be used to open far away chests, activate switches, slow enemies, heal your party, and provide light in dark rooms. A second person can use the mouse to control the firefly as well, adding what is kind of two player experience to the game. You are also able to craft and equip Oculi, gem stones which grant various buffs to the player depending on the type and slot it is equip to. If you know what colours make what when mixed, you will handle the crafting system just fine.
For me the game was basically glitch free as well minus one glitch that has appeared a total of three times, one for each play through. While not game breaking or altering, the glitch many happens when I fight an enemy midjump, which sometimes seems to cause the game to not render Aurora's hair, effectively making her bald for the duration of the battle. Other than that the game gives me stable frame rate the entire time with no other glitches so you should not have to worry about any of that.
Lastly, and most disappointing of all, is the fact that the game requires the use of uPlay. Yes, it requires it. If you do not have uPlay you will have to download it to play this game for what I can only conceive as double DRM. If you launch the game through Steam it will automatically open up the uPlay service and have you register the game if you have not yet. Please note that this registration only apply to one uPlay account and cannot be moved so once it's registered you cannot use it with any other account. Should you delete your account or anything the game is effectively gone. After uPlay launches you will have to hit play, at which point uPlay will then launch Steam and then the game itself. This is by far the biggest draw back to the game as uPlay itself is not all that great and it may be a deal breaker for some people who do not already have uPlay on their computers. This also means that you will want to make sure your specs are above the recommended level as your computer will, as far as I know, run both Steam and uPlay at the same time which can heavily drain resources over time.
All in all Child of Light is an incredible game, though very short for the price tag given (at full price.) If you like artsy games, turn based rpgs, witty poetry, and a cute story the game may be for you, but just be warned that uPlay will try to impede your progress the first time you boot it up and then less so every time afterwards.

What an enchanting game.
It feels like a fairy tale with rpg elements. Like a well illustrated children's storybook come to life in video game form. RPG combat system is classic with a few updates. A lot of the tactical element of the game centers around altering how quickly you or your enemies can attack. If you can attack your enemy when their initiative meter gets into the red zone, you can interrupt them potentially setting them back an entire turn. And you have multiple options for affecting that timing.
While your attacks are turn based, you have a fairy companion controlled separately by the mouse who can heal you, or slow down your enemies and operates in real time.  Out of combat this same companion can interact with objects on the map that Aurora can't reach in a variety of ways allowing two people to play, one operating Aurora with the keyboard and the other controlling the fairy with the mouse
The trailers do a pretty good job of letting you know what you're in for and the beauty and grandeur of it all holds up throughout the game. Its proof that you can have a beautiful game without demanding that your video card spit out the maximum number of polygons and photorealistic textures and next gen lighting effects. As shown here, with some actual art direction, you can do so much more with so much less.
The story is a basic coming of age tale combined with a heroes journey. Young Princess Aurora seemingly dies in bed only to wake up in a strange new land. Able to see haunting visions of her own father falling ill from grief as he mourns her passing, she must explore her new world and try to find her way home while making friends and enemies along the way.
One annoying thing was the decision to write the game in rhyming couplets. I know that this was done to hold with the storybook fairy tale conceit but it started to wear thin for me rather quickly and had me wishing that they'd just speak plainly. But I am a childless 35 year old man (what are you looking at me for? Maybe I want a change of pace from the high octane AAA experience every now and then), so your mileage may vary. I've seen plenty of comments both ways from other people. I will say that if you find the dialog annoying, its usually not terribly essential to read all of it apart from getting side quests and there's not a huge amount of it anyway. The soundtrack and the art still make for a plenty beautiful experience even if the dialog doesn't work for you and the gameplay should be plenty fun for any fan of classic rpg gameplay.
But other than that, everything about this game was great. Nice change of pace too. And again speaking as a childless 35 year old man, I found that it didn't get to "twee" for me, so if that was a concern for you, don't worry. Its also a short game for those of you who have lives.

Personally, I really enjoy this game. Admittedly, it has its down-sides but its pros outweigh the cons and I would recommend this game to anyone.
I found that this game is fun whether you are playing alone or online. I completed the game twice on my own and tend to mess around and do side quests with friends and people online. I completed all the missions, got all the weapons and played for hours just just jumping from rooftops onto unsuspecting zombies who subsequently got decapitated. However playing online either with friends or strangers is fun whether or not you talk to each other or not. I played this game, with three other people, for four hours straight, not talking to them but instead listening to music and I still had a blast with them. Playing with friends who you can talk to really is one of the great joys of this game, especially when random stuff happens with causes you to laugh uncontrollably.
However, it has to be said that a few things in this game either just don't make sense or don't seem to me like creative game design. For example, the first quarter of the main story missions in this game are basic fetch quests that don't really amount to anything apart from allowing you to learn the map and learn how to deal with zombies. The game does pick up after this though and soon you're doing missions that actually seem to have a point, especially when you enter Old Town. Furthermore, the weapons at the beginning of the game are too weak to kill even one zombie without your character running out of breath. The zombies at the beginning of the game take around 10 hits to the head to die, however this mechanic does almost force you to use one of the games' main selling points to traverse the map; parkour.
In the late game, it's a joy to run around both the Slums and Old Town, drop kicking, slicing and stabbing each and every zombie you see. You will rarely use guns in this game but they are fun when you do use them. Although landing a headshot is basically the only way to one-shot the standard zombies, the rest of the infected types can survive a fair whack of shots before going down, the only types exempt from this are probably the Viral and the Toad.
The zombie types; the zombies, Virals, Goons, Toads, Boomers, Demolishers, Volatiles, Screamers, Bolters, Bombers and the Night Hunter. Most of these are pretty original apart from the zombies, Virals, Toads, Boomers and Demolishers which feel oddly stolen from other zombie games, such as Left 4 Dead. However, the other zombie types are creative and each require a different tactic to deal with them, which I like. The Night Hunters are people online who join your game through the Be The Zombie mode. I really like these Night Hunters, however I feel unless its an experienced player who has invaded your game, or you're playing alone, the Night Hunter is at a huge disadvantage as the players can drain its power with the UV flashlight, then it only takes a few hits to die.
The characters in this game are mostly one-dimensional and I never really felt any attachment to any of them. From the get go, I already knew a character who was going to die and what the main plot twists in the game were going to be, so I wasn't shocked when these things eventually happened. I'll give it to this game, there were two characters that I didn't expect to die from the start, although for one character, this became very obvious eventually.
The night gameplay was terrifying in the early game as you couldn't do anything to stop the pursuing Volatiles. But in the late game, you could eventually fight them off. I know most of the weapons I use can one-hit the Volatiles if i hit them in the head. This took away the terror for me as they don't damage me much either. If the volatiles' attacks became more damaging and they had more health, then maybe I would once again sprint for a Safehouse whenever it got to 21:00.
I have the Season Pass for this game and so I have all the DLC. My favourite is the Bozak Horde as I enjoy the tense, fast-paced running that is required throughout. The Bozak Bow that you get for completing all twenty trials and the special bows you get for completing them in a certain amount of time are fun to use too. However, the other DLCs are either useless or too easy. I haven' t found much use for either of them, except for loot farming in the Cuisine and Cargo quarantine zones.
I believe this review of this game has gone on long enough and, although many people will not even see it, I enjoyed writing it. I would recommend this game to anyone but especially if you have friends to play with. The mods in this game are fun too, as mods always are. Mods do stop you playing with people online unless they have the same mods installed. Overall, I would give this game an 8/10 as it is very fun to play by yourself or others. Slaughtering zombies is fun and the different zombie types make for interesting gameplay.

This is a great update of the original XCOM. It doesn't go for copying the original, but for getting the feel and many of the general aspects the same, while having it's own style. If you just want to play the original XCOM, build multiple bases, have more than a dozen soldiers on a mission, and have a bit more in depth interceptions and engineering mechanics, and absolutely broken psionics, the original is still out there. But this game will have you crying over your top soldiers being turned into paste, cheering after you take a huge risk to save the mission and succeed, having to make tough decisions as to your next research and what to do with your limited cash reserve. And that, I feel, is what makes it a good XCOM game, as well as a good game in general. The addition of named characters is kinda just meh for me, it's nice to have officer bradley relaying important mission info, but the escort NPCs are just grating on the ears. The best part of the voice acting is the different languages spoken by your soldiers based on their nationalities (might be the expansion that enabled this feature, or a patch, can't remember, but it wasn't in the game when it launched).
The expansion, enemy within, is a must if you like the base game. More options, more tough decisions, more maps and mission types (and one particularly nefarious one in Newfoundland), and they beefed up the sectopods (which really didn't have as big of an impact in the base game, due to it being common to just gang up and slaughter them in one turn before they become an issue).
Multiplayer is fun, but for me, I've rarely played it. The single player is where it's at for me. Short death matches with my squad isn't really the XCOM experience for me. If they added coop where'd you'd have to work with other xcom bases around the globe, that would be fantastic. But they don't have that.

It's been a while since I've fallen in love with a game as hard as I have with Divinity: Original Sin. It is a game with many glaring flaws, and those flaws are part of the reason I've come to love it. It's not everyone's cup of tea, but those who can stomach its initial few sluggish hours will find a meaty turn-based RPG that pays thorough respect to its CRPG predecessors like Baldur's Gate.
Those familiar with pen & paper RPGs, as well as roguelike elements, will feel right at home here. Combat is tough and involved. The game uses mechanics familiar to paper players while being relatively accessible to modern gamers (none of that THAC0 nonsense!). Larian has developed a smart, stern RPG that offers its charm in its unforgivingly old-school game design with absolutely zero handholding. Very few map markers. No quest arrows. Why am I surrounded by level 15 invincible enemies at level 10?!
If you like Dungeons & Dragons or TBRPGs in similar veins like Shadowrun Returns, you owe it to yourself to play Divinity: Original Sin. Best enjoyed with a friend who will antagonize you.

A great mix between Diablo 2 and Path of Exile, the combat has real weight, the story has real choices, the customization is deep, and the mechanics in the game are awesome and have a welcome complexity to them. The atmosphere of the game is incredible and the builds you can make are truly unique. Awesome game so far.
Quickly becoming one of my favorite RPG's (let alone ARPG). The world is highly immersive and while the animations are not as flashy as Diablo 3, they are buttery smooth and there is a true weight to them. When my character slams his 2 handed mace into an enemies face, the squish and splat have weight. When my character teleports to an enemy and spawns poison spikes from the ground (ohhh yeahhhh) they are palpable and effective. Everything comes together in this game to give it a very grim feeling, from the story to the blood splats and sprays of gore, to the random strangers you meet.
While the voice acting is spotty, the writing is well done, and the main city has a Fire Link shrine feel to it, where strangers you meet along the way will tend to congregate. You can communicate with them and some will have quests for you, some will have impacts on the city itself, some will turn out to be evil and they will attack you in a fit of rage. The choices you make in game have real outcomes, not some phony choice system that changes some insignificant thing. If you decide to skip through the dialog, you could end up burning down an entire village or killing off an important quest character. This is something you don't see executed this well very often, especially in a game that carries the hack and slash stigma.
Which brings me to the combat itself. Yes it has a weight to it, but is it good? The answer, shortly, is ♥♥♥♥ yes. This is the meat of Grim Dawn, and it's the Kobe Beef of ARPG's. Builds come in the form of "whatever you want" and if you structure your character well, you will be able to take on the toughest modes.
There are so many skills to choose from and so many passive buffs you can work into your build through the PoE styled Devotion Grid. Each class is composed of 2 masteries, so of the 6 masteries, you can combine 2 and pick skills from each tree to form your character. THEN you can pick up skills from special items, equipment enchantments, devotion skills (which are like addons to pre-existing skills, procs generally) and relic skills. This helps you mold a character that YOU want to play.
The lack of randomized content is a breath of fresh air as well, unexpectedly. Every inch of the game world is well crafted, creating very unique level design, unlike the repeating similarly textured corridors of ARPGs. The world is a place you can actually explore as the secrets and hidden areas are ACTUALLY hidden and hard to find. Going through the same areas on new characters I find something new every time. It's nice to be able to truly explore and battle my way through an ARPG and it feels fresh and fun as hell.
At only 30 hours in, there is so much I have yet to see and do. I am excited for what's ahead to see and explore more beautiful landscapes and blow more monster's to pieces.

Grim Dawn has plenty of content for those that decide to stick with it all the way through and decide to go even further with additional difficulties or try other classes and class combinations. One thorough playthrough on Veteran (Enhanced Normal) took me around 39 hours with a mix of single player and co-op. The hours per dollars spent ratio is fairly high; however, the experience isn’t problem free. The game performs well on everything maxed and only dropped frames when too many effects were going off. So turn down some of those settings if you’re using a weaker rig and planning to have some co-op fun.
Unsurprisingly, the world in Grim Dawn is grim. Humanity is struggling to survive amidst the warring factions all vying for control of the world. The quests aren’t revolutionary, but what kept me interested was the world building aspect. Journal entries waiting to be discovered are scattered all across the land. Some of them are very well written and have tones that range from sad to gross to horrifying. Other entries will give you some history or act as a bit of flavor. The game uses darker shades of color and litters the world with rotting dead bodies, ancient dungeons, mines, and many enemies to slaughter. The game is separated into four acts that all have a distinct visual style and map layouts. Some layouts were better than others and didn’t make you walk around too many blocked paths. I felt much more invested in the world than Diablo 3’s (I disliked most of D3’s story) and grew to dislike one of the factions in GD because of how gross they were with human lives. Let’s not forget that this game is an ARPG and the story isn’t the main focus. So let’s move on to the gameplay.
This game has a slow beginning pace in regard to acquiring skills. This pacing can become even slower if you decide to take on two classes because for the first 50 levels, you’ll be making hard decisions on what skills you want to give your 3 skill points. You can stick to one class and be a purist which lets you specialize and access the later skills much faster, but I prefer mixing things up. To access later skills you have to put points into a mastery bar to unlock them. This means dual classing can put you at a disadvantage if you don’t have a good plan in mind because specializing with your damage abilities far outweighs having a bunch of weak ones. Many abilities can have passives that enhance it even more, which makes specializing very potent. To err with skill point allocation is human, but the game is very forgiving with skill point refunds
It starts out fairly cheap and slowly increases in price the more you use it, but I’ve used it for over 120+ skill points without destroying my wallet.
Grim Dawn also has a Devotion system which reminds me of Path of Exile’s giant passive tree, but smaller. The Devotion system is made of many constellations which mostly provide passive bonuses and some on-chance abilities which can result in meteor showers, whirlpools, a shield, and more. You must find and cleanse shrines out in the world to earn Devotion points and most of them are out of the way or hidden. Every completed constellation provides affinity for unlocking more powerful constellations which makes things complicated. Planning will be required here since refunding skill points is more difficult. You’ll need Aether Crystals (a material) and iron bits (the currency) for each point.
For my main character, I went with a Druid (Shaman + Arcanist) that heavily used the refund system to create a fun character that could handle the challenges of the game set to Veteran. My character underwent some drastic changes as she went from a melee focused lightning Shaman with a pet and some Arcanist abilities to a cold/lightning Arcanist that later added two aether/fire skills found deep within the tree. I mainly used Olexra’s Flash Freeze, a damaging AoE freeze attack; a Lightning Nova from an Amber gem; and Trozan’s Sky Shard, basically 3 ice meteors. I greatly enjoyed freezing all the enemies on the screen and then following up with the other two spells. Eventually, I picked up Aether Ray for that single target beam of death feeling and Devastation to complete my AoE build. The spells and skills are satisfying and impactful once you have your arsenal together. Some of them send the enemies flying. You should definitely use the refund system to maximize your character’s potential.
The game has crafting and it’s the kind of crafting where you make one item that’s then needed for another, more powerful item. Example, 3-4 pieces make 1 complete ingredient. Item A, B, and C each require four different complete ingredients. Item Q requires A, B, and C. This kind of progression is tied to crafting materials and Relics. It also lets you try and roll rare gear if you have the Scrap, but I wouldn’t recommend it unless you’re trying to replace very low level gear. You can farm materials off of specific monsters, including bosses. To repopulate a world, you’ll need to exit to the main menu and then start the game again which goes by quickly for my system, but still isn’t fun to do. The crafting system requires enough farming to the point of multiple restarts or playthroughs in order to make the more interesting items. In my case, I couldn’t make a Relic I strongly desired because I didn’t find the right blueprint drop for one of the ingredients over my 70+ hours on that single character which made me sigh repeatedly. Still does. I had all the other pieces that went through the process.
Finally, there’s a reputation system in play. Enemy factions will grow stronger as you kill more of them which results in better drops. Allied factions will offer more items from their faction merchants. They carry good equipment and make sure you stay appropriately geared if the drops were not in your favor. You can do bounties for a faction to increase your reputation with them, complete relevant quest, or kill the monster types they dislike. Bounties are vaguely described kill quests and not very interesting.
Grim Dawn has functional p2p online co-op which works out pretty well for the most part. You’ll never have to worry about servers shutting down or server maintenance, but at the same time, you better make sure all players involved have some decent connections since one of you will be the host. The only disruptive things I’ve noticed were some rare desync issues where you can lose track of the other player’s true position (summons will follow the real deal) and some dead monsters/enemies that stayed behind in odd positions, their bodies normally decay to nothingness. Some player abilities will synergize well together. In my case, I used my max level Olexra’s Flash Freeze to reduce the enemies’ fire resistance by 106% which greatly benefited my co-op partner who dealt 80-90% fire damage.
-
Grim Dawn is a fairly good ARPG that should keep you entertained for many hours. For me, it has a low replay value. It’s a game that I might check on every now and then. I do have an interest in seeing what future mods might be able to accomplish once the tools are ready since the other ARPGs I play are online only. You can also use a trainer with GD with no issues online or offline. Should you decide to give this game a chance, I’ll point out two useful resources for beginning players:

A Visual Novel written by russians? That piqued my interest just like Katawa Shoujo did, which was made by members of 4  chan. In general, VN's not written/made by a japanese company should turn out quite interesting (not always good, but interesting nonetheless) as they aren't that much influenced by the japanese culture. Japanese Highschools, japanese character archetypes, you name it.
That's why Everlasting Summer offers a different experience for someone who has already read some Visual Novels, but at the same time it performs well as a Novel for a beginner.
The first story arcs revolve around the girls and the camp and how Semyon's relationship with the girls will change him as a person. The "secret" route (and to some extent the DLC) however focuses on the mysterious world Semyon landed in. This mix between romance and mystery is well done; The spacing and the writing is great, though the story is often pretty predictable...except for Miku's route, that was ride from the beginning to the end and the name of the achievement for this route fits perfectly: "What is this I don't even...". What I should mention though is, that while not a completely new idea, this mysterious world is pretty well "designed" and keeps the story really interesting; Especially that not everything will be explained about it and inviting the reader to make own assumptions.
The artwork sadly wavers from Triple-A quality to mediocre fanart, which sometimes damages the atmosphere as characters change the art-style from one scene to another. Good thing is that doesn't happen that often.
The soundtrack is pretty good, though there are better ones out there with tracks that stick in one's mind. But still, it does it's job.
One thing worth mentioning is the implementation of the workshop, which opens up the option for altermate endings, continuations or completely new story arcs. Right now, there aren't many english mods, but that should change in the future.
Overall, I can only recommend this Visual Novel. The story and especially the world is darn interesting and I'm sure you won't be disappointed and/or bored by it.

After all these years, this is still one of the go-to LAN games for my friends and me. There is something so incredibly cool about seeing your LAAT's turrets (manned by the people sitting at the computers around you) rotate about their mounts and unleash laser beams with a BZURRRK sound as you continuously pick up and drop off respawned troops to infiltrate an enemy crusier during an assault match. Or ya'll just say ♥♥♥♥ that and fly around the map doing strafing runs and laughing as the fighters trying to take you down can't land enough hits to counteract the vehicle-auto-repair bonus you give since you're playing as a Pilot Class.
And yes, the game is pretty unbalanced as you've likely heard. I've seen campers make it into an AT-ST on Endor and continually blow away respawning players as they fruitlessly attempt to dash out of the nearby base's only exit to grab the other AT-STs sitting there. And the Mos Eisley map has a spawn area that is essentially a giant bowl. Only players with jetpacks can make it to the top rim, where they are mostly free to pick off respawning players from below; this wouldn't be a problem except that, when playing during the Galactic Empire era, only the Empire has a jetpack class (the reverse is true for the Civil War Era, where the Clones have a jetpack class but the Separatists don't).
Online matches are almost always easy to find, but they can be (and very often are) difficult due to the skill (or aforementioned knowledge of balance issues) of seasoned players.
But even still, I completely recommend this game due in no small part to the modding community. For example, are you curious about the first Battlefront, but don't want to buy a physical copy? Well one mod basically brings it in its entirety (with some truly excellent maps that should have been carried over to begin with) into BFII. There are numerous user-made maps, campaigns, and characters. And there are various graphical update mods that greatly improve the look of the game.
Even beyond all this, there is the hero class (Darth Vader, Yoda, Jango Fett, etc.) that becomes available during some match-types after a certain number of points have been gained. There is also an interesting (but ultimately not very meaty) strategy-ish game mode where you continually choose a galactic path to fight through, and on each new planet select a perk (which may greatly boost the abilities of your troops) to bring with you when you join the battle on that planet's surface (at which point the game is mostly like the typical Battlefront everybody recognizes). How well you do in that battle determines you next available choices of planets to wage war on, as well as the perks you can take into your next battle.

This game is probably the best bang-for-buck game purchase I have ever made. It is deeply challenging, imensely fun, highly addictive, and infinitly replayable. The music is fantastic, giving the down moments between battles a calm, soothing feeling, which is then shattered by the rush of the next battle - dodging missiles, thwarting boarding parties, putting out fires, and frantically trying to coordinate your weapons to rip through your opponents shields and destroy their ship. The challenge is amplified by the decisions that must be made at each new location; the events are varied enough that you are consistently surprised and terrified, and the choices have a great balance of transparency without it being obvious which should be picked. Do you give these stranded travelers some of your precious fuel in the hope that they will reward you with an epic new weapon? Do you engage these pirates who are beseiging these refugees knowing that they are more well armed than you? Do you have time to visit the store to repair your hull before the rebels seal off your only exit? Most likely, it won't matter - in the end, you're still gonna die, but that will just give you a chance to start a new game and make new choices and face new trials. It's all exhilirating, all fun, and totally worth your money.

This is a wonderful JRPG adventure with well written, funny characters. The main character, Neptune jokes around quite a bit but knows when to be serious. It feels like an Anime that you play, in more ways than one. The combat is turn based but the attacks are flashy and pretty sweet to look at. Getting tired of basic attacks? You can unleash a powerful flurry of attacks using SP (mana/magic) or your EXE charges (built up from using any other action in battle). And as you level up, more basic attacks can be unlocked and substituted for your current attack combo.
The story is quite intricate and complex, yet it takes it's time and makes sure you understand what's going on. The tale is mostly told in text boxes accompanied by lightly animated 2D characters. And by lightly, I mean they react to what's being said when dialogue is rolling and they sway gently when nothing is being said, so they they all feel alive. And the story is filled with plot twists and at any moment, a joke could pop out of nowhere, or the characters would break the fourth wall  addressing the scene or another character's behavior.
Enemies all drop something upon death that is unique to that specific enemy, and the bestiary keeps track of which enemy drops what and what zone they could be found in. These materials are used to unlock items in the shop and complete plans. Plans do everything from modifying the game mechanics as a whole, modifying the items harvested in each zone and unlocking new items in the shop.
The next few items are nitpicks because this game is a port from the PS Vita from what I understand. So i know that there may be a lack of memory left over for these details. and I'm willing to look past these
Enemy variety is new and fresh and the variety is wide. Some enemies will be the same in both model and texture exactly and the only difference visually will be the names. This trend isn't all that noticeable until you look at the bestiary. Certain enemies have a specific element attached. I found no use for the elemental attacks because it never seemed that I recieved a benefit from them at all. I know there was probably a system in place to address that but I just wasn't interested enough to care, since there was no internal way to know what attacks would be effective for each enemy (like final fantasy's Libra). Or maybe I just didn't understand the enemy's design hinted at the weakness, and I'm at fault here.
Dungeons, stages, levels share motives and share styles. You won't notice it at first but as you progress through the game, levels will repeat shape and style with very slight changes and a new set of creatures. but they are mixed up enough that a return to a familiar layout isn't that bad.
The problem with both of these nitpicks is when you return to an area to collect materials from an enemy, some of them look exactly the same. All run down factories share the same "Bit" design and skin. So the besiary keeps track of what you need.
All in all, it is a fun freakin game and I highly recommend it to any fan of anime and JRPGs. 8 out of 10

I will preface this by saying that I've played both seasons and DLC of The Walking Dead, but have not played either the Borderlands or Wolf Among Us seasons. The comparisons I make are between the Telltale Games of Game of Thrones and The Walking Dead.
Thoughts:
There is something about the way Telltale Games designs their games, and at the heart of them, are excellent storytelling. They find a way to get you to gravitate towards a character or despite another, but they go one step beyond TV or comics by giving you the key to the storytelling. Everything is in your hands, and this Game of Thrones is the very same. They introduce a house not currently covered by the HBO show, but keep some familiar faces to ease the transition. The art style is similar to their other series, but with differences that make Game of Thrones different from the other three.
Now about the game:
The controls take a couple to several scenes to get used to, but similar to season two of the Walking Dead, with much more reactionary sequences. Button mashing and quick QTEs :)
Voice acting is quite good, with very familiar voices (and faces") if you watch the show.
Free roam is similar to other series by Telltale, with slow walking and good interaction with other characters.
Some of the scenes have weird face movements when characters are speaking, but it is few and far between.
Pleased with the control of multiple characters, a difference between The Walking Dead that is welcomed.
I am very happy with the new installment and glad I can finally write a review.
TL;DR - would recommend, if graphics are more important to you, then stay away; great storytelling reminds you how well made a game is.

In the Deadly Tower of Monsters, you play as♥♥♥♥♥♥Starspeed, a hero who's crash landed on the alien planet of Gravoria... Wait, actually you play as Jonathan Digby who's playing the role of♥♥♥♥♥♥Starspeed in the movie the Deadly Tower of Monsters... Wait, actually you're playing as three different people in the DVD commentary of the Deadly Tower of Monsters by Dan Smith, the director of the movie, accompanied by an audio engineer Patrick.
The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a unique and weird action-adventure game that is an homage to old school B-movie sci-fi films, it is quite short but it more than makes up for it with the quality of the overall experience.
Pros
- Weird and unique.
- Visuals, effects, sounds and the commentary make you really feel as if you're playing the DVD commentary of a sci-fi B-movie.
- Well-executed humour that will make you smile.
- Voice acting is amazingly bad but in a good B-movie way.
- Gameplay is fun whether you're bashing man-apes on the head with a giant mace or shooting them with a ray gun.
- Climbing higher and higher on the tower over the course of the game is quite epic.
Cons
- I played the game relatively quickly and didn't go out of my way for collectibles but I beat the game in 3h.
If you like unique and weird games, if you're a fan of ACE Team (Rock of Ages, Zeno Clash, Abyss Odyssey), if you're a big fan of B-movies especially science fiction then you can hardly go wrong with the Deadly Tower of Monsters.

Got through about half the game before I uninstalled out of frustration. I'll cover the major parts of the game, no sound/music/story rating though I did like the music, brief and repetitive as it was.
Gameplay: There are I believe 4 maps in total, you have "levels" which consist of doing different objectives on the same map, a main objective and (usually) 2 optional objectives. You earn coins for doing more objectives which allows you to buy weapons/outfit pieces. Outfit pieces increase your "coolness" stat which gives you some perks like being able to make everyone dance around you (it's like a crowd control button) or a passive ability that gives enemies around you a chance to join and defend you. Additionally you have a "pocket" stat which increases your max coin capacity, never hit a point where I came close to maxing out but I kept my outfits upgraded. Other stats include: survival, guns, and strength. You increase them all by use and they all give perks at certain milestones. You can build a few buildings and a tower on designated plots but I never really needed them up to the point I quit.
Control/Camera: They've made the control much better with time, having watched some older videos the shooting looked very awkward. Luckily it's been made more standard as far as tps control goes barring getting caught on some corners it felt fluid enough. The camera though...I'll get into that last.
My issues:
First: My survival stat glitched and maxed itself after I got blown up by a bomb on the 7th or so level. It's supposed to raise itself by taking damage so maybe that was why? Either way it went from a small blip to a full bar with all the perks that come with it which I really didn't like. It made me impossible to kill, sucking any kind of challenge away.
Second: Enemies randomly spawn in pairs of 3, no matter where you are. Normally this isn't an issue, blast them and move on but if one spawns outside of your vision while you're zipping around a map trying to do the other objectives, one could spawn close enough to attack a base or person that CANNOT die/be destroyed or it's game over but they never state before-hand that they're essential. I spent a good chunk of time on one level screwing around and finally finished only to be told "my friend died :(". This♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off a great deal and it kept happening. This becomes a serious problem later on when you have followers whom you cannot command to stay behind and they get killed very easily, failing the mission. Speaking of followers the AI constantly gets stuck on the environment, your pet/followers almost always get left behind and if they're essential it is a coin flip if you'll be able to make it through the level.
Third: Survival maps/open world performance is abysmal. The open world update came out in april so I assume they've moved on. It had a (beta) tag on the front so fair enough, problems expected but the survival mode was much worse for some reason. After 3 minutes of a survival map my fps dipped to 10 fps, regardless of how many enemies were on screen.
Fourth and the final nail in the coffin: The camera. This in combination with my frail allies caused me to quit. If your camera gets at a certain angle or something is behind/above it, your guy will shoot anywhere but where you aim. Sometimes he'll shoot up, other times he'll shoot straight ahead where he faces. It got so bad on one of the chapter 3 levels that I just got too fed up and had to throw in the towel.
I don't really like giving negative reviews, especially to indie games but I had all I could stand. If I could I would put a "maybe" recommendation as it's a pretty fun game when it wants to work and I would still recommend it if you could stomach some technical problems and don't mind repeating the same level potentially multiple times because of a bug or stray enemy. However if you're easily quick to anger after losing progress (like me) due to something other than pure gameplay you'd be better off passing on this.

A great idea with so much style! That's about all it has to offer, however.
It's a DICE game, so expect a super trendy visual style. These are the same guys that made stuff like "bluish hue soldier with an orange highlight walking towards the camera", boy that was a good game! So stylish. Well, this game is different - it's mostly white with simplistic geometry and stylised textures - so sleek, so minimalist.
It's also an EA game, so don't be surprised if you find that all your nostalgic and stylistic appreciation for this title is nullified within the first 30 minutes due to technical issues. Whatever the initial idea for this game was, it came out through the EA development and marketing cycle a vapid broken mess
Mirror's Edge as a
sounds amazing - parkour, some light combat, focus on movement and momentum over painstaking looting and exploration. And this is why so many people like it. Not for what it is, but for what it conceptually represents. It's cool to like a seemingly small game that's pretty much an anti-game when compared to the other titles from the same studios... However, Mirror's Edge is not that game.
You remember it for being cool, smooth and innovative. Well, keep it that way and don't spend any money on this game today if you're hoping to relive the joy, because you're likely to get burned just like I have.
It
runs poorly. I played it when it came out and it was laggy. Played it again a few years later and it kept crashing. Even today, with a PC far beyond the dreams and imaginations of its developers at the time,
And not just a humble error and retry, no - the whole screen goes white and you have
options other than restarting your PC (by flipping the switch, the game won't let you switch tasks). Unacceptable, especially for a game this simple. So that's 3/3 times when the game behaved poorly or straight up didn't work - three different systems, three different attempts spanning almost a decade.
The controls are
awful. Stuff like extremely sensitive mouse (lowest possible sensitivity and still the slightest nudge turns me 180 degrees) is just lazy QA. Stuff like jumping/timing mechanics not being explained, that's just lazy design. You'll have to watch the training NPC demonstrate the jump to you over and over (in an unskippable sequence) just so you can give it one more try and fail and be forced to watch the NPC do the moves again (from your own perspective no less, so you have no idea what they're actually doing when they're jumping). This applies to all missions too, so it's a "make it or load" grind with all the promised fluidity sucked right out of it.
This game should cost $5 at most. It should run damn near flawlessly. It doesn't and it doesn't. If you get it for free, go for it and see if it crashes - you might be able to enjoy it for a moment, but I think you will more than likely leave it to rot in your library after 30 minutes of playing.

The design concept - not just sharing the setting of 50s B-Grade Sci-Fi movie, but actually being a B-Grade Sci-Fi movie, complete with "DVD commentary" - is a good one and works well for the first 80% of the game. However the addition of an unnecessary plot-twist, poor keyboard-and-mouse controls and generally paint-by-numbers game-play mean that, while the game starts out well, the fun quickly leaches out of the game.
On the positive side, the game looks good - in a suitably bad sort of way - and it doesn't feel as though it has a lot of filler (despite the afore-mentioned poor plot choices). The dangers of playing on a tall tower with few railings is mitigated with a button that will teleport you back to where you fell off and a jetpack that lets you land softly. There is also a teleport mechanism to move between check-points, but it is rarely necessary (and unfortunately easy to forget when you do need it).
On the bad side the poor controls come face-to-face with some platforming sections where the 3D relationship of the platforms you are on is not obvious. The boss fights are generally low-challenge affairs with little creativity (although the giant octopus was at least fun). In game-play terms you will have seen it all before, the monsters follow all the usual patterns. The power-ups don't feel like they give much of an advantage and you have to complete challenges or find objects to gain them.
The merely mediocre is the character changing mechanism, they all play differently, but there is little reason to change characters for 95% of the game until you reach the points that require a certain characters skills. Similarly the weapons don't give you much of a reason to swap around once you have found a favourite (there are exceptions: dinosaurs vs. rocket launcher being one of them).
Overall it is a game with a good concept that starts off feeling good, but slowly stops being fun as you realise there is little other creativity involved.
