Using "an old scifi b-movie made into a game" as a setting, The Deadly Tower of Monsters is about 8 hours of fun action platforming that manages to utilize most of the potential of that idea.
As a fan of funny-bad b-movies and scifi-movies where people's imaginations are way bigger than their budget or means, this game felt like it was tailor-made for me: The concept is you're playing an old, unintentionally humorous b-movie with the director's commentary track enabled. The title probably gives away enough about what happens in the "movie".
The game is viewed from an isometric angle most of the time, but there are some sections where you're flying or shooting downwards that have a different viewpoint. Basic movement of running around and beating or shooting stuff with your main and sub weapons feels fluent enough. Although there's a main objective to go for the game gives you a bit of freedom in exploring the accessible areas where you can find materials for upgrading your weapons.
There are three playable characters and you can switch between them at-will at certain points in the game. They do have some movement and ability differences and you're required to use some of them in order to progress through some sections. The best part though is that the characters are voice acted and at least for the hero it's done in a hammy, William Shatner-esque way.
The visuals also keep with the theme and have some nice touches to them like emulating the good old movie goof of being able to see the strings that move the enemies around. Speaking of utilizing the setting, most of the enemy animations also look choppy in a stop-motion -kind of way and there's even an option in the game settings for applying a VHS-type grain on the picture.
There aren't too many negative things I can bring up. My biggest complaint is that it could've used more music on the soundtrack as you tend to hear the same themes a lot after playing for a while. I also didn't like the ending (or maybe about the last 10% of the game) but the positive bits far outweigh the negative ones.
I'm not sure if I'd recommend it to someone who doesn't find the concept appealing but I thoroughly enjoyed it. Comedy is a difficult thing to nail as it depends so much on who you're trying to target with the jokes and the game succeeded in making me laugh out loud a good amount of times.

NOTE: XCOM 2 WAS JUST ANNOUNCED. BUY THIS GAME NOW IF YOU WANT TO UNDERSTAND ANYTHING AND ARE PROBABLY GOING TO PURCHASE THE NEXT ONE.
Almost perfect in my books. If you're here because you played the original, you won't be disappointed, but maybe a little sad due to the dumbing down of XCOM in general. I've never played the original, but I plan on picking it up on steam, or using OpenXcom to give it a go (OpenXcom is a clone of the original Xcom, but free to play and is easily moddable if you want to change things). I say the game is dumbed down compared to the original because of the lack of large micro management and the rather fun/stupid ways to get results. In the original, you could strap a dead man switch onto a soldiers grenades so when he dies, he blows up, taking out enemies or allies. Basically, you could send in a kamikaze unit for fun. In this game, you can't, it's basically tactical, rational choices only. Also, the game is short compared to the original (from what I've heard), but you can switch on a second war setting to make the game longer, or download a mod called the Long War to drastically increase the games length. The game is also perfect if you're a series veteran or a newb to the series, like I was. If you're new, there's tutorials for you, and an easy difficulty for you too. If you're new but want a challenging but fair game, or if you're a veteran but want to play a more relaxing game of Xcom, choose Normal, as it's challenging, but fair. Veteran? You may want to choose classic, as it brings the difficulty to par with the original. Veteran, played this game fully once or more, and a little crazy? Try impossible, and if you want to go even crazier, try impossible ironman.
TL:DR
Buy if you think you'd like it, you probably will.
Buy if you're a veteran, you'll probably like it.
Has a community that makes good mods to improve the base game and it's DLCs.
Is challenging, but fair, and can be made harder at the players discretion.
I recommend getting during a discount, as this game is 2-3 years old now. Also pickup the DLC, as it adds a new story, missions, customizations, and more.

Since this is a revival of an old franchise, comparing it to the old titles is somewhat inevitable, but I'll try to keep it short. I've played X-COM: Apocalypse back in the day, and had a lot of fun with it. The reboot greatly simplified things, to say the least. I remember having to carefully consider which weapon and armour I wanted to give my soldiers, so they could fight efficiently without being weighed down too much (they all had an alotted amount of time units per turn, which greatly diminished as you added stuff to carry). Which kinds of ammunition and how much to bring? Having to manage several bases, vehicles and staff added to the complexity of the game. One thing I did not overly enjoy at times were the levels - while they certainly made interesting futuristic settings, having to search a 16 level office building for one roaming alien was more than a royal pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ Also, the extreme complexity didn't exactly make the game beginner friendly - young me would have a steep learning curve ahead.
X-COM: Enemy Unknown massively simplified that. No more office skyscrapers, only one base to manage, standardised squad equipment and only one troop transporter (although admittedly X-COM could solve much of the especially early game problems by just building two more of those!). The game enjoys forcing you to choose from one out of three missions every so often, only allowing you to help one country while having to ignore the other two requests, allowing the aliens to cause panic in those countries. Especially early on, this is sort of an uphill battle as you don't have the resources to effectively lower panic level.
Base Management has been massively overhauled. You only have to manage one base now, carefully planning where to place which building, as there is a compound bonus for similar things being close to each other (so for example two laboratories next to each other will give you an additional bonus). Scientists and Technicians don't have a skill level anymore, and act like a resource now, lowering the price for your projects, buildings and technologies the more you have. Carefully distribute your funds between producing new equipment for your soldiers, digging out more building spaces, maintaining and protecting your satellite network and of course building new facilities, sometimes required to advance in the plot. The technologies are fairly interesting, and the rate of progress is rather quick - you usually only spend a few days researching something you've never seen before. For some reason, I remember that to be much slower in the old days, although this change is not exactly unwelcome. Equipping your soldiers is fairly straightforward, although I must say I found the variety of weapons and armours to be somewhat lackluster, but that might be just me.
This brings us to the next huge chunk of the game: combat. Each soldier has two actions, which can be used for movement, shooting, using an ability or guarding an area - an option you should use generously. Soldiers will automatically take cover if they are near an obstacle, although it seems the aliens critted regardless of the protection granted by the environment. Seems to have been somewhat more balanced in Enemy Within, or it was just the RNG hating me. There are a few different objectives (saving civilians from alien terror, extracting and escorting a VIP out of a battle zone, and just generally killing every alien), and a few special missions on unique maps. Speaking of the maps, there is some repetition after a while, and they seem somewhat small, leading to battles feeling a bit directed. Don't get me wrong, though, they are still entertaining and satisfying for the most part. After each mission, your surviving soldiers might level up and learn a new skill, making them increasingly powerful in battle. The first levelup will assign a class to your soldier (you can purchase an option to skip that one later), from there they move down a skill tree with two options for each levelup.
X-COM: Enemy Unknown looks really nice, especially compared to the games of old, and the extensive tutorial guides you through the beginning of the game quite well. However, this leads me to one of the main problems I had with the game: since you are mostly guided by your advisors and always have some sort of overarching objective to deal with, the game feels a lot less free and more... directed than the previous ones. While the technologies are certainly interesting, there is not as much variety as I remember and would have liked to see (although Enemy Within added several pretty nice aspects to the game). Killing aliens is still satisfying, and offers an overall polished experience. Fans of the franchise might, however, miss the complexity they loved. After all, I do recommend it though, as despite all my complaints, I still had a great time.

Child of Light is a turn-based roleplaying game with a very distinctive pseudo-storybook graphical style, written entirely in rhyme. Many of its mechanics are reminiscent of Final Fantasy X – including some painful dialogue.
Gameplay
The game consists of two portions: environmental navigation and battle.
Environmental navigation is actually a bit tiresome; at the start of the game, the player can only walk and jump, but very soon they gain the ability to fly around the 2D environment, eliminating all of the platforming elements in the game very early. This has a somewhat negative influence on gameplay speed, the player must explore an environment from top to bottom to find all the items and secrets, greatly increasing the amount of space which needs to be explored. In parts, it works decently well, but frequently it is tiresome, and only a few environments full of puzzles and traps are even remotely interesting to navigate.
There are no random encounters in the game; rather, monsters appear and wander around on the screen, and will attempt to pursue the player if they see them. The player will be “ambushed” if the monster runs into them while their back is turned, and will ambush the monster in turn if they manage to run into the monster’s back. This means that most of the time, the player will ambush the monsters, as not only is navigation simple, but the player controls a small ball of light which can be used to temporarily stun the monsters, in addition to healing the player between combats and activating some switches and puzzles
The game’s combat is actually reasonably sophisticated. The player controls two characters in combat, and faces off with up to three enemies at a time. It is somewhat reminiscent of Final Fantasy X in many respects; the player can switch out their characters at any time during combat, including replacing KOed characters with another character, and different attacks have different speeds. However, unlike Final Fantasy X, there are two different speeds which matter: the base speed of the character, and the speed at which the character acts.
There are two portions of a gauge at the bottom of the screen; the first portion represents the time spent between turns, while the second, smaller section represents the time spent charging up to attack or perform some other action. Each action has its own speed through the second portion of this, and if someone is attacked while they are charging an action, their action is interrupted and their turn is reset into some random (or semi-random) portion of the between-turns section of the gauge. As such, the player can interrupt enemy attacks, or the enemies can interrupt player attacks. There are some means of protecting yourself from such things, and some monsters will automatically counterattack against certain types of attacks (physical or magical) or against attacks made while they’re charging their actions.
The characters are actually quite varied, with each character having their own skill-set which is unlocked via a character-specific skill tree. Each character has their own set of abilities, and there are two characters who are primarily magic users, a warrior who can force enemies to attack him, a character who focuses entirely on speeding up or slowing down allies and enemies, a couple of physical attack characters, and some support characters. Gauge manipulation, interrupting enemy attacks, exploiting enemy elemental vulnerabilities, and applying the right status ailments while keeping your own party healthy are all important. The ball of light you control while navigating the levels also appears here, and can be used to slow down enemies or heal your allies – it is almost always better to slow enemies, though, as that prevents them from doing damage (and makes it easier to interrupt them) much more than healing yourself does.
Unfortunately, after a while, the battles become a bit routine; while the first set of enemies in an area are new and fresh, after a while they become very routine and can be defeated via a very samey set of actions in the same way that Final Fantasy X fights often went. This makes many of the fights in the game fairly dull, and while they’re skippable, the bosses, which are much more difficult, basically require you to beat every other enemy in the game so that you’re the proper level to face them.
The boss encounters tend to be the highlight of the game; they’re the most enjoyable bits of it, and tend to be a bit different from other encounters, mostly in that the bosses and their companions tend to be more dangerous, quicker, and more prone to retaliation and inflicting annoying status ailments that require you to actually think on your feet. Even still, I got through the game without getting a single game over, and I suspect that most players will do so as well; indeed, I was left with an overabundance of items at the end of the game and used them with wild abandon against the final boss, as I had hardly used any prior to that point.
There is also an equipment system, in which craftable, equippable gems which are acquired over the course of the game are put into slots and have various static effects on a character and their statistics; these can be used to add elemental damage types to physical attacks, grant bonus damage, make a character tougher or more resilient, or even increase the rate of xp gain.
While this system seems neat in theory, I had the xp-gain gems equipped to my characters’ body slots for the entire game, and never needed to remove them to mitigate damage. Moreover, I pretty much figured out exactly how I was supposed to equip all of my characters quite early and from there on out it was just a matter of marginally improving my equipment over time – not the most exciting thing in the world, but it gave some sense of progression.
Presentation
The game is reasonably well-presented; the game tries to go for a sort of storybook style, with the characters appearing almost like paper cut-outs or things from a storybook, and the monsters having a similar stylized character. The music and sound are both reasonable enough, but a lot of the dialogue – delivered entirely in rhyme – is pretty awful. Sometimes it works well, but other times it falls down and is kind of painful to read.
Final Summary
Child of Light is not a bad game, but it isn’t exactly thrilling either. Everything about it is a decent enough idea, but in practice, it only shines on rare occasion. The game takes on the order of 20 hours to complete, and has no replay value; while there is a new game + mode, there is little reason to play it.

NOTHING BUT GAMING CULTURE AND KATS!
All games have a realm they are best suited to. Mass Effect is an excellent single-player example, Populous is one of the best God games out there; FTL, the standard for roguelikes. So when it comes to multiplayer games that are not only fun, challenging, and fresh but that allow you to drop a hot mess on your buddy's head, no game is better suited than Crawl.
But how to best describe a game that effortlessly packs together arcade style multiplayer alongside RPG friendly player progression and item usage? Well if I had to use a single word to do so, I'd say something along the lines of...bananas.
This game is ♥♥♥♥ing bananas.
First off, the premise. You and up to four other players (bots are also an option) are tasked with defeating the final boss in a dungeon crawler style series of levels that contain all manner of hazards from fire-spewing torches to Zelda style porcupine bricks that careen from one side of the map to the next. At any given moment, one player is the human in search of the end of the dungeon while the rest are either floating apparitions that collect globs of ectoplasmic goo to use as a weapon later on or to possess vile aberrations; each of which possess' it's own unique approach to dispatching the lone human paragon.
Monster progression is tiered and each tree provides a different approach and selection of satanic beasts you will be able to choose from. This includes, but is not limited to, Cthulhu (+3 Lovecraft boner), Skeletor's misogynistic cousin, and a barfing carp or, as I have come to know it as, "Barfamander."
Yup, it's sort of like Army of Darkness got drunk and had a sloppy ♥♥♥♥ with a desperate Pokemon.
You'll spend a great deal of time possessing traps as you chisel away at the human in play in the hopes that, by killing them in a Shogun Assassin style arterial splash of blood, you will land the final blow and thus become the human until the same fate befalls you. It's a fun give-and-take that means that anyone can end up being the winner regardless of points or skill level (although the latter certainly factors in).
Fun Steam based additions have been somewhat regular and made the title a real gem as far as replay and for the creepily glitched out visuals and sound that operate like an NES on meth. Got a few bucks to spare with the buddies you love to hate most?
Get your Crawl on.

Get ready for nostalgia, and a lot of it.
I first played this game as a kid at a couple different friend's houses and fell in love with the game.
STORYLINE
You are a member of the 501st at the Battle of Geinosis. From there you are given different missions that start in the Clone Wars. Order 66 is given and you witness the fall of the Republic and the rise of the Empire and then the fall of the Empire. all of this while still a member of the 501st. The missions are straight forward and objectives are given one right after the other. Some are easier than others but over all, not bad. The only thing I would have changed is some of the space missions, but space missions are optional. Overall 9/10
GRAPHICS AND THINGS OF THE LIKENESS
Gameplay is pretty smooth. I personally never had any issues, but that may be because of my pc. My pc isn't the best but it runs pretty good for me. No lag, fast loading. I have no complaints. Graphics wise, it's not that bad for a 10 year old game. It has that old game feel that makes you nostalgic. A somewhat blocky appearence to the maps but thats to be expected. The characters look very smooth for their time, not extremely blocky but not completely smooth, but like I said; Smooth for their time. Overall 9/10
REPLAY VALUE
There are a few different game modes that I'm going to mention. First, and my personal favorite, Galactic Conquest. This is a turn based mode. You can play as any of the sides in the Clone Wars and the Galactic Civil War. You take turns moving your fleet across a small galaxy, conquering the galaxy. You win when you have control of all star systems and elliminated all enemy fleets. This mode can be played 4 times before you start repeating. It's completely random which adds more to the fun. the only thing I don't like about this mode is the number of troops that you have in a fleet. 150 points to win on land and you need to score 180 points in space. The number of points you get for completeing "objectives" is a lot for the win point to be 150 or 180. So for that I give 7/10.
The other mode is Instant Action. Pretty straight forward. you can make your own map list and when you hit launch, it goes through all the maps in your list. It also allows you to edit some settings like the number of points you need to win, number of troops on land battles, how often special characters show up, and more. This is where I have the most fun because I can make a map list that will be exactly how I want it. Only complaint is you can't play both Clone Wars and Galactic Civil War on all maps. Some maps are exclusive to one era. for that 8/10. Overall for replay value I would give 8/10

This is my first time ever approaching a Hyperdimention Neptunia game and to be honest, I had no idea what I was in for. I thought it would be a "OMG LOOK AT THE BOOBS JIGGLE" game. And let me tell you that while some jokes revolve around boobs and fanservice, that is not the main focus. Not by a long shot. I also played with a controller exclusively so I have no opinion on keyboard controls
This is a wonderful JRPG adventure with well written, funny characters. The main character, Neptune jokes around quite a bit but knows when to be serious. It feels like an Anime that you play, in more ways than one. The combat is turn based but the attacks are flashy and pretty sweet to look at. Getting tired of basic attacks? You can unleash a powerful flurry of attacks using SP (mana/magic) or your EXE charges (built up from using any other action in battle). And as you level up, more basic attacks can be unlocked and substituted for your current attack combo.
The story is quite intricate and complex, yet it takes it's time and makes sure you understand what's going on. The tale is mostly told in text boxes accompanied by lightly animated 2D characters. And by lightly, I mean they react to what's being said when dialogue is rolling and they sway gently when nothing is being said, so they they all feel alive. And the story is filled with plot twists and at any moment, a joke could pop out of nowhere, or the characters would break the fourth wall  addressing the scene or another character's behavior.
Enemies all drop something upon death that is unique to that specific enemy, and the bestiary keeps track of which enemy drops what and what zone they could be found in. These materials are used to unlock items in the shop and complete plans. Plans do everything from modifying the game mechanics as a whole, modifying the items harvested in each zone and unlocking new items in the shop.
The next few items are nitpicks because this game is a port from the PS Vita from what I understand. So i know that there may be a lack of memory left over for these details. and I'm willing to look past these
Enemy variety is new and fresh and the variety is wide. Some enemies will be the same in both model and texture exactly and the only difference visually will be the names. This trend isn't all that noticeable until you look at the bestiary. Certain enemies have a specific element attached. I found no use for the elemental attacks because it never seemed that I recieved a benefit from them at all. I know there was probably a system in place to address that but I just wasn't interested enough to care, since there was no internal way to know what attacks would be effective for each enemy (like final fantasy's Libra). Or maybe I just didn't understand the enemy's design hinted at the weakness, and I'm at fault here.
Dungeons, stages, levels share motives and share styles. You won't notice it at first but as you progress through the game, levels will repeat shape and style with very slight changes and a new set of creatures. but they are mixed up enough that a return to a familiar layout isn't that bad.
The problem with both of these nitpicks is when you return to an area to collect materials from an enemy, some of them look exactly the same. All run down factories share the same "Bit" design and skin. So the besiary keeps track of what you need.
All in all, it is a fun freakin game and I highly recommend it to any fan of anime and JRPGs. 8 out of 10

Is the game good? Yes. Is the game worth £22.99? In it's current state... no. It isn't. While this game may be very well written and feel like an actual episode of the show, in it's current state it just isn't finished.
The game in it's current form (Episode 1 only) is just incomplete and ends too soon. For £23 you expect a long and interesting game. But instead you're left feeling dissatisfied as the game ends just as things get interesting.
You are essentially paying for a 2 hour introduction scene. When all chapters are release then this game will definitely be worth the money. But at the moment, it isn't. Sadly.
PROS:
-Incredible voice acting (With the known characters being voiced by the actual actors from the show)
-Well written and interesting storyline
-Well paced
-Lots of decisions that really make you think and act on instinct
-Has a replay value
-No bugs. Generally a very well made game
-Characters are incredible and you really feel like you are in the situation and feel as if every decision has serious weight
CONS:
-Graphics aren't great. Textures constantly changing quality depending on the camera angle
-Not much time to choose speech options. Many not giving enough time to hear dialogue and read options. (Makes some moments more tense and interesting though)
-Can't skip cutscenes and speech in replays
-Very limits options menu.
-TOO SHORT! 2 Hours is not the length of a game you release for £22.99
-Finishes just as the action picks up making you frustrated after spending so much time building up to that moment
Long story short. Great game. But it isn't finished. I don't care what you say. TellTale or not. This is a terrible way to release games. Release it all in one or don't release it at all.

A sort of twin-stick shooter that combines combat with exploration and platforming while ascending the titular tower and murdering loads of aliens. the aesthetic here is 'cheesy 60s sci-fi flick' and it extends that to having the director of the film commenting as you play as if he was recording director's commentary for a DVD release. The visuals are solid with all the enemies looking like guys in monkey suits or plastic alien masks and it's all very well put together. You get a multitude of different weapons, each with upgrades, and three unlockable characters to play with. They even take good advantage of the tower climbing mechanic in that sometimes you need to change your viewpoint to look down to lower levels of the tower and murders flying aliens as they approach which makes for a nice change. Sounds good right? Yeah, no so much. On paper everything's there but the execution really isn't great across the board. The in-game currency required to upgrade weapons is really hard to come by so you're not going to see much change there; which doesn't really matter because the clunky repetitive combat renders all the weapons pretty similar in use (especially the melee weapons which are almost completely interchangeable). Talking of repetitive, aside from a couple of missions set off the tower which give more room to manoeuvre, climbing the tower itself become a bit of a chore after a while. The visual design does change things up admirably and you'll very often get new enemies to fight, but nothing actually changes as you spiral your way up the tower so it doesn't help much. Boss fights are rare and boring; the 'shoot down the tower' stuff is unwieldy and annoying; the platforming sections are an♥♥♥♥♥♥ache due to some quirk of the pseudo-isometric viewpoint rendering vertical distances pure guesswork; the three characters are exactly the same to play with except having unique specials which are almost never used (except in random rare cases where you need to switch to a different person for five seconds to get past an obstacle); etc. It's actually more fun to play than I'm making it sound there but there's just so much of it that's completely half-baked. Less weapons (or more upgrade currency), proper twin-stick shooter combat and a little bit more variety and it could've been something really special but I can't really recommend it as it stands.

A joy to play from start to finish, a love letter to gamers.  It's like a goofy Prototype, a perfect direction for the series after Saints Row 3.  One of the funniest games I've played, too.  What are you stupid, buy it.

Gameplay:
Let’s start with the parkour, the whole core of the game, is an absolute blast. The feeling of running, jumping, sliding, and clambering over things feels wonderful. It has the best sense of motion of any game I’ve come across. Then you start hitting kinks. Grabbing onto things can be incredibly finicky. Oh sure you can climb up this ledge but not this slightly different ledge or the bars you swing on which you can grab just fine if jump into them from below or straight on but Gravity have mercy on your soul if you try to latch onto one from a downward angle. And finally things can come to a complete crashing halt when you’re being chased and have little to no time to set up a jump or look for a path.
Then there is the hand to hand combat. Oh lordy lord the hand to hand combat. Sure, fighting the basic cops is no problem but when fighting the tougher melee opponents it’s like slamming each other with beanbags filled with lead shot. Thankfully most of the tougher battles can be cheesed by using the slide kick. And the gunplay? Well that’s surprisingly competent for a game that’s not about gunplay. It’s not Quake or Half-Life but it works and didn’t make me want to pull my hair out.
Graphics:
This is another place where Mirror’s Edge really shines. Everything has a base coat of bright white contrasted with vibrant reds, blues, greens and yellows. It is truly a great case of proper art direction over mindlessly throwing high poly models and high res textures at things. It’s still a very pretty game to this day. Then we come to the hideous 2D cutscenes. Why they didn’t just use the 3D assets for all the cutscenes is beyond me. I’m probably being a bit nit picky here but it’s a bit jarring coming from the gorgeous 3D environments to what looks like cheap Flash animation from the early 2000s.
Plot:
A hyper generic near future dystopia. Only we’re not given any info on how the current ruling party is being oppressive, or why the bad guys are bad guys and why the good guys are good guys. Hard to believe it was written by Terry Pratchett’s daughter.
In closing Mirror's Edge Is something I really wanted to love more.

This is a very enjoyable 3rd person action game, that lampoons the vibe of cheesy 1950's movies.
It's presented as if it were the director of a movie called "The deadly tower of monsters" giving an audio commentary for a dvd release. So he will make amusingly droll asides about how bad the animation is (which is superb at looking like old stop motion animation), or how naff the design of everything is (beautifully naff - perfectly captures that era)
Everything about the production of this game is spot on when it comes to mocking its inspiration. The graphics are tasty, the music is gloriously retro, the voice acting is cheesy, and it is pretty funny too.
Gameplay wise its a responsive mixture of shooting / melee and platforming, with some nifty boss battles and cool little touches. This element is strong, but fairly straightforward. I wouldn't say the presentation is carrying this aspect, as it is fun on its own, but there's no question that its campy vibe  elevates everything on the whole.
I really liked it - it has something that AAA games lack. Beyond the sense of humour it is doing a lot with a little, and somehow seems more impressive than (most) games that cost four times the amount. At around 6 hours to finish I don't think it's bad value for the price, considering there's no filler or duff bits and it's good fun.

I'd say the dollar to hour ratio is perfect. If you enjoy small characters in a giant world then this is right up your alley. The game reminded me a little bit of old Army Men Games for the PS2.
The controls are a little wonky if you play with a controller. But for the price you are paying for this full fledged cutesy sandbox, it's worth it.

I was bashing a horde of  paper-crafted zombies with a huge flaming matchstick when it struck me that playing Squareface is a decent amount of fun.  The charm of the game had gotten to me.  My  mission quest had me pushing a  giant skateboard of craft supplies across the room, zombies coming at me from  all sides.   I was laser-sighting tiny zombies with my gun near a vacuum cleaner and grinning from ear to ear. Squareface just oozes creativity, even down to the menus and zombie finger mouse pointer.   There are shortcomings for sure, but  it does a good job of creating an inviting game atmosphere.
At first glance from the cover art, it just looks like another cubic character game.  I’ve seen tons of these lately, so it barely peaked my interest.  However, once the game started I immediately had a “this is cool” moment.   There’s a sort of whimsical Double Fine vibe here that reminded me of the first time i played ”Psychonauts”.   It’s that charm that will likely ride you through the game, as every level seems to bring something just a little unexpected.  For an action adventure RPG with shooter and melee gameplay, i was pleasantly surprised.
We begin as an amnesiac who finds himself in a world that apparently resembles the confines of my teenage bedroom.  It's all there; video game controllers, remote controls, guitars, and of course paper-crafted man-dolls strewn all over the floor with little guns.  You are a tiny paper figurine come to life in this world.  After an intro on some game mechanics, you are led by an old man to discover some tribal paper-doll struggles within this bedroom.   You get your best Rambo face on and run into the fray with guns blazing and your matchstick swinging.
There are four main areas to explore in the house.  You start off in the bedroom, make a daring excursion to the bathroom, followed by an escape to the kitchen, and finally end up in the living room.  Each area has several mission levels with a variety of goals to achieve in order to move on to the next mission.
One thing that did confuse me a bit was understanding which mission goal advances me forward to end the mission.  Sometimes, it was all three goals but occasionally I would be doing one goal and suddenly the mission would come to an end before I could finish the next goal.  This may frustrate those who love to get achievements.
Progression seems fairly well paced, but most of the RPG customization comes from the multitude of options you can purchase with the coins you retrieve from your kills.
The first choice should be your costume.  Level up your coolness and wallet size with costumes options such as hats and coats.  I personally went for the items that maxed out both of those.  This enabled me to get as many coins in game as I could and convert zombies into lovestruck minions who help fight by my side with just because I’m uber cool.
Guns are also upgradable, but my favorite was getting a katana.  It just made melee a lot more fun to slice through hordes of zombies rather than continually shooting them.
There are also Pets you can have along with you who range from a variety of animals such as cockroaches to a manned tank.  These pets can also be set to attack on sight, which can help when the zombie hordes come running for you.   Some of these are unlockable as you play, but the better pets are available for purchase with your game coins.
Inside every level is a  “Funerales” merchant who allows you to purchase one ticket for 10 coins to get your life back should you die.  I thought he might have extra tickets or other items for sale, but he only sells the one ticket to you.  Beyond that, you can pay 200 coins to revive yourself in the event of multiple deaths.  This is helpful as it really progresses the game along nicely without the need to redo a level again in order to move forward.  That’s not to say the missions are easy.  The end missions per level can become quite a challenge.
The day i started playing was just after the first release of controller settings in the game.  With a xbox 360 controller in hand, I went right at it.  One thing you’ll notice is you cannot zip through the menu by pressing buttons. Instead, you must use the right joystick and slowly click the right trigger like a mouse click.  After that, the movement of the character is very fluid without much slowdown. I did notice if i swung my melee weapon I would move about enough to fall from a ledge.  Also, targeting was very sluggish.  On the sniper level, it was virtually impossible to keep the laser sight still with a controller.  That was the only instance where I had to alternate between a mouse and a controller, though.  If using the controller I’d suggest trying the game with mostly melee action because aiming is not going to be a quick action.
For an RPG, the story was a little sparse.  If you are looking for character development, story arcs, drama, or intriguing dialogue you will be disappointed.  What I found is each mission level started with a tiny amount of dialogue with perhaps an extra line here or there towards the end.  Don’t expect to get attached to characters or find more than a barebones storyline during the gameplay.  The game is more about the game world than the story.  That’s not to say the story is bad, but it certainly lacks depth for an RPG.
While not a must play title, Squareface is certainly a fun romp through a household battleground.  Where else could I fight to the death on top of a toilet seat firepit?  It’s got originality and style.  You can feel the studio spent time giving the game world a quirky persona.  Even the missions carry this through.  I would finish a harrowing gunfight mission to follow it up with another mission where I could set the zombies on fire with a stove burner or shred them with a cake mixer.
I did encounter a few odd geometry issues where I would get stuck in place.  Occasionally, my allies would block my shot while I was sniping.  Even lovestruck zombies would attack my thumbtack barricades, destroying my cover.    This can frustrate the gameplay a bit, but in general you work around it without too much trouble.
The weakest part of the game is the lack of full RPG storyline.   In an RPG I’m usually expecting to find a story with a larger measure of narrative.  Squareface does not have that and it becomes more of a shooter action game than anything else.
Towards the end of the game, the levels do feel a bit rushed.  Compared to the rest of the game, the last levels conclude rather quickly.
Overall, I say it’s worth a play if you have some extra time and want to enjoy a moderately short action RPG that’s different than the norm over a weekend.  The creativity of the environment in Squareface is the highlight of the game compared to the story and gameplay.  If traversing the confines of a kitchen counter with little zombies and running about condiments for cover sounds like a good time, by all means give it a go.  Do keep in mind that story and gameplay take a backseat to the gameworld.
DISCLAIMER: A game key was provided for review

Well, well, well... Of all of the roguelike, couch co-op indie games out there, Crawl has to be my favourite. The atmosphere of the game is just creepy enough to send the willies up newcomers, not to mention the new intro cutscenes narrated by the magnificent Old Shrimpeyes. I don't know what that man eats, drinks or starves himself of to get that kind of voice, but whatever it is, I want it.
Intro and Atmosphere aside, Crawl is just a boatload of fun to play. I picked up the Steam Link recently and said box of goodness has proven itself to be quite good at processing these pixel-style games. It's situated in my living room, so I of course went on to have a real couch co-op experience with a few mates which consisted mainly of ghostly noises and violent screaming. The graphics are great, especially when running at 60fps as you get to watch the current human shifting fearfully from hall to hall before being set upon by rats, spiders and goblin grasshopper thingies, all of which are controlled by either bots or the people sitting next to you.
The best part is, if you haven't been human for a while, you gain Wrath every time the lucky fellow levels up, which in turn allows you to evolve your goblin grasshopper thingy into a rock-lobbing giant. This system of EXP for the living and Wrath for the dead makes the game a lot fairer and keeps things interesting in a long runthrough.
Overall, I'd recommend Crawl for anyone hankering for some old fashioned jolly cooperation; I can't remember what I bought it for because I was a pre-release funder, but whatever it costs now, it's worth it!

You'll wear out your mouse button clicking through every line of dialogue and exposition in this game; it's given to you single sentence by single sentence. It's worst in the game's prologue, when you're doing nothing but clicking through Semyon's dreary restlessness.
This is a visual novel, and the bulk of the story is your life at a Soviet youth camp, where you spend a few days trying to catch up on sleep, trying to make it to meals on time, and trying to do all the tasks that the camp coordinator gives you. But the story is given plenty of time to develop, and you're given lots of opportunities to get to know the other campers - most of whom are attractive young women with somewhat stereotypical personalities. The character artwork looks more like something from DeviantArt than professionally done, but the backgrounds are gorgeous, and the sound fits the mood.
But it's the end of the story where things get interesting and set the stage for another go-through (or several more). Unfortunately, given the sheer length of time it takes to click through the story sentence-by-sentence, once is enough for me.

I can honestly say that this is the best game I have ever played, the brilliant map generation and effective AI make every game a new experience. The base game is fantastic but cannot compare to the masterpieces of Gods and Kings and Brave New World, the DLC for Civ V introduces a new level of gameplay that gives you more control and more options on how to manage a civilization, and destroy your opponent’s. Being able to play against your friends is amazing, the challenge is no longer against an AI that you cannot reason with but against an opponent that understands the fundamentals of the game and responds to them and your actions in a way that makes it feel like you are indeed guiding a civilization in a complex world. But... if you thought it was going to be that easy you are wrong. The multiplayer in Civ V is the most poorly coded element of any major game I have ever encountered. A game with 3 or more human players is guaranteed to crash/resync/devour your soul on a regular basis. But I still play it because once again this is not only the greatest strategy game of all time but one of the most entertaining things money can buy. With the recent release of Civ VI I can only say that this game will go down in history as a revolutionary game that will undoubtedly stand the test of time.

Telltale's Game of Thrones is pretty much what you would expect from a Telltale Games title. It's another interactive narrative experience just like the Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, but this time, it's centered around the Game of Thrones universe. For those watching the TV show, the game starts right at the end of season 3, at the red wedding. You know what I'm talking about.
That said, I really liked the first episode for Telltale Games Game of Thrones. It captured the essence of the show quite well in all aspects of the narrative, and even if you're not a big fan of video games in general, this is a must play for those who like the Game of Thrones books or TV Show. You play from the perspective of 3 different characters with very distinct roles. They all know each other, but they never actually meet, at least not in this episode. Like the TV Show, it's constantly jumping from character to character giving you these very different perspectives. From the mind games of King's Landing to the war games of the battlefront.
As I've mentioned before, in terms of gameplay, it happens pretty much as you'd expect. Lots of dialogue and different options which will cause a direct impact on the game. What certain characters think of you, whether they trust you or not, is all up to the way you choose to respond to them.
From time to time, there will also be some action sequences with quick time events which Telltale just doesn't seem to be able to let go. I'm really not a fan of these, I'd much rather be watching a cutscene than doing these quick time events. Pressing keys at the right time, is not what I'd call good gameplay mechanics, and most of them don't even matter, because even if you fail to press a key in the right time, it's barely going to change anything. I wish they'd just drop this feature entirely in the future, or replace with something that would actually be compelling to do, because every time I see these button prompts, I can feel my eyes suddenly rolling upwards, it's kind of a reflex of mine.
The soundtrack and voice acting are flawless, or close to that I would say. The actors of the show actually voice their own characters and they do a superb job of it.
Visually, the game is okay. It's not impressive, it's not crazy good looking, it's just okay. I can live with it, but some character models do bother me to an extent. Margery being the worst case, I don't think they were able to capture her face very well. There are good models though, if we look at Cersei and Tyrion, they look spot on, but from time to time, some wierd faces will appear. Also, why the hell did they try to recreate the intro from the TV Show? It's by far the worst looking part of the game. Look at those textures, that is horrible, and was completely unnecessary. This doesn't add anything to the game at all, so it's very weird that they decided to include it.
But these complaints feel very minor when compared to the good things that the game has in general.
There is although something I noticed after playing through the game twice. The game is fine for a single playthrough but when I played the game a second time to see the actual impact of your choices in the story, I was actually very disapointed. You can't change anything major. Characters will talk to you differently, they'll seem to trust you more or less, but there aren't any significant changes in their behavior or any major events. You can't save any character from dying, if they die in one playthrough they'll die in any other, they'll go to the same places, they'll interact with the same people at the end. This was kind of a bummer, but it was something that I only discovered after playing the game twice. I'll tell you this, Telltale is really good at creating the illusion that your choices matter in this episode, but at the end of the day, they really don't change a thing. That's not to say that your actions won't have a more meaningful impact in future episodes, but right now we can't say for sure.
Overall, very positive feelings about this game. Telltale and Game of Thrones go very well together, and I can't wait for the next episode, because as usual, this one ends on kind of a clifhanger, but that much was expected I guess.

Squareface:
~~~~~~~~~

To be vertically challenged can be difficult at times (I know, I am one of them). Can you imagine being two inches tall, having a square face, a body made of paper and you being stuck in a room with a giant human? But that’s not the worst of it - there are other two-inch figurines who are running after you to shred you apart!  And you thought hiding in the corner of the room was a good idea! Not in Squareface!
Squareface is a Third Person/ Action/ Adventure game where you take control of a miniature paper figurine. At the start of the game, your figurine will appear in a box laid on the floor with “ School Project”  written on it. This first mission is really a nice tutorial and will explain how to interact in the game with other figures, use items and more.
Squareface has several rooms in which you will be playing. The first room is Stevo’s room, the giant human I mentioned above. If you think Stevo’s bedroom is a mess, just wait until you step into the bathroom! Oh, and be careful with the water, it does not gel very well with paper figurines! Then you will be in the kitchen and in the lounge room. There is also a boxing ring stage which will be full of interesting challenges.

Within each level, you will talk to other figurines be given tasks to accomplish; achieve them without dying or without losing a structure (if required) to win and move to the next stage. Usually, there are three tasks per mission and if you manage to complete all of them, you will be rewarded with coins which you will be able to spend on new and better weapons (melee, main and side), pets or on your character customization. Just a quick mention on pets. They are in the game to help you carry coins but can be used to attack enemies, too. I’m saving coins to buy the great Hamster - this is going to be fun!
Your figurine will lack firepower early in the game but as you progress and collect coins, you will quickly be able to upgrade your arsenal. There are plenty of weapons to buy and help you along your quest.

Gameplay-wise, the levels are really fun! There are boxes to search for goodies (ammunition, blueprints, etc) laying around the levels and use you flashlight for a faster search. In the ammunition one, you might pick up mines, water balloons (to slow down your foe) or grenades to eliminate them. They will leave a coin at the place in which they have fallen - just run over the coins to collect them. There are different type of enemies to defeat, from small (half an inch, how bad they must be feeling) to monster paper figurines. Some will have melee and others will have range weapons. Enemy towers and other giant obstacles, the likes of the mighty and smelly thongs is one of them! Hold on, I have not finished. You can drive cars and also build camps with defence towers, barracks (you will get additional figurines to fight at your side), warehouses and workshops in some missions.
I like the graphics and artworks, they are just great! The only negative is the camera, in my opinion. Every now and then the camera just goes totally weird and you need to move your mouse in a circle a few times, then the camera comes back to normal.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Plenty of weapons, enemies and pets
-	Well-designed levels
-	Cool concept and universe
-	Fun gameplay and character customization
-	Print and make your our paper figurine
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	This camera bug (if it is) is annoying. Needs to be fixed
8/10

On some rare occasions, a game is found which seems not only close to flawless but proves an absolute joy to play. A game like this stands up in a crowd and says, "Hey! You remember fun? Try this, maybe!" The Deadly Tower of Monsters is such a title. In perfect honesty the author nearly feels an aversion to publishing any opinion on The Deadly Tower of Monsters, as it feels like it would fall short of doing the game justice.
To summarize, The Deadly Tower of Monsters is effectively a platforming video game incarnation of Mars Attacks: a perfectly satirical nod to the greatness that was the pre-3rd millennium sci-fi B movie. Looking at it, one gets a vague notion that the developer ACE Team may have originally intended a slightly different product, and partway through the life cycle decided, "You see these stitches? That faulty lighting? Yeah, we do too!" and ran with it in a new direction like it was out of style. Every cliche and trope of 19xx's science fiction makes an appearance while the indomitable protagonists♥♥♥♥♥♥ Scarlet, and... Robot, in the interest of saving the downtrodden population of an oppressed planet of ape-people, try to overthrow a maniacally space-evil space tyrant in space.
Where The Deadly Tower of Monsters shines is its decision to not simply center on a sci-fi tale released to DVD, but the story behind FILMING the kitschy goodness of the same.
To expound, the game's every aesthetic choice leans toward showing the strings holding up miniatures, throwing way too many antennae on absolutely everything, overlaying the player's actions with metanarration by an offscreen hilariously delusional production team, and universally displaying film grain over the camera's vignette. From the game's start screen, an over-the-top director Dan Smith is offering commentary on the making of the ersatz film and the history behind the characters, plot, actors, props, and completely irrelevant trivia about the filming process. The running commentary is a solid part of what makes the game amazing; from hilarious one-liners about the stars experiencing mid-life crises behind the scenes to Bastion-esque dynamic descriptions of the player's actions on a moment-to-moment basis. Voice work for the whole "cast" is actually the weakest part of the game in places (trying just... a little too hard for a cheesy effect and overplaying its hand), and it's still perfectly suited to the whole experience. The Wilhelm scream makes a mandatory appearance in numerous places, and other stock sound effects are mixed into an original library just enough to show self-awareness while keeping accusations of being lazy or uncreative all the way in the next town over. Meanwhile, the score could be thrown over any Godzilla feature ever created without anyone the wiser - an odd but compatible choice for action-platforming adventure.
Visually the game manages to pull off a neat trick by adopting a Duck-tape-and-prayers asset style, and lavishing an inordinate amount of effort on the quality of both the Duck tape and the prayers. Disparate sci-fi movies from decades past are united in a weird, compelling blend. Within minutes of starting the player encounters soldiers with needlessly decorative armor. They run into stop-motion dinosaurs. They may get eaten by a giant fish thing right at home in The Creature from the Black Lagoon. They swat little flying bat things that have actual wires holding them up. They will almost certainly stop and gander at the trees throughout the environment, as most of them are shiny enough to give away a faux nature (which is doubly clear when rampaging foes sometimes just topple them over). There are dozens of smaller touches one notices over time, like how the cursor actually faintly lights up the environment in dark spots, interspersed title cards straight from a silent movie, and fingerprints smudged all over a perfectly good lens flare. Eventually the player will be forced at length to admire the modeling of Christmas light covered dogs stuck in vacuum cleaners, people stuck in too-small squid costumes and squirting ink everywhere, and a gigantic sawblade wielding mechanical space chameleon. It is distinctive, it is ludicrously self-aware, and it knows exactly what look it wants to achieve... and it nails it flawlessly.
In terms of gameplay, The Deadly Tower of Monsters divides itself into two very well defined zones delineated by most action platformers: action and platforming. In the former camp lies interesting, slightly awkward combat with close-range and long-range elements, and occasional set-piece scenes involving climbing parts of the Tower just ahead of rising danger. Said awkwardness in combat is one of the few things about which complaints exist; not that it plays badly, but that it looks... profoundly unnatural at times. Regardless, foes are ludicrously varied, and might do things like repulse grainy blaster fire, or highly encourage use of specific characters' special skills. Dodge based parrying is perhaps unnecessary for most of the fighting one does, but the supplication to "get gud" should be heeded by the midpoint at the latest. Branching and linear upgrades allow one to really carve out a niche style, and establish particular rhythms with favored weapon/skill combinations, in spite of the "merely human" method of ungainly swings of maces and antennae swords and the like. Switching one's tools becomes a necessity at times, though, and although the combat controls are generally extremely simple it remains fresh for a really long time. In a very neat touch, the game has a vertical shooting gallery element; get close to an edge, and the protagonist of choice leans over with a special ray cannon, able to demolish targets far below, or prevent enemies from ascending to their altitude and reinforcing an already vicious group of adversaries.
In stark contrast to the fighty stuff, the titular Tower must be climbed so as to unseat the overlord ruling it with an iron fist. This involves going up and down between teleport checkpoints at times, as well as more conventional running around to explore the many hidden and less hidden locales. Perhaps the single most iconic aspect of the game, though, is the free-fall. Head to a high spot, leap off, and plummet at a rate where dodging and weaving out of the way of oncoming projectiles is possible, but foes can also be dueled with blaster fire on the way back to earth (Sorry, Gravoria) just before triggering a recall function that returns one to the original jumping spot. In a word, awesome. It manages to combine the tension of aversarial scenarios with a really profound sense of just how big the scale of the Tower actually is. One of the better organic moments in the game was one point during an encounter fight where a stronger foe managed to land a heavy hit with a space flail, knocked poor♥♥♥♥♥♥Starspeed off his precarious ledge about forty or fifty stories up, and initiated a completely unnecessary but exhilirating descent through several layers of fire breathing pterodactyls and UFO attackers, ending with a just-in-time jetpack touchdown on terra firma. It was that altercation in particular that really hammered home just how much care went into this title when ACE Team embarked on its quest for producing more amazing games.
The Deadly Tower of Monsters is truly excellent and deserves recognition for the spectacular efforts in making it look and sound a notch above the rest. It shows that, when a team decides to undertake a project, cut out anything like an attempt to take themselves seriously, and polishes the thing so much the previous paint job begins to come out, the result is not simply space-great, but space-magnificent.

Child of Light is a
game. The art has a lovely watercolor look that adds to the fairytale feel. The music is really well done, too - evocative, supporting but never overpowering the action. However, the story is short and to reiterate, it is a
, so if you want an epic campaign to save the world, this isn't it. This is a story about a child growing up, learning to become a leader, how to deal with loss and betrayal, and how to be everything she needs to be - strong, caring, gentle, noble, and powerful.
One of the strongest points of Child of Light is the combat system - there are about four to six things you have to keep track of simultaneously, and it gets crazy. The real-time turn-based combat was immensely fun - you can only battle with two of your party members at a time, and often the enemy has three combatants that attack at different moments and at different speeds. Learning to control the firefly and shift your party members in and out of the fight in order to combo-stunlock the enemy is a wonderful challenge that really never gets old.
I really enjoyed the diversity of characters here. They come in all shapes and ages and sizes, and all the characters become strong, with their own motivations and stories. In one case, it's a girl being strong for her depressed brother. In another, it's an orphan out for vengeance on the people who killed her parents. There's a mage out to prove himself to his elders. A disgraced warrior out to restore his honor. A boy who wants to win a fair lady's heart. Major points for not sexualizing the female characters, especially as two of them are about 7-10 years old.
You can't customize your characters' weapons/armor. You can change the stones attached (called Oculi in the game) to add different stats, but you have the same weapons throughout the game and there are no shops and there is no currency. The Oculi are pretty strong - there's the usual RPG combining and there are other stat boosts in the game, but overall customization stays relatively simple.
Perhaps the weakest part of the game is the dialogue - I personally liked it most of the time, but I agree with other reviewers that sometimes clarity is sacrificed for the sake of rhyme. If you hate Shakespeare and can't stand poetry, this game is not for you. The rhyming dialogue gives a sometimes immersive, other times jarring feel - when it works, it's hilarious. When it doesn't, it's just plain bad.
tl;dr:
Pros: beautiful art & music, great combat system, short and fairly casual storyline, wonderful cast of characters
Cons: dialogue is hot or cold, game is relatively short, limited customization

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Squareface is a 3D, third-person-shooter, action and role-playing game. The game actually reminds me a lot of the Toy Story movies because of the setting and the visuals. You're a little square faced person made of cardboard and paper, trying to figure out what's going on in your world. You'll explore various areas and take on new missions in each level to explain your existence and your environment.
--------

The thing that sticks out most about this game is it's visuals. The art assets and style are great. The character design is quite nice despite everyone looking like boxes, and of course you can customize your character with different accessories and expressions that are unlocked through playing the game. The terrain and environment look great and really fits the theme of the game.  The game really gives off that toy box feel since you explore the world so close to the ground. The stages are all very colourful and despite so many things being on the screen at once, it somehow works and again, does fit in well with the motif of the game. Any mid tier graphics card and CPU should also have no problem running this title as it is not that demanding.
--------
The sound assets are decent. There's a few nice background tracks to the game and I haven't noticed any of the sounds or songs becoming repetitive or bothersome. The guns and other weapon noises aren't too bad and the sounds that are created when interacting with objects or terrain are also fine. Sometimes it seems like the background music doesn't really match up to what is happening in the game or doesn't fit with the theme of the game. It is a minor gripe but it does make things feel a bit off once in awhile.
--------
The mechanics of the game are solid. You use the WASDs keys to move around, use the mouse to aim, and left click to shoot the weapon you currently have selected. You do have sort of a hot-bar, and it will fill up once you find the different items, weapons, or traps that go in each slot. You can customize your weapon load-out before selecting a stage to better fit your play style. There are quite a few different weapons you can acquire in the game, and each with their own damage output, rate of fire, and ammo capacity.
There are some melee weapons also available, but one thing that irked me specifically, is that one of my melee weapons was bound to the "Q" key, and that's fine, but hitting the "Q" key did not switch to that weapon. Instead, it swung/used that weapon, and then clicking the left button continued to shoot the current gun I had equipped. This meant that every time I wanted to use my melee weapon, I had to keep mashing the "Q" key, when I would have preferred to switch to it, and then click my mouse to use it. It is a very obscure rant, but it bothered me quite a bit throughout my play.
Through each stage you're usually running around shooting up zombies, collecting coins and completing whatever objective you have. There are various types of enemies, each with different strengths and weaknesses. After you've completed the objective you can move onto the next level. Each stage has different objectives as well as optional side objectives (that yield bonuses or unlocks), and some are actually quite unique. You can also go back to previous stages in the main menu if you want to replay them or complete any side objectives that you may have missed.
Your coins that you collect throughout each stage are progressive and can be used to purchase power-ups, pets, allies (that help you fight till they die), cosmetics and other various things. As you continue to play, your skill level in certain categories will increase (indicated by a visual bar). These skills dictate what things you can customize your character with, depending on how filled the bar is. There are also different vehicles to drive and some elements of base-building within the game that I have not fully explored yet.
--------
I had fun with the game for a bit, and I can see how people would enjoy it. The graphics are nice and it's a very neat setting. However, I wasn't very comfortable with the way the camera angles were. It might be just me but it always felt like the camera was not low enough or not high enough, and it made shooting enemies very weird. I tried to fiddle with the settings in the options, though it only made it worse. The game almost felt like it should have been an open-world sort of game, with a bunch of side missions, and I think I would have liked the game a lot more if it went in that direction instead of having a stage after stage sort of progression. Not saying that I don't like it now, but it feels like there was some missed potential. It's worth mentioning that you can print out a blueprint for a paper-craft version of your character.
Thanks to the Devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

Were they really so desperate for sequel hype that they had to end it like THAT?!
Yes, the game is challenging. Yes, the art is beautiful. Yes, the gameplay is simple but enticing, taking what is clearly a grid-based mobile port and making it into an intricate turn-based strategy game where each move must be calculated lest one's enemies (who always outnumber you, by the way) beat you to within a bloody inch of your life (as some battles you can lose and not get a Game Over). And yes, the choices that you make really feel like they have weight, with each one possibly leading to life-and-death of party members.
But that ending... It makes the game feel incomplete. The story of the world is that a horde of grey-skinned creatures called The Dredge (a very original name for the bad guys, unless you count Guild Wars 2 or Titan A.E.) are overunning the land and two separate caravans of people and varl (basically giants with horns and not one female amongst their entire race) must come together to address the threat. Along the way, they learn that the world is coming to an end and that up until recently a giant serpent (who I can only assume is this world's version of Jormungandr, based on the heavy Norse influence) was planning to eat all. But it turns out there's an even bigger threat up north that threatens the world.
So, what is this threat? Never addressed.
What the frack is that serpent thing? Never addressed.
How does anyone plan on stopping these duel threats? Never addressed.
Oh, sure, they give some vague mumbo jumbo about what everything is, but nothing concrete. Nothing that would possibly diminish one's need to buy the inevitable sequel merely so one can find out what happens. Plus, a lot of characters have relationships established with eachother but are never brought to what feels like a full arc.
Ultimately, I can't recommend this game. It feels way too much like The Amazing Spider-Man films, with far too many elements left open and just stopping in the middle of everything leaves the game feeling unfinished, like they were just getting to the next part of their story when suddenly the devs or the publishers decided to chop it up into pieces and lazily sell each piece as its own game.
Sure, the game has it's merits. But it's not worth $20, pretty art or no. Buy it while it's on sale or try it during a free weekend, but don't pay full price, because this isn't a game with a full story. It's a game with about 1/3, maybe 1/2 of a full story.

This is only the second visual novel I've played, and the first was several years ago. It was a good re-introduction to this game genre, and won't be the last I play. The protagonist is Semyon, a 25ish reclusive guy living in a city in modern (21st century) Russia, who falls asleep on a bus and wakes up to find he's at a summer camp in the Soviet Union.
There are too many good points to list them all here, and I hope I don't forget any of the most important ones. The music (by Sergey Eybog, and by Between August and December) is outstanding and does an excellent job of setting the mood. The character art and backgrounds are all very well done. The "gallery" images are of inconsistent quality but many are very good. But that's all dressing - a visual novel, like any other story, is about plot, characters, and setting. The plot is well done, a dating sim game on the surface with a deeper plot that starts to become evident by the end of the first play-through and which isn't fully realized until you've explored all of the endings. The characters are enjoyable and well-developed, and the girls Semyon interacts with all turn out to be interesting and usually likeable in their own way. The setting, a pioneer camp in the Soviet Union in the mid-1980s, is used to good effect to tell the story. There are plenty of puzzles and surprises, and plenty of love and relationships, to be discovered.
And now for the problems. My biggest complaint is how at times the dialogue and storytelling gets belabored and drags on and I just wish it would hurry up and get to the point - if I were beta-reading for a fiction writer (which I've done), there are places I would tell the author to tighten things up. All the pictures of Semyon show him with his hair over his eyes, which I gather is a trope used in many visual novels but it still bugs me. Sometimes the characters get too over-the-top emo (especially the one I found most likeable at first, but I can't say much without spoiling).
Despite a few problems, it's an excellent game overall, one that will have me mulling over parts of the story for quite a while.

Like others are saying, this is basically a horror version of Clicker Heroes and clicker games like that, so if you like those games and horror, I recommend this game. If you don't know if you like clicker games, here is a little background on them:
Clicker games are typically casual games that require more time (and clicks of a mouse or tap of a screen) than thought. You can rarely just sit down for hours at a time to make big progress--like most games. Clicker games typically require an extended amount of idle time where they collect resources when not played for you to spend once you play again (most gather these resources even when the game is closed and many have ingame stores that offer various boosts if you use real money). For people who don't have much time to play games, who like to multi-task, or who want achievements (not always fast ones), these are perfect.
I feel the best part about this clicker game is the imagery. If you're like me, then you like getting achievements from or just playing casual clicker games but are sick of the childish graphics. I know I could care less for kiddy images, so I'm loving this clicker because it's adult and horror themed. It even splashes blood on the screen as you click! I love that and look forward to seeing all of the different creatures and bosses.
One word of caution: This game doesn't handle internet connection issues well. It seems to keep track of most (if not all) of my progress when my connection is lost, but it also has to be closed out and won't restart until the connection is back.
I will update this review as I play the game more and/or if my opinion changes in that time. :D

Based on the TV adaptation of the Game of Thrones series by G.R.R. Martin, this is a worthy start to a new episodic series from Telltale.   Having played the first episode, here are my impressions:
-- Story takes place between seasons 3 and 5 of the TV series..... or, in A Storm of Swords, if you're more of a book fan.  I use the term "fan" because the that is what the game is designed for.  You are meant to be quite familiar with the plot, characters, places, etc. and the game does very little hand-holding, pretty much plunking you down right in the middle of action.
--  Fairly decent visual representations of actors from the GoT TV series, with the actual actors voicing their game counterparts.  Voice work is decent and serviceable.
-- Visually, game is not as harshly cell-shaded as Walking Dead, or Tales from Borderlands.  It has a more....watercolor-painted feel to it, which appears to suit the game well.
-- For me, at least, game felt to somewhat "drag" in the middle.  Although I understand that the goal was to introduce characters and establish plot connections, I found it to be somewhat tedious.
-- Illusion of choice is still there and going strong.  You still get to choose, as is customary with Telltale, but quick research after I finished let me know that in a few spots, it didn't really matter what I chose, certain events were gonna happen anyway.  For the rest....we'd have to wait and see :3
I will amend the review as more episodes come out, but for now, Telltale has my attention.  I'm curious to see how the game will develop.

I decided before I started the EW playthrough in earnest, I had to know what I was getting myself into, so I went on Youtube to find a playthrough of it. I ended up finding this awesome Finnish guy named Zemalf (pronounced Che-malf?), and he did a playthrough on Impossible Ironman (hardest difficulty). He managed to go the entire playthrough without losing a single soldier. I managed only losing one, although it was a stupid mistake. There were a few times where certain troop movements and areas made the game stop responding,  resulting in a hard reboot (of the game). I made sure not to make the same movements into the same areas next time, and was able to avoid further bugginess.
If you're going to play this game for the first time, or are about to buy it, make sure you know what you're getting into. This is XCOM baby! And it will wreck your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥left and right! Be prepared to lose troops if you eff up, and the rage that ensues. Did I mention that this was my first XCOM game? I'm in love with it and this series. I truly hope Firaxis decides to make another one, because this game will change your life (okay, maybe not). A true-to-the-spirit of the original XCom, this game is a great example of the right way to go about paying homage to the classic games of the past.
The new remake captures the spirit of the original - tactical, turn-based gameplay with the ever-present threat of merciless death to one or more of your squad members - while updating it with high definition, 3D graphics and a host of modern graphics and improvements.
If you played and loved the old XCom, you must play this.
If you never played the original game, but enjoy turn-based tactical combat games, this is the cream of the crop.
I have some minor quibbles... I'd love to see an enemy base map that recreates the size and open-ness of the old game's base assaults. For me, the Temple Ship in the final mission doesn't stack up as well; it's a very linear experience, whereas the old game's base assaults were vast, sprawling adventures reminiscent of a dungeon crawl.
But minor quibbles aside, this game is well worth the price. I highly recommend it.

First, the art; Little Nightmare's artist is something from the wonderful imagination of both Tim Burton and Hayao Miyazaki (specifically I got vibes of Spirited Away).  The gross, horrifying, unique look of all the characters in this game are what I play these types of games for.
Second, the music; The musical team for this game matched the creepy and eery feeling that the rest of it gives off.  I don't know if there is a vinyl record of this score, but I'll definitely be keeping my eyes out for one.
Lastly, the gameplay; Every level/section of the game has you hiding and escaping the clutches of these hungry monsters and it has my heart racing every single time.

You set your flagon of ale down in the viking hall and sit in front of the lovingly crafted chess board with its austere yet beautiful playing pieces. Across from you is your opponent, a weathered veteran covered in scars, tattoos and sporting a thousand yard stare. The game seems simple enough and yet as it progresses, more and more depth is revealed. The atmoshere around you grows heavy as you and your opponent ponder your moves and you become caught up in the narrative that unfolds before you, even as your pawns die in droves. As you maneuver your pieces for the final checkmate, you realise that that's what this game has been all about. A seemingly simple enterprise with a f%$#ing great story, a$$loads of atmosphere and, despite its indie production values, wonderfully crafted aesthetics.
You decide that once your hangover clears, you're coming back tomorrow to the longhall for more.
