The combat is turn based in a very "XCOM" way, and was intricate enough to keep me entertained.  Pay attention to the (Very short) tutorial in the beginning because when they mention how damage is calculated, they don't mention it again.  Basically the damage that you do (Strength) is the same stat as your hitpoints.  So if you go down 5hp in the enemies last round of attacks, you can now do 5hp less damage.  Furthermore, your damage has to equal higher than the enemies armor.  So if they have 9 armor and you have 12 Strength, you're only going to do 3 damage.  Untill we start factoring in willpower bonuses.
With so many choices so often the game has a very high replayability.  Different choices mean different heroes to fight with or against and with so many characters to care about it just pushes that higher.
The only downside I had was the ending.  The game ends so abruptly I had a hard time believing it was actually over (as the credits scrolled across my screen.)  I actually typed into google "Banner Saga Ending?!" and saw many, many folks who were as maligned as I was by the abruptness of the ending.
I hadn't realized when I embarked upon my journey with Banner Saga that it was going to be a trilogy, so the storyline is continued in future games.  If I had known that I would likely have still bought the game and played the same as I had but I just don't think that it was stressed enough from the get go, what I was getting for my moolah.
With all of that said and done, buy the game.

Sandbox type games are everywhere these days. Whilst not necessarily a bad thing, this can create a diminished quality in the product available. A poorly made sandbox game is a terrible thing. You can see, feel and almost taste the complete lack of attention given to it. Saints Row IV is not one of these games. Volition have thrown so much love into the game, crafting a huge steaming pile of fan service, that you cannot help but find it endearing. Whilst, arguably, the environment and NPC's may not feel as "alive" as those in Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row more than makes up for that with fun. In fact this is the driving force behind the whole game. Whereas SR 1 concentrated heavily on the thug life, SR 2 began the trend for fun, kicking it up a new gear for the third game before ultimately becoming a rollercoaster ride of insanity for the fourth installment. Some fans may prefer the varied environment of 2 or the seriousness of the original but if you are capable of human emotions, something in the vast menagerie of 4 will appeal to you. In fact, whether you choose to keep it old skool and cruise around steelport in a low rider, or super run up to an enemy and drop kick him wearing a hot dog suit, Volition has got your back.
The customisation available helps players craft an identity all their own. You could be a street thug, a super hero, a ninja, a schoolgirl or something unique like a punk cheerleader with a giant dog head. Whatever you choose, the option is likely there. SR IV is also filled to the brim with enough guest stars and cameos to make any new players moist and existing fans fill their pants with a fresh load of love. Put simply, GTA may bring the realism (not counting Trevor) But Saints Row brings the fun/k!

It's a game like this where I wish there was a middle option between the thumbs up and thumbs down button. To be clear, the only reason I hit the thumbs down button is because -I- don't like the game on a personal level. Do I recommend this game? This is one such title where whether the line between love and hate is drawn by the reader's personality.
For instance, if one has never picked up a Visual Novel before, this might be perfect; the game is free, allowing newcomers to dip their toes in the VN style of storytelling. Bonus points if players are into romantic anime/manga; things may feel familiar to them, and there are quite a few references to anime/manga to be made.
But what if the player is the type who doesn't like anime cliches or the semi-fantasty coming-of-age stories this type of medium often tells? This absolutely won't appeal. Then there comes the removed content: the Steam version of the game removes all nudity, but also removes certain segments of the story that help it make sense. Putting it in isn't necessarily better either; one might get the full story, but does one really feel comfortable with risque content of young women? Panty shots of underage girls just make me feel dirty.
Onto the content itself, the game is essentially a dating sim: follow a girl (or none, or several), have adventures, live happily ever after (or not). The Russian background is fairly unique, and the subject of communism, Stalin, and the USSR frequently come up, though not to the point of being invasive to the player; it is simply the stage being set. The game gives lots of replayability, with many endings depending on your level of commitment to each person - which makes sense on some level, however the decisions start to matter matter from very early on and may make your first playthrough unpleasant if you want to get to know the girls BEFORE getting tied up with one - like normal people.
That being said, there are a LOT of endings, and a LOT of secrets. The game was made with replayability in mind; on redundant playthroughs, you'll have the options you selected previously grayed out - you can still select them, but it allows you to see what choices you've already made so you don't accidentally do the same thing twice. At least one option doesn't even become available unless you've gone through one playthrough, acting as hidden bonus stories if you happen to touch upon the right notes during your playthrough.
Fortunately, the game also likes to keep its choices varied. Sometimes you'll pick between making one of two people happy, but sometimes you'll also pick between making someone happy and just shrugging them off. Sometimes you'll have the option to investigate a specific event or ignore it completely which can open up more choices. By making the consequences of each choice a bit more complicated than 'pick between the one you like better', the game wants to make you think about what you're doing, and does it alright.
However, while the number of ways to take the story is diverse, the amount of little dialogue choices (the kind that don't affect a game's outcome) feels lean. At times, the main character will say things that disagree with what the player is thinking, with no way to opt out. Extra dialogue choices would have also helped in places where the game is the same on every playthrough; I was skipping a heck of a lot of text on subsequent playthroughs because it was the same dialogue.
The lack of dialogue choices and ambiguity of some decisions might even end up catastrophic - my first playthrough, I ended up inadventently romancing a girl I didn't like with no way to hit the breaks andohcrap it's the morning after. Officer, I swear, I wasn't given an opt-out button for two days, It's not my fault!
And that about sums up Everlasting Summer. Would I recommend it? Not for myself; not my kind of romance. But for someone who likes dating sims in general, or just wants to experiment with the genre, this is probably the most accessible game of its kind and there is no penalty for trying.

The gods are dead. The sun never leaves the horizon, shining on boundless wastes of tundra. The land is torn between men, giants known as varl and armored creatures known as dredge, neither carry any reason to trust each other. A new day dawns, and the world is at the brink of turmoil, weary of old wars, always anticipating new wars; nearly void of hope. In such a time, you take the role of leading a caravan across frozen wastes to its destiny.
You play the parts of many characters, make their choices and endure the consequences while discovering the beautifully weaved tale of the realm. Each and every character that you lead tell a story of their own in this Nordic, war-thorn saga. Each choice that you make affects your chances of survival, and makes you approach one step closer to your destination. The setting is incredibly rich, expected from any proper RPG game. Every road, landmark, settlement, mountain or forest; every region depicted on the map contains its own local history. The lore is complete and refreshing.
To begin with, the game contains a diverse gameplay, bringing together elements of adventure, role-playing and strategy games. The adventure elements are directly affecting the story, and the outcome of your choices twist and turn to present you alternative destinies. Combats are turn-based in isometric maps, and gameplay is fairly easy to grasp. Yet 'fairly easy to grasp' quickly turns into 'hard to master'. You are able to level up your characters with renown, a kind of currency that you may gain through heroism either in adventure choices or by slaying your adversaries in battle field. Alongside leveling, you are capable of gathering minor and major items to enhance your heroes furthermore.
presents a direct example for my reason to become a gamer: a story to be told. The game satisfied all my expectations thoroughly. I do not wish to present any spoilers, but it is safe to declare that the story of the realm is not finished in this game. Good news is that
is in development. Cheers!

I enjoyed this much more that I thought I would.  It's a mostly enjoyable visual novel, with a few gripes and hiccups along the way.
Firstly, the art sits somewhere in the uncanny valley.  At times it looks just fine, then at other times it's just a bit off.  But the backgrounds are often quite detailed and of high quality.
The 4 main heroins all have some problems.  Slavya just kind of generally exists, and isn't very compelling. Ulyana is generally a but too impulsive and often idiotic and immature, but that's kind of the point... or something. Lena is... yeah... this isn't going to be what you expect, and it doesn't feel as well executed as it could have been. Alisa's rout was by far my favorite and the one that I didn't expect to enjoy first going in; the mysterious events that occur on day 4 were much more engrossing and left a more lasting impression, and the ending feels more organic if still a bit stiff.
The extra route for Miku (Almost literally Hatsune Miku) did a wonderful job turning the game on its head. A wonderful surprise to enjoy.
The Final/Harem rout did a pretty good job wrapping up large parts of the mystery and providing more lasting closure to the story.
Add in the DLC extra kinetic novel rout for more story-line shenanigans, arguably the most compelling rout, but it is HIGHLY recommended you play all of the original routes before playing this.
And it's all FREE.

Dying Light is the follow up game to Dead Island from the polish developer Techland, but will it be worth your time ?
Dying Light puts you in the shoes of Kyle Crane a GRE operative sent into the Turkey city of Harran to find a man named Rais who is a political figure gone rogue who has a file that could destroy the GRE. When you arrive there you find yourself fighting against Rais and helping other survivors led by Brecken.
The story is this games biggest weakness. The story is beyond horrific, with much of the plot holes not making much sense. Not to mention throughout the game you meet a lot of characters and the game expects you to be emotionally attached to them in the more emotional moments in the game. But that is impossible when the characters you meet are incredibly stupid. Almost all the characters are useless and you find yourself not caring for any of them.
The gameplay is amazing and is  a massive step up from the previous Dead Island titles. The combat is way smoother and not as clunky as the combat in Dead Island. But of course the biggest reason this game is so huge is the parkour system. You can free run and climb up everything you see and it all works perfectly. It's incredibly fun just to take time off of doing main missions and just explore Harran at your own pace. The game also has a day and night cycle where during the night it's pitch black and more dangerous zombies emerge out of the dark corners of Harran. Early in the game night is the most frightening thing in the game as the zombies become stronger and faster.
Graphics are top notch, everything looks outstanding maxed out, both the city and the slums are designed really well to fit the fast paced action of the game.
The CO-OP is also a big feature in the game, but it feels kinda out of place with this game. Every character is Kyle Crane and it sort feels out of place. Not to mention the Prologue and the end game are both played Solo only so don't expect to jump into CO-OP straight away.
The "Be the zombie" mode is also quite interesting. It's pretty fun to play as the zombie and it's also quite intense to fight the zombie as well. But there is a massive problem with this mode. It's incredibly hard to find a game, because as soon as you join a game the host drops out. But there is an awesome reward if you beat your opponent.
The soundtrack is beyond amazing. The soundtrack is awesome 80's synth music and makes you feel like a zombie movie like Dawn of the Dead and some great movies from John Carpenter.
I played the game CO-OP from the start. To complete every main quest, side quest and every quarantine zone took me 23 hours. After finishing the game you can always go back and explore Harran. There are also a lot of parkour challenges around the entire city so you can go play those. Not to mention the "Be The Zombie" mode, there is a ton to do in the game so you can expect hefty amount of play time.
The game ran smoothly from start to finish. Never dropping any frames whatsoever, so if you have a strong rig, you shouldn't experience any issues. But there are still a ton of bugs, but nothing game breaking.
Dying Light is a great game and a major step up from Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide. While the story is horrific the game is fun enough to play through at least once.
Final Rating:
8.5/10 - Worth Purchasing

OVERVIEW
Overall, this is a good game.  The main positive is that it strikes a good balance between simplicity and depth.  It is easy to learn, but challenging to master.  The main negative is that the challenge is not well-balanced throughout the game.  The beginning of the game is brutally difficult; the end of the game anti-climatically easy.
CONTRAST WITH THE ORIGINAL
XCom: Enemy Unknown is not just a remake of the classic XCom: UFO Defense; it is a fundamentally different game based on the same premise.
Enemy Unknown is a simpler game than UFO Defense.  In Enemy Unknown you manage just one base (not eight), fight with squad sizes up to six (not twenty-six), and develop soldiers with six attributes (not ten).  The simplification eliminates some of the tedium of micro-management, though it makes it a less free-form game.  Missions have more story behind them, and that gives them more variation than the two standard missions of UFO Defense (landing site and terror site).
GAMEPLAY
Much of the game is spent on the tactical battlefield, where your soldiers fight different varieties of aliens.  The tactical portion of the game is simple enough that it is easy to learn, but still deep enough to allow for a wide range of tactical options and creativity.  The combination of battlefield graphics and UI work together well, and it is easy enough to see at a glance the battlefield situation.  The battlefield screen could have benefited from freer camera movement options, but that is a minor quibble.
A secondary part of the game is the strategic portion.  Back at the base, research priorities are set, equipment manufactured for soldiers, and decisions made as to what missions to take for what possible rewards.  There is not a lot of depth to this part of the game.  Many decisions are obvious, though there is still room to make meaningful decisions about worldwide panic management and equipping soldiers.
TUTORIAL
In addition to a proper tutorial, you get three NPC advisors who explain game basics as you go along.  The tutorial portion of the game does a great job at teaching game mechanics and using the UI; I was able to play the game right away without ever opening up a game manual.
However, the NPC advisors give dreadful tactical advice.  Commander Bradford will teach you to hurriedly dash your soldiers into the middle of danger without support.  Though explosives are your best early-game weapon, Dr. Vahlen will scold you for using them.  The story goals they give you are not always your top immediate priorities.  I suspect that a big reason many first-time players find this game so hard is because they made the mistake of trusting the advice of their NPC advisors.
DIFFICULTY
The biggest flaw in the game is that the difficultly is front-loaded.  The hardest part of the game is surviving the first game month.  You start with rookie soldiers who are prone to have panic attacks at the sight of their own shadows.  The aliens they face outmatch them in terms of ability, carrying weapons far superior than your rookies' conventional weapons.  The beginning of the game- where the new player is inexperienced- is that part of the game with the smallest margin of error.
Aliens will get tougher as the game progresses- but XCom soldiers can progress much faster and close the gap by mid-game.  By the late game, the aliens hit a ceiling where they get as tough as they will ever get.  The ultimate ceiling for XCom soldiers is higher than for the aliens, and there are no time constraints preventing you from hitting that ceiling.  Whereas the beignning of the game can be quite brutal, the end of the game can be an anti-climatic cakewalk.  The game is most fun in the mid-game.
ENEMY UNKNOWN / ENEMY WITHIN
The Enemy Within expansion is not so much an expansion as it is a fleshing out of Enemy Unknown.  Every bit of content from Enemy Unknown is included in a game of Enemy Within; if you have both, you are missing nothing if you ignore Enemy Unknown and start immediately with Enemy Within.  Enemy Within adds a lot of extra options early on; if it is all overwhelming, a new player might consider playing one game of the less complex Enemy Unknown first and then moving to Enemy Within.  Otherwise, there is no reason to play Enemy Unknown instead of Enemy Within.
Enemy Unknown is a fine game without Enemy Within.  However, without the extra battlefield maps included with Enemy Within, Enemy Unknown may not have as much replay value.
CONCLUSION
I enjoyed playing the game several times, and I can see myself coming back to it for another play in the future.  I regret paying full price for both Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within when they were released; however, the XCom Unknown Complete Pack (plus frequent sales) make it a good value.

AFAIK this is a pretty well known, well reviewed, well hyped game. But I didn't fully understand it at first, so in case you're in the same boat, here's a quick explanation: Its a "rouge like" which (most importantly) means that it deliberately wants to stop you from saving your game. It will allow you to save and quit, so you can continue playing later. What you might try to do (because it seems like a good idea) is save so you can reload if it all goes wrong. This completely misses the point. The fun in the game is that your decisions count and there is no way back, which raises the stakes considerably.
TL;DR: Don't get pissy when you realise you can't save, that's the point.
Now that's out of the way, here's some commentary on the game. The graphis are top down and simplistic. The whole thing is simplistic actually, you pick a ship, you have a crew, you tell your crew to man certain functions of you ship, decide what to power and then head off to explore the universe. You can and should pause at key moments, allowing you to balance what you power, where you shoot and what your crew are doing without losing time in a battle. And that's it. It seems sort of stupid and pointless, and ultimately you'll probably get blown up. And you'll want to stop playing. But you might wonder how far you'd get if you just played one more time and before you know it, it's Tuesday.
I haven't yet played the updated version (if its out) but am looking forward to it. Once you've played it for a while, the storylines do start to repeat so the expansion is appreciated. Plus its free! Ultimately, this is one addicting game and if you like space, strategy, narrative and clicking, you should probably check it out. Or not. It's really up to you.

Bite Size Review - Mirror's Edge
The Good:
- Bright Colours
- Great Looking Design and Art
- When it works, it does feel good
- Puzzle solving can be really satisfying (when there are no enemies)
The Bad:
- The Story is boiler plate stuff, rebels vs big crops
- The developers thought it would be a great idea to have enemies in the levels, always shooting at you
- The story takes itself really seriously, and just feels kind of dumb at times
- First Person Platforming
- Fighting/Shooting feels awful
- You are going to die, A LOT
The Verdict:
Imagine a game like Portal or Portal 2 if in every level they had enemies constantly shooting at you, as you were forced to either fight them in awkward combat, or to solve the puzzles as fast as you could while taking damage. Now that sounds like an OK game, but then instead of portals make the puzzle solving be first person platforming (which can be extremely frustrating) and you pretty much have Mirror's Edge.
I was really excited to finally play this game after years of hearing about how good it was. But as I started playing (expecting rooftop levels and puzzle solving to be the main focus) I suddenly realised that the game constantly throws enemies at you and forces you to make split second decisions that more often then not end with Faith plummeting to her death to the city streets below. If it sounds stressful reading this, it is because it is. It would be OK if the last few levels had bullets flying but I swear this game has enemies after you constantly and does not give the player a break. The art style and presentation of the game is amazing, and I loved looking at the levels, but those moments where I could at my own pace were few and far between due to the enemies. The combination of enemies and so many falls that instantly kill you really made this game frustrating.
It may be a bit unfair to say, but this game really is like putting lipstick on a pig if that makes sense. If you took away the art style and presentation of the levels with it's white buildings and coloured objects that looks great and removed the female protagonist I don't think many people would look at this game with rose tinted glasses or even had liked it when it was first released. I feel like most reviews back then would have been low scored with the tag line "at least they tried something a little different". I beat the game, but every time I thought about going back and doing it again I just reminded myself that the game play was really not enjoyable, and the only thing the game had going for it was the art. It's for that reason that I can not really recommend it - go look up some screenshots of this game and enjoy those, but give the game a pass.

Okay. First thing's first. I'm not going to say that this game is life-changing or breaks the boundaries between videogames and art, or that it is even an incredible game...but that's not a bad thing. Just because this game doesn't break any new ground or pose a philosophical question, doesn't make it a sh**ty game. Modern media has created this idea that for a game to be respected, it has to make people view the world in a new light. Well, guess what? This is Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball. It's a game about robots on roller skates, often with moustaches, zipping around a disco with flashing lights and electro music, throwing balls at eachother. It hasn't provoked any reaction in me to make me go; 'Dear God!!! My life has a new meaning!!!'. Instead, it made me say; 'Ohh I'm gonna kill this skate-riding robo-sunnuffab**ch' (this was actually a genuine reaction). I like this game. It's fun. It's quick. But the best part about this game's fun-ness, is the fact that it's stupid. Goat Simulator, is stupid. It's funny at first (the amount of time I found Goat Sim funny for can be measured in themtoseconds), but it's not fun. RR-DDD is impressive in the amount of pros it has, despite the strong overtones of stupidity. It's tight controls and fun visuals have given me some good times. It's a little pricey, and a price drop or a sale might be necessary before it's entirely worth investing your money in, but don't let the price stop you if you like an FPS which requires a decent level of tactical skill (I'm looking at you Call of Duty). If the price is too much for you personally, try it out with a friend who already owns it. It might not be your cup of tea. As I say, it requires some tactical practice which may not be something you want in your robot related disco-shooters. However, if you're not a fan of tactical strategy games and like some fast-paced fun, I recommend this game greatly, along with a few games like Awesomenauts (easier) or Ratz Instagib (much harder). In conclusion, I give this game an 8.5/10. It's cool, but is lacking in areas which I won't go into, because I really don't want to put you off. It's fun, and you should give it a go. Why the heck would you listen to me anyway? I'm a random dude off the internet.
Finally, I don't think that this game is incredible or brilliant, but that's okay. You know why?
Because it's a game about roller-skating robots in a f**king disco.

So in all seriousness this game definitely exceeded my expectations. I thought it'd be a relatively stubby tower full of dull monsters... nope. The enemy variety was extensive and it was kind of refreshing to see most of their animations done in a stop-motion type of way. Without the cause being framerate issues
. The gameplay was solid; The jetpack platforming, weapon variety, the combat, how the enemies drop pickups and not to mention the collectables... It reminded me of 3D platforming games from the good old days, with a top-down/isometricish twist. Needless to say this game gets you pretty high, and free falling once you are is ♥♥♥♥in majestic!
The story was interesting to say the least... I'd elaborate on that some more but it'd just be spoilers. However, I will say I liked how this game played on all the major cliches of B-movies. Even for someone like me, who doesn't frequently watch b-movies, I still understood the humor. The commentary did actually make me laugh a few times, and I went in thinking it'd be cheesey/cringe-city. It was, but not as much as I thought it would be. It was the misogynistic humor that made me laugh the most, especially in this day and age with all the feminism.
Right when you start the game, before even getting to the main menu, the games either gonna make you laugh/smile or anger/annoy you with its commentary gimmick. If you're part of the group that laugh/smiles, you're in for a good time.

I wanted this game as soon as I saw the trailers, and I wasn't disappointed. In fact, I've played it everyday since I got it. I now use an iBuffalo Classic USB gamepad; the same goes for it, although that might just be because it's a new gadget and hasn't been broken in yet. Both control sets work great! Word to the wise, though: As of now, you can't adjust the gamepad controls in the main menu; you have to start a game and then use the controls menu that appears immediately after.
The developers are still working out the kinks, I imagine, and they're adding new content all the time. Sandbox type games are everywhere these days. Whilst not necessarily a bad thing, this can create a diminished quality in the product available. A poorly made sandbox game is a terrible thing. You can see, feel and almost taste the complete lack of attention given to it. Saints Row IV is not one of these games. Volition have thrown so much love into the game, crafting a huge steaming pile of fan service, that you cannot help but find it endearing. Whilst, arguably, the environment and NPC's may not feel as "alive" as those in Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row more than makes up for that with fun. In fact this is the driving force behind the whole game. Whereas SR 1 concentrated heavily on the thug life, SR 2 began the trend for fun, kicking it up a new gear for the third game before ultimately becoming a rollercoaster ride of insanity for the fourth installment. Some fans may prefer the varied environment of 2 or the seriousness of the original but if you are capable of human emotions, something in the vast menagerie of 4 will appeal to you. In fact, whether you choose to keep it old skool and cruise around steelport in a low rider, or super run up to an enemy and drop kick him wearing a hot dog suit, Volition has got your back.
The customisation available helps players craft an identity all their own. You could be a street thug, a super hero, a ninja, a schoolgirl or something unique like a punk cheerleader with a giant dog head. Whatever you choose, the option is likely there. SR IV is also filled to the brim with enough guest stars and cameos to make any new players moist and existing fans fill their pants with a fresh load of love. Put simply, GTA may bring the realism (not counting Trevor) But Saints Row brings the fun/k!

Disclaimer: I was generously given a free copy of Detour with the understanding that I was expected to review the title after spending some time with it.
Detour is a puzzle game which tasks you with creating a safe route for a truck to pass through a hostile city.
Now the bad part. This game runs atrociously. The first thing that struck me when starting up the game for the first time is the inexcusable amount of latency when using the software cursor. The delay between my mouse movement and the cursors response on the screen varied anywhere from 0.5 to (not exaggerating) 2.5 seconds! If you’re really desperate to play Detour, your first priority should be to enable Hardware Cursor in the options menu. Following the debacle with the laggy mouse, I noticed there were a fair few grammatical issues with the level selection text. Typically with low budget/hobby games I sort of just overlook this, especially when the narrative is, for all intents and purposes, irrelevant to the actual gameplay. Unfortunately, after seeing the issues with the cursor, these errors were much more eye catching and set a precedent in my mind that this was either shoddily put together or unnecessarily rushed to release. Then I began the campaign. I actually quit midway through the first level just to activate Steams’ FPS counter and boot up Fraps to confirm my suspicions: this isometric mobile-port style puzzle game was running at 16 FPS on a GTX 680 and an overclocked i7-2600k. I suffered on through a handful more levels just to know what the game was trying to be, and as intriguing as the concept may be, the performance of this game is just abysmal.
Revolution of FPS shooters, started here. The wait for HL3 never ends.

The decision to recommend this game or not was made based on me answering the question "Would I play the second part?" Sadly, the answer is "Hell no!"
Yes, the game uses a unique art style, and both audio and visual components are fitting to the viking setting. Yet the "game" part of the game ended up being a complete let-down.
The way the game is presented and set up one would think the developers try to discourage you from save-scumming and thus put more weight on your decisions. "Every decision you make in travel, conversation and combat has a meaningful effect on the outcome as your story unfolds."
Unfortunately, as I found out, this translares into "The outcome of any decision is arbitrary, and you're most certainly going to be punished for taking any decision, that tries to avoid combat."
I would argue, that if the outcomes of your actions cannot be even roughly predicted, the description should state that "every decision is meaningless".
Losing key characters? Supposed to make you care for the rest, in reality makes you annoyed and frustrated at the game and the developers.
Thinking that decisions between dickish and polite actions should at least influence the morale of your caravan in a predictable way? Nope, everything's totally arbitrary.
Have not came across any situation, when the amount of people in your caravan would play any role whatsoever. But since I kept expecting it, ended up spending all the renown on food supplies, and never had enough to buy a single artefact, let alone keeping my troops promoted.
The fiddliest experience of equiping the artifacts before the battle is further augmented by characters taking off after the battle WITH your artifacts. And since the saves are only done automatically, rewinding the last hour to rectify that was too much of a hassle. So I guess the devs achieved their goal of eliminating the save-scumming - I just couldn't be arsed...
tl;dr a "killing characters is so grown-up" attitude to the storytelling with your decisions governed by a random number generator. The only sure way to have any positive outcome is to always choose combat. A cool art piece, a mediocre game.

I picked up this game while searching around for free games to pass the time with. I had never played a visual novel before this one. I hardly expected anything at all from this one, maybe a few laughs at the ridiculousness of it.
I'm not really sure what it is about this game, maybe the combination of characters, amazingly varied original soundtrack, completely unique story, sense of immersion and atmosphere all blended together and really struck a chord with me. I chugged my way through an ending over the course of a few days, and along the way fell in love with the game. Once I got that ending, there was a gaping hole inside of me that wanted more. So I went for another ending...then another...then another until I had eventually completed all of the endings.
It's so apparent as you go through the game that the devs put so much time, effort, and love into this game. Between the 60 or so original tracks, the 20-30 hours of gameplay if one goes through all of the endings, and the vibrancy of the story and characters, it's amazing what was accomplished with what seemingly little resources they had.
I still love this game today, and hold it in regard of being one of my favorite game experiences. I do still listen to that awesome soundtrack, and get nostalgia for that very first time through. I do wish that I could go back and experience this game for the first time again, it was a wild ride that I won't forget.
Even if you aren't a fan of visual novels, I'd still recommend at least giving this game a try, it's free after all.

This is coming from a guy who has only heard of these games in passing before now. I had no idea what to expect when I was thrown ino this world. Good thing I didn't get time to prepare! Right from the get-go, this little lady Neptune, I had seen around the internet captured my attension, and she didn't let go!
From what I read online after Neptune herself commented, "They really changed the story with this remake!" They really did change the entirety of the thing and it's suggested even those who played the original get into this too.
Let's talk about what this game is. Hyperdimension Neptunia is a traditional JRPG that parodies every bit of gaming you can imagine. From locations, like Halo Mountain and the Hyyrule Snowfield, to the discs upgrades which allow you to 'create' games like CoD and other such that give you awesome stats, to the fact they've stolen some Tales Of Series Hi-ougi (Mystic Arts). This game is a wash with references to Gaming, even Visual Novels like Stein's Gate get a nod. For those of you raised on gaming, this is a tribute!
The Combat system is the games most polished and strongest point. It reminds me of a far better version of the old Quest 64 Battle system, On your turn you move within a certain circle on the battlefield to approach or get away from enemies and then unleash your combo attacks to ether build upyour EXE gadge for specials, break attacks which lowers the enemies guard bar for extra damage if it's depleted, and simple power attacks for damage. The characters have their own set of combos.
Speaking of the characters, they're fantasic, you have the four Console Patron Units, and Company self inserts, alongside of oneliner joke characters like Maryo and David Snake.
There are several weaknesses in this title however. First of all, level design, the 'dungeon' areas are lazilly constructed and most are carbon copies, like seriously they litterally just copied and pasted the exact same locations with different enemies. Sometimes its nice that you don't have the feeling of, OH♥♥♥♥♥♥BRAND NEW PLACE, but the level design is simply lazy. Of course all the enemies are recolors too, but this is a JRPG, par for the course.
Another problem is localizaton. It's bad, the dub is obsence, we're talking 4kids tier, the translations are censored and oftentimes wrong. I hope Idea Factory International does a better job for next ime becuase the character voices aren't going to improve, they're all set! At least they give you Japanese Voices.
One other thing of note is this game is extremely grindy. As people discoveraround the level 10 mark you're going to have to grind hard. Luckilly the guides on Steam are solid and will assist you in time saving, but there are people who can't stand the grind.
All in all, especially with these weaknesses, if you can feel yourself enjoying the characters and the combat system alongsie of the strong story and the references that abound. I feel like you'll love this game and won't mind the repitiveness of the level desgin. Thus I reccommend it.

When I first started playing HyperDimension Neptunia Re;Birth I wasn’t sure if I liked it or not. The story and character interactions seemed somewhat reminiscent of the Disgaea series.   As I’m a rather large fan that series I was sure that the story would keep me going through the game. But that wouldn’t be enough to make me recommend it to friends.
That first night I put about two hours into the game advancing the story and figuring out the basics of the combat.  The second night I played about four hours and advanced the story. The third night I started doing the mini-quests and messing around with the dangerous enemies in dungeons.  I had about twelve hours in the game at that point I had just finished chapter three and started chapter four.
I’m now thirty hours in and just started chapter five. The story seems to be a little short but the amount of side content is huge.   At this point, I’m very happy with the battle system and still find enemies in the side areas to reasonably difficult however the enemies in the story line dungeons have been trivialized due to my doing side goals for so long that I’ve wound up severely over the level the dungeons are designed for.
The odd part it I didn’t find myself to be grinding the whole time I was collecting drops from gather spots or enemies for items or weapons.  The few times I wasn’t doing that I was trying to do the dangerous monsters to challenge myself.
The Combat in the game is designed really well preventing you from face rolling through enemies unless you’ve really leveled up.  The combat uses a three attack type system divided by break, power, and rush.  Enemies have a guard bar and a health bar while the guard bar is intact they take reduced damage from all sources.  This is where break attacks come in they do minor damage to health in exchange for dealing high damage to the guard bar.  Power attacks are the opposite they do a great deal of damage to the hp but almost no damage to guard. The rush attacks focus on building the EXE gauge which deals with finishes and large damage super attacks.
The game is absolutely a blast for me and I wish that I had heard of the Neptunia series sooner.  I highly recommend this game to anyone that is interested in it.  It also has plenty of references.  “Go Ancient Dragon, I choose you!”
Tl;dr The game is a blast but it’s easy too get lost in side content and make the story content to easy.  Totally recommend this game for anyone that enjoys comedic story’s like Disgaea or games with some depth to the combat system.

Mirror's Edge managed to be a paradox: a pleasant surprise and a complete disapointment.
To explain:  The first hour or two of MIrror's Edge is extremely unique, engrossing, and fun.  Parkour is the central theme as you run around the city on the roof tops, climbing up walls, and making ridiculous jumps.  That's cool, it's great.
Unfortunatly the fun doesn't last.  Very quickly, Mirror's Edge descends into repitition and uncreative solutions.  The way that you solve puzzles and traverse the landscape in the first thirty minutes is the EXACT same way you solve puzzles and traverse the landscape for the rest of the game.  The scenergy changes but the gameplay never manages to diversify.  Everything becomes a slog as you perform the same jumps and runs as you did before.
On principal, Mirror's Edge offers exciting gameplay you just dont see a lot.  In practice, it needs a lot of work both in options it gives the player and level design before it becomes a good game.
I would like to see the formula executed right, but sadly that just isnt this game.

Personally, I really enjoy this game. Admittedly, it has its down-sides but its pros outweigh the cons and I would recommend this game to anyone.
I found that this game is fun whether you are playing alone or online. I completed the game twice on my own and tend to mess around and do side quests with friends and people online. I completed all the missions, got all the weapons and played for hours just just jumping from rooftops onto unsuspecting zombies who subsequently got decapitated. However playing online either with friends or strangers is fun whether or not you talk to each other or not. I played this game, with three other people, for four hours straight, not talking to them but instead listening to music and I still had a blast with them. Playing with friends who you can talk to really is one of the great joys of this game, especially when random stuff happens with causes you to laugh uncontrollably.
However, it has to be said that a few things in this game either just don't make sense or don't seem to me like creative game design. For example, the first quarter of the main story missions in this game are basic fetch quests that don't really amount to anything apart from allowing you to learn the map and learn how to deal with zombies. The game does pick up after this though and soon you're doing missions that actually seem to have a point, especially when you enter Old Town. Furthermore, the weapons at the beginning of the game are too weak to kill even one zombie without your character running out of breath. The zombies at the beginning of the game take around 10 hits to the head to die, however this mechanic does almost force you to use one of the games' main selling points to traverse the map; parkour.
In the late game, it's a joy to run around both the Slums and Old Town, drop kicking, slicing and stabbing each and every zombie you see. You will rarely use guns in this game but they are fun when you do use them. Although landing a headshot is basically the only way to one-shot the standard zombies, the rest of the infected types can survive a fair whack of shots before going down, the only types exempt from this are probably the Viral and the Toad.
The zombie types; the zombies, Virals, Goons, Toads, Boomers, Demolishers, Volatiles, Screamers, Bolters, Bombers and the Night Hunter. Most of these are pretty original apart from the zombies, Virals, Toads, Boomers and Demolishers which feel oddly stolen from other zombie games, such as Left 4 Dead. However, the other zombie types are creative and each require a different tactic to deal with them, which I like. The Night Hunters are people online who join your game through the Be The Zombie mode. I really like these Night Hunters, however I feel unless its an experienced player who has invaded your game, or you're playing alone, the Night Hunter is at a huge disadvantage as the players can drain its power with the UV flashlight, then it only takes a few hits to die.
The characters in this game are mostly one-dimensional and I never really felt any attachment to any of them. From the get go, I already knew a character who was going to die and what the main plot twists in the game were going to be, so I wasn't shocked when these things eventually happened. I'll give it to this game, there were two characters that I didn't expect to die from the start, although for one character, this became very obvious eventually.
The night gameplay was terrifying in the early game as you couldn't do anything to stop the pursuing Volatiles. But in the late game, you could eventually fight them off. I know most of the weapons I use can one-hit the Volatiles if i hit them in the head. This took away the terror for me as they don't damage me much either. If the volatiles' attacks became more damaging and they had more health, then maybe I would once again sprint for a Safehouse whenever it got to 21:00.
I have the Season Pass for this game and so I have all the DLC. My favourite is the Bozak Horde as I enjoy the tense, fast-paced running that is required throughout. The Bozak Bow that you get for completing all twenty trials and the special bows you get for completing them in a certain amount of time are fun to use too. However, the other DLCs are either useless or too easy. I haven' t found much use for either of them, except for loot farming in the Cuisine and Cargo quarantine zones.
I believe this review of this game has gone on long enough and, although many people will not even see it, I enjoyed writing it. I would recommend this game to anyone but especially if you have friends to play with. The mods in this game are fun too, as mods always are. Mods do stop you playing with people online unless they have the same mods installed. Overall, I would give this game an 8/10 as it is very fun to play by yourself or others. Slaughtering zombies is fun and the different zombie types make for interesting gameplay.

If nothing else, a very unique game.
I certainly enjoyed playing it, and my experience in parkour only made it better. The only thing I'd say wasn't true about it was that it seemed to use wallruns as a way to get higher, which is unfathomably difficult, if at all possible. Other than that, everything certainly felt right, right down to scrambling at the wall when you don't reach the ledge.
Certain parts were very frustrating to me, but rarely because of a flaw in level design. More often, there'd be a chance glitch that'd leave me helpless to do anything, or an occasional overpowered enemy. (I'm looking at you, tazer guns.) I was able to get past the latter by telling myself it's probably what would actually happen, except for the second-to-last huge combat section, which left me fuming.
The story is nothing incredibly special, though I will say that it's not one of the over-saturated kinds. In parkour-related media, though, it seems to be an easy out. Essentially: big-brother type future, traceurs act as couriers. It did bug me that they were using wireless technology to communicate, especially since it's a main plot device.
I found it interesting that they chose all of the main characters to be female, where most of the supporting roles were male. It's nothing I would change; for the kind of things Faith does, it's definitely more believable as a woman. It was also nice to see no hint of romantic subplot.
Overall, a wonderful game, despite the glitches making it feel more indie. The combat system, while frustrating, was decently tuned, and it was gratifying to disarm enemies. As for the parkour aspect, just next to spot-on. The Runner Vision was a nice touch, not to mention the jargon made for the world that helped so much with the immersion.
tl;dr: Great game for non-traceurs, and certainly agreeable to traceurs. The combat sections were whack, though.

Child of Light is a warm dreamlike, sugar coated, fuzzy and light game about a princess that does stuff. You'll get no spoilers from me. The game is easy to play, easy to pick up, easy to get into, and a joy to explore. As I am writing this I haven't finished the game. But I wanted to write it since it is on sale and maybe many of you are on the fence about it.
Graphics
Like a warm fire on a cold winter day. This game shows you a world where its ok to lean back a little and smile. The use of color and the smoothness of the animation, gameplay, short cutscenes and overall world are fantastic. Everything looks like a childrens book. And that is a fun and happy place to be.
Gameplay
It feels like there are almost two games here. In one you lazily float around in the world and collect items. You get to see all the cute buildings in the sky and solve increasingly difficult puzzles. And in the other game you have a turn based rpg. Where you can costumize your team of characters (via skill trees) and have an influence on their equipment. The combat is fast paced and fun. There is room in it to improve and really become quite good at it. Overall the gameplay is enjoyable and there really is more game than you think there is at first glance.
Sound

The rhyming way the story is told really does make you feel like youre in a childrens book and further engages you in the world. DETOUR is a real-time highway-simulator strategy-game developed by Sandswept Studios. The objective can be summed up as
. DETOUR gets increasingly complex with weapons, buildings, and opposing AI or Human Players (in Multiplayer).
You work for a construction company over seen by
. I can't actually remember that guys name, I just know he sure looked like bob the builder, but wasn't friendly at all.
As you progress through the game you are faced with different NPC's who are competing with you to get their trucks across the finish line. Sometimes they're all facing the same direction, other times you're pitted head-to-head with 3 NPC's against you.
DETOUR itself starts out very simple, and attempts to teach you the basic concepts as you play through, although the explanations are quite wordy and I concluded “I'll learn the hard way, I don't feel like reading”.
As in most real-time strategy games, you reach a point where you can no longer click fast enough to compete, so you need to learn the keyboard shortcuts to keep up with the other players/AI. Unfortunately the keyboard short cuts are 1234567890 and some of the “F1-F2-F3-etc.” keys.
There are four categories of “build-able” objects; Roads, Trucks, Weapons, and Buildings. Roads are are used to cross different map terrain. Various truck upgrades can be purchased to speed up or defend your trucks. Weapons can be used to destroy, or impede other players/AI progress. And Buildings are limited but you can build ground turrets, air turrets, satellites and more.
Multiplayer can be challenging and fun, however getting to that point is a whole new kind of headache. Naturally there are connection problems depending on the physical location of the person you're playing with, but just trying to CONNECT to that persons game can take nearly five minutes. And then sometimes you might get disconnected from that persons game.
Not to mention you need to probably arrange a game with a friend, since there aren't enough people playing the game that you can just drop in and play with a random person.
Now we come to my biggest complaint about this game... the achievements are painfully tedious. There are 28 achievements in DETOUR. After beating the game for the first time I had literally 4 achievements.
Most of the achievements in DETOUR are actually
unlocked in multiplayer mode. And none of them are quick unlocks, you need to coordinate with 3 other people for some achievements, but a handful of achievements can be unlocked with just another person (1 vs 1 matches).
DETOUR is priced at $4.99, for an indie game that's a pretty fair price. I personally like to spend one hour in game for every dollar, that will easily show up on my game time, because... ...unfortunately connecting to a 4 player game requires about five minutes of restarting and reconnecting DETOUR.
The single player campaign will take about an hour or two, depending on how good you are at strategy games.
Story: irrelevant – I didn't feel like reading the day I did the campaign.
Gameplay: the core mechanics were mostly solid, but there were graphical errors, and multiplayer connection problems. Achievements: Agonizingly long to work on these and un-soloable. Not an easy 100% completion game. Price: the price is a little high for how much time the average player will spend on the game.
All in all, DETOUR has a number of flaws and I haven't particularly enjoyed playing it. That probably means most “normal” people won't like playing it. However if you're looking for a game to play with a friend, this will give you several hours of entertainment, and even more hours of connection problems.
I recommend this game to Indie-Game Supporters, Strategy-game-fans, and achievers who aren't daunted by several hours of coordinating with others to obtain 100% completion.

Everlasting Summer at first glance seems like your typical Japanese dating simulator that you supposedly play for the "plot." At first, I'll admit, I downloaded this free to play visual novel for that "exact" reason, however, I was in for a major treat.
With there being 13 alternate endings one can achieve in their playthrough of Everlasting Summer, there are various turns the story can take depending on your decisions. I really had no clue the changes could be so drastic until after my first playthrough in achieving Semyon's bad ending. I was intrigued by the fact that the story could end in a different way, so I consulted a walk-through guide taking you through which decisions lead to which routes. I straightaway noticed the difference in outcomes once I made a different (seemingly un-)major decision and was positively delighted when I finished with a
different ending than my initial one.
So far, I have completed 4 of the possible 13 alternate endings and I will definitely continue to discover the other endings and, in turn, discover and understand the characters on a truly deeper level. The feels I got from a certain ending (not telling which) truly inspired me in terms of game development. This is what video games should be: interactive stories that parallel those of books and movies. That is what I truly believe the gaming industry is moving toward: becoming a media to convey deep stories on par with those of great literary works and blockbuster hits, and Everlasting Summer is a fine example of that.
tl;dr: I would pay to play this free to play game, download it.

What is there to say about The Banner Saga?
It's near-perfect for one. The visuals are wonderful 2D Disneyesque paintings. The soundtrack, though somewhat sparse, really hits home when it's allowed to shine.
The real pillars of game design, though, story and gameplay, are what really holds the thing together.
The gameplay is split between dialogue choices, travelling supply management, and turn-based tactical skirmishes. The skirmishes are masterfully done, although a bit easy for strategy veterans like myself (still haven't played the game on very hard, though). The travelling sections are what caught me, I'd almost always go for days, sometimes weeks, without supplies, watching clansmen and soldiers fall left and right. Really, though, there are very few consequences for it, besides a last stand segment near the end where your warriors slowly tick away buying time for you to do things. It felt both forced and pointless, and while it helped my immersion early on, I realized that it didn't matter about midway through the game.
The dialogue ties in more with the story, which is a mix of Walking Dead style branches and convergence (some things will happen no matter what you do) and meaningful decisions. There was only one point in the game where I felt one of the plot trees failing, and you'll know it when you get there (although it can also be skipped around with some finagling.)
As for the story bits you can't control? Feels.
Too many feels.

Damn it all, this game has brought out my inner weeaboo. Other than the anime style though, all in all a great well rounded, fun RPG. Stunning looking special moves, awesome HDD Transformations (Basically Mega Evolutions), no overly complicated battle interface, simple as you have a certain area that is shown that you can put damage into, how you aim it depends on whether or not you will take out 1, or take out 5. Story is compelling, full of comedy, puns, and many MANY references. Fun Plan system which lets you alter the game however you like. Enemies too hard? Use the Plan system to weaken them and give you a little edge. Enemies too weak for your tastes? Turn that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥up to 11 with the Plan system. The Plan system is basically like built in mods, that you unlock over time. You like character customization? Boom, there are different outfits for all the useable characters that not only change their clothing, but their hair color and eye color...... Ok I will admit it's not the BEST character customization, but it's still fun in it's own aspects. The game has a great leveling system too, each new dungeon you enter obtains enemies that are not only stronger, but actually give out enough more exp than the enemies in the last dungeon that you don't hit a ceiling, and end up having to spend a good amount of time to gain just 1 level. An example of this is, you need to gain a total of 40,000 Exp to level up, the enemies at the most recent dungeon give out around 2,000-3,000 Exp per battle. At most takes about 10-15 minutes to level up your characters. (Did I mention as long as they are in your party and are alive, they all gain equal experience? It's like Exp. Share from Pokemon, but actually an EQUAL share. Cool right?) All in all I'd give this game a 10/10, Great, compelling, comedic, all around amazing story along with a great battle system and cool looking special attacks and HDD Transformations, with great plot development, fun and challenging boss fights, tons of references from titles such as Pokemon, Space Invaders, (an anime that has a contract signing little pink thing, I forget the name of it), comedic stereotypes, and a fair share of fourth-wall breaks, leaves this game as a must buy game for almost anyone! Definitely my new absolute favorite JRPG game. I've had it for barely a day and a half, and I already have 18.3 hours spent into this beauty. 10/10 would recommend, definitely worth the price. 10/10 would binge-play this game.

Detailed review (May include spoilers)
South Park: The Stick of Truth (TSOT) is a turn-by-turn combat role-playing game based on the Comedy Central TV show South Park. The game was developed by Obsidian Entertainment and South Park Digital Studios and published by Ubisoft. The game was met with its fair share of delays but finally made it to players hands on the 6th of March 2014.
You play as the New Kid (who Cartman gives the name:
) who was just moved to South Park leaving behind a mysterious life which is later revealed in the game. You've moved in and head outside to find Butters battling another boy. You meet Butters who introduces you to the Kingdom of Kupa Keep (abbreviated to
) consisting of the main characters Cartman, Kenny and Butters.You choose a fighting class
and have your first fight and get your first look at The Stick of Truth. But quickly after you are introduced to the town and Kupa Keep the enemy team, The Elves consisting of Stan, Kyle and Jimmy, attacks and takes The Stick of Truth. From there you'll get thrown into the most random story line with
and so much more that will keep you entertained for hours and hours. Any South Park fan should have this game! It's pretty much a must have for any South Park fan!
Although just because of the great story line it doesn't mean it is without flaws. The turn-by-turn combat aspect of the game is used way too much. I get it's the main aspect of the game but it does get boring after a while. But there are bits thrown into the turn-by-turn combat sessions that will really catch you by surprise. Controls will also get pretty complicated and the hotkeys will be forgettable. I always find myself hitting the inventory button just the access the quest book because I forgot the hotkey.
Another main issue that will greatly affect how to experience TSOT is the censorship in some areas. I live in Australia and a big chunk of the scenes in a certain part got censored. You'll find the same censorship in Europe and more parts censored in Germany. Not sure about anywhere else. But thankfully someone has created a patch you can download to get around the censorship which worked perfectly for me (I did get a few visual glitches with cut scenes after installing the mod but I'm not 100% certain it was caused by the mod). It's pretty much a must have if you get this game. Just Google "South Park The Stick of Truth un-censor" or something along those lines and you'll find it.
But there are so many great things about this game that the flaws can be overlooked. I love this game and if you have the money (you should probably wait until a sale to get it though since the price is pretty steep) and a good sense of humor you should absolutely get the game!

Even for a visual novel, there's very few options to really choose which path you take through it. Honestly, your character keeps asking himself to make choices but makes them for you. Because of that it's really hard to get into.
On the plus side, the images on screen change fairly often to reflect the things happening in the dialogue. Not sure how I feel about the mature warnings I'm seeing in other reviews. Guess we'll see when I get there.
The whole thing seems very abstract. You're left hanging with no real plot to grab ahold of. No traction in the story. If mysteries compel you to read forward, this is probably for you. The art is very simplistic to say the least, and there's a decent amount of music invilved it seems.
Verdict: Considering it's free to play there's no reason NOT to recommend this title to people who are fans of visual novels. It's really the only reason I'm playing it, because it's free. It seems interesting, but slow going with no real plot, and many missed opportunities to allow you to make decisions for yourself. As usual, your character is some introvert idiot with no grasp/ concept of the situation. Unlike other visual novels though, your character uses big words showing some signs of intellect. Play at your own risk of wasting your time though.

Dying Light is the follow up game to Dead Island from the polish developer Techland, but will it be worth your time ?
Dying Light puts you in the shoes of Kyle Crane a GRE operative sent into the Turkey city of Harran to find a man named Rais who is a political figure gone rogue who has a file that could destroy the GRE. When you arrive there you find yourself fighting against Rais and helping other survivors led by Brecken.
The story is this games biggest weakness. The story is beyond horrific, with much of the plot holes not making much sense. Not to mention throughout the game you meet a lot of characters and the game expects you to be emotionally attached to them in the more emotional moments in the game. But that is impossible when the characters you meet are incredibly stupid. Almost all the characters are useless and you find yourself not caring for any of them.
The gameplay is amazing and is  a massive step up from the previous Dead Island titles. The combat is way smoother and not as clunky as the combat in Dead Island. But of course the biggest reason this game is so huge is the parkour system. You can free run and climb up everything you see and it all works perfectly. It's incredibly fun just to take time off of doing main missions and just explore Harran at your own pace. The game also has a day and night cycle where during the night it's pitch black and more dangerous zombies emerge out of the dark corners of Harran. Early in the game night is the most frightening thing in the game as the zombies become stronger and faster.
Graphics are top notch, everything looks outstanding maxed out, both the city and the slums are designed really well to fit the fast paced action of the game.
The CO-OP is also a big feature in the game, but it feels kinda out of place with this game. Every character is Kyle Crane and it sort feels out of place. Not to mention the Prologue and the end game are both played Solo only so don't expect to jump into CO-OP straight away.
The "Be the zombie" mode is also quite interesting. It's pretty fun to play as the zombie and it's also quite intense to fight the zombie as well. But there is a massive problem with this mode. It's incredibly hard to find a game, because as soon as you join a game the host drops out. But there is an awesome reward if you beat your opponent.
The soundtrack is beyond amazing. The soundtrack is awesome 80's synth music and makes you feel like a zombie movie like Dawn of the Dead and some great movies from John Carpenter.
I played the game CO-OP from the start. To complete every main quest, side quest and every quarantine zone took me 23 hours. After finishing the game you can always go back and explore Harran. There are also a lot of parkour challenges around the entire city so you can go play those. Not to mention the "Be The Zombie" mode, there is a ton to do in the game so you can expect hefty amount of play time.
The game ran smoothly from start to finish. Never dropping any frames whatsoever, so if you have a strong rig, you shouldn't experience any issues. But there are still a ton of bugs, but nothing game breaking.
Dying Light is a great game and a major step up from Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide. While the story is horrific the game is fun enough to play through at least once.
Final Rating:
8.5/10 - Worth Purchasing

XCom is a tough nut to crack.
If you suck, it will not hesitate to laugh at you, mock you, and kick you in the ribs. It will make you hurt and it will not let up. You are XComs ♥♥♥♥♥.
But if you're good? XCom will still laugh at you, but it will be less derisive, and between the screams of Berserkers who totally got rope-a-doped back and forth by two Assaults.
In short, XCom is that rare game that manages to be really hard, but does so without a lot of unfair loading of the die or stacking of the deck. If you lose, it's because your placement was poor, or you didn't utilized the right troops, or you took for granted the Low rating for an abduction. Highly recommend, and I'd have to give it a 9/10. A solid, strict, and fun game that, as much as it pisses me off, is great fun all the same.

I just polished off The Deadly Tower of Monsters.  The premise is simple:  You are watching a VHS of an old low budget 50s pulp sci-fi B movie while the director records the commentary for the DVD release.
You control the characters (leading man, space woman who has never seen a man, robot) through a sort of 3D action-shooter-platformer, complete with VHS video artifacts, cheesy sci-fi soundtrack, and the director commenting on the actors, the filming, and the oddities that don't make any sense (like how player deaths were just footage accidentally left in, or how much the prop guy hated having to re-build all of the crates that got smashed.)  The gameplay was fun, challenging at times, but not really tough on normal difficulty.  There were optional collectibles, weapon upgrades, basics skills, and special abilities.  The story has you climbing a massive, massive tower that goes from ground level to orbit, and at any point you can look down and see the entire thing, or even jump off and fall all the way down to any point you'd been at previously, landing with your trusty jetpack at the last second (and you could always teleport back.)
They pull off the B movie schtick brilliantly.   The VHS effects really work, and the look is spot-on.  The 'monsters' you fight are obviously guys stuck in a rubber suit, and if anything flies you can clearly see the wires.  When larger monsters appear, they're animated in such a way that they look like the were filmed using stop-motion photography.  You carried two melee and two ranged weapons from a large selection, all typical fun sci-fi nonsense (including one blaster that was obviously an electric razor, and one gun that was a small vacuum.)
My only real complaints were that the last chapter's narrative kind of went off the tracks, and that some of the special abilities were never really communicated to the player (I still don't know exactly what the big bubble thing that everyone had actually did.)  It was a little too easy at times, but again, I played on normal.  It was still tough enough that boss fights required some effort, but never to the point of being dull or frustrating.  It was the perfect length for that, too, being maybe 4-5 hours.  Any longer and it would have gotten tedious, but it was fine for that length of time.
Not a perfect game, but a ton of fun and a great setting.  Maybe a 7.5/10.

There is a lot to love about this game. The art is beautiful, the story is enchanting, the combat is solid though improvable.

In that light it doesn't look so pretty anymore, and the story isn't one, it's a fragment, in the middle of a much larger story that is hinted at but never explored. In light of the sudden ending, some game mechanics actually stop making sense (which is to say, everything to do with travel is ultimately pointless cause the pros and cons you're supposed to weigh turn out to be irrelevant to the story and you could always have chosen one way and been better off for it).
While this is a beautiful game still, it's half of one at most, and the sudden end is just heartwrenching in so many ways. I can't recommend anyone buy this with a good conscience. As much fun as you might have along the way, it'll only leave you unsatisfied.

Dying Light is the follow up game to Dead Island from the polish developer Techland, but will it be worth your time ?
Dying Light puts you in the shoes of Kyle Crane a GRE operative sent into the Turkey city of Harran to find a man named Rais who is a political figure gone rogue who has a file that could destroy the GRE. When you arrive there you find yourself fighting against Rais and helping other survivors led by Brecken.
The story is this games biggest weakness. The story is beyond horrific, with much of the plot holes not making much sense. Not to mention throughout the game you meet a lot of characters and the game expects you to be emotionally attached to them in the more emotional moments in the game. But that is impossible when the characters you meet are incredibly stupid. Almost all the characters are useless and you find yourself not caring for any of them.
The gameplay is amazing and is  a massive step up from the previous Dead Island titles. The combat is way smoother and not as clunky as the combat in Dead Island. But of course the biggest reason this game is so huge is the parkour system. You can free run and climb up everything you see and it all works perfectly. It's incredibly fun just to take time off of doing main missions and just explore Harran at your own pace. The game also has a day and night cycle where during the night it's pitch black and more dangerous zombies emerge out of the dark corners of Harran. Early in the game night is the most frightening thing in the game as the zombies become stronger and faster.
Graphics are top notch, everything looks outstanding maxed out, both the city and the slums are designed really well to fit the fast paced action of the game.
The CO-OP is also a big feature in the game, but it feels kinda out of place with this game. Every character is Kyle Crane and it sort feels out of place. Not to mention the Prologue and the end game are both played Solo only so don't expect to jump into CO-OP straight away.
The "Be the zombie" mode is also quite interesting. It's pretty fun to play as the zombie and it's also quite intense to fight the zombie as well. But there is a massive problem with this mode. It's incredibly hard to find a game, because as soon as you join a game the host drops out. But there is an awesome reward if you beat your opponent.
The soundtrack is beyond amazing. The soundtrack is awesome 80's synth music and makes you feel like a zombie movie like Dawn of the Dead and some great movies from John Carpenter.
I played the game CO-OP from the start. To complete every main quest, side quest and every quarantine zone took me 23 hours. After finishing the game you can always go back and explore Harran. There are also a lot of parkour challenges around the entire city so you can go play those. Not to mention the "Be The Zombie" mode, there is a ton to do in the game so you can expect hefty amount of play time.
The game ran smoothly from start to finish. Never dropping any frames whatsoever, so if you have a strong rig, you shouldn't experience any issues. But there are still a ton of bugs, but nothing game breaking.
Dying Light is a great game and a major step up from Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide. While the story is horrific the game is fun enough to play through at least once.
Final Rating:
8.5/10 - Worth Purchasing

WARNING: Do not play this game unless you have watched up to Game of Thrones Season 3 fully, it contains heavy spoilers and NO spoiler warnings!
With that out of the way:
Very engaging and game of thrones-esque storytelling. It's also very suspenseful knowing that you literally are playing the game of thrones, so you either win ... or die, and dying does not necessarily = game over. Quite mature and well thought out. Episode 1 definitely sets up some epic sh*t for the future episodes.
Beware, if you don't know about Telltale Games, it is basically a really long interactive conversation cut scene, with little to no combat (which is limited to basic QTE's), which I usually dislike, but if you enjoy the drama and conversational nuance in Game of Thrones, then this is the perfect platform for a GoT game for you. In fact, I'd argue it might have been even better game design to leave some of the action QTE's out.
Best Game of Thrones game out so far, which doesn't say much, if you know how bad the others are, but if you like Game of Thrones and appreciate the drama aspect, then you should definitely play this. Also, my favourite Telltale Games, although I may be biassed due to my love for GoT.
SPOILERS FOR THE STORY
*****************************
I felt the story (mine may differ from yours) was redeemed by the "celebrity" cameos (especially Cersei and Ramsay Snow) and the very GoT-esque twist at the end. I felt the main characters you control were lackluster and almost generic, and the really potentially interesting characters (Lord Gregor Forrester, Rodrik, Asher etc.) are either absent temporarily or permanently.
I feel the replayability and effect your choices have, as well as the great scenes with the cameo characters (Cersei and Ramsay Snow) really save the game, and luckily it looks as though (Ep. 2 preview) it's only only gonna get better, and I can't wait.

I can honestly say that this is the best game I have ever played, the brilliant map generation and effective AI make every game a new experience. The base game is fantastic but cannot compare to the masterpieces of Gods and Kings and Brave New World, the DLC for Civ V introduces a new level of gameplay that gives you more control and more options on how to manage a civilization, and destroy your opponent’s. Being able to play against your friends is amazing, the challenge is no longer against an AI that you cannot reason with but against an opponent that understands the fundamentals of the game and responds to them and your actions in a way that makes it feel like you are indeed guiding a civilization in a complex world. But... if you thought it was going to be that easy you are wrong. The multiplayer in Civ V is the most poorly coded element of any major game I have ever encountered. A game with 3 or more human players is guaranteed to crash/resync/devour your soul on a regular basis. But I still play it because once again this is not only the greatest strategy game of all time but one of the most entertaining things money can buy. With the recent release of Civ VI I can only say that this game will go down in history as a revolutionary game that will undoubtedly stand the test of time.

As soon as the title sequence of castles and cities rising over the map of westeros happens, I'm hooked.  I admit I am shamelessly a huge fan of the books and HBO series (I even own the "World of Ice and Fire book".  That is one the games biggest strengths and weakness.  There is no introduction to the source material, in fact if you don't want it spoiled for you don't play this game!  I repeat, do not play this game!  However, if you are a fan there is much to enjoy about this game.  I've also played Telltale's Walking Dead series and this game is really no different, well written characters, tough decisions, quick time fights, and countdown timers.  The first episode is a little slow and lacks the emotional impact that WD had, but I imagine things will pick up as the series progresses.  You can tell Telltale lovingly recreated the look and feel of the HBO series, and I was blown away by the use of vioce actors from the series.  The characters are very interesting, and I love the new location of Ironrath.  I was a little dissappointed to see that the Forrester family seems to be a bit of a rip off of the Starks.  There are enough differences to make me move on.  My other concern is that death needs to make a larger impact in the story, what I mean is, when I played the WD a death was emotionally jarring for me and the characters.  So far the deaths seem a little meaningless since I barely know them.  I'm hoping this will change as I get to know the characters more.  Overall I am impressed, look forward to what they have instore for us.

Five out of five for this game. XCOM provides a fun and fairly simple strategy game experience that is backed by an amazing and replayable storyline. It's rare to find a game with a good story that you can replay and still have a different story experience. I found myself getting attached to characters and feeling some emotions I haven't felt since I went through the Mass Effect series. Aside from a great story experience that allows you to save the world the way you feel is best, the gameplay is really fun. It's simple enough that you won't get confused, but fun and versatile so you won't get bored of it. The campaign progression (research, mission choices, etc.) is like a game in itself outside of combat. You have to strategize on and off the battlefield to be succesful in this game. My only complaint deals with the multiplayer. Playing against friends with teams you've customized is a blast, except for when the game freezes or glitches in some other way. I've only had this happen in multiplayer and it's not a huge issue, just one worth mentioning. If you see this game on sale, snatch it up, because this game is a great investment even at full price.
