XCom is a tough nut to crack.
If you suck, it will not hesitate to laugh at you, mock you, and kick you in the ribs. It will make you hurt and it will not let up. You are XComs ♥♥♥♥♥.
But if you're good? XCom will still laugh at you, but it will be less derisive, and between the screams of Berserkers who totally got rope-a-doped back and forth by two Assaults.
In short, XCom is that rare game that manages to be really hard, but does so without a lot of unfair loading of the die or stacking of the deck. If you lose, it's because your placement was poor, or you didn't utilized the right troops, or you took for granted the Low rating for an abduction. It's rarely, if ever, because the game gave you the top 5% of a 95% hit chance, or because an alien wandered right into your LZ on their first time and scattered into flanking positions.
Highly recommend, and I'd have to give it a 9/10. A solid, strict, and fun game that, as much as it pisses me off, is great fun all the same.

Child of Light is a bit of a rarety on steam, for several reasons.
1st, it needs you to install some third party pseudo platform from ubisoft. If that's a sticking point for you then don't read any more, because the rest of the review is quite positive.
2nd, its kinda in the realm of a visual novel, but without any of the drag along standards that keep visual novels geared towards older teens. If you want a story driven game that you could relax while letting your kid brother play at your grandma's house, here you have one.
3rd, this is a short and easy game. Not that this is bad, just different. None of that "Hours into a dungeon and still no save point." The whole game took me just over 12 hours on casual setting. There is something to be said for an easy dungeon that is just long enough to chew that last piece of rhyming dialogue, before the next one.
Graphics are top notch, though it is getting rare to see a new game that graphics aren't awesome in. Still worth mentioning, because its not about detailed realistic graphics that a hudred people coded together in a secret room any more. Instead what makes graphics shine is grabbing onto an artistic vision and being true to it throughout the game, which Child of Light definitely does gorgeously.
The music is okay, at least what there is of it. It felt a couple of times like they ran out of funding for their orchestra only 30% through the recordings. Some silence here and there, and a couple of somewhat obvious loops.
Personally, I very much enjoyed this game. I really hope to encounter not a sequel, but a series of games based on this style.
Here are the subjective numbers:
10/10 graphics
4/10 music and sound
9/10 story
0/10 first person shooter experience
8/10 game experience
10/10 storybook experience

Simple is the best word to describe this game, but it does so in a way that makes it great.
It's not overly dificult even on expert, but it still has a fresh take on combat in a turn based rpg. It's simmilar to the active time mechanic of games like Final Fantasy 7 but also offers ways to exploit and master it.
The crafting system is made up of combining gems to increase its power and effects. Simple, but effective; it offers more depth than it initially looks as each gem has different effects based on where you equip it.
Some complaints I have with it (besides the Uplay requirement) is the constant rhyming throughout the game; while most of it is fine, some can be a bit jarring to listen to. So if tou get put off by the rhyming then this won't be the game for you. Another thing is the useless DLC almost all of it is just pay real money for crafting gems that you can easilly get in game anyways. Even the golem one which adds a new party member is useless as he is much weaker compared to the rest of the party and won't see much active time in battle.
Like good art, good story, and a colorful cast of characters in your RPG? This is the game for you. Hate rhyming, fairytales, or princesses? best to skip this one.

Let me to start off by stating what's obvious for anyone who played this game for more than a minute: Claiming that this game has anything to do with vikings, the historical viking era, Norse mythology or even anything remotely related to the misconceptions and myths regarding vikings and their religion, is complete BS.
It's like saying that the tv series of True Blood is based on the historical accounts of Vlad Tepes, Bram Stoker's book Dracula or the historical myths about vampires that originated in the Slavic region of the world.
True, The Banner Saga has humanoids depicted with horns, which may be interpreted by some to be Viking helmets. It also has area names that bear some resemblence to Scandinavian regions that existed in the viking era or in the mythological tales, but that's about it. If you expect characters like Odin, the Fenrir wolf, Thor or any events as depicted in Norse mythology or the tales of Snorri Sturluson, prepare to be deeply disappointed as this game's story is a mockery of everything viking.
If you have no interest nor knowledge of the vikings or their mythology, The Banner Saga might be far more enjoyable than it was for me. I like the game mechanics, the graphics, the different characters and how you get to play "both sides" of the story.
I really try to enjoy the game, and I am sure it'd be easier for me to do if the game creators would leave out their horrendous attempt to make it "viking-themed". Unfortunately, it spoils the entire experience for me.

This is not a fun game, this is an experience. The choices you make will be hard, and there's almost never a right one. Thinking about the choices in a video game sense won't help you either. oh you bought all the supplies from a store so you know you'll have food? thieves stole it. The combat is spot on, in some of the best strategy combat I've ever played. It's hard, tight and engaging, almost never will you get through a battle without someone falling. The story is interesting, and you'll find yourself caring for the characters in your party or hating them, especially when they make decisions for you, sometimes even against you. It adds to their personality and makes them feel more like people. This game has an incredibly strong sense of narrative, lose a battle, you'd expect it to just ask "try again?" like most games would, but it doesn't, losing a battle is like making a choice, it will affect what happens to your party, how people treat you, and what decisions you are limited to.
This is not a game for the faint of heart, no because it's scary, or intense but because of it's ability to make you stare at the screen and think "well, what the hell am I supposed to do now?". The game makes you care about this group of people that you control and must lead to survive, going to the ends of the world, or to death.

Detailed review (May include spoilers)
South Park: The Stick of Truth (TSOT) is a turn-by-turn combat role-playing game based on the Comedy Central TV show South Park. The game was developed by Obsidian Entertainment and South Park Digital Studios and published by Ubisoft. The game was met with its fair share of delays but finally made it to players hands on the 6th of March 2014.
You play as the New Kid (who Cartman gives the name:
) who was just moved to South Park leaving behind a mysterious life which is later revealed in the game. You've moved in and head outside to find Butters battling another boy. You meet Butters who introduces you to the Kingdom of Kupa Keep (abbreviated to
) consisting of the main characters Cartman, Kenny and Butters.You choose a fighting class
and have your first fight and get your first look at The Stick of Truth. But quickly after you are introduced to the town and Kupa Keep the enemy team, The Elves consisting of Stan, Kyle and Jimmy, attacks and takes The Stick of Truth. From there you'll get thrown into the most random story line with
and so much more that will keep you entertained for hours and hours. Any South Park fan should have this game! It's pretty much a must have for any South Park fan!
Although just because of the great story line it doesn't mean it is without flaws. The turn-by-turn combat aspect of the game is used way too much. I get it's the main aspect of the game but it does get boring after a while. But there are bits thrown into the turn-by-turn combat sessions that will really catch you by surprise. Controls will also get pretty complicated and the hotkeys will be forgettable. I always find myself hitting the inventory button just the access the quest book because I forgot the hotkey.
Another main issue that will greatly affect how to experience TSOT is the censorship in some areas. I live in Australia and a big chunk of the scenes in a certain part got censored. You'll find the same censorship in Europe and more parts censored in Germany. Not sure about anywhere else. But thankfully someone has created a patch you can download to get around the censorship which worked perfectly for me (I did get a few visual glitches with cut scenes after installing the mod but I'm not 100% certain it was caused by the mod). It's pretty much a must have if you get this game. Just Google "South Park The Stick of Truth un-censor" or something along those lines and you'll find it.
But there are so many great things about this game that the flaws can be overlooked. I love this game and if you have the money (you should probably wait until a sale to get it though since the price is pretty steep) and a good sense of humor you should absolutely get the game!

Before playing this game one must ask themself "Deep within do I want to be a cute little girl who can beat everything up and transform into a no longer cute but voluptuous woman who can rain destruction down onto even the most powerful of foes?" If your answer is anything but "yes" then stop reading. I heard a bit about Neptunia from a friend of mine, but I never gave the game much thought. After being released on steam and looking at the screenshots I knew I had to play it especially since it's a JRPG. In the end I thought this was a very fun game with a charming atmosphere, a good game to play to unwind.
Pros:
There's a fair bit of the game that has voice acting, and the acting isn't really bad (it's only really bad if you look at lipsynching in which case there really isnt any...dialogue trails away from the character's mouth movements)
After getting used to them, the controls can be very intuitive.
Cons:
Button mapping, despite being a PC port of the game it still shows all the buttons of a playstation controller. This took me some getting used to but after rebinding a few keys here and there I was good to go.
The in-between: Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1's level scale felt a bit strange to me. There are points in the game where you can be "underleveled" but take on enemies with great ease, and other times where you can be incredibly "overleveled" and still feel like you're making zero progress.

WHY IS THIS FREE??
The visual novel is very well written, sometimes really surprising and all in all a lot of fun. There are a few flaws in this. A few of the pics are quite low quality, while others (Lenas Route for example) are AAA-material. Nudity, romancing and such are not at all generic and feel quite right. At one point, I thought to myself "yes, finally a protagonist who acts like a normal person!". This game is everything between adorable friendship simulation, philosophical journey into one's soul, juvenile relation drama to straight nightmare game from hell. Getting the girl tends to become a bonus, not the main objective, which for me was seeing all the possible storybranches and outcomes, because they are so interesting and compelling.
So once again: Why is this free? It is a 10h+ experience, and a powerful one indeed. Support this developer in any way, maybe buy the soundtrack from their website, donate to them. I want more quality VNs like this!

This "game" seems like it's an unfinished romance game that only a few of the dozens of choices your character makes got programmed, yet all the story elements from each possible choice were left in the story which unnecessarily muddles the overall tale. The character himself is written like the typical animé teenager that is so annoyingly awkward around girls and unsure of his own feelings (despite any definitive choices you try to make with your few choices as the player) that he only ends up with the girl you choose more or less accidentally.
The fan service is minimal and the "sex scenes" are neither illustrated nor described and given the innocent and naive nature of the character it would have made more sense to simply leave these scenes out entirely, possibly improving the story.
Despite these shortcomings, the story itself isn't bad. Unfortunately the same cannot be said for the interface which requires you to click the mouse or hit a key on your keyboard for each individual line (sometimes a single word) of the several hundred (or possibly thousands) of lines of dialog which really slows the story down. If there were an option to display an entire paragraph at a time or allow you to scroll the text either using the mouse wheel or have it autoscroll at a user defined rate you could enjoy this as an interactive story, but as it stands, anyone with even rudimentary reading skills will find reading the massive amount of text painfully slow.
If the developers ever turn this into a proper romance game or interactive story it could be quite good, but until then give this "game" a miss.

This game is from the Devs of Dead Island, Techland. And if you have played Dead Island, its graphics were AMAZING at the time. And I love Techland for showing me the whole zombie genre. +Very optimizable (AMD R7 250, AMD FX 8320, and 16 GB of RAM, all low settings at 720p, getting 30-47 FPS.)

Update: After 51 hours (Excluding hours I left the game running and didn't play,) got all the Achievements for the Game. I enjoyed this game so much that it's literally the only game I actually bothered to do Achievements for. Also the first Game I actually decided to do the Trading Cards for. This is definitely a great casual Game worthy of many playthroughs.
Really surprised with this title so far (14 hours into the Game at the time of this post.)
The Story is quite... Interesting. It is not your typical straightforward story. The Basic plot is that the CPUs are in the middle of a Console War. Yes, a Console War. This is where your Story starts off. If you can comprehend that and the fact that the game has a lot of 4th wall breaking context to some times insult its players and have wacky dialogue, the Story is for the most part Satirical all the way through, which is very interesting, and I actually like it.
One main piece of advice I can offer to any one interested in Re;Birth 1: I recommend one of two things.
1. Watch the Anime. (The Anime is an adaptation of the Game, and takes place some time after the other games. Main reason I list this is because it's a good way to get used to the Characters, and if you can handle the wacky / cheesy dialogue in the Anime, you'll fit right in for the Game.)
2. Grind. Grind. Grind, and buy Item Upgrades / make the Upgrades VIA Plans at every opportunity they become available.
People say that this Game is pretty easy. Maybe if you played it before it came to Steam, that is understandable, but this Game is by no means easy. It is actually VERY hard / some times frustrating.
The Game runs Eight Chapters. If you are not grinding / purchasing upgrades at every opportunity, you will notice how hard this Game can be when you get halfway through the 2nd Chapter. The other problem is that the Bosses have a lot of RNG to them, where they can either do a Normal hit to you, a Powerful hit that might kill you, or an Attack that hits all of your Party Members in close range, even if they aren't even in front of the Boss. Reviving your Party Members when they get downed is also RNG, because from what i've experienced in my own Playthrough, the Boss likes to immediately attack and kill the person you revive almost 90% of the time before it switches to one of your other party members. If you're coming into this game thinking that you'll blow through it without using Healing items or Game Over'ing at all, you're in for a rude awakening.
Get used to how the Dungeons look in the first two chapters of the Game, because you're going to be seeing them all the way until the End. I can't knock them on this because if you can tell already that the Game doesn't take itself seriously and that it mocks a lot of things, especially in the Gaming world, you could see this as them mocking Games that use the same Layouts constantly.
Soundtrack is also pretty decent, but a lot of areas unfortunately use the same background music way too often. Can't knock this either for similar reasons that I listed for Dungeons.
If you can get past all this, this is definitely a very fun game, albeit very challenging as well. Would definitely recommend to any one that likes JRPGs, and I look forward to the rest of the Series coming to Steam.

After playing over 100 hours of Mirror's Edge, I'll give my opinion and you can take it as you wish.
The game is fantastic fun, but that doesn't mean it's easy and never irritating, it has it's fair share of bugs and infinite tricks and strategies to learn. You can play through the game once and have some fun struggling with parkour, or you can push yourself to learn other tricks and feel fantastic as you blaze through the levels. The levels, even though linear, do require a large amount of focus and memorisation, especially as you increase what tricks you use.
If you play through the game once and feel satisfied, then that's great, but you're missing out on the most charming aspect.
If you enjoy the game and want to enjoy yourself more, then I recommend watching some speedruns, both with glitches and without, and see if you want to pull off mind-warping tricks like they do.
This may be one of the only single player games I will ever play repeatedly because even with it's problems, the payoffs are so big that you feel like a god if you manage them.
tl;dr - The game has glitches, and isn't easy, but with a little bit of time, it can be a replayable experience that promotes constant improvement.

I will be honest, Telltale "games" are not much of games but well crafted enjoyable stories. There really is no choice. The illusion of choice is what is most prevelent. There are no two ways a story plays out, only two "choices" and one outcome regardless. So do not expect a telltale game to every REALLY give you choice that can CHANGE the story. That being said, and taking the game for what it really is, here are my further thoughts
Would I recommend this game? If you love Game of Thrones yes, absolutely. For 6 episodes 30 dollars is reasonable with the first episode ccoming in at around 2 hours long, if you play slow and do everything possible. I really enjoy the stories characters who are well voice acted and engaging. It helps drive the story and you care for your characters and the people who you are playing and "protecting" I still think Wolf Among Us is the best thing Telltale has done and I hoped that GoT would offer ACTUAL CHOICE. Alas it is just another Telltale Interactive story. It does feel a bit rushed, and honestly Telltale can't get away with the Cell shaded "style" forever. They need to create a better engine that looks better and runs better, no blurring, jaggies or other graphical blemishes. That being said its not about graphics or ACTUAL choice its about a well crafted story that is enjoyable to play and experiance.
If you like interactive stories, and well crafted and acted ones at that. Game of Thrones is for you. The series could be one of Telltales best if they start offering more ACTUAL choice and deepen the story which I am sure they will, it can be a fantastic "season" of Game of Thrones.

This game is exactly what i was looking for when i bought it. And sadly enough i love it so much that i HATE it.
Let me start with the positive side. First of all, this is a SOLID RPG. Turn based party combat, and more phat lewt than you can shake a stick at. Every aspect of this game seems to surround you with a very deep level of immersion. The battles are challenging, and rewarding. Now for why i hate this game. The good is in fact what makes it bad. It's deep. Very deep. Right now i play with a moderately tight budget as far as time goes, i might get an hour maybe two occassionally during the week.
First of all equipping, and levelling up/speccing 4 characters for a party can be incredibly tedious.  Especially early on in the game when you are still figuring out what's good, what works, etc. Secondly, I tend to be a very thorough person when it comes to looting, so it is a moral obligation to check every square inch of the region before moving on. The crafting system is brilliant, with more ingredients/recipes than you'll ever be able to try in one playthrough. This being said it is not unusual for me to spend an hour or two crafting with the wiki open on my steam overlay.
All of these things being said, it tends to make the overall game progression seem very slow. Which is why i just cant seem to keep myself focused on the game.
Despite this game not working for me, i still strongly recommend it to any fan of the RPG genre.

"The Deadly Tower of Monsters" is a fun little diversion that banks it all on the player loving the humor and the undeniably well-executed b-movie style just enough to overlook some shortcomings in the design. This certainly did pay out in my case, as I've often found myself enjoying the movie references, the jabs at b-cinema and just the game's overall art direction, which is consistently on point and never truly runs out of ideas, moreso than I did enjoy the actual action. Not to be misunderstood, I had some legitimate fun blasting "stop motion" dinosaurs, underpaid extras in monkey costumes and space alligators, especially with that colorful arsenal of ludicrous sci-fi weaponry, but there's still no denying that "Deadly Tower" is not an excellent action game by any means. The twin stick shooting is a bit bland, the platforming can be utterly atrocious (luckily, there are only three or four rather brief mandatory jumping sections in the game) and the camera can be a nuisance at times. Still, though, the good outweighs the bad, and so I recommend this game to anyone who's looking for some twin stick action with style, especially to those with a knack for old b-movies and low budget sci-fi.

For the complete experience, get both the original and the enemy within expansion.
Although I have personally not played the original game for MsDOS, this game has proven to be a very entertaining remake. From what I have seen, it remains faithful to the original source and includes many new elements that are refreshing to see.
The positive:
-As there are a multitude of tactics to go back and priorities can be mixed up every time, it is easily possible to replay the game whenever you want. Although the maps and some of the crucial missions will stay the same, base building, soldiers themselves and when you get which abductions or other missions changes all the time.
-The difficulty of the game is completely up to you. With 4 different difficulty levels that in between easy or normal vs classic or impossible have a huge difference in how the AI behaves and how cover helps out this is something that I feel is done tastefully. Additionally you can use second wave options to make the game even more challenging. Lastly, for those of you wishing the real thrill of the game, go for ironman mode in which savescumming is combatted.
-The combat is hugely centered around having knowledge and having strategy. From the beginning the odds are against you. The enemies start out with plasma weapons and amazing accuracy as well as mind control abilities. However, when carefully dealt with, you should be able to manage. Additionally, base building itself is a large term project in which you should weigh out how you are going to contruct the facilities to get the bonusses (which you so need on impossible) and when you are able to do so. The game is structured towards having you make critical decisions here.
-There is one particular mission in enemy within that really flips everything on it's head and is the hardest out there. For those of you reading this who have played it, you know which one it is. The key to winning here is to learn how to use the environment, making sacrifices and of course a healthy amount of luck.
The negative:
-While I respect the choice of going for RNG mechanics, the consequences can be rather dire. If you have your veteran soldier die on the field through a critical hit from a distance you have little chance of striking back and part of the squad panicking as a result, it might be over very soon. And while having your top squad die shouldn't be the game over there, you'll be struggling to catch up for the rest of the game. Luckily you have explosives.
-The difficulty of the game isn't linear. It starts out easy enough, then gets significantly harder all the way up towards the point where you almost have laser weapons (or should be having), which hits the hardest part of the game and then it becomes a breeze as soon as you have plasma weapons. The hardest mission in the game is definitely not the last one.
Otherwise, for anyone who likes strategy, I can recommend this game. A popular mod that is raved about on the internet is Long War and as it changes some core aspects of the game, I recommend checking it out as well.

RPG games are my forte, but I do love me a music game.
I define music games in two branches; those that have strict music and those that have freedom. Both have their qualities, and are fairly equal but Beat Hazard Ultra brings something.. new to the table.
Essentially it's a top-down shooter, space themed. Your mission is to shoot enemies - that spawn based on your music, using weapons - that spawn based on your music, combining multipliers - that spawn based on your music, to gain masses of points - that increase based on your music.
The theme here is obvious.
Now many games afford you those kinds of perks(!) already, but BHU has another trick up it's sleeve; Online Co-Op.
It's a great feature that most games these days needs to include, and BHU does it with minimal fuss. Sure, both players need the same music for it to work in most cases, (sometimes they don't? It's a weird system..) but the point is, it has it and it works -damn well-.
A game as challenging as you make it.

I grew up as a kid watching Creature Doube Feature, a weekend show that'd play two horror/sci-fi films back to back.  Of course, most of the movies played came from the 50s 60s and 70s, which is how I came to love Godzilla, the Forbidden Planet, and a host of other B movies.
I saw this game advertised, and thought it looked a little silly.  As I watched the videos, though, I decided it looked awesome; the right blend of self-deprecating humor, action and nostalgia.  I made the purchase - and I'm glad I did.  The running commentary (as you play the game) between the director and the sound engineer recording it is inspired.  The developers/designers put some serious thought into entertaining the gamer, and they ended up making a game I never would have thought I'd enjoy as much as this.
You can play one of three characters, and can switch them back and forth throughout the play-time.  One thing to be aware of is that unlike the weap[ons you pickup throughout the game (which can be used by all characters), the special abilities apply only to the character who discovered them.  It's a tiny inconvenience at worst, but it does give each character more flavor than the differences between the voice actors and some graphics.
There's some overlap between missions/quests and game achievments, which I thought was a bit odd/lazy - but this game is hardly the only one to do that.  While there's action, the game is more of a puzzler than an action/shooter.  I've found that playing on hardmode makes it a good challenge.  The graphics bring the nostalgia to life, and on my system they do the game justice, cartoony lush and fun
I love this game, but I sorta doubt that this kind of genre has legs.  Instead, it has the feel of being original/unique, and something that an imitatation would invariably screw up.
Bottom line: fun and casual and full of references to the kind of stuff I loved as a kid.  Well-worth the purchase :)

Despite the occasionally clunky controls and unruly camera, I can't help it I loved this game.  It legitimately felt to me as though I were playing a B-movie and I as the player was present in the sound booth where the obnoxious director was telling horrifically hilarious anecdotes of his time on the set.  How you will feel will depend on how forgiving you are to a game in which you can kill a claymation Apatosaurus with a lightsaber while the director says he didn't believe the scientists who said they were carnivores.  To me, a few missteps in gameplay and interface are forgivable if the concept is unique, the dialogue is well-written, and it all looks and sounds great.  The Deadly Tower of Monsters isn't a great work of art that will shake the medium of video games for years to come, but if you like meta-humor, hammy actors, and the B-movies of yesteryear, this may be a game for you.  It's a fun romp through a movie I really wish was real, and when you've played it you will wish that too.
Pros:
+ Hilarious writing
+ Great Weapon selection
+ B-Movie Aesthetic
+ Epic feeling of the Tower
Cons:
- Clunky controls
- Erratic camera
- Lackluster survival mode

The Banner Saga is a wonderful game worth being played. The story and lore are rich and entertaining. The game presents many choices for you to make over the course of it, and it feels fluid and meaningful. The combat, at first glance, made worry the game would be hard, but once you get used to the mechanics, it's nothing to sweat over. The combat is fun and rewarding. Sometimes you may be down to the last person in your party with three dredge left and miraculously survive. You just have to be careful not shoot yourself in the foot with your decisions in the combat. But even if you do, it doesn't seem to matter much. You may lose fighters and supplies, which is where you can get messed up if you're not careful. All in all the game is amazing. I enjoyed my eight hours. The only complaint I have is the abrupt ending, like many other reviewers comment on. But it's whatever. The ride was fun. I'd recommend picking it up on sale for $5 to $10. But if you love world-building, Nordic inspired lore, and turn-based combat, maybe the full price would be worth it to you.

I found the combat incredibly difficult and unforgiving which would be ok, normally. I'm a fan of the Dark Souls series so I'm no stranger to that. However, this game doesn't seem to reward you for anything. After a battle or war, win or lose, I never felt I accomplished anything. I always felt I was just sending my fighters into a slaughterhouse. At best, you will get an item for winning a battle. Win or lose, I always felt like I lost. More people died, more people left, more enemies attacked, people betrayed, it just never stops. Near the end of the game, the story starts picking up, important people are introduced, and you feel like maybe you can win. Then, you beat the final boss, people die, and the game just ends.
To conclude, while the game is interesting, the art is beautiful, and the music is phenomenal, it just isn't very well executed in my opinion. This is a game, and I never actually had fun. I always felt defeated.

The cons
- if you don't like a story that involves reading with little to no voice acting, this is not for you
- if you don't like slow paced strategy combat similar to XCOM, this is not for you
- There could be some more customisation options for the characters clothing and weapon designs but it doesn't matter as much

When Killing Floor 2 launched out of early access, it still wasn't worth picking up over Killing Floor 1. The gameplay was refined and changed into a more open run-and-gun style, and KF1 had a wealth of custom maps, skins, enemy types, and just general fun shenanigans that made for a great multiplayer game with your friends.
Over time, Killing Floor 2 has surpassed its predecessor. There are more classes available to switch up your style of gameplay, there is the same breadth of custom maps to try, skins are now customizable accessories for different parts of the player's outfit, new bosses & enemies change up the gameplay, and players can unlock free items by completing rounds or completing daily challenges and weekly challenge mutators. There's just so much to love, and Tripwire gives it all to you free (though you can buy cosmetics if you so choose.)
If you like co-operative shooters—especially wave-based survival games like this—Killing Floor 2 is a blast. The continued support of Tripwire and the community build upon the game tremendously, like the classic PC mods for UT or HL. So if you ever do find yourself tiring of the same old "Please kill them before I'm eaten alive," just come back later and enjoy all the new stuff the game has to offer you.

This first-person platformer game is disappointing. At first glance it appeared to offer interesting gameplay based on parkour, as well as nice artwork, but the implementation leaves much to be desired. Despite the apparent "open world" environment, levels are very linear. Yes, the player character runs on rooftops and inside large buildings in a big city, but the doors, windows, gates, vents etc. are blocked, locked, or just unbreakable, except for a specific path which the player has to find, often while being shot at. There are pipes, crates, planks, and other objects in the environment, but player can't move or otherwise use them to create new paths. There are armed enemies and the player has ability to fight, but combat system is subpar. And yet for some reason the story has the player character frequently go directly into the midst of said armed enemies, particularly in the last few chapters, making the combat system more conspicuously annoying. The lacklustre plot doesn't help either. Would have been better if it has actual "open world" environment, better combat system, and perhaps ability to bypass confrontations altogether (e.g. by sneaking around enemies or creating distractions). Overall, after completing it, I feel that while this game may be interesting when it was first released, it isn't a good use of time and money today.

For the complete experience, get both the original and the enemy within expansion.
Although I have personally not played the original game for MsDOS, this game has proven to be a very entertaining remake. From what I have seen, it remains faithful to the original source and includes many new elements that are refreshing to see.
The positive:
-As there are a multitude of tactics to go back and priorities can be mixed up every time, it is easily possible to replay the game whenever you want. Although the maps and some of the crucial missions will stay the same, base building, soldiers themselves and when you get which abductions or other missions changes all the time.
-The difficulty of the game is completely up to you. With 4 different difficulty levels that in between easy or normal vs classic or impossible have a huge difference in how the AI behaves and how cover helps out this is something that I feel is done tastefully. Additionally you can use second wave options to make the game even more challenging. Lastly, for those of you wishing the real thrill of the game, go for ironman mode in which savescumming is combatted.
-The combat is hugely centered around having knowledge and having strategy. From the beginning the odds are against you. The enemies start out with plasma weapons and amazing accuracy as well as mind control abilities. However, when carefully dealt with, you should be able to manage. Additionally, base building itself is a large term project in which you should weigh out how you are going to contruct the facilities to get the bonusses (which you so need on impossible) and when you are able to do so. The game is structured towards having you make critical decisions here.
-There is one particular mission in enemy within that really flips everything on it's head and is the hardest out there. For those of you reading this who have played it, you know which one it is. The key to winning here is to learn how to use the environment, making sacrifices and of course a healthy amount of luck.
The negative:
-While I respect the choice of going for RNG mechanics, the consequences can be rather dire. If you have your veteran soldier die on the field through a critical hit from a distance you have little chance of striking back and part of the squad panicking as a result, it might be over very soon. And while having your top squad die shouldn't be the game over there, you'll be struggling to catch up for the rest of the game. Luckily you have explosives.
-The difficulty of the game isn't linear. It starts out easy enough, then gets significantly harder all the way up towards the point where you almost have laser weapons (or should be having), which hits the hardest part of the game and then it becomes a breeze as soon as you have plasma weapons. The hardest mission in the game is definitely not the last one.
Otherwise, for anyone who likes strategy, I can recommend this game. A popular mod that is raved about on the internet is Long War and as it changes some core aspects of the game, I recommend checking it out as well.

The western film industry has thrown out old fashioned 2D animation, as if it's the poor girl who puts her heart into her work for overlord Disney but can't seem to bring in the same income as her newer, shinier 3D bunkmate. So it's ironic that 2D has found a new home with videogames, an industry known for almost exclusively working with the same computer animation that got the poor girl kicked out in the first place.
"Oh boy!" said the recently evicted child, "You won't regret this video games industry! I'll work hard to make some of the prettiest games you've ever seen!"
And "pretty" is the best word to describe the hand-drawn "Child of Light", with its gorgeous aesthetic and colourful backgrounds that changes from blotches of dark grays, greens, and blues to intense purples, reds, and yellows.  All of this is magnified by Coeur de Pirate's beautiful soundtrack, which works together with the visuals and sounds to create a wonderful atmosphere that communicates all the wonder, fear, and emptiness without saying a word. And thank the gods for that because the words everyone speaks are structured into rhyming couplets that will either can be ignored at best and painful at worst. I suspect a lot of the game's other problems comes from this gimmick as well.
The story is meant to be a fairy tale, so I wasn't expecting a deep and thoughtful story, though what's there is well paced until the end, when everything starts feeling rushed. The main heroine, Aurora, is transported to the magical land of Lemuria, where she meets a colourful, if a bit shallow, cast of personalities. While Aurora is likable and even relatable at times, she's the only one of gets any sort of development in the whole game which is disappointing because what little is there is still enjoyable. They barely have any dialogue together, obviously because trying to get them all to rhyme makes the whole process twice and difficult and half as enjoyable for the audience. One character in particular later on was especially disappointing. I'm not going to spoil anything, but suffice it to say that the game misses a golden opportunity for a great moment between the character and Aurora near the end.
Besides all that, the gameplay is what glues the whole narrative together, and I must say that Child of Light deserves a big golden star for managing to make the Final Fantasy-esque battle system fun. I've always considered the JRPG's gameplay to be some of the dullest in all of video games behind point-and-click adventure games and paint drying simulators, but Child of Light manages to add some life into the stale, stagnant genre by adding a slowdown and interrupting mechanic. You and the enemy share a single ATB gauge that's split into two sections: waiting and casting; if you manage to hit an enemy while it's in the casting section, it will be pushed back on the gauge, buying you some extra time. The enemy can do this to you, but you can negate this by defending, which also makes your next turn faster. Another thing Child of Light deserves a cookie for: finally making the defend button not translate to "waste time doing bugger all" as you plan for enemy attacks to get in the right position. And that's the magic word: PLAN. When you play on hardcore mode with the speed on maximum (which I highly recommend you do) the battles become more like a strategy game as you predict the enemy attack and measure out your time for buffs, healing, attacks, and defending, optimising your situation by switching out characters to take advantage of each one's special skills. Theoretically, you can beat a horde of enemies without once getting touched if you plan out your fights well enough.
Child of Light has a few problems, mostly regarding its writing, but the spectacular visuals, music, atmosphere, combat system, and charming main heroine are enough to over look most of its flaws. Just keep in mind that you'll need to install UPlay to run this game; also, if you have a laptop with an integrated graphics card and processor, this game will run like absolute♥♥♥♥♥ If you only have a laptop instead of a PC and you still want to play this game, I would suggest getting the console version.

Child of Light tells the story of Aurora, a daughter of an Austrian duke who finds herself transported into the land of Lemuria. She soon discovers her destiny is to recover the sun, the moon and the stars, for she is
Through this tale Aurora groups with a diverse range of characters, each with their own tales and struggles. The land of Lemuria has grown dark, and in this world you fight on in search of your father, who has become ill and is dying. Very few games create such an emotional and memorable experience in story telling quite like this.
Child of Light is a turn-based, role-playing-game that has a strong emphasis on exploration, atmosphere and lore. There is tonnes of collectables hidden throughout the world for you to seek out and collect. These collectables range from crafting materials to additional lore, which alike the game, takes form in beautiful poetic form. Child of Light has beautiful writing, whether it be in cutscenes or in simply talking to NPC's around the world; every piece of dialouge is artistic in every sense of the word.
Few very games can truely be classified as artistic, in recent years it seems that a beautiful game is one that is graphically realistic, this is not the case with Child of Light. This game is far more imaginative and inspired that any game I have played in recent years, and it shows. The art style for this game is very 'child-like', but in a positive way. It compliments the games narrative and atmosphere perfectly from beginning to end. Where Child of Light shines most however, is the soundtracks. From the heart-plucking moments to the up-beat boss encounters, every soundtrack is perfectly conducted and adds an entire new layer to atmopshere that is rarely seen in video games. Any moment a new soundtrack would kick in, I would pause for a moment and just listen. Whilst playing this game, I went so far as to just refuse any distractions that would remove me from the experience; an experience that beautiful, emotional and engaging.
The turn-based combat is also another truimph over games of it's genre, it's fluid, refreashing and requires strategy. In combat, you can control two characters at any given time. There is a bar, split into two sections, the 'wait' period in which all characters in combat will slide towards the 'cast' period at a given rate, depending on their stats. Once each character reaches the 'cast period, you can select a number of actions ranging from switching characters, casting spells, using potions or fleeing. There's a great deal of stategy involved and in many cases, especially boss encounters, the game can be quite the challenge. Once either all your characters are dead, or the two selected and out in combat die, the game is over and you continue from your last save. Battles are a rewarding experience because you're almost always guranteed for at least one character to level up, and from this, you can spend points into generous skill trees that differ from character to character.
Child of Light is a simply amazing experience in every aspect. The lore is emotional and creative, the soundtracks are amongst the best in recent gaming and the gameplay is varied and rewarding. From the beginning to the end, you'll make decisions, you'll solve puzzles and watch Aurora grow on her journey. This isn't just a great game for it's price, it's a great game, full stop. I
urge anyone who is interested in stories, role-playing-games or just looking for something new to pick this up and try experience it.
Child of Light is a masterpiece. Very few games offer such a complete experience in such an inspired form, and honestly, I'm finding it difficult to name a single game I've played, ever, that I've enjoyed as much as the experience on this.

Child of Light is exactly what the creators at Ubisoft Montreal intended it to be. It is a beautiful piece of gaming, with amazing visuals courtesy of the UbiArt engine, a soundtrack that can only be described as haunting, and the storybook tale of a young girl named Aurora, trying to return to her father, an Austrian Duke. The land of Lemuria, where Aurora finds herself, is fantastical and a blast to explore, and all of the dialogue in the land is completely in poetic verse. Every RPG player who has even a little bit of childlike wonder left in them should definitely take the game for a spin. But beware, a fairy tale story is just that: a fairy tale. Don't expect epic character development or combat.
That being said, Child of Light doesn't need to be epic to succeed. Aurora's journey is one of simplicity; she does not wish to defeat a great evil, nor fight for a crown — she simply wants to see her father again. To do so, she must rescue the moon, sun, and stars — apropos goals for this type of adventure. Throughout her journey, she meets plenty of allies who fit the fairy tale mold; a circus performer looking to join her troupe and an anthropomorphic archer mouse who wishes only for the heart of his beloved are some of the first to join the party. Each and every character speaks in a rhyming verse, and while this is certainly engaging to read, I can't help but think that some of the lack of character development comes from the unique structure. While all of the characters have their moments, many seem to lack depth beyond simple quips that carry the meter.
Still, this young girl's journey is one that is worthwhile, and it's backed by some of the best 2D visuals I've ever seen combined with a brilliant score. To say that Ubisoft Montreal has created a visual masterpiece wouldn't be hyperbolic; the watercolor-like portraits and sweeping vistas are complemented by a strong artistic vision. Environments like dark forests and the innards of a giant golem kept me exploring, but I wanted to see what I could do around every corner. Each place Aurora visited made me sit up and listen to the music.
Beauty does come with danger, however, as fire, spikes, and other danger await Aurora as she flits about the 2D landscapes. While Aurora can fly almost immediately upon entering Lemuria, some of the platform elements are frustrating. I've never been a fan of damage or status effects being inflicted outside of battles, something that frustrated me to no end in Bravely Default, and I died without ever entering combat more than once. To be completely fair, some of this was simply a lack of care on my part, but I never felt like these sections provided anything to the journey. Had I simply solved a puzzle or continued along, the experience would have been almost identical.
The combat is more satisfying, with its combination of elements from Final Fantasy X and Grandia. If you've ever picked up GameArts' Grandia games, combat will feel like second nature: a gauge runs the bottom of the screen which displays when characters will act. Once a command is selected, the icon runs through the cast section until execution. Depending on the power or type of attack, the cast time might be incredibly brief or very long, but commands of both friend or foe can be interrupted if they are attacked while casting. In Grandia, timing often felt a bit random, but Child of Light improves it with the use of Aurora's firefly companion, Igniculus. Controlled with the right analog stick (or a second player), activating him on enemies will slow them down, allowing the chaining of interrupts. His power isn't infinite, though; it must be recharged either with items or by moving him to plants that exude energy to absorb.
That's not the only depth in the combat, though, as only two party members can be on the battlefield at any time. When it's any character's time to act, they can swap with another one of the various party members. Elemental weakness is important in Lemuria, so going up against a group of fire enemies means you'll probably want to switch to the characters with water-aligned abilities. The battle system is entertaining enough, though I did start becoming tired of it after a while.
To take advantage of the different elements, planning outside of battle is important. Different gemstones, called oculi, provide unique bonuses and elements when they are equipped, and I made sure to have a character on hand with fire, water, and lightning as their primary attack elements. Some gems have less traditional bonuses, like being able to manipulate the action gauge. Three gems of the same type can be combined to create more powerful versions. This, alongside the three-pronged skill tree for each character, provides enough customization to make each character feel sufficiently unique.
It's very clear just how much care and thought went into the development of Child of Light. It might not be a vanguard experience for fans of the genre, but there's enough depth to keep veterans interested. The charming story lacks a bit of depth, but with enough going on to tug at the heartstrings, it's easy to recommend Child of Light. As long as you can remember a time in your childhood where everything felt new and beautiful, there's an enjoyable experience to be had.

Detour
Construction Multiplayer
Sandswept Studios
Sandswept Studios
is a multiplayer-focused construction game developed and published by Sandswept Studios. This is going to be one of the shortest reviews I've ever written and recorded, since the game is pretty simple to describe.
Really poor graphics: absence of many animations, boring background, poor particle effects and
Your goal is to build a road that goes from one point of the map to the other so that your trucks can travel there, while also trying to destroy the roads built by your adversary. The end. There are multiple objects that you could use, but it pretty much becomes a game of "the one who builds the road first wins", while in the singleplayer challenges you will have little to no problems since the AI is braindead and predictable.
As I've already said, beating the AI is really easy, while in multiplayer you will spend more time using dynamite and hoping that your enemy doesn't notice you rather than using any real tactic.
There aren't many sound effects, and the ones that are there aren't all that polished. The soundtrack is really uninteresting and annoying when playing, and you will find yourself muting it to preserve your sanity.
28 Steam achievements and multiplayer mode will make you come back if you were enjoying the experience. Singleplayer challenges will be beaten pretty easily, but you can try beating your highscores.
Overall, Detour is not a game for everybody: it is very easy when playing solo, and it lacks strategy in multiplayer. I recommend buying it only when on sale, since its price drops a lot. Otherwise, don't buy it.

Little Nightmares is a stygian grotesquerie from the mind’s eye of a madman. Yes, it's so good that I had to whip out my five dollar college educated words to describe it. It’s been quite awhile since I’ve beheld such a perfect dance macabre of creepiness. Something that would send sickly shivers down my spine. Told yah I was gonna use my big words. Well on with the review.
You play a little girl named Six. All she has, it would seem, is a yellow rain slicker and a lighter. Six is deep in the bowels of a vessel called The Maw. You need to get her through it by using stealth and solving very imaginative puzzles. That describes it as a usual puzzle platform, but the Devil is in the details and these details are down right satanic.
Every element of Little Nightmares is fine crafted and they all fit together perfectly to form a beautiful game.Ddetailed artwork creates an early twentieth century nightmare environment. The audio, whether it is music or ambient sound, backs up the landscape perfectly. Even the small touches. The way everything rocks slowly, or the way objects are a bit askew, making it tricky to get about. I loved the little gnomes that scurried around, or when Six stepped on a sponge and it made a squishy noise and water flew out of it. It’s these little things that make it all so very worthwhile. The people are the best. Grotesque caricatures that are just… sick. Filthy cooks that wobble around a garbage dump of a kitchen, picking their noses over the food  is but one example of the horrors that await you.
The puzzles are creative, fun and not too easy. Between solving them and avoiding being killed in a disgusting way by an even more disgusting creature, I had a great time.
The game could have been longer, It took me about 30 hours to play.
Little Nightmares is one of the weirdest games I’ve played in a while. I highly recommend it.

Friends become enemies become friends again in this feverish beat-em-up where you will die the hero, only to see yourself become the villian anyway.
This puts a very unique spin on an already established genre, and it does it in a way that makes it stand out against the rest as an example, a goal for how to change game mechanics while maintaining the fun factor.
HOW IT PLAYS
To start, it plays like Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon in a sense. Instead of shooting, there is hack n' slash combat. That is where similarities end.
When the game start, what happens is a wonderfully crafted, simple yet effective backstory is given as to the 'what and why' of the game. The 4 heroes (up to 4 players or 3 AI) are reduced to 1 while the other players(or AI) now become the spirits. Those spirits are now your enemy.
It is the Hero's job to reach at least hero level 10 and kill the boss, all while surviving the traps and monsters that lurk in the dungeon. To do this, the hero will need to stock up on gear and weapons found in the Blcksmiths shop.
The spirits are tasked with taking down the hero by means of possesing the traps and summoning runes that lay marked on the floor. Those summoning runes turn the spirits into 1 of 3 monsters from their "monster loadout". Once one of them kills the hero, they then take on the role of hero, slayer of ghouls and the fiends they possess.
Throughout the game, the hero levels up and sometimes gets rewarded with gold by finding interactive objects or dealing damage to the hero as sppirits. The spirits on the other hand evolve by earning their own currency gained by causing harm to the hero or when the hero levels up.
It is a fun and rewarding back and forth game that is surprisingly well balanced with no bugs that I have encountered. I bought this game just a few days before I found it was also part of my Humble Monthly quite some time ago. I did not request a refund from steam for my purchase however because this game is easily worth the money I paid. I would recomend this game to anyone who has local buddies (or can play solo) and loves dungeon crawlers.
OTHER THINGS AND STUFF
Things it could improve would be to add online functionality, and more diversity to the level design, although neither is required for this already magnificent game.
Go give the game a chance!
Edit: After spending more time in this game, my review still holds. If anything, I think higher of this game. It is truly something special. They have added more voicework, nee items, a new boss, new mechanics, and new monsters to control. The developers have truly pulled through with this game. Please, go out and play it. It's a hellova good time.

This "game" must not be called a "game".

(This review will be a little longer, as you do no have the time to read it, look for another game. Then this game does not suit you at all... You can try to give a long or short review on Everlasting Summer - but no matter how many words are used for this... it is not possible to describe this the way it deserves)
First of all, I did not know that there even exist so-called Visual Novels (VN, as I heard).
Or to be more precisely, that this is the name for it.
As I read the description of ES, I thought this will be the typical japano-dating-game-style. As a kid I once liked them a lot, but now I would have immediately lost all interest of this game... but thanks to the other reviews.
They were in a way that positive, I was so curious about this game - I had to download it. And this was one of the best decisions in my life!
You are Semyon - a grown-up-man who managed to get into a pioneers camp. In the 80's. You are much younger now - 17 years old - and have no idea how you came there and what you shall do to return to your proper life.
This question is constantly in the narrators mind... but you have not much time to search for answers. In the camp there are other pioneers, always trying to have a talk to you and there is a camp leader which personal slave 24/7 you seem to be. Quite annoying, huh?
My first opinion while playing this game was like "what the ?! I do not have many options to decide on... at which point can I influence the story???"
After some hours I started to realize: I do have some options, maybe quite a lot [and you have a lot!] but the passages between my decisions are so well and lovely written that it seems as an eternity first... but as continuing ES you get caught by the story and you CANNOT stop reading this. (30 hours playtime in 4 days do speak its own language)
As it behaves when you finish a good book, the same it does when finishing ES. You are happy of the time you spent with it, but you feel sad as if you have lost a very good friend.
After my first playthrough, I went back to the reviews again... and what did I read? 13 different endings?!?
13??
So you really have a lot of influence to the story...
So I started to play this again... and again... and it just got more interesting!
You learn so much new about each character and its behaviour, you learn a lot more of how and why this happens. And you really, really have to complete each ending to understand what is going on.
I just finished with this piece of glamorous art and I am happy... satisfied.
You do understand the behaviour of the protagonist more, the older you are yourself. Often you catch yourself compairing to him, because many aspects just fit to you - big compliment to the creators of the game.
Well as I do not want to tell too much about the details, I think I'm done with my first real review of a game.
If you managed to come this far: thank you for reading

download this game. It is for free, and it seems to interest you that much that you read through my review!!!
When something is that catchy, that you feel uncomfortable when you have to stop with it, then it has to mean a lot...

This game is pretty good.
The pros:
- It really shows, at all times, what a difficult situation you are in. Having to worry about supplies, morale and squad stats was really interesting.
- The characters are well designed and written. The writing of this game is amazing.
- The story is nice, sometimes feels like a GRRM novel. Deaths and♥♥♥♥♥♥included.
- The gameplay is a bit different from other turn-based strategy games, and it feels good, although not great.
- The visuals are amazing. Really amazing. The soundtrack is also beautiful. This game is a piece of art.
The cons:
- It's not much of a game that allows replayability. I've only had one run (around 10 hours) and I feel satisfied with it. Not many reasons to go back.
- You have to take some decisions without much information, which may or may not lead to some catastrophic events. You may feel cheated sometimes :-)
- Some minor difficulty spikes, so if you are a casual gamer only interested in the story, you may need to turn down the difficulty. But nothing to be afraid of.
- Kind of slow to get interesting, but with around one hour in, you may find yourself really into the story.
Overall, I rate this game as 8/10. Great addition to your library if you are looking for a  good story and amazing visuals.

Another fantastic Telltale installment. Much like The Walking Dead S1, S2 and The Wolf Among Us, there is excellent writing and dialogue as well as art direction. For this game, Telltale has a slightly different tone, heading into high fantasy with Game of Thrones.
This is based off of the TV show, so if you haven't caught up there will be spoilers for that. There will be MASSIVE spoilers. This will be following from the taile end of season 3 all the way to the end of season 4. It conveniently makes a nice recap game for season 5, while also throwing its own twist into the story.
You play as several people connected to House Forrester, a family that served under the Starks. Each character is unique, and given the new aspect of multiple perspectives, I thought it really refreshed the formula Telltale had established with TWD and TWAU. Writing-wise, still excellent dialogue and situations, and a lot of it was very appropriate to the characters or the show itself. The writers did well in keeping the consistency of the tone of the show. It is dark, dramatic, and full of intrigue, and, in a departure from their previous games, full of gorey violence much like the show. Also, if you did not like the excessive "sexposition" of the show itself, it may be of interest to you that this game (from the time of this writing) has none.
Art-wise, Telltale changes their formula and rather go for a comic book style model for their characters and environment, they opted for an oil painting like texture. The characters still get that slight Telltale cartoon-ish vibe, however, they definitely look much more realistic now. Also, for the characters that we know from the show, they got a lot of the models to look almost perfect to the actor's faces - and to top it off their voices are in the game too. To really drive the point that this is indeed the Game of Thrones universe, they created an opening just like it. A very good touch of fanservice for fans of the series.
Some minor complaints do have to do with some glitches (I had Lady Forrester float behind the fireplace in one scene) and some of the situations just seemed ridiculous or silly and I questioned why they had the character doing that.
Overall, another solid release from Telltale. It's a bit pricier than normal because this game comes with 6 episodes, NOT 5. If that's a deal breaker, pick it up when it goes on sale.

Okay, okay, I'll thumbs up this game. But it comes with a large "BUT".
In this case: ...but it's not so much a game as it is a mod of a game. Seriously: if you've told me I was actually playing an UT2004 modification, I would have believed you, and I've played plenty of those.
So the game plays as if it was made ten years ago...does that make it bad? No. Not at all. Even the graphics and sounds aren't that important, as there is clearly plenty of time spent on the gameplay. RRDDD plays very smoothly and has very addicting gameplay. The AI is okay (again: I think I recognize UT's bot behavior), it has stakes, franctic action and modes to keep you going.
I'm not really sure how in-depth the skill ceiling really goes, but with this sort of game, it's most likely more than it might seem. Still...if you ask me, you shouldn't be playing it for attempting to be the best. You should do it because you want to have a good time with friends. The game just screams LAN-play.
Anything else? Well...the mod-quality unfortunately shines through the campaign. Its arcade-y style has no progression into it and is more an attempt to keep you busy. There are barely any levels (though that means there aren't any bad ones either), you'll get bored of the visuals fast and even faster of the music (I get chiptunes...this is just not good, IMHO).
In short: this is one of those games I don't intend to play again, but of which I'm glad I've got them in my steam account. It's something to keep in mind when having a LAN with a mix of hardcore shooter veterans and other gamers...I assume this'll blend in with everyone.

So, I just finished this bememoth of a CRPG. And I find myself in a bit of a pickle. Usually when I finish a game, if I've stuck with it for its duration, I feel very strongly one way or another as to whether or not it was good.
I don't feel that way this time.
So then, how do I review a title that both provided some of the most enjoyable RPG action I've played in years, but that also occasionally threw up a baffling design decision that detracted greatly from the overall experience?
The answer, I think, is that I recommend the game, but warn you lovely people.
Divinity: Original Sin wants you to like it. That's immediately evident. The first third of the game is a constant stream of reworked CRPG tropes, a strange mishmash of the familiar, and you know what? That works. That works extremely well. It fuses Fallout and Baldur's Gate into something honestly beautiful. It's funny, it's clever, the plot's central mystery unfolds with a refreshing lack of cynicism and delicacy that's all too devoid from most modern games, it looks great, it runs smoothly, and most importantly, the combat is an absolute treat. Learning to use elements to manage enemy lines and unleash ridiculous combo attacks is one of the best things I've done in a game this year.
But Divinity starts to fail you. It creeps up slowly. Around the 40-50 hour mark, you start to notice that very little has actually been happening. The game spirals to a satisfying enough conclusion, but the sense of adventure and refreshing take on the old-school is slowly lost.
And then Divinity decides to flip players the proverbial bird and introduce loads of forced stealth sections, the most egregious of which found me actually holding my finger to the quicksave key.
Some would argue this is part of the experience. I'd counter that things change for a reason. I didn't play CRPGs in the 90s because I wanted a quicksaving simulator, I played to have an adventure. Divinity offers 30 hours of a truly classic CRPG, and 40 of a middling one.
This is enough for me. The genre has been sorely devoid of great new games for a long time. But, I reiterate, this is a recommendation with an attached clause: don't expect a gamechanger. Don't expect to not have to fight Divinity on its own terms. This is a CRPG, with the warts you've forgotten about securely in place.

The first-person perspective is a little odd for a move set normally confined to third-person action games. You'll find the camera shakes around a lot, and those prone to motion sickness might very well have some issues playing through, particularly while performing quick-turn wall jumps. Yet the jitters and distortions you'll see onscreen really enhance the sense of immersion here, something further strengthened by the way DICE includes Faith's limbs. In some first-person games you're just a floating gun, but in Mirror's Edge you'll frequently see Faith's hands as she grasps at ledges, legs as she curls into a somersault, and feet as she kicks through windows. It grounds the game with a sense of realism that's contrasted against the often dreamlike quality of action and setting.
Buildings are drenched in white, sometimes blindingly so, and oppressively bright color motifs applied elsewhere in the world make everything seem ordered, sterile, under control, and entirely at odds with the way Faith is able to cut freely across the rigid, rectangular, and seemingly unyielding environments. Sound, too, underscores this theme, with the pattering of footsteps and Faith's perpetual breathing punctuating a soundtrack of bubbling electronics, bolstering the sense of the otherworldly.
Relative to how powerfully this world is presented the storyline doesn't match up, with minimal information given regarding the world's fiction which, strangely enough, works to the game's advantage. DICE's withholding of narrative detail fits in perfectly with the mystique weaved by the audio-visual components. The way it's presented, however, could use a lot of work. The crudely animated cut-scenes that crop up between action sections really need to go, as their flimsy presentation and the hammy lines of dialogue are totally at odds with the game's strengths and effective only at ruining the sense of immersion.
Combat is another weak spot; it's something that you'll occasionally need to engage in, but it doesn't work as well as the platform-hopping mechanics. The initial required fight sequence will momentarily kill the game's urgent sense of pace, but provided you put in a little time it's possible to get used to the finicky disarm mechanics and thereafter bash your way by enemies almost as easily as you would wallrun across a gap. Assuming you stop to pick up enemy firearms you'll find the shooting mechanics to be pretty rudimentary, though then you're getting away from the point of the experience.

Dying Light is an action survival open world game presented in first-person perspective. It may be squalid and zombie-infested, but Dying Light's city of Harran isn't a depressing wasteland – it's a vibrant, ambitious, open-world playground. It could be similar to previous zombie-survival you had played like Dead Island maybe? But here, buildings are for climbing, the undead are there to be destroyed in creative ways, and there's always something interesting to be discovered nearby.

Pretty interesting story.
In summary - Kyle Crane is GRE agent who is tasked with recovering data from the overrun city of Harran that could cure the virus rampaging throughout the city. The virus transforms the victim into a zombie like creature or into special mutations of that. After getting bitten inside the city, Crane has to blend in with one of the two main factions of the city, while staying undercover to try and recover that data. But he may have bitten off more than he can chew.

The FPS perspective makes it looks realistic and incredibly fun as in you are really exist in the game world where you roam an urban environment devastated by a mysterious epidemic.
Scavenging to craft - Make your own weapons, medicines and bold your pockets by looting some trashes, boxes, lorries, zombie corpses, and etc . Crafting also comes with delight various level weaponries.
Scavenge for supplies to send back to the safe zones.
Team up for missions in multiplayer mode - Engage in competitive challenges, or just run around and bash zombies together. It was fun; they even have mini challenges with your partner throughout the multiplayer mode to earn some achievements.
Invade other people - in Be the Zombie mode. But it is sometimes frustrating because most of invaded players always immediately quit or even disable for being invaded.
Weaponized your self - Discover a new rare blueprint is most blithesome feeling in this game. It’s so rare! You won’t expect it will be placed in that kind of place.
You are leveling up as you are surviving, parkouring, and beating some asses! Especially in the nighttime.
Set up traps – Players can also use environmental traps, such as spikes and electrified fences to kill the infected.
Throwing stars, tomahawks, etc. are ranged throwing weapons that can be aimed and used to take enemies out silently from a distance. They are silent and do not summon virals, unless you use them to ignite a gas tank.
Explosives are either in the form of grenades (thrown and explodes) or bombs (which attract then explode). They all cause noise and attract virals.
Molotov cocktails spread fire where they're thrown and will ignite the infected. Can often spawn virals after using.
Support items each have their own role, flares repel zombies, firecrackers distract them, and the UV flashlight for stunning infected at night. There is less used items like the Pyza Suit which lets you glide.
The slow motion combat is gory and so cool!
Last but not least, when you have unlocked grappling hook, here comes the spidey !

when nighttime comes everything changes. The zombies get faster and stronger and new mutations called, Volatiles come out to ruin your day. Good night and good luck.

Dying Light control scheme seems pretty familiar and at the same time highly customizable, with a couple of unique elements. In high pressure situation your survival in the game will depend on your performance and how quickly you react, thus, if you want to improve your gameplay and effectiveness you should take maximum advantage of your custom key binding scheme.

Really atmospheric and warm with a great depth of field. The blood and gory while slashing the zombies especially while slow motion are fantastic.

Definitely will come back. Ive replayed a couple times – especially to finish all the side quests.

I am a classic RPG player.  Final Fantasies, Breath of Fires, Star Ocean etc.  Over the years I have fallen out of love with these games generally: They are long, the turn based combat is boring, and I don't really have the time to focus on character building.
Then I discovered Child of Light.
This game is awesome.  It presents the world in a very simple 2D way.  It is easy to get around and relatively easy to remember what you are doing.  There are characters and party members that keep it interesting, and the character improvements are both in depth enough to satisfy strategists as well as simple enough to keep track of what you are able to do.   Each character carries a skill tree which you can unlock as they level up, unlocking new abilities.  You can see the whole tree, so all you have to do is decide what you want to get, and go in that direction.  There is also a small crafting section using gems that is in depth enough to be interesting, but not so bloated that I feel I may be missing out on something important (and thus have to scroll through pages of crafting guides).
Child of Light is also the most relaxing RPG I've played.  Both the music and art style are calm and relaxing.  However, my blood still gets pumping during the battles.  The game uses a simple element system and a few status effects and an "Interrupt" mechanic to keep the turn based battles engaging and interesting, as well as downright challenging sometimes.
Heavily recommend.

Saying Little Nightmares was good is an understatement. While it wasn't quite "amazing," it was definitely a lot better than "pretty good." Now, the story takes a dark turn. I'm not sure how to feel about this. But, even without knowing anything about the characters or plot, you can clearly see the descent of Six's situation as well as behavior. This is ironic however, because as Six ascends each level of the Maw, getting closer to the light, her character grows darker and dives deeper into something quite sinster.
I loved the artistic design for the game. Typically I don't like creepy things or anything from the horror genre. Each one of the creatures gave me the heebie jeebies, but at the same time, it's part of the charm of the game.
Confusing at first, chaotic fun from that point on. Admittedly I played against hard bots to start, and couldn't work out why I couldn't do anything as a ghost (which I was 99% of time).

Originally planned as a DLC for Saints Row the Third,
was released as a full  fourth installment in the Saints Row series that took an over-the-top turn with Saints Row the Third. It's pretty clear that this is the direction they want to keep going and
sure dropped yet another load of over-the-top on the series with this one... but is it good, or just a disappointment to the Saints Row series?
The Pros:
· An over-the-top ridiculous story that'll quickly place you in a Virtual Steelport, but it feels like a whole other city than in Saints Row the Third...
· ... most likely due to the fact that you have a wide array of cool powers at your disposal. The simulation allows you to jump incredibly high, sprint almost three to four times as fast as a car can drive, use freeze blasts, fire blasts, kinetic powers, ground stomps, and so much more to fight against Zinyak and his Zin Alien troops.
· In terms of over-the-top, it sure ups the Third a few notches, but also recovers some of the characters that were simply forgotten in Saints Row the Third. You'll get to meet characters from previous Saints Row games and you'll be able to do a ton of sidemissions for them in order to make them become Super Homies.
· Aside from the Homies sidemissions, there are tons of activities in Virtual Steelport you'll want to check out. Fun sidequests, sharply written story missions, countless collectibles and many more.
The Cons:
· Due to the many overpowered abilities I could use, I never felt like I needed to drive a car or challenge myself in combat. Once your guns are upgraded to the point where you have unlimited ammunition and your powers have low cooldown, it's just a matter of spamming those and spraying.
· I'm afraid they can't take the series higher without making it a downright parody to open world games. Saints Row the Third felt like an immense chance from the previous titles, but
is twice as over-the-top. If they want to do anything fresh, they'll basically have to go higher or do something miraculously entertaining without it being a step back from the last two titles.
The Visuals:
· They might look like Saints Row the Third's visuals, but they're absolutely fantastic. Alien structures' lights will flare across the city, walls and roads will glitch under your feet as you charge a powerjump, animations look solid and smooth, characters and environments are beautifully done... These small details make the game look like an improvement that hides under a cover of Saints Row the Third's graphics.
Final Verict:
· To answer my question at the beginning; it's a bit of both. I didn't have the Saints Row-feeling I wanted from
, but I definately had tons of fun playing through it. 8/10.
