I'll be honest. Grim Dawn is a difficult game. It's difficult to chose a class, Every single class I've tried is just flat out done amazingly well. As a HUGE fan of aRPGs, I've played them all, bought them all, have them all in some capacity. Literally. Almost every damn one ever released.  Grim Dawn is light years ahead of anything released lately or in years, as a matter of fact. I'll give it the "I've played it for 75 hours and still haven't finished it" review. I'm not going to go into minute details. Just know the game rocks, and does it hard.
Graphically the game is like the Dungeon Siege games amped up on steroids and blasted in amazing detail. Remember playing the first Dungeon Siege and having your jaw drop at how beautiful the scenery, the verticality of it all played out? Grim Dawn has it in spades. Wonderful vistas, creepy forests, scattered and desolate deserts, creepy temples and underground dwellings and caves, and the ever wonderful "secrets" that are scattered generously. The attention to detail is astounding. You'll find libraries full of books you can actually see, candelabras giving faint light on a desktop, small envelopes and letters scattered and blood spattered walls and streaks of death. Character armors and weapons are done very nicely and enviroments are teeming with sudden death if you're not careful. Weapon procs and effects are dazzling and spell effects will light up your immediate vicinity and give you a feeling of invincibility as you're hammering away at a bad guy with your lightning mace and destroying absolutely everything in sight. Pets come to your aid as you find yourself in a jam, if needed of course. Lighting everywhere trickles in spots and corners and enemies are cloistered in a room awaiting your arrival with surprise weapons of destruction.
Then you hear something walking. Stomping around, awaiting you. But where? You can't see them yet, it's dark, but you know they're there. Waiting. They'll come at you speaking curses and whispering death spells. The ambient music surrounds you with calling birds and trickling waters of a stream as you hear your pet walking and get a little scared. Just for a second. Major NPCs will speak to you in full dialogue and you'll be listening because it is important what you do. You'll find small pages of torn books and letters that flesh out a darker and sad secret, or maybe you'll find the reason the horror you're searching has done the things it has done. It will freak you out, just a little, that this world exists and you're tyring to help save it. Then you'll be searching for the terrors in the night as the music picks up and you know you're in the right place at the wrong time.
With a fully active mini map you'll still get lost in the vastness of the areas. You'll be searching for that special cave and come across a tomb. What waits for you inside is not a friend in need, or is it? NPCs will try to trick you from time to time and you'll be listening and reading for clues on the insanity that is the Grim Dawn. Ample storage space that increases from time to time will guarantee you're ready for anything, as long as you have that idle minute to look. Portals open at your beckon and you're guarateed safety if just for a minute to catch your breath. Then you'll leave again, with a better weapon, a shinier talisman, an upgraded pair of boots for your journey. You'll have discovered a full Devotion religion that will better prepare you and your pets for what lies ahead. There are NPCs awaiting your arrival to help guide you on your journey and better explain the evil in the dark that awaits you, then they will ask you to go kill it.
THIS is Grim Dawn. Easily one of the best aRPGs I've ever had the opportunity to experience. It doesn't neccessarily re-invent the arpg wheel, but it soups it up with the best engine, the most horsepower and the best kit and then lets you go on your merry way. Oh, and the view is pretty awesome too.

There is not much strategy involved aside from 'build roads everywhere you can to block everyone' (Goldmines first so you can afford to keep blocking them), and 'throw explosives at the other players'. As for competitive, don't bother. It does not have a lot of skill involved aside from who can build the fastest(Which in itself is a matter of being the fastest at clicking). Addictive? Definitely not. Play it once, maybe twice. Third time with friends and then you´ve seen it all. There is nothing to come back for, and I would say it is severely lacking in replay value.
At least it is realtime, and with 4 players throwing explosives it is chaotic so you can at least count that as a plus if you enjoy that sort of thing. For the single player challenges, they do take some effort, though the 'humour' involed in it is certainly not my kind. You are essentially challenged by a bunch of stereotypes which eventually end up teaming up on you. And then it just sort of ends.
Detour is a game that sounds good in theory, but just doesn't cut it in practice. Maybe it was a good idea on the idea board that just didn't get fleshed out right, maybe they just lacked the skill or knowledge to make it work. But either way I would recommend against buying Detour - Your time is more valuable than any sale price

I have only two very minor quibbles with the game:
1. The character art is a little distracting compared to the background art.
2. The English translation needs a proofreader to go through it and correct all the misspellings and bad grammar.
That said, I loved both the character and background art (that's why it's a minor gripe). The first scene I saw when I started the game was breath-taking and I just stared at it before continuing, and the art continued to be beautiful.
The characters are all interesting and fun, the only one I don't really like is Miku. I rather like Alisa, her somewhat-yandere personality is really entertaining. So far though, I like Lena the best.
I haven't finished the game yet, but I already wish this had a yuri version, not a big fan of het romance - that's not to say I won't read and enjoy it though.
The writing at times is a bit stilted and robotic, but I think that might be in part because it wasn't originally written in English. My Russian isn't fluent enough for me to read the original and form a proper opinion about its writing quality.
I tried to make it through the mine without looking up a guide, but after my third time in the crystal cave, and second time at the miner camp I was just too tired (it was nearly 3am). xD
* Semyon's route was bizarre and a little sad, it had a bit of a Twilight Zone feel to it so it was interesting.
* Finished Miku's route and holyshit what a mind♥♥♥♥... do not play this at 1am with the sound up because it's creepy as hell lol.
* Ulyana (Yuliana?)'s route was fun and silly and the good ending was full of hope and warmth and made me cry a little at the very end. I won't spoil the ending, but Ulyana looked really pretty.
* Slavya's route was kind of... different. It wasn't really what I would have expected of such a girl, but it was quite enjoyable. My favourite part was definitely the scene of her standing at the bus stop in her winter coat. It was quite a beautiful picture.
* Lena's route was just plain weird. I liked her shy character, but the story was just off in left field lol. And not the good weird like Miku or Semyon's either. It left an unfullfilled taste when it was done. I did however like how he realised that he could just stay in the Sovionok world and live there, so that was a nice touch.
* Alisa's route is by far my favourite. She seemed more like a real person than the others. A well-written tsundere, and I do love a well-written one lol. The good ending was... meh. It wasn't bad, but it left a lot to be desired. After finishing her route, I read the official (?) mod-ending for Alisa, and I liked it much better - it made more sense for her to join Semyon, than it did for her to be a girl in the crowd. It also made the ending a lot happier too; the original ended on a hopeful note, so it wasn't complete rubbish.

This is my review of Game of Thrones, the latest title released just yesterday by Telltale Games.
This game is of course based on A Song of Ice and Fire by George R. R. Martin. It looks and feels very much like the TV show. However, it’s not based on any storyline in the show. Nor is it really based on any storyline in the books. This allows them the creative freedom to tell a completely new story within the world without worrying about messing up canon, although as you’ll see there are appearances by many of the series’ favorite characters, all of whom are voiced by the actors who play them in the show. And the characters in the game look just like the actors in the show as well.
It’s best to think of it as a sort of serialized storytelling adventure in which you’re able to play a minor role. Though you’re lead through the story by the nose, Telltale has done a great job of giving you just enough control to get emotionally invested in your character.
Now you’ll note that I said “serialized” there. That is because this game, the one that has released and that I played, is only the first episode of five. Telltale has promised to release another episode every five to eight weeks, and you get them ALL for the up-front price of $29.99 at the time of this review. You’ll get about ten hours of content in the end, and that’s without ANY replay, and you’re going to be tempted to replay this game, although I’ll discuss later whether you actually SHOULD.
What are the game mechanics? Primarily, the game mechanics are dialogue selection. You get to choose what to say in response to the people who speak to you throughout the story.
There are other, minor mechanics, but to be honest, it’s all about choosing what you say. Your words have a BIG impact on how people react to you, although not necessarily how the story plays out, as we’ll see in a moment. It feels COMPLETELY appropriate to the Game of Thrones universe, where a lot of interesting characters sit around and talk a lot, and very occasionally stab each other violently in the face.
I can’t normally do thorough graphics reviews because my computer is NOT a great gaming rig. However, this game runs perfectly fine on my computer with the graphics and resolution turned all the way up, so if you don’t have a great computer, you’ll still probably be able to play it.
There are some minor graphical issues. Occasionally cloth will simply melt into someone’s body, and there’s some slight aliasy-looking stuff around the edges of characters in the game. In the final analysis it’s not that big a deal, but it was occasionally distracting, and distraction sucks in a game that relies completely on its ability to immerse you in narrative.
Despite that, though, it’s hard not to call this a very pretty game. Game of Thrones feels like you’re watching some ancient tapestry in motion. It’s a great aesthetic, and my hat’s off to them for it.
The game had no bugs that I could see in two playthroughs, and the sound design was fantastic. In particular the voice acting was, in my opinion, simply superb. Bad voice acting could absolutely have ruined the game. Instead, with very, very strong voice acting, every interaction felt real, meaningful and important. Peter Dinklage in particular is in fine form, and it really did feel like I was chatting with Tyrion Lannister in King’s Landing which of course is just awesome.
So let’s talk about the story. I will make one statement right up front: if you are not already a fan of Game of Thrones, certain parts of this story will feel VERY confusing and you should probably avoid it. The story starts right up front with one of the most important events in the entire series. But anyone coming to the game without ANY knowledge of the world will be incredibly confused. Similarly, when later in the game you meet Queen Cersei, there’s a tremendous amount of tension because you know Queen Cersei will kill you at the drop of a hat. However, you only know that if you’ve read the books or watched the show. So for the uninitiated, this game is probably a definite do not buy, because you will not fully get the story, and this game doesn’t have anything going for it besides the story. However, if you are a fan of the books and/or show, the story is simply great.
As for Telltale’s treatment of the subject matter...well, it’s EXTREMELY hard to get into specifics without massive story spoilers. Instead let me simply say that Telltale does not pull any punches. This game is about as Game of Thrones as Game of Thrones gets, and at one point you will want to fling your computer through the window.
Now I have to tell you what I didn’t like about this game. Actually I didn’t just dislike it, I felt profoundly disappointed. And that is the level of choice and influence you can actually have in the game. Throughout the story you are given many, many choices in dialogue. The choices are made out to be very important. In fact, the game CONTINUALLY reminds you how important they are by adding little tags at the top of the screen that say, “So-and-so will remember that.”
However, I’ve now played this game through twice. The first time I played a very sort of Lawful Good character, following the rules and trying to be the best person I could be. Then I said, “I’m going to play this through again, and this time I’m going to Game of Thrones the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.” So I played a much more Chaotic character, with shows of strength, decisive, definite action.
And you know what changed? Not an awful lot.
Characters reacted to me differently, and sometimes those reactions were great to see. But in the end, all the major broad-strokes plot points happened the exact same way.
At that moment, the replay lost its luster for me. If I couldn’t make any significant changes, then what was the point of replaying the game and making new decisions? Especially since Telltale won’t let you skip through dialogue scenes. You have to watch them, and hear everything everyone has to say all over again.
So, final analysis: What’s bad about this game? Well, at this moment in time, you’re only getting two hours of content for about thirty bucks. You’ll get more in a few weeks, but if you’re selective with your spending, it might be better to WAIT those few weeks and get more bang for your buck, or wait for the inevitable Steam sales and get the game at a discount.
And then of course there’s the lack of any ability to make real, significant changes within the world, and that’s a major downer on a game that builds so much false sense of power into the choices it gives you throughout the story.
But what’s good about this game? Well, the aesthetic is very pleasing, the acting is simply fantastic, and the story immersion is some of the best I’ve ever seen. You really do feel like you’re in the Game of Thrones universe. Does this make the game insanely fun? No. Does it make it incredibly compelling? Absolutely.
Who should avoid this game? Anyone who has never read the books or watched the show. This game simply is not inclusive enough for you, and relies heavily on your knowledge of the source material. Also anyone who wants more true power of choice in the world.
Who should pick up this game RIGHT NOW? Diehard fans of the series who simply can’t wait for the show to come back on the air, or for George R. R. Martin to write the next book. It DOES feel very much like watching a very long episode of the show or reading a few excellent chapters in the book.
Who should pick this game up WHEN THE FULL SEASON IS DONE? Anyone who likes the books and the films. At $29.99, the full series will almost certainly be worth at least one playthrough, and maybe more.
Thanks very much for reading.

Dying Light is an action survival open world game presented in first-person perspective. It may be squalid and zombie-infested, but Dying Light's city of Harran isn't a depressing wasteland – it's a vibrant, ambitious, open-world playground. It could be similar to previous zombie-survival you had played like Dead Island maybe? But here, buildings are for climbing, the undead are there to be destroyed in creative ways, and there's always something interesting to be discovered nearby.

Pretty interesting story.
In summary - Kyle Crane is GRE agent who is tasked with recovering data from the overrun city of Harran that could cure the virus rampaging throughout the city. The virus transforms the victim into a zombie like creature or into special mutations of that. After getting bitten inside the city, Crane has to blend in with one of the two main factions of the city, while staying undercover to try and recover that data. But he may have bitten off more than he can chew.

The FPS perspective makes it looks realistic and incredibly fun as in you are really exist in the game world where you roam an urban environment devastated by a mysterious epidemic.
Scavenging to craft - Make your own weapons, medicines and bold your pockets by looting some trashes, boxes, lorries, zombie corpses, and etc . Crafting also comes with delight various level weaponries.
Scavenge for supplies to send back to the safe zones.
Team up for missions in multiplayer mode - Engage in competitive challenges, or just run around and bash zombies together. It was fun; they even have mini challenges with your partner throughout the multiplayer mode to earn some achievements.
Invade other people - in Be the Zombie mode. But it is sometimes frustrating because most of invaded players always immediately quit or even disable for being invaded.
Weaponized your self - Discover a new rare blueprint is most blithesome feeling in this game. It’s so rare! You won’t expect it will be placed in that kind of place.
You are leveling up as you are surviving, parkouring, and beating some asses! Especially in the nighttime.
Set up traps – Players can also use environmental traps, such as spikes and electrified fences to kill the infected.
Throwing stars, tomahawks, etc. are ranged throwing weapons that can be aimed and used to take enemies out silently from a distance. They are silent and do not summon virals, unless you use them to ignite a gas tank.
Explosives are either in the form of grenades (thrown and explodes) or bombs (which attract then explode). They all cause noise and attract virals.
Molotov cocktails spread fire where they're thrown and will ignite the infected. Can often spawn virals after using.
Support items each have their own role, flares repel zombies, firecrackers distract them, and the UV flashlight for stunning infected at night. There is less used items like the Pyza Suit which lets you glide.
The slow motion combat is gory and so cool!
Last but not least, when you have unlocked grappling hook, here comes the spidey !

when nighttime comes everything changes. The zombies get faster and stronger and new mutations called, Volatiles come out to ruin your day. Good night and good luck.

Dying Light control scheme seems pretty familiar and at the same time highly customizable, with a couple of unique elements. In high pressure situation your survival in the game will depend on your performance and how quickly you react, thus, if you want to improve your gameplay and effectiveness you should take maximum advantage of your custom key binding scheme.

Really atmospheric and warm with a great depth of field. The blood and gory while slashing the zombies especially while slow motion are fantastic.

Definitely will come back. Ive replayed a couple times – especially to finish all the side quests.

This is another hidden gem on steam that would give Ricochet a run for it's money. Robot Roller Dodgeball is dodgeball that knows no boundaries and puts everyone playing at risk. Such an extremely simple "FPS" game made with care and precision.
In Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball, you control one robot whose face you can customize. The controls are relatively simple and require precision aiming more than anything. Think of CS : GO type of game-play movement and that's essentially what you get. The catch? Your robot is on one wheel always rolling around somewhere. There are primarily nine directions you can direct your robot in, all in which will move it at a constant speed. This clonky directional movement can be interrupted and perfected thanks to the mouse. To shake-up the game and to keep it away from being bland they added a jump feature (which you can hold down longer for a bigger jump) and a boost feature, in which both are extremely handy. The game has more game modes than I have fingers on one and possibly two hands. My favorite game feature is their incorporation of basketball or "hoops" as they call it. The player can hit other players with the dodge ball, but there is one golden ball that needs to be used to score a point. To do so, the player has to throw the ball on one side of a square floating in mid air by the other teams spawn point. There is also a free for all setting for the mode. Other game modes feature (team) deathmatch, score battle (first team/person/robot to x amount of points), elimination where one by one team members get knocked out and wait for the next round, super ball where players have to keep hold of a certain ball to accumulate points, grand prix where players have to race around a map, horde (single player) where you face up against one robot (then two, then three etc...), and finally training. Any game willing to add variation deserves some credit, and disco dodgeball definitely deserves a high five or two.
Besides game modes, players can pick up random power-ups found spread out throughout the map. Some power ups include larger ball, fire/laser ball where it can't be stopped, jet pack to stay in the air longer, boomerang balls, and even a super boost that replenishes boost a lot quicker. How do you pick up a dodgeball? You'll find them laying around everywhere after people start throwing them. They are pretty hard to miss as white globes on the floor will glow brightly. They've also put in a feature where you can CATCH a dodgeball. It's a hard skill to master as you have to point at the ball but results in an opponents quick death. Throwing power can be modified the longer the mouse button is held down. This is useful if you'd like to ricochet your ball off a wall to hit someone on the other side of it.
themselves are a nice twist and keep everything simplistic. There is nothing wrong with being simple as it keeps the focus towards the game. If you are sensitive to a bunch of different lights going on and off you might want to take some precaution.
themselves are neat, subtle and sort of quiet, but neat. The music is what protrudes the most at all times. One thing I noticed graphically was when hitting an opponent with a ball, instead of the opponent blowing up or the ball stopping in it's tracks, there's a little recoil when hitting an opponent, then they blow up. This is a tiny feature that makes hitting an opponent with a ball that much more rewarding.
The price is a bit steep I must say but if a sale comes around, I'd say pick it up! Also, for the wary, the servers are sort of empty at times but there are bots to keep it interesting. You will find some stragglers once in a while playing.

Little Nightmares is a puzzle-stealth-platformer videogame of sort with horror elements developed by Tarsier Studios. The game allows the player to experience the story of a little girl in a yellow raincoat named Six, who is trapped in a huge ship called the Maw, where she's expected to be killed and eaten by the resident guests just like the rest of eerie place's children prisoners. Six must navigate the huge, mechanical monstrosity and avoid its dangerous guardians in order to achieve freedom.
If you've played games like Limbo or Inside in the past, then you already know what you are in for with Little Nightmares: you must navigate the various locations with your little protagonist while avoiding undefeatable huge monsters and manipulating the environment to your advantage. Six can also and will die if you screw up what you are supposed to do, which adds a "trial and error" quality to the whole thing. Truth be told, this game is unique in the measure that it achieves a good balance between stealth and platforming sequences.
The two issues people may have with Little Nightmares boil down to two, which are:
1) It's very short lenght, since the game can be finished for the first time around three or four hours at worst, with following runs being able to be much, much faster than that. It can be argued that the game takes you in the main places of the Maw, but the whole thing is so interesting and captivating you can't help but desire more of it. It's worth mentioning that Little Nightmares features collectables/side quests hidden in the levels in order to give you an incentive to replay them, but someone could find them just akin to extra padding.
2) At the time of this writing the huge monsters (or "the bosses") of the game can sometimes get themselves stuck into elements of the scenery or otherwise not do what they are supposed to do in a given sequence. Since the game features a lot of scripted scenes, which are necessary to go forwards, an enemy getting stuck means you'll have to restart from the last checkpoint manually. That said, this issue is not that common.
If you can get over the short lenght, however, Little Nightmares can reveal itself to be a very interesting and tense experience. The rather unique art style of the game as well as the general quality of the gameplay make for a very horrific and grotesque adventure which still manages to challenge the player with hectic levels and one cruel twist after another

I'll be honest. Grim Dawn is a difficult game. It's difficult to chose a class, Every single class I've tried is just flat out done amazingly well. As a HUGE fan of aRPGs, I've played them all, bought them all, have them all in some capacity. Literally. Almost every damn one ever released.  Grim Dawn is light years ahead of anything released lately or in years, as a matter of fact. I'll give it the "I've played it for 75 hours and still haven't finished it" review. I'm not going to go into minute details. Just know the game rocks, and does it hard.
Graphically the game is like the Dungeon Siege games amped up on steroids and blasted in amazing detail. Remember playing the first Dungeon Siege and having your jaw drop at how beautiful the scenery, the verticality of it all played out? Grim Dawn has it in spades. Wonderful vistas, creepy forests, scattered and desolate deserts, creepy temples and underground dwellings and caves, and the ever wonderful "secrets" that are scattered generously. The attention to detail is astounding. You'll find libraries full of books you can actually see, candelabras giving faint light on a desktop, small envelopes and letters scattered and blood spattered walls and streaks of death. Character armors and weapons are done very nicely and enviroments are teeming with sudden death if you're not careful. Weapon procs and effects are dazzling and spell effects will light up your immediate vicinity and give you a feeling of invincibility as you're hammering away at a bad guy with your lightning mace and destroying absolutely everything in sight. Pets come to your aid as you find yourself in a jam, if needed of course. Lighting everywhere trickles in spots and corners and enemies are cloistered in a room awaiting your arrival with surprise weapons of destruction.
Then you hear something walking. Stomping around, awaiting you. But where? You can't see them yet, it's dark, but you know they're there. Waiting. They'll come at you speaking curses and whispering death spells. The ambient music surrounds you with calling birds and trickling waters of a stream as you hear your pet walking and get a little scared. Just for a second. Major NPCs will speak to you in full dialogue and you'll be listening because it is important what you do. You'll find small pages of torn books and letters that flesh out a darker and sad secret, or maybe you'll find the reason the horror you're searching has done the things it has done. It will freak you out, just a little, that this world exists and you're tyring to help save it. Then you'll be searching for the terrors in the night as the music picks up and you know you're in the right place at the wrong time.
With a fully active mini map you'll still get lost in the vastness of the areas. You'll be searching for that special cave and come across a tomb. What waits for you inside is not a friend in need, or is it? NPCs will try to trick you from time to time and you'll be listening and reading for clues on the insanity that is the Grim Dawn. Ample storage space that increases from time to time will guarantee you're ready for anything, as long as you have that idle minute to look. Portals open at your beckon and you're guarateed safety if just for a minute to catch your breath. Then you'll leave again, with a better weapon, a shinier talisman, an upgraded pair of boots for your journey. You'll have discovered a full Devotion religion that will better prepare you and your pets for what lies ahead. There are NPCs awaiting your arrival to help guide you on your journey and better explain the evil in the dark that awaits you, then they will ask you to go kill it.
THIS is Grim Dawn. Easily one of the best aRPGs I've ever had the opportunity to experience. It doesn't neccessarily re-invent the arpg wheel, but it soups it up with the best engine, the most horsepower and the best kit and then lets you go on your merry way. Oh, and the view is pretty awesome too.

I've wanted to try this game since I saw it randomly in Game Stop one day, I had given up consoles entirely by then though.
Fortunately they've released it here.
The game is quite frankly addicting, the characters are likeable, the combat is enjoyable and challenging and there's plenty of content for RPG lovers who like to do a little more than the story. I'm currently 60 hours in, Levels 110-126 on my characters and have barely scratched the surface of the optional content. Most people who enjoy RPG's will at least want to collect all the equipment and finish their characters progression, I'd say I easily have another 40 hours to go before then.
You do however need the DLC to get to level 999 and have all the extra items and battles that have kept me busy. Otherwise the game is about 40 hours long with some side content that probably adds another 10-20 hours.
It's worth the price, I've been playing the game non-stop.
Now let me list and explain some things people may not like to help you with your decision.
First off, there's several repeating dungeons, that is to say the textures and design will be quite similar and there's also no shortage of pallete swapped enemies. If you're the type who needs the little details in order, this game might do too little in that regard for you to be able to play through it.
Second, it's a bit grindy, at absolute bare minimum you'll be grinding 5 levels per dungeon between/during story quests. That's the minimum, with that you'll still lose a few times and struggle a bit. It's not that bad since there's ways to level up a lot faster but it should be noted, if you don't like the old fashioned concept of having to grind a bit once in a while then this game may annoy you early on and post game, seeing as post game is essentially a huge grind for the ultimate equipment you need to defeat all the optional bosses and what not.
Third, being a first time player I noticed that early on the combat made me feel very restricted, almost like sometimes I was losing due to the battle systems limitations and quirks rather than my skill or level. For instance, there's a little indicator for the order of turns that enemies and your characters will take, a character or enemy may appear to have two turns worth but if your character attacks too many times in the turn then that turn disappears and the enemy takes their turn. It's extremely difficult to plan moves until you learn how to work around it, essentially you need to take less actions if you need an extra turn with that character and even then it sometimes still doesn't work out like I think. Later on the combat at least feels less restrictive, as you grow stronger more of your attacks become viable with the right equipment. Early on you're basically forced to do your basic combos and mix in a skill attack when possible. Later on they introduce EXE's, making your skills less valuable and then later still your regular skills become viable again once you're equipped in a manner that lets them do damage.
For example, one character may do abysmal damage due to resistances of the enemy, you may have to deal with that for a while until you can equip them with certain abilities before you can really do more than scratch these enemies. This is pretty much the experience with the boss battles early on, they have ridiculous physical resistance and more often than not your attack will not suffice, unless you've grinded more than 5 levels.
That said the first problem is not constantly present, there are a few unique dungeons, but definitely not as many as one would like, the third problem resolves itself as you work around the quirky battle system and equip your characters properly.
A good tip would be to equip all your physical characters with anything that can give them "ignore enemy traits" or "ignore enemy category" this nullifies the irritation of facing bosses with high physical resistance when your characters early on are physically based.
I've enjoyed my time with the game much more than I have most titles these past years, it's not perfect but it is highly reminiscent of old JRPG's and everything that worked in them works here, character progression is fun and rewarding, the characters push you through the story quite well, particularly the villain who actually makes you wish you could phyisically whack her with the broad side of a huge great sword. Of course this happens because the heroines are likeable and seeing them suffer at the hands of the villain makes you squirm, which is a sign of well written personalities in characters if you ask me.
Despite it's flaws if you like JRPG's there's no reason not to pick this up. If you're having a hard time, get the Plutia, Peashy, and Histoire Battle Entry DLC, they're extremely useful throughout the game and will make your experience easier if that's your thing, it certainly was for me since I only wanted to do minimal grinding during the story.
Pick it up if it sound like it's for you, there's plenty of content and challenge to be had and with a relatively large amount of characters..., Neptune, Compa, IF, Vert, Noire, Blanc, Plutia, Peashy, Histoire, Tekken, CC2, MAGES, Uni, Nepgear, Ram, Rom, and a few more whose names escape me at this moment, there's no way you won't find any likeable characters to fit in your party. There's so many I forgot the names of the ones I used the least which was due to preference. Some of those named above are also DLC but it's so cheap you might as well grab it.

Ok calling all RPG fans....
Grim Dawn was made just for you if you liked
Diablo 1 or 2, PreSkyrim Morrowind cycle, Throne of Darkness, Van Helsing, Titan's Quest, or any of their closest kin.
The opening plot starts with you being possesed, tortured for inforrmation, and being hung. The hanging exorcises the aetheric infestation (4th dimentional being has no desire to die stuck in your body). Your rope gets shot down and the game starts with you enhanced body being asked if you're willing to redeam yourself and help save a small parcel of humanity. No spoilers there folks, watch the trailer (nicely done).
The setting is as if someone took magical Renaissance era Europe added a touch of the old West, a dash of Tesla, and iced it all with some Soloman Kane.
Graphically
You've got the 3 person top down angle camera view.
And well folks... while the detail level isn't bad. This game is dark, grubby, and crumbling in looks. A while one occationally gets to walk through areas like this
more often you'll get dungeons like this and darker
I turned up my brightness. Cause everytime I was in a dark area at night. Even with light enhancing items, it was bloody hard to see. Which is realistic (and can be nice in a horror game) but I personally don't find it fun in a dungeon crawler.
Audio
30% of NPCs have voice acting. The rest speak only in text format. The hacks, shots, grunts, ect are worthy; but nothing special. The background music is your typical ignoreable mood enhancer stuff.
Gameplay
Now here's where it gets enjoyable. It's your standard mouse point directional walk, left click attack, right click ect.. with the customizeable 2 layered slots for potions, spells, special attacks, and the permanent spot for your personal rift portal (that your lovely modifed humanity grants you). A great class system and you'll get to choose 2 of them eventually. Then you get you devotional choices once you restore your first shrine (on a nice astrological skill map). Your inventory will expand with some quests. You have a storage chest and the ability to send items to your other characters. You get enhancement bits to add to your items. Once you help the blacksmith, the ability to craft.
And if all that seams familar to you (to any core rpg player it should) there's the truth of this game. The developers have taken nearly every well working gameplay aspect from all the games before and used them.This isn't a bad thing even if it's not truly inovative. It's nostalgic without being hokey.
There's also multiplayer available.........
Overall
I really think if you ever enjoyed a 3 person view RPG you should buy this. It's a premium experiance and a excellent dungeon grinder.

Take on the brutal world of transport trucking. Will you be able to take on your foes and make sure that your routes stay intact so that your trucks can meet their quota? Well that's what it takes in the game Detour, by Sandswept Studios. This real-time strategy game will have you on the edge of your seat trying to keep up with what is going on in the game as well as devising new plans to meet your goal.
Graphically this game isn't at the top of the food chain, but there's enough here to make you feel pulled into the game. Each level is on a grid based system and in those grids you can find opponent's roads, hills, mountains, protestors, rubble, buildings and more. You'll also notice that in every level there is one corner of the grid that has a checked flag pattern, that's your ultimate goal.
So lets get into what it is about this game, well there's definitely a good number of single player scenarios that you can take on, each one, of course, ramping up in difficulty, however, there were definitely some of the later stages that I breezed through in comparision to earlier ones. Now that might be because I got used to the flow of the game or perhaps luck. Either way I definitely was relieved when after a hard level I was able to breeze through the next one.
This is definitely an interesting game, but it definitely has some flaws and quirks. The first one has to do with the lack of voice acting, look I understand not everyone has the budget to do that, but at the same time if you're going to have a "Sims" voice do SOME of the dialogue, you're going to need it to do ALL of the dialogue. It was really odd when the first speech bubble has random yammering (aka Sims talk) and then the very next one greets you with silence.
Now as I stated this game is challenging, but the issue that I have is that the challenge, for me was more so about trying to control the game, and not so much playing the game. You see developers definitely thought in depth about giving the player many different options to play around with in the game, the only issue is that getting to them is a PAIN.
Here's the deal, you have four different sections of choices that you can play around with, each has at least 3 different options in it. Think of it as a menu bar. The problem is that if you try to go the mouse scroll wheel route not only is the y-axis flipped but scrolling will not only cause you to select each section but each choice within that section before going to the next section.
There is an alternative, you can use the keyboard, which once again I found cumbersome. You see you're going to be using WASD to move around the grid to see what all there is to see, but you can use the arrow keys to select the sections, this time it will just select the sections, but once again the y-axis is flipped, which is beyond disorienting.
Here's the deal every time I have to make a decision, especially if I have to change sections, I have to take myself out of the game and try to figure out how the hell I'm going to do what I need to do, and that takes away from what should be my main focus, the actual game. Perhaps they should have found a simpler way of making choices, or maybe remove some of those choices, but as of right now the controls are so cumbersome that this game isn't fun.
There's definitely something there, and you definitely need to bring your A game to really do well in this game, but with such a barrier as your choice of selections in the game and the inability to easily make choices, this game might need to be left alone for the time being. This game gets a 6.1 out of 10.

Coming to my overall experience.
I was sceptical since this was my first visual novel period. I actually wanted to try it and started with this one because it costs not a single dollar and the reviews were pretty good.
The first hour might have lost me but I stayed and it drew me somehow into its world (get it? because the protagonist also gets into another "world").
I liked the characters and the overall sound (ambient and music). Since I knew, there would be several endings I really started working hard for  one I liked most. It actually worked out pretty well for some time. I mean the character at some points is a bit dumb with his decisions but most decisions I actually did myself got me closer to my goal....you know...getting that one girl you like best.
Now at the end I'm a bit surprised and heartbroken.....As you might have figured out, I did not really get the ending which I really wanted. All my work was for nothing. And I really like, that this depresses me. This vn gets to my nerves and actually makes me regret some decisions.
Not many games have touched my heart as much recently nor have other stories in movies or books ever done so.
So about the visual novel itself. You cannot really argue about since the price it is free to play.
I guess it was part of a freetime project and most likely very few developers.
However, there are some things to point out:
First of all I already mentioned the very decent sound. There was nothing too special but it always fits the situation.
The backgrounds are well drawn and are somehow in contrast to the characters. I did not really have problems with that but it definitly gave me a bad first impression since they might be the weakest part of the game.
Also having minor translation problems but meals and people are explained so you don't have to google words you might not know.
What else is there left to say? I'm eager to get my ending of desire and also trying out other visual novels thanks to Everlasting Summer.
Of course, it's not really a game, but a nice story with good accent on the characters and as for me those were very welld spent 8 hours. They probably should make a remake with polished graphics and sell it.....I would buy it then.

I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys turn-based tactical combat and some light reading.

I'm not all that far into this game but it has made a strong impression already.
This is a top-down RPG not dissimilar to something like the old Baldur's Gate.  You have a party of 4 adventurers that you control via the mouse like Diablo, until it comes to battles, when things shift into a turn-based mode.  It uses all the classic enemies like orcs, skeletons and that sort of thing.
It is difficult to come to grips with in the early stages, it does little to explain things to you.  The battles are finely balanced and if you mess up at all, expect to die.  If you wander into a high-level area, you're toast, don't even bother trying.  As you figure things out though, it becomes apparent just how many options there are in this game.
The real delight is in the combat, the way you can combine elemental effects rewards creativity in approaching how to defeat your enemies.  e.g. in the early stages, I relied quite heavily on my pyromancer to set up an area with flammable oil.  I'd then lure enemies onto the oil and set it on fire.  That is an extremely basic example of the sort of thing thats possible.
The quest system is weak, there are times you don't really know what you're supposed to be doing, and a walkthrough is definitely recommended.
The graphics are a bit of a mixed bag, some of the environment and character models don't look all that great close up, but the pyrotechnics on display in the battles more than makes up for it.  At times it is spectacular to watch.  The sound and music are good, with reasonably good voice acting.  Some of the arguments your characters get into are quite amusing too, there's a good roleplaying element there.
All in all, this is one of the best RPGs I've played in years.  It has a steep learning curve but with a walkthrough at the start, once you get rolling, it's a fantastic entertaining game that rewards creative approaches to the problems/combat it poses you with.
Highly recommended.

The devs put in a lot of effort to make this game, so it's only fair that I take some time to put down my thoughts about it in more than just a one-liner ^_^ Here we go...
-------------------
There's lots of it. Don't get fooled by the 4 overworld maps like I did - Each one takes many many hours to complete. There's a good enemy variety, but most of it is fantasy standard: Orcs, spiders, skeletons, ... They can have some nice/surprising abilities though. You'll spend quite some time in your inventory comparing stats of the tons of items you find and trying out some crafting recipes. Completing every (side-)quest and doing almost everything D:OS has to offer took about 105 hrs on hard difficulty - It's a long game but doesn't overstay its welcome. You'll see everything on a single playthrough except for some alternate consequences of choices you make. They aren't significant enough to justify playing it again though. However, the different char progressions and party setups do. For example, I never tried a stealthy rogue approach and rarely used witchcraft. Also, I highly suggest keeping an eye on the mod scene as those guys made me enjoy rpgs up to 4 times as long as intended...
-------------------
It's turn-based - each turn, a character gets action points depending on his stats to spend on movement, attacks or using items and once you're done, another character or enemy gets his turn.
After using a spell/skill, there's a cooldown to prevent you (and your enemy) from using those high damage AoE spells every turn.
A very cool aspect of the combat system is, that many spells work together or with the environment in some way. See a puddle of water? Electrify it and everything standing in it. Enemies enjoying some toxic gas? Throw a fireball and make it explode around them. Dragon Age 1 did something like this, but D:OS takes it even further.
Of course enemies and yourself have resistances and immunities to elements, forcing you to adapt your strategy.
-------------------
In general, it's far more difficult than most modern rpgs and the only one since Dragon Age 1 that managed to kill me. Repeatedly :D Once you get used to how everything works, it's a lot easier than what you might expect though. In any case, the difficulty is too inconsistent - Early-game is quite hard because you have few good spells available, then in Luculla Forest and Hiberheim it gets a lot easier and then difficulty spikes again for a short time on the last map only to drop to zero near the end. Imho it SHOULD start fairly easy and then gradually get harder - I have yet to play a game that gets this right though (and it's probably impossible because difficulty is so subjective...) Except for one instance the game is not unfair - you always know exactly WHY the enemy wiped the floor with you.
I like that the game randomly throws some bosses in your face - "Here, have a giant spider for no reason!" - and some of them like the Braccus Rex battle really require you to come up with a good tactic. The final boss was a big disappointment though and got boring quickly because you are so overpowered by then that it requires just time, no effort.
-------------------
You get 2 main chars + 2 additional ones you can hire either in the area Cyseal or in your "base". On lvl-up you spend points in the usual rpg stats (strength, intelligence, ...) and a variety of different skills (like elemental magic). Every now and then you get to pick a special, powerful trait. You can develop your party however you want - there's nothing stopping you from making a fireball throwing warrior.
-------------------
The writing is excellent with some highly enjoyable dialogues, but the story itself is... well, not bad but nothing special either and also pretty much linear. However, D:OS does a good job to keep you interested in what's gonna happen next. Most of the story is experienced in-game but every now and then you get a cutscene with a narrator talking over some artwork, which is pretty neat.
Quests are pretty much rpg standard, but they are well written and often involve interesting characters. In many of them you get to make a choice and (if you activated AI personality or playing co-op) argue with your partner about how to do things which is often hilarious, especially in co-op. Sometimes your choice even has some consequence later in the game, although none of them is really significant.
-------------------
Not much to complain here: Inventory management works pretty well with all the automatic sorting options. Technically there's a limit of items you can carry based on weight, but it's not like Diablo where you have to return to town every 10 minutes. In fact, with 1 high strength warrior I never reached the limit once because even full plate armour doesn't seem to weigh too much.
For every char you get 5 bars with 10 slots each where you can put skills/spells/items for quick access via hotkeys. For late-game mages that's not enough for EVERY spell, but you won't be regularly using every single one of them anyway.
Sometimes it's easy to misclick and accidentally steal stuff or chuck a fireball where you didn't want to though.
-------------------
Effects are great and the music is absolutely fantastic. I'm not sure how many tracks there are, but I never got bored with them. There's little voice-acting (mostly for the 2 main chars) but the few parts that are voiced, are done quite well with talented actors.
-------------------
Because I've been playing on a rather old PC (E6750, 4Gb Ram, Radeon HD4800) I wasn't able to try maximum settings, but even on medium the game looks pretty gorgeous. Most of the time you'll be playing zoomed out pretty far out but it's nice that it also looks good up close. It's very colorful with nice animations and spell effects - having half the screen explode with a meteor strike feels quite satisfying :) The world has been handcrafted very carefully with a lot of attention to detail and also offers more variety than you might think at first glance - Just when you get a little bored with grassland you stumble into a burning forest, get teleported to a frozen castle or stand on a ledge that essentially looks like the one in Mt. Doom :)
-------------------
On my old system the game runs smoothly on medium - I guess you COULD play it on high on such a system if you're ok with occassional FPS drops. With my 32-bit OS I had the nasty problem that the game froze and ultimately crashed when saving after about 20 minutes. However, a fix mentioned on the forum worked just fine and I was able to play the following 105hrs without any crash/freeze. Saving/loading takes some time (~30s), but considering the amount of data that needs to be saved/loaded, I suppose that's still ok.
-------------------
Surprisingly few. There's some items you should be able to get with telekinesis, but the game tells you you "can't reach" them for some reason. In Hiberheim I encountered what I think was a scrapped quest. There was also some treasure I didn't get, because an item I needed wasn't in the game. I couldn't finish one of the last sidequests, but I killed everyone involved so I'm not sure if that qualifies as a bug... ;)
-------------------
Is it perfect? Nah. But in terms of complexity, depth and atmosphere it DOES shame many rpgs of recent years made by bigger companies with a much higher budget. Some will tell you that with D:OS, there's finally an "old-school" and difficult experience around again, but I don't care about that. The important thing is - D:OS is a very well made and atmospheric rpg that really shows the devs love, passion and understanding for the genre.

Child of Light is an RPG reminiscent of the JRPG genre, but with beautiful 2D visuals. A tender and linear game with simple controls but deep systems.
(Visuals)
One of the selling points of CoL is certainly its artsy visuals, masterfully implemented on the UbiArt framework, the same from Rayman Origins and Legends. The landscapes vary from dark sceneries to rivers of lava, but one thing that remains constant is the extremely high quality of the artwork invested onto all moments of normal gameplay and battle.
(Systems)
The battle system is a very strong point of this game. Typical strategies from JRPGs are present, with strength or defense buffs and elemental weaknesses, but there is a huge focus on timing here. In a system similar to the ATB from classic Final Fantasies, allies and enemies need to wait until their icon reaches the casting bar to choose an action. The interesting part is that while the character is casting, its action can be cancelled by hitting it with an attack. Making the system even more deep, you can slow one or the other enemy by keeping your mouse pressed on it, to adjust things to your favor. This battle system demands a lot of focus and strategy to optimize your performance, and that is why I liked it so much.
(Story)
The story is told in a very poetic way, and I consider it very soothing.
The narrative is made in form of poems: every single dialog in the game rhymes. It seems that bothered some people, but that didn't happen to me.
(Conclusion)
Its best points are the very well executed art style and the battle system, but the rest has close to no flaws too. If I had to name a flaw, I would say that CoL lacks the learning of new skills to expand the explorability of the overworld, like in a metroidvania game.

I very rarely write reviews for games, but this is, by far, the most unique, enjoyable, humorous experience I have ever had playing a game. I believe I played for ten hours, and I didn't play a single other game until I finished this one. Moreover, I will most definitely be revisiting it soon.
Usually, when game journalists say a game has a unique story, they're just compensating for crappy gameplay and trying to elevate games to the "true artform" they wish it to be (even though every game is already clearly art). This game has it all: a story that is unheard of in the gaming universe, humor to please you endlessly, fantastic gameplay that ramps up in difficulty when you're ready, 24 different and upgradeable weapons, and a look that you just won't find anywhere else.
Basically, you are playing through a 1950's B-level sci-fi movie (with absolutely hilarious and true-to-life "commentary" from the "driector" nd his "interviewer" throughout every scene and even the menus, as if the game is actually a DVD of the "movie" through which you're playing), and the sheer creativity in what they have done with the concept is astounding.  Some of your powers are ever based on the fact that it is, in fact, a B-level sci-fi movie. You also have three unique characters you can play as at any time. You have multiple special powers, some unique to their characters and required to solve puzzles to get pieces for upgrading your equipment.
The game also has extremely enjoyable and organic-to-the-setting side-missions that you can complete for the chance to upgrade your skills and abilities. It forces you to try new tactics to defeat enemies and search every nook and cranny of the eminently treversible terrain to find all the game's secrets.
Ultimately, I give this game my highest recommendation. I've prbably bought over 400 games in my life, and I've only ever finished maybe less than a dozen of them. Not only did I finish this one, but I did it without playing any other game until I completed it!
You simply must get this game. It has everything: combat, puzzles, exploration, and everything else you expect from a triple-A game, but with the most unique aesthetic and story I have ever seen. Try it now, and reward the developers by buying it at full price (I don't know if I've ever said that before....)!

Crawl is simple but brilliantly executed multiplayer concept. One person plays a hero traversing a dungeon, and the other players play as the dungeon and enemies.  When a monster kills the hero they take his place. The monsters are generally "weaker" than the hero so they need to both work together and compete to get the last hit.
The matches are fairly short, usually lasting from 15 to 30 minutes which doesn’t feel like too long. The balancing mechanics are well designed, and players make comebacks regularly keeping the game close - the longer you play as a monster the better off you are if you become the hero, but wait too long and you might lose.
The hero and monsters feel good to play, and the players are given several customization options at the beginning of each game allowing them to choose a group of monsters to play as. There are also additional perks which offer variety in play styles.
There is a learning curve to the game, and understanding the different resources you have to manage and knowing each monster can be confusing to newer players. The mechanical simplicity helps a lot with this. Crawls biggest problem is that it currently has only local multiplayer and really needs online multiplayer.
Crawl is intensely fun and extremely well designed. It is easily one of if not the best local multiplayer games available on steam, and an amazing value for its price. If you can get a group of three or four people together to play I highly recommend it.

Yet another game that i would like to press "Mixed" instead of a yes or no recommendation. Grim Dawn still has a ways to go before i would consider it a must play. It has qualities that lead you to believe the creators kind of ran out of steam half of the way through the story and map creation process. Meaning they probably had a lot more idea's for what they wanted to do yet they didn't have time or resources to make it happen.
The maps for one are big, and I mean big not really in a good way more like content filling. They snake around and are barred off at almost every juncture. Its actually quite frustrating to clear them honestly. Where they could have put a hole in a stone fence to save you from walking 100 yards they instead made the fence bigger, or put a stone barricade to force you to go around. Dungeons are few and far between and are usually comprised  snaking passagways or repetitive floors.
The story is basically non-existent. I've beaten this game 3 times now and really don't have a clue what was going on besides a demonic invasion. You get lore items to help but they are usually filled with extremely long paragraphs you probably wouldn't want to read.
As far as character creation, gear, skills, its average really. After building a couple characters you will find yourself wishing they added more classes. And in the end regardless of what class you build or what stats you put in, the success of your character is still going to be dependant on the gear you got. Its just up to you if you want to farm and grind through oversized maps and repeditive dungeons to get it towards the end of harder modes.
The game itself doesn't seem to be optimized very well. Crashes for me are not just game crashes but desktop freezes. Meaning my whole computer will lock if the game becomes unresponsive and i will be forced to manually restart. Getting disconnected from multiplayer servers randomly are not uncommon, and screen shuttering / low fps are also issues i've noticed.
Still though I don't want to completely harp on this game. The creature creation, map atmosphere, and music are great don't get me wrong i could write 5 more paragraphs about the good, but it's a tough tough task nowadays to make a great one of these types of games to stand up to the classics of the past.
My overall take of Grim Dawn is its a slight revive of Diablo 2 with a lot of Titan Quest sprinkled in, though lacking the big production value of both those games. Is it worth playing? Maybe, if you are seasoned with D2 and Titan Quest then yes do play this, its good just to see what a new take looks like. But if you've never played top down arpgs' or are kinda on the fence about them I would probably look somewhere else.

When you play this game, it actually looks like you're watching a South Park episode when you're walking around. You travel around the town, which has finally been laid out and you can go all over the place, and even see businesses like Tom's Rhinoplasty as you walk about. You can talk to tons of characters in the show, there are heaps of references to many episodes throughout the series by means of items you find and their descriptions, and the story is hilarious and fun from start to finish. You get to make your own kid and play as any of the classic roleplaying archetypes: Warrior, Rogue, Mage, and Jew.
Each class/archetype has its own skills and would play a bit differently. Hanging out with Cartman and friends as they do their childish shenanigans is a blast, and the combat in the game consists of turn-based RPG mechanics. It's rather simple, and you only control two characters, but they have somehow managed to make it so entertaining that both people who love turn-based RPGs and those who don't really like them often enjoy it. I have two friends who don't like that sort of gameplay at all, and they both love this game. In fact, this is the only single player game one of those two friends has bothered to complete in about 15 years, other than Portal.
The game is just as zany and wild as the show, and if you're a fan of South Park, you should definitely check it out. Anyone unfamiliar with it or who doesn't like South Park may wish to avoid it or approach with caution.

Having seen most of the content, ultimately I can't really recommend this title. It isn't horrible by any means, and there are plenty of things to like. The artwork is very well done, the music is quite nice, it has some interesting, even  profound ideas, and it did keep me intrigued enough to keep playing and see all of the good endings. But at the end of the day, there are too many problems that dampen the experience.
Everlasting Summer plays out like a cross between a dating sim and an interactive mystery novel, and unfortunately falls rather flat in both areas. In order to pursue one of the girls, you have to build up enough points by performing certain tasks that make you look more favorable in their eyes. The first problem is that it's very unclear about whether or not you are doing the correct action or not. For example, there is one point where one of the girls gets a package from the infirmary, and you have the choice between asking her about the package, or not asking about it. I correctly guessed that she would prefer me to not ask about it, but someone might think that the correct answer would be to ask her about it, as that would show that they care about her well being. And there are a number of times where the correct answer is completely counterintuitive.
Another big problem is that there are only two possible endings for each girl, a good one and a bad one, the bad one being if you didn't get enough points, and the contrast between them is rather jarring. For example, in the case of one of the girls, in the good ending you end up getting married, have two kids, and have a wonderful life together, and in the bad ending the girl and the main character end up committing suicide. This would be bad enough, but the sequence of events leading up to both endings is exactly the same until the very end, where the two paths divert rather abruptly. Extremely unrealistic, and means that the player pretty much has to use a guide in order to guarantee the good ending.
Another big problem is that there really aren't that many choices. I understand that if an author gives the reader too much freedom in a choose your own adventure type of game, they'll spread themselves too thin, but the limited choices in this game impede your ability to really feel like you're contributing to the story, especially on subsequent playthroughs. I appreciate that they added in a feature that allows you to fast forward through scenes you've already experienced, but when the player is encouraged to skip most of the content just to have a go at one part they haven't seen yet, that's a problem. The lack of choices really begins to be noticeable when the main character starts saying and doing things that you would never do, but aren't given any alternative options to choose from.
Finally, the game doesn't work as a mystery novel because it leaves too many unanswered questions, and ultimately will waste the player's time analyzing problems that are never resolved. I'm not saying I wanted to know everything, but the game was too ambiguous on a lot of matters, with many mysteries popping up and either never being resolved, or being resolved in extremely anticlimactic ways. The most egregious example was with the Miku ending, where they do an excellent job of building the suspense and horror of an uncomfortable and frightening situation, only to throw it all away by making it all be a dream, which is one of the cheapest cop-outs of all. The converging stories, as a whole, are a bit of a mess, and while they do keep the intrigue going long enough to warrant multiple playthroughs, ultimately it doesn't make up for the fact that it's really not all that well written.
I'll close this out by going over a few more of the things that I liked. I liked how each of the girls had a distinct personality, and how they were at least somewhat realistically proportioned, and not obscenely stylized. The fact that the game is free is also definitely a factor to consider. If this game had cost me money, I would encourage people to avoid it like the plague, but the fact that it's free does mitigate that issue.
In the end, if you are at all interested in this type of game, you'll probably find something you'll like. I admit that I did. But ultimately, the time I spent with this title was not worth it, and I cannot recommend it.

I'm going to recommend this game, but with the following warnings and criticisms:
1) The combat is fundamentally flawed by what I have to attribute to not enough/intelligent QA testing and some design choices I would have left out, namely that the level differences appear to follow a WoW mechanism, so even +1 level over your characters is gigantic.  You will do less damage to the higher level while at the same time missing more and hitting them less often - and they will do just about x2 your damage on every hit.
2) Attacks of Opportunity:  A good idea and works for many games, but opponents either have an abundant supply of APs or the design never took into account facing or put a limit upon how many 'Attacks of Opportunity' could fire off for one enemy in a single round.  So, don't think just because something is facing away from you that you'll be able to dash off, even if that same bad guy just got an 'Attack of Opportunity' a second ago on one of your allies.
3) Line of Sight:  This can be extremely frustrating sometimes.  Look carefully at your elevation especially or you're going to send an arrow into the dirt when you can't afford it.
4) Get used to the Quick Save button.  I'm not kidding.  Don't be ashamed to use the Quick Load either.  Sometimes you'll just get into fights that you can't win and you should mark them on the map and deal with them after you level (or add more npc followers).
5) Fights seem to all be geared towards a large player group.  Address every fight as if your life depends on it, because that's how every fight seems to be designed.  Room-for-error is minimal.  Be VERY careful when you are clicking because the mouse can go from pathing to a targetting in a millisecond if your mouse strays and that can land one of your characters right in the middle of mobs, and I've had it happen at the worst moments.
6) Music soundtrack reminds me of King's Bounty.  This is good often but sometimes odd.  I would have gone a different route with the composition personally, but that's just me being picky.
7) Some sounds seem to be overlooked.  If anyone ever hears a fountain's water, I'd be curious to know.  I'm running 7.1 speakers.
8) No day/night cycle, at least not in the first act so far?  Odd choice.  Kills a relatively easy point of immersion.
9) Some bugs.  I've experienced a crash once in-game and several when attempting to exit.  Nothing that's caused me to lose game time yet, thankfully.
All-in-all, Divinity: Original Sin is a beautiful RPG with some unique twists on combat mechanics.  It mostly succeeds so far, though I'm sure I'm still early into the game.   I'm having fun and that's what matters.  I'd like to not find myself yelling in frustration during combats so often though, but believe me, I'm going to be stacking my group at every opportunity from this point on as a result.  My class choices may not have been optimal and I'm keeping my group small, so consider that before you get deep into the game.  I certainly will if I ever do a replay through myself.

Yes, some of the quests are unfair. Yes, the game has some rough edges. But I have yet to see any decent PC RPG that didn't have some bugs. Heck, PC RPGs are such a big, lumbering animal, it's hard to envision every scenario that the player might carry out. PC RPG fans already know this.  This really is a successor to the Infinity Engine games of yore. Hammer that "Buy" button now if you know what this means. However, if you're still on the fence or new to this type of game, keep reading.
The reason I focus so much on the game's percieved shortcomings is that it they aren't really shortcomings at all. They're simply artifacts of a genre that that doesn't coddle the player. It's up to YOU to figure out how YOUR character and YOUR party will handle a situation. Whether it's by hacking down the locked door with a sword, carefully scouring the surroundings for a key, talking the skeleton guard out of opening the way for you or having the perception to notice the switch hidden behind the picture that unlocks the door, the choices are yours.
Divinity: Original Sin presents an astounding breadth of player choice that encourages endless tinkering, trial and error or just out-and-out hack-and-slash gameplay. It has a huge world to explore and the adventure unfolds slowly and deliberately. Combat is measured, precise, highly tactical, and difficult without ever being unfair. There's an excellent crafting system in the game that encourages experimentation. There's a fully fledged RPG construction kit included in the game. And there's honest to goodness co-op mode, a feature that hasn't been seen in a PC RPG since Baldur's Gate.
Seriously: What are you waiting for?

If you're a fan of the original Divine Divinity (or the series as a whole), you will not be disapointed with OS. Staple mechanics are here (lock picking, pyramid teleporters, crafting food and potions by collecting ingredients out in the world), some of which are recognisably the classic Div Div systems (the skill-up system is pleasingly familiar, whilst also being greatly expanded), and some of which are fresh new additions.
Perhaps best of all for series fans, the lore, setting and characters are all intact. The Legion are around in their various garrisons and forts, Arhu is on-hand to dispense wisdom and advice, and, of course, the Source is present and correct (or  rather, corrupt).
Beyond Div's simultaneous 2 character system works even better in OS. In fact, it's chalk and cheese, and any painful memories you may have of that game's controls, or the notorious Fergus will be wiped away. Your group can be split up and easily managed just by dragging the portraits around, so no worries there.
I never thought isometric RPGs could get better than Div Div, but OS takes the crown.

Is it worth the price label? I'd say yes if:
*You enjoy fantasy games.
*You can appreciate the fairytale atmosphere.
*You can appreciate the rhyming dialogues.
*You're a connoisseur of entrancing game soundtracks.
*You have a completionist attitude, and want to finish the game (which, in this case, ties in with the previous bullet point - the credits song is too amazing for words)
*You've heard of Coeur de Pirate, and realize she wrote the songs for this game.

D:OS is very similar to many traditional RPGs like the Infinity Engine games (Baldur's Gate etc). The view is top down, game is turn based and focus on party & space management, so if you liked those games you'll probably feel at home.
The game has a lot of good stuff that can surprise you. It's not completely open, but it's open enough that you don't feel like you're forced to walk down a corridor or something. Your biggest restrictions are usually going to be facing monsters of higher levels than yours, but with a good enough team you can still deal with those 'soft' barriers and just explore the way you want to.
The combat system resolves a lot around elemental manipulation. Basically, elemental spells in this game modifies the environment, which could be used for your advantage. For instance, you can drop oil on the ground, then set it on fire to cause damage over time. You can cast rain to create ponds of water, then use lightning spells to stun all enemies in the pond. These are very important during the early phases of the game since your characters usually have very limited options.
Character building is neat. It's possible to build absolutely overpowered characters that just break the game, but I think it's absolutely fine for a PvE game like this. Magic/skills are fairly diverse, it's not blazingly amazing but fits the game. A lot of elemental madness to tinker with.
It's not without problems though. The game's story is relatively weak. The writing is something you'll expect from a Divinity game, it's cheeky and not very serious (which can be a huge turn off if you're into a good story). The game is also very long, 80+ hours if you just try to finish every quest. Part of the reason is because battles take quite a long time and the fact that you have to spend quite a lot of time traveling. The combat, while very difficult early on, can be a breeze later when your characters have already been fully developed.
Overall I'd highly recommend. Do take note that it's quite time consuming though.

Do you like Titan Quest? Do you like post-apocalyptic environments? This game is for you.
Some of the Grim Dawn development team are folks that worked at Iron Lore, the developer that made Titan Quest, and it's built on the same game engine. You can kinda think of Grim Dawn as a bit of a "spiritual successor" to Titan Quest.
I threw down on this game back in April 2012. I played around with it a little during the pre-alpha and alpha phases. I had MASSIVE stability problems that ultimately led me to abandon it until things were a little more polished and bugs worked out, and of course, I was further distracted with other things.
So, I finally jumped back in when I read that it was content-complete and officially released. I'm not very far in, but I haven't experienced a single crash since, absolutely smooth sailing. In the past, it would've crashed on me at least three times by now, but seems we're good to go so far. My video card config has changed dramatically, not sure if that had anything to do with increased stability, but at any rate, it's never run this stable for me before. I can finally enjoy this game I paid for 4 years ago.
The game world is beautiful, much more detailed and attractive than I can recall the last time I played it. I'm still discovering a lot of things that weren't there the last time I played, like the devotion system, for example.
Grim Dawn falls under the hack/slash/loot ARPG category and formula. If you dig games like the aforementioned Titan Quest or Diablo II or Dungeon Siege (referring to 1 and 2 only), etc, then you may want to check out Grim Dawn, I'm confident you won't be disappointed.
