A 2D strategy game from a top-down perspective that isn’t a tower defense. Now that is something you don’t see very often on Steam. Don’t worry, there will be plenty of defense and offense going on, but it’s packaged in a different scenario than a run-of-the-mill fantasy setting involving the undead and their beef with the plants. Raid on Coasts is about the perpetual combat from the Middle East. A daring Steam debut from Outlaw Wars, a one-man team which relies on player feedback, not just taking advice into consideration.
Two superpowers fighting for control of Yemen and its coasts. Why is it a strategic location worth starting WW3 over, don’t ask me. It’s never properly explained other than shown as an objective on a map. The first and so far only mission implemented in the Early Access is a raid featuring both the amphibious landings of the Russian Federation or the rapid response from the land-based army belonging to the United States of America. I’ll remind you that Yemen isn’t part of NATO and it has been plagued by civil war since 2015. Neither the insurgents nor the Yemeni government, are playable factions at the time of this writing.
With motives unclear, we’ll simply move on and presume that this scenario is part of the unforeseen future. But not too far ahead, since the armies sport contemporary equipment. Or at least the US troops do, since the Russians seem to be disadvantaged from the start. While still in use (as far as historical accuracy is concerned), the T-72 is outclassed by the M1 Abrams in nearly all regards. Sure, a main battle tank won’t secure towns (you need infantry for that purpose), but they’ll “level to the ground” any opposition so they’re ideal for the modern frontline.
Raid on Coasts is being powered by the Construct 2 Personal Engine. I don’t mind the change of scenery from Unity, but any game that doesn’t have screenshot support, has already shot itself in the foot. Fortunately, the developer has addressed this issue within a few days of my review. Other than that, the sprites are skillfully drawn and they prove that even an RTS can benefit from a more unconventional perspective. The unit roster will receive more troops in subsequent updates, but even as it stands now, you’ll have plenty of options which sadly don’t take into account the map diversity just yet. As in, that single map can only get you so far. The Yemeni coastline will surely accommodate more battlefields soon enough. Just be aware that the current version of the game is indeed in an Early Access phase.
No narration or voice acting, but the troops on both sides of the front feature a handful of repetitive lines that really need some attention from the developer. Perhaps the Russians will actually speak Russian for a change? This isn’t the infamous airport level from Modern Warfare 2 afterall. A proper soundtrack at this point, would be like icing on the cake but one can still hope, right?
Top-down or not, the gameplay will be familiar to all strategy fans. It’s a real time formula that places less of an emphasis on strengths or weaknesses and more on sheer numbers and how fast you can cover/conquer the ground. There are three types of strategic locations: big or small villages and oil refineries. The former may be converted into military bases capable of recruiting all the units you need, while the latter shall keep the mechanized segment of your army, on the move. As simple as that. Securing those locations depends more often than not on the size of your dispatched forces, but having some bazooka/RPG squads tagging along for the ride, is a sound plan. They’ll make a short work of the tanks which are the true threat to your success.
Air units are implemented in a limited manner. Bases can be upgraded to 3 maximum tiers and on the last one, you gain access to AI-controlled attack helicopters which defend the HQ or bombing runs from jet fighters stationed on aircraft carriers off the coast. So the Artificial Intelligence really won’t allow much room for maneuver, if you thought that you can control warplanes directly. On the map I managed to play and test out, most matches last for about half an hour, depending on the difficulty you select before starting the mission. You can obviously choose between the aggressors or the defenders while the newly added Steam Achievements should unlock after reaching the correspondent objectives.
I’m really glad that Outlaw Wars slashed the initial price tag in half to better reflect the Early Access stage its project finds itself in. The potential for a full fledged campaign is there and within time, I shall readdress the rating to reflect that. The game is in dire need of a lot of things, starting with more maps and missions. An expanded unit roster, especially for the ill-equipped Russian faction, would certainly reflect the current historic status of ongoing modernization. The T-14 Armata, for example. That tank would make target practice from a T-72, to say the least.
Edit: Screenshot support has been added.
+ Pleasant graphics.

+ Interesting concept and execution.
- Needs more maps/scenarios.
- Limited sound selection.
- No Steam Trading Cards.

South Park: The Videogame. Very, very faithful to its license indeed, and it definitely succeeds in recreating the SP atmosphere in videogame form. This is not a full-fledged RPG though - there is barely any choice at all besides character customization and development. The story is completely linear and dialog is one-sided with the player character being always on the receiving end. On the bright side, combat is surprisingly developed, with some elements like button-mashing and QTEs feeling strangely refreshing, rather than annoying. Enemy variety is ample too. Can't say there is any replayability though, because all skills and perks are combat-related, and you could max out most skills in one playthrough anyway, and player class does not really affect gameplay that much. There are also metroidvania elements with parts of the world locked behind ability wall, with required abilities being unlocked via story progression.
Interface and controls are rather clunky in some cases. Certain abilities like buddy command for example, are nothing more than gimmicks with one or two uses per buddy in the whole game.
With all that being said, if you are not a fan of South Park - steer clear. This game is obnoxious as hell and includes farts,♥♥♥♥♥♥ dookie people, hobo hunting, anal probing and the list goes on.

Battlefront II is an old game now and has stood the test of time.  Even compared to modern shooters it is still fun and has many modes, elements and features not seen in many modern shooters. The game contains many fun and exciting game modes that are enjoyable for a long time after purchase.
The campgain will be the first mode that most play.  The campaign is simple and is similar to its predecessor.  Since this game came out prior to Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith, it will loosely follow the events leading up to the movie.  The gameplay for the campaign, multiplayer and other modes follow a simple capture the command point style.  Through the campaign you will be introduced to the game mechanics and character classes.  In all though the story is somewhat boring and seems to be hastely thrown together in order to have the game released for the movie.  I would also argue that the campaign is more difficult and maybe slightly less fun than its predecessor.
There are a few differences in Battlefront II.  One is that there are playable heroes and elite characters that can be unlocked in battle, and these aren't just limited to jedi and sith.  In Battlefront I each side would be aided by an almost undefeatable jedi or sith.  This has changed in Battlefront II.  The special heroes are unlocked after a human controlled character has unlocked enough points.  These heroes vary in type and abilities.  There are also more elite level classes that are unlocked after a certain points threshhold has been reached.  These new heroes and classes are some of the many things that add a lot of freshness and replayability to the game.  The second main addition to the game is space battles.  These battles include dogfighting and destroying enemy fleets.  An interesting ability in these modes is that engineers can repair the fleet and brave soldiers can attempt to land, invade and destroy ships from the inside.
The other modes in the game are largely unchanged from Battlefront I.  These include instant action mode where friends can play versus bots, galactic conquest which is a risky style strategy game, and online multiplayer.
Overall Battlefront II is a great game and makes me long for Battlefront III.  The campaign is not the best, and definately not a selling point on its own.  The most fun will come from galactic conquest, instant action and multiplayer with friends. If you have not tried any of the Battlefront games, this is a must try, especially on steam sale.

In my opinion this is the best ARPG currently on the market. It plays a lot like Diablo 2 and Titan Quest but with nice graphics.
It is a loot-based game which focuses on boss farming to acquire good loot (like in Diablo 2 and not like in Diablo 3 where you farm whole areas to get loot). While your character gets better when you level up and spend points on your stats and skills, you can be godlike when you have godlike gear.
The game has 6 "pure" classes with its own skill tree. You can dual-class which gives a total of 21 possible classes (15 dual classes and 6 pure classes). The skill system is very in-depth but still easy to understand and the possibilities of different builds are very enormous. The max level is 85, after finishing the game at normal difficulty you will be around level 50 and there are two more difficulties.
There is also a Hardcore mode, multiplayer, an extensive crafting system and an achievements system.
Overall a very good game, I would recommend it! The replay value is really high and if you like ARPGs you can expect a few hundred hours of fun from this game.

Update: A recent update to the game has apparently fixed the "Runglish" translation and it should now be much easier to read. This pretty much negates my only complaint about the game, so TLDR upfront: Play it. It's free. Do it right now.
Before I start listing how much I really enjoyed this game, I should point out the game's biggest flaw: It's translation. Almost every single line of dialog in the entire game has some sort of gramatical error or typo. It's almost as if they just copy-pasted the entire script into google translate. I had to re-read parts of the game multiple times to truely understand what was happening. It honestly makes the game feel like a chore to read.
With that said, the fact that I even kept playing the game is a testament to how well done it is. Without spoiling too much, it's a russian dating sim. This fact alone is interesting, dating sims not made in japan are quite rare. Unlike most dating sims I've played, however, the overarching story is a mystery and solving it is a central theme. The game has 14 endings: 6 good ends, 5 bad ends, 2 endings that could both be considered the "true" ending as they both give points that help paint in the big picture, and a free DLC story that also helps answer some questions. One of the worst endings in most dating sims, where the main character ends up with nobody, instead does a great job in getting the player hooked. It raises even more questions, and (at least in my case) makes you want to keep playing in order to find out what exactly is going on.
I feel like I got extremely lucky in which endings I got my first and second playthrough, as I feel both of those endings were the most interesting prior to the true ends. On the topic of endings, you need to have gotten a good ending in order to get one of the last girl's ends, and you need to have gotten all of the good endings in order to get the "true" ends. This means that if you're not willing to go through the game multiple times (which is helped by the ability to skip text at a fairly fast speed) then you're probably not going to get full enjoyment.
And onto my final point, the game's free. Completely free. Try it out, even if it turns out the game's not your cup of tea it didn't cost you a dime.

I understand why a lot of people do not like the 4th episode of Volition's critically acclaimed series. With the superpowers we now have the game is a bit too over-the-top. Also, there's no real new area here as the city of Steelport remained the same. It looks a bit different due to the alien invasion (actually, the huge alien ship in the air looks stunning and is pretty cool), but the areas remained the same.
So, in essence, Volition only added a new storyline which now sees our favourite gang pitted against the invading forces of an alien race. And the battle mainly takes place in a Steelport which is not a real city but the virtual reality version of an already destroyed place. So, as a nod to Matrix we, just like Neo, can easily do in this world whatever we want. With the superhuman abilities we can run up on the sides of buildings, can leap forward to great distances and following a charged-up jump we can glide in the air for a long time. This gameplay is similar to the one we had in Prototype so those of you who liked that franchise will see that this one plays pretty familiar.
The downside this approach brings with itself is the fact that as you unlock fast running pretty early own there's no real point in driving any car in the game as getting from point A to point B is much easier by running, jumping and gliding instead of using any vehicles. In fact, later on running right next to people or cars make these fly away due to the sheer force of your fast speed so to a certain degree getting into a car while running is a bit difficult.
However, if you think about it Volition could not have gone in any other direction. After all, in The Third we already kicked the arses of the rival gangs of Steelport and even fought the government's so-called STAG programme. So, taking one step forward was obvious towards aliens. And the jokes and hilarious moments including some excellent cameos of famous people (Keith David, Roddy Piper, Neil Patrick Harris) are still there.
And this was always the real deal for me: how funny this franchise was, how silly the missions were and how great dialogues the Saints had. When completing the story and the game's many side missions I clocked around the same number of hours I did with The Third. For me, the 4th installment of the Saints did deliver and I think Volition did a great job once again.

Think about a person. Your closest friend, the one that you trust the most in life; your platonic life-partner. The Bill to your Ted. Starsky to your Hutch. Simon to your Garfunkel. This is the man who you would leave your children to in a sudden passing. The best man of your wedding. The one person in this world that you can rely on moreso than anyone else.
If you play Divinity: Original Sin with this person, they are also now officially Hitler.
You have created the modern day Hitler. Congratulations.
"But Thalarios, that's an incredibly offensive thing to say."
Well ambigious voice, I'll give it to you that it's a bold claim. But let me tell you why you've resurrected the late Führer from the depths of Hell, and I'll do so in 250 words or less.
Divinity: Original Sin is a single and multiplayer fantasy roleplaying game brought to be by the powers of Kickstarter. It puts you and a friend in the world of Rivellon to combat evil magicks and fight goblins and orcs and whatever other fantasy creatures they decide to throw at you. Skeletons probably. But what you didn't realize is that this game was brought to you by M. Night ♥♥♥♥ing Shamaylan because, plot twist, your real enemy is the godfather of your children, Hitler.
Are you going to play a melee hero? Your friend will obviously play a ranged hero, of course. And if you go ranged, they'll go melee. "To balance out the party" they'll say. "It'll be more fun this way." And you'll agree to this, because you are innocent to their true nature. I guess you never took Social Studies. Maybe you were too busy getting handies behind the football stadium from Victoria Blangfield.
And in the first couple fights, you'll laugh with him and say "Wow this turn-based combat is interesting! Did you see that explosive barrel you shot did damage to me?"
"Yeah." He'll say. "Yeah ain't that something."
"We better be careful about that stuff!" You'll trail off, too busy taking in the ambience of the game.
He won't reply.
You'll fight a few more encounters, and you'll laugh nervously as you get caught in his charges, or as his flame arrows ignite the ground you walk upon. Maybe he's just learning. I mean you're only level 1.
Flash forward.
You're level 5, enclosed by skeletons on every side. The claps of thunder above are the only thing that keep you awake through the pain and constant downpour of rain. But you know with your next turn you can finish the skeletons off. One mighty bladestorm is all it'll take.
You look at the iniative at the top of the screen.
Hitler is next.
"Hey man, hold your action until after I use my bladestorm. You can pick off any that are left," you pause for a laugh, "If there are any!"
There's a moment of silence before he speaks.
"I'm going to use my electric arrow to crowd control them all." he says.
"What? No, don't do it man." You're unsure if he's joking or not. "You're gonna CC me! It's raining, the electric will CC me!"
He doesn't say anything. You see his character charging up the shot.
"Come on man just let me do it!" You're reduced to pleading now. Pathetic, shameless pleading.  "We'll just finish this fight and then we can save so I can go grab those tickets to see Maroon 5 before they're sold out. The show's gonna be so sick bro!"
Too bad Adam Levine was born after World War 2. He let's the electric arrow loose. Every single skeleton resists his stun.
It's your turn now. Oh wait, Hitler just crowd controlled you. The skeletons beat on you until nothing's left but a bloodied pile of armor and regret. It's Hitler's turn. Oh look, another electric arrow. You haven't said a word since his last turn.
Stun fails again. He dies to the skeletons. Fade to black. Reload screen. Silence.
"I'll catch you later man, gonna hit the sack. Same time tomorrow?" he says and before you can answer he logs out.
You drive 45 minutes to get the tickets. They're sold out.

Child of Light follows the story of Aurora, a princess who has fallen into a deep sleep and awakes in the mythical land of Lemuria. Along the way Aurora meets strange friends who help her fight through the monsters of Lemuria in order to save her father from death. The game takes on many aspects of well known fairy tales such as Sleeping Beauty and is written entirely in iambic pentameter.
The Pros:
Combat - Combat is done in a jrpg style. It is indepth as well as entertaining. How combat centered the game will be is determined by your difficulty level. If you're the type of person who only wants a casual experiance and a story, great, you can breeze through the combat on easy. For those of you who enjoy a challenge, bump up the difficulty.
Art - If you take one look at the beautiful watercolors of Lemuria, you will see why so many people are drawn to this game. From dark forests to high cliffs and to under water palaces, the artsits behind Child of Light never fail to deliver a stunning, graceful, and beautiful scene.
The Cons:
Characters - All though it's obvious that Ubisoft Montreal wanted to make the game feel like a classic fairy tale, they may have succeeded all too well. The characters, though unique in their own way, vary little from their classic archetypes. Overall this has damaged the game for many people.
Overall, I would say buy the game. If you're overly concerned about the flat characters, buy the game when it's on sale. The experiance was enjoyable enough to play through it at least once, although I suspect that eventually I will play through the game again.

Upon first playing this, I was surprised at what a high quality game it is. Although checking the developer, I saw that they had made a couple of other games I really enjoyed, Zeno Clash 1 and 2 which are fantastic.
TDToM has got a lot of polish and everything looks and feels great. There's a lot of variety in the gameplay and combat and the level design is very innovative. Since you are climbing a giant tower, at any time you can just jump over the side and plummet through the air in freefall, picking up secrets and diving through rings as you fall. Then when you hit the bottom, just teleport back up to where you jumped from. Sometimes you'll want to backtrack to access previously locked areas with a new tool or weapon - no problem, just leap over the side and hurtle towards the general direction of where you want to end up.
The humor is pretty clever and will make you smile as you hear references to old and modern movies. The Director says some funny things and the art design is set up to look cheesy and fake. There are strings connected to the flying monsters and the robots are made from vacuum cleaner parts.
All in all this is a very innovative and cool game. If you like top-down ARPG's like How To Survive or Torchlight, you'll love TDToM. If you're looking to play something fresh and new you'll probably like it as well.

At first, I only thought of buying this game. I never really thought it was worth it.
Then, it went on sale.
(Do give off some credit, my friend actually bought this for me)
My friend bought the pack of four games to send to three other friends, and that was me and two other "chosen ones".
We were like "Why the Hell not? Seems pretty cool."
Then we got into the world. First of all, we were pretty amazed by the graphics in the game. We played through, and the free-running was an awesome addition to the game. For once in a game, it was okay to run from an enemy, from roof to roof escaping hordes of zombies.
And of course, the combat. You don't just have one option of combat; you can do a variety of different moves or use the environment around you to take out opponents. Not just "grab a weapon and swing at them" like a lot of other games, but using the spikes set up around the world to impale the creatures, drop kicking them into the spikes. In some way, throwing them off roofs. As they run at you, grab them and trip them over your foot and stomp on their heads afterwards. (There's some more that I could list but I can't list them off the top of my head right now.)
The story is also pretty good, nuff said.
And multiplayer is fun. This game, I find, was good multiplayer and singleplayer, but fooling around with your friends or running from nightmares at night is probably the most fun I've had in a co-op zombie game.

PROS:
The easiest way I can describe it is that it's concept reminds me of The Legend of Zelda but only if one character plays as Link where you're a little guy with a sword and the other plays as Ganon where you summon monsters of all kind after the little guy with the sword. It's a really fun concept and I can see Powerhoof is trying to take as much advantage of this as they can, which of coarse is FREAKING AWESOME! I like how you don't even need to power up all the eldritch stones to activate the portal to the boss and how it's a different monster with it's own unique mechanics depending on how many you have powered up.
This game is also a good example of how a video game doesn't need a real story what so ever to be enjoyable because it could leave your imagination up to do that if you wanted to like how it does for a silent protagonist's personality or motives. You can imagine the human as a hero and the ghost(s) as the villain, or the human as the villain or the ghost(s) as the hero(s), or there could be no good guy here at all but instead just poor souls fighting over a change at freedom and riches like a bunch of hungry wolves fighting over a dead rabbit. The possibilities are endless to what it could be happening down in the caverns.
CONS:
As fun as the game is and as much as I hate to admit it, the only thing that could make it complete is if they do put together a little online feature where you can play with friends from all over. Sure it's got local co-op AND I know that it's still on there to do list, but my point still stands that online is the only thing that's missing. But even with online still yet to be a reality, the game is pretty solid even when playing by yourself. Though when I played it by myself, I couldn't help but notice there's some slight kinks in the ghosts' AI. But it's still early access and these kinks do seem pretty minor like sometimes the ghosts would stay stuck in a corner for some reason, interracting with a trap that you're no where near which only happened once for me and they stopped obviously as soon as I left the room.
ALL IN ALL:
Really solid game, enjoyable even when playing by yourself, still waiting on that online even after a year and a bit but they can take there times since I'm sure they're getting to that soon.

It uttelry boggles me that this game is currently rated as "very positive" in relation to total overall  user reviews. The parkour is cheesy, the combat mechanics are horrid and tediously unnecessary (i.e. strike enemy, walk backwards, strike enemy, walk backwards...you see where I'm going with this). Weapon degeradation is the worse I've ever experienced in a game (nothing like watching your "metal" hammer deteriorate before your eyes after striking a "fleshy" zombie a few times). Come on! Steel hammer vs. human flesh...the degredation is borderline game braking, to the point of wondering whether or not the developers understand that metal is not similar in durabilty to that of cheap plastic - that principle has seemingly escaped them.
It's a casual game geared towards mindless persistence based player progression. Let me lay out the game in black and white:
- Start
- Obtain mindless mission with weak plot given to you by a parkour instructor that was looking to train/teach potential clientele prior to the zombie apocalpsye??!! What the...
- Jump from rooftop A to rooftop B using annoying "parkour" skills
- Avoid horde of Zombies
- Attack small group of zombies using various weapons with awkward stats
- "Level up" - if that is what you call it in this game
- Collect metal parts to repair the weapons that are continuously damaged in the process of beating down zombies while leaping around like a wannabe dare devil
- Obtain another mission....rinse and repeat
Oh yeah! Don't forget about the tower the game is centered around. It is "full" of people that are somehow reliant on "just you" to do all their work for them (yeah! the main base of operations is saturated with incompetent helpless souls). They have weapons, they have the numbers, but they can't collect the continuous airdrops that bring in their desperatly needed medical supplies; which, are only guarded by 3 or so humans each time - I guess only a single human being is capable of such a task - *rolls eyes*.
If the aformentioned information hasn't made you reconsider purchasing this game, at least make sure to buy it when it is $20 or less. Simply put, this game is not worth $60 when taking into consideration other titles that are avaialble. Otherwise, just buy/rent/borrow a cheesy zombie movie and watch a few parkour "fails" on youtube. That alone is far more entertaining, in my opinion.

This is a really goofy game, which you will probably have guessed if you have watched the trailer. Basically it's a parody of the old sci fi/monster flicks of the 50's and 60's, with their camp stories and dodgy special effects. In fact, the game actually recreates the stop motion style animation from those old films. The effect is actually pretty good and like a lot of other stuff, really sells the premise. I normally hate effects like film grain in my games, but with this title, it's just such a part of the atmospere they are aiming for that for once I kept it on. Another amusing feature is that the whole game is themed as a commentary by the director being recorded in a studio for the upcoming release of the movie on DVD. It's pretty funny stuff and the director himself is an over the top caricature of the cliche egomaniacal self deluded Hollywood mogul. It's all pretty corny but it fits the vibe and made me smile.
I just wish the game behind everything was as good as the premise. Its pretty much standard action adventure fare. You'll collect different weapons, collect different coloured cogs with which to upgrade those weapons. You'll solved side missions that will get you skill points that you can use to upgrade basic character stats like energy and health regeneration. You'll do some basic platforming and beat the crap out of a whole ton of monsters. There are some basic puzzles, some of which can only be solved by one of the three playable characters/ None of it is actually bad, its just not anything you haven't done in  other games before. I think it just feels like more of a shame because the premise begs for a more solid gameplay experience. It never really rises above okay. Probably the best and most unique part of it is climbing the tower itself. The tower really goes way way up, and you can jump off and pretty much fall all the way off back to the ground levels where you started without seeing a single loading screen (And to get some secrets, you will have to). This really adds to the tower's sense of scale and is definitely a highlight.
I do recommend this game if you dig the theme. I had fun with my playthrough, but I couldn't help wishing for a more unique gameplay experience.

Battlefront II is an old game now and has stood the test of time.  Even compared to modern shooters it is still fun and has many modes, elements and features not seen in many modern shooters. The game contains many fun and exciting game modes that are enjoyable for a long time after purchase.
The campgain will be the first mode that most play.  The campaign is simple and is similar to its predecessor.  Since this game came out prior to Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith, it will loosely follow the events leading up to the movie.  The gameplay for the campaign, multiplayer and other modes follow a simple capture the command point style.  Through the campaign you will be introduced to the game mechanics and character classes.  In all though the story is somewhat boring and seems to be hastely thrown together in order to have the game released for the movie.  I would also argue that the campaign is more difficult and maybe slightly less fun than its predecessor.
There are a few differences in Battlefront II.  One is that there are playable heroes and elite characters that can be unlocked in battle, and these aren't just limited to jedi and sith.  In Battlefront I each side would be aided by an almost undefeatable jedi or sith.  This has changed in Battlefront II.  The special heroes are unlocked after a human controlled character has unlocked enough points.  These heroes vary in type and abilities.  There are also more elite level classes that are unlocked after a certain points threshhold has been reached.  These new heroes and classes are some of the many things that add a lot of freshness and replayability to the game.  The second main addition to the game is space battles.  These battles include dogfighting and destroying enemy fleets.  An interesting ability in these modes is that engineers can repair the fleet and brave soldiers can attempt to land, invade and destroy ships from the inside.
The other modes in the game are largely unchanged from Battlefront I.  These include instant action mode where friends can play versus bots, galactic conquest which is a risky style strategy game, and online multiplayer.
Overall Battlefront II is a great game and makes me long for Battlefront III.  The campaign is not the best, and definately not a selling point on its own.  The most fun will come from galactic conquest, instant action and multiplayer with friends. If you have not tried any of the Battlefront games, this is a must try, especially on steam sale.

I love this game. I honestly enjoyed it very much. I was able to buy this game during a good sale and so I was really pleased with the value for money of the game. Though completing the game was faster than I imagined, it turned out to be a pleasant surprise because it felt worth it. Also because I know that there's going to be a sequel.
Just several things as to why I think this game is worth playing/buying (on a sale if possible):
1. Soundtrack/Music: Absolutely wonderful. I have to say that the music had a huge part in giving the proper atmosphere and mood throughout the game. It makes no wonder as to why the Soundtrack is being sold. It gives a beautiful and extremely adequate pairing with this nordic, medieval game.
2. Art: The game shows a unique style of art that is not like the other games that boasts on some high-tech digital art rendering but classic and beautiful drawn art or seemingly drawn. There is no want for skill involved in the making of the game, even the landscapes and sceneries involved are pleasant to see.
3. Story: Playing the game left me wanting for more. I immediately got myself immersed in the storyline of each character. You can tell that the background of the story is quite rich and has a lot of potential, truly gives you the unique feeling of living in the medieval ages or the nordic ages which I crave for.
4. Gameplay: I enjoyed the mix of the RPG and strategy that the game uses. It is simple enough that it doesn't overcomplicate things but interesting and versatile enough that there is room for strategising and being challenged. Additionally, the game provides players with decision making options that alters, whether significantly or not (Most consider not), the story line. This dependence on the user decision is what is lacking in most RPGs today and it is very nice to see it being used here. Although not an open world type of a game, it gives a certain feeling of freedom and adventure.
For these reasons I recommend this game. Especially if there's a sale, very worth it. I guess one thing I love about the game is really the potential it has to be developed into a classic masterpiece. I hope it does reach that level. Nonetheless, I think everyone should give this game a try.

I have 159 games in my Steam account. I have never felt the need to review a game until now. This is the game Diablo 3 should have been and in one respect, the game Diablo 2 should have been. Besides all of the other high points brought up by other reviewers the following points are what make it the best Diablo type game I have ever played.
1. All of the areas are connected and not sealed until you complete a quest. This suites my play style enormously. I spend most of the game charging ahead as fast as I can until I need to go back and level up because I can't go any farther as my character is not strong enough. When I feel so inclined I will complete a quest or perhaps read some quest  related  material and that is priceless. Play whichever way you want.
2. No Torchlight/Diablo 3 style large ramps connecting areas in dungeons. There are actually doorways to make a stand in and structures and dungeons feel and look realistic because of that architectural decision.
3. Not just a handful but tons of claustrophobic dungeons that definitely gives the game the feel of descending into the dungeons of  Diablo for the first time.
4. Lots of monster variety. I have played 48.7 hours to date and just found a new monster type this morning in another dungeon linked to a quest. Outstanding.
5. Many of those quests so instead of blowing through each difficulty level simply to get to the next one I want to take the time to immerse myself and explore the world.
6. Shotguns. I carry one around as a swordfighter just to take some potshots now and again.
At $25 this game is a steal if you are a fan of the genre.
(I did not like Titan Quest if that makes a difference to anyone.)

Everlasting Summer's main strength is its metacommentary on the nature of visual novels, or at least that large subset of visual novels based around choosing one of some number of girls to pursue as a romantic partner (often to the exclusion of all others). It's interesting enough, and all of that could be grafted onto any of those other visual novels without a great deal of difficulty. But commentary alone does not make a game, and all the meta stuff is built around a straightforward example of that same genre, which example unfortunately isn't all that great.
It's slow. It's repetitive. The different characters' routes don't branch off until fairly late in the game, meaning there are a whole lot of scenes with every girl that play out the same no matter what you've already said to them, and you have to go through them all over and over again. Even in full skip mode, this takes a while. The same basic dynamic is at play in most conversations, so even once you finally get onto an individual route, you can skip most of the new dialogue without fear of missing anything. Fortunately(?) only maybe half the girls are particularly likable to begin with, and even one of them is secretly psychotic, which... pretty much goes unremarked upon. But you need to woo
to get into the real meta stuff, as well as consult a guide or else make some very specific guesses. (Should you eat an apple or not? Who knows?) And along the way, it feels like about a quarter of everyone's lines are "it's nothing" and variants on the same, as everyone does their best to avoid saying anything about themselves at all, especially the player character. Even when characters have sex they can't quite bring themselves to mention what they're doing, and words like "relationship" or "girlfriend" are simply not part of the lexicon.
Graphics vary. The sprites aren't perfect but are certainly attractive, and almost everyone has huge breasts, in case you're into that. The 10-year-old (or whatever) girl doesn't, but the game does make sure you see her panties pretty much every chance it gets. Some of the CGs are pretty, others not as much. Nudity is brief. Sex is possibly all consensual, but making that clear was obviously not a priority, given the pained expressions and frequent lack of framing. There's some variety in music tracks but nothing incredibly memorable. Programming is mostly just primitive RenPy stuff, apart from the card game, which claims to be based on poker scoring but... isn't. (Unless there's some Russian version of poker where straights don't exist and two pair beats three of a kind.) Honestly none of the graphics or music or anything are
, and they could make for quite a pleasant experience paired with likable characters and less repetitive dialogue and game structure, but that was not to be.
(Note that I do not speak Russian. The English translation is clumsy, but if you do, that clumsiness won't be an issue for you and you'll probably understand more of the jokes. Besides, there's talk of the translation improving over time, so I didn't focus on that.)
(Yes, it's free. Yes, it had a troubled development that probably excuses a lot of the writing problems. But neither of those facts mean you should actually play this.)

I understand why a lot of people do not like the 4th episode of Volition's critically acclaimed series. With the superpowers we now have the game is a bit too over-the-top. Also, there's no real new area here as the city of Steelport remained the same. It looks a bit different due to the alien invasion (actually, the huge alien ship in the air looks stunning and is pretty cool), but the areas remained the same.
So, in essence, Volition only added a new storyline which now sees our favourite gang pitted against the invading forces of an alien race. And the battle mainly takes place in a Steelport which is not a real city but the virtual reality version of an already destroyed place. So, as a nod to Matrix we, just like Neo, can easily do in this world whatever we want. With the superhuman abilities we can run up on the sides of buildings, can leap forward to great distances and following a charged-up jump we can glide in the air for a long time. This gameplay is similar to the one we had in Prototype so those of you who liked that franchise will see that this one plays pretty familiar.
The downside this approach brings with itself is the fact that as you unlock fast running pretty early own there's no real point in driving any car in the game as getting from point A to point B is much easier by running, jumping and gliding instead of using any vehicles. In fact, later on running right next to people or cars make these fly away due to the sheer force of your fast speed so to a certain degree getting into a car while running is a bit difficult.
However, if you think about it Volition could not have gone in any other direction. After all, in The Third we already kicked the arses of the rival gangs of Steelport and even fought the government's so-called STAG programme. So, taking one step forward was obvious towards aliens. And the jokes and hilarious moments including some excellent cameos of famous people (Keith David, Roddy Piper, Neil Patrick Harris) are still there.
And this was always the real deal for me: how funny this franchise was, how silly the missions were and how great dialogues the Saints had. When completing the story and the game's many side missions I clocked around the same number of hours I did with The Third. For me, the 4th installment of the Saints did deliver and I think Volition did a great job once again.

What King of Dragon Pass could have been, as a turn-based strategy game rather than resource management / Viking Spreadsheets.  Beautiful illustrations, extremely atmospheric, interesting plot (pseudo-norse clans running around with giants), and a smoothly polished squad-based combat system.  The gameplay is split about equally between combat encounters, and choose-your-own-adventure / visual novel style decision-making.
The combat system has two big components -- armor and strength.  Strength is both an attack stat and health, and armor lowers an attacker's effective strength.  There's a stat for how good you are at breaking armor, willpower points you can spend to deal just one more damage or move one more square, and another stat that lets you spend more willpower points per action.  I haven't seen a system like it before, but I am growing to like it.
A+, if you see it on sale and don't buy it you're nuts.
[EDIT] : It's worth noting that it DOES end very abruptly, and seems to be episodic in nature (which could have been more clearly marked..?).  It sort of feels like the game ends immediately after a midboss, though I couldn't put my finger on why.  Probably because they were running for most of the game -- and then their plans don't change after the boss dies.  Either way, I will be playing through it a few more times to see how the story goes with different decisions.

Having played FTL through multiple times, and fallen in love with the game over and over, I can officially say you should take what I'm about to say with a grain of salt. With that out of the way, I love this game.
Story
The story of FTL is a simple, yet effective one, providing just enough backstory to set the player into the universe. The galaxy was controlled by the Federation, a coalition between humans and various other races, such as the robotic Engi, and the hyper-intelligent Zoltans, until the Rebellion came. Humans were fed up with being equal with other races, and led a successful rebellion against the Federation, all but destroying it. You are the commander of a small Federation cruiser, holding the only information that can help the Federation win the war. Your task is to fly through the galaxy, racing against the Rebels, to get to the last Federation base, and inform them of the weakness of the Rebel fleet.
Gameplay:
FTL is played from a top-down perspective, with you, the player, in control of a spaceship, requiring you to manage weapons, shields, engines, etc. to keep the ship alive in the depths of an unforgiving galaxy. When I say unforgiving, I mean unforgiving.  Just about everything is out to get you: Pirates, Rebel Ships, and Giant Alien Spiders make up only a tiny portion of the people who want to tear your ship apart peice by peice. You have to survive the constant onslaught with just your wits, carefully balancing your systems and crew to quickly end conflicts with as little damage as possible. In between events, you jump from point to point on a map of your current sector, which can hold shops, distress signals, and other miscellaneous warp points. As you travel through the galaxy, you'll acquire new crew, weapons, and systems to fight the ever-stronger enemies, in an arms race to the Federation Base, culminating into a final boss fight that will put your ship, and your skills, to the test. This game is not easy by any stretch of the imagination, and even on easy mode you will find yourself dying over and over. If you can get past the difficulty curve of the game, you'll find that it offers a very deep and rewarding experience, which will keep you coming back time and again.
Visuals:
The visuals in FTL are simplisitic, and two-dimensional, this doesn't mean that they are bad however. The game's art is fantastic, with the various ships, weapons, and aliens all having a unique look that suits their particular traits. The environments in this game are gorgious, with backgrounds of deep space, nebulae, and planets that never seem to get old.
Writing:
FTL's writing is funny, adding a bit of levity to an overall tense game. Many of the random events are incredibly out in left field, and the writing capitalizes on this, such as in the case of the aforementioned Giant Spiders. That said, the writing isn't all jokes, and also does a fantastic job of building the universe. In many of the encounters you are offered a chance to let enemy ships surrender, with really humanizes each encounter, and provides a moral dillemma with each ship you encounter. Often the rebels really aren't that dedicated to the cause, and are just average joes conscripted to help, and whether you should kill them or not is up to you.
Music:
One of the best aspects of this game is it's sound design. This game has one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard in a video game, with beautiful ambient music to accompany the lulls in the action, and tense tracks during tough battles. All the music in FTL is very electronic, most easily described as a mix of Chiptune, Ambient, and Trance. The music is relaxing enough to play a long session without getting boring, and engaging enough to keep you on the edge of your seat during some of the harder fights in the game. The sound effects of the various weapons, crew, and environmental hazards all fit perfectly, and can repeat without ever sound grating or annoying. Overall, the sounds and music in FTL add just as much to the experience as the visuals, if not a bit more.
Problems:
For all that I've said about the game being fantastic, it does have a bit of a flaw that some people may find irritating. The way you unlock ships straddles the border between a good progress system, and an annoying grind, especially with many of the type B or random event ships. To unlock Type B cruisers, you must complete two of the corresponding ship's achievements, which can be anything from a normal run, to a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ (I'm looking at you Rock Cruiser.) On top of that, there's a secret ship
which has two methods of unlocking: Complete a series of random events, dependent upon about fifty thousand different dice rolls going perfectly, or beat the game with every other ship's (excluding the new Lanius cruiser) Type A and Type B configurations.  That said, none of the ships are objectively better than the others, and are really just built to suit different playstyles.
Final Thoughts:
FTL is a great game that will provide hours of entertainment, for a bargain price of $10, about the same as going to a movie. If you feel that FTL might not be the game for you, I recommend waiting until it goes on sale to try it. For those of you intrigued by the concept of a spaceship simulator, or like strategy games, buy it. You won't be disappointed.

It's officially Telltale Season, folks. Mere days after Tales From The Borderlands (which I quite unexpectedly loved) comes another hotly anticipated license (or rather, license of a license): Game of Thrones, the game based on a hit TV show based on a series of very big books. As it usually happens, Telltale game tells an original story with a number of similarly original characters (and some cameos from the critically-acclaimed main cast), but how truly original it really is? The answer so far is: not very.
The whole episode felt like a re-imagining of George R.R. Martin's story and settings with different names and faces. Telltale writers knew how much people like Starks, for example, and the Forrester family you play as (or at least, they make up two out of three POV characters so far) are just that: a watered-down less important version of Starks. Here we have a noble family of Northerners plagued by misfortune. They're not Starks though, they're Forresters. Here's the matriarch of the family, widow to her slain Lord husband. She's not Catelyn Stark though, she's Lady Forrester.  Here's their young inexperienced son, who has to grow up quickly and learn to be a proper lord. He's not Robb Stark, however. His name is young Bob Dylan... sorry, Ethan Forrester. As for their eldest daughter, who is totally not Sansa Stark, but Mira Forrester, well, she is in King's Landing, surrounded by hypocrisy and intrigue... Well, you get the idea. For Pete's sake, they even have a Forrester clone of Rickon!
There's very little about the first episode that actually feels new. Familiar terms like "small council" are uttered, familiar names are spoken, and some familiar faces are shown, and that's almost it. Telltale dedicated too much time to shameless fan service at the expense of their own storytelling, and that leaves a bitter aftertaste.
Presentation also deserves some gripe. Just last week I was singing praises to Telltale Tool's unexpectedly good performance in Tales From the Borderlands (the game didn't stutter at all during action scenes displayed at a breakneck pace). Game of Thrones, however, looks and performs significantly worse. I assume this has to do with more "reality-oriented" art style (compared to TFTB and also The Wolf Among Us) that the engine often fails to handle. As a result, everything and everyone looks just a tad more realistic, but significantly uglier. Not the best trade-off, in my opinion.
And despite its many shortcomings, I still liked it. It was more or less a fun (that's probably not the right word to use here) experience, and I'm looking forward to the next episode, but this story just has to pick up from now on. Game of Thrones of the Show of the Book has to stand on its own two legs, stop flaunting its considerable TV show assets and make me care about its own ostensibly original characters and their exploits.

I like it.  It's a bit too over-the-top at times (the director can get a little annoying with his commentary) but overall this is quite an enjoyable action game.  The B-grade sci-fi movie trope is a lot of fun, and while the jokes are juvenile at times, it wasn't enough to make me dislike the game; But do expect to groan loudly at the purile humor.
I very much enjoyed the ability to upgrade weapons and character traits, and while most of the powers were underutilized (most of the time being used as plot-drivers, ie: Need ability X to cross here), they were varied enough to give you some relief from using the same tactics over and over.  It was possible to mix it up and that's fun.
The vertical component to this game coupled with the open-world-like map feels great and helps the game from wearing out its welcome too soon.  Back tracking is necessary if you want to unlock everything, but a liberal spread of teleporters and the ability to teleport back to a ledge you fell off of makes this fairly painless.
The downside?  The camera.  You have no control over it and at times it feels like the camera is out to get you.   The first problem is that it can pick strange angles to view the action, but mostly what got to me is how slow it transients when you are falling.  For example, some of the jumps required strict timing, and when you leap into the air and the camera sort of pauses before adjusting -- and does so at a leisurely pace -- it would mean I'd miss something or crash into a pipe or ledge I had no idea was there.  This becomes particularly frustrating when you're looking for secrets;  I spent most of my time just trying to trick the camera into showing me something so I could learn if it held a secret or not.
The game also feels a little too easy, but the developers have a Hard Mode (I recommend enabling if it you're a vet of twin-stick action games like this) and a Survival Mode to offset that.
A very solid game worth about 10 hours of play, with an enjoyable tongue-and-cheek subject matter and enough hidden secrets to make you want to take your time and really get to know the world.  I recommend it.

First of all, let me clarify that I've played this game much more than 86.8 hours.  I originally bought the retail version in a store.  I don't even remember where or when.  Once Steam had it for sale, I bought it again.  I figured I'd have two copies in case a friend wanted to try the game.
Second, this game, and more importantly it's mods, have consistently been tops in my heart as my favorite game of all-time!  The original Starcraft is second place.  Everything else I played for awhile and stopped playing or only playing it sparingly.  Mount & Blade is the only game that I always come back to.
Why do I like it so much?  To me, it feels like a true First Person knights and armor game where my skill actually matters and you can create an army that grows in skill with you, the more they fight, gain experience and don't die.  Your skills in healing and surgery, for example, helps to prevent them from getting killed.  Instead, they'll more likely get knocked unconscious.  Saves you time on recruitment.  However, if you rescue prisoners from an enemy army, then you can get a large amount of reinforcements quickly.
Army:  Best part of this game is the option to either ride solo and fight in tournaments, bandits, help townsfolk, cities and trade goods to make money that way or fight and make money.  The other option is to recruit townsfolk and/or hire mercenaries and build up an army to fight with/for you.  Every time you defeat an opposing army, you loot them for coins, items and the ones you knock unconscious you can sell to slave traders or keep for ransom money (enemy lords).  Plus, with an army, you can conquer enemy towns and cities for a lord you pledge loyalty to OR you conquer everyone yourself and take the whole map for your own kingdom.  Some mods offer more options in this area and also include storylines where you have to defeat the whole map before an incoming invading army arrives.  Takes awhile but is very fun along the way.
As for mods, TLD (The Last Days of the Third Age / Tolkien mod) is by far the best and most mod of them all.  It adds many enhancements and custom everything to the original game, and Warband if you prefer that one, and then follows the events of the books for you to carry out.  The only downside is that it's always been very buggy unless you follow their instructions on best setup to use.  My other favorite is Sword of Damocles.  It adds new units and tons of new items as well as additional town and city options, new barracks and unit generation tools, plus that storyline above about the incoming invading army. =)
Archery:  My archery skills, for example, rely on my aim, not just mashing buttons.  For example, I've hit targets I can barely even see (have to use the zoom feature to see if my arrow was close) and I'll get a hit or a kill.  When I do, it'll tell me the difficulty of that shot.  My favorite is hitting moving targets on my horse.  I have to aim like you would in real life.
Swordplay and Blocking:  They are a bit more structured, but they still have enough variety to make it interesting.  You have to block, for example, the same direction as the incoming swing or they'll hit you.  Swinging your unlimited options of weapons varies in less ways than archery but in reality, you're not going to swing a staff or sword or a mace in too many different ways.
NOTE:  Warband adds more variety of swings, but the swings feel super short and awkward so I never got into anything past the original M&B.  I wish they would've added the option to use swing mechanics of the original or Warband.  Forcing the WB mechanics on me was a mistake.  Main reason why Original is so superior and why there's still mods being made and updated for it, in my opinion.  Plus, there are so many great graphics, weapons, horses, armor, story and gameplay improvement mods that Warband is not needed.
P.S. Mods (Use Map Settings) are the reason I played Starcraft I for so long as well.
Armor:  Armor plays a huge role in how long you survive a battle.  Damage is calculated by damage - armor.  The higher the armor, the less damage you'll take.  If the damage is lower than your armor,then you won't take damage, it'll just sound like a thud.  Also, make sure you cover your feet, legs and hands with high number armor or you'll get weakened down quicker when riding your horse, charging the enemy.
Game Damage Settings:  Default is you take less damage than you damage bots.  I find that fair because there are those lucky shots the bots can get in from time to time, for big damage, like from lances or head shots.  That's why I never use total realism or 1:1 damage settings to offset those lucky shots.  I play like an epic King who has the best armor you can buy, the fastest horse you can buy and the best weapons you can buy.  When I say "buy", I mean that you can find at the various towns and trade for.
"Cheats":  You can turn on cheats in the main loader.  That just means you can use certain keystrokes that gives you coins or experience, depending on what screen you're on.  Same for your army.  Gives 1000 coins or exp every time you hit the key combo.  This is nice because it helps me setup scenarios and backstories of my own to my characters I create.  If I'm a wealthy noble who decides to leave his lands to help fight against whatever, it stands to reason that I'd already have my own set of armor, weapons and horse(s).  The cheats help me to afford what I think this character would already have.  Or, if all you want to do is fight, then you can edit your exported character txt file to have all the high level skills you want, so all you have to do is start the game, use that character and you're saving yourself a lot of grind time.  Lots of options there.  You can do the same for your armies.  Just give them experience to the level you want them to be and off you go.
Summary:
Pros:  Mount & Blade is my favorite game of all-time because I really do feel like I'm in the game, playing how I want, with my own story, while also allowing for mods that give you various stories you can choose, new weapons, armor, horses, diplomacy options, unit creation options, different factions to choose from with their own strengths and weaknesses.  It's strategy meets First Person RPG.  Very unique.  Nothing else like it.  Absolutely love the game!  Recommend you play the original game in it's default form to get all the mechanics and gameplay down.  Next, try Sword of Democles and finally The Last Days mod to really immerse yourself in a different world.
Cons:  Original graphics are very dated but still way fun because of the gameplay.  You can improve them with mods.  You can improve the items graphics as well.  Also, the original story is open-ended, which is fine for awhile, but once you conquer everything, that's when they start to rebel, so you still have more to do.  If you're into RP, then this is fun.  However, if you want an end-game, then the mods are the way to satisfy that itch.  There's subtle mods that only add small upgrades and storylines.  Then there's complete redesigns, like TLD, that change even the map and towns.  So really, the cons are really subjective based on what you prefer.  I personally value gameplay over graphics so these cons are more of a sidenote. =)
Love this game!  It goes on sale all the time.  Get it cheap with the other games in the series and give it a real chance.  You'll be glad you did.  The only reason you wouldn't is if you don't like solo game or are hung up on the dated graphics.  Warband adds multiplayer and improved graphics, but because of the different swing mechanics, I didn't like it.  However, as a new player, you wouldn't know the difference so starting there might be good for you.  =)
Mount & Blade FTW!  Thanks for reading. =)

The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a third-person action game based on the styles of early b-movie sci-fi. The gameplay is in fact meant to be a tape of one of those early films that is now being narrated over by the Director for an audiotrack on some 'upcoming DVD release'. This means there are regular gags, motifs, and dialogue based on the assumption that your gameplay is all part of some 1950's movie set. It's humorous and engaging.
The campaign focuses mostly on climbing the Deadly Tower of Monsters! which is an insanely tall tower reaching from sea-level up into space. Each section of the tower is themed after a different sub-genre of b-grade sci-fi, and one of the things I appreciated most was how thorough the game was with its art direction. The game touches on a lot of instantly recognizable genres with instantly recognizable costumes, weapons, and creatures/enemies.
The game is on the fence for me as to whether it holds much replay value in the campaign. The gameplay is short, but it's an appropriate length for the simple combat mechanics. There is an accompanying survival mode and a set of non-trivial but easily attainable achievements which will likely keep your attention for a short while after the campaign.
As a minor criticism, the weapon system, while just as beautiful and humorous as the rest of the game, is mostly superficial. There are some different effects of using different weapons, but for the most part there are only two weapon types and the late game weapons are only moderately more deadly than the early game versions. This becomes most obvious in survival mode. The weapon system however does incentivize you to explore the map for upgrade parts, and in that regard is a wise design decision as it introduces the player to more of the map, but it does little to make combat more interesting.
Many of the negative reviews are critical of the 'Director Commentary'. I personally found it an entertaining and welcome edition to the game. I felt that it added a lot of flavor to the milieu. The humor is very tongue-in-cheek though, which I appreciate is not everyone's cup of tea.
Do I recommend The Tower of Deadly Monsters? Absolutely, 100%, if you enjoy playful humor and retro-futurism I wholeheartedly recommend this game!

For starters, ignore the time on record I have on Steam. I've beaten the game on X1 and got it a second time on Steam. Yes it's that good.
Dying Light starts off with you starring as Global Relief Effort agent Kyle Crane jumping out of the back of a cargo plane and parachuting into the city of Harran, a place once excited to be hosting the Harran Games, something like an olympic tournament from what I could gather, only now Harran is full of undead. In the center of this mess is Kadir Suleiman, a man who stole files belonging to the GRE connected to finding a cure to this outbreak.
After your landing goes astray you are nearly beaten to death by a group of yellow-dressed men who work under a guy named Rais. If the brutes act this way, surely their king can't be any better. After taking some head trauma you shoot one of the guys only to have a horde of infected surround you. One of them bites you and you become infected yourself, but it isn't long until survivors wrapped in blue bandages from The Tower ward off the infected and save you.
This is the intro to Dying Light. This is what your goal is, who will help you, who will hunt you, and what happened and will happen to the city.
Features:
-Easy day cycle with normal zombies and mutants, and a challanging night cycle that will make you avoid every encounter you come across.
-2 Open world maps with several smaller linear ones.
-Varying melee weapons, types, levels, and modifications.
-3 Skill Systems for combat, parkour, and progression. All their skills make sense for the categories they are in too.
-Decently lengthed campaign with plenty of side missions.
-Safehouses to clear out and unlock.
-Quarentined zones that tell the story of the first signs of outbreak.
-Easter eggs like Mario and Plants Versus Zombies game modes hidden in the maps.
Pros/Cons:
-Parkour is fun as hell in this game.
-Can't really find anything wrong with this aside from it being too easy from time to time, but I won't compain because it is fun and I'd like it to stay as it is.
-Characters are memorable
-Facial animations aren't too convincing with very minimal nose, eye and eyebrow movement, plus there are moments where the faces snap from track to track.
-Combat is well done for being mostly melee weapons. Aiming at the leg does leg damage, at the head does head damage, and the skills you aquire do what they say they do.
-The two-handed whirlwind attack is VERY picky with what two handed weapons you can use. My biggest complaint about the game is that.
-Open world with a lot of vertical gameplay.
-Falling to your death and dying will kill you more often than the infected.
9/10. If you want a zombie slasher with a good story, open world, day night cycle, or a protagonist who tells the antagonist to "shut the f*** up already" during a speech, get this game.

Round of applause from the artistic community to Ubisoft’s Child of Light. Following the beautifully watercolored tale of the young Aurora, a young girl from 1895 Austria, Child of Light takes you on a journey through the afterlife that is written in verse and so artistically designed, you forget you’re playing a game and not reading a child’s storybook. The game begins with Aurora’s awakening in the lost fairytale continent of Lemuria, after her untimely death to a strange sickness. You journey with her on her quest to return home and to her father, as she fights against the dark creatures of the Queen of the Night. Fighting to retrieve the stolen sun, moon and stars, Aurora’s quest takes you across giants, creatures of the night, and even friendly companions that accompany you along the way. With fight mechanics similar to that of Final Fantasy, battles within the game aren’t difficult, and her flight ability proves easy to maneuver throughout the game. Her firefly companion, Igniculus, accompanies you from the start of the game, controlled easily by your mouse. He proves to be a helpful friend during battles when he slows down your opponents and collects HP and MP for you and your travelling companions. The gameplay mechanics themselves have no real fault, and the skill tree and crafting system is a bonus for anyone who loves character development in terms of skills and levels. As much as there is kudos needed to be given for the gameplay, the beautiful story and settings of Child of Light are the real money-makers of the game. Seen purely in the beautiful aesthetics of the game itself, the game plays out as a child’s nighttime story, with beautiful colors and aesthetics to match it. It’s watercolored scenery and characters paint the game into a masterpiece of artwork - effortlessly depicting Aurora’s tale in the style seen in children’s books. Partnering the game’s gorgeously painted graphics are the precious details placed in the gameplay. Essentially crying out the amount of love and care put into the development of the game, they aren’t small things missed by the player. Aurora’s flowing red mane of locks alone shows the time and effort spent by designers to depict her strong and formidable character, despite her small size and age. The minor details of Aurora’s crown falling off during battles and her firefly companion’s sarcastic commentary are only a few of the touches that the Child of Light developers included that proves the game was crafted with attention and love of detail. The music of the tale is superb and fitting for the game, wonderfully matched with the Aurora’s journey and it’s beautifully detailed settings. Child of Light is a tale of heart, beauty, and creativity, all available to be enjoyed by any player of any age. Ubisoft succeeded in crafting a game of beauty and artistic design, and has earned a definite win in my book.

Some games are bad, some games are good, some are so good you just feel that you have to tell everyone around about them. Especially about such games like DToM which are unfairly unknown to the wide audience.
The Deadly Tower of Monsters is one of my best purchases in Steam in all times.
It's hard to describe its genre: it's a platformer + hack'n'slash + metroidvania. Set in a sci-fi B-movies setting with odd but amusing plot. But the most brilliant thing in this game is its concept:
there is a high, INSANELY HIGH tower, and you have to reach the top of it. It has different sections with unique enemies, challenges and platforms, but at the same time the whole tower is a single solid level. You can always go back without any loadings. At any time you can just jump off the tower and reach any section of it you've already passed (to unlock items and gain collectibles with the help of new characters and their skills) and then just teleport back and make your way to the top! It's just absolutely mind-blowing to watch how you start from the ground and end up in space among planets and stars. And you can always jump down, fly for couple of minutes and safely land with your jet pack. Absolutely genius idea!
Music is great, voice acting is awesome, retro movie style is provided with the help of different effects like film grain, claymation style animated monsters... everything to make you feel you are in a 60's sci-fi B-movie.
Do you know that feel of being bored in the last part of most games? When you just can't wait for the game to end? Playing DToM I didn't even notice how the time passed and suddenly the credits began. Finishing the game took me 7 hours and I really felt like I need more. Completing all achievements with the one from Survival Mode took me 2 hours more. By the way, achievemеnts are rather easy to unlock and some of them are pretty fun.
I would recommend this game to everyone. If you seek some fresh entertaining experience this is definitely your choice. You can even buy this game at full price to support the devs. I heard that this game was free in PSN and it's really sad that corporations like EA or Activision get tons of money for their generic AAA crap while really talented studios get nothing for their work.
Bravo, ACE Team! Amazing work! I am really looking forward to the sequel!

Child of Light is one of those games I long heard about yet never gotten around to actually play it. I regret not playing this sooner.
This is the first game in a long long long time where i felt compelled to finish, sure the story might not have strayed too far away from a typical fairy tale, but the journey was an incredible one. If you were ever read a fairy tale, or were told a story about a magical land somewhere when you were just a kid, this will bring some of those memory back, It almost felt cheezy, but then agian, what fairy tale story ended in an unexpected way to us adults. For a fleeting moment, I went back to being a kid, accepting that the road to victory over evil, while all but assured, does have a few bumps on it. Not many games out there can do that for me.
That's enough on the story front, I did not read a single guide, just used all the ingame tutorial to help me along the way, got lost and became really confused serveral times before eventually finding my way. all the while loving the combat system, although not without a few curses thrown in there when things did not go my way.
It is worth noting I played the game on Expert diffcultly, I am by no means a "good"  player, but I did enjoy the challange it presented, some of the boss battles took serveral tries, some of the roaming mobs kicked my♥♥♥♥♥when I tried to play greedy. but with a few tweaks in the Occuli(essentially "gear") and party combination, i was able to take down everything without having to back track and farm levels.
The combat system definatly took some getting used to, being turn based but not really turn based, while it was very well done and very enjoyable, making a traditionallly turn based game very very smooth in combat, it also made some skills very confusing, ( X skill lasts Y turns.) It was hard to tell exactly when a "turn" starts and ends, but visual ques are there to help you, and they are very well presented, you will have no problem telling what buff/debuff you have at any given time, but how long do they have left? well, I couldnt really tell until they fall-off along with the visual ques.
according to the Uplay unlocks, I have completed all but 2 side quests in the game, the side quests are usually fairly straight forward, you will end up picking them up along the main story and doesnt take muccch time to do, I mostly stumbled onto them while trying to reaching the next zone. or got lost in a maze and ended up in the side quest objective.
overall 9/10 game.
P.S i love the artstyle and Coeur de Pirate's wonderful music,

mount&blade may be the best game about medieval life ever made. granted, games about the medieval era are few and far between, but they usually focus on adventure or strategy. In comparison, it's difficult to easily describe Mount & Blade, but it's a bit like a medieval version of sid meier's pirates. it is part action game, where you can ride into battle, swinging a sword to hack your opponents. it's part role-playing, as you control a character that can level up, learn more skills, and even climb the ladder of feudal society. It is part strategy game, as you hire and train a company of soldiers that fight alongside you in battles. and it all takes place in an open world where you choose to be as noble or as dastardly as you want to be.

Beat Hazard is, well... Insane, to say the least. If you watch someone experienced playing the game on the hardest difficulty, you'll see what I mean.
Lights flash, ships explode, and wave after wave of enemies relentlessly piles upon you, all to the tune of whatever music you choose. The harder difficulties have a near-vertical learning curve, but once you have mastered the game, it is one of those games you can just pick up and instantly feel awesome about.
The Ultra update is worth every penny. It makes the game easier in some ways, harder in others. The new bosses are tricky and require different tactics than what classic BH players are used to to beat.
In short, it's an unmissable game, unless of course you can't handle the bright strobing effects, which are way more intense than any screenshots would have you believe.

I will keep it brief, but here are five reasons why you MUST BUY Little Nightmares! Not Rent or borrow, but buy!
1) As a puzzle game, Little Nightmares is unique in that it combines horror and problem-solving with an added sense of fear (no jumpscares btw), in an environment that always changes and you can explore wildly.
2) The controls of the game are great, and the main character flawlessly follows your actions, and thus you can immerse yourself in the story
3) The use of sound and visuals is outstanding, and I genuinely hope that this game receives awards for it, as the atmospheres of the game are so well founded and thought through that I can't name any games similar.
4) The villains in the game are really something to look forward to, and beating their challenges proves to be fun and rewarding, and really add a sense of adventure to the game.
5) And finally, the game's story finishes with a mind-changing message that you won't realise until the end, but will soon realise that it has been clear all the way throughout.
Overall, 10/10 game, I would love to see more development into the series (not a sequel but maybe DLC), and I fell in love with this game only after an hour of playing it. This game will definitely be one that sticks in my mind for a long time

The fact that this game is completely free of charge, with new content added by zealous, comitted creators and modders alike, this could easily get an auto-reccomend.
The strange tale of Semyon in the equivalent of the scouts in 1980's Russia is a story about deep personal connections between himself and the various young women in the game, though sometimes compared to its contemporaries, it can feel shallow, and the art could definitely use some minor improvements here and there.
I wanted to get the negatives out of the way, because there is quite a bit to love here. The various romance options have for the most part unique and interesting personalities. Unlike many of its contemporaries, its difficult to pidgeonhole any of the characters into a particular trope (though some do come close,) and the characters feel three dimensional and fairly dynamic. I feel like the inclusion of the secret endings a bit... anachronistic and not fitting with the mood, but by the time you go for all the endings in this game, you'll be invested enough in the story of everyone attending the camp, including the main character.
Overall though, well written, the characters are memorable, and its long enough to let the story breathe and short enough to not make it feel like a slog to get the endings, which add pieces to the story at large.
Once again, completely free of charge with modders and talented, devoted devs adding new content. I would say if you're on the fence, go for it and try it out.
