Some don't like this game because there's not much choice.
Facts are there isn't a lot of choiceand in some conversations I would've said different things than what the player character would have said.
Some don't like this game because boobs/anime/it's an eroge/it's a VN/it's a dating sim.
Honestly, I've never been one to like dating sims (look at my most played games) or anime, or any of the things above. I never hated them but never really thought it was for me.
Anyways this game kinda changed that. Sure there's women with large breasts and sex if you add the hentai patch. However the focus is on the characters and the relatively mature themes of what to do with life, the nature of existence, and the excellent plot, and most importantly, the effects of one's actions on others. The writing apart from the funky translation is good, but if you've talked to actual russian girls they tend to say things the same way so there's a degree of veracity to it.
This ties in well with the nice soundtrack and excellent background art.
Also of note is that each ending really has a different message and life lesson. Is it a little corny? sure, but at the same time it feels like it was a good use of my time and made me really feel. Not only one emotion, but probably every ending will bring a different range of emotions.
Then once you've finished all the basic girl endings, the game takes that and throws it out the window. It goes to almost Tarkovsky levels of insanity and mind/reality bending and will make you super confused. Think through it for an hour, put the pieces together and you'll realise the developers were either blackout drunk or genius when they wrote the overarching story. Then, you truly have experienced this game.
Overall, if I was to describe this game in 3 words? Feels, thoughts, experience.

A fun ARPG but not very special.
There are some cool things in this game, you can combine two classes at level 10 but then you still have to spend a lot of points to be able to unlock the skills you want. So you don't know if you will like you class by level 30ish. With each level you can add some points to attributes, but spending them in your class bar that unlocks skills also raises your stats so it feels a little redundant.
There is a reputation system that rewards you with being able to buy high end gear and equipment upgrades that add damage etc. This goes paired with the many items that you can use to augment weapons, so you can end up with a weapon that is upgraded twice.
Constitution is a gold/yellow bar on top of your health, when you are out of combat your health goes up and consumes constitution in order to regenerate. You can refill it by finding meals in the world (no inventory items for eating). But this mechanic seems a little slapped in there for good measure and never really feels like it adds that much to gameplay overall.
There are also shrines you can restore for points to spent in a passive skill tree with constellations that contain different upgrades and abilities that you can put on top of the abilities that you have already learned.
Grim Dawn tries to differentiate itself from other ARPG's but doesn't really stand out that much from the standard ARPG gameplay. It is however a lot more casual than Path of Exile for example, which is pretty hardcore, and because of this it is also a lot more fun to play just a few hours of whenever you feel like it. And it's also hard enough to sometimes challenge you a bit.

Everyone knows about SR and what it is. I don't intend to simply reiterate knowledge that virtually everyone has about this game. Instead, I'd like to talk about what this game is like after you've finish the campaign. Now, most people stop playing sandboxes a little while after they beat the campaign and fart around for an hour or so. If you're like me, though, and you have a nasty habit of sinking a few dozen extra hours into titles that don't every techincally end, then you probably give a crap - like me - about what they're like in the "end game." Simply put, you can do everything in SR4 that you can in SR3 plus the super powers. This is good, and it's also bad. It also cheapens everything else a bit. You don't HAVE to use the super powers, but why wouldn't you instead of driving around having armed shootouts with the police on a crotch rocket. You'd think the latter was cool enough to justify doing regardless of whether or not you had the super powers, but the fact that there's no consequence to losing your bike, missing all of your shots, etc. makes the whole experience feel fabricated. Ultimately, it feels less fufilling to pull off a motorcycle jump onto a roof top that you'd've had to call a helicopter to reach when you can literally just walk up the side of it. The super powers are nice, but if you want to fool around with stuff that isn't related to them - which some would argue is the majority of the game - you might want to go play SR3 instead. Buy it for the campaigne and new mechanics, but don't think of it as just SR3 plus superpowers.

Secondly, while I realize this is quite a new game (and an idle clicker at that), it would be helpful to have a FAQ built into the game. Some features (such as the character screen, equipment, and illnesses) are pretty esoteric without context.
Overall it's a decent achievement farming game, but those few nitpicks detract from what would be an otherwise pretty standard clicker experience.

In short, bang for your buck (especially seeing it only costs you a wooden nickel).

No spoilers in this review.
Being both a fan of the books and the film this was a great way to further immerse oneself in the world of G.R.R Martin. This is a definite buy for Game of Thrones (GoT) fans.
Story: As above it is brilliant. Telltale have managed to bring House Forrester (the house you play as) to life with main characters from the books appearing in a way that does not feel forced. Telltale also managed to capture the grim and bloody nature of the books and at the same time the ever changing political landscape that we see in the GoT series. And this is where the game shines, the choices you face and there outcome really allow you to get invested in the characters that you are playing. However, the biggest potential flaw this game could face is that your choices don't matter to the extent that they might alter the ending a little bit but not drastically, only time will tell if this happens or not.
Gameplay: Pretty similar to any Telltale game. M and K (or controller) are used to control the characters in the story as well as dialogue options selectable during the game that can and will affect the world with QTE being used for combat.
Graphics: Again similar to all Telltale games. You will either love or hate them.

The soundtrack was good also.

Although, I wish there was more to this game as it's really easily completable. Cutscenes are really low quality, low framerate, compared to the actual game.

In short: An extremely good classical RPG.
For the elders:
I wouldn't say it's on par with Baldur's Gate 2 or Torment, but yet it's not far behind either. It will surely bring you good memories. They mixed new stuff ( coop, better UI, ergonomy and graphics) with good old stuff which made good cRPGs good at our time. Plot is very nice, and gameplay very addicitve (I personally spend hours crafting stuff).
For younglings: This is the best game for you to introduce you to a great game type which was left aside for a good while. If you like this one, you're on a great path, which will include (in any order) Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Arcanum, the two first Fallouts, and Planescape Torment (My all time favorite).
It might be harder than your average game, but like every game (not just video games), overcoming the difficulty is proportionnaly rewarding.
9/10 A must buy.

First off, this game needs a sequel or even a DLC of some sort. I can't even begin to explain how much this game blew my mind! From the beautiful graphics to the soundtrack and everything else, this game is simply outstanding and not to mention REALLY addicting as I actually went back to get some of lanterns I happened to have missed during my first playthrough.
As someone who is a huge horror fan, I can definitely say this game succeeded in terms of making me scared. From start to finish, the game leaves you in suspense wondering what's going to be around the next corner. Little Nightmares perfectly replicates the idea of being a child in an unfamiliar environment who doesn't understand what's happening to and around them. This is one of the aspects that I personally find great about this game.
The only negative I'd say is that the game doesn't really give you any sort of indication of what you're supposed to be doing at certain points. Sometimes I was unsure of whether to grab onto something or climb up somewhere but overall, everything else is pretty straightforward.
I've read some reviews on here about how the game could be longer but honestly? I think it's better off being short and sweet rather than dragging on for longer than it needs to. However, as I've said, a DLC or sequel would be awesome as I'd really love to see what happens next!
Little Nightmares is one of the most original and immersive horror/adventure titles I've played to date. Even if you're not into games like this, I still think it's worth a try :)

Gameplay - The gameplay is the best part of this game. It is turn-based and very open to many playstyles and strategies. It is fun (but also frustrating) experimenting to find out what works. Some battles are ridiculously hard if your party is not prepared. Sometimes you have to rely on cheap tatics (kiting, pre-emptive attacks, exploits) to get through some battles, which I'm not a fan of. The exploration aspect of the game is a little more frustrating. It is very difficult to know what to do sometimes. Item drops for me were terrible - I put in 40 hours and got only moderately good gear. It makes the game feel very grindy like Diablo 3. 7/10
Graphics and Engine - Art style is detailed and interesting and graphics are fairly good quality for the isometric perspective. 8/10
Story - This is where this game falls apart for me - it's all text based. I find it hard to engage or care about any of the characters. Most main characters, sidekicks, and NPCs are generic and uninteresting. The story also suffers from being semi-serious, as it makes for less motivation to do the quests. 4/10
Overall - Recommended, but don't play this for the story. 7/10

Grim Dawn is the long awaited spiritual sequel to Titan Quest, the now classic ARPG that bridged the gap between Diablo 2 and more recent games such as Torchlight and Diablo 3. Unlike most looter ARPGs, Titan Quest was set in established mythology, mostly Greek with a sprinkle of Asian. Grim Dawn on the other hand features a completely original world set after a destructive event of which the game draws its name. Your character begins on the ground beneath the gallows after the people of a wayward settlement hung you for being possessed by an Aetherial. Apparently Aetherials are an evil race of beings from beyond the veil aiming to conquer the world, because they apparently inhabited it before regular folks did. You begin helping the people of Devils Crossing, the settlement that previously hung you because hey, what else are you supposed to do. Throughout the game you learn more about the Aetherials, their place in the grand scheme of things and their mortal enemies the demons of the void, the worshipers of Ch'thon.
That leads me to one of the very interesting aspects of this game, the fact that not all enemies are the same. By that I mean Aetherials will not fight along side the Ch'thonians, they will happily kill eachother. Wandering the world of Grim Dawn, you will often come across enemies of different factions fighting eachother. The game tracks your involvement with the different factions, killing mobs and bosses will progress your various "hatred meters" which at given milestones will cause new and more powerful bosses to spawn in the world.
The same goes for the various friendly factions scattered around the land. Doing quests and bounties for a given faction will improve your standing, as will killing mortal enemies of that faction. Improving your standings will give you the opportunity to purchase unique gear and upgrades, as well as special quests. This all serves to bring some well worth life to the world, which often gets swept to the side in favor of your character being a demigod demolishing everything in his/her path on the road to more shinies.
This brings me to the nuts and bolts of the game, the character progression. Like Titan Quest, character creation amounts to nothing more than selecting gender. You pick your feller or lady, in my case often a lady, and are thrusted into the world with a stick and plank to fend of the walking dead. You whack a couple of them and the game screams DING! giving you the option to choose one of six classes, or masteries as they're called here. Great, six classes is what you'd expect from an ARPG. You take your pick and progress steadily through the beginning of the game and you reach lvl10 and DING! you get a second pick of the aforementioned masteries. Character creation in this game is actually the pick of two out of these six masteries, giving a grand total of 15 potential classes. As far as I know that is unprecedented since original Titan Quest. The rich amount of build opportunities in this game is reason alone for an ARPG fan to try it out.
Like Titan Quest, you pick your masteries and are awarded with three skill points per level. These are not only distributed among active or passive skills, they are also required to further your individual masteries. Every skill in a given mastery requires a set amount of mastery levels, meaning you have to balance the points you get per level up between skills and mastery. There are also three main attributes; physique, cunning and spirit. They can be mostly summarized as health, physical damage and magic damage respectively. They do not define your character as much as skills and masteries, but they do gate gear requirements and optimization.
This brings me to the meat and potatoes of a game like this, the loot. At the end, we all play games like this for the ever elusive legendaries. In most loot games gear is typically comprised of a few types per level or tier for each bodypart, with varying degrees of enchantment, as well as a few special pieces with significant power and unique abilities. In Grim Dawn though, there are basically two tiers of "legendary". There are the blue "rare", which have unique design and often special abilities. Then there are the actual purple "legendary", which have even fancier designs and even more powerful abilities. Many legendaries provide abilities that even outshine regular skills. Did you loot a legendary weapon that doesn't fit at all with your character? You could most likely build an entirely new character around that one weapon, just put in the shared stash and return to it whenever you want to. If that weapon happened to be way below the level cap, there's guaranteed to be max tier gear suitable for your character. There are rares and legendaries a plenty to suit every mastery combination you can think of. I have not even mentioned relics, components and augments. Safe to say, this skinner-box has some hella juicy treats.
The only complaint I can bring is the relative lack of endgame content. There are the aforementioned faction quests, there are also repetable randomized dungeons, but there are no leaderboards or global stat tracking. For me personally this hardly matters, the main focus of the game is leveling and progressing new characters. I have put in hundreds of hours and I have never reached the level cap (lvl 85) simply because when I reach the later parts of the final difficulty, I have a freshly formed character build in my mind that I happily start fresh with. I have several characters over lvl 70, but right now I find the most joy in my latests lvl 40-ish glasscannon mage, whom I started simply because there was a single skill I wanted to explore (Chaos-transmuted Aether Ray).
All in all, this is the best ARPG experience I've had since original Titan Quest. The loot is phenomenal, the amount of build freedom and variety outweighs my experiences of both Diablo 3 and Path of Exile. Crate is a personable developer who seems dedicated to their game and I have no doubts they will continue to support this game for a long time. I have heard rumors of a planned total of 10 masteries, which would give this game an unprecedented amount of character freedom. Even if that turns out to be false, the amount of content available right now is well worth the price of admission, and then some.
TL;DR
Grim Dawn is the spiritual successor to Titan Quest. It features a similar dual class character progression, all six masteries are varied and unique, all combinations are valid choices with gear to match.
Unprecedented player choice in terms of progression and character builds.
A faction-based world where enemies of different factions fight eachother, while friendly factions provide unique gear, quests and upgrades depending on your standing. Faction interation is tracked globally, if you kill a significant number of a given hostile faction they will spawn special bosses.
Incredibly rich amount of gear with effectively two tiers of "legendary" pieces. Gear is tailored to every type of mastery combintation you can think of and most of the high level stuff have unique abilities associated that more often than not outshine regular skills.
Lack of endgame might disappoint some people, though in my opinion the focus of the game is leveling and building new characters, not grinding at max level. There are distilled endgame dungeons which provide an effective way of endgame grinding, though starting anew with a fresh idea is far more rewarding.

A solid, if not horribly ground-breaking, Visual Novel.
Clearly inspired by Visual Arts/Key, in the way it combines romance with mystery and supernatural elements, although it isn't nearly as great as any of Key's classics (Kanon, Clannad, Rewrite, etc.).  Still, the Russian setting is interesting, the characters are generally well drawn (for the most part), the arcs generally make sense (again, for the most part), and there is certainly enough here to keep your interest if you're a fan of the genre.
That being said, there are a few criticisms/points of warning.  First of all, this is NOT a good starter Visual Novel, if you aren't familiar with the genre already.  Go elsewhere.  Second, at times the game tries to be too mysterious for its own good, and instead just gets confusing.  I'm tolerant of a little bit of "what the hell is going on" as long as it is explained later--but it's not always explained later.  (Mostly... but not always.)  Third,  they are working on polishing the English translation, and boy, does it need it.  The language is almost always understandble, but it is often stilted.
So if you're like me, you loved Plantetarian, can't wait for Clannad to hit Steam next year, and are looking for something to read in the meantime: Give Everlasting Summer a go.
And if that previous sentense made absolutely no sense to you, then you should play a different game.  Try Planetarian or Analogue: A Hate Story; if you love those, go find Katawa Shoujo, and if you like it to, then come back here.

When you get past all of the chatter about the potential of this game looking better on a PC, and all of the yip-yap about Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball being "just another" first person shooter, and all of the lip-flapping about this game not being able to compete with the very best games on PS2 or GameCube and you actually sit down and play the game on your Xbox...you're in for one hell of a game.
The only thing people need to be concerned about when it comes to this game is how soon they're going to get it and where they're going to find the time to play. With a story good enough for a full length novel, audio and visual elements as detailed as any you've ever seen and excellent pacing, This game is the reason for Xbox and vice versa. Bungie has brought to the Xbox the game that will prove hundreds of thousands of naysayers wrong (about the system and thegame) and bring sweet relief and joy to those who've been biting their nails and pacing in circles waiting for Microsoft's machine to arrive. Hype is one thing; reality is another; Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball on Xbox is one of the best things to happen in videogames.
Features:
Situational First and Third Person perspectives.
Role-based, cooperative multiplayer team game
Play story mode as a single player or cooperatively with another player.
Choose from a variety of conventional human and powerful alien weaponry
Vehicles include marine jeeps and tanks to alien flyers and hovercrafts.
Squad based combat.
Enjoy the action with 5.1 Dolby Digital Surround Sound and Widescreen playback features.
The Story
Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball takes place in the far future where mankind is locked into a brutal war against a race of aliens known as the Covenant. These dudes are seriously evil. They wipe out entire planets at a time, and they are so fast at doing so that we poor humans are unable to get much information on them before they nuke us into oblivion.
The horde of aliens is getting closer and closer to Earth with the clock quickly ticking down before they completely annihilate our race. Finally the line is drawn. In a massive battle near a human planet, only one ship survives: Pillar of Autumn. The commander of the ship decides to lure the Covenant as far away from Earth as possible so she programs the ship's AI to jump to some random location in the opposite direction of the home system.
Eventually the ship arrives at a distant area or space where they find both a gas giant called Threshold and its small moon known as Basis. This wouldn't be so strange except for the fact that they find a giant ring construct floating between the two objects, which is about 10,000 miles in diameter. Unfortunately for the small ship, the entire Covenant battle fleet had followed them and arrived in the system shortly before.
When you boot up the game, you're knee deep in the middle of the Autumn being evacuated. That giant ring construct is Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball and the secret that it holds is the part of the story that will be up to you to discover.
Gameplay
Before we get into the nuts and bolts of how Halo plays, I'd like to share a few of the quotes blurted out in and around the IGN offices and other places as passers-by were enraptured by a glimpse of Bungie's first person superstar.
"Are those guys fighting with you?"
"Drive the Jeep! I wanna see the Jeep!"
"Damn, this feels like a movie!"
"I thought the fun part happened already."
"How come the enemies speak English?"
You will fire roughly 4 million rounds at all sorts of alien creatures and vehicles by the time you reach the end of Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball. It's definitely a first person shooter with the emphasis on shoot. But it's how you're motivated to deal all of that damage that makes the experience so enjoyable. And I'm not referring to the backstory of the game either. The artificial intelligence of the enemies is sophisticated enough and increases in difficulty at such a nice steady pace to that you are literally getting better the more you play.
There are a handful of basic enemy types that you'll encounter in Halo including the small annoying Grunts, force-field wearing Elites, shield carrying Jackals, terrifying Hunters and the good old cloaking Elites --they carry cool energy swords that you don't want to know about. Each of the different enemy types behaves and attacks according to their specific "personalities" and so there are tactics in dealing with each.
Grunts are basically chicken-ish and so they like to attack when they have plenty of backup and run away once you isolate them or show your aggression. The magic is in how they express themselves. When Grunts run away they only get so far and hide behind cover before they muster some more courage and pop out again. You simply pop them at will with whatever weapon you have handy.
Elites have an entirely different plan. They have shields, just like you, so they're more likely to go toe-to-toe. Once you get their shields down, however, they panic and become even more aggressive with a running melee attack of some kind. Since their shields are down, your best bet is to smash them with a melee attack of your own with whatever weapon you may be carrying. How often have you gotten frustrated in other FPS games and wished you could just smash the enemy in his side-chewing mouth? An up close and personal attack with the butt of your assault rifle is one of the more underrated joys that Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball will bring you.

If you're looking for a game that is beautiful to look at with simple controls and light content that doesn't require a large investment of time to finish, look no further than this game.

Saints Row IV may not have as much story as its predecessors, but if you are a fan of the previous games, you'll likely enjoy this one as well. There are a lot of references and characters from previous games that show up that spice up what otherwise might be a new set of activities for Saints Row: The Third. While it's true the city is largely the same Steelport as Saints Row: The Third, I actually prefer that due to the superpowers. A new city would have lots of little things to explore. The superpowers are not particularly conducive to that as you'll be sprinting faster than any car, scaling tall buildings in moments and gliding across the city. Driving and walking through the streets is likely not going to be oft used here. The superpowers give quite a different feel to the combat. While you still have an arsenal of weapons alongside the superpowers, it doesn't feel too overpowered (until you start upgrading abilities). There's some story but a lot of it is just thrown in without much explanation. And more often the minimal story is just flimsy pretext to force you to go out and complete the various activites/side-quests.
Overall it's a mixed bag. If you're looking for a fresh Saints Row game and new story you're likely to be disappointed. If you enjoy Saints Row games and want a little more zaniness, this might pique your interest. For me, the amount of activities and references to previous Saints Row games made this a lot of fun for me. But once done, I would more likely play around in Saints Row 2 or 3.

Then, it went on sale.

My friend bought the pack of four games to send to three other friends, and that was me and two other "chosen ones".

In some way, throwing them off roofs. As they run at you, grab them and trip them over your foot and stomp on their heads afterwards. (There's some more that I could list but I can't list them off the top of my head right now.)
The story is also pretty good, nuff said.
And multiplayer is fun. This game, I find, was good multiplayer and singleplayer, but fooling around with your friends or running from nightmares at night is probably the most fun I've had in a co-op zombie game.

FTL: Faster Than Light
like a roguelike; one must manage their resources carefully to survive as long as possible and every decision is important. The mechanics are simple and consistent, the interface is informative, and the controls feel natural; nothing is overdone.
The variability in ships, events at beacons, and sector layouts afford FTL its high replay value. Playing as the captain of a ship, one will most certainly meet a stressful situation in which there is an overwhelming amount of things to keep track of: ordering crew to repair rooms, man systems and contest invaders; opening blast doors out to space to suffocate fires; targeting weapons onto an enemy ship; all the while juggling the options of continuing a fight, accepting a surrender, or fleeing before its too late. It's exhilarating.
The Advanced Edition update only made things better, introducing a host of slick UI enhancements, providing an improvement on an already great experience.
I highly recommend FTL: Faster Than Light to people that like games. And everybody else.

---------------------
Well lord and behold, this great fast paced arcade game got tons of new additions added to it. What was once just a simple survival score attack game, now has an arcade/story mode, and more playable characters! Either they had already planned to add more, or they listened to the fans and reviewers and gave us more, like playing as the other characters! Even getting the original actors is a huge bonus. Same great witty lines just like the movie.
I never even knew they did this till I felt like playing this game again and saw it with my own eyes. Once again I suck at this game, but had a BLAST playing this again. Still love that damn smexy soundtrack.
In Arcade Mode, you progress by completing waves of enemies to get to the boss fight. I was skeptic on how the bosses would work, but they worked out real good. Instead of being stuck where you could only attack and not move, you move by holding the buttons, which you need to dodge the boss attacks before he becomes vulnerable to you spamming the attack button to lower its health bar. Very cool. As you complete the section, you get to play as another character and do it all over again, but each character plays a little different, and the boss fight being different as well.
Kung Fury plays your normal press a button to use your amazing kung fu skills to obliterate your enemies. Can take 3 hits before you die.
Hackerman was the hardest for me, and could not pass his level in arcade mode. You have a "HACKING" bar you have to fill up by targeting enemies till it fills up, then you can blast everyone at a distance with his hack gun, which kills everything in 1 or 2 hits. Can only take 2 hits before you die.
Barbarianna is by far my favorite. She plays in a 5 hit combo style. Your first 4 hits are a melee and build up the combo, then your final 5 hit is the mini gun, which kills everything on which ever side of the screen you click on. Can only take 2 hits before you die.
Triceracop plays much like Kung Fury, minus the kung fu and uses guns to shoot the enemies in the groin, but has slightly more range, and a lot more health. Can take 5 hits before you die.
Some people claim that this got worse? They say that the controls are not as responsive as before, but honestly I didn't notice anything.
If this game wasn't a must buy before, it most definitely is now with the extra content, and for only $3! You can't go wrong with it.

I have to say this game is unique.  It has a flavor to it that really makes you want to stay.  The voice overs are not be taken seriously, it’s all meant for good fun.  So if you are expecting Oscar winners for "best actor/actress" you will be disappointed.
Allot of people think this game is a sandbox which it is not.  There are specific quests that have to be done in order to attain your goals.  In my 1st play through I played it like a sand box and then had to back track half a dozen times to finish a quest or do that puzzle I was avoiding ( as I hate puzzles, I view them as busy work ).   The enemies never re-spawn so if you think you can grind your way to level, forget it.  The game has 20 levels officially however, I was able to hit level 23 on the 2nd play through which will give you an idea of all the things I missed on my 1st game.
Character classes, while abundant can lead you astray as there are a specific number of attribute, skill and talent points to be earned in the game.  So a class that has 3 key elements will be far easier to level then one that has five!  So that battle mage that you are drooling to play, you will find is quite difficult to be really good at casting or combat.  While the pure mage or pure fighter will be much easier to play and become very powerful.  One of the nice feature is that any class can learn any skill, provided that you put points in the base skill.  For example if you want everyone in your party to be able to heal, then you all need 1 point of skill into Hydrophist which is water magic.  The amount you can heal is based upon intellect and intellect is not an attribute that a fighter can afford to dump points into as an example buut that party member can still heal.
Combat is fun especially with elemental magic involved.  Unlike other online RPGs and many solo games, you cannot kill a fire elemental with fire magic.  Cast a poison cloud then set it on fire for a nice explosion!  Cast a rain spell and get everyone wet, now watch your aim and electrocute the enemy, but if you are too close you can also stun your whole group as well :P  Many people have stated in Utube and the like that they had to do a battle over and over and over and I have to admit a few times I wanted to change the difficulty, but all that does is lower a mobs health nothing more.   So plan your moves and save often if you reach a point in a boss battle that you don't want to do again!  You can save in combat obviously!
Are there bad things about the game, yes!  Mostly things that create tedium, such as inventory management, passing items back and forth.  One character does the blacksmithing for example and one does the magic identification work.  Now, unlike many games, once an item breaks in combat it is not gone forever.  Keep a spare item to equip and repair it.  You can pass an item to the member of your group, have them repair it and pass it back.  It takes a turn to re-equip it though.
Crafting is something you may want to google as there are some very well done lists on what to mix together with which item to make this or that.  As an example you can make food items for buffs in combat.  I don't know about you, but I love pizza :)  Ok take a tomato and crush it with a hammer and you get sauce.  Now grind some wheat with a motor and pestle to make flour.  Mix water with the flour to get dough.  Now mix the dough with the sauce and get pizza dough and pop that into a forge and you get a really good pizza although it’s just a cheese pie :(  Experiment, if it can be done it will happen, you get a window.  If it can be done but your skill is too low there will be a message.
Vendors can wipe you out financially if at least one party member isn't skilled in bartering.  You can add points and there are always a maximum of 2 gear items that will add to that skill.  Five is not the limit as most might lead you to believe.  One of my characters has 5 skill points in barter and two gear items and it counts.  My last game I amassed 1 million in gold as an example.  But then again I am a total "loot ♥♥♥♥♥"  lol
Skill Books are useful for ideas on how to craft but are not meant to block your crafting at all.  You can still craft metal items and not read any books on metal crafting.  Since there are no cut and dried recipes, the books are meant to make you think about what you can do.
One thing about vendors that is quite annoying is the vendor only sees the character that opens the vendor window.  So if you are trying to buy skill books for another member you will have to know what they have learned by your memory or write it down because as you mouse over an item it will say  "you have already learned this spell" or it will say in red "you don't know this spell".  Well if your barter character is a mage then it’s pretty safe to assume that they will not have learned any of the fighter skills.   Even if you toggle through the menu and show your fighter as the active character, the vendor still only sees the one that opened the window.  So it’s a bit of a pain to open chat with each party member, note down what is needed, and then switch back to the member with the barter skill to actually make the purchase.
Boss Battles changed in a recent patch that supposedly "fixed" the balance.  I notice allot of bosses run to a far corner of the combat area and stare at the wall and do nothing for 4 or 5 turns while your party is killing all the minions.  When the last minion is killed it wakes up, but it’s too late, he is going to "sleep with the fishes"  lol.  So, Larion dropped the ball here somehow.   One boss battle was against an elemental casting boss.  In my first 2 play throughs and one co-op that I play, the battle was a long drawn out slug fest and many times the whole group was on the verge of a wipe.  After the last patch my party killed this boss on the 8th turn vs the 24 turns it took before!
So in closing I feel the game is worth every cent of its rather low price.  It is released, but publisher is constantly updating and tweaking.  There are elements that hint at a sequel to carry the story on.  Warning though, if you are the sort that needs to be held by the hand with quest markers and little glowing dots on the ground so your know where to walk, don't buy this game!

This is a little gem of a game where the isometric 3D shooting and fighting and platforming isn't that innovative but the sheen on the game is clearly a labour of love.
The premise of the game is that this is a schlocky 1950s sci fi movie undergoing a DVD release with a director's commentary.  So the entire artwork for the game uses the most modern technology to duplicate sub Harryhausen stop motion animation.  This is great fun and during the course the game there is barely a cliche from the genre that doesn't get thrown at you.  I can't over state how much the overall look and feel of the game adds to it.
Gameplay is good.  For most of the game it's not the most challenging so you rarely get stuck for very long anywhere in the game.  There's one of the later monsters that becomes tough because it is only vulnerable from the rear and nearly at the end there's a tricky platforming session where even the guy on the Let's Play video has to have three goes at it.  The layout is incredibly linear for the most part taking place on a narrow staircase leading up the tower but there is the odd location where I've had to backtrack to complete another section of the game to maintain onward progress.  Pay attention to instructions where given and if you find yourself at a rocket you can't activate retreat backwards to the large platform below you and go through another exit to find one of the best series of scenes in the game.  You have the choice from part way through the game of playing as the rather wooden All American hero, the blonde bombshell Emeror's daughter, or the man in a suit style robot.  They have unique special abilities and sometimes you'll need to use one rather than the others to progress.
The inventory and upgrade screens don't have the visual imagination of the main game.
This game is as far from shovel ware as it's possible to get.  A clear labour of love the developers love for the genre they are parodying comes across in every scene and the director's commentary keeps the game fresh even when gameplay doesn't vary that much.  Definitely worth buying when it goes on sale.

4 out of 5 stars -- Pleasantly surprised at the game's high quality, despite lacking certain features.
Pros:
1) It's quite an original concept with classic anisotropic top-down style combat, similar to Enter the Gungeon (but nearly as unforgiving).
2) The director commentary is hilarious is you like a mix between dry wit and silly humor. Imagine Fred Willard being... Fred Willard. You know that role he plays in every movie? It sounds just like him and he acts just like him. That's basically the director commenting throughout the whole game. Some other reveiwers got tired of him, but I personally loved it, so your mileage may vary.
3) The soundtrack is perfect. It sounds like it belongs in a Rick and Morty game.
4) While reminiscent of retro movies (and brilliantly so), I also got a very strong retro platformer vibe from it. The game frequently reminded me of Banjo Kazooie. It pushed a LOT of nostalgia buttons for me.
5) The style is beautiful and captures old low-production sci-fi thrillers to a T. It's extremely well done. Some monsters even move in claymation style, which I thought was a fine touch.
6) Supports 1920x1080
Cons:
1) The camera is a bit stiff. I wish you could pan it just a bit to see a little farther off the tower, since in this game you often have to jump off the tower you're climbing to get collectibles, so not being able to fully see where you're going gets to be a little tiresome. On the plus side, you can respawn up on the ledge you jumped from with a simple button press. And eventually you'll be able to see everything if you just go high enough in the tower, so it's not like the camera is barring you from getting that.
2) This game is a lot of fun with a gamepad, but unfortunately they didn't see the need to make the buttons rebindable (keyboard users can rebind at will, don't worry). For some reason they didn't bind anything to the left trigger, which would be perfect for cycling through your specials. I'm not sure why they dropped the ball on that one. Otherwise the stock controls are pretty good, though of course rebinding buttons would be ideal.
3) Can't change the mouse sensitivity. I have no idea why they didn't include this.
4) The rings weren't programmed very well. It's hardly an issue, but it can take you out of the fun when you pass through a ring and it doesn't register. (This is more for people who have already played it).
Playing music is fun.

Best nightmare I've ever had, that's for sure! Little Nightmares is an immersive experience, excelling in both audio and graphics it simulates a spooky atmosphere. I find myself coming back to this game in spite of having finished it. There's something so charming about it all, particularly our odd little protagonist, Six. Her design is simple, withholding elements of her character just enough to sustain that air of mystery. The overall plot is rich with possibilities -- let it be known that it requires the player to concoct their own theories and understanding; there's still a lot that needs to be accounted for. It's both effective and intriguing, but I do hope the developers intend to reveal little tidbits about the story soon enough. I'm aware there's comics that delve deeper into the lore that mightn't otherwise be apparent in the game, so that's always nice. I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the horror genre, but I recommend that you take your time to look around and appreciate the atmosphere. You won't properly experience the game if you simply rush through it. I find it to be rich in artistic quality, it's always worth looking around at even the littlest things! It's just such a breathtakingly beautiful game, what with lighting, depth perception and the overall design of The Maw. It's the opportune place to be scared stiff!

I really wanted to like this game. The combat isn't bad (though it's not inspired either -- the lack of terrain features combined with the suicidal "gank the weak ones" AI combine to make it all feel very gamey) but the story is just not interesting.
If you're going to go with the whole "the world is doomed" plot line you have to give me a reason to care about this world. However, all the characters felt flat and uninteresting, and with a few exceptions they were just variations on the 'generically ok person' template. The visual design was not very interesting -- everything looks like a 70s cartoon and all the characters basically wear the same outfits.
Also, the game occasionally ambushes you with choices the ramifications of which are not really possible to understand at the time. This is a big narrative mistake; it's not really clever writing to "trick" the player into making a bad choice when there's no way to understand what the choice actually is. Actually gripping choices in a game come from making a hard choice between two equally good (or bad) outcomes, not from simply trying to pull a gotcha on players.
There are lots of VERY good RPGs out there. There's no reason to waste your time with one like this unless you're really desperate for something to do.

So I just completed my first playthough of Grim Dawn and I am very pleased with it. Anyone who ever played the currently unsupported prequel Titan Quest will be pleasantly surprised with this installment. The formula is almost exactly identical which I believe to be a very good thing. There are graphical improvements and minor design changes that enchance the experience, but overall at its core it is a true (Diablo) game. It took me about 50 hours on my first character run completely solo, It's a rather large game. It does the typical New Game + after that where you can continue leveling up agasint harder repeat enemies. A great game to play with a friend or two. My complants are minor, but I do feel the online navagation is not all that comfortable to use. It does work, I connected to a local friend without any issue but a more distanced friend we just could not get into the same game together. It is the same format as Titan Quest however I wish that format was updated on and a bit more user friendly. I can also say the same thing about Inventory management, everything in the inventory windows seem to feel so small and... grim to me? Fitting I guess but some of the fun in this genre of game is finding that nice piece of bright and colorful equipment and makes you go "ooo so pretty!" Not to say impressive gear isn't available I just wish the icons and inventory managment were more "flashy". Last there is no "cutseen" or visual indication that you have moved on into the next Act. Whatever. Those are all very minor complaints and there are plently of positive things I can rant on about this game but most are a repeat on how I feel about Titan Quest. If you have never played either game think about this one as a solid Diablo 2 remake with an element that I absolutly praise, the ability to reset your skill points and change your builds (for in game coin known as iron bits). You also pick your class after you create a character and you can have 2 classes for mix/matching. Class choices however are not reversible. Overall an absolute georgous game with minor destructible terrain and some enemy physx that can be hilarous when you bash a skeleton in with a giant warhammer =3. I highly recommend this game.

I initially went into Grim Dawn with low expectations. Maybe it would be a dark fantasy Titan Quest at best. To say Grim Dawn surpassed my expectations would be selling the game short.
Core gameplay is standard genre fare; grind enemies into a fine paste and collect items off of their dead bodies. The combat itself has a nice weight to it, my Blademaster felt like a whirlwind tearing through groups.
Progression uses the dual skill tree system from Titan Quest. A first tree is picked at level 1, and then the second is picked at level 10. There is no restrictions on mixing trees, so a variety of different builds are available.
Skills in the tree aren’t just selected, a player is given three points on level ups to use.  A player can either choose to level up masteries, which has skills at 5 point intervals, or one of the aforementioned skills. This system forces a player to choose between immediate returns of available skills or investing in mastery points to unlock stronger skills.
In practice the system mostly works, but can cause some pacing issues towards the end of a skill tree. Around Act 3 there was a huge difficulty jump, and the skill to finish my build felt like it required too much investment in masteries to unlock.
Itemization is average for this type of game. Most of the items are just straight stat boosts, but the character is given plenty of choices for damage. There are ten resistances available to the player and enemy. All of the resistances see use without one over shining the rest.
It is important to note that Legendaries are treated as end game build defining items. They start dropping at level 50, or around the end of the first difficulty.
Where Grim Dawn really sets itself apart from the genre is the story and atmosphere. The game starts out with a cutscene to give some exposition about aetherials invading the world. Then the player is dropped into a post-apocalyptic world.
From here the player isn’t given much in the way of outright story. Instead hints are dropped about how exactly civilization collapsed, the history of the world, humanities place in the three way war that is being waged, and much more. The main plot is more or less the player trying to survive, eventually becoming a ‘hero’ because frankly the developers need a reason to explain why my Blademaster has killed 24,500 enemies.
The atmosphere is what brings everything together. From the get-go it is established that this is a terrible world. Other games have tried the dark fantasy thing, but often feel sterile despite there being blood and corpses everywhere.
A set of notes that drop in an area tell a story. A family of four is fleeing the aetherial invasion and food is scarce, but there are rumors that the cultists who have risen up to fight the aetherial invasion will provide shelter to anyone willing to join. The family is forced to join the cult. In time the mother starts to buy into the ideology while the father just grits his teeth to make sure the children have food. The story ends with the women realizing that the family she joined the cult to protect would be safer as sacrifices to the blood god.
As mentioned before, the cult has risen up to fight the aetherials. Make no mistake, these cultists are no friends of anyone sane. The aetherials sole goal is to claim the world for themselves, enslaving humanity in the process. The remnants of an empire are caught in the middle trying to fend off both sides while reclaiming civilization.
This three-way war is illustrated in gameplay through encountering cultists and aetherials fighting each other. When the player engages one side, they will keep on fighting. At times they will side with each other to fight the player, but there has been times where they simply ignore the player and continue their assault, as if accepting the help.
The game is loaded with small scenarios that provide opportunities for choice and consequence. There was a man lying in the road bleeding out, and according to this man was betrayed by his partner. Either way he was dead and there was nothing I could do to help him. Except to honor his last request to track down his killer.
I do so and the person begs me to let them explain what happened. He explains that the man lying in the road was indeed his partner, but he acted in self-defense to stop the ex-partner from♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥his daughter. There is no other NPC in sight. What do I do? Is the daughter hiding or am I be being played a fool?
The attention to detail in all of these things give the world an authenticity that the genre hasn’t had in a long time. Since Diablo 2 in fact. Yes, it’s that good.
This isn’t the game for someone wanting a fun 1,000 hour min/max item grind; that is Diablo 3. This isn’t the game for someone wanting to replay the game 50 times trying out off the wall builds; that is Path of Exile. This is the game for someone who wants the fun gameplay of the genre with a well realized dark fantasy world.
Crate Entertainment is a studio to watch. I know that I’ll be watching for the first Grim Dawn expansion.

This is worth every penny the devs could ever ask you for it.
Seriously, they could have went with 59,99€ triple-A release price and it'd still be a bargain for a game of this caliber.
+ Feels and sounds like the old Diablo games, very dark and foreboding. Overall the game just has a really good atmosphere.
+ Most of the great mechanics from Titan Quest like dual classing make it to this one as well.
+ Combat is fun from the start and gets increasingly better the more abilities you get. A nice contrast to the rather slow start in the games of this genre most of the time.
+ An absolutely MASSIVE world, i've heard the game takes around 30 hours to finish on your first run. (Considering Path of Exile and Diablo 3 both take around 12-16, GD truly feels enormous.)
+ Tons of different enemy types, each new area introduces new ones as well.
+ Mostly solid voice acting and writing.
+ Good game to play solo, much more story oriented than PoE for example.
+ Great loot, nice looking gear too.
- GD shares the same engine with Titan Quest, which means the visuals are pretty dated compared to other games of the genre.
- The levels are huge, but all of them are hand crafted. Meaning there aren't randomly generated dungeons...
- ...Which takes away quite a bit of the replay value and possible endgame content.
The last point which i make might be a dealbreaker for most of you, and it was indeed a pretty big thing for me as well at first. But honestly, such a thing can also be taken positively. While there aren't randomly generated areas, they are designed very well compared to PoE etc. If you can get over this point i guarantee you'll have a great time with the game.

Saints Row 4 left me with some very mixed feelings. Having played and loved Saints Row 3, I bought this game to see if it would live up to my expectations. It did, in part. My review will contain minor spoilers, most of which can be ascertained from the trailer, however.
In terms of audio, the voice acting was very well done. Two of the voice actors from the previous game could be heard in this one, which was a pleasant surprise. Nolan North also made an appearance, but not a subtle one. During the character creation process, you get an option to choose his voice for your character, and his name appears explicitly, which was interesting. I found some of the writing in the dialogs between characters genuinely funny, and the developers have spent a lot of time thinking about how the characters interact with each other. For example, when you are accompanied by your homies, you will discover different conversations between the characters depending on who you chose to accompany you, with some quite interesting results at time. However, I didn't believe that the soundtrack behind the game, was impressive as SRIII. There were a couple of good moments, but nothing compared to the Power descent on the penthouse, from SR3.
The story itself felt a bit disjointed. I felt in a few occasions that I had no idea why I was doing this mission, in the context of the game. A lot of the side missions were a lot of fun, but didn't make any sense in terms of the story. They feel placed there as filler. Also, the concept of taking over a city in the simulation felt a bit artifical as well. If the "overlords" of this existence were smart enough to build the simulation, then they must be smart enough to prevent all the activities going on inside. I wasn't expecting the story to be fantastic, that isn't an element Saints Row is known for.
I saw a lot of fun items, especially weapons and vehicles. However, I felt that there was a lot of reuse in assets also. The map is pretty much identical to that of Saints Row III, with the exception of some Alienification. I felt a little bored spending the majority of my time in the same old city. Certainly, there are plenty of new locations, but you'll spend 90% of your time in Steelport.
So in summary, this game is a fantasticly mad sandbox,  which gives you the freedom to do anything. You'll enjoy the game if you can swallow another 20 hours in Steelport.

This visual novel is incredibly fascinating. The story has particular elements that truly make it interesting and themes that are effective food for thought. The overall plot is definitely the most powerful aspect of the game, as the storytelling is just so brilliant in the many ways it shows the detail and perspective of our protagonist, Semyon, and how no one decision will ever be the best decision you can make. I found that out early in the game, because even though it may have said one thing, it would change how the story went quite a bit. Which leads me to my next point: there are many endings you can get. As of now, I've only gotten two; each ending seems to require a full playthrough of the 5+ hours it takes to complete a single playthrough. From what I've seen, I can almost guarantee that these endings will be the best parts of the novel, as the author reveals an incredibly large amount of information in the endings. The soundtrack is utterly fantastic for such an indie game, and with each scene it's extremely compelling. Action scenes will be hyped with rock music, romantic moments will get much more atmospheric with light piano, and the light tunes playing throughout are pure earcandy. The audio is well recorded as well. Fanservice is minor and very infrequent, so you'll have to play something else if that is what you seek (EDIT: Apparently there is a 'Restoration Patch' for hentai and stuff so if you're into that, then I invite you to utilize a search engine to do so). My only criticism is that at times certain scenes seem to drag on unnecessarily and throughout the game you can see translation errors in spelling and grammar, though neither of these are gamebreaking by any means. I definitely recommend giving Everlasting Summer a go.

BEFORE READING THIS PLEASE UNDERSTAND THAT I HAVE ABOUT 30 HOURS IN THIS GAME, BUT MOST WERE IN OFFLINE MODE BECAUSE MY GAMING PC WAS FIRST GETTING SETUP.
Anyway, Dying Light is a zombie game created by the makers of dead island. I actually liked dead island unlike MANY people because the gameplay was geuninely fun. However I was turned off from the humor, as it took away realism of an  apocalyptic zombie scenario. Dying Light COMPLETELY CHANGED THAT. It has a revamped style of combat and gameplay, AND OH GOD FINALLY A GOOD STORYLINE. WHEN IS THAT EVER SAID IN ANOTHER ZOMBIE GAME?

-THE GAME PUNISHES YOU FOR MAKING LOUD NOISES SUCH AS SHOOTING A GUN! This adds realism that I craved so much before I found Dying Light.

Visual novels are always a crapshoot, but I have to say this one is well worth the time.  What's amazing about this game are how seamlessly the story works, no matter which path you choose, and the ideas and issues it raises.  In fact, there are completely horrific outcomes, absurd and bizarre twists--but they all work within the story and even the framework you're given.  Playing through to the end becomes a neccessity, and you are rewarded with a completely new set of ideas and philosphical questions.  I started this game wanting a bit of fluff over the holidays--and then I got hooked.
I will say that the one con to this game is that the translation is kind of bad.  You'll have no trouble figuring things out, but the language could definitely use a lot more polishing. On the other hand, the different paths/stories are engaging enough that I easily overlooked the language issue.

FTL: Faster Than Light
like a roguelike; one must manage their resources carefully to survive as long as possible and every decision is important. The mechanics are simple and consistent, the interface is informative, and the controls feel natural; nothing is overdone.
The variability in ships, events at beacons, and sector layouts afford FTL its high replay value. Playing as the captain of a ship, one will most certainly meet a stressful situation in which there is an overwhelming amount of things to keep track of: ordering crew to repair rooms, man systems and contest invaders; opening blast doors out to space to suffocate fires; targeting weapons onto an enemy ship; all the while juggling the options of continuing a fight, accepting a surrender, or fleeing before its too late. It's exhilarating.
The Advanced Edition update only made things better, introducing a host of slick UI enhancements, providing an improvement on an already great experience.
I highly recommend FTL: Faster Than Light to people that like games. And everybody else.

Man I have always loved this game.  The gameplay is exciting, and the art style is distinct and has it's own atmosphere that you can get immersed in.
I've always been impressed at how they managed to make a game out of free-running, something that seems very organic and wouldn't lend itself very well to a video game, or at least very difficult to capture.  But they certainly achieved that, and in an interface that feels intuitive as well.
It's very timing based - jump so that the top of the metal fence will be at the apex of your jump, and when she reaches it, she will gracefully vault over and maintain her momentum.   Press it too late and she'll jump and slam into it, hanging from the edge and pull herself up, climb over, and drop down to a standstill, so you have to build up your momentum again.   It's genius, that it "makes sense" to you physically and feels right, and yet is also an enjoyable game mechanic.
You can steal an enemy's gun and breifly engage in FPS gameplay.  Very briefly, because you will never pick up new ammo for the gun, she will cast it away when it's spent.  I liked this, it made for some really bad♥♥♥♥♥moments and opened up other ways to get out of a situation, still using your parkour abilities to out maneuver the enemy.  For better or for worse they removed this in the sequel Mirror's Edge Catalyst, and I can't agree or disagree with that.  They want to keep it purely about parkour, and have a legitimate sounding explanation (the weapons are high-tech and bio-locked to the owner).  So you don't get the thrill of an FPS session, but more focus is put on the parkour, and they go into more detail with it there too.
You MUST have an nVidia graphics card when you play this version of the game.  This will enable PhysX and a lot of "dressing" will be enabled in the levels.  On paper this might sound superficial, but it really heightens the action.  A mini gun on a helecopter rips the tarp in front of you to shreds as it opens fire, tattered cloth blowing away in the wind.  Shards of glass rain down around your ears as the enemy shoots at you while you run through a hallway with tall glass windows.  Don't underestimate the emotional impact this effect has.  I played it on an AMD card and forgot about it, then wondered why the game felt so empty and lifeless in the action sequences I previously remember playing.  When I looked into it, I got my education on PhysX, and was so annoyed I immediately sold my AMD card and got an nVidia one again.  (This has less relevance now since most games are console ports and devs can't justify putting effort into effects that a very small percentage of their user-base will see).
I've had many movie-like moments in this game, that were completley born of the dynamic combat and free-running system.  It takes a very special game to achieve that.   Spend time learning the controls and making them second nature, and you have a really good game with an exciting story, for very cheap now.
I personally believe the art style holds up, even if it may appear a bit flat and lacking detail by modern gaming standards.  That was 2009 remember, and they did a damn good job.
If you're a fan of the Game of Thrones TV serie, you will love this game.

This review is a bit late because I thought I wrote it but I had only made my preliminary notes on it while playing the game and hadn't ACTUALLY written my review, because I'm an idiot.
Sorry guyz
Anywho, Mirror's Edge follows Faith Connors through a narrow strip of the City of Glas, a setting which looks like it would be a beautiful open world type area, BUT we didn't get that until 2016 whenever Catalyst came out. Which was meant to be a sequel then a prequel and now is.... Kind of a prequel kind of a reboot, people are pretty divided. The point is the series has kind of been in development hell.
Bellyaching about that aside, the game has a decent storyline which is told through these cartoony cinematics. Which was really different than most other games that had come out in 2009. This is good. The game, however, tries to tell a deep story with a lot of edgy characters with shady pasts that we don't get any kind of background on. And while this could be accomplished with 2D styled animation, it.... just doesn't fit in with the tone of the game. This is not so good. I can see why some people enjoyed it, but it didn't sit well imo.
Let's talk about gameplay. I hope you like moving forward and occasionally telling Faith to jump or dash, then getting angry whenever she DOESN'T do what you said. As far as difficulty goes, there isn't much difficulty that can be attributed to anything other than glitchy gameplay.  I feel like the game also didn't know what it wanted to be. One second, you're running in a straight line, and the next minute, you're at a standstill trying to either sneak around enemies or getting shot at. To me it didn't flow very well, it felt choppy, like the true essence of the game was being stifled by the combat or puzzle platforming sections. Motion isn't fluid, it's like a river that has been dammed up, it still flows, but the flow is choppy at best.
As far as the story goes, it is shallow. The one twist in the game (which has been spoiled for pretty much anyone with an internet connection) can be EASILY seen coming. I purposefully avoided content pertaining to this game because I had beem told there was one twist in the entire game, and it would be spoiled really easily, and I STILL saw it coming. And usually, you feel satisfied with a game's ending. The story gets wrapped up all nice and pretty unless the devs KNOW there will be a followup. Not here though. The end, without spoiling anything, sets up for a sequel that never comes. The story doesn't start to get good until the last few chapters of the game, and then none of the questions that arise gets an actual legitimate answer.
And my last gripe... THE ENTIRE GAME GETS RETCONNED. "Oh but the devs wanted to go in a different direction." I hear you say. "But Pokemon Master 503, you loved Tomb Raider and it got retconned!" NO THESE ARE NOT THE SAME SCENARIOS. Tomb Raider got retconned by DIFFERENT COMPANIES. Also, most games that get retconned HAVE MORE THAN ONE GAME IN THE FUDGING SERIES.
As far as bang for your buck goes, this game doesn't really give it to you. It's a game based on speed, with time trials for all the chapters and everything, but other than going forward a la Sonic the HedgeHog, the gameplay doesn't really vary all that much. Granted there wasn't much gameplay to vary.. Ten hours is all it took for me to gain 100% completion. And while this would be okay with, say, an indie game, this game was a AAA title, with huge marketting behind it at the time. If I'm not mistaken, it sold for full price back in '09, and to me 10 hours of gameplay would NOT have been worth the full price tag. It's not even worth the current $20 price tag to be completely honest. If you're gonna pick up the game, pick it up on sale.
Verdict, go play Catalyst. It's ten billion times better despite what IGN said.

Do you remember the original Neverwinter Nights, Baulder's Gate, or Pool of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor?  If so, this game will score some major points with you.  It is turn based, which at first delayed my purchasing of it.  After a couple of hours in and a few battles under my belt, I realized that it is actually a huge benefit.  I have had more fun with the combat in this game than I have with action games (like NWN).
Combat:
The combat is turn based, but that is a good thing.  You can setup the battleground and you have a lot of time to think about how you are going to proceed.  The environment can react to what is done to it.  Mix poison with fire for explosions, cold with water to create freezing, air with water to create electrified surfaces/clouds...  etc.  You can throw things around while in combat.  Want to light up that boss?  Throw that oil or poison barrel next to him and have your mage/archer hit it will something fiery.  Archers getting the best of you from a range?  Create a smoke screen so they cannot see you.  Melee enemies chasing your glass cannons?  Put some ice on the ground or throw the enemy half way across the battle field - make him land on his allies for additional damage to them as well.
Crafting:
There are guides online for recipes - and for good reason.  While the books and such you find around the area hint towards recipes, they do not provide all of them - or perhaps I did not find all of the books.  To craft, you just drag an item over another item.  It is much like "Alchemy" (the game) in that sense.  You could spend a while just trying to combine everything until you find all of the recipes or you could just go online and find them there.
Questing:
There are a lot of quests in this game.  I did not find any of them to be disappointing in terms of entertainment.  I often found the side quests to be more entertaining than the main storyline.
Exploration:
There is a lot to do and plenty of subtle secrets to find.  This game rewards (or severely punishes) the curious.  Save often.
Main storyline:
While it was intriguing to a point, I did not gain a real attachment to it.  There was no cataclysmic climax that the characters (or me as a player) really felt attached to.  While it is a story that wraps around the characters, it doesn't really seem attached to them.  Your role in the game seems more like an extra character than the main character at times.  Don't get me wrong, it was a good storyline, but I would not buy this game for that purpose alone.

Have you ever wanted to play a B-Movie?  This game gives you the opportunity.
Altus/Ace have perfectly captured the environment and overall vibe of low budget science fiction movies in the middle of the last century's American Cinema.
The game is built using the Unreal Engine, so all the capability of it's graphical system is present.  However the presentation is different from typical unreal game, instead of a first-person or third-person view point, TDTOM is played from a third-person isometric perspective that can shift when needed.  (During jump/freefall sequences in particular)
I feel that's one of the game's strongest points..  it feels stunning visual sense, as you continue to play you really get a sense of the height of the Tower.  At any given moment the players jump off the ledge and free fall all the way to the surface.  There's a wonderful sense of vertical space to the game, I feel that the level design is imaginative and quirky.  Incorporates physical puzzles, a bit of platforming, and character specific obstacles.  The setting never left me bored.
In addition to an interesting overall design scheme, the game has two choices for post-processing of the overall visual aesthetic.  "DVD or VHS", I played the game using both.  In "DVD" the visuals are pristine and crisp, giving the player the feeling that they are looking down at a live diorama starring yester-years fantasy of the future.  In "VHS" It Coats the experience in a veneer of nostalgia, Conjuring the atmosphere of an old CRT monitor.
The dialogue and cutscenes in the game are somewhat minimal, but what is there absolutely nails the feeling of classic Sci-fi Cinema.   it brought to mind many late nights in my youth spent watching old movies about robots and aliens on my black-and-white television.
The opinions on the next subject mixed in different reviews, but I'm going to give you my take..  throughout the game there is a running "director's commentary".  I found it to be smart funny and well written, hitting the bullseye, sounding like a has been movie director from several decades ago.
Even with a couple dozen deaths I didn't find it to be too repetitive or find myself wishing to turn it off.
The combat is fun and works well with a controller, not the highlight of the game, but enjoyable.
There is a weapon and character upgrade system to help in your survivability toward the end of the game, along with unlockable special abilities, some of which are required to pass certain points in the progression.
If you're looking for a game that strays off the beaten path, and takes a detour to places strange and distant.  Here it is.

I initially went into Grim Dawn with low expectations. Maybe it would be a dark fantasy Titan Quest at best. To say Grim Dawn surpassed my expectations would be selling the game short.
Core gameplay is standard genre fare; grind enemies into a fine paste and collect items off of their dead bodies. The combat itself has a nice weight to it, my Blademaster felt like a whirlwind tearing through groups.
Progression uses the dual skill tree system from Titan Quest. A first tree is picked at level 1, and then the second is picked at level 10. There is no restrictions on mixing trees, so a variety of different builds are available.
Skills in the tree aren’t just selected, a player is given three points on level ups to use.  A player can either choose to level up masteries, which has skills at 5 point intervals, or one of the aforementioned skills. This system forces a player to choose between immediate returns of available skills or investing in mastery points to unlock stronger skills.
In practice the system mostly works, but can cause some pacing issues towards the end of a skill tree. Around Act 3 there was a huge difficulty jump, and the skill to finish my build felt like it required too much investment in masteries to unlock.
Itemization is average for this type of game. Most of the items are just straight stat boosts, but the character is given plenty of choices for damage. There are ten resistances available to the player and enemy. All of the resistances see use without one over shining the rest.
It is important to note that Legendaries are treated as end game build defining items. They start dropping at level 50, or around the end of the first difficulty.
Where Grim Dawn really sets itself apart from the genre is the story and atmosphere. The game starts out with a cutscene to give some exposition about aetherials invading the world. Then the player is dropped into a post-apocalyptic world.
From here the player isn’t given much in the way of outright story. Instead hints are dropped about how exactly civilization collapsed, the history of the world, humanities place in the three way war that is being waged, and much more. The main plot is more or less the player trying to survive, eventually becoming a ‘hero’ because frankly the developers need a reason to explain why my Blademaster has killed 24,500 enemies.
The atmosphere is what brings everything together. From the get-go it is established that this is a terrible world. Other games have tried the dark fantasy thing, but often feel sterile despite there being blood and corpses everywhere.
A set of notes that drop in an area tell a story. A family of four is fleeing the aetherial invasion and food is scarce, but there are rumors that the cultists who have risen up to fight the aetherial invasion will provide shelter to anyone willing to join. The family is forced to join the cult. In time the mother starts to buy into the ideology while the father just grits his teeth to make sure the children have food. The story ends with the women realizing that the family she joined the cult to protect would be safer as sacrifices to the blood god.
As mentioned before, the cult has risen up to fight the aetherials. Make no mistake, these cultists are no friends of anyone sane. The aetherials sole goal is to claim the world for themselves, enslaving humanity in the process. The remnants of an empire are caught in the middle trying to fend off both sides while reclaiming civilization.
This three-way war is illustrated in gameplay through encountering cultists and aetherials fighting each other. When the player engages one side, they will keep on fighting. At times they will side with each other to fight the player, but there has been times where they simply ignore the player and continue their assault, as if accepting the help.
The game is loaded with small scenarios that provide opportunities for choice and consequence. There was a man lying in the road bleeding out, and according to this man was betrayed by his partner. Either way he was dead and there was nothing I could do to help him. Except to honor his last request to track down his killer.
I do so and the person begs me to let them explain what happened. He explains that the man lying in the road was indeed his partner, but he acted in self-defense to stop the ex-partner from♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥his daughter. There is no other NPC in sight. What do I do? Is the daughter hiding or am I be being played a fool?
The attention to detail in all of these things give the world an authenticity that the genre hasn’t had in a long time. Since Diablo 2 in fact. Yes, it’s that good.
This isn’t the game for someone wanting a fun 1,000 hour min/max item grind; that is Diablo 3. This isn’t the game for someone wanting to replay the game 50 times trying out off the wall builds; that is Path of Exile. This is the game for someone who wants the fun gameplay of the genre with a well realized dark fantasy world.
Crate Entertainment is a studio to watch. I know that I’ll be watching for the first Grim Dawn expansion.

This is worth every penny the devs could ever ask you for it.
Seriously, they could have went with 59,99€ triple-A release price and it'd still be a bargain for a game of this caliber.
+ Feels and sounds like the old Diablo games, very dark and foreboding. Overall the game just has a really good atmosphere.
+ Most of the great mechanics from Titan Quest like dual classing make it to this one as well.
+ Combat is fun from the start and gets increasingly better the more abilities you get. A nice contrast to the rather slow start in the games of this genre most of the time.
+ An absolutely MASSIVE world, i've heard the game takes around 30 hours to finish on your first run. (Considering Path of Exile and Diablo 3 both take around 12-16, GD truly feels enormous.)
+ Tons of different enemy types, each new area introduces new ones as well.
+ Mostly solid voice acting and writing.
+ Good game to play solo, much more story oriented than PoE for example.
+ Great loot, nice looking gear too.
- GD shares the same engine with Titan Quest, which means the visuals are pretty dated compared to other games of the genre.
- The levels are huge, but all of them are hand crafted. Meaning there aren't randomly generated dungeons...
- ...Which takes away quite a bit of the replay value and possible endgame content.
The last point which i make might be a dealbreaker for most of you, and it was indeed a pretty big thing for me as well at first. But honestly, such a thing can also be taken positively. While there aren't randomly generated areas, they are designed very well compared to PoE etc. If you can get over this point i guarantee you'll have a great time with the game.
