Saint's Row IV is/was hilarious fun. I haven't played the previous installments of the franchise, and started straight into SR/IV which convinced me mainly because of the attributes that caused a many other fans headache: the added superpowers.
As a former veteran of the good old (and unfortunately also gone) MMORPGame City of Heroes/Villains (Superhero creation), I was looking for something that would fill the fun void that was caused when NCSoft shut down the game's servers and the Super Heroes and Villains soared into the evening sky for their last time.
But back to this game here:
The main thing you gotta know about Saints Row is that: it can't be taken seriously, yet you can't just classify it into just one game genre either: It's part 3rd-view-shooter, it's part adventure game, it's part exploration, and a whole fistful of fun if you're into character customization and generelly hilarious fun whatever the hell you decide to get up to.
You are able to collect a whole arsenal of all sorts of exotic weapons, out of which the "Dubstep Gun" will be the most memorable one, trust me. You can achieve them by completing missions, mini-side-tasks, races, platform challenges, collecting in-game stuff, and next to weapons, you'll also earn more character customization add-ons. (You always wanted to go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on your characters, making them look as wacky as possible? - This is YOUR game here, trust me!)
Once completed, you'll always be tempted to go back in again from time to time, just to wreck some havoc in the in-game city. It's like a real life anti-stress solution! ;)
So, that were my 2 cents about the game here... hope you'll have fun!

Everlasting Summer is a free visual novel. It's a (recurring) story about a man who steps on a bus during the winter, quietly nods off to sleep while an old Soviet melody is playing and... he wakes up alone in the bus at a Russian pioneer camp during the summer.
If you thought that was bizarre, then you're thinking the same thing as our protagonist, Semyon. Are you going to find out what happened to you? Or do you pursue socializing with the local pioneers? With a bunch of routes and endings, Everlasting Summer is sure to give you an interesting experience with a variety of endings.  In the end, there's also a story holding the subsequent playthroughs together.
Complete all the endings for the best experience!
Everlasting Summer was originally a Russian VN, but it has been translated to English. EDIT: Translation is fixed.
In terms of graphics, the characters and backgrounds are nicely done, but the CG is inconsistent which can be jarring. But since CG is only a small part of the game, that can be forgiven. (Again, the CG isn't bad, it's just inconsistent with the main style of the game.) The backgrounds are the most impressive and varied.
The soundtrack contains a ton of tracks. In fact, the soundtrack might be one of the best things about this (free) visual novel. The main theme is memorable and there are some good-sounding tracks. The soundtrack also does a great job giving you the right feeling for each scene.
Regardless, Everlasting Summer is a solid read, and for the amazing price of free, you can't go wrong with this. If you enjoy visual novels this is pretty much a good pick. If you want to give this kind of storytelling (visual novel) a try, this is a good point to start if you can stand the inconsistent art (which is a minor complaint.) The story is pretty damn good so you probably won't mind.
Final verdict:

It is pretty much what you get on your first playthrough (or readthrough?), although the story is intriguing enough that your curiosity commands you to go on with a second playthrough, and then a third, and then...
By the time you are done, you realize you have just enjoyed one brillant little masterpiece of a mindf***, that gradually reveals itself as a serious existential meditation on love, life and the very nature of reality. Grim Dawn is a great game.
It features a complex yet rewarding character building system, satisfactory combats, epic boss encounters, and countless equipment to loot or tinker. Masteries, skills, item grant skills, devotions, you name it. The customization is so rich that you can play it forever.
Graphic is a little bit unpolished comparing to some AAA titles. But the atmosphere and world presentation are spot on. The environment feels unique and attracting, more importantly, it expands naturally and lore friendly. There is no sudden “gap” between stages and sceneries.
Story wise, Grim Dawn has an intriguing background setting, and OK main quests. It did not explain or explore deep enough to the origin of main events, therefore I felt less heroic after beating the bosses. It however does offer interesting and interactive side quests, and those are actually much better and involved than go-and-fetch quests I did in other RPGs. And THAT Easter Egg, I was laughing so hard while fighting, that’s so unfair!
All in all, Grim Dawn offers excellent aRPG experience and high replay value. It’s not another mindless hack-and-slash RPG (although some builds do click and mash a lot), and it just feels right in every way I wanted.
So hell yeah, I recommend this game to you all.

If you liked titan quest, you will most likely like grim dawn.
The game play is similiar, with ability to pick two classes and mix them giving decent amount of class combinations, they also took a dip to path of exile and made a zodiac tree system, that reminds me of the poe skill tree slightly, exept it's tied to devotion points that are tied to shrines and that are limited.
My biggest gripe with this game is that the areas are fairly large and as they aren't most parts randomly generated, you end up knowing what is where pretty fast making several game plays less interesting.  Also due the largeness of the map, the distances between bossfights or objectives leave a mark in your sanity. Usually games fix this issue by creating advancement illusion by making zones so that you are constantly going up or down stairs. With Grim dawn however,  since you mostly are in open areas, it feels you are just running in large field bashing enemies with not that much to do between.
By far is not Grim Dawn a bad game though, just less "hectic" and engaging than some of it's compeditors.
The game gets exponentially harder later on with team play and harder difficulties though, forcing you to pick abilities that focus on survial, the builds that allow you to just blast trough most things and kite about as class cannon aren't that usable in this game.
For example I am using druid ( Arcanist / Shaman), that has really good area slow mechanics ( thorns 75% slow, chance to root), that is ideal for kiting type of play, however lot of bosses and some teleporting creatures ignore all slows and roots. Meaning it's less effective.
Also in team play game seems to heavilly favor attacking caster and ranged classes.
I am playing with my friend who is pure two handed damage dealer, we are talking about a person who hits 3-4 times harder than I do, because I have more of cc /utility build, yet all monsters and bosses keep agroing on me, letting him to just move  to  their backside to do free damage, even then it takes really long time to kill some mini boss creatures, and this is merely on veteran diffucult.
As for the game appareance factors, I'm bit conficted, terrain looks mostly awesome as well as do all the effects, but the player charecters are just plain ugly to my eye, it creates a weird contrast in the game.
Anyways, give it a shot if you are in to the genre, I don't particularly regret getting it, but I ended up playing it lot less than I intended.
Perhaps  I just am more poe person.

For the unacquainted... 'Crawl' is a dungeon crawler with fluid pixel gameplay and mechanics. It, in its current build, it is a 4 player local multiplayer game where the friends you play with are the monsters, bosses and environmental hazards you must overcome. One player plays as the human, whilst the rest of the players take control of the ghosts of comrades that were slain by the human. If a ghost manages to kill the human, that player gains humanity and takes the place of that human. All players must fight amongst each other for this humanity, reach level 10 and kill the boss (of which, each player takes control of a section of the boss). As the human improves, the ghosts/monsters evolve stronger too. This chaotic and entertaining Indie game has brilliant potential, updates and adds new content quite often.
If you ever see this game on sale and have at least one local friend also possessing a mouse and a keyboard, I urge you to buy this game and support this games development. It is a game that would be enjoyable to a wide range of individuals regardless.
When online eventually comes to Crawl, It instantly becomes a must buy hands down.
Give the game a chance. It is constantly improving.
A purchase that you will not regret.

Serious Review:
This game plays basically like blind survival mode from One Finger Death Punch (OFDP). If you've played OFDP before then you'll know whether that was something you enjoyed or not.
If you haven't played OFDP, then the simpleist way to explain this game is that it consists of two parts... the main menu, and a score attack mode. There are a bunch of different controls available (a,d, left and right cursor, lmb, rmb and everything on a controller.. and that's just what I've tried!), but they all end up doing one of two things. Attack left, or attack right. You don't move in this game, you stand still and attack enemies when they enter your range. The attack range is never shown to the player so it's something that has to be learnt through trial and error.
Now that the gameplay is outta the way, I personally love everything about the feel of this game. The sprite animation is crisp, and is a joy to watch, the music is great. The sfx of the quarter being feed into an arcade machine at the start of each run as well as the way the window is shaped all add to the retro arcade machine vibe. Biggest problem I have is that every time an attack connects the screen does a yellowish-white flash which can get a bit irritating at times.
TLDR: A crisp game, that'll be great if you enjoy score attacks, or survival modes. But don't be expecting any story or upgrades/collectibles.

Conclusion:

Did RPG's of last few years lack many things that were important for the legends of the genre?
Yes, they did. They lacked cool parties (last game with this feature made somewhat good was first Dragon's Age), good stories, interesting worlds, turn-based combat and many, many other things.
Divinity Original Sin is a dream come true for RPG fans, it takes a lot of good things from classic DnD (not only computer games) and continues Divinity Saga in very good fashion.
I'm recommending this game to everyone who liked Baldur's Gate/Planescape Torment/Icewind Dale/Neverwinter Nights/Dragon Age and I think that Fallout fans that don't fear fantasy settings will find themselves in here as well.
I don't recommend this game if you hate turn-based combad, or are turned off by lots of talking (hey, this is an RPG after all, it's about playing a role, not only fighting everywhere!).
If you haven't played earlier parts of the saga (chronologically according to Divinity universe events in this game take place between Dragon Commander and first Divine Divinity game) - you will miss out lots of humour. Most of the story doesn't rely on your knowledge of other titles from the series, but is connected. Fans will recall familiar characters, and will notice that they are playing a part of something that was "ancient history" during the events of Divine Divinity.
Summing it up:
If you like classic RPG's (not only party-based), enjoy Larian Studios humour and want to see how modern RPG's should be made - try this game.
If not - you can still try, maybe you'll enjoy something new :)
Have fun!

Grim Dawn is a great game.
It features a complex yet rewarding character building system, satisfactory combats, epic boss encounters, and countless equipment to loot or tinker. Masteries, skills, item grant skills, devotions, you name it. The customization is so rich that you can play it forever.
Graphic is a little bit unpolished comparing to some AAA titles. But the atmosphere and world presentation are spot on. The environment feels unique and attracting, more importantly, it expands naturally and lore friendly. There is no sudden “gap” between stages and sceneries.
Story wise, Grim Dawn has an intriguing background setting, and OK main quests. It did not explain or explore deep enough to the origin of main events, therefore I felt less heroic after beating the bosses. It however does offer interesting and interactive side quests, and those are actually much better and involved than go-and-fetch quests I did in other RPGs. And THAT Easter Egg, I was laughing so hard while fighting, that’s so unfair!
All in all, Grim Dawn offers excellent aRPG experience and high replay value. It’s not another mindless hack-and-slash RPG (although some builds do click and mash a lot), and it just feels right in every way I wanted.
So hell yeah, I recommend this game to you all.

If you liked titan quest, you will most likely like grim dawn.
The game play is similiar, with ability to pick two classes and mix them giving decent amount of class combinations, they also took a dip to path of exile and made a zodiac tree system, that reminds me of the poe skill tree slightly, exept it's tied to devotion points that are tied to shrines and that are limited.
My biggest gripe with this game is that the areas are fairly large and as they aren't most parts randomly generated, you end up knowing what is where pretty fast making several game plays less interesting.  Also due the largeness of the map, the distances between bossfights or objectives leave a mark in your sanity. Usually games fix this issue by creating advancement illusion by making zones so that you are constantly going up or down stairs. With Grim dawn however,  since you mostly are in open areas, it feels you are just running in large field bashing enemies with not that much to do between.
By far is not Grim Dawn a bad game though, just less "hectic" and engaging than some of it's compeditors.
The game gets exponentially harder later on with team play and harder difficulties though, forcing you to pick abilities that focus on survial, the builds that allow you to just blast trough most things and kite about as class cannon aren't that usable in this game.
For example I am using druid ( Arcanist / Shaman), that has really good area slow mechanics ( thorns 75% slow, chance to root), that is ideal for kiting type of play, however lot of bosses and some teleporting creatures ignore all slows and roots. Meaning it's less effective.
Also in team play game seems to heavilly favor attacking caster and ranged classes.
I am playing with my friend who is pure two handed damage dealer, we are talking about a person who hits 3-4 times harder than I do, because I have more of cc /utility build, yet all monsters and bosses keep agroing on me, letting him to just move  to  their backside to do free damage, even then it takes really long time to kill some mini boss creatures, and this is merely on veteran diffucult.
As for the game appareance factors, I'm bit conficted, terrain looks mostly awesome as well as do all the effects, but the player charecters are just plain ugly to my eye, it creates a weird contrast in the game.
Anyways, give it a shot if you are in to the genre, I don't particularly regret getting it, but I ended up playing it lot less than I intended.
Perhaps  I just am more poe person.

This is an 'on balance' No vote, rather than an OMIGAWD don't play this crap.
It's ok, especially at the start, it's all the fun of Titan Quest.
But then as time goes by you realise that in the first hour of play, you have seen all the game has to offer.
1) The art direction is non existent.  There's one area with a smattering of snow, but basically what you see when you start the game is what you see when you finish.   The Titan Quest games had incredible art direction, lots of different themes all of which were impeccably designed.   Grim Dawn has two themes, grim overground, grim underground.
2) All fights are the same, they just vary in how long it takes them to die. Occasionally you might relax a bit too much and get jumped by an elite and die.  But the combat rapidly reaches the point where it ceases to change.  You will be fighting the same way in the same environment for the next 40-50 hours
3) Itemisation.  You will spend the vast majority of your game thinking "nah, don't want that"  I finished the game on Veteran with the same sword I picked up around lvl 30, never saw better.
4) Story... What story?  I actually had to go and search the web to be sure that I had actually finished.   It was one of those "Really? Was that it?" games.   There are a pitiful number of quests which is particularly problematic for faction.
5) Factions.  Pointless, you will not max faction without grinding for that specific purpose.  The quests may get you to respected for some, maybe.  If you want to max a faction the bounty quests give like a 1000th (may be a slight exaggeration), you need to grind.  ♥♥♥♥ that, I don't grind.  If you can't make content to get me there, I'm not going to spend days repeating dreary boring crap to make up for it.  Don't GRIND people, don't do it, make them produce a game!
6) Levels,  All the lvl 50 legendary gear?  You will finish the game before you hit 50 unless you grind (see above, don't grind!)
It's a pale imitation of the Titan Quest games, and they have totally missed what was great about those games. The most glaring omission? Decent art direction, the graphics are good, fine, no problem.  The art directions is just dreadful, borderline non-existent.
Go play Van Helsing or something, better looking, more varied, better story, better everything.  It pains me to say this as an avid Titan Quest fan and a kickstarter backer, but there you go.

I've logged over 25 hours with this game and while I would recommend it to anyone who enjoyed Diablo 2 or 3, I will warn you that it gets very grindy very quickly. Also, expect to retrace your steps a lot, their is a ton of exploring to do but often little direction as to where to start looking next. While this is not, in and of itself a problem as the scenry is gorgous and their is tons of stuff to do (and a never ending supply of enemy mobs to wade through) there are few waypoints or shortcuts so you can expect to tread over the same patches of ground a ton of times. This becomes maddenlingly infuriating later on when the areas start looking like mazes and you need to walk for 15 minutes just to go what would be linearly a short distance.
I love the dual class system that functions like Titan Quest's did, but its easy to end up with a bunch of low power abilities that become a chore to manage. I am significantly less impressed by the loot system which ends up like Diablo 3 where you have tons of crap that you don't need and barely have the time or inclination to actually sort through it.
All in all, I would give it 3 and a half to 4 stars out of 5. If the pace of the gamplay was accelerated a little and the loot system was revamped so that loot was worth managing, it would be perfect.

This is one of those games that makes me wish there was a "Kiiiiinda" button in the steam recomendations. Let's cut to the chase here. Ok? This game is a clicker game. I know, hard to believe taking on account it's title. And that's probably its biggest issue.
Its graphics are pretty freaking great, the sprites are detailed and the design awesome, specially if you get the references. Howeeeeeeever... Its a clicker game. This seriously makes me wish it was a horror adventure game, either RPG or point and click, and the sprites were actually characters and/or enemies that acted in interesting ways. But it's a clicker game... I think you're starting to get the problem here.
Frankly, if you are a writer/designer (either by job or hobby) and like horror (like me), you probably will find this game really interesting, I know I do, it serves very well to fuel your imagination, by the means of presenting you with interesting graphics that sadly have no story or mechanics of their own, so as inspiration for other creators it's awesome... But not as a game... Because it's a clicker game.
So let's review it from the clicker standpoint... Well it's of the Clicker Heroes school of thinking, not the one I like most, but that's ok for a clicker game... For a clicker game. However it does have it's problems:
To begin with, the gear. It comes waaaayyyy too late into the game, for probably hundreds of rooms you'll be running around naked, which is just hillarious. For the most part it's just teeth (the basic currency) that you can do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥with besides upgrading your minions.
The minions themselves, well they look ok, but they have no story or character at all. Remember how clicker heroes added little stories to the upgrades that talked about the personality and history of the heroes? This has none... Which is really sad because they look painfully interesting.
Same with the enemies by the by, this needs a bestiary badly. And same for the main character, but you know, at least that's average instead of bad... For a clicker game. Tho it has the sin of not having any interesting event like cookie clicker either, seriously, it's kinda sad when the lovecraftian grannies from CC actually managed to scare me more than the unholy abominations of this game.
All in all, this is a giant waste of potential. It looks great, its designs are awesome, it would make for an awesome horror game... But instead it's yet another clicker game. It's not like I can say that they were lazy, they weren't, the designs and graphics are way too good for that... But it's a god damn clicker game, and not even that good a clicker game at that...

Despite what you might think just looking at the screenshots this game actually has less fanservice and anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t than you'd expect. Sure there is fanservice scenes spread throughout, but the real core of the content is the parody aspect of the game and the 4th Wall Breaking antics of the cast.
For those of you who don't know, the Hyperdimension Neptunia games are an affectionate parody of the game industry. Much of the humor is based around references that go from the obvious like Mario, to the almost ridiculously obscure like the SNES-CDROM ordeal. That's not to say that is the only source of humor, indeed much of the fun comes from the surprisingly diverse cast with each character having their own little quirks that make them stand out.
As for game mechanics, it is fairly basic turn based system, however there are some notable features that are pretty neat. The order in which each character on the battlefield fights is determined by their stats, once it is their turn the player is allowed to move a certain distance with the character (once again determined by stats, which can be changed via equipment and the usual level ups), and then the character can use a basic attack with a range that is dependent on what weapon their using. The basic attacks are split into three variations, Break, Power, and Rush; each with their own uses in a battle that is best explained in-game. Each character has a variety of skills that are usually just special attacks, healing abilitites, or buff/debuff techniques, these drain the characters SP bar once used. The characters also have access to EXE skills, which are super moves that tend to make fights much easier. The first EXE skill is obtained when a character reaches level 25, and is essential to boss battles. Note though that EXE skills can not be spammed since they use up a bar on the EXE gauge, which has a max of 4 bars and can only be filled by giving or receiving damage.
Also important to point out is that character are seperated into two seperate groups, the CPUs and the Makers. The CPUs are unique in that they have a second form in which their stats are boosted and in general just become all around better in direct combat. While the Makers have a wider variety of skills that are better in the support role, though they are still capable of dealing good amounts of damage. While most people tend to just stick with the CPUs since their HDD modes make fights easier, some battles require the skills from the Makers that the CPUs lack. Combined with the Lily Rank system and the bonuses those grant (for example the heroine's (unlockable) sister Nepgear allows the character she is paired with to deal damage pass the limit of 9999), and you have surprisingly deep party customizing options.
It should also be noted that level grinding is very much needed in this game due to boss difficulty ramping up at certain points. The grind isn't too bad, but it isn't uncommon for the idea of level grinding to turn off a few people.
The PC port is actually quite good considering it was done by a Japanese developer, basic but in no ways unplayable. The framerate is a massive improvement from the PS3 titles, and the graphics actually look like they belong in this generation of games now. Note that in the option menu the resolution states that the max is 1600x900, this is only for Windowed mode and as long as you have the game in fullscreen it should default to your monitor's resolution. If you are having issues you can try going into the program files and editing the .ini configuration file manually to set your resolution (make sure to set the file to Read Only after doing so). There are also some issues with DLC at the time of this review, but the DLC are minor additions and are not necessary to enjoy the game at all (though the addition of characters with an HDD mode like Plutia do make some sections easier).
*EDIT* As of right now the resolution and DLC issues appear to be fixed (at least for me) so the previous section is irrelevant now.
In conclusion, if you are a fan of JRPG's or just a fan of Anime related products then Neptunia Rebirth is a decent addition to your steam library. The upcoming games that will be released have the same forumla with minor changes (biggest being the addition of a fourth party member during battle), but it is worth getting them for the different stories and humor alone; so those are also good purchases if you want your money's worth.

I've never reviewed a game before, despite having hundreds of games and being a Steam member since Steam was a thing.  I'm lazy that way.  Deadly Tower of Monsters is a game worthy of promotion.
I normally find twitch-and-jerk jump-and-shoot type games boring.  This game is the sole exception.  Just the sheer goofy fun, the retrofuturism and 'googy' design, the self-referential fourth-wall breaking humor all combine into a game that is a joy to play.  And when you think you're mostly through, you find out there's a lot more to go.  When you get high enough, diving off to shoot targets, catch rings, or reach hard to achieve platforms is fun.  Well worth the price.
That's not to say there are no Cons.  The three characters are largely interchangeable.  I rarely wanted to go back to a swap station to change to another character just to get their 'special ability'.  The weapons were cool and fun, but the melee weapons were all very similar.  The ranged weapons worked differently enough that some were better for certain attacks than others.  I got through the entire game without levelling my character up more than 1/3 of the skill levels necessary, so the game lacks a difficulty level option to make opponents tougher (or easier).
If you've ever watched Flash Gordon, Buck Rogers, or any retrofuturistic video and smiled, you will like this game.

Following that I was baffled and perplexed and still shouting angrilly about such thigns as "those THINGS from before, what about that!" " or THAT thing! that thing was there for a few times and now its just NOT THERE?! "
The game left me asking questions that it did not answer, and with the 2 gig of space on my hard drive , I was expecting more story telling than this. Upon research, I found that this game was to be the first in a trilogy. The ending itself under THOSE circumstances, is good, like the final chapters of a book that you eagerly await to read the next, giving closure where closure was needed, and leaving trails and questions un answered to continue giving you an urge to see how it plays out.     This how ever doesnt equate well to the fact that the game is so large, the price that comes with it, and the fact that you want more to it. Do I say this is a bad game? oh hell no.
Combat is one of the most balanced and defined of its genre. I would have liked to see more of some aspects, such as characters you meet mid game that had amazing abilities, but that would getting into spoilers. The abilities were all unique and made sense, the mechanics were "Easy to learn, hard to master" and just..GOOD. ..they were...they were so good...
I both liked and didnt like the Renown system where, essentially, its used for everything. Food, Gear for your heros, leveling UP said heros...did I mention food? Because this game likes to go Oregan Trail on you and suddenly you get hit by bandits and lost 3 days of food from your 4 days of food you had on the carts. Or perhaps you REALLY wanted that high level item, spent more renown than you should have to then level up someone to get to wield it, only to go 4 days with no food in the entire caravan because someone decided to eat what equated to 2 days worth of food just to level up once, fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... and HEAVEN HELP YOU if said character dies from a choice you make, because he will be burried with said amazing item. Congrats, you are now starving, and have nothing to show for it. Now that is not to say their deaths were "Bad" as it was all about story telling and ussually based on your decisions, making you realize..anyone could die. The game doesnt force connections to characters, you get them on your own after seeing who they are through the story and through their actions. Which brings me to my next point!
The story telling though, my God...it was like watching a masterpiece of these people's lives unfold and intertwine before my eyes, seeing strands fall to the side, or be burned assudner, only for some to mend, some to rejoin where once ends were flayed, or others to simply be woven in to help the twine become more than the sum of its parts...Only to watch the entire cord be splayed out like a drunken room mate you dont remember having after a party because ya dun goofed up and its entirely your fault that Billy is going to jail-..uh..I mean...yeah, your choices have consequences, but thats the great part about this. This whole cord thing ofcourse an analogy for the fact it's "Banner Saga" and ..ya know..threading and-..oh never mind.
In closing, yes, get this game, play its story, play it again and again to see where other paths and decisions may have lead you, to see how other characters react to different choices or party members, the game is still very much worth it in my opinion, just...please know that if you were in it for the long haul, sorry, but your closure is in another castle.

This is a huge problem however, and although there are many similarities between LN and Playdead games, Little Nightmares must be viewed as a fresh title to truly be appreciated.
I found myself frustrated when attempting to solve many of the puzzles in Little Nightmares because they seemed to be too reliant on trial and error, where in either Playdead game the solution is almost always attainable on your first attempt. In a game that relies on suspenseful gameplay to stimulate the player, puzzles should be challenging but not to the point that a puzzle should need to be attempted several times. The excitement in playing games like this is the rush of being able to figure out how to stay alive in a high-stress situation. Unless you grew up watching old movies like Clash of the Titans, 20 Million Miles to Earth, The 7th Voyage of Sinbad, Jason and the Argonauts and any other number of Ray Harryhausen or Harryhausen-esque pictures or you love film in general, you'll really be missing the point of The Deadly Tower of Monsters which would be a shame; strip away the B-movie aesthetics of the game and you're left with a mostly unremarkable but mindlessly enjoyable top-down beat-em-up that pits you against everything from evil apes to flying saucers to giant ants
The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a game developed by ACE Team and published by ATLUS. The scenery looks cobbled together from cheap rubber and styrofoam. Enemies are either obviously stuntmen in suits or stop-motion effects. Many times, you can see the strings holding them up or the boom mic appearing in cutscenes. The plot is authentically nonsensical. Every facet of the aged Hollywood magic that made those films what they were is present, correct and jammed full of obscure references and Easter eggs; rarely has a game shown so much devotion and love to its subject matter
Not quite as endearing, however, is the commentary track that runs throughout the playtime. The Deadly Tower of Monsters is presented as a DVD re-release with the director and his production assistant firing out quips every thirty seconds or so and while it's been exhaustively written and is fairly humorous on occasion, there is just far too much of it. A lot of times, the two voices will be jabbering on, fully subtitled, while you're trying to hack your way through a major battle or set-piece so you wind up missing what they're saying by way of trying to concentrate on not getting crushed by a plasticine brontosaur
There's a metric arseload of weapons to grab as you go, some far more useful than others, which can be upgraded with cogs that you find as you progress. Annoyingly, your loadout only allows for two ranged and two melee weapons at a time which wouldn't be a huge deal if the game didn't force you to find a terminal every time you wanted to change them. The worst part about this setup is that every time you pick up a new weapon, one of your current ones gets elbowed out of your inventory. Having fun with your ultra-powerful Tesla cannon? Not any more! Have this crappy flamethrower instead! Even better, have it while you're being literally SWARMED by waves of killer ants!
The character stat upgrade system is more pleasing and innovative. You're not rewarded with skill points by way of XP; rather, the game has you complete various objectives, many of which are completely optional. While you'll usually get one for killing a boss, taking down a giant dinosaur with a knife is all on you. It adds depth to a game that is, at times, lumbered with mechanics that sorely need it
Still, The Deadly Tower of Monsters has more than enough style and bare bones playability to be worth a try, especially for fans of the genre it inhabits. It's a forgivingly easy game; you can make it through without a good deal of the upgrades available but as a love letter to those creaky, weird and wonderful pictures that entranced me as a kid, you'll find none better!

As somebody who loves Diablo 2 with a fiery passion that edges on peverse, and someone that just couldn't get into Torchlight 2 for some reason, and was utterly uninterested in the world and characters of Van Hellsing, Grim Dawn has finally satisfied my needs for a modern Diablo 2.
I think the biggest thing that Grim Dawn gets right that most other D2 clones fail to recognize is having an actually interesting world with a good premise. It starts off by just throwing you in blind and doesn't tell you much other than you were possessed, but as you explore the world you find journal entries that give you insight into what happened.
Much like Diablo 2, Grim Dawn has a dark world where horrible things have happened. You awake in the apocalypse, the world is ending and only a tiny sliver of humanity remains to fight back. The world is filled with gruesome tales and your decisions(that's right, you actually get to make quite a few as you progress) can frequently have nasty unintended consequences.
In other words, the setting is wonderful.
The second thing this game does right is have a good skill system with satisfying special abilities. Too many Diablo clones fail because their progression system just feels dull, here you are always eager to level up because it gives you new or more deadly abilities.
The combat has a lot of weight to it, and when you smash an enemy with a crit or a special attack it feels super satisfying as their corpse flies away from you with an explosive thwack!
Length: no idea, not even done on my first play through, wayyy over 30 hours worth of content though. At 25 bucks this is a steal.
Loot system is basically Diablo 2's, maybe not quite as good as D2's but that may be the nostalgia talking. There is a ton of loot to find, and it encourages you to try other classes and builds as you find epic loot for those classes.
Overall, this is a fantastic game. And if you've been waiting years for something to scratch that Diablo 2 itch like I have, then this is definitely a game you need to try.

Difficult decision, since the game is not awful, but there's just too much frustration involved for a 5 hour game, so it's barely a "no". Get this during a discount perhaps.
So, the game's goal is to climb the deadly tower of monsters. In order to do so you will have to fight, fight, fight and jump occasionally, but mostly fighting...and walking. The problem with the fighting is that it's awful...god awful. It's not a real brawler, it's not an ARPG, it's "something". You basically control your character from a weird elevated camera position that is 95% fixed (you can wiggle a bit, but that's it). The camera will screw you over multiple times I guarantee you. Apart from that you have a basic melee and ranged attack, as well as a dodge roll (block if you time it right) and a few special abilities, which are mostly pointless in combat. Doesn't sound THAT bad until you actually get to fighting stuff...let's just say the combat is not fleshed out at all. Hitboxes, attack animations, tells, etc. all of those need more work, especially the interaction with your character. It just feels jarred and as a consequence you'll take more damage than necessary. That in itself wouldn't even be the worst part, but some (most) attacks knock you flat on your♥♥♥♥♥and your character takes about 5 seconds to get back up...this happens quite frequently. I know you can dodge or block the attacks, but when it feels like that it's easier to do that in Dark Souls, which is pretty unforgiving in that regard, something went wrong.
Not to mention that some checkpoints are pretty far away and if you die, everything respawns. Also, some enemies can also be (very slowly) defeated by special abilities. At least I didn't find a weapon that would make a dent in them. Extremely time consuming and annoying. Oh, also, ♥♥♥♥ the targeting in this game...seriously.
Apart from the combat you will collect different coloured cogs, complete "missions" (aka achievements) and gather gold. Gold is left behind by enemies or in breakable objects...you will have way too much of that. I think I had 40,000 at the end and couldn't upgrade anything anymore, because...to do so you need said cogs, which you can find throughout the game. Not sure how many are in there, but I only got enough to upgrade about 4 weapons to maximum. Nowhere near enough to make use of the 12 or so weapons you actually get access to...especially later in the game. You also need gold to upgrade your character, but wait, you can ONLY do that once you get an achievement. That's right folks, you need to complete achievements to get more damage or more life or whatever. I got to level 11 of 30 or so. It's basically busy work if you want to get stronger. Maybe an interesting idea, but I don't like it.
The main reason you will be playing this game, however, is the story and writing. While the story is that of a C class sci fi movie you're actually replaying the movie with the director's commentary (and that of the audio technician), which can be pretty hilarious (do not turn VHS audio mode on or everything is completely garbled and sounds horrible). It does drag on at the end though, so even this isn't 100% great...
Graphics are ok (activate VHS mode here for the real deal). And that's pretty much it. If you are a patient player and don't get frustrated that easily, pick this up when it's on sale.

This is one of my new favorite games on Steam, hands down. Like a normal Dungeon Crawler, you go from room to room fighting off monsters. However in Crawl, the players play as the monsters, all trying to attack the main player. The goal of the game as a monster is to kill the human player and take their place, while the goal of the human is to kill as much as possible and gain XP points. You win the game if you're the player and you go into the boss room and destroy the boss. (The other players also control the boss too!) However, you may only do this at level 10. If the players fail to slay the boss 3 times, the player who fought the third time is removed from the game forever. (And I'm not kidding, it actually deletes your name!)
If you have friends locally, this is for you. Just grab a couple of controllers. And no, unlike 70% of steam games with controller support, it DOESN'T need to have XInput. The devs of this game were sure to incorporate as much controllers as possible. As long as it has a USB that you can stick into your computer the controller probably works. Did I mention the game only uses 3 buttons and a d pad? (2 not including the start button) Haven't tested it, but this should work in theory:
If you want one of the best local play experiences you'll ever have, buy now. Also the game devs are really active in the community pumping out updates like mad.
Positive Features:
-Up to 4 Players Locally
-Single player mode with AIs
-TONS of controller options
-Innovative control scene
-Active Devs (As of now)
-Low Price
-High Repeatability
-Cabinet mode (You may hook the game up to an arcade machine!)
Negative Features:
-No online support yet. May not come for a while. Don't buy the game hoping for online support, it's clearly not it's focus, although it may come in the future.
Overall, this game is wonderful locally. If you're having a party or just inviting friends over, this is a must have. It's still fun with bots, but not as good with other people, I haven't played much single player but I know it's kind of a mixed response, some like it and some don't. I like it though.
Also you can fight Gabe Newell. He hits you with his custom skinned digital knives. 10/10

This game is one that dared to be different, for better or worse.
The movement is really nice, if a little clunky on occasion (some hitboxes are weird).
The most tedious part, I would say, is the combat, but I think that it makes sense; of course fighting against people with assault rifles while unarmed would be really difficult.
The story is good enough, if underdeveloped, leaving a lot of it to the background. Although, in a lot of cases, this is quite good, because it allows people who don't really care about the story to just play.
The one thing that this game really captures, though, is the pure adrenaline, especially in some of the later levels, where you sometimes manage to escape with barely any health left.
Probably the best part of a game is its visuals. The visual aesthetic, with it's gleaming whites and bold colours ages really well, leaving the game able to hold up against newer games, while being much less hardware intensive.
Overall, I would recommend the game, but keep in mind that if you suffer from motion sickness, it is not exactly great for that, and I would recommend spending a bit of time figuring out how to adjust the FOV.

I still remember the fight. Two shambling skeletons, swinging lazily at the shield of my battered warrior. My sorceress, in the background, incanting a lightning spell. "I've got this." I said to myself. The spell went off with the clap of thunder, arcing over the warrior's shoulder and slamming into the first skeleton. The sense of victory quickly turned to surprise and then disbelief however as I realized that I had created a bony lightning rod, which was currently in the process of electrifying the pool of blood my warrior was standing in. He was stunned. An easy target, even for a skeleton.
This has been my experience with Divinity: Original Sin. The schools of magic interact in fantastic ways, and knowing how the system works will mean the difference between annihilating your party in a heartbeat or vaporizing that trio of goblins threatening your ranger. This is a game that does not hold your hand. You will need to think, you will need to pay attention, you will die, and sometimes you might get a little lost. But the rich RPG that the developers have put together here will reward you for your effort with a deep story and satisfying gameplay. Those of you who have tried to play co-op in games like this know that it usually involves a lot of standing around bored for the second player. Not so here. The developers have addressed that issue with co-operative dialogues. Characters can discuss certain decisions or events amongst themselves and agree or disagree as they wish. If you've missed games like Baldurs Gate, Neverwinter Nights or Icewind Dale, then pick this up. It is a gem of a game, and I highly recommend it to anyone that loves RPGs.

As I'm a hardcore fan of Telltale games, thought of giving a review for the first episode. Note that this review isn't biased to the dev.
Since I'm a big GoT fan , instantly got this, was not worried at all about the story and the decisions. The story is in parallel with the tv show especially , since the characters, voice acting and some elements of the story are alike. You represent House Forrester, atleast to a certain degree and you won't be confined to one character like in TWD or TWAU. This is somewhat similar to 'The tales from the Borderlands' as the story is given from multiple perspectives. It's a good take by Telltale games imo especially since you know the gravity of your decisions and how they'd affect you as another character. Moving on to the plot. The story so far , atleast in the first episode was top notch and I got to say I was pretty skeptical about the game after seeing how Polygon gave it a 6.5. But just for now the story has been great. The way it shows how major effects of the book/show affect minor houses is brilliantly executed.
The decisions are playing a major role like they've played in the previous Telltale games. But this time around like Totalbiscuit said, it's solely not emphasizing on dialogues and etc, but rather small ones like "taking this" or "not taking this". The weight of your decisions are felt by your own playable characters as they have to go through them. This game thus far have been the best Telltale game with hard decisions for me. It's not only that, they manage completely to nail the grim nature of of GoT. This game isn't rated R, it doen't certainly have boobies, but holy cow it's violent. In a good way which is what Game of Thrones is all about.
Moving on the the gameplay, the devs have used the same gameplay elements they have used in previous games, if you are looking for a button smashing, sword blazing GoT, THIS ISN'T THE GAME FOR YOU. Point and click mechanics and quick times events have been in the game so far with nothing new gameplay wise. The voice acting was excellent, especially since they were done by some of the original cast. Not to mention some of the scores from the original series. However the only thing I have against this game is the new graphics they have used. It doesn't look bad, but it seems a bit muddy and unpolished in a way. At times you can see some of the textures blur for no reason, that's something Telltale should work on. And the weird animations of characters can get clunky at times. Improvement from these two departments would have made this game a much better experience for consumers. But then again no one plays Telltale games for graphics.
Overall this game is pretty damn good. You should note, if you haven't seen the TV show nor read the books, be sure to do either of them. Because this game is heavily based on the what has already happened in the series so far. Hopefully Telltale would release other episodes rather quickly than what they did with TWUA but for now if you already have the game, you'll be playing it a multiple times to see what could have been if you had taken another choice. I'd give it a solid 9/10. However this may change with the coming episodes. For now it's an excellent game.

Maybe it was because I played the game completely co-op, but the combat was just insanely boring. Add to that a few long "Explore the Town" sequences that, coupled with another player, are just long, tedious, and confusing due to one player talking to an NPC while the other is having trouble keeping up with the conversation.
The combat is a shame because the mechanics of it, the element system, debuff/buff system, etc is really good and invites player customization, but it is in its execution that it becomes a boring waiting game full of long, drawn out turns with long, elaborate cast times that really amount to nothing special.

There are very few games that have legitimately freaked me out like XCOM: Enemy Unknown\Within. Not the type of jump scares or grotesque images one might find in the standard horror offerings you could pick up, but from the sheer pressure of opening up more of the map. Will you find that meld you need for that MEC upgrade or maybe just a Sectopod ready to take a giant dump on your day? Do I want to save the country that will give me money that I need now or save the country that will give me scientists that I will need later? Do I really want to fast-forward the days to get to the next event or, do I want to take this chance to shower off my feelings of ineptitude for losing a Major sniper and half the civilians on that last Terror mission I botched?  The only other game that has given me greater feelings of accomplishment and more moments of sheer frustration and bitterness in a single sitting would have to be the original.
Saying that:
Some of the more hardcore turn-based players or UFO defence fans might not appreciate the more streamlined nature of the modern sequel, trading some of the deeper elements of the original for an easier to understand interface and progression tree (...and base building and organization management for that matter). The inability as well to pick more than one event to investigate on the campaign map feels like a very artificial way to ramp up the difficulty. The adding of Exhalt in the DLC with new game modes made me want to play these modes against the aliens and, while a challenge in their own right, feel kind out of place as their own faction, could have just been added to the alien's roster as human sympathisers/experiments/brainwashed units. Indeed the lack of control compared to the original (It was a micromanaging nightmare at times, but made you feel like the "Commander".) will most definitely put off many of the fans of the original. The multiplayer is a HUGE disappointment, this is a game that begs for CO-OP campaign or some sort of horde-mode. Instead, you get a very bare-bones offering of 1 v. 1 that, while fun, feels like a last minute tack on.
Graphics and sound are good, but will not blow anyones socks off whatsoever.
Yet, all that said, it remains one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I have ever had, one that offers a different experience every time I've played it and one that is easy to get comfortable with on the lower difficulties before turning you into a sock puppet on the higher difficulty settings. The ability to customize your soldiers and upgrade them with various items and skills is done in a ways that makes it to your advantage to mix and match who you bring out for missions without making any one character overpowered.
If you play this in the hopes that it will allow you to revisit the old game, you are better off buying the old game. If you are like me and can look past the streamlining work that was done, you will have a bloody great time (just be sure to buy Enemy Within as well).   A-Must-Play!!

Another fine RPG from Larian studios, but not without it's faults.
Original Sin is a very open ended RPG, and truly they have succeeded on this front, almost to a fault. No areas are off limits and it's very easy to stumble into an area quite over the party's head. The game is built around these freedoms and the engine and game systems in place do a fantastic job at allowing you those freedoms. There was one point where this freedom was troublesome for me, and I eventally arrived at a point where I was unable to progress and unsure why. Some google research led me to a "quest" (not in my journal) that I needed to do in order to do another thing... to do another thing... to progress in the story. I don't want to give more details, as it would be spoilers, but needless to say there probably should have been a quest entry for the initial "wall" that I hit.
All that aside, the game is very well done. The combat is fun and the enviornmental interaction is all top notch. The skills are interesting and you can make quite a few different types of characters. Combining spell effects leads to interesting combinations and allows you to think outside the box in order to overcome battles that may have otherwise been too difficult for your party.
What the game makes up for in open-endedness, it lacks in story. The story isn't awful, by any means, but the above-mentioned "wall" that I hit made it so I basically put a pause on the story for 75% of the game and then was rushed through all of it hours before the finale. Sort of silly.
Graphics are good, writing is acceptable, and I encountered very few bugs.
Overall, would recommend, but don't feel bad if you have to look at a guide online a few times.

I think I just played it through in one sitting. I will... need to play this through again. So many choices. So little advice. Tense, edge of your seat action when all you're doing, for the most part, is... responding to dialogue options. Smart writing, every bit on par with the novels or the TV series. Excellent production values. Entertainment for days.
HOWEVER, and I feel I must in good conscience caution you all... if you are the type who try for a "perfect playthrough" where you make all the "right" decisions, this game will be your undoing. Morning may find you huddled over your monitor, your clothing in rags, your nails long and your hair unkempt, chanting to yourself, "but the other option, precious... what if we chooses it? What if, precious?" Your friends and family will shun you. Neighbors will recoil in horror. Cats and other small animals will back away in fear. But will you turn away? No, you'll say. So many more permutations. What if I choose option 3 this time? Will it be different? Will I find happiness for these characters?
You will not. This is the world of George R.R. "I Love The Taste of Your Despair" Martin, and Telltale has certainly evoked the Bearded One's true intent. Sorrow shall follow you all of your days no matter what choices you make, until you are cold and hollow within.

I had gotten this game with my video card, and have had it for a while, just now got to playing it and have beaten it, and I had to tell others how beating this game feels in a spoiler free retelling of my reaction
".....THA HELL ARE THE CREDITS ROLLING ALREADY FOR?! WHA-I-BUH-I DUN EVEN! WHT ABOUT THGAT THING! AND THE OTHER THINGS?!"
That was my reaction to completing the game. For the TL;DR crowd...
-=[[ THE PROS! ]]=-

-=[[ THE CONS! ]]=-
- "Short Game"
- Ending that will make you rage almost as much as some people raged over Halo 2..almost..not THAT bad but...yeah.
- Seriously, Dat Ending, WHY is 2 gig of my hard drive needed for this!? GIVE ME MORE DAMN IT!
- ....why isnt there more game? ; . ;
- Can I list how GOOD the story was as a bad thing?...Cuz I want more and its not there to be had!

Anywho, where was I for the readrs? AH yes,  "WHERE DAFUH IS REST OF GAME?!"
Following that I was baffled and perplexed and still shouting angrilly about such thigns as "those THINGS from before, what about that!" " or THAT thing! that thing was there for a few times and now its just NOT THERE?! "
The game left me asking questions that it did not answer, and with the 2 gig of space on my hard drive , I was expecting more story telling than this. Dont get me wrong, I fully and whole heartedly recomend this game! just know that....eh..it will leave you wanting more, not that that's a bad thing per say, I just...hope they actually FINISH it.
Upon research, I found that this game was to be the first in a trilogy. The ending itself under THOSE circumstances, is good, like the final chapters of a book that you eagerly await to read the next, giving closure where closure was needed, and leaving trails and questions un answered to continue giving you an urge to see how it plays out.     This how ever doesnt equate well to the fact that the game is so large, the price that comes with it, and the fact that you want more to it. Do I say this is a bad game? oh hell no.
Combat is one of the most balanced and defined of its genre. I would have liked to see more of some aspects, such as characters you meet mid game that had amazing abilities, but that would getting into spoilers. The abilities were all unique and made sense, the mechanics were "Easy to learn, hard to master" and just..GOOD. ..they were...they were so good...
I both liked and didnt like the Renown system where, essentially, its used for everything. Food, Gear for your heros, leveling UP said heros...did I mention food? Because this game likes to go Oregan Trail on you and suddenly you get hit by bandits and lost 3 days of food from your 4 days of food you had on the carts. Or perhaps you REALLY wanted that high level item, spent more renown than you should have to then level up someone to get to wield it, only to go 4 days with no food in the entire caravan because someone decided to eat what equated to 2 days worth of food just to level up once, fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... and HEAVEN HELP YOU if said character dies from a choice you make, because he will be burried with said amazing item. Congrats, you are now starving, and have nothing to show for it. Now that is not to say their deaths were "Bad" as it was all about story telling and ussually based on your decisions, making you realize..anyone could die. The game doesnt force connections to characters, you get them on your own after seeing who they are through the story and through their actions. Which brings me to my next point!
The story telling though, my God...it was like watching a masterpiece of these people's lives unfold and intertwine before my eyes, seeing strands fall to the side, or be burned assudner, only for some to mend, some to rejoin where once ends were flayed, or others to simply be woven in to help the twine become more than the sum of its parts...Only to watch the entire cord be splayed out like a drunken room mate you dont remember having after a party because ya dun goofed up and its entirely your fault that Billy is going to jail-..uh..I mean...yeah, your choices have consequences, but thats the great part about this. This whole cord thing ofcourse an analogy for the fact it's "Banner Saga" and ..ya know..threading and-..oh never mind.
In closing, yes, get this game, play its story, play it again and again to see where other paths and decisions may have lead you, to see how other characters react to different choices or party members, the game is still very much worth it in my opinion, just...please know that if you were in it for the long haul, sorry, but your closure is in another castle.

Everlasting Summer looks like your usual Japan-inspired dating-sim visual novel but you know something odd is going on when the name of the company making it is "Soviet Games" and the title screen greets you with hammers, sickles and Lenin busts.
Don't get me wrong, this really is a Japan-inspired dating-sim visual novel, but it takes place and has been made in Russia so you should expect lots of quirky stuff even when they are just trying to fit a stereotype. The premise is that you are a twenty-something internet addict with no friends and passions, who get sucked in a 1980 Pioneer Camp, the Soviet version of boy/girl scouts, before the Berlin Wall collapse. Trying to understand what the hell happened to you and how to get out from the Past you got stuck into turns out to be only half of your quest, while the other half is, of course, getting acquainted with all the girls in the camp, have sex with them, and live amazing things you couldn't experience in your actual, dull, apathetic timeline. Over the course of 7 days you will make some sparse choices that will decide what ending you get access too. This is weird cause at first it totally looks like you couldn't choose much, but the game has 13 VERY different endings and I would say that this is where it shines.
I got undeniably hooked when I realized how different the story can get based on what "branch" you pick. The problem is that without a guide, and after your first clean playthrough, it isn't clear at all how to get into a different branch or what you could have done differently. But as soon as you try to get a little deeper into the mechanics you'll realize the amount of story(es), for a game of this kind, is quite huge. This doesn't change the fact that Everlasting Summer is definitely too long in some sections and the writing is uneven at best, which might have to do with a different cultural style from what I am used to, I'm not sure. The different endings though, including a few crazy ones, are interesting and while some interactions and dialogues are beyond childish, there are also times when you can appreciate the education background of the writers.
The characters get more interesting through replays, since the first trip through the 7 days don't leave much room for their personalities, but whenever you take a different branch you get to know them better. As I mentioned before, this is the strength of the game: the 13 endings paint a whole picture. I am not a completionist but this is one case where you can only really say you finished the game when you got all the endings since only then you will really know Sovionok Camp and the story of the guy who got trapped into it.
The character design is weird at first, as pretty much everything that wants to look Japanese but it's not Japanese, but you'll get used to it soon and will probably appreciate it after a while, and the background pictures/paintings are honestly beautiful. Finally, the 1980s Soviet Union setting is just unbeatable.
Don't forget to download the Hentai patch from the official website, since the Steam version will just give you a black screen where you are supposed to see sex or breasts. It is not much at all, this is not a hentai game, but it's better to see all the stuff instead of censorship blankness.

You could be forgiven for thinking that Tarsier have been making horror games for years prior to this game's release, and indeed you could also be forgiven for thinking that they have been working with the PC for as many years; such is the quality of the gameplay, audio/visual design and performance of the game.
Turns out this is their first multi-platform game and their first horror title. More surprising still is that their previous work was LittleBig Planet and Tearaway Unfolded, which makes the kind of confidence on display here all the more surprising.
Preamble aside, Little Nightmares is one of the best horror titles I've played, and one so distinct in its visuals, themes and mood that the relatively short three and a half hours of gameplay I racked up not only satisfied me entirely, but also held its own against the spine-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly terrifying Outlast 2.
So let's break this down blow-for-blow, shall we?
-Performance/Graphics.
Little Nightmares is breathtakingly gorgeous. Tarsier clearly brought the full power of Unreal 4 to bear on the game and it shows through even on lower settings, with higher settings being stunning. Six's lighter for example, is particularly impressive, casts long and eerie shadows while also bathing the nearby areas in a sickly off-golden light that flickers, dulls and sways with the lighter flame. Lighting aside, textures, effects and other such goodies are all present, accounted for and impressive.
More impressive however, is perhaps just how well the game runs, given that the developers so evidently unleashed a gamut of tasty graphics and physics on the game. With some tweaking, I was able to run Little Nightmares at a fairly stable 30 FPS in 4K on a humble R9 280X with only an A10 7700K to back it up. When taken down to 1080P, I was free to ramp up the settings with abandon.
The only failure I could spot here is that - this being a horror game - the unfortunately mandatory film grain (WHY! GOOD LORD WHY!) and its equally insidious twin Chromatic aberration both rear their ugly heads by default. While they can be turned off to reveal the game's full, Coraline-esque visuals, they are unfortunately packaged together in post-processing, which forced me to turn that off entirely because whatever else might have been packaged in that setting, it wasn't worth putting up with having the gruesome twosome of terrible effects going on.
-Audio.
I played on a 4K TV, so I can't tell you much about deep subwoofer notes or careful surround placement, but the sounds you get to hear here are all very well engineered and presented. Music is minimal and only used to emphasise certain parts of the game, while ambient sounds and the horrible noises made by the monsters in the game all work to keep you very much ill at ease, even given the game's calmer and more reflective moments. Perhaps nicest here is that when you die, there's never a loud musical sting to go with it, and instead you're treated to the suitably squishy and dull sounds of Six crumpling like a sack of potatoes if she falls from too great a height, or sounds of struggling and slimy slipping as she gets attacked by massive leeches. It's all somewhat natural-sounding, and all so very nice.
-Controls.
Rely on Horror pointed out that the game is difficult to play with a keyboard and this would seem to be one of only a couple of things that would indicate the developer's relative inexperience with the platform. However, I play all my games with a controller by default because I'm a horrible person, and I'm pleased to report that the controller scheme for the game is not only sensible and fairly intuitive, but fellow controller users don't even have to use Big Picture, because Little Nightmares features native DS4 support - a welcome rarity indeed.
In addition, the way that Six moves around feels refreshingly heavy and believable: She is - after all - a weak and malnourished child, and so controlling her feels a strange mix between pleasantly responsive, but satisfyingly weighty. There's no noticeable input lag, but Six takes just a little time to change direction, which is accompanied by fantastic animations, which I'll get into later.
Finally, I noticed one bug where the menus all moved by two increments only when I used the controller, but this was easliy remedied with the use of my mouse.
-Gameplay.
Gameplay here is firmly a case of the traditional hide-and-seek-or-die, spiced up with well-executed platforming that takes up more of the early chapters of the game. As mentioned in controls, the interestingly weighty way that Six moves makes all the platforming much more tense, as Six doesn't turn on a dime like a character in a regular platformer, but seems to be a completely independent physics object in and of herself and so has to turn around or climb with her body and limbs like an actual human. This adds to the tension, as while Six SHOULD make a jump or grab a ledge, there's always a little air of uncertainty as she flails her arms around or lands on something just a bit too heavily.
Furthermore, the character animations in the game are all painstakingly realised, reaching Uncharted 4 levels of polish: Six runs on skinny, gangly legs with a tangible sense of unsteadiness, taking huge strides because she's just so small, and when you hit a small obstacle, Six blunders awkwardly through it, tripping realistically on the knee-high cans and babies' blocks. Even smaller gestures like the way she looks round when you try to move the camera and the fact that when you respawn after a death, Six is never just standing, she's usually sitting down or lying on the floor all come together to make you feel like Six is an actual tiny person, not just a character.
Beyond that, the story presented to you is pleasantly vague; Six wakes up in a world much, much bigger than she is and must escape; that bare and simple premise forms a great framework from which the game hangs all manner of narrative flavours, like the ever-present threat of being eaten, the mystery of who Six is and how she got there, what's up with the gnomes and some far less pleasant things that lie deep in spoiler territory. What is perhaps most interesting about the story and gameplay is that the game really DOES play on childhood fears; there's no overt sex and high-impact violence here, and no blood either. Instead the kind of scares you're presented with here are far more abstract and eerily familiar. Things like falling to your death, being attacked by giant leeches, being caught and put into a cage, being turned to stone and being eaten alive are the sort of things you'll be faced with and in all cases, the deaths are just plain unsettling, with one that my friend encountered being particularly horrible.
Though not a visceral, in-yer-face horror experience, nor a particularly psychological affair, Little Nightmares stands up on its own peculiar breed of surreal and creepy horror that - while it never elicited a scream or a jump from me - simply worms its way under your skin and sticks there throughout the whole game. It's a subtlety I appreciate and one that helps set it apart as very much its own thing; distinct from Playdead's shadowy and starkly contrasted offerings by way of its design and visuals and distinct from the likes of SOMA or Alien: Isolation in its more abstract and moody themes and more relaxed pacing.
-Final thoughts.
Congratulations! You read through my wall of text!
In finality, Little Nightmares is a wonderfully realised little toybox of creepy treats, and one which I had to go over with a fine-toothed comb. Some may lament the game's short length, but I found that being able to play the whole thing in one sitting only added to the experience.
All told, I don't usually dish out reviews, but I enjoyed myself with this title so much that I had to write an in-depth review for anybody interested in the game to find. Needless to say, I'll be keeping an eye on Tasier Studios in the future.

Everlasting Summer is not a game.
No, I do not mean that in the sense that "visual novels are not games", or "This doesn't deserved to be called a game", but more so in the idea that Everlasting Summer attempts to defy what a game or even a traditional visual novel is. Rarely have I ever come across a piece of media that has had such an emotional impact on me in quite this unique a fashion. Sure, the usual check-marks of the average VN standard are here; Somewhat bland protagonist (initially), fairly black and white choices, and fanservice rewards for reaching certain endings (see the XXX patch of the game's original version for more details) just to name a few. However, Soviet Games turned the standard on its ear when developing this project in ways I never even imagined. 
After my first blind playthrough, I received a bad ending. However, it wasn't bad in a fashion I'd come to expect from other VN of the same dating sim nature. This stems from the fact that, while most games with a similar idea might try to focus purely on the realtionships the characters build, Everlasting Summer chooses to turn every encounter, good or bad, into a type of growth (or degeneration in a few cases...) for Symeon, the main character. From the start Symeon is shown to be a blank slate, much like any other sim protagonist. However, it quickly becomes clear that that isn't the full extent of his character. Symeon has a definite personality with multiple established traits. He's a shut-in with multiple, unspoken issues who has always opted to stay locked away in his room and communicate with the outside world through a computer screen, talking to people that, for all intense and purposes, aren't really there. As such, when he finds himself swept away to a summer pioneer camp after falling asleep on a bus in the middle of winter with no rhyme or reason, he must find a way to cope with a situation he has no experience with, spending his time forcibly getting to know people, looking for answers, and finding out things not just about the people and setting around him, but also about himself. 
Keeping this in mind, the first ending I got wasn't a punishment, but instead a learning experience, showing me that not every bad situation necessarily has to have a bad outcome. In the end, it all comes down to what we do after the situation passes that decides our futures. As such, I was encouraged to immediately play through the game again and get the good ending of the romantic partner I'd initially chose, and while the main idea of the ending wasn't massively different, I did feel like the second play through was worth my time for what the good ending added to the experience. slight touches and differences are what really make the choices in this game carry decent emotional weight. What's more, once you finish both playthroughs of one character, you'll be hooked and dying to figure out what happens to Symeon in the other situations you passed over. Out of all the Visual Novels and choice dependent games I've played, this was one of the only ones that felt as if it demanded me to get every single outcome and ending possible. What's more, each individual ending helps you understand a little something more about either Symeon or the Sovionok Pioneer Camp, meaning you'll have an even bigger reason to keep coming back to help piece together each individual story-line into one massive story-web. 
I want to say so much more about this game, but I'm afraid I might spoil some crucial plot points if I keep going, so I'll leave the rest to you, the player. 
In short, this is a game that refuses to be a game. The main character is his own character, not just a suit for the player to wear and experience a simulated feeling of personal choice through. You will care about Symeon the more you play, and you will be drawn to see where each road takes him. On top of all of that, this game has one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard in my storied history with video games, ranging from soft and classic rock to fully orchestrated pieces and techno-bit tracks, and I could honestly recommend it, even without all the other positives I've already mentioned, just for its musical score alone. Go download this game. Right now. It's free, and minus some personal preference on certain endings (we all have them) and some minor grammatical errors in the English dialog (it's a Russian Game Studio, so cut them some slack), there is no reason for anyone not to play through this wonderful game... no, this wonderful experience.

Insanity Clicker is essentially a Reskinned Clicker Heroes.
You click on the monster to kill it, and you only progress to the next level when ten enemies are killed on the most recent level, or you've killed the boss on levels of multiples of 5. As far as I know, progression is impossible whilst offline, as is a usual weakness with this mechanic.
As you kill monsters, you gain currency. In others, it's usualy Gold, here it's Teeth. Functions identically however, as you purchase pets, which are your main source of increasing your Damage until Ascensions, at which point you'll gain a special second currency, likely named Spirits. These are most likely used to purchase upgrades that are effective across each run, inbetween ascensions.
As you upgrade your pets, you can unlock spells. As far as I have seen, there's the typical arrangement of spells. Click Damage boosts, Drop Increases, Gold per click boosts, spell power increase, spell cooldown decrease, essentially every skill in Clicker Heroes is here.
There's an auto-progress mode, a very negligible array of options to only turn on/off music, sounds, or any other audio in the game, turn on scientific notation numbers, and other graphical on/off modes.
There's also a button for Fullscreen.
I'm personally/currently unsure of what Illnesses are, but I imagine they're not too different from Clicker Heroes' Ancients, essentially requiring Ascension Currency to purchase/upgrade upgradeable objects which give scalable, and powerful boosts, some of which may be infinitely upgradeable or not.
There is also an Idle mode, but as far as I know, it only serves to collect teeth for you.
As far as the above, mostly all of them are basically in Clicker Heroes, the only one that isn't, is the Idle Mode, due to the effect always being on.
The graphics look rather nice however, being highly detailed, with each character looking nice and creepy if not horrifying, with each art asset looking like it fits in with one another very nicely.
Haven't listened to the music, but I imagine it's fairly decent.
You do have the option of dressing your character, choosing between male or female, and being able to dress them with weapons, shirts, pants, underwear, shoes, socks, pets etc.
Only... as far as I know, there's absolutely nothing to do that with yet.
Altogether though, I can't really recommend the game. It's too mechanically similar to Clicker Heroes to really justify it's own existence on the same platform as it.
That being said... if you want a game that's almost mechanically identical to Clicker Heroes, this will be in your area. It's personally not a game I can enjoy too much.
