If your only contention for Dying Light is that it is
, then you must not hold games to a very high standard. Considering that Dead Island came out almost six years ago without the advantages that Dying Light has today, I'd say that Dying Light has not brought much new to the table and has failed to surpass Dead Island in most ways.
Dying Light and Dead Island both share the same loot system. Simply put, it is a color spectrum that shows the rarity of the items that you'll collect from quest rewards or random pillaging around the world. This is no different between either game, save for the actual items that can vary from game-to-game. If Dying Light truly wanted to surpass Dead Island, I would have liked to see far more crafting components and more intuitive mods.
Speaking of mods, they're mostly the same across both games. Both games employ an elemental status effect with electricity, freezing, flammability, and poison. The varying statistics of damage on these modifications are clearly different, but nonetheless the same across both games. I would have thought they might get more creative in Dying Light with their modifications, but they disappointed in that aspect, as well as the looting.
The narrative for both Dead Island and Dying Light are both equally
. Both games have cardboard characters and a predictable storyline that bordered on the goofy. What comes to mind are the antagonists of Dead Island and Dying Light: Ryder White and Rais, respectively. These characters are calcuable in dialogue, actions, and their own personal anecdotes, which makes them about as cringy as you can get.
I would have expected Ryder White coming out of a game like Dead Island because I believe it was intended to be asanine to begin with. Dying Light, which was created to harbor a more serious tone (quotes from the developers themselves), has not created a loving antagonist simply because they tried far too much on crafting something that would rival that of other AAA-title antagonists. Conclusively, I would have expected so much more from Dying Light's character development, especially since it is several years ahead of Dead Island.
Branching off of that, the personality of many characters doesn't line up entirely with their dialogue. The protagonist, Krane, is a huge part of this problem. If you look at the quest where you have to pick up money from various fishing villages for Rais, his dialogue consistently changes from threathening to compassionate.
If you want to see for yourself, go to the third village on the questline and talk to Morgan. When Krane enters, he acts more passively than his previous encounters, "Don't shoot the messenger, I don't want this just as much as you do." Within nearly two seconds, he threatens Morgan by saying how easy it would be to burn the entire village down, in leiu of the fact that he could have easily bartered his services with Morgan instead of being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
This type of bipolar attitude with many of the characters is another glaring example of how poor they have been developed. They are so bare-bones that they don't even have a personality that they're able to stick with consistently throughout the entire narrative of Dying Light.
As for the gameplay itself, I think Dying Light succeeds with flying colors. The zombies in the game are incredibly fun to toy around with, the weapons are fun to craft, and the night-time races against Volatiles give for an enjoyable day/night cycle. However, I can't give Dying Light a recommondation simply because of that.
Dying Light, to put it bluntly, has not brought anything new to the table in a market that is saturated with zombie games. With the crafting/looting system being recycled from their Dead Island franchise and a story that is nothing but a disappointing pit of effortless backstories, cardboard characters, and an uninspiring landscape - this game is not getting a recommondation from me.
Dare I say: Dead Island reskin, with parkour dlc.

If you enjoy the click genre of games, then this one is not disappointing.  It's a successful use of the Cookie Clicker formula with a darker twist, making the mechanics familiar and easy to get into the game.
Pros:
- The game has many unique monsters, well rendered and different (which could count as something less cohesive, but I enjoyed seeing what was next).  Even the sexy female ones have a horror flare that is both amusing and interesting.
- Good pacing.  I only played a bit over an hour but it seemed to advance more steadily than, say, Clicker Heroes.  I never hit that WALL where you just have to let it run and walk away, and while that may have been further on, I felt it was a good, steady balance of furthering your place on the map and powering yourself up.
Cons:
- The blood spatter effect (labeled as 'special effect') quickly overwhelms the game.  Yes, you can turn it off, but the monsters become static and there's not much life to it.  I can't confirm it, but turning off the effects seemed to turn off chests and the bugs as well, as I never saw a single one (but got an achievement for getting 10 chests, go figure).
- The critical hit shake, and this is a big one because it's the reason I have to stop playing.  At some point you'll start getting critical hits and true to clicker form, everything shakes.  Unfortunately, by everything, I mean EVERYTHING, from your interface to the icons to the buttons, it all jumps.  You can imagine how unpleasant this is to look at if you're critting a lot.  There's no option to turn this off.
That's really all I can give it after the time played, but it was interesting enough for a recommendation.

Incredible game! When I first started following this game, I was put off by the amount of dialog that seemed to be present.
That is not an issue.
The dialog, while verbose, is broken up into easily read portions. Conversations are handled in logical ways. I have yet to run across any dialog that I wanted to "skip through". All of the dialog has added something to my experience, just as it should in a quality RPG.
The shear amount of things to do is incredible. I usually play my RPGs as a “good” guy; You know the type. I won’t steal, trespass, or try to break the game’s progress. Divinity WANTS you to do those things! Once I let go of my lawful tendencies, the game opened up on a whole new level.
Sneak into a house and rob in blind? Check.
Bust open a shop door? Check.
Murder an NPC for her possessions? Check.
Dig up a grave or three for lofty loot? Check.
In fact, had I not done at least a bit of this the game would have been much harder so far. This speaks truths to some aspects of real life experience as well. Not that I have ever done anything like that listed of course, but its possible out here, and possible in Divinity too.
Then there is the lovely, turn based, tactical combat. Personally, I haven’t seen enough combat! This system is enjoyable enough that I think it could be a game unto itself. Rain on a fire based enemy, zap it with a water based spell, and cause massive bonus damage, just as logic would dictate. Fire and lava on the map will actually heal those fire-based dudes, too. Nothing feels quite so bad as when that badass sword swinging melee fighter runs off, steps in lava, and heals for 3000 points (When he only has 150 HP to begin with!). Knowing you have to kill this thing in one turn so it can’t heal really puts the pressure on.
Opposite to that, catch on oil slick on fire. The fire will spread all over and enemies enveloped by it act accordingly, sometimes casting rain spells of their own to counter. Of course, casting rain now makes then wet, and they can be more easily frozen. I love this system, and many combinations exist. Poison arrow bombs. Electricity streaming through a newly created rain puddle. Teleport that bad dude into a lava flow for virtually instant death. SO MANY OPTIONS!
Exploration. The game is HUGE! I have about 25 hours in and have not completed the first area yet (I am told 100 hours for a first playthrough is not unreasonable). I am only at level 6 with my characters, too. I have found a way to “skip” past a lot of the content in the first area, but the next map harbors enemies that start at level 9. So, while possible, it’s not advised. The game does not put up an artificial barrier to block your progress (Or hasn’t so far). In the first town I was warned by the city guards that I was not strong enough but they would still open the gates for me, leaving the choice up to me.
The game will require some thinking outside of the box. Some of the boss fights you will face can be brutally hard. But with the proper application of strategy and using the tools at your disposal, all fights seem fair. Nowhere did I feel I had been cheated, either in battle or in the puzzles. And if you do feel so, the quick save and quick load function can be used anywhere.
So, tl;dr? If you even remotely liked Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment, this game will scratch that same itch.

I know I'm bucking a massive trend by not recommending XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but I think is important to distinguish why this isn't as good a game as the overwhelming recommendations indicate. I feel the game's flair leaves an incredible first impression that's not actually reflective of core gameplay and this is really skewing the reviews in a positive direction.
The graphics/audio are glorious. The UI is slick and fancy. The game was reliable enough (hung on me once) and I had no significant problems with any aspect of the game.
Where the game lets itself down - as well as the heritage, which 2k have exploited to the maximum - is that Fireaxis have dumbed it down a lot for marketability reasons, creating a game that is initially easy and fun but sacrificing the depth and nuance that made the originals so engrossing.
Once the novelty of the prettiness wore off, I soon found it a tedious and shallow affair that slowly became less fun and eventually I stopped playing altogether long before I completed it.
Gone are soldier stats. Instead you get soldier classes and a simple skill path with 1 or 2 choices at each level (with previous choices not affecting future ones). Soldier builds soon become templates and this detached me completely from the characters. It may be easy to understand, but it is boring.
Gone is full control over soldier load outs. Certain classes get certain weapons, there is unlimited ammo, and you get one extra slot. None of the micromanagement that plagued the originals, but at the expense of control. Grenades are almost surplus due to this the limited single extra slot, curtailing yet another aspect of the game where you had to balance ammunition, grenades, and supplements like (health kits etc).
The AI is dumb and predictable. Generally the aliens don't move until you find them, then seem to have no real intelligence in their tactics. Their general lack of awareness of your squad until you 'trigger' them just flies counter to any logic about an advanced race. You can blow aliens to bits but in the next room the next batch sit there patiently in blissful ignorance. Again, easy at first, but ridiculously boring as the game winds on.
The tactical time-unit based combat of the originals is replaced by the current trend of 2 actions per turn. It is literally child's play. You run a guy into cover and shoot, or you run forward to trigger enemies then retreat. At first the simplicity of it makes it immediate fun, but after several hours worth of doing the same thing over and over again, it becomes a very monotonous affair.
The original game's missions were tense affairs. You had to balance movement with being ready for a firefight. You had to balance safety and long distance shooting with conserving ammunition (coincidentally making grenades very important due to their destructive power). Going through doors was a dangerous moment. Time units made positioning and setting traps a slightly tricky task - which gave a player something to master. Your soldiers could only see the direction they were facing, and enemies moved independent of previous engagement. None of this is present in this remake, so you just edge through the map wiping them out as you encounter them. You can run into a room then out completely safely. There's just no surprises once you've experienced each map/enemy a couple of times.
The base management seems to be straight forward. Again, easy at first, but down the line it ends up being just another template in a game of template soldiers and template tactics in template missions. Eventually you'll just feel you are stamping your templates without much thought and no longer engaged in the game. Maybe late game adds a few things, but from what I could tell (without really getting deep into it) it was still just more template stuff.
One major bug bear that just made me cringe every time I saw it was when snipers jump out from behind cover to shoot which just looks so silly. They can't see particularly far either! After the graphical flair wore off, I felt I was playing a game designed by managers and marketing - it'd looked amazing but was built to get great reviews.
Well, I have to give it to 2k/Fireaxis, it worked.
To the reader: if you want a game that will keep you coming back for more, look elsewhere. I probably won't play this again.

XCOM Enemy Unknown, what do I have to say about this game?  Quite simple, I love the game.  Turn based strategy games aren't usually my type of games but I recently have gotten into playing them more and thsi one is definitely one of my favorite.  I usually stay in the realm of real time strategy games such as League of Legends but this game is a very enjoyable games.
This game has a simple concept when it comes to gameplay, in between fights you are tasked with managing your base which is seen as the last stand of human survival from the alien invasion.  During fights you are allocated a certain amount of moves each turn that you use to maneuver your men among the battlefield and engaging enemy soldiers.  When engaging enemy soldiers it is not 100% guaranteed to hit your target, before taking your shot at the enemy target it will tell you the percentage it is likely to hit to give you the chance to not take the shot and come up with another move to make.
There is a multi-player side to the game where you go into a 1v1 with a friend or stranger online, depending on the settings of the lobby you will have a certain amount of currency to use in crafting your squad to use in the battle.  Once in the game it will work as if it is any other battle during the campaign, the game will progress until one of the squads is defeated and a winner is determined.  You will have many options of how to create your squad so you have the choice to use your limited currency to either make a small squad full of high quality gear or a larger squad full of lower quality gear, personal preference and experience will help you decide which type of squad will best suit you.
The campaign of the game is quite simple and very easy to follow, the basic idea of the game is you will build up all your resources and gain experience on your different soldiers all in preparation for the last mission that will become available to play after a certain point in the game.  Once the last mission is completed it will be game over and you would have won.
Overall this game is very enjoyable offering many things to do within the game, you have many upgrades that you will need to acquire before attempting the final mission and there are multiple ways to upgrade your soldiers and gear them up so every player should have a way that they can make their squad into the squad they want.  The multi-player side of the game I found most enjoyable playing with friends, however I didn't find playing with strangers very fun, that may very well be just me as everyone has their own way to enjoy games.  Bottom line this game is very fun and I recommend it to anyone looking for a good turn based strategy game and if anyone hasn't yet played a turn based strategy game then this one is definitely a good one to start with.

The Deadly Tower of Monsters is the best ACE Team game I’ve played so far. It seems fairly well polished, has a neat theme, a funny out of touch narrator, and a great sense of scale through its use of the vertical space since you are making your way up a gargantuan tower. TDToM does come with a handful of issues though that can be mitigated somewhat.
The combat is a mostly pleasurable experience. You have basic attacks, a strong attack (charged basic), a jumping attack, a roll/parry button, powers, and ranged attacks. One of the more satisfying things is how enemies will often harm each other. You can use it to your advantage with smart footwork and the ragdoll physics only make it better. It can feel simple at times, but nailing down the parry allows for some satisfying counters because it’ll group parry. If 3 close projectiles come at me, I can reflect them all back and that works on multiple melee enemies too if they’re close enough. Understanding the enemy’s timing is the only hard part since there are plenty of enemy types.
Progression occurs as a good pace. As you play, you’ll discover a variety of weapons. They all have different properties from each other and are introduced in a way with the most powerful ones being acquired last. You can upgrade your favorites to make them even stronger and change them visually. Upgrades are acquired by spending cogs that you can find hidden around everywhere. These weapons are shared across the three different characters that you’ll control one at a time. Each character also comes with a different power that they can use to overcome the occasional obstacle or overwhelm your opponents. Powers are unlocked over time and can be a chain lightning attack, a dash, a mine, an AoE push, and more.
I’m a big fan of the theme of this game and how it presents everything. The narrator is there speaking as if he were providing audio commentary on a DVD. Many of the enemies are presented as an old, cheesy sci-fi movie type of deal with guys in various monster suits, bats on strings, and really big bosses. You’ll see some stop-motion animation going on with some of them too. The level design really lets you know how high you are the further you go into the game.
The ending was uh… weird. Not sure how I feel about it. I guess it was okay.
The game does have some negatives that made me sigh a couple times. You need to touch a checkpoint in order to save progress which makes accidentally falling to your death taste real bad after finishing a big battle or completing a large platforming section. You can teleport to any previous checkpoints at will, so use that to your advantage and don’t forget to touch one before doing something risky such as skydiving a long way down with little health. There are a few easily killable enemy types that can completely stunlock you into death if you’re cornered by two of them. Stay in the open and away from the walls when you run into them and don’t forget about your powers. Finally, there was one section that involved plenty of stairs that went by real slow. Thankfully, that was the only portion of the game that had me bored and it isn’t too long.
So, if you’re looking for a good 5 hours or so of some quirky fun that was fairly consistent throughout, The Deadly Tower of Monsters would be a fine choice. If it’s on sale, definitely consider giving it a go.

Beautiful is the only word that comes to mind when asked to describe Child of Light. From the amazing fantasy world of Lemuria to the delicate flow of the soundtrack and from the immersive combat system to the underlying theme of the story, Child of Light becomes the beacon of both hope and inspiration that a great RPG can exist in this generation of gaming.
The world of Child of Light is incredibly stunning and very well realised as the fairy tale setting comes to life as though right out of a children's bedtime book. Reality is but an ember within this brightly shining flame of fantasy galore and I can't help but stop and marvel at the beautiful world during my travels through Lemuria.
This existing beauty is largely due to the fact that everything within the game is made to look as though it was painted in watercolour. Whether you're floating around as Aurora or admiring the character portraits during conversations, the art style brings out a sense of nostalgia and fondness, reigniting the subconscious memory of famous old fairy tales. Do they have talking mice? Check. How about midget magicians? Check. Sword in the stone? Double check. All of these, in aesthetically attractive watercolour art.
The world is fully fleshed out with a soundtrack that is truly remarkable, memorable and addictive. As you cruise through the skies of Lemuria, you can't help but give your mind over to the soothing draw of the violin or sway your head to the catchy tune of the piano. The solo effort of Béatrice Martin creates a bridge to your emotions that latches on and never lets go, long after finishing the game. The battle music, however, makes use of a whole orchestra to generate fiery fierceness and a potent cheer during its climax that would be sure to instill an everlasting feeling of power and hope within the player.
Gameplay in Child of Light is akin to what I would call a turn-based active time interactive system. Why interactive? This feature comes from your buddy, Igniculus, who can be used to slow enemies and heal Aurora and her allies. The active time turn-based system acts independently of Igniculus (controlled with the mouse) and depending on your timing in slowing your enemies, can be very useful or horribly detrimental. This dynamic shows off even during the first battle and is something I found to be engaging and very fun to play with.
Finally, Child of Light tells the story of Aurora, a young princess who finds herself in Lemuria, in search of her father who is at death's bed. While the story remains as such, the underlying theme is what I found to be the actual journey, the actual idea of the game. Child of Light isn't just a simple fairy tale, it's a light-hearted coming-of-age story. Even after finishing the game, it's strange to say I've become attached to Aurora's journey and maturity.
The only gripe I have with the game is the length of it because having done all the side-quests, optional bosses and collected all the confessions, I've only logged in about 13 hours. Of course, the price compensates for that and I'm quite used to playing properly lengthy JRPGs which obviously does not compare.
Child of Light, to me, was well worth the money and I can not be happier to say that such a great RPG is now present on the PC. The game was short but incredibly sweet and I can't help but keep diving back into it, not to do anything else but gaze at and absorb its beauty. After all, having the ability to fly, I wanted to simply float along and smile.

A revamp of the PS3 release. Re;birth 1 removes the bland and tedious of the first game (but still enjoyable) and replaced it with goodies from its mk2 sequel, primarily its semi free-roam battle system, as opposed to the original's FF-sqeue turn-based combat, all while still maintaining its charm and eyecandy fans have come to expect and love. Console jokes and character conversations also include references and jabs at the first game, giving players who played the original PS3 release a good chuckle or two.
Being a Vita port, the game doesn't run on native 1080p, but it's not a deal-breaker. In fact, I find it very well optimized for a port aside from its post-release issues and glitches. Gameplay is fluid and 'breathing' character portraits bring life to its cast during dialogue. Best played with a controller, a KB+M is fine but navigating character movement and camera angles with two sets of movement keys while inputting commands isn't fun.
Highly recommended to anime and VN fans, or anyone who falls into the niche JRPG segment of the market.

I only game on the PC so this is the first time I'm introduced to the Neptunia franchise, but I love this game so much.
In this game, the grind is real; and if you don't grind enough, bosses will just one hit KO your characters. Also if you are a forgetful person like me that doesn't save very often, prepare to get wrecked as there is no autosave so you will have to start from your last save. Of course, there are save points before major boss fights and that always helps, so if you do get the game, remember to save ever so often.
About the DLC, the DLC characters are kinda overpowered, buy it only if you want to support the developer. The game is basically easy mode considering Plutia's and Peachy's EXE Drive (read: Super Attack if you don't own the game yet) will take a big chunk out of a boss mob's HP bar. The colosseum mode added by the DLC is quite fun but requires even more grind as the mobs introduced there are even harder to burst down.
A major flaw I found with the game is how they sort the 'Plans' to re-make items, which is very apparent when you go to the accessory category. This won't bug you unless you are keen on customizing your character as inventory sorting is still bearable and doesn't make it a pain to find consumables you need.
Story wise, the game is basically satire based on the 'Console War' debate. There's constant referencing to other games to the extent that characters are named after games or game developers. Is it a good story? I don't think so but it's pretty funny most of the time. The voice-acting is also great; I listen to the Japanese voices as the English one is missing a lot of lines even in the beginning moments.
1080P IS HERE!!!

I first saw Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball on the Steam store during Early Access. I was interested in this game because of the Disco Dodgeball part of the title, as I am a fan of the disco genre. I bought the game after it left Early Access. As I was introduced to this game, I was treated to a flashy arena filled with bright colors and entertaining disco music. This game has both single player and multiplayer, but it places more emphasis on multiplayer since it puts you, a rolling robot with one wheel, against other rolling robots. You are either with the red team or blue team. Your robot looks strikingly similar to Claptrap from the Borderlands series.
Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball looks like a first-person shooter, but the weapon you use is a ball inside a futuristic looking arena with ramps, robots from your team, and robots from the opposing team. The game emphasizes combat with that ball and you can score one hit kills just like your opponents can do to you. There is never a dull moment in this game, as the music is always rocking and your robot is constantly running around the arena either trying to knock out your opposing robot or trying to avoid getting knocked out. It takes some time to master the skills of advanced movements such as blowing up a robot while in mid-air or blowing up a robot with a ricochet hit. So, this game is wildly different than traditional first-person shooters.
The main mode is deathmatch, which requires your team to reach a particular score before your opponent does by scoring knockouts with your ball. There are powerups scattered around the arena that can give you an edge, such as a boomerang, higher jumps, extra ricochets, bigger balls for easier knockouts, easier targeting, etc. There are many other modes that enhance replay value with the main objective of scoring team points that have nothing to do with scoring knockouts. For example, hoops is a basketball-like mode that requires your team to find a specific ball to shoot through a hoop for a point and the team that shoots the most hoops wins. This mode puts your movement skills to the test because shooting hoops is extremely difficult while constantly moving. You will have to learn to use the brake key in order to shoot accurately. Another interesting mode is capture the cube, a mode that requires you to steal a cube from your opponent and race with the cube to place in your domain for a point. While the main goal is to score points with the cube, you can use your balls to knock out opponents to increase your personal level. Increasing your personal level will allow you to buy certain upgrades for future matches such as gears and other equipment. Other than teams, you can opt for free for all (FFA) competition in each mode. FFA requires all robots to compete for themselves, meaning you score for yourself and not for a team.
Those who are used to first-person shooters will feel right at home because the mouse/keyboard configuration is familiar. The mouse is very effective in moving your futuristic robot in all directions. You can learn to catch balls thrown at you so that you can throw them back at your opponent for quick knockouts/kills. Mastering your movements can help you score creative kills which will increase your personal/robot level. Creative kills include the aforementioned killing in mid-air, ricochet kills, and long distance kills.
One cool feature in this game is the ability to hit the F5 key to record the last four seconds of your gameplay. Recording the last 4 seconds of gameplay will be saved as a .gif file. You can place the .gif file in the artwork section of your Steam page to show off your sudden kills and talented moves. This type of recording is very rare for any video game.
Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball is an exciting game in terms of gaudy graphics and gameplay. I wish there were more music available, especially American disco. The music in the game sounds like European disco only, but it’s still very entertaining and will keep players upbeat. There are many levels of arenas with wildly different shapes and many modes that have different goals for scoring and winning matches.  I recommend this game for its looks, gameplay, and extremely high replay value. Kudos to Erik Asmussen for making a fine indie game.

One of the best local multiplayer games ever made. My friends and I have played this almost every week without fail since launch - it's that damn good. When we meet new people who claim they're into games, we vet them on this and see if they have fun or can appreciate the depth of game mechanics. We love this game because there's nothing like sitting shoulder to shoulder with a pal and howling with rage at a stolen kill, laughter at a horde of slimes causing a human to suddenly play a Shmup, or roars of hype when a close bossfight comes down to the wire. My short recommendation for this game is
. But now let's get to why you should.
CRAWL is a local multiplayer game that involves between 2-4 players. One player is a human, and the other 1-3 are monsters. Every time a monster kills a human, whether it being done as a monster, as a possessable slime, or a controllable trap, that player will become the human.
This means that the three non-human players must work in a loose alliance until the very last minute, because there can only be one human!
The other gameplay mechanics are a bit more complicated than that, and I'll explain the most complicated one, the leveling system and the asymmetrical nature of the players:
-A player possessing a human can kill monsters to gain XP and continue leveling up. This primarily adds extra health and to the human and gets the player closer to a boss run, since only characters with level 10 or higher can do boss runs. Humans get better gear and stats by accessing shops. They use gold that they gain primarly while being a monster (I'll get to that later)
-Nonhuman players control ghosts most of the time. Ghosts can possess pentagrams to spawn as monsters and fight the humans. They can also control traps or collect ectoplasm while they're in Ghost mode to drop slimes, which are weak, autonomous/controllable monsters that can be dropped at any time. This is useful for trapping a human in a room, since humans must kill all monsters before leaving a room. Slimes aren't too strong on their own, but if the human's health is low, and/or the room is full of traps, they can be utterly devastating. All players can level up their monsters at the end of a round. Nonhuman players can also all control a boss monster Voltron-style, with each player controlling a limb or head and working together to kill the human.
Now here's what keeps this asymmetrical gameplay balanced from a progression standpoint. As other players level up their human forms, all the other players get "Wrath", or monster XP. So as any given player human(s) get stronger, the monsters of the other players get stronger. This keeps the players' monsters roughly scaled with players' human forms, and it means that people who are especially good at playing only humans or only monsters may be in for a dramatic uphill battle once they get out of being a human/monster for an extended time.
Also, while players are monsters, they gain gold by hurting or killing the human. HOWEVER, this gold can only be used when you're a human! This means that someone who's been a monster for a long time will most likely have strong monsters, a lot of gold, but low human levels. Even if you can buy out the shop, you'll still be a pathetic creature of flesh until level up or reach the shop to get some assistance.
There's a lot more stuff going on here as well. Single-fight upgrades that require slime/gold/human health sacrifice, spells, dodge rolls, blink teleports, poisoned food, magic staffs, frog hexes, cursed weapons (that make you insane), repeating crossbows, Gabe Newell, I could just keep going on and on. Let's just say there's a LOT of content packed in the core game, and different human/monster builds play very differently from each other. There is also a ingame database to keep track of all the traps, monsters, and items, and even a monster/boss duel mode, where you can practice as a human or as a monster to improve your skills.
The only drawback I could say about this game is the fact that it doesn't have online multiplayer, and that it is quite different in terms of gameplay flow when you get started for the first time. The online multiplayer aspect is not a big deal. This game plays at a fast, almost twitch-like speed, and lag would utterly ruin the experience. As for the gameplay, a gross approximation I would make is classic Zelda crossed with Dark Souls, but the monsters are hilarious jerks because they're your friends sitting next to you! But really, it's a bit of a gross approximation - CRAWL is one of a kind. And the devs are great guys. They provide substantial updates to this game - not very often, but it's only 2 guys and they take the time to address balance issues while adding content during updates. They'll even talk to you on their Facebook page and respond to emails you send them.
I'll say this though: if you ask them about online multiplayer, they'll tell you that they'll finish the game first then add it later, so don't get your hopes up.
Anyway, get it, my personal GOTY every year since it launched because it's just so damn fun.

Play until you start feeling like a boss.  Just do it.  Ignore reviews, all of them, positive or negative.  Just hang in there.  I promise that if you have any inclination for an open world, "collectible" and diversion based platform, even the most rabid Saints Row purists can be swayed.  I was one of them.
The story is awesome.  Not, say, Squaresoft awesome, but my favorite GTA is Vice City and although the story for SR4 does not match it's epic proportions the story is absurd enough to just
.  Yes, Volition really likes to push the envelope, sometimes in ways that make you scratch your head as to why they thought this and that would belong, but the voice acting is so gosh-darn great and the individual characters all possess attitudes similar to those you'd expect from characters dropped into such an insane and bleak world.
I did not give this game a good review at first.  I was so excited for it.  I played SRTT with my kid on her account when it came out and honestly it was so much fun.  There was a lot missing from 4 that I really wanted to see.  Without giving much away, some of the creative options for vehicles aren't really present, which was a HUGE turn off.  Things I can still enjoy doing in the 3rd game are not really possible in 4.
Another favorite game of mine is the Prototype series, and 4 borrows heavily from those games in the most genuine and passionate ways.  There are certain elements of platform games such as these that make one feel like they have a LOT of freedom, things that make me feel like the old days of playing Mario 64 and such.  Freedom takes on a whole new meaning in games like these, which is why ever since the 3rd game I cannot even force myself to get interested in GTA anymore.  See, you start getting stats and abilities in a metroid-vania sort of way but with every upgrade you start noticing that sure, anyone can go cause a larger-than-life military involved crime spree, but the elements added to Saints Row IV actually made me and my family try to avoid those wanted stars.  The absence of real gang presence scared me at first but the game does a really good job at including enough "stuff" to do that I found us repeating challenges more often than just starting new missions.
I don't really care how much carnage and wonton chaos a game wants to offer, because it's one of the best things the Third did in their giant middle finger to the rigidity of the GTA series.  However, the Fourth installment made me feel like even though the devs pushed the envelope even further, they broadened the gap between going around spraying everything with rockets and actually competing in events and DLC that just "fits" in a game like this.
This game is such a nice break from my main game, the Battlefield series, in that it helps alleviate the frustration and stress that other games can cause.  Replayability is a shoe-in, and the character customization options, combined with a world that although small can still surprise you every once in a while, turned the game from feeling like it lacked direction into a game that knew exactly what the players would enjoy doing.
I got it for free with a Never Settle bundle but I have bought it on sale and on full price for the rest of the family.  Worth it.  Co-op is better to us than even SRTT, because most of the time you can be on opposite sides of the map doing your own thing but then join back up to do some awesome stuff together.  Great game.  Support the franchise, support the creative liberties and the innovation.  Play it with an open mind and give it a chance, and you will have a LOT OF FUN.  Period.

OVERALL: Great game 9/10
This review is based on having just finished the game after about 200 hours on difficulty: NORMAL.
Dying Light is a great game if you like Far Cry, Mirrors Edge, Stalker games, the 28 Days/Weeks Later movies and Walking Dead TV-series. Its a mix of all these, and a great mix it is.
Upsides (90%) are the big open world, the freedom, sidequests, exploring, the horror of being hunted all the time, the creepy mood, the graphics (although heavy on GPU), the music, the freerunning/parkour which works perfectly 90% of the time, the gathering of resources, the trading, the crafting and the character building. This is where I spent around 180 hours of my time in Dying Light and loved every minute of it. I could have gone on forever, but I ran out of things to do eventually :-)
Downsides (10%) are a pretty bad single player campaign (the last half where the game designers ran out of good ideas and just wanted to make your life a frustrating hell is really really bad. Especially the final section up against Rais men was done really badly by the designers. I was excited and looking forward to this section expecting a good fight, as my character was well levelled up, had good weapons and good skills, but was let down bigtime). Also  the controls when doing very difficult climbs left you uncertain about what a particular move would result in, often ending up making you fall to your death.
This game is absolutely great despite its downsides and I really recommend it if you are into one or more of the games/movies/TV-series I mentioned above.
*** RECOMMENDED PLAYSTYLE ***
I recommend that you spend most of your time having a blast exploring the Dying Light world, gathering resources, doing sidequests, building your character, having fun with all the different weapons/mods. I would also recommend that you put the main quest on hold at the point where you are to go to Rais fortress in OLD TOWN and rescue Jade. This is the part where the main quest starts to suck. So put the main quest on hold here and finish all you want to do in SLUMS and OLD TOWN, before going further.  Also, level your character well up on AGILITY before entering OLD TOWN, as this place really tests your freerunning skills. Lastly, I would avoid using the Grappling Hook, as its a big immersion breaker (it belongs in a DC Comics/Marvel world). I only used it as a last resort if I could not find any other way of progressing. Note, that you CAN continue playing after finishing the main quest if you prefer, however I felt discouraged to do so by the bad ending.
I hope you found this review helpful. Enjoy this great game :-)

Let me start this off by saying that I really enoyed Saints Row The Third as its own game. I know some people didn't like it because it strayed from the path that had been set for it in Saints Row 2, but I don't mind, and I really enjoyed the comical and raunchy nature of it.
That being said...
I feel like after playing 50+ hours of Saints Row The Third I have very little to do in this one.
It's kind of nostalgic seeing the same stuff again... but not that nostalgic, actually, not really nostalgic at all. In fact, it's just ♥♥♥♥ing boring. What I enjoyed about the previous title, aside from the comical aspect, was taking over the city from opposing gangs, and being able to take the city like a badass, at the pace I felt comfortable. I had 100% of the map before I even finished the story quests.
It's not as if you can't do this in SR4, but after already doing it in the same city, in the exact same engine, there is no longer that sense of exploration there. I pass by where a hangout used to be and just say "Well that's ♥♥♥♥ing stupid, guess there's not much I can do about that."
As cool as the super powers are, even if they feel a bit cluncky at times, I really think they take away from the game as a whole. Why the hell would you spend your money upgrading a car or a weapon if you could just upgrade your super abilities for cheaper, and get around faster? Being forced into using the incredibly well done driving and customization system in many ways makes the game more in depth, and tuned to not only your style of play, but your style over all. The same goes for the weapons. You can easily play through this game with only the use of the penetrator and your fists on the hardest difficulty, where as making weapon upgrades vital to your success in the previous title very much catered to how you wanted to play.
Ofcourse these systems was not removed, but just made inviable throught the addition of super powers.
Games such as GTA and Saints Row serve a greater purpose than to just be sandboxes to♥♥♥♥♥♥around in, and that is to be works that criticize a society's idiocy and vices. Each game that attempts to tackle this will do it in a different way, and in Saints Row 4, they chose to satirize... themselves.
You would imagine their choice to be very meta about this title could be funny, but for some reason, to me, it just wasn't. The desire to criticize their own choices when developing their title seemed to me to just take away from the game. You could see this in the opening infiltration sequence, clearly trying to parody the Moderm Military Shooter genre, but instead of being overly stupid and filled with QTEs, along with some snide remarks from the characters to make it their point clear, they chose to do it exactly how you would expect any Modern Military Shooter would do it, and it became incredibly boring and lost it's humor.
Then we come to my single largest gripe. The map.
Listen, I love Steelport, I've spent plenty of time driving around finding easter eggs, taking over oposing gang territory, and doing stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥like running into the military outpost to try and get a helicopter early game. These things are all good and fun, but the fact is I'VE DONE IT BEFORE. MULTIPLE TIMES. I AM NO LONGER INTERESTED IN STEELPORT.
The map is actually the exact same, with no updates to graphical fidelity that could give it a small amount of validation that this kind of thing is okay to do to your customers. Last time I checked, you payed close to the same price on the release of this title as you did on the release of the previous title, so why the hell are we getting the exact same assets we already payed for? The only alterations made to the map made it worse, and doing♥♥♥♥♥♥like running into a military base became utterly pointless when you're given super powers.
Final Thoughts: The game started out being developed as a large DLC expansion and it should've stayed that way. They did very little, in terms of the gameplay and the map, to constitute a new game to be sold at retail price. The game has become exactly what it set out to parody. If you're eager to purchase this game, do it when it's on sale, because chances are, if you played a lot of the previous game, you won't really like this one.

To explain exactly why I love the story of Faith the runner so much, let's go back about a decade. Xbox 360s were the console of choice found in most high schoolers' homes, and the rise of online play lead to an immense popularity in shooters. Call of Duty: World at War was a highly anticipated release, and Battlefield: Bad Company had been the start to a now dominant industry player. Ironically, DICE was the same company to pull the gun away from the player, and to place the focus entirely on fluid, free movement.
I rented this game from my local Blockbuster upon its release and was
. The world was stunning, the music was beautiful, the freerunning felt amazing and fluid, and its minimalist theme and simple control scheme engrossed me. 10 hours later, I sat reeling. I could not put into words why I loved what I had just experienced. It is only recently, in reciting what made the game so unique to me, that I can understand what captivated me.
Mirror's Edge was fresh and original. It shunned many popular but hackneyed game concepts, and in doing so truly set itself apart.
Mirror's Edge still plays perfectly even today. Yes, it is a hit or miss game: you will love it or hate it, its playstyle isn't for everyone. But it holds significance to me, and to my perception of the game industry as a whole. It showed me that 'breaking the norm' could lead to something completely wonderful and absolutely unforgettable. Its separation from other games in its time helped form my gaming tastes, and left me searching for games that do things differently. It may not have been a financial success, but, thanks to DICE's work, it left a permanent impression on me.

Star Wars Battlefront II. Well what can I say, it's pretty much Battlefield set in the star wars Universe so what else is there to say? It is a well respected and one of the most played game son the orginal Xbox Live and still has a decent fan base today. for it's time some pretty decent features, especially for a game on consoles. Battlefront II, like the first game, is based around 2 armies fighting, usually for control of objectives. There are 4 playable factions; The Republic, The CIS, The Empire and The Rebellion. The armies only cross over in campaign, such as the Empire fighting Clone Troopers and Jedi. In the other modes the games are played Republic VS CIS and Empire VS Rebellion.
It might have missed a few features from the first game such as flying vehicles in ground battles and the ability to go prone. But it did add a lot of decent things too. Like the ability to play as heroes such as Han Solo, Yoda, Chewbacca and Luke Skywalker as well as villians like Darth Vader, Darth Maul, Boba Fett and Emperor Palpatine. It also added SPACE BATTLES!!! Yes, it did take out flyers from the ground game but put them in space where  they are a lot more fun to fly then they were in the first game.
Let's talk about the features now. Starting with the campaign, which still holds up compared to a lot of games even after nearly 10 years. The campaign has some interesting features such as in most missions you will only start with a small amount of reinforcements (basically your teams lives, which are used by everyone on your team). These were increased with every objective but still meant that a few mistakes or a lot of A.I. deaths could cause you to lose the mission as soon as you started. While that could feel cheap at some points it does add a sense of acomplishment when taking a hard objective. There is a also a sort of progression system in some levels with the drip feed of units and vehicles as well as heroes.
The consoles versions also had the option to play the campaign, or in fact all modes in split screen which is really where the fun is at. Unfortunately the PC version, as a far as I know, does not include the ability to play the campaign in co op but it still has the multiplayer modes and is the only platform where it is still possible to play online.
Aside from the campaign there are a few other modes; Instant Action and Galactic Conquest.
Instant Action is a simple mode but has plenty of game types: Conquest, XXXL, Hunt, 1-Flag Capture The Flag, 2-Flag Capture The Flag, Space Assault, Assault (With Playable Heroes on Land), Space 1-Flag Capture The Flag.
Conquest is very similar to the mode in Battlefield. You have a certain amount of lives, usually around 200, and there are multiple objectives to capture on the map. Capturing these will increase the rate the enemies lives are reduced. Once the oppposing teams reinforcements reach 0 you win.
XXL is a rather unique game type. You are placed right in the thick of the fighting pretty much from the start and it can get rather overwhelming because of the sheer amount of units on the field. As this mode is only availible on Hoth and Geonosis there are a large amount of Vehicles, including the large At-AT's (Empire) and AT-TE's (Republic).
Hunt is also rather unique as it gives you control of indigenous units like Ewoks, Wookies, Jawas and Sand people. There are usually two different units for the indigenous side while the opposing team ususally only has access to one unit such as the Imperial Sniper against the Ewoks, or the Magna Guard against the Wookies. The goal is to reacha  target amount of kills before the other team.
1-flag capture the flag is, as you might have guessed, a CTF mode with a single flag that both teams must try and capture.
2-Flag Capture The Flag is just a stock standard CTF mode, cap the enemies flag while keeping your own secured.
Space 1-Flag Capture The Flag, just 1-flag in space, the flag is only obtainable in a spacecraft so things can get hectic.
Space Assault, a little bit different to the land modes. There are no objectives to capture but there is a point limit you must reach before the enemy. You get points for killing enemies and destroying ships, also for destroying capitol ship hard points suchs as turrets and engines.
There is another Assault  mode availible only on Tatooine. In this mode you only have access to heroes. Same objective as Space Assault but the only way to earn points is killing other heroes. While this mode is fun, it can drag out with a maximum point limit of 300 and each kill only gaining you 1 point. Still a great amount of fun with others.
Now onto Galactic Conquest. This mode is a sort of minor RTS mode, you control fleets and planets and use income to unlock troops and various, temporary, boosts. These boosts can include the ability to use a hero for one match, all your troops have a minor health regen, or all your enemies vehicles start off damaged. Each individual battle is still played like normal, you only move your fleet in an RTS style section.
The objective off Galactic Conquest is just that... Galactic Conquest. The side to own all planets wins, simple as that.
It's a good game, even to this day. While not pretty, it's graphics aren't terrible and the animations are fine for something so old. It is also relitivly cheap, so it's perfect for anyone looking for a Star Wars themed combined arms warfare game. Try it, you wont regret it.

1) The artwork is fun, but as has been said elsewhere, not quality on par with the concept.
2) The narrator is a one-trick pony, and annoying after a very short run. Profoundly annoying.
2) The animations and controls feel wooden. Some have excused this as a function of its "vintage look" aspirations, but I don't buy it. Those monster movie days were days of practical effects. It should feel "real world", not... "modern poorly optimized". I see nothing that looks like it's even trying to be stop-action. Which made me sad.
When I bought the game, I played and dropped it in an hour or so, for the reasons described above. I didn't review, because I was optimistic, thinking updates would improve it. But every time I come back, it's that same old feeling: great idea... disappointing execution.

An exellent, albeit linear, narrative constantly interrupted by flawed turn-based combat. The Banner Saga boasts great visuals and beautiful soundtrack, character design is spot-on, reminiscent of older cartoons, while still being true to the nordic theme and as historically accurate as a fantasy saga can be.
The flaws lie in the gameplay, particularly in the fact the game concentrates too much value on Renown. It's the currency with which you buy food, amulets and level up heroes. It's also not that easy to come by, since it's mostly rewarded from killing things and winning battles (although you, very rarely, gain some for a choice).
The game alternates between frequent combat sections, where you and the enemy alternate in turns, regardless of numerical advantage. Combined with the fact strength is both HP and how much damage you can deal, this system encourages the player to not kill oponnents, but, instead, harm them until they all have low HP, only then should the player start the killing.
The fact renown is used for everything also limits character choices and story decisions. You'll be encouraged to be a psycopath, partaking as many battles as possible to gain extra renown. To make matters worse, there are no real consequences for such choices.
Morale is almost meaningless, only awarding a few extra willpower points at the start of the battle. Supplies are also meaningless, seeing as fighters aside heroes have no effect on war outcome, as long as you win your battle (usually a charge, since it puts you against more enemies, which equals more renown), a team of 5 heroes could win a war against thousands of dredge.
Downed heroes come back with injury whoose duration and severity depend on game difficulty setting. Ironically, these same immortal heroes can die arbitraly during text-based events while travelling.
While I haven't been able to finish the game yet (always get bored by the game before being able to do so), I've seen users complain the story actually ends abruptely, leaving space for an obvious non-advertised sequel. The Banner Saga is actually just a first episode, despite not being advertised as such.
EDIT: I have finished the game on a new playthrough, and the ending is indeed abrupt, with a short (non animated) cutscene right after a rather easy boss fight (just ignore every dredge and focus on the boss). Even if it's part of a trilogy, a game must feature a relatively complete story (compare it to a movie such as "The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug" and you can see how this kind of ending is unsatisfying). A bit more recently, the store page was updated to reveal banner saga as the first of a trilogy, despite that not being the case on release date.
To summarize: The Banner Saga has great visuals, soundtrack and (linear and relatively unfinished) story, but it's held short by bad gameplay which ranges from silly to frustrating, removing almost all immersion or tension the well written story can create.
If things don't get better in the sequel, I think stoic should give up on making games and start writting novels or animated short films.

It's a nice game, I really like the graphics and the setting, it's supposed to be some type of parody of horror movies from back in 50's, the entire game it's supposed to be the film, you have three characters to choose from all with different power ups that matter just in very specific situations, frankly i've just been using the robot because I like how he looks, the characters don't trascend into the custscenes, in them a specific character will be used, that being said, the cutscenes are ok, they're clearly are trying to be funny, mimic certain aspects of the "b-movies" from back then, all of this is perpetually narrated by the director of the supposed film that you're playing, I think this game it's enjoyable mostly if you know what the game it's referencing and making fun of, or rather, paying homage in it's entirety.
Altho the other thing that keeps me playing it's it's simplistic gameplay mechanics, you can carry two regular melee weapons, and two ranged weapons, but there are tons of different weapons that you'll get by just progressing through the game, frankly the thing that kills me it's that there's an upgrade system for this weapons that's extremely difficult to use, mainly because the upgrades are only obtained through playing the game naturally, but mostly, through exploring and finding secrets, etc... The game it's so massive and convoluted tho, that finding this secrets proves to be a rather jarring chore, be that as it may tho the upgrades are incredible changing not only the damage outpout of your weapons but also changing how your weapons visually look, it's great.
The weapons are also pretty varied, you may have at one point a simitar, or a flamethrower, my favorite so far it's the whip, which it's great for staying on the outside while still hitting hordes of enemies.
The enemies are pretty varied, each and every single one of them satirizing some movie, or monster from the horror films from the 1950's, it's great, at one point you might be fighting some monkeys like in Planet of the Apes, or in another moment you might be fighting a fly with doctor's clothes similar to the original fly movie, the game even makes a reference to it by having the director saying it's paying an homage.
It's really a nice game, I do however recommend playing it with "hard mode" set to on, it made my experience immensley more enjoyable than when I started playing the game just without it. Plus it's not impossible, it's actually pretty balanced and engaging, I really like it.
Overall I really think it's a very nice game, it's just a very fun game to play casually and the commentary from the director it's hilarious for the most part, it can get repetitive after a while, but overall it's been great, I really feel as if we need more games like this one that take risks while satirizing films in a decade in which films ironically enough took risks, not so much because of taking them as much as because the filmmakers were always experimenting with them.

As a student of Game Design, I'm about to tell you, in graphic, bloody detail, what this game does WELL, what the game NEEDS to do, and what this game needs to FIX.
WELL:
-The art. The monsters are well made, gruesome, and a few border on the "horror porn" genre...specifically a female monster with swords for feet, holding herself off the ground with tentacles, with her legs spread like "come kill me, master."
+5 points.
-Presentation. The game starts with no ui, no nothing. Just a monster. You click it, you kill it, and from there you slowly unlock the features of the game.
+1 point.
-The "heroes." I was going to put this in the FIX section, as you start with
and then you get a...cobra. No. But by the time you get into the game and are starting to enjoy yourself, you get some kind of freaky man eating plant, a cybernetic redhead named lilith, and an OK reskin of the plant as a freaky robot tentacle.
...I'm noticing a lot of tentacles.
+5 points.
-The fan service. Part of this is the horror porn, but when a game let's me beat down Nyarlathotep with a knife and a bat, I'm game.
+ 1 points.
NEEDS:
-A tutorial. If you've played incremental games since cookie clicker classic, you won't need one...but how is a new comer to the clicker genre going to understand right off the bat "teeth since last amnezia (and yes, that's how the game spells it)? How is a new comer going to figure out that yes, this is how we do things here in clciker land, go make a sandwich and turn on south park?
-2 Points
-Polishing. Not a lot, mind you. It's just that, at the moment, this is a reskin of clicker heroes. An INTERESTING reskin, but a reskin just the same. This game needs to differentate itself from its competition, and considering it's a horror themed clciker, I can see a million ways to do that...
...Just PLEASE, no cheap jumpscares. You can do so much better than that, game.
+-0 Points
FIX:
-The sound design. You get a looping song that sounds like a track from one of those atmospheric halloween CDs for 5 bucks at walmart. Sound FX
I guess? A weak sounding punch-like noise for each click, a sort of scream when an enemy dies...that's about it,
-3 Points
-The special FX. EVERY click, every single one, splashes the screen with way too much blood. I'm trying to appreciate the monsters (Here's looking at you, sword feet~) and I'm blinded by blood splatters. Come on, game.
-3 points
-The art. I realize this was in the WELL category, but...I'm seeing some very familiar art. A Pyramid Head knockoff, some splatterhouse fanart...At the very least, use stock photos, game. Don't steal from artists.
-2 points.
Overall- 0 points. The cons and the pros balance each other perfectly, which kind of captures this game to a T.

OVERALL: Great game 9/10
This review is based on having just finished the game after about 200 hours on difficulty: NORMAL.
Dying Light is a great game if you like Far Cry, Mirrors Edge, Stalker games, the 28 Days/Weeks Later movies and Walking Dead TV-series. Its a mix of all these, and a great mix it is.
Upsides (90%) are the big open world, the freedom, sidequests, exploring, the horror of being hunted all the time, the creepy mood, the graphics (although heavy on GPU), the music, the freerunning/parkour which works perfectly 90% of the time, the gathering of resources, the trading, the crafting and the character building. This is where I spent around 180 hours of my time in Dying Light and loved every minute of it. I could have gone on forever, but I ran out of things to do eventually :-)
Downsides (10%) are a pretty bad single player campaign (the last half where the game designers ran out of good ideas and just wanted to make your life a frustrating hell is really really bad. Especially the final section up against Rais men was done really badly by the designers. I was excited and looking forward to this section expecting a good fight, as my character was well levelled up, had good weapons and good skills, but was let down bigtime). Also  the controls when doing very difficult climbs left you uncertain about what a particular move would result in, often ending up making you fall to your death.
This game is absolutely great despite its downsides and I really recommend it if you are into one or more of the games/movies/TV-series I mentioned above.
*** RECOMMENDED PLAYSTYLE ***
I recommend that you spend most of your time having a blast exploring the Dying Light world, gathering resources, doing sidequests, building your character, having fun with all the different weapons/mods. I would also recommend that you put the main quest on hold at the point where you are to go to Rais fortress in OLD TOWN and rescue Jade. This is the part where the main quest starts to suck. So put the main quest on hold here and finish all you want to do in SLUMS and OLD TOWN, before going further.  Also, level your character well up on AGILITY before entering OLD TOWN, as this place really tests your freerunning skills. Lastly, I would avoid using the Grappling Hook, as its a big immersion breaker (it belongs in a DC Comics/Marvel world). I only used it as a last resort if I could not find any other way of progressing. Note, that you CAN continue playing after finishing the main quest if you prefer, however I felt discouraged to do so by the bad ending.
I hope you found this review helpful. Enjoy this great game :-)

This game is my absolute favorite--although the storyline is a little confusing and the graphics are just okay, the mechanics are wonderful.  I learned that I really enjoy parkour-oriented games, and Mirror's Edge delivers on this and then some.
It's a very engaging game and it forces the player to strategize, sometimes in stressful/time sensitive situations.  I didn't really love the fighting sequences, but they did a good job of keeping the game interesting throughout the campaign.  I also would have liked for Faith to have her own weapon (perhaps with limited bullets or something), but that's just a small aspect of the game.
The level design is really quite clever and does a good job of diversifying the locations while keeping the same basic mechanics in place.  There's jumping across rooftops, climbing down storm drains, and traveling through buildings.  There are also time trials on "playgrounds" for further play after the campaign has ended.  Along with the time trials is the "speed run" feature, which involves getting through certain chapters in a set amount of time.
I've logged a good amount of time on this game, but it's pretty quick to play if you're skilled.  It could easily be finished in one or two nights if it's your second time playing the campaign.  That's where the time trials/speed runs come in--I've played only a few of them and I think they're a great addition.
Overall, this game was absolutely stellar.  It's very fun to play, and there's plenty of content beyond the campaign to keep you busy.  I
recommend purchasing Mirror's Edge.

Yes. Robot Roller Derby Disco Dodgeball. Robot Roller Derby Disco Dodgeball is a game about robots rolling around dodging balls in a disco-rave environment. You will dodge, duck, dip, dive, and dodge until your parents yell at you to please just stop playing that epilepsy simulator. The game is a treat, aesthetically and otherwise, but especially aesthetically. Let me explain: The environment is beautiful, but also essentially a giant equalizer with pretty flashing colors. The music, of course, is not only in sync with said equalizenvironment, but very pleasing to the ears. It gets you going, and keeps the game going. The gameplay is gloriously colorful high octane fun! The controls have a momentum to them, and may take some adjustment. Shooting isn't per pixel where the crosshair is, which is good. The ball may bounce off the edge of a hoop or narrowly miss your opponent until you really learn to aim well. You'll also be pleased to hear you can catch and block the ball, not just dodge! There are CTF, king of the hill, and many other gamemodes to keep you occupied.
Now, on the other hand, I did encounter some problems. But only some! Very very few even...but they should be mentioned. First off, in my first few times trying to play, I ran into a wealth of strange settings bugs. No steam overlay, couldn't get into gamemode. Then that worked, but the controller wouldn't look around. Restart again, controller works, but can only change the sensitivity with the mouse. The only other issue besides the ocassional bug (that I only ever had at the very beginning, all smooth now!) is the sticky terrain. You will get stuck on the corner of a ramp, or even on players, because the game kind of defaults to jumping you when you do. Probably because of that sweet momentum!
So keep on rollin', folks, and remember to dodge, duck, dip, dive, and dodge!

Child of Light is a basic 2D adventure through the fantasy land of Lemuria. The princess, Aurora, has died and her papa has lost hope, but with the help of unusual friends there is no time to mope. Aurora battles darkness with friends anew, hoping to see this spiritual adventure through. Magicians, jesters and warriors unite to give the princess one last chance. With each battle won, Aurora makes her advance.
The attractive world of Lemura is rendered with Ubi-Art Framework, but the lack of noteworthy gameplay starts to hurt. Aurora walks or flies across colorful landscapes, stumbling upon treasures and wishes.  Wishes ignite your friendly orb of light and treasures prevent you sleeping with the fishes. The orb stuns foes left and right, but minimal exploration makes the adventure slight.
As you collide with foes, you are thrust into a contrived battle pose. Battles have your friends taking turns to eliminate foes counting three. But the nature of the combat propels enjoyment far out to sea. You jostle to deal elemental damage to susceptible foes, yet constant interrupts keep you on your toes. Once you become a master tactician, bosses turn interrupts into a war of attrition. Some bosses succumb after half an hour, making boss battles repetitive and sour. Combat is tolerable at best - how much you can endure is the true test.
Just as the world lacks excitement, the un-voiced dialogue becomes an indictment. Exactly as this review is written before you, the authors were smitten with rhyming too. Some might think it funny or clever, but it becomes like persistent bad weather. If instead you find this readable, then you’ll likely find the narrative tolerable. Know that there is little that proves enlightening, even as you battle forces most frightening.
If Lemuria is the land we are sent to after death, try to avoid the reaper long after your last breath. If you insist on buying Child of Light to get your arty platforming hit, don’t complain when you discover it’s quite sh…

A dark setting, cultists and demons abound!  Gameplay is familiar to anyone whos ever played any action RPG, story is fairly well done, gives an incentive to keep moving.  The class system is the same system used for Titans Quest, with slight variation.  Choose a class on first level up, then a secondary at level ten,  making a fairly wide selection of builds possible.  Crafting is done well enough, but isn't groundbreaking by any means.  The "choice and consequence" touted in the description doesn't really affect the story, it's a psudo-choices, do you belive this man when he say he's innocent? do you talk him down if he's aggressive? do you kill him outright? He doesn't matter in the slightest, do whatever you like.  There's only one choice that matter for factional gear rewards as far as I can tell.  Which brings me to the factions, a neat addition and take on this kind of system.  Every monster you kill, every quest you complete etc will give faction with one or more factions, enemies hate you more, friends like you more.  The higher your faction gets with friends, you guessed it, new rewards to buy from their quartermaster.  The more your enemies hate you, and this is the neat part,  the harder they try to kill you.  More mobs spawn, more champions spawn, eventually up to nemisis class enemies. haven't fought any of those yet.  All in all, a fine game, well worth the price if you like dungeon crawlers with some character to them.

I'm not sure what prompted me to get HNR;B1. Yes I play Japanese videogames, yes I watch a little Annie May, and hell I even listen to Hatsune Miku. However, I'll be deep-fried in damnation before I tolerate uguu moeblobs crying over baka oniichan and the lack of senpai-noticing. That's not what this game is about though. The art might give you that impression, and there is some fan-service, but I dare say the best qualities about HN are the characters and writing.
HN is broken up into 8 chapters. Typically there's plot, then shopping, more dialogue, random people handing you "plans", dungeons (both forced & optional), and then more plot. It's a standard setup and if you know what you're doing and/or skipping dialogue this game can be quite short. I wouldn't recommend it though, because the actual game portions aren't the greatest. From what I've read, this edition of HN is a massive improvement over the original in terms of exploration and combat. This must mean the first version was really dire.
Getting around is handled via a map-screen, with dungeons representing the only "on-foot" portions. While the dungeons include various niceties like no random encounters, the lay-outs tend to repeat quite often. We're talking the exact same lay-out, and the enemies that populate them tend to be the same creatures you already fought, except stronger. There's no other way to say it, the dungeons in this game are weak. At least they're short, and they aren't bogged down by elevators, lots of stairs, and mind-numbing puzzles.
The combat fares a bit better. It's turn-based and over-time you develop combos. There are three types: rush for building EXE meter (super moves), power for straight damage, and break for taking down shields. There are a variety of other skills like healing, buffs, and so on. The roster of playable characters eventually blossoms to over a dozen as well. It sounds like a lot to take in, but for the most part this is not a difficult RPG. There's very little strategy aside from "use a lot of super moves" and the ever-important "heal when you're low on HP". If you're getting slapped to heck and back, it's probably because your level isn't high enough. Late-game grinding isn't really a hassle either. A lot of optional super-enemies drop enough exp to level multiple times in a single battle. I suppose the level of difficulty can vary greatly, depending on how much leveling you do. Some players might find more entertainment in avoiding optional fights, so that every regular encounter is hard-fought. Eventually though you're going to become OP, you can't resist it.
Most of the grind in this game is in finding all of the materials. Those plans I mentioned earlier add things to the game. New equipment, new abilities, more dungeons, and so on. They require materials stripped from the cold dead flesh of the monsters that you kill. This is best tackled with a guide. The in-game "Nepedia" is nice, but it pales in comparison to a guide from good ol' gamefaqs and the always handy CTRL-F.
Materials (along with corpses) can also be turned in for quest rewards (if applicable). Quests are interesting in that completing them can raise & lower shares. The gals of HN are always talking about shares and their importance in the console war. This never really becomes a factor until 1) the ending and 2) the acquisition of hidden characters. It's something to keep in mind. I guess I should mention that aside from the ridiculous "millionaire" achievement, HNR;B1 isn't bad if you're a completionist. Doing everything (aside from some DLC) in the game took me less than 30 hours. I have played through the Vita game as well. That first play-through took about 30-35. If you don't skip cut-scenes, the length is more than reasonable.
Notice the lack of character discussion in this review. Yeah, I'm not going to spoil the best aspect of the game. The cast of Neptunia is great, and the voice-acting (both ENG & JPN) is very well-done. I mean okay yeah, it's cute girls, some of whom transform into something exceptionally form-fitting, but the dialogue is rarely dull. Aside from a couple (expected) interactions, the cast doesn't get too hung up on the standard Annie May tropes either. Call me shallow, but I also got a kick out of all of the videogame references.
The most amusing one to me is Neptunia herself. The other goddesses are Leanbox, Lastation, and Lowee. Since the plot of this game involves a console war, you can guess what those names refer to. So what's the deal with Neptunia? Back in the mid 90s, Sega was planning a console that combined the Genesis & the 32X. It was called Neptune. Honestly, I can't think of a better system that represents Nep-Nep, she is quite a random character.
So yeah, I recommend HNR;B1. As far as J-RPGs go it's not particularly great, but it has so much charm I can overlook its faults. Also, it's appropriately-paced and the port isn't too bad (although I had to switch to XP compatibility due to constant after-battle crashes). Don't write this game off simply because you visited the community hub and saw a few questionable images.
