To preface my review, I must say that Everlasting Summer is a visual novel style of game. Expecting to control a character in the traditional way is misguided, because that is not how the game is played. A visual novel is just that, a novel that tells a story through narration (traditionally, and as is in Everlasting Summer, through text) and a simple use of pictures and character images. If you prefer your games to get right into the "action" with little introduction, narration, or verbal/textual description of the events transpiring, then this game is not for you. If you are, however, a fan of games that revolve around story told to you, or are just a fan of books and stories in general, then this might be something to check out.
When I saw Everlasting Summer as a free game on steam, naturally, I was intrigued. I had never really tried the visual novel style of game, but as an avid reader I figured that I could find maybe the same kind of enjoyment that I would find in reading anecdotes with pictures. I was wrong, in a very good way.
What Everlasting does very well is tell its story utilizing a wide range of emotions. At first, I wasn't sure about how connected I was going to get to the characters, but with the first introduction to the Pioneer Camp Sovionok I was soon attached to the main character that the story revolves around, Semyon. Everlasting Summer setup Semyon's life in a very relatable, realistic way, and throughout the story there is a feeling of development in Semyon, some realization of an awakening.
The other characters of Sovionok are also very interesting and well written. The story and game revolves around Semyon making decisions that impacts his relationship with some of the girls around the camp, eventually leading to his desire to want to remain with them in a romantic relationship, a very different situation to when he arrived. While the game does still contain nudity (to some degree, though if that IS your thing, there's a very simple way to reactive it fully) and sex, it isn't a leading theme, but a result of choices (though sometimes it can be over apparent). The characters grew on me, and by each ending I too, like Semyon, was hoping that they could remain together.
Combining the superb storytelling full of emotion with the fact that the game contains Steam Workshop support (a VERY unexpected, but highly welcomed addition) that allows users, and even the developers, to release changes, additions, or entirely new stories built around Everlasting Summer and its style of game.
There are some places that Everlasting Summer falls short, however. The translations from Russian to English can be poor at times, and I saw a fair share of spelling and grammar errors in the English version. There is also a sense that maybe some points in the game have been skewed in translation, but I do not speak nor read Russian, so I cannot be for sure. Some things about Semyon's thought process and logic seem far fetched or cheaty at times, though this does not happen often.
All in all, Everlasting Summer does what it's meant to well: tells a story in a very emotion rich, beautiful way. The characters are full of personality and can really hit hard at home with events that occur. Everlasting Summer had me smiling, angry (in a good way), overjoyed, and even in saddening tears. If you enjoy storytelling and maybe don't mind the few sexual things, then I would highly recommend Everlasting Summer, even if you (like me) haven't tried the medium of Visual Novels before.
tl;dr:
PROS
Very rich storytelling.
Emotion filled (both in the story and for those partaking).
Relatable and deep characters.
Steam Workshop mod support.
CONS
Many spelling and grammar errors in the english translation.
Sometimes a sense of being "lost in translation".
A few 'illogical', out of control deicisions.
Sometimes a little bit too much sexualization.

Definitely one of EA's more unique titles, and probably the best parkour-focused game you can find right now. If you're new to the series, play this and skip the largely disappointing Mirror's Edge Catalyst.
Gameplay-wise, the game feels pretty good to play once you get a handle on the controls. It can easily be played via a controller or keyboard+mouse; the latter option will give you a slight edge in gun battles, but since the game can be completed without touching a gun (except for one part where you have to shoot a police van) it doesn't matter what you use. The controls are awkward either way at first, but the more you play the more natural it'll start to feel. And once you get used to it, you'll probably wish that more games had similar mechanics. While Mirror's Edge might look like a FPS at some times, it's a platforming game above all else. Levels are presented in a linear fashion and you progress through like you would in any platforming game; using the enviornment to vault, swing, and crawl your way past obstacles. With only 9 levels, the game is on the short side...but it definitely has some replayability if you're looking to speedrun it. Gunplay may leave a little more to be desired; it feels clunky, and Faith can't carry ammo so when she disarms an enemy she can only use the rounds that are already in the gun. Apart from pistols and SMGs, guns will also considerably slow Faith down, no doubt an intentional move by DICE to emphasize that you sacrafice speed for power by picking up a weapon. Again, this doesn't matter much since guns are an entirely optional feature.
Graphically, it's a very pretty game. The game can be a little too bright sometimes, with it's pre-baked lighting and strong bloom effects, but overall it uses Unreal Engine 3 pretty well. The artstyle is fantastic; set in a near-futuristic dystopian city, the colorful city skylines make for a great view as you dance along the rooftops. Combined with a fantastic minimalistic HUD, the game presents many opportunities for gorgeous screenshots if you like to toy around with video game photography.
Moving on to presentation, Mirror's Edge has the same appeal that a cult movie would. The story is far from perfect with average voice acting, poor pacing, and a somewhat anticlimactic ending. That being said, it was still done effectively. If the story does anything good, it's world building. I found myself wanting to know more about the events leading up to the game's story, about the city, about Faith herself. The cutscenes will probably remind you of those old Esurance commercials, but they eventually grow on you. The soundtrack is pretty well done too, with the music from the final level being exceptionally good. Overall, the game is very obviously far from perfect and yet still charming in it's own unique way.
Mirror's Edge has a small but dedicated and enthusiastic fanbase for a reason. It's not for everybody and it's certainly not the best game in the world. In spite of that, it's aged well for an almost 10 year old game. It's got some of the best platforming mechanics I've seen in a first person game, although there's still a few frustrating trial-and-error segments. All in all, I think it's worth at least one playthrough...certainly more for a budding speedrunner. $20 might be asking a little much, but when it goes on sale it's a must buy in my opinion.

Notes before installing/reading review:
This is a clicker game. There is no significant gameplay to speak of. Some clicker games have more than others. If you are unaware of what a clicker game is look up Cookie Clicker, which stands as a good representation of the formula.
Also, this is not a Horror game♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it doesn't give any impression its trying to scare you it just has monsters and such in a Horror environment. An example of a game like this might be splatter house or bloodborne. Both games could scare someone but ultimately are using Horror as a visual theme, this game does the same. Referring back to cookie clicker, its just replaced the cookies with monsters.
Review:
As far as clickers go its not a bad game.
One thing I like visually is the currency (teeth) fall from the monsters when defeated and actually sort of knock around the bottom of the screen and collide with the health bar and such. Most clickers just drop the currency at the bottom in no certain visual effect.
Speaking on the visual effects, when the game starts its not strictly presenting itself as a clicker. It starts out with no HUD or anything and as you kill the first couple monsters, options open up and so does the upgrade panel. I found this to be an interesting way to start the game and sort of involve you in the theme the game is going for.
Now I've said enough positive things, there are a few things that bug me.
It doesn't explain the click is considered your blade, you sort of just learn that from your first upgrade. This is dispite the fact you dont see a blade anywhere not even in the character screen in the upper left.
In fact, a lot of the game seems ot assume you've played a clicker before and can translate the terms over from one to the other. If you highlight the teeth counter at the top, it mentions these are your teeth till next amnesia.. What amnesia, when did I have amensia the first time? Im assuming that like most clickers, you'll get to a point where you can do a prestige reset, you keep something but lose everything starting over with a small/minor benefit to the next playthrough, like a newgame+
A negetive review I read mentioned this was a cashgrab. I honestly searched and didn't find any, if it pops up at some point I havent seen it. The only place I see it asks for money is when you go out of your way to look for it, otherwise its not going to offer anything. I read other reviews that say that you gotta pay to use the boosts...but they are boosts they're intended to make it easier so of course you're going to have to pay.
Another mentioned stolen art from other games. Okay sure I see that, but honestly the game is a clicker, if you're looking  for something original you've already lost the point. These are idle games, you see the art for literally seconds if that.
Overall:
If you want a clicker game for idling, this is a different take on that genre and not a bad one. Not as interactive as others, but definitely not boring and plain.
Acheievements appear simple, realistically just rewards for playing the game over a period of time as its simply click a bunhc of times, kill a bunch of monsters, go through the amneisa a bunch of times. Might take you a while to get them but they dont rely on anything special to occur that wouldn't happen through simple playthrough.
TLDR VERSION:
Pros:
Its a simple clicker game that has decent visuals, stolen or not.
Visual affects that other clicker games dont have
Presentation better than most clickers.
Cons:
Text can be difficult to read sometimes
Appears there may be some translation issues from original language but not a lot nor distracting
A lot of unclear terms that may only make sense to those familiar with

ToC
===
1. WORD OF WARNING TO BUYERS!
2. Game Review
3. Personal Notes
4. Overall
1. WORD OF WARNING TO BUYERS!
=========================
If you are yet to play XCOM: Enemy Unknown, and you've purchased the XCOM: Enemy Within expansion pack, you better off know that XCOM: Enemy Within is ONLY an extension for the contents in XCOM: Enemy Unknown (aka Addons and improvements pack). IT IS NOT a sequel.
Which also means, that if you wish to play the expansion XCOM: Enemy Within, I do NOT RECOMMEND you playing the original XCOM: Enemy Unknown and better of start playing immediately from XCOM: Enemy Within, as all of the XCOM: Enemy Unknown story campaign is replayed!
Imagine my shock to find out about it when I was all exciting  to continue the story of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, then I launched the XCOM: Enemy Within, just to find out that I actually play the same story from the begining.. I sure don't want others to experience that.
I feel this should be told to buyers as I was lead to believe due to the high cost and marketing of the game, that XCOM: Enemy Within is much more than some tweaks, addons and extra missions... but for now I won't be discussing the expension pack, as I'm yet to play (or should I say "replay"?) the game.
The second word of warning to buyers who wish to play this game is to remember to Drink, Eat and Sleep.. These three things are very essential to your survival and I really can't remember when (if ever) I was playing a game and getting so deep into it, that I can't even notice or sense my own real life physical needs -- yes, it was that bad.
2. Game Review
============
-The Good:
As a gamer who heard of and played some of UFO: Aftermath and the free Open Source game, "UFO: Alien Invasion", I was amazingly shocked at how GOOD is XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
The game creators succeeded very well in their excellent effort to make you feel like the Boss of a real Super-Secret/Super-Heros-Company aka a Super-Meaningful-Calling, giving you the "We're gonna save the world!" feeling about it.
Everything from the polished graphics, awesome music, sound and atmosphere.. I mean, the game creators could have just re-create a simple Chess game and make you fall in love with it!
XCOM series are known for their very detailed and complex game structure which gives you freedom to manage things on your own ways and eat the fruits of you're own hard work. Such freedom can often be overwhelming, but non-the-less, extremely rewarding!
XCOM: Enemy Unknown has an EXCELLENT difficulty and complexity balance and I deeply hope that future games made by anyone, would learn and get inspired from the way XCOM was designed.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown also offers a difficulty variety for all kind of players. Difficulty can be tweaked for the Hard Core fans and masochists a like.
-The Bad (Cons):
There are minor bugs in the game that show up, however not often but can be annoying non-the-less.
1. Load / Save Game menu is out of order.. YES, unbelieable, how many times I had to be looking long minutes over my many game saves at the menu, looking for the right one to load back... Quiet frusturating, especially when you are "in-the-flow" of the game and then you just.. stop for not less than a minute (in good timing).
You would have expected that the latest game save would be at the top of the menu, or in a bad case, the buttom of the menu.. but nither is the case. More often than not, the Game Saves are allover the menu. Some are in order, some get lost. Rarely I couldn't delete a save entry not until I tried to delete another, unrelated one.
2. Graphical Gliches, rarely you would see a charactor holding a weapon in a complete wrong direction when firing it, or the game Camera would just go out of order when killing an Allien (tends to happen when playing in Huge Allien Ships missions ( the kind of missions you start already aboard the UFO ships) -- Also noticed on Alien Terror missions, at the moments when the Alliens kill civilians.
3. Dead-Screen-Time. Sometimes you get that annoying feeling that the game is controling your timing, not you (aka the player, aka the client, aka the buyer). The game doesn't allow you to pause or ESCcape while the alliens make their move. I can't even go to the restroom for a second their or else I miss what was the alliens move..
4. Exteremly rare is a bug I had when I was asked in a trade to give away a few weapons I had in storage. I was required to give 4 of them. I had 3 in stock. So I factored a 4th gun, but still couldn't make the trade, the game didn't recognize I bought an extra gun for the trade. (Com'on, all the game had to do is +1 on it :/ )
5. Telekinetic Field ability doesn't stop grenades. Using it, will force all playing Alliens that carry grenades, to throw them and hit you.
Those are the bugs I remembered as I wrote this review, all of them are minor, kind of a little bit annoying because they feel like the developers could just tweak and fix them up by now (The game was relased in 2012). I wouldn't expect such bugs still exist in the game, and it almost feels like the developers don't care. Again I'm NOT saying they don't, no way that they don't... I'm only saying that it feels careless and that gets to me a little because I made an affort to buy the game (currently I'm unemployed = no income = still buy the game which is a high price game), and anyone else who bought the game made enough of an effort, for some a little bit more of playability...
Well.. If it's not completely broken, it doesn't mean that it ain't broken..
3. Personal Notes
==============
What made me buy the game was the game's demo. It really did it for me and I also recommend you download the play it, so you get an idea about the game.
This is a bit of personal, but when I saw on the Demo game that they put in Israelis, I was thinking "What a cool company! they put up all different countries, including mine, politics aside". I was surprised there were no Israelis on the full, paid product. I was wondering why, if that's a political issue all in all? As an Israeli, seeing a game mentioning Israel ,gave me a really good feeling, not just about the game but about its makers aswell. When there were no Israelis in the final payed product that I played, I was highly disappointed and felt cheated about it. It felt personal and a little bit offending. As if their marketing brought in political views. It just came off with a bad taste to it..
4. Overall
=======
With all the cons, the game is fun in an overwhelming way and made so good, I'd love seeing more games adapting the genre and its features. The kind of strategy games that in volve you in them both Logically and Emotionally and give you freedom to pursue your way and enjoy the benefits (And YES. RPG games tend to fall in for what I just described, but RPG games are focused around the player(s) and characters with world around them, and usually not in position of power and decision making like a strategy game would -- XCOM is more kind of a very concrete in detail, Strategy/RPG game)
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is the best form of strategy game I played to date. It is maybe the best combinition of a storydriven game with freedom I ever played. (Regarding freedom and story, for me it's more or less like the feeling I had with playing the original Deus Ex 1 game)
If you wish to play its extension pack XCOM: Enemy Within, go a head and start playing XCOM: Enemy Within from the get-go. Don't start a new game over XCOM: Enemy Unknown, as XCOM: Enemy Within, would just play the exact same game all over again, just with more features and extra story pieces.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within, is a must have for everyone who wants to do something meaningful at the hour of need and crisis and in the event of an Allien invasion to Earth! Because in XCOM, YOU ARE IT!
Hope I was helpful to you and that your head ain't hurting.

FTL combines real-time-strategy with an unfortunately rarely paired theme of ship combat.  The game takes place solely on a singular ship with just a few crew members and by incorporating resource management and role-playing mechanics it reaches strategic depths few games see at this price point.  If there is an argument to be made that the greatness of a game comes from its elegance, FTL would likely be the paradigm.  The way energy is managed, levels are gained, the way exploration takes place, and the way shots are timed are all balanced perfectly.  This harmony means every decision the player makes is consequential, and although these consequences are delivered often in the form of brutal punishment, FTL manages to escape from being unfair.  That said, be prepared to put in dozens of hours if you hope to unlock all the ships - this game is tough!
I'd imagine anyone who is a fan of real-time strategy games would appreciate this, but this game is targeting a larger quick-to-play audience and those that would like to play full RTS games but don't have the time to commit will find this a perfect match.
Overall, this is a tremendous accomplishment and ranks currently in my top five in its price range.  It would easily take first place if it had more content, which isn't small on its own, but with such an original design, it leaves me wanting a deeper game.  It would be great to see it develop multiplayer and ship editor mechanics or possibly even a long form version of the game itself.

So this, to start off, is the first Telltale game I have ever played. And if the others are even remotely this good, then boy have I been missing out. I will leave this review short and spoiler-free. Telltale's Game of Thrones is an excellent interactive movie-like experience. The story is gripping and if episode one is anything to go by the next five episodes will be grand indeed. However this is an interactive movie, you use QTEs (Quick time events) when whatever cast member you are playing as gets into some kind of fight, you will not be doing the actual fighting yourself. You also spend most of the game talking and interacting with the game's well written and well voiced cast. So if you are the kind of person that does not like excessive amounts of dialog or does not like QTE's then this game is probably not for you. However if you are a person that likes lots and lots of dialog, well written stories and does not mind a few QTEs mixed in, than I can recommend Telltale's Game of Thrones wholeheartedly.
If you can stand the "OH GOD MY EYES" factor this is quite the blast to play. And the Ultra DLC improves the game significantly.

In overall essence, this game is very enjoyable. There is no doubt that games created for large franchises are largely created by nobody-developers that inevitably fail to deliver a quality game to meet the standard of its product. That is why I was glad to see Telltale games had developed a game in the series of Game of Thrones, based on the HBO show itself (not the book series).
In Telltale's version of Game of Thrones, you play as the many members of House Forrester, an old northern house faithful to House Stark for generations. When trouble makes its way to the north, it's up to your decisions on behalf of your house to survive.
Right from the beginning you are thrust into the story that is familiar to both readers and watchers of the series. After an iconic event at The Twins, stronghold of House Frey, you must begin the tide of difficult choices for House Forrester. True to the series itself, Telltale Games has crafted a series of decisions that seem to equally have just as many good outcomes as bad. Despite my best efforts, I questioned whether each decision was truly the right one to make. It is in that tug of war that the game captures the best of the series. If you enjoyed the third, you may not like SR4 immediatly; it takes a while to get into the story.  The things that made SR3 fun - pushing people around, driving cars like a maniac, feeling like a boss - all of this is still there, but it's all irrelevant.
Those super powers are the central mechanics of the game, along with the usual arsenal of guns you can find at your local Friendly Fire.  Which is nice but the story does take a while to take off.  So in the mean time, you feel a sense of loss: you don't drive cars anymore (no need), you don't push people around (don't care), you stopped caring for the city and the personal stories of the people (for one reason, you're running so fast next to them that you only catch the first and second words of their sentences).  OK, some missions force you to still do those things but they kind of feel out of place.
But this is where the game shines in true SR tradition:  the story starts to go wild, the weapons are over the top, you go in and out of the Matrix for more challenges and weapons and more allies join you in your fight. Then, the game isn't that bad, anymore.  And later, these enemies are beggining to really kick your butt.  The story evolves and the city starts to take another dimension on its own.

The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a wonderful subversion of pulp sci fi movies of yore.
The game is narrated by the (fictional) director of the (fictional) movie, The Deadly Tower of Monsters. Without a doubt, the strwength of this game, and the main reason to play it, is the tremendous ambiance and tone. The devs clearly have a strong affinity for cheesy, B-movie sci fi and boy does it show. From the VCR film grain to the not so subtle strings attached over pterodactyls, this game nails it’s aesthetic and hits it out of the park. It has cheesy one liners, an evil doctor, and a main hero named♥♥♥♥♥♥Starspeed. What more could you want?!
As far as the game itself plays, it’s perfectly serviceable, if nothing special. It’s your standard fare third person action game where you get two melee weapons and two guns.  Your arsenal is varied enough that it keeps the game fresh but there are clearly ones that you should use (the flamethrower). In addition, there is a sizeable amount of enemies that you encounter each with increasing difficulty as you ascend the deadly tower. My main gripe would have to be the checkpoint system, it’s not great. Many times I was set back two or three confrontations earlier that led to somewhat tedious moments. Thankfully, this didn’t happen enough that it severely hampered my experience but it was definitely annoying.
The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a blast to play if you have any affinity towards The Twighlight Zone or old sci fi movies. This alone carries the game through its 5 hour runtime. If you have no connection to that setting, then the game may be a bit dull for you, however. That said, I am excited to see what this studio does next and would love a follow up to see what shenanigans old Dan Smith is up to.

After becoming an independent publisher, Techland's newest zombie survival game, and successor to their Dead Island franchise (now owned by Deep Silver) blows me out of the water, and is stunning both visually and mechanically. The parkour system makes a somewhat stale genre much more exciting. It adds flavor to the stale combat most games boast, and this game makes full use of it.
After completing the main story singleplayer, I can say that it's one of my favorite games, and one I hope to get the DLC for.

Pros:
-Amazing graphics
-Parkour is insanely fun, well designed and useful
-Gameplay feels nice
-Inventory and collecting loot feels nice and is well designed
-nice skill tree that feels good and leveling up is at a good pace
-Nice variety of special infected
-Steam Workshop and Custom content
-Co-op (I haven't even touched it yet)
-Nice story
Cons:
-Gameplay may eventually feel repetetive
-Normal zombies somewhat weak (could be a good thing)
-I often find I don't have to fight most of the special infected due to parkour (see next paragraph)
-Not many players in Be the Zombie mode (since I last played)
-I didn't find myself needing to roam around much at night (thought that may just be me)
This game is amazing. It's graphics could definitely be the best for a fps game as of the time of this review, and it's new parkour mechanic is refreshing, and has even led me to search for more games like this (tried mirror's edge, but this game made it's somewhat dated parkour system and graphics feel lacking and less fluid). I often find that I run rather than fight (my personal playstyle in this game), leading me to take full advantage of the parkour system. The combat system on the other hand is still good, but it's similar to existing combat mechanics, and along with most games, it could get repetitive.
I felt the story was good, but others have argued that the Dead Island games had better, more compelling stories. The main story took me around 23 hours to complete, and there are plenty of side quests and challenges left for me to complete. In addition to those, there are custom maps and content via the Steam Workshop, many of which are very good and can easily double one's playtime (with time and an already growing community, and more importantly mapmakers of course). Overall, you will get your money's worth of playtime from this game.
The upcoming Following DLC set to release in February of 2016 looks great so far and includes improvements to the base game, both visually and mechanically. It also adds cars, but is set in "the country," a less populated rural area, with open fields and more dangerous enemies. While the addition of cars (and highly customizable ones at that) and a more open area, I fear that parkour will be less utilized, thought that has yet to be seen.
Sorry, if this review looked like a rant, but overall, I would rate this game a 9/10

In the Banner Saga you play as the eponymous Banner Saga, a sentient temporal anomaly that has developed hive mind capabilities as well as the ability to display it's own thoughts and mental images on an interactable 2D grid of pixels.  The hive mind has taken control of several people within its own created universe and deigns upon you the responsibility of choosing every important action that these people make.  Their minds are distorted into believing that they have made these decisions themselves and that they have full agency and control over their own lives.  Often, when a decision arises, time will become frozen all throughout their universe and they stare blankly at you, awaiting your decision.  Their vapid expressions are like children who have not yet learned how to coax a thought from their own brains and who never will.  When you do pick a option time resumes and they all act as if everything is normal, perhaps because they do not experience anything during the frozen time, or perhaps because they lack the mental capabilities to comprehend it.
I fear spoiling what some may find as an interesting discovery, but I feel that I should warn you now that nothing in this game is real.  The whole world is a fictionalized thought experiment, meant to elicit some sort of feeling from the viewer, perhaps one of empathy, or of omnipotence?  I suppose the precise emotion is unimportant and that the real goal is to use this perverse fantasy as a sort of mirror, a tool whose only function is to see exactly how it affects you.
At night I feel my thoughts slip back to this world and its inhabitants.  If I told one of these people to throw away their own life for me they would do so without concern, thinking it their own idea, finding their own motives.  What does it mean to say that I am responsible for a life that has never existed, one that never had any agency other than what I chose?  Am I only responsible for them insofar as I am responsible for any action I make that only affects myself?  Does that make them an ideological extension of myself?  What have I gained by guiding them to the end of their road? What have they gained?
i find these questions to be much too vexing.  I would recommend not dwelling on them for long but instead finding some solace in a book or game.

I should start by saying I am a person who is deeply rooted in Eastside Hockey Manager and any hockey simulation will always be compared to that on any basis. Sure, EHM is dated now but I don't compare games to how it is now, but rather, my memory of it. I know what a monumental task that is to live up to, one’s memory of a favorite game is always seen through rose colored glasses and makes this comparison all the more difficult.
Let's talk "Wow" factor. FHM has gone leaps and bounds past where it came from. Like any good sports sim, it started a little rough around the edges but managed to be enjoyable. Now though it has blown past EHM, so this will be the last time I compare them.
FHM still has a long way to go, don't get me wrong, anyone who loves sports sims as much as I do will always find something more they want or expect from a game like this and my list has plenty of suggestion. Though nothing is broken (so far) in this seasons game and that is a nice breath of fresh air. My biggest gripe right now is how obvious the Rangers researcher is very bias, how on Earth is JT Miller one of the top players in the game? Baffling.
I am excited now for where this game is going because though not a lot is new this season, it runs better and feels smoother, so it might be the version just before a big addition to really make this game take off? I hope so.
It still lacks that major thing that FM has, which is feeling like you are in an immersive sports world, rather than the center of it, where the sports world happens around you. OOTP has the ability to get busy with making sure your lineup and pitcher is correct game after game, in a hockey sim there is a little bit less to do, so you can sometimes feel like you are just pressing the button and that is the game for periods of it. Not that this is a terrible thing, I like to zoom through seasons and see the results but if you choose to have a head coach you are not doing very much at all, and if you choose to be coach you end up doing too much.
I hope to be able to set my lineup and tell my coach to use what i want him to in the future, and set the "Goalie starts" screen myself and expect my coach to use it my way, this would add a measure of immersion that games like FM and OOTP have, rather than full on automation. My coach can just coach the games in side the game, that is his job!
But with all of that said, this game is a gigantic leap past my expectations. The streamlined feel of setting up a game to just playing through season after season and watching history be written (or rewritten if you play historical games) is satisfying.

Introduction:
Mirror's Edge is a game made by DICE and produced by EA. The game costs 19.99 USD at the time of this review, whether the price of this great game goes down anymore is yet to be determined. Sales for this game can be pretty common and can bring this games price down to under 10$ so keep that in mind if you are penny pincher like me.
Gameplay: If you haven't already noticed from the trailers, videos, and screenshots that the store page shows. This game is first person oriented and will involve alot of running, jumping and punching. There are guns in this in which you can use against your enemies, but that would go against the very principle this game is trying to convey to its audience. Your main goal is to avoid conflict as much as possible and parkour your way out of your problem. Jump, duck, slide, wall run, zipline, these are all options you can have at your disposal when running through these missions. Although always taking the runner route is easier said and done because these enemies have some pretty good aim, and when you feel you must fight it can be a bit of a pain. Fighting is mostly an up close and personal matter, with enemies getting progressively tougher with armor as the game progresses. You can disarm your oppenents and take their weapons to use against others, but that would hamper your running abilities (Unless you steal a pistol). Your best bet when dealing with numerous contacts would be to out run and take them down one by one. Time consuming, yes, but it will make you feel much more accomplished. The feeling of running is exhilarating and is the best  feature of this game, and solving the levels "Platforming" will be the best rush you can get. Especially when it means running away from baddies.
Graphics: This game is pretty dated, all things considered. It was made in the early era of the PS3 and Xbox 360 era, and it still holds up pretty well. The city you run through looks pristine and vibrant with color, its urban environments have alot of variety and you could just stand there and appreciate its many details. While there are a few cutscenes in the main game engine (all shown in your first person perspective) the main story cutscenes will be of normal 3rd person perspective but with a twist. The scenes have an interesting 2D CG kinda anime style (Not the kawaii kind). The animation is really fluid and unique to this game only as far as I am aware.
Story: The story as is the length of this game, is pretty short, depending how well you do and how quick you can figure out your enviroments to progress through the levels. The story follows Faith, a runner of Eurasian descent whose main job is to deliever packages for clients who don't want their messages jacked by higher government powers. I will try not to go into spoiler territory, but the story goes into a more noir crime drama and less on the package delivery. Those packages are there, but as collectable items and there is about 30 of them that can be found throughout the game.
Extras: Remember those collectables I mentioned earlier, they tie in the the extras tab on the main menu. This is a big bonus in my book because I greatly appreciate seeing all the work and concepts that go into making a game. Its a rare thing  to find in a game these days. This is also where all the cutscenes are located and the entire soundtrack for easy listening. This game also has time trials, which is this game's soft multiplayer aspect. Seeing who can get through the level fastest and who is the best runner. You are going to need an EA account for leaderboards placement and things, although the mode can be played offline. You will just be racing yourself which is fine in my opinion.
Options: Whether you care about option menus or not, you can skip this part of the review. The options for this game are enough for this pc port, you got your graphic choices, V-sync, and other graphical options. Since this is an old game, I wouldnt expect many PCs to not be able to run this game smoothly, but it is nice to know that they are doing there job. Controls are re bindable with mouse and keyboard, and there are multiple control schemes if you are using a controller. All your sliders for sensitivity are there too.
Final word: As of writing of this review I have 5.5 hours of playtime (may be higher if I play more in the future), but it truly shows how short the campaign is. Probably less if i didnt die so much. But the time spent was alot of fun, alot of those play time hours may go to perfecting your parkour speed running skills for this game, it may also go to the hunt of those packages. And let me tell you, those things are not easy to find. There is a hint for finding them, but its not the best hint, essentially find the runner symbol painted on a wall or object in the world, when you see that then there should be a package nearby. And that is the end of this review, for a game as short of this, it really should be experienced. You wont be disappointed and since there is the sequel to this game I will have to get myself a copy and compare. So if you are looking for a fun experience, buy this game, especially on sale. (There are sadly no achievements for this game on PC)

The Stick of Truth is an oddity in that it's not only faithful to the material, but good too. You really couldn't ask for a better South Park game. It looks and sounds identical to the series, and is just as gleefully offensive. But it's also a very decent RPG, with rich customisation and slick turn-based combat.
You are the new kid , and you've just moved to the not-so-sleepy Colorado mountain town of South Park with your parents. There are enough bits and pieces in the character creator to make a fairly accurate depiction of yourself, and I enjoyed seeing a little paper me sharing the screen with Cartman and co. in what is essentially an episode of the show. Don't worry about what name to enter when you're given the chance, though—everyone refers to you as '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' regardless.
From the start, most of South Park is free to explore. Wandering its streets and plundering its houses, I was struck by how detailed it is. There are secrets, sight gags, and show references everywhere , and thorough exploration is rewarded with weapons, costumes, and other useful loot. It's a big space, and nearly every building can be entered, from Tom's Rhinoplasty and South Park Elementary, to the houses of all the main characters. The whole game is dense with jokes and Easter eggs, even down to the hundreds of sellable junk items. A lot of love has gone into designing the world.
As you explore your new home you're drawn into a clash between the humans, led by grand wizard Cartman, and the elves, led by... well, I won't spoil the surprise. Cartman recruits you into his army and you're given a selection of classes to choose from: mage, fighter, thief, or jew. Yes, really. Each has its own special abilities, but there are no limits to what armour and weapons you can equip. The two factions are fighting over the titular Stick of Truth, a mystical artefact of great power that, according to the kids, allows the bearer to the control the Universe. But really it's just a stick.
The writing is what you might expect from a South Park game. It's crass, it's satirical, and its parodies—of video games, RPGs, and high fantasy—are keenly observed. Nothing is out of bounds for Matt Stone and Trey Parker, and the game will no doubt stir some controversy. But that's why South Park exists, and I'd be disappointed if it didn't . The show has been ruffling feathers for almost 20 years and I'm glad the game hasn't pulled any punches. A few scenes in the PC version, including Randy Marsh being violated by♥♥♥♥♥♥probing aliens, are censored in certain regions, but they amount to a fraction of the game. I'd consider some of the stuff that wasn't cut to be more controversial.
The war over the Stick gives way to a larger story involving a UFO, a government cover-up, and a virus that turns people (and kittens) into Nazis. But there are opportunities to stray from the story in the form of sidequests. You'll help Al Gore hunt down the elusive ManBearPig, fight Mongol warriors in the Tower of Peace, reunite Mr. Hankey with his missing kids, and dozens of other distractions involving characters from the show. A few are 'collect X things' filler, but most are entertaining and reasonably lengthy, with rewards including the ability to summon, among others, Jesus to help you in battle.
The combat is where Obsidian's involvement becomes clear. They're the studio behind the likes of Fallout: New Vegas, Knights of the Old Republic II, and the forthcoming Pillars of Eternity, so they have some RPG chops, which is evident in South Park's excellent turn-based combat. There's genuine depth here, with status effects, damage modifiers, stances, buffs, debuffs, and customisable gear. It's most reminiscent of the Final Fantasy games, but with a South Park twist. Fling a turd at an enemy and you'll inflict 'grossed out' status, causing them to keel over and puke, while red-headed enemies' 'Touch of the Ginger' ability lowers your defence. It's snappy, fast-paced, and requires some strategic thinking, but bar a few bosses, it can be a little too forgiving on the default difficulty setting.
Real-time elements give the combat some added flavour. You can block by hitting the right mouse button just as an enemy attacks, and most spells and abilities involve some kind of player input to pull off properly, usually in the form of simple, unintrusive minigames. To use Jimmy's bardic powers, performed with his magical lute, you have to complete a short rhythm-action sequence, while the new kid's fart powers (think Skyrim's dragon shouts, but funnier) are timing-based. These make combat feel more hands-on and dynamic than your average turn-based game.
There's a lot of gear in the game, which greatly expands your ability to customise your character and comes with interesting buffs and modifiers. Combined with 'strap-ons', which add additional effects to weapons and armour, this gives you scope to make some unique character builds. As you face enemies with different strengths and weaknesses, you'll find yourself regularly changing costumes to adapt. Much of the fun in the game—that is, the RPG beneath all the jokes and pop culture references—lies in experimenting with the vast array of gear and strap-ons you find as you play. This might be the first time in PC Gamer history where the word 'strap-on' has appeared three times in a paragraph.
The problem with reviewing The Stick of Truth is that I can't really talk about my favourite bits. Being surprised is half the experience, and you won't believe some of the stuff it makes you do. I had to stop myself calling people over to my monitor in the office to see whatever ludicrous thing was happening next. It's one of the most unpredictable, and consistently entertaining, games I've played, which is all the more impressive when you realise that the only reused assets are enemies. Every scene is handcrafted and animated, which is remarkable for a game that lasts between 15-20 hours. The summons and late game special attacks, including one where Cartman overloads his V-chip by repeatedly swearing, are a joy to watch. They've somehow made the famously low-fi South Park feel lavish .
And I laughed. A lot. It's puerile, yes, but not in the dimwitted way the execrable Family Guy game was. South Park's humour has always felt very knowing to me, with its tongue wedged firmly in its bum cheeks. The show marries schoolboy fart jokes with dark, witty satire, and the game is no different. It also manages to steer almost entirely clear of the trap a lot of comedy games fall into, where they joke about something while actively making you do it. See Far Cry 3 spin-off Blood Dragon mocking boring tutorials while making you sit through a boring tutorial for a recent example. The comedy here is never at the expense of fun, even when it's poking fun at gaming cliches.
There are better RPGs out there, but no one's buying The Stick of Truth just for that. You'll probably buy it because you like, or at least are familiar with, South Park, and as an extension of that series it's pretty much perfect. That it's a decent game underneath it all too is a pleasant bonus. Above all, it's just a wonderful piece of entertainment. It's surprising, surreal, packed with jokes, and rarely frustrating. I didn't get bored once across the 17 hours it took me to finish the story and most of the sidequests, and it kept me laughing consistently until the credits. If that isn't worth 90%, I don't know what is.

FTL combines real-time-strategy with an unfortunately rarely paired theme of ship combat.  The game takes place solely on a singular ship with just a few crew members and by incorporating resource management and role-playing mechanics it reaches strategic depths few games see at this price point.  If there is an argument to be made that the greatness of a game comes from its elegance, FTL would likely be the paradigm.  The way energy is managed, levels are gained, the way exploration takes place, and the way shots are timed are all balanced perfectly.  This harmony means every decision the player makes is consequential, and although these consequences are delivered often in the form of brutal punishment, FTL manages to escape from being unfair.  That said, be prepared to put in dozens of hours if you hope to unlock all the ships - this game is tough!
I'd imagine anyone who is a fan of real-time strategy games would appreciate this, but this game is targeting a larger quick-to-play audience and those that would like to play full RTS games but don't have the time to commit will find this a perfect match.
Overall, this is a tremendous accomplishment and ranks currently in my top five in its price range.  It would easily take first place if it had more content, which isn't small on its own, but with such an original design, it leaves me wanting a deeper game.  It would be great to see it develop multiplayer and ship editor mechanics or possibly even a long form version of the game itself.

(Note: Please disregard my playtime. I have about 24 hours played offline.)
Forget about what you know of common RPG tropes. Forget everything of what you thought you knew of how they go and how they all behave. This game is anything but your standard fare RPG in the veins of Final Fantasy, Skyrim or Fire Emblem, Lord of the Rings or even Dungeons & Dragons for that matter. This game completely takes all known RPG tropes and flips them all upside down onto their heads and repeatedly farts in their faces. Or rather, it takes certain RPG elements and instead does something completely new and innovative while at the same time completely lampooning - and then harpooning - every single RPG with merciless and hilarious razor sharp dialogue, one-percenter fart jokes and tasteless gross-out humor that would never fly in your typical episode. And that's how you would have to view this as: An interactive episode of South Park, where a new kid has come to the quiet little mountain town where it falls upon him to make some new friends at his parents' behest. Along the way, the new kid comes across a conflict between the humans of Kupa Keep and the Drow Elves over a mystical artifact known simply as the Stick of Truth, for whomever holds the Stick has control over the entire universe. In simple terms, Cartman's up to no good once again and Kyle is having none of that. Or perhaps maybe you bought what Cartman's been selling and there are times when he does make some good points.
But, if you know the show like I do, you would know that there is always going to be some crazy things that happens in the little mountain town and OH BOY DOES IT EVER. Just when you think you've been hit with the worst, the game reminds you that yes, it does in fact get MUCH worse. How awful or flatout horrendous does it go? To be honest, I can't even go into detail with the things I've seen this game throw at me. Because knowing the Steam people, I'd be dinged no matter what it is I brought up. So how about I skip right to the end and say this: The only way you're ever gonna know is if you play this game yourself. But whatever you do, be sure to bring a bucket, a helmet and wear a five-point safety harness, because it'll get sick really quick.
The combat of the game goes something like this. As your turn comes up, you have a chance to use an item first before launching either your melee attack, ranged attack or class-specific ability, thereby ending your turn afterwards. This also applies to your party members, too, depending if it's Butters, Jimmy, Stan, Kyle, Cartman, or Kenny as on top of having class-specific abilities, they also have character-specific abilities that you can use without their turn ending if you didn't use an item beforehand, giving you two opportunities per character and per turn. It might break the flow of combat for some, but I will explain as to why this is actually necessary. As your enemy attacks, you can block their attacks actively, allowing you a chance to counterattack if you time it just right. It's extremely important that you watch your enemy closely to see what they'll do and then react accordingly. If you screw it up, you'll end up paying for it when you see your characters' HP levels in the red or get killed, under a series of status effects that can cause damage over time, can kill you in a set number of turns or render your attacks next to meaningless, so make sure that you stock up, beef up and then waylay your opponent with everything you got, because they'll come at you with just as much if not more. You can even summon special characters if you're in a real tough spot, except they can't be used for boss fights. On top of that, they can only be used once a day, so you'll need to be especially mindful of this. Although, the gripe I have is that you can only have a max party size of two and you're responsible for taking care of whoever it is in your party. I personally wouldn't worry too much about Kenny, as he won't stay dead for long if he does bite the big one at any point during combat. To sum it all up, timing is everything.
For those of you who want to take a more sneaky approach, you can take out your opponents before combat even starts sort of like what you could do in Wild Arms (maybe, but I could be wrong in that regard), awarding you with EXP and items you can loot from their bodies by simply watching the environment around you, wherever you might be at that point in time and look for glints or colored cracks. More often than not, it'll usually be just a collection of junk that you can sell for a quick buck or two. In addition to this, you can also run around the town smashing whatever's destructible for some loose change here or there as well as grabbing collectables along the way. On that subject, you can even gain Perks as you make more and more friends, allowing for further customization for your chosen class.
Now, despite South Park itself appears to be a small town, the map itself you can travel through is surprisingly big, as you'll come across loads of familiar locales like the school, the police station, City Wok, Mr. Slave's house, all of the boys' houses, Tom's Rhinoplasty, and further beyond. Everything here is there for you to explore, so long as you have the right method or key for getting into said places. You can also use Sir Timmy's Fast Travel if you don't feel like wandering around the town in order to get from Point A to Point B, so there's a pretty slim chance that you'll ever get lost. If you do, then you're pretty much on your own. Or hey, someone will find you. Eventually. Graphically speaking, this game looks like, sounds like and for all intents and purposes feels like South Park. As I had mentioned before, you'd have to look at this like a typical episode from the show, and you'd be pretty hard pressed to think otherwise.
In terms of controls, they may require some degree of getting used to, but you'll get the hang of it, especially when it comes time to harness the power of your farts. If that doesn't work, you can order one of your buddies to do a job for you, be it Butters healing someone, Kenny using his feminine charms to distract someone or having Stan call over his dog Sparky to pee on something. Either way, if there's a problem, it can be solved. Usually by whacking something with a stick really hard.
All in all, this game put a huge smile on my face when I first saw it many moons ago and upon viewing it with a fresh pair of eyes, I can safely say that without a shadow of a doubt that if you are a South Park fan and/or an RPG fan, this is the game for you. If you are neither of these? Welp. Can't help you there. Although, the trope of Your Mileage May Vary needs to come into full effect here, as the main quest is rather short and may take you anywhere from about 10-12 hours and maybe 15-20 if you do all the sidequests, grab all the collectables and befriend every character in the game. At the same time, however, it's just enough for me, as I know I can pop into this game once more just to uncover more secrets and giggle like an idiot at the things I find or can do. On a final note before I send you on your way is that there are some who might say that in order to get the most enjoyment out of this game is you have to turn up the difficulty because it's not that hard hasn't really played very many RPGs, since I found a pretty decent amount of challenge in certain spots, but I might also have to agree that as long as you keep it on Normal you'll do fine, but I kinda doubt you'll get anything different if you boost it up to Hardcore other than maybe bragging rights. But overall, it all comes down to a few key things. Reflexes, item management, knowing what your enemy is weak against and what skill will inflict the most damage and when and where to use it effectively. In conclusion, yes I would recommend this game if not for the RPG experience, then for the fact that it's a proper South Park game.

Brutal and unforgiving, but keeps you wanting to come back.  A fantastic turn based strategy game that challenges your tactical decision making skills and your ability to adapt when things go wrong.  Outside the battlemap, the base mangement mechanics challenge your abilities to prioritize the right projects at the right time to maintain an edge over the alien threat.  The game loses some steam near the end when your team becomes so powerful that the aliens cease to threaten you in most engagements, but that point usually comes near the end game anyway and the variant rules and higher difficulties will encourage you to play again and again.  The Enemy Within expansion's use of Meld Countdown timers will force veteran players to juggle smart tactical play with aggressive advancement, and the Exalt missions present a unique switchup to the standard alien sweep and clear missions.  Highly recommend for turn based tactical gaming fans, fans of the original XCom, or rogue-like genre fans.

Backed this on Kickstarter and generally I'm quite happy with the final game despite some questionable design choices. So far I have finished the game once on veteran difficulty with rifle-wielding soldier/demolitionist.
The good:
- Solid action RPG gameplay
- Focus on single-player and multiplayer with friends, this is the way I have always played action-RPGs anyway
- Dual class system allows a lot of build variation and generally works quite well
- The art style fits the world well, even if it makes the maps somewhat repetitive
- Veteran difficulty was a good challenge level for the first playthrough
- Lots of secrets and hidden areas, exploration is encouraged
The bad:
- Auto-leveling enemies, this is just lazy game design that I really dislike
- Monster design in general is very boring, very few of the enemies are memorable. Even most of the bosses just feel like slightly stronger versions of normal mobs

If you're planning on buying this game for the Solo Campaign, just don't. From a Solo point of view, if that game was not set in the Star Wars universe, it would be complete and utter garbage. Not only is the AI completely idiotic, your teammates are completely useless - they get mowed down like tools, and even if they do reach the objective, they can't accomplish it - YOU have to do it. They can't capture points. They can't destroy items. They're just extras, meatbags to make you feel you're not alone - except you are. You will have to take on those enemy squads all by yourself and be the one-man-army, because you can't expect any help from your allies.
Aside from that, the campaign is totally asymmetrical - the "CPU" side does not obey the same rules than you. For instance, YOU have LIMITED reinforcements, THEY have INFINITE. That's the age-old flaw of all second zone FPSes - infinitely respawning enemies. You're going to have to throw yourself at a brick wall up until it breaks; there's no attrition war here. There's no "let's do it carefully" here. You have to rush the respawn points and capture them, because the longer you take, the deeper in♥♥♥♥♥♥you get - because your reinforcements are dwindling but not the CPU's.
If those two little details had been corrected, this would have been at least an acceptable game. I'm guessing that in Multiplayer, both sides have limited reinforcements and you have more players to make up for the uselessness of the AI-controlled soldiers, so it ought to be more enjoyable than the utter piece of crap that is the solo campaign.

After becoming an independent publisher, Techland's newest zombie survival game, and successor to their Dead Island franchise (now owned by Deep Silver) blows me out of the water, and is stunning both visually and mechanically. The parkour system makes a somewhat stale genre much more exciting. It adds flavor to the stale combat most games boast, and this game makes full use of it.
After completing the main story singleplayer, I can say that it's one of my favorite games, and one I hope to get the DLC for.

Pros:
-Amazing graphics
-Parkour is insanely fun, well designed and useful
-Gameplay feels nice
-Inventory and collecting loot feels nice and is well designed
-nice skill tree that feels good and leveling up is at a good pace
-Nice variety of special infected
-Steam Workshop and Custom content
-Co-op (I haven't even touched it yet)
-Nice story
Cons:
-Gameplay may eventually feel repetetive
-Normal zombies somewhat weak (could be a good thing)
-I often find I don't have to fight most of the special infected due to parkour (see next paragraph)

This game is amazing. It's graphics could definitely be the best for a fps game as of the time of this review, and it's new parkour mechanic is refreshing, and has even led me to search for more games like this (tried mirror's edge, but this game made it's somewhat dated parkour system and graphics feel lacking and less fluid). I often find that I run rather than fight (my personal playstyle in this game), leading me to take full advantage of the parkour system. The combat system on the other hand is still good, but it's similar to existing combat mechanics, and along with most games, it could get repetitive.
I felt the story was good, but others have argued that the Dead Island games had better, more compelling stories. The main story took me around 23 hours to complete, and there are plenty of side quests and challenges left for me to complete. In addition to those, there are custom maps and content via the Steam Workshop, many of which are very good and can easily double one's playtime (with time and an already growing community, and more importantly mapmakers of course). Overall, you will get your money's worth of playtime from this game.
The upcoming Following DLC set to release in February of 2016 looks great so far and includes improvements to the base game, both visually and mechanically. It also adds cars, but is set in "the country," a less populated rural area, with open fields and more dangerous enemies. While the addition of cars (and highly customizable ones at that) and a more open area, I fear that parkour will be less utilized, thought that has yet to be seen.
Sorry, if this review looked like a rant, but overall, I would rate this game a 9/10

In The Banner Saga, you're dropped into a place where the sun never sets, the Gods are dead, and the world seems to be crumbling away. The land is inhabited by humans, horned giants known as Varl, and the odd and often off-putting villains, the dredge. You trek across lush valleys and frozen wastes with a caravan of followers, attempting to find safe haven from the dredge invasion. During your travels you experience a number of battles and events all of which greatly affect the well-being of your caravan. It's your job, in the game, to keep them alive, well-fed, and in good spirits. And, for me at least, that was very, very hard.
Despite my inability play the game with any kind of aplomb, I really liked The Banner Saga. The game was developed by Stoic Studio, via funding from Kickstarter. They made inventive use of that Kickstarter money and they put out a game that, for the most part, works really well.
There is an impressive sense of hopelessness and inevitability in the game. Alex Thomas has created a world of characters who are eternally dour and are well-aware that life is short. A grim visage plays across nearly everyone's faces. Smiles on characters always come tinged with bittersweetness. As if to say, "this is all very nice, but it's going to end, as all things do."
One of the cooler aspects of the game are the dredge. The creatures you end up fighting most often. I read in an interview they were attempting to stay away from common fantasy tropes like orcs and goblins. If that's the case, the dredge are a resounding success. They're weird, mysterious, scary, and cool all at once. The sound design had a huge impact, I think, on making the dredge so intriguing. The sounds they make are a strange mix of mechanical and organic. You're not told much about them, but they still seem to have a mythic quality. They feel very real in that world.
The reason I backed the game in the first place was because of the concept art they displayed at the outset. The game is a treat to look at, and the art by Arnie Jorgensen is by far the best thing about it for me. Jorgensen pulled heavily from Eyvind Earle, whose work you may know from Disney's Sleeping Beauty. It makes for other-worldly landscapes that look familiar but are clearly not our world.
The economy of artwork may bely the sheer amount of effort Jorgensen must have put in. All of the art is wonderful and cleverly applied. The illustrations of cities are particularly impressive.
I was worried I wouldn't be able to enjoy the game because I'm traditionally not a fan of the strategy genre. Not so with this one.  The battles were a lot of fun, despite some issues I'll describe later. I believe John Watson is the mind behind combat in The Banner Saga. I can't say how it stacks up with other strategy games, but I found the battle to be dynamic. And the addition of some really smooth and impressive animation made it that much more enjoyable.
My biggest gripe with the game was I often felt at a loss. The tutorial portion at the beginning must have passed me by because I never felt like I had a real strategy going in to battles. This could be due to my lack of familiarity with the genre, overall. But I played the majority of the game without leveling my characters up. And so I was losing most of the battles I was fighting.
I found several tutorial videos online, later, that would have been a great help. I really want to play the game again, now that I have a grasp on how it's supposed to work. (I think)
I enjoyed The Banner Saga a lot. There were a few story points that were left open in the game, so I'm hopeful there will be a sequel. And even if there isn't, I'm excited for what Stoic Studio will put out next.

I awoke.  Not to my soft king size bed, as usual.  Not today.  Today I find myself on a cold, metal, bed.  To my absolute horror, a twin size bed.  Like a pauper.
I scream.

Sometime later, I calm myself.  There has to be a decent bed in this place.  Somewhere.  I just have to find it.
My surroundings give me little comfort.  A pair of broken night stands sit near my bed.  Two.  Why two?  I don't know.  Maybe this is a hotel?  I check for a Gideon Bible.  No.  Not a hotel.
I look for clothes.  Boxers.  Blue with lighter blue stripes.  Nice.  Not the best start to the day, but it could be worse.  There could have just been a shirt.  Shirt with no pants doesn't go well with my complexion.
I look back at the bed.  That's when I see it.  Some weird thing in a wheel chair with what looks like medical equipment inside it's body.  I know, deep down, I have to fight this thing.
A punch?  A kick?  Maybe both?  No... not today.  I look up at the ceiling.  Bats.  How the tables have turned.
I point at the wheel chair thing.  The bats attack.  It dies.  I yank out it's teeth, as is tradition.  I point at several other weird things around the room.  Half naked girl with a broom(?), computer guy with a TV head(?), dude with a sword and a sack over his head.  They all die to my bat onslaught.  More teeth are mine.
I look around.  Cobras.  Scorpions.  A box with tentacles coming out of it.  The very things I've spent my entire life training.
I bribe my team of critters with handfuls of teeth.  As we all know, snakes love teeth.  With my menagerie of stuff, I boldly walk down the hall, killing.
You may have thought this was a horror story.  It is.  Just not for me.  I am Random Critter Man and I am only wearing boxers.  I am the horror.
Additional information!
I can no longer recommend this game.  As I check in daily to upgrade my fleet of things killing the (horror) thing, I find I spend an additional minute to use skills.  I click frantically for 30 seconds, teeth flying here and there.  Click click click.  As I click, a message pops up saying something about amnesia.  There's a new button that appears right where I was clicking and I have clicked again before realizing this.  My horde of creatures evaporates, like they never existed.  My bag of teeth?  Gone.  My father, Santa Claus, and my mother, the Tooth Fairy... they'll be disappointed.  All I wanted was a giant bag of teeth to hand out to good little boys and girls.
Alas, this was not to be.  The game trolled me.  I find myself with my lone bat friend still in my boxers with no teeth.  I click the big X in the top corner and find "delete local content" because I am not doing this crap again.  I'm surprised I wasted my time doing it the first time.

Gripping. Brutal. Depressing. Beautiful. These are the first words that come to mind, grasping for a way to describe this game. I feel like gameplay is the best place to start in describing a game, so consider the combat. Turn-based and simple seeming at first glance (with each unit having one active, skill which automatically levels up, and one passive skill, which doesn't), the "health is damage" element makes every hit hurt. You hear the sound and see the little animated guy stagger and think, "we're all gonna die," and you're sometimes right, and then Egil dies. I can only name one game to have had this feature in the past, an old Gameboy Color title named Legend of the River King...
So anyways, grim terror all around, right? You're in charge of two different massive groups of people from opposite ends of the world whose storylines intertwine as they flee an endless invading army of tree-sized replicas of Disney's Iron Giant (tm) - which are similar to humans except for having really thick armor, which you usually have to hurl your puny humans and awesome giants (did I mention you control massive horned nordic giants created when a god crossed humans with some kind of magic Ox?) against repeatedly before damaging their health, and then Egil dies.
The music is nice, and they put a little bit of voice acting into some random scenes narration as your little grimdark 80s Disney army slowly walks across doomed countrysides, constantly interjected by storyline pop-ups wherein mostly bad things happen, or you get something good but it causes a tragedy later, or Egil dies, or all of the above. I would describe the game's feel overall as Last Unicorn meets Gears of War/Dark Souls, except maybe don't praise the Sun here, because did I mention the Sun just stopped in the sky for no reason? Hail to the Great Serpent.
Spoiler Tips: Try not to starve to death, fight whenever possible to afford rations, don't level up or put gear on the people who are going to be randomly killed off (and their gear vanishes when they do so), rest maybe, and don't level like any of the varl but Hakon and Gunnulf (Gunnulf can also die unless you shout at him a lot). Don't level Egil, he's going to die. I know, he's useful, but he's also not going to make it. Not your first time through. It's like surviving your first run in Sunless Sea, just get over it.

MIrror's Edge is a first person parkour game developed by DICE and published by EA games. Personally, for a game that was made 10 years ago, the graphics are stunning and I thoroughly enjoyed the dystopian city setting in the future. However, the story was very short and there several things that could be improved.
Pros:
- Very good graphics, especially for a game this old.
- Amazing first person parkour experience in a wonderful setting.
- Storyline was overall quite strong.
- The cartoon-ish cutscenes were really interesting and gave out a different flavour but I don't think it was neccesary.
Cons:
- Story was too short.
- Free Running was great but it was implemented in a way where exploration is limited.
- No subtitles during the actual gameplay, only during in-between cutscenes.
- Combat controls were mediocre.
Overall, this was a good experience especially when you have nothing to do and are willing to spare a few hours. However, I would not recommend getting this game at full price, definitely worth waiting to buy this game during a sale.

I can sometimes be a picky gamer. Every now and then a game will come out that I really had no interest in but somehow end up giving it a try and being capivated by it. XCOM Enemy Unknown is an example of such a game. No game is perfect, but I pretty much loved every aspect of this game. The combat especially, I had so much fun leading squads of soldiers agaisnt the aliens. The close quarter urban combat and turned based combat was exhilarating to me. I also very much like the feature of perma death (especially on Ironman mode) for your soldiers. Losing a decked out ranked up veteran officer is painful, and your next mission suffer because you have to take a red shirt with you, who has a slim chance of living. I also like the constant challenge the game throws at you, just as soon as you feel like you are snatching victories easily from the Aliens they send something new out that gets half a squad killed, and you have to learn to adapt to that new threat. But that feeling once you win by the skin of your teeth from a hard fought battle is hard to top. Excellent gameplay like this really makes me hand it to the devs of this master piece.
The other spectrum of XCOM is the base and resource management. You can research alien technology found on your missions, upgrade your soliders, manufacture new weapons and armor, launch air strikes, upgrade fighter jets, etc. If you bought the must have Enemy Unknown expansion you can search for psyhic abilities amongst your troops or turn some of them into powerful cyborgs with flame throwers and mini guns. There is also a world council you have to appease and do missions for or fall out of standing and be denied funding from that country that did not approve of the XCOM project.
XCOM Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within is for sure on my list of best games I have ever played. I highly recommend this game to anybody, and if you do purchase it be sure to get the expansion Enemy Within it is a must have!

EDIT: After another playthrough and watching the commentary video (and the release of Dragon Age: Inquisition) I've decided to give my review another chance.
The things I said below still stand, but after a less-critical look at Divinity: Original Sin, I have whole-heartedly changed my harsher opinions. As an Old School, classic RPG it fills the void I felt after DA:I. Hell, I apologize to Larian for being a fool. They did a great job with Divinity, and I wish them success in their next two RPGs, which I will most certainly buy and support on Kickstarter.
Thank you Larian for making a game that can rise from the ashes of the cRPG wasteland (not a callout to W2, that game was sweet too) and make something great.
(OLD, HARSH REVIEW BELOW)
It's with a wee bit of reluctance that I have to vote a NO on Divinity: Original Sin. Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad game by most standards, but it just feels off somehow.
For starter, the first thing that bothered me immensly was the male hero model. Seriously? Why did he have to be a gigantic meathead? No gigantic meathead like that would make a believeable rogue or mage. It just looks like a joke.
The second thing was the skill system. At first it looks interesting, lots of options and veriety. Sadly, you'll soon come to realise that it's only an illusion and that advancing these "skills" only unlocks extra slots for the real skills, which are all learned from books. The trait system looked cool, it reminded me of Fallout 2, but even that wasn't enough to save the skill system.
Third was combat. Again, at first it was addictive as heck. For me it was a modern Final Fantasy Tactics, a game that I loved back in the day, and still hold in pretty high esteem. The animations in Divinity were really good, both graphically and immersivley. The environment and spell combos were new and exciting, the magic looked good and the effects of them, like ememies disintigrating to ash from lightning, or charred corpses from fire, were good for a laugh and a triumphant grin. Most the enemies were pretty impressive, large foes and creepy undead, and a good variety of things to kill. But, again, it never progresses really. You end up using all the same combos you used at the beginning and it really just ends with who has the better crowd control.
Fourth was load screens. I can handle a long load screen or two but this was crazy. It was like playing Morrowind on X-Box, the screens take minutes to load. This isn't a huge deal, but when your two hours of playtime has fifteen minutes of loading it ends up feeling like watching a movie on TV. Long enough load times for me to think about playing something else anyway.
And last and most important : The writing. My god. For a game touted as the next Baldur's Gate II the writing was lackluster, to be polite. I've spent countless hours playing both BG 1&2 as well as the enhanced editions, to firmly deny that the writing even comes *close* to either of those two epics. I cannot stress enough that it is *not* the writing that lends people to believing that Divinity is akin to Baldur's Gate, it is the isometric view. That's it.
Anyway, it's still a pretty good game, just don't have too high of expectations going into it. If you think Divinity: Original Sin is the next milestone in CRPGs, you're probably wrong.

The first episode of Game of Thrones: A Telltale Game Series has all the staples of both George R.R. Martin's (in)famous series as well as what we expect from Telltale's games. The tough choices carry extra weight in this installment. Almost every choice is difficult, and you're presented with several in the first episode alone. Along with introducing you to a new cast of characters, who aren't quite as compelling as established characters (yet), the game allows you to interact with some of the famous faces of Westeros.
Ultimately, I greatly enjoyed this episode. the graphics are unique, and not as bad as you'd expect looking at the screenshots. The voice acting is, for the most part, excellent (a few minor characters have inconsistent accents, but nothing horrible). The music mixes some new tracks with some Game of Thrones soundtrack staples, but it all works very well. The story is, of course, excellent. Compelling and with a few unexpected surprises. However, the only complaint I could come up with regarding the plot is the lack of exposition for those unaffiliated with Game of Thrones. While I think it is playable for non-fans, the experience would be diminished, and a lot of confusion would ensue. However, for those who DO watch the show/read the books, the experience is fantastic. There is a moment early in the first episode where you don't realize where you are for a few seconds until the camera pans and you realize: "Ooooooh....This is THAT part". Ultimately a great experience so far.
