As a huge fan of Game of Thrones, and the A Song of Ice and Fire series, I appreciate that Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series is the first official game that delivers the kind of quality fans get from the books and show.
This is a violent virtual choose-your-own-adventure set in Westeros, in which you play from the perspective of members of the Forrester household. The pacing is a lot like the books, with chapters that alternate between several "point of view" characters. Although there is some outright action and combat, many of the decisions you are called upon to make rely more on diplomacy and tact than your martial skills, and as the series is constantly showing, decisions have consequences.
The artwork for the game is really striking, from the trademark opening sequence familiar in the HBO series to the locations where the action is set. Some are places that we've been in the show (which is maybe a little too convenient honestly but still fun to visit), and some are new to the video game but everything still fits seemlessly in the world George R. R. Martin has established and the HBO series has visualized.
Though the main characters are new to the game, members of a small Northern house mentioned only briefly in the books or show, they do (again, conveniently) interact with a handful of characters familiar to viewers of the show. Happily, all of these are voiced by the same actors who play the roles on HBO and so the voice acting in the game is one of the strongest parts of a game that already comes in strong with its story, music, artwork, characters, and design.
If you're looking for a quality gaming experience and good serialized story set in a rich and well-envisioned world, Telltale games comes strong in its first offering in the Game of Thrones series.

I wanted to like this. I really did. And I did, but far less than I expected. I'm disappointed with the wasted potential of this game. I'm flagging my review as "not recommended" because I just wish Steam offered a neutral option.
The 2D art is beautiful. The soundtrack is pretty good. The cast is diverse, something that's rare in video games. The dialogue is all written in rhymes. The battle system has more depth than it seems.
But the game feels hollow and rushed.
One example I'm sour about is this one. When you acquire the power of flying, very early in the game, there is a really cool cutscene that makes flying seem really magical. And it's just right at home in the game's universe. It strikes the childlike chord of your heart. And then you're able to move. And your character flies in a *really* stiff way. The complete opposite of the cutscene. It feels like a slap to the face.
Another thing that grinded my gears is that the game doesn't really try to say anything (maybe except vague messages about motherhood). It's as generic as "good vs. evil" gets. And there aren't some cool story themes hidden between the lines as well. It's disappointing considering that besides the protagonist (who undergoes a really cool transformation two-thirds into the game), there is barely any character development at all. The story doesn't have any complex twist and turns either. You find yourself wishing the game had some sort of lore... anything at all that could give the story as much depth as the beautiful artistic direction has.
The battle system is really nice but there's a big difficulty spike out of nowhere halfway through the game that requires a bit of grinding to go through (one particularly annoying boss). That's really the only part which requires grinding. In this childlike gleeful universe, this doesn't feel right. You battle with two characters at a time maximum, and can switch between them. They all have a distinct set of skills, which is an interesting mechanic, because while I dreaded this at first, I think it feels better to rely on more than just two people ever. Some of them are too situational though.
The menu system, for inventory and leveling, takes you really right out of the game. It feels... insanely gamey and unintegrated, basically. It just cuts to complete silence, and it's kind of a pain to navigate through, especially when choosing your skills to level up. The skill "trees" (they're actually mazes on the menu!) are convoluted for no sensible reason. Nothing about the menu feels right at all. It breaks your immersion.
All in all, this game feels like a lot of wasted potential. Maybe Ubisoft didn't allocate enough resources or didn't let the guys have enough time. It's one of those games that really have something going for them but just don't reach for their opportunity, and it's heartbreaking.

Beautiful artwork and design, wonderful soundtrack, traditional turn-based JRPG-like game play, and everyone speaks using poetic rhyme!

The story is very simple, but it adds to the charm of the adventure the characters go through. While the over-all story can be confusing and even a bit anti-climatic at times, it does not take away from the overall feel of wonder the game tries to inspire. You will certainly encounter strange looking allies in the game, but you may find many of them relatable.
What truly drew me to game in the first place is the artwork! 'Child of Light' has some of the most amazing artwork and design I have seen in a 2D game. Just take a look at the trailers and images! In my opinion, this alone supports a play-through of the game. The world illustrated is vibrant and mind-blowing, a true feast for the eyes. It is definitely worth a look at (pun intended!), and I would recommend it for any JRPG fan and/or lover of art.
Update: I purchased "The Golem's Plight" DLC a while back, and it basically adds in an additional quest and a new playable character/ally. I would recommend buying the DLC before playing the game - if you want the Golem. Buying it after beating the game makes it rather pointless (it's basically back-tracking), unless you plan to replay from the start.

Well, I started to play this out of a whim ... and was sort of surprised. I can´t say that I didn´t like the girls Endings, but they where ... well,  sort of okayish at best. As a Horror-fan I definetely liked the Sasha/Miku Route. But Yulyas route ... well, that one has been in full cry. I guess it´s almost safe to say, that we´ve got one of the games here, which becomes better the older YOU are when you´re playing it. Perhaps its just a personal thing - I don´t really know, nor do I actually care - but, I suppose the older you are, the more you have actually experienced in your life, the more you´ll be able to understand what the protagonist is thinking about, what is bothering him. On the other hand - it actually manages it, to give you this slight nostalgic feeling. Which is interesting in a certain way .... I grew up in western Germany, in the late 1980s I was a little bit younger than Semyon. I should not really be able to compare my expiriences to the life of an adolescent in the late years of the sovient union. It might be a side effect of this game, a wanted thing - or whatever you prefer to call it ... but darn, I can relate. It sort of feels familiar. Okay, it wasn´t called Pioneers - we had boy scouts, like in the states. But ♥♥♥♥, some memories surely came back. It actually leads me to some sort of conclusion, I´ve had heard some while ago: It doesn´t matter where you live, where you´ve grown up - the basic hopes, wishes and desires remain the same - anywhere. So - I´d like to tip my hat to the developers, for granting us an interesting experience here and I hope this won´t be that last game we see from you.

You know, I really want to thumbs up this game because I love the SR series...but I just can't.  While I did enjoy the game to a certain extent, it felt...I dunno, depressing, redundant, and not satisfying?  Welcome to Steelport...again.  Its the same city as last time (which is close to half the size as Stilwater), and most of the fun is gone.  Remember all those diverse soundtracks and entertaining news clips you heard in vehicles?  Well, you're not going to get much this time around, because you'll find you use your super running powers rather than car jack in this game because you're faster and have better control.  Guns?  Sure, you'll use them to supplement your blasty powers but they are fairly lackluster too.  Many reviewers have said that this game feels more like an expansion for SRIII than a new game, and I have to agree with them.
Ultimately its a Saints Row game in "The Matrix".  Is it a bad game?  No...I guess not, but it will probably remain the black sheep of the series if more are made.  Frankly, without spoiling the story or ending beyond what they tell you in the summary, a much more fun and better idea for gameplay mechanics are revealed at the ending of the game as a story element.  So, based on the ending credits let's hope there is a SR5 because it could be quite fun.

Using the engine and many gameplay elements from Saints Row the Third, this game is even goofier (not always a good thing) and much, much tighter. A lot of the filler from SR3 has been scrapped (or even skewered in the DLC, which is totally worth it if you can grab it for 75% off, aka the Steam Sale magic number).
Ignoring the 'infamous' (wahwah) take on superpowered games, SR4 is also a love letter to the series and its fans. I grinned at all the callbacks to the series' roots, and feel this was more of a natural sequel to SR2 (still the best) than its predecessor.
Highly recommended, especially during the sales that are becoming more and more frequent.

Backed this on Kickstarter and generally I'm quite happy with the final game despite some questionable design choices. So far I have finished the game once on veteran difficulty with rifle-wielding soldier/demolitionist.
The good:
- Solid action RPG gameplay
- Focus on single-player and multiplayer with friends, this is the way I have always played action-RPGs anyway
- Dual class system allows a lot of build variation and generally works quite well
- The art style fits the world well, even if it makes the maps somewhat repetitive
- Veteran difficulty was a good challenge level for the first playthrough
- Lots of secrets and hidden areas, exploration is encouraged

Gripping. Brutal. Depressing. Beautiful. These are the first words that come to mind, grasping for a way to describe this game. I feel like gameplay is the best place to start in describing a game, so consider the combat. Turn-based and simple seeming at first glance (with each unit having one active, skill which automatically levels up, and one passive skill, which doesn't), the "health is damage" element makes every hit hurt. You hear the sound and see the little animated guy stagger and think, "we're all gonna die," and you're sometimes right, and then Egil dies. I can only name one game to have had this feature in the past, an old Gameboy Color title named Legend of the River King...
So anyways, grim terror all around, right? You're in charge of two different massive groups of people from opposite ends of the world whose storylines intertwine as they flee an endless invading army of tree-sized replicas of Disney's Iron Giant (tm) - which are similar to humans except for having really thick armor, which you usually have to hurl your puny humans and awesome giants (did I mention you control massive horned nordic giants created when a god crossed humans with some kind of magic Ox?) against repeatedly before damaging their health, and then Egil dies.
The music is nice, and they put a little bit of voice acting into some random scenes narration as your little grimdark 80s Disney army slowly walks across doomed countrysides, constantly interjected by storyline pop-ups wherein mostly bad things happen, or you get something good but it causes a tragedy later, or Egil dies, or all of the above. I would describe the game's feel overall as Last Unicorn meets Gears of War/Dark Souls, except maybe don't praise the Sun here, because did I mention the Sun just stopped in the sky for no reason? Hail to the Great Serpent.
Spoiler Tips: Try not to starve to death, fight whenever possible to afford rations, don't level up or put gear on the people who are going to be randomly killed off (and their gear vanishes when they do so), rest maybe, and don't level like any of the varl but Hakon and Gunnulf (Gunnulf can also die unless you shout at him a lot). Don't level Egil, he's going to die. I know, he's useful, but he's also not going to make it. Not your first time through. It's like surviving your first run in Sunless Sea, just get over it.
10/10

This game is amazing! The story is fun. The art is beautiful. The music is perfect. It is hard to articulate the awesomeness of this game. I found myself genuinely concerned about keeping everyone alive. The story kept drawing me in.
I read a lot of the negative reviews but most of them surround the desire to have every single choice in the game changed the entire outcome of the game. There is an overall story. You are progressing an overall story. If you take the path on the left or the right wont change that. But the paths may change what you encounter and how you reach your destination. For example in one part I chose to go a longer route to avoid combat (because I needed peeps to heal) but that decision was hard because I may not have had enough food to get to the destination. Ultimately I ended up in the same place but the route brought us there with less food (potentially no food if I took too long) where the other route would have been faster but we may have had more people die during battles. Your choices do affect the game in a variety of ways but the story is progressing forward.
The only negative thing I would say about the game (which I hope they change) is that you only have one resource (renown) to buy supplies and to level up characters. So you end up having to choose between feeding your people or using your experience to level up characters. This was annoying because story-wise that doesn't make sense. How do you buy food with renown? I had battle-harden characters with numerous kills at low levels because I couldn't afford to raise their level and keep the convoy alive. Which in turned was rough because then I had artifacts that I couldnt use because my characters were low level.
With that said, it was still fun because every choice you make in the game has a consequence. I could level up my characters (which I did once) and have less food. Or have weak fighters and hardly be able to protect my convoy.
Anyway the game is amazing. It says I only have 15.6hrs on here (as of this review) but it felt like so much longer (in a good way). I felt like I spent a lifetime with those people in my convoy.

This game is amazing, it is so unique and entertaining throughout.  The style and presentation doesn't lack at any point, the design is wonderful and charming if you enjoy old Sci-Fi movies. Sometimes you need these special powers to continue climbing the tower or to get collectibles, but it isn't overplayed.
The game isn't short, but it isn't long and dragging out. Speaking of climbing the tower, when I bought it and when you begin, you start climbing and it's like ok cool we're climbing this tower. But at a certain point you're just like damn, I'm climbing so far! And eventually you fall, or you get curious and jump off, and you just keep falling! That was a perfect moment for me when I first skydived down the tower all the way to my death(because I forgot to save my jetpack fuel to slow the fall).  It never got old skydiving and enjoying the scale of the game.  It really pulls off the verticality well, the fighting isn't hard but it isn't an easy tedious task, the different weapons bring a little bit of variety to combat, the presentation is great, the music is so fun and on-point, the whole climb feels tense and interesting. I'm a fan of this studio's games, but I was still blown-away by how much I enjoyed  The Deadly Tower of Monsters.  The game is worth beating if only for the ability to skydive all the way down to the bottom, teleport back, then do it all over again.  Can't recommend it enough.

Quick Review-
Battlefront II is among the greatest entries to the Star Wars franchise. Movie liscensed games have gotten a poor reputation as of late. Games like Thor, Green Lanturn, and Star Trek Online feel like rushed messes intent to quickly cash in on initial sales. Big icons like Superman and Aquaman have yet to have a game that is actually playable.
But then there are Star Wars games. Sure, there are a couple duds, but for the most part, George Lucas' iconic series has been treated well in the world of video games. We all remember great titles like Knights of The Old Republic, but not as much praise is thrown at the Battlefront series.
If you are not fimiliar with Battlefront, here's a quick rundown:
>You can chose your side in each battle: Republic or CIS / Galactic Empire or Rebel Alliance
>Each faction has a set of playable classes: each has their own version of a Rifleman, Sniper, Engineer, and Heavy Weapons.
> Each faction has 2 unique classes. For example, the Rebels have a Wookie Warrior and Bothan Spy, while the CIS has Magnaguards and the renowned Droidikas.
>You can battle on foot, find a land vehicle, or pilot a ship.
>Several game modes - Conquest, CTF, and Assault for example.
Conquest is a bit like a King of the Hill mode, where you can win 2 ways - capture and hold all of the Command Posts, or destroy your enemy and deplete their reinforcements. There is the standard 1 and 2 flag CTF, and Assualt has 2 ways of playing it. The standard is Space Battles. Space battles are often overshadowed when talking about Battlefront II, but I don't mind the change from fighters on the regular maps to a full space combat mode, personally. The other way Assualt can be played is on Mos Eisley. You choose your side, as usual. But this time, you choose between Heroes and Villians, and play as all of the iconic characters from the movies. Unfortunately, Mos Eisley is the only map this is playable on.
As for the story mode, it's way too short. It will only take you about 3 hours to complete the campaign. Luckily, there is plenty of replayability in the Instant Action feature, which is where you will be spending most of your time.
Overall, the game is what you would expect from an online 3rd person shooter based on Star Wars.  Fun, fast-paced, and full of nostalgia bonors. Final Verdict: 8/10

Little Nightmares is often terrifying yet always beautiful. Coming from Swedish studio Tarsier, Little Nightmares is the studio's first original title after years of contributing mostly to Little Pig Planet titles for PlayStation. Tarsier really got to flex their creative muscles with this one and in the process, created a dark and enjoyable platformer.
When you first lay eyes on Little Nightmares, it’s hard to not immediately think of INSIDE. While this comparison may be apt, it’s also not entirely fair as INSIDE was in intense development for years and is frankly a masterpiece in my eyes. Little Nightmares is certainly a good game but to compare it to INSIDE would not be fair to either game.
Little Nightmares tells the (intentionally) vague story of a little girl named Six who is trying to escape from the Maw. In her three hour adventure, you’ll encounter grotesque beings and a number of scares along the way. The game walks a tight line with its horror elements and manages to mostly pull off everything it’s trying to do. Mostly. For every close escape I experienced in my time with the game, I also had a frustrating amount of trial and error moments that stunted the pace of the game for me. There were a handful of sections where I feel like the only way that you can figure out what to do is to fail first. Now this is not a bad thing per se, but it can kill the momentum of the game. I felt that this was particularly prominent due to the finicky controls. Reminiscent of Shadow of the Colossus, the grab animation didn’t always seem to work correctly and there was some funky collision involved. This wasn’t a huge issue but it hindered my experience overall and I feel could have been a bit more refined.
Minor mechanical issues aside, the things that Little Nightmares does right, it knocks them out of the park. The attention to detail and especially the sense of scale are superb and really help the game world create a solid and cohesive sense of place. While that place is certainly ugly, the devs made it a very pretty ugly. I found Little Nightmares to be one of the most screenshot-able games I’ve played this year. While the story was definitely vague, I still enjoyed its themes clearly relating to gluttony and vainness. I also enjoyed the (intentional?) nod towards Spirited Away towards the end.
Despite some frustrating trial and error segments and some mechanical flaws, I thought that Little Nightmares was a thoroughly enjoyable experience and a stellar original debut by an indie studio. I certainly plan on keeping an eye on Tarsier on the future and look forward to what they create next.

I am a great fan of the diablo series, but this game feels like how diablo 3 should feel.
You start off in some small city and from the first moment in, I felt it to be ''just right''. Even when they used the same engine as Titan Quest, the graphics in this game looks amazing and stunning.
Its like the developers didnt want ANY place in this game to look like it has been created on a hurry. Every single bit of environment you encounter looks just right. The trees, the little abandoned cottages, the looks of mobs. As far as I have played, which isnt that much yet, even the most outlying places looks great.
I am a fan of multiplayer, and the way this games handles the ''drop-in'' and ''drop-out'' of multiplayer works like a charm. Indeed, they dont support their own servers for multiplayer, but they did an awesome job here. No port forwarding needed. Just enter if you would like to play single player, multiplayer using LAN or INTERNET, or joining one of those. Everyone with a decent connection should not have any problems with this game playing over either Lan or Internet.
The dept of this game overall is amazing. The skilltrees, the devotion points (Points that can be acquired through shrines around the world), the dual specialization, the different classes. The blacksmith who can craft amazing and lots of items and add-ons for your character. The shared stash tab, so you can share items between other characters instantly.
Although Grimdawn is an ARPG, the different playstyles you can combine with or without friends feels so good. I have played a lot of RPG's and ARPG's before, but Grimdawn feels like something ''new''. Not the standard hack and slash experience, but something feels different in this game. All the variation in it makes it so great. You even have an option to turn your camera around, so if you're bored with this game (I cant image why), you could turn the camera 180 degrees and its like you're playing a whole new world!
Would I recommend this game?
Well definitely I will!
And that for only 25 euro's? Thats amazing!

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is one of my favorite games. It is a tactical turn-based strategy game taking place during an invation by hostile aliens and puts you in control of XCOM, earth's primary defense against the invaders. You play the role of the commander and through the course of the campaign you get to train soldiers, build facilities, research alien technology and retaliate against the alien menace.
The alien designs are highly imaginative as are the designs for the weapons and armor of the X-Com operatives. The graphics are highly detailed given the dearth of information on the screen at any given time. The enemy AI changes based upon the difficulty setting and is meant to tax the player. You will feel the pain when a soldier you have been using a lot and have trained to a high level dies in combat. There are several types of battles with different goals; some are simply to defeat all the enemies. Others require rescuing a specific character and escorting that character back to the ship. Sometimes you have to rescue civilians or disarm bombs. There are also over 120 maps so it doesn't get too familiar. All of the maps are very well designed, sometimes with dead ends to separate your squad!
The simulation parts between battles are a lot of fun too, and there is some challenge in deciding what facilities to build, which upgrades to choose and what to research especially when funding is scarce and you are facing panic in nations that needs to be pacified so they do not withdraw from the XCOM project, meaning less revenue for you down the line.
A really nice touch is how all of your soldiers have a unique appearance (duplicates happen though it is not common) and a first and last name and country of origin. They also earn nicknames when they level up, which gives a feel to the soldiers having their own personalities and lives outside of XCOM.
The expansion, Enemy Within, adds covert ops missions that ties into a side mission of shutting down EXALT, a rogue group that wishes to use alien technology to overthrow the world as well as new maps and challenges, medals that can be awarded and boost your soldiers' power and the ability to create either genetically enhanced soldiers or MEC soldiers, cybernetic soldiers in Battlemech suits. It does not add more content beyond the endgame, unfortunately. The story still ends when you take the fight to the aliens.
I absolutely recommend XCOM: Enemy Unknown and the Enemy Within expansion. It is one of my all-time favorites.

This game is the original Mount and Blade, the classic that spawned the series of the same name. Admittedly, it lacks many of the features and improvements Warband has, including multiplayer. Indeed, if you are new to the series, I suggest playing  Warband first.
This does not mean that this game isn't worth playing, however. It is still extremely fun and addicting to play, and is a testament to how amazing the core mechanics of the franchise really are. The original offers a very similar, but different expierience to Warband, with a different map, different faction soldier equipment, a different Marshall selection system, and only 5 factions.
If nothing else, perhaps the biggest reasons to return to this game are the many classic, unique, and memetic mods that will never see a proper port to Warband, like 1866 (the first, and currently still best Wild West mod), The Eagle and the Radiant Cross, The Wedding Dance, Gangs of Glasgow, and Solid and Shade to name a few. Also, fans of the Warband versions of Prophesy of Pendor, The Last Days, and Star Wars Conquest may appreciate the classic versions available on the OG.
I fully recommend it to veteran M&B players that are curious to see how it all started, especially when it's on sale.

Divinity: Original Sin is an enchanting walk down memory lane for me, with a camera position that reminds me of Diablo, and elements of Dungeons & Dragons behind every choice. I'm heavily reminded of Baldur’s Gate with this series, and that is not a bad thing in any way. The gameplay is turn-based, and I feel the combat couldn't have worked any other way. The nervous tingle you feel when you are so close to your next target but are short on action points is second to none for me. The rogue class in particular was exhilarating for me, stealing all the paintings in town and pickpocketing guards with reckless abandon. Exiting the starting town with over 17,000 gold in pocket and every revive scroll is a wonderful feeling.
I feel as though there is a synergy between all the classes, and some classes don't work as well with others. Running a Ranger with a Fire Mage, for example, is quite hard when the Fire Mage puts up clouds of smoke you can't see through. You could also play with an Ice Wizard who “accidentally” stuns you. And there are a fair share of game breaking bugs that I encountered within the first hour of gameplay. Such as breaking down a gate while on the other side, and getting trapped because the game registered the gate as still closed even though it was in splinters below my feet.
Basically, you need to play this game. Even if you have to play it by yourself because your friends are jerks, you still need to experience this game in some form. It's incredible.

Child of Light is a fairy tale about Aurora, the princess of Austria (?). Falled into a fantasy world, she lives an adventure to save her family and her people, and she also discovers her own marvellous destiny.
The visual design reminds of old child book illustrations; it is beautiful, although sometimes silly and mushy (...why girls' hair are always horizontal, moved by an omnipresent wind lol?) ...the story and the character design (thanks to the quests she takes, Aurora meets many original characters) are well conceived, also some unexpected plot twists are present.
Rpg features are reduced to quests and characters modification via trees of abilities, but do not expect visible customization or complex character study: you may choose random evolutions and they will equally functions.
The turn-based combat system with the action timeline is generally easy, but also smart and it requires a good amount of reasoning and resources management.
A positive note about the music, that will remain in your mind.
Another curios aspect of the game are the dialogues and narration... all of them are in rhymes. That's cute but... at least in the italian version, no metrics are provided by the authors; for this reason, some sentences just sound contrived and stupid. Such as... not fairy/inspiring characters, but childish idiots who force their own speaking to put rhymes in it at any cost.
The idea is cool Ubisoft, but if this is the goal... next time, please hire an experienced poet!

Crawl is an excellent four player local competitive game, with a well defined style and a lot of heart. You're four lost souls damned to wander an unholy dungeon, fighting to escape through exerting your will upon the frail flesh which happens to pass before you. As a spirit, you are ever at odds for when you inhabit the hero the other spirits seek to displace you, and when you are a spirit, you must be the one to strike the killing blow if you would escape. Once you've advanced your hero to a sufficient level, and subsequently discovered a portal, you can go through it to face a monstrosity which may end up inhabited by all your foes. Fail there, and return to the dungeon, until someone escapes, or you collectively fail too often.
If Crawl has a flaw, and you do not agree that the flaws are at times inherent to the beauty of a piece, it is that the game loop is secured around four players. If you do not have four people, you will need to fill the remaining slots with A.I. which - while quite capable - is not nearly as unpredictable and thus exciting as a human player.
Purchase a copy, invite three of your friends, and prepare to writhe - no - crawl your way back to the living.

First of all, I am a huge fan of the "South Park" TV series.

It's got everything you need from watching the show; it's hilarious, the gameplay is fun, and it honestly feels like South Park. No other way to explain it.
You can definitely play and greatly enjoy this game without knowing anything about the TV Show, but it's great that items and side quests all relate to episodes of the show in one way or another.
Of course, no game is perfect, nothing is.
The game is too short for $40CAD. I finished it twice on console, each playthrough taking under 12 hours [console]. In my opinion, any game that takes less than 20 hours to complete should be $20 or less. That's just me though. I have to say, even though there isn't much quantity, the quality can make it seem worth it to some people.
The game is locked at 30FPS. I don't really care that there are no graphics settings, because it's supposed to look like South Park. I just feel like the game was directly ported from console to PC without much work done at all to make it a better experience for the PC.
To sum it up, The Stick of Truth is definitely worth it for South Park fans, and general comedy fans alike. If you wholeheartedly believe in quality over quantity, definitely go for it.
Obviously, try to get it when it's on sale. I honestly wouldn't be able to justify $40 for such a short game.

This is a port of a Playstation Vita game that remade the first of the Hyperdimension Neptunia series on PS3.  You can already read what the game is about so I'll essentially only rate it on content.

This is a really good port by a company that, to my knowledge, has never made a pc port of a game before.
The game is half off, and at 15.00 it's a steal, even at 30.00 it's pretty good.  The dlc is a really good value being like 7 dollars all together full price. Support this for more Japanese games, and for future entries in the series.  The second should be on its way as well.

This review may contain spoilers, continue reading at your own risk
South Park: The Stick of Truth is a light-RPG set in the South Park universe following all of your favourite South Park characters through your adventure through the Stixk of Truth. Depending on your options the game does infact change your experience; BUT I wouldn't take this too sereiously as nearly all choices result in a humuorous outcome.
The graphical fidelity is true to the show, stimulating the experience of being in a 10+ hour long episode of South Park. The graphics are pleasant to look at and there are no real complaints to have about the graphics. In some cases textures for explosions were purposely made to look like a low budget movie for the humuorous effect. Overall the developers nailed this section with pleasant graphics that are easy on the eyes- allowing me to play for countless hours straight.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a light-RPG turnbased comedy game, just by reading this it sounds like the developers had implemented strategies from Game Dev Tycoon into their game- but yet again, I just cannot complain. The gameplay is wonderful, it flows perfectly: nothing too difficult that players may not understand, nothing to easy that the players feel unaccomplished after a fight. The main characters from the show are offered to you to be your 'Buddy' which is essentially a partner that you also control in fights (which also have use dfuring quests too!). Each character offers different abilities and play styles to allow major change in the combat which I believe stopped it getting stale. I used Butters as he was my favourite character from the show, offering witty one liners and exciting abilities I once again have to say the developers absolutely nailed this section.
First off with the voice acting. Trey Parker and Matt Stone, the people who voice act all of the well known characters from the show, do the voice acting in this game! Honestly to me this is insane, the voice acting is exactly the same as the show offering the player with maximal amounts of immersion. The music was enjoyable, it offered humour in certain stages of the game. Giving the player battle music, walking music, and even music from Jimmy The Bard! Not really much to say about the SFX, not very noticable or effective in chnaging the game.
I believe the comdey aspect of this game needs its own aspect. Even if you aren't a fan of South Park's crude humour I believe you will still find a good laugh in this game every once in a while. And is you are a fan of the humour in South Park, this game was made for you. Nazi's, offensive language, suggestive humour, blunt humour, and even more. This game is a love letter for South Park fans.
South Park™: The Stick of Truth™ has revistalised my urge to play video games, I have been in a drought of never being able to finish games just through the lack of desire but this game allowed me to burn through it with pure enjoyment in 2 days! I played for 7 hours in one day, I was fully immersed for the whole experience all the way to the credits rolling. This game is a modern masterpiece and unlike most video games based off popular media, this game is not a cash in. This game is a must play for absoulately everyone. The crude humour, the graphical fidelity, the immersion created by the voice acting and the exciting gameplay allow this game to be one of the best games I have ever played.

It's hard, really ♥♥♥♥ing hard,  even on easy. There's a huge learning curve some people will have quite some difficulty with I know I did. The difficulty spikes and often times when you lose you feel like it was outside of your control. You can be on full Hull, full missles with an Extra shield at the start of the game. Then you make a warp and end up in an unwinnable battle for example. I played Pixel Piracy in Alpha when the difficulty was literally broken and you couldn't save. The difference was even though I probably died more in that game at that time, every life was a different experience since the world is procedurally generated. Pixel Piracy since then has been updated quite a bit and is a pirate version of FTL almost. Although if FTL had let me torrent their game first I wouldn't of bought it. Some people seem to think my issue is that it's hard, that's not the case. My issue is that no matter how far I get I always restart in the same place. Which means when learning to play you repeat the same content over and over again. It made me often want to stop playing after dying just because I didn't feel like replaying the start of the game again. The game gets more fun the longer you play, but the difficulty spikes randomly. This means you can go from feeling like your farming ships to getting wrecked by the next one you encounter and being forced to restart. Sometimes you can run away but it's often not really worth it because unless you have money for repairs etc. You're just likely to die in your next encounter. I don't know if this is just on easy but The AI will attack random parts of your ship such as the door controls. Which doesn't make any sense to me. To me some of the games features feel shallow to me, I understand it's not meant to be a sim and the focus is meant to be on ship management, and crew micromanagement. For example I wish there were more options with crew member other than just different races. The fact that I've played betas with more depth tells me they didn't want that aspect to be like an RPG. I would just of liked a higher level of customization, and to be able to build your own ship. Although I realize I'm asking for an entirely different game, but another one of my issues is getting the other ships is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥which are either a process of trial an error or a process of meticulously following an online guide with a bit of luck and skill. I'm not saying FTL is a bad game, I'm saying it's hard to get into and it's not very inviting to new comers. I'm also saying I feel like it had the potential to be much more than what it is, because even something as simple as a difficulty curve would of made a world of difference. I prefer Pixel Piracy over this title although it's difficult to compare the two. If you beat the game on hard your first try, you've probably played games like this before. In conclusion I haven't experienced a learning curve like this since playing minecraft tech mods. Because due to the almost complete lack of a tutorial you can either learn through trial and error or by watching a bunch of youtube tutorial videos, and playing with a wiki open. The problem is most of the game is fairly unpredictable, but I don't think I should have to watch a youtube video if I want to learn how to play the game effectively. I'm not saying it's a bad game I'm saying it's difficulty and it's curve are a fault, and when combined with rogue like elements. It leads to a ton of repetition that sometimes feels unfair. Because the hardest part of any game like this is getting started, then once you're going it's mainly luck that you don't run into something absurd then run into something after that while going for repairs. I don't mind randomness but it doesn't make the experience feel fresh, it just makes it feel unpolished. Since the start of the game still feels the same even if the encounters/stores have all changed places. It doesn't stop it from feeling the same as the time before. The problem is you need to be sort of lucky with your encounters because if you can't afford ammo/repairs then you're screwed. Since the only consistent way to get money is to pillage other ships etc. Which without full HP or Ammo often means your death especially if you're even slightly outmatched.

First take notice of the amount of hours I have played. Realize that some portion of those hours actually was from me banging my head on the keyboad trying to beat the last boss battle during my first playthrough, which was on the hard difficult setting where I limped my way to the ending in the final chapter due to a few "bad" choices along with a flawed supplies mechanic that is still manageable for the most part. The battle was so difficult that subsequently in an update through various aspects the bellower was nerfed a bit primarily on lower than hard difficulty, but also characters brought into the final boss battle are no longer injured beforehand. Given this realize that I definitely am aware about the flaws of this game and that this review is based on the updated version having done multiple playthroughs.
In short here are the positivies and negatives about the game:
Positives: 1. In many ways an ehanced Oregon trail type of game.
2. Interesting world environment, plot, characters, and ambiance from music selection
3. Combat can be challenging and fun (look up combat gameplay before hand though as this opinion could vary)
Negatives: 1. Poor resource mechanic where renown earned from choices and battle is used for both upgrading characters and purchasing supplies to prevent starvation (managable largely except special care should be taken in chapter 2 to avoid buying supplies as much as possible until chapter 4.)
2. Oversights such as supplies in Frostvier during chapter 4 automatically being about 3 days worth regardless of what supplies were in chapter 2. Also renown spent and items can be wasted if characters die or leave... you can load though.
3. Hard difficulty is unforgiving especially given negative # 1 and certain poor choices so avoid until after first normal playthrough (trust me). Normal difficulty should still be fine for most people and easy should be... well easy.
4. This one is not that negative, but can be annoying. You can not save manually it saves automatically over time. There are plenty of places to load though, which I know from... first hand experience.
False Top Review Complaints: 1. Choices don't matter/impact the game. 2. The story goes nowhere
1. Your choices have a direct consequence on the size of your forces, the difficulty of combat, certain limited character dialogue, what events occur, and whether characters live or die. Obviously as in any RPG choices only matter as much as you asign them. If you don't care about your caravan or the characters in your party then of course they don't matter, but to claim they don't impact the game (or in a way you would like) is ridiculous. There is a difference between choices impacting the game and not being satisfied with what one expects or wants out of a choice's impact. I would agree choice impact regarding camp dialogue is limited and not as deveoped as I like, but it's not game breaking.
2. This first banner saga game is soley about surviving the dredge threat. The varl perspective portion of the playthrough, which involves completing a certain objective despite the dredge threat is actually no different. If you make certain dialogue options you realize your actions are actually helping/attempting to end dredge threat albiet indirectly. To complain that the game is about running from the dredge then making a final stand is similar to complaining that the reapers were not eliminated as a threat in Mass Effect 1 or that Oregon trail is about surviving until reaching a certain city. The first game of any trilogy is about setting up the environment and getting gamers to know and bond with characters and the story. It is about concluding a portion of the story, while leaving enough open for there to be more. The bellower isn't some random boss. It is some sort of champion of the dredge that is primarliy a large part of how the dredge are able to win against (almost) any threat. I really don't want to spoil certain story elements about the dredge or the reasons behind what is going on. Just know that there is a lot more than get to point a and fight some boss.
Recommendation: Buy this game at a price you find acceptable. If you are used to paying $60 for a game then the $20 price should be fine. For everyone else used to steam prices I am sure this game will be on sale at some point as it was in the past especially during steam summer sale. If the price is $10 anyone should buy it, while $15 or $20 is probably more for RPG fans looking for a good story, with some mechanical game flaws as mentioned, that will only be even better in the sequel.

Verdict: Many of the reviews on Steam do this game a massive disservice. I understand, I do. It's not what they were expecting. Like most gamers, they want to feel empowered, feel like they are affecting the outcome in meaningful and tangible ways. This is not that kind of game. This game is about disempowerment and despair, accepting consequences you cannot change, and showing resilience in the face of the end of the world. Most of the choices are between outcomes that are bad or worse, and you will feel like you have chosen poorly very, very often. But therein lies the magic of this game; when you fail 9/10 times, the 10th time brings incredible pathos when you miraculously succeed against terrible odds, when a comrade unexpectedly returns, when you find that timely cache of supplies to sustain your march just one more day. It is an emotional antidote to the automatic success meted out by most video games these days.
I can't recommend the Banner Saga enough. It is one of the most engaging and affecting experiences I have had in a game. 10/10
Story: This game is driven far less by the story as defined by specific plot elements, and far more so by the general feeling it engenders through its overall presentation. Information is seldom just handed out; as the player you have to infer a great deal from subtle hints. Characters are elusive and rarely forthcoming but, even if their role is brief, most hint at significant hidden depth. Many things are left open and unexplained in the end, and that is exactly how it should be. 9/10
Gameplay:  There are two main elements to the gameplay: the simulation element where you manage resources and make decisions for your followers, and the turn-based (and sometimes punishing) tactical battles. The simulation part is simple, but wrenching. There are never enough resources to go around, and never a simple choice. Consequences are unforeseen and permanent. The tactical part is standard but given added depth by the armour-break system. Some players will be frustrated by the criminally short range of archers and other distance fighters, but it feels right that there is no hiding on the battlefield. Battles often feel unfair, but that fits the game perfectly. It’s one of the first games where, when a hero dies, I accept and mourn the loss rather than reloading an earlier save. 8/10
Graphics: The art and presentation is the soul of this game, and it would not feel the same without it. Everything is rendered in a beautiful, hand-drawn style, with layered backgrounds to add a sense of depth and distance. 10/10
Sound/Music: The sound and music are both excellent, and the soundtrack is worth downloading. The ambiance in every scene is incredibly atmospheric and immersive, despite its simplicity. Less is more in this game, and sometimes there is nothing more solemn than a winter wind.  10/10

Original review:
I really, really want to be able to recommend this game - Eastside is showing its age as the NHL continues to evolve, and there's not much else on the PC so far as hockey goes. But in its current state I can't recommend spending $40 on FHM 4.
I've run the 2017-18 NHL season three times now to test things out. I've been playing as GM, controlling all roster moves but giving the AI control over the lines and tactics as head coach. I really like a lot of things about the game - the trade AI doesn't seem out of whack, the tactical system and line chemistry system works well, the sim times aren't outrageous even with quite a few worldwide leagues running in the background. But the longer I've played, the more issues I've seen. In just my most recent season alone...
Even with these issues I've actually been pleasantly surprised at the state of the game, but that's because I remember the low bar set by FHM & FHM 2. I skipped FHM 3 altogether and decided to buy this year's version mostly to support continued development of PC hockey games. FHM 4 is fun in a way those previous games weren't and I'm sure it's going to improve through patches as hockey season goes on, but it's still not quite there yet. I can't imagine anybody who's really choosy about the money they spend on PC games would be happy with this product given the steep asking price.

I've just finished the single player campaign for the first time, and i really enjoyed it.
Pretty much about an alien invasion trying to take over the earth. I did not expect much else coming from such a plot, hence I was surprised to find out about the backstory of every different unit that we were facing throughout the game in the last mission. Although it would be nice to be able to extract more information from the final boss,such as explaining what was purpose of achieving 'ascension'. (I killed it within 2 turns so maybe more could be revealed if the fight draged on)
This is a turn based strategy game but it is special in a way,your units does not have hit the enemies all the time. Your units have a certain % to hit the enemy and that is affected by cover, terrain and distance (perhaps even more). To me, this is a unique and refreshing game mechanic that makes the game much harder yet more enjoyable to play. Sometimes, there are a few WTF moments when you realise your units can 'see' the enemies through walls and then shoot through it. There were also a few grindy moments in between research time for researches that is needed for mission progression. I hate grinding but that is forgiven because of its short duration.
The game is also quite balanced. The purpose of upgrading gears is to even the playing field against tougher enemies rather than to overpower them. You still have to be careful with how you manuvure your units even when they are equipped with the best gear in the game.(e.g Your colonel assault can still die to the likes of thin men if you recklessly charge forward to shoot in their face) One complaint i have is that i find plasma rifles too weak in comparison to heavy plasmas and plasma sniper rifles, would be nice if the damage increase by a unit or two.
However, i have a major problem that I did not ever encounter in other games but this game has it. In the last mission, there are 'invisible doors' that cannot be opened quietly, causing me to forcefully get my unit to rush through the door and get caught in a very bad position. The Elite Muton that was summoned by the final boss was armed with an 'invisible gun' and caused my game to crash when the it tried to shoot. The Elite Muton problem was fixed after restarting the game but the 'invisible door' is still there.
I bought this game during the winter sale and i definitely recommend it at full price if its within your budget. Now I am going to attempt the harder difficulty.

The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a third person perspective action game, set in a retro sci-fi film title. Releasing from ACE Team Studio, who are known for Zeno Clash and Abyss Odyssey.  The story is based on two astronauts and their robot friend.
Game play is from the third person perspective above their heads. Firstly one of the game’s biggest flaws is the camera angle; it is in a set position on each frame, which means it can be very hard to look where you really want to especially when it comes to some of the puzzles. There are two sides to the gameplay mechanics; the platforming side, and the action side. The action parts of the game are your standard hack and slash style; with different weapons available throughout the game for you to use and upgrade using the game’s currency system.  There isn’t really anything standoutish about the combat system, other than it just works and does as it intends to do, as well as being easy to control and grasp. The platforming side of the game is one which I wasn’t keen on. It surely can’t just be me who is sick to death of jumping puzzle style. The camera angle of the game doesn’t help on the platforming at all. With the awkward camera angle makes any sort of jump you need to make, more of a guessing game.  Thankfully the platforming is few and far between, still a small gripe though!
The art style on show in Deadly Tower of Monsters is done in a cartoon, retro look. The camera filters which are also used throughout the game are to add to the effect that you are watching an old film, and it does it very well. It wasn’t my favourite aesthetic in the world; but I can appreciate the look and feel they were going for. The soundtrack and voice acting are all really spot on too. With the voice over and narration being a key feature for the game, adding plenty of comedic value and fourth and fifth wall breaking too.
This game is by no means easy; there aren’t any difficulty settings, so what you get is the same experience throughout. A lot of the game can be overpowered by simply grinding on monsters for more gold and “cogs” which are the games currency system for upgrading your skills, but a lot of the game will come down to how good the player is, rather than how powerful the character is. The end boss fights are a real challenge, and will require you to try and try and try before finally successfully conquering them.  Even some of the more regular monsters in between boss fights will cause concern amongst some.
I finished the game in a little under six hours. There is a handful of side missions you can take part in, but none of them add anything to the story, nor reward you extra skills; purely just extra content. Some of them you run into whilst playing through the main story, whilst others you have to go out of your way for. For me I was quite happy completing the ones I found naturally, I had no real urge to go seeking them.  There isn’t any replay ability factor in Tower of Deadly Monsters; it’s a completely linear story line. The co-op mode may make a second run through viable with a friend, but you may as well just make your first run through co-op and save yourself the time.  There is a hard mode added, but that will be for a small group of people who’ll take that upon themselves to play.
Technically, I had no problems at all. The game runs very well even on 4K.  The frame rate did not drop below 60 at any points. I would recommend people playing this game use a controller, simply because it is easier to handle and you get the most out of the game play with a controller over a keyboard and mouse.
To sum up, The Deadly Tower of Monsters is your run of the mill OK game. The most redeeming factor about the title has got to be the narration and comedic value it brings. Dying Light is a survival/horror game based on Crane, the main character and a GRE operative whose mission is to retrieve a document containing valuable info about an epidemic disease which converts humans into something, that was supposed to be recovered by a agent known as Rais, leader of one of the two factions in the city.
+ I expected the game to be another Dead Island, turns out I was wrong. The combat system variety depends on skills that you gather by fighting through zombies, which is important depending on a players style when dealing with a enemy.

+ A pretty big map, fully lootable, including lockpicking, hidden caches, and puzzles.

+ Great fun in co-op after the "Be the Zombie" expansion.
+Really good story
- FPS drops at some points, but doesn't affect gameplay much.
- Toxic community
Dying Light is a very good horror/survival game with a enormous size which promises a great succes for the developers to keep bringing new content to such a terrific game.

I tried to be as thorough as possible, so It took about 80 hours for a single playtrough on high difficulty level.
i'll just put here some pros, cons and conclusion and be done with it.
Pros.
+ Complex, but at the same time easy to understand and pretty well balanced combat mechanics. If you are familliar with basic concept of Action Points and know something about physics you will have no problems with that.
+ You are free to experiment with your character progression, combine different schools of magic and abilities. You can have the total of 4 characters in your party, 2 of them you can create at the beginning.
+ In battles on high difficulty, instead of putting you against some fat meatbags, this game most of the time offers a reasonably effective sets of opponents with different roles. They are combining their abilities, using potions and even 1-time scrolls. So it is fair to say this game is pretty challenging.
+ Effective crafting system you can experiment with just combining random items together. You can cook food, mix potions, add stat boost for your weapons and armour. Base items that you create yourself are always the same level is your character, enchant them and you have solid equipmet at any part of the game until you find some good legendaty loot.
+ Seek, and ye shall find. Seriously, if you asked to find something - you gotta find it, literally. You wont have any marks on your map. I thought its gonna be annoying and boring as hell, but it turned out to be highly enjoyable experience for most of the gameplay time.
+ Tons of unobvious treasures, quests and other secrets.
Cons. No game is perfect, D:OS is not an exception, every pros have some downside in itself.
- At the very late game (which is not that big part to be honest) everything becomes a boring routine. A big chance you'll just wanna run trough it as fast as possible.
- Camera control is lacking some flexibility, it messes up with indoors gameplay, especially in combat situations when you sometimes cant see the enemy and click on him unless you select top-down mode, which isnt pretty.
- Terrible inventory management.
- In some puzzles even if you figured put what to do - you will still have to find the buttons which are small and hard to press because of the camera.
- I know this game is focuses on gameplay, not the characters, but i doubt it could've hurt the gameplay if they were more "alive". Seriously, they rarely talk, the companions are just dummies with small background story, few lines of dialogs and 1 personal quest which they will give you at some point. Yes, you can even select AI personalities for your main characters which leads to some funny situations and the argument that can be decided with rock-paper-scissors game, but it rarely makes any sense because you'll just want to make YOUR decision anyway.
Conclusion? This is the first RPG game i truly enjoyed since The Witcher 2.  Solid, challenging and rewarding gameplay experience. Plenty of well-written texts and dialogs, fairy neutral storyline which you may like, but can easily ignore and enjoy the gameplay if you dont like it. Larian made a statement that they will continue to support this game, and right now they are working on new difficulty level and further polish. Most likely i will play this game again when they do that.

This review may contain spoilers, continue reading at your own risk
South Park: The Stick of Truth is a light-RPG set in the South Park universe following all of your favourite South Park characters through your adventure through the Stixk of Truth. Depending on your options the game does infact change your experience; BUT I wouldn't take this too sereiously as nearly all choices result in a humuorous outcome.
The graphical fidelity is true to the show, stimulating the experience of being in a 10+ hour long episode of South Park. The graphics are pleasant to look at and there are no real complaints to have about the graphics. In some cases textures for explosions were purposely made to look like a low budget movie for the humuorous effect. Overall the developers nailed this section with pleasant graphics that are easy on the eyes- allowing me to play for countless hours straight.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a light-RPG turnbased comedy game, just by reading this it sounds like the developers had implemented strategies from Game Dev Tycoon into their game- but yet again, I just cannot complain. The gameplay is wonderful, it flows perfectly: nothing too difficult that players may not understand, nothing to easy that the players feel unaccomplished after a fight. The main characters from the show are offered to you to be your 'Buddy' which is essentially a partner that you also control in fights (which also have use dfuring quests too!). Each character offers different abilities and play styles to allow major change in the combat which I believe stopped it getting stale. I used Butters as he was my favourite character from the show, offering witty one liners and exciting abilities I once again have to say the developers absolutely nailed this section.
First off with the voice acting. Trey Parker and Matt Stone, the people who voice act all of the well known characters from the show, do the voice acting in this game! Honestly to me this is insane, the voice acting is exactly the same as the show offering the player with maximal amounts of immersion. The music was enjoyable, it offered humour in certain stages of the game. Giving the player battle music, walking music, and even music from Jimmy The Bard! Not really much to say about the SFX, not very noticable or effective in chnaging the game.
I believe the comdey aspect of this game needs its own aspect. Even if you aren't a fan of South Park's crude humour I believe you will still find a good laugh in this game every once in a while. And is you are a fan of the humour in South Park, this game was made for you. Nazi's, offensive language, suggestive humour, blunt humour, and even more. This game is a love letter for South Park fans.
South Park™: The Stick of Truth™ has revistalised my urge to play video games, I have been in a drought of never being able to finish games just through the lack of desire but this game allowed me to burn through it with pure enjoyment in 2 days! I played for 7 hours in one day, I was fully immersed for the whole experience all the way to the credits rolling. This game is a modern masterpiece and unlike most video games based off popular media, this game is not a cash in. This game is a must play for absoulately everyone. The crude humour, the graphical fidelity, the immersion created by the voice acting and the exciting gameplay allow this game to be one of the best games I have ever played.

I don't think The Banner Saga is a very well executed game. The ideas are certainly there, the story is interesting, the music is excellent, but gameplay-wise, it has some pretty egregious design problems.
Consider that players replaying the game regularly consult a guide to check when certain characters might die, in order to not waste resources levelling before that point. Then consider that on your first run, you don't have that - you have the option to choose from an assortment of characters, spending your points (renown) on whoever you please. But while they can die from your negligence, they generally don't: they die from purely unpredictable events instead.
Well that's how surviving in a viking wasteland is, yes? That's how it should be!
The trouble is that this is not FTL - a run is not 1-2 hours, it's 10, and it isn't replayable if you find yourself trapped with a now-useless team after luck decides to screw you. It's harsh, and adds to the tone of the game, but it's also ruinous. Save-scum, save-scum.
Double-edged sword that may be, I can see the justification for it. What I can't justify, at all, is that the game essentially does nothing with it's random encounter system. Events pop up and you're faced with options. Based on my runthrough of the game, I'd say you get positive outcomes maybe a fifth of the time. Further adding to the harsh climate of the game, etc, etc... the trouble is, your options tend to lie in shades of grey between the -right- thing and the -wrong- thing to do in any given case... and THERE IS ZERO DIFFERENCE. They're all dice rolls, and that I started at a point of angelic service to my fellow survivors and slowly arced towards commiting horrible deeds for my tribe caused not one change. It was dice rolls all the way through; you get nothing in exchange for that guilt, and seeing what emotional impact it has on the player to decide, I'll murder this person in front of my (character's) daughter, when you take the plunge and hit that button ----> dice roll. The same dice roll. 80% of the time, it goes bad, and you feel worse.
(On a lesser note, a gripe: this game totally does not have good animation, as nearly everyone is excited to share. It has a very cool art style, but central story beats aren't illustrated; they're all just text... including the climax.)
I leave off with one thing. The final boss is very very poorly designed, requiring a combat style the rest of the game would punish (rushing in a straight line forward), and I didn't/couldn't finish with the team I had, and I now have no intention of continuing with this franchise.
Cross your fingers. You might find the telepathy to make the right decisions, and the game might be fun!
For me it was a lesson in negative reinforcement.

Having never played a previous game in this franchise, and not being disappointed and/or annoyed by the wacky path this game takes, I can safely say that Saints Row IV is an extremely fun game.
The writing in this game isn't the best, and maybe I'm just spoiled by Borderlands 2, but it certainly brings laughs.  However, the comedy in this game rarely comes entirely from the dialogue.  Most of the time, the situations that you, as a player, find yourself in, are where the game truly shines in the humor department.  You'll be walking down the street, when suddenly, a lazer-shooting cat will assault you, forcing your character to launch counter-measures with a large alien bazooka.  You can be surfing on top of an airplane as your friend drives it into buildings.  The pure randomness and un-equalled freedom in this game allows it to become a zany super-powered romp through an alien simulation.
I do have a few complaints with it though.  The fact that you are granted extremely helpful superpowers early in the game, almost immediately gets rid of the need for driving a car.  Your freeze, fire, or psychic blasts eliminate the need for a gun.  I guess the game is trying to grant you freedom to use whatever you want, but maybe they should've nerfed the powers a bit.
All in all, Saints Row IV is a hilarious, fun, and gorgeous game.  The co-op is excellent, the customization is mind-boggling, and the scale of the world is very good.  This game is a joy to play, even with some mild gameplay problems.

I've just finished the single player campaign for the first time, and i really enjoyed it.
Pretty much about an alien invasion trying to take over the earth. I did not expect much else coming from such a plot, hence I was surprised to find out about the backstory of every different unit that we were facing throughout the game in the last mission. Although it would be nice to be able to extract more information from the final boss,such as explaining what was purpose of achieving 'ascension'. (I killed it within 2 turns so maybe more could be revealed if the fight draged on)
This is a turn based strategy game but it is special in a way,your units does not have hit the enemies all the time. Your units have a certain % to hit the enemy and that is affected by cover, terrain and distance (perhaps even more). To me, this is a unique and refreshing game mechanic that makes the game much harder yet more enjoyable to play. Sometimes, there are a few WTF moments when you realise your units can 'see' the enemies through walls and then shoot through it. There were also a few grindy moments in between research time for researches that is needed for mission progression. I hate grinding but that is forgiven because of its short duration.
The game is also quite balanced. The purpose of upgrading gears is to even the playing field against tougher enemies rather than to overpower them. You still have to be careful with how you manuvure your units even when they are equipped with the best gear in the game.(e.g Your colonel assault can still die to the likes of thin men if you recklessly charge forward to shoot in their face) One complaint i have is that i find plasma rifles too weak in comparison to heavy plasmas and plasma sniper rifles, would be nice if the damage increase by a unit or two.
However, i have a major problem that I did not ever encounter in other games but this game has it. In the last mission, there are 'invisible doors' that cannot be opened quietly, causing me to forcefully get my unit to rush through the door and get caught in a very bad position. The Elite Muton that was summoned by the final boss was armed with an 'invisible gun' and caused my game to crash when the it tried to shoot. The Elite Muton problem was fixed after restarting the game but the 'invisible door' is still there.
I bought this game during the winter sale and i definitely recommend it at full price if its within your budget. Now I am going to attempt the harder difficulty.

"Do you recommend this game?"
NO, not at this price and not in it's current state.
Do I like the game and see the potential?
YES, this sim has a high ceiling and I hope and pray I can change this review to a thumbs up sooner than later.
Seriously... when you are charging $35+ for a game, at least have some fundamental standard that you prioritize.  I don't want to play a simulation game where basic things are broken like sorting on certain columns, or a back page function that doesn't remember your last configuration/filter.
If simulation games 20-30 years older can do exactly what you're trying to do and have done it extremely well in the past, that should be the "standard" you try to at least reach before you present anything furthermore. Zero excuses in my opinion.
Aside from the headscratching "Dev, why can't you not sleep just for a night and fix the most obvious unsightly detractions", this simulation is very rewarding and I am actually enjoying the brunt of the mechanics.
Simple obvious polish is all that is needed, for instance when both teams are the same trim color, the text labels will use the same color for both teams, which is annoying and confusing when you are trying to immerse yourself in the details, it's like trying to watch two teams wearing the same uniforms.  Also a game puck indicator that seems to follow a hidden random agenda to what the play by play is actually saying, or penalty countdowns which start fine, but executes in a completely 'F- failed function coding class' buggy mess.
Plusses:
- Real players/teams. The NHL/PA licensing is great and this is the type of sim I will love to tinker around with in various historical fantasy tangents
- Engine that is more believable than smoke & mirrors at this point. Text play-by-play retty much reminiscent of Championship Manager 01/02 (Football Manager before it went 2D) and that era of sports sim engine.
Minuses:
- Unpolished, untested, sloppy coded front-end, broken functionality that is there but not working properly under various contexts
- Setting a player trade with a team and finally clicking "Offer trade" leading to home screen with no indicators/prompts/results and then going back to the trade window manually has the same trade ready to go/repeat into loop-of-nothing. Seriously, how the heck do I trade a player?
- Resolution settings seemingly not working at all (fixed default regardless of what I set including after a restart)
- Momentum meter doesn't seem very realistic or in tune with the action being portrayed
- Puck indicator that seems to have a mind of its own compared to the action being portrayed
- Game engine playback settings that don't stick and have to be reset every game
- No player comparison
- No line presets
- No steam cloud save
(my opinion after open-minded 6 hours of casual play)

I haven’t seen a game pull off the super cheesy lines inspired by B movies made back in the day since Unstoppable Gorg. That game was a tower defense game, though, with goofy villains and flying saucers. The Deadly Tower of Monsters (TDTM from here on out because golly that’s a long title) pulls it off in spades. The setup is a director coming back to record some audio commentary for the DVD release of the movie he made a while ago. He talks rather passive about things like people dying on the set to the cost of certain features and complaints by stars: it’s all very entertaining.
The whole game is run in a 60’s style of aesthetics with creatures that look like they are stop-motioned captured (love that T-Rex and the squid people). Keep in mind though, that this is the director doing the narrating while you play. If you die, he criticizes the one playing the video footage for getting bad footage since the scene never happened that way in the original film. It was mocking you and still explained it off (if you were worried about continuity and how they would talk about it). I died so much at one point that the one helping with the footage asked the director why they kept all of these reels when they weren’t  shot correctly. They really put a lot of thought into the narration and I love how they comment about almost everything.
The combat works fairly well, I did favor the melee over the range attack. It always feels like you do more damage than using the lasers and such. (I’m looking at you Tesla Gun.) Smaller melee weapons are faster and quicker guns are weaker, yadda yadda yadda, I wield the biggest stick and tank with my face! That’s not to say that things will always be that way throughout the course of the entire game. There are cogs of different colors and worth littered throughout the game and you will use these cogs to upgrade your weapons. Obviously there are more difficult ones to get and some that I just don’t understand how to get at this point in the game, but with exploring you’ll find enough of them to fix the weapons up to play the way you want to… or at least start in the direction you’ll want to go in. There is a good variety of different weapons that will get handed to you as you progress, upgrading them will be dependent on your determination to explore and gather the various types of cogs.
You’re given three adventurers to play around with in TDTM, and I used to feel that this was one of the few negatives I had with the game. They all felt like the same character to me. Whether it’s with the combat in general or jumping, there didn’t feel like there was any major difference in how they operated/controlled. If I had to ask myself if that’s a bad thing, I would say not completely. In the fact that they all felt the same, that means I could switch it up between♥♥♥♥♥♥Starspeed, Scarlet Nova and Robot. While I love Robot’s name, for some reason I loved to play with… Mr. Starspeed.
It was about the time that I was getting fed up with some golden cogs that I couldn’t figure out how to get that I realized that specific characters had different talents. The first one to really set itself apart was Robot. He had the ability to slow time down and that opened my eyes to being able to progress further and get some cogs that were impossible before hand. Now, with the other characters starting to show me their moves, it’s starting to feel like the characters are a bit more fleshed out than I had originally thought. Granted, as you obtain new abilities, you slowly remember places that gave you pause and caused your brain to hurt an hour or so back and realize that this game will have some back tracking. I was almost bothered by this until I discovered that all of the characters could fast travel up and down the tower (a power I had originally thought to be given to Scarlet only). This is what I get for assuming.
Score: Gewd.
With the characters getting more fleshed out and more weapons getting unlocked, the world seemed to open up even more. The narrator doesn’t stop from shining with the humorous comments and the game continues to be visually fun throughout. Something stops TDTM from being super compelling to play without a desire to stop. I find it rather easy to play, but other games continue to easily pull me away. That is not to say that it’s not worth picking up, but I think one should be in a specific mood to play this type of game. TDTM is a action-platformer, RPG and while fun, there is something that stops it from being great. I wish I could articulate my point better, but sometimes you just don’t know what you just don’t know.
