A common belief has arisen that suggests the industry can no longer support the development of mid-tier titles — that the middle has fallen out. All signs certainly seem to point to this conclusion.  Sometimes though, a game comes along that shakes off such insinuations, and shines a light on the potential of the middle.
Child of Light is one of the brightest examples — carving out a nook in the space between the Indie scene and the Triple-A arena. Many of the talented people at Ubisoft responsible for the development of Far Cry 3 were involved in the creation of Child of Light, and the same level of dedication to polish and quality shines through.
The narrative unfolds as one might expect; as if read by a parent to their child as they are tucked into bed. The tale begins with Aurora in eternal slumber — having laid her head upon her pillow, seemingly unable to ever again awake. As her father spends his days at her bedside you learn about the close connection between the two, and the despair that has gripped him — affecting his ability to rule the country. Aurora awakens to a more precarious scenario, trapped in a dream-like world alone, with only her wits to aid her.
From the stark contrast of light and shadow to the vibrant use of color amidst the backdrop of the pop-up storybook setting, the world of Lemuria feels warm and inviting. What I discovered upon awakening in the realm was a far more bleak and somber affair than I had expected though; a world of humor and light overtaken by darkness. That isn’t to say that the world is devoid of either. In fact, both are found in abundance throughout Aurora’s travels across the land.
While at first glance the game dons the facade of an average platformer, the mask is soon peeled back to reveal its true nature. As Aurora is bestowed with the gift of flight a sense of freedom and fluidity plucks the player out of the mundane, allowing them to effortlessly take to the sky — instilling a sense of liberty that, sadly, few games ever offer. With such a simple concept introduced, the game opens up into so much more.  The environmental puzzles are few and far between, and I found myself wishing there were more of them to tackle. A gust of wind here or a thorny labyrinth there offers up the occasional challenge as the player zips around the world. Sometimes an intriguing puzzle will prove more difficult a distraction, but ultimately serves as nothing more than a minor hindrance to progress.
In every corner of Lemuria, there are people in need assistance, dark creatures that need slaying, and caches of loot that need looting. Indeed, the inhabitants of Lemuria, choose curious and perplexing locations to store all their valuables, and Aurora and crew feel no compunction about liberating these artifacts from their hiding places. Most often, these items manifest as useful potions or permanent stat boosts. Because… well, video games.
Frequently, the player will come across precious stones known as Oculi. These stones form the basis of a simple yet effective crafting system. Through careful consideration, the combination of these varied Oculi can create larger, more powerful variants — each with useful passive effects.
Early in her journey, Aurora finds a spiritual guide of sorts in the spritely firefly, Igniculus. This indispensable little helper pledges his assistance to Aurora, and sticks by her side throughout most of the roughly twelve hours it will take to complete the game. Aside from fetching loot from chests that are just outside the player’s reach, and collecting orbs of restorative energy, Igniculus plays a vital role in combat. With the ability to blind opponents to slow their progress on the timeline, Igniculus’ utility proves second to none.
The combat in Child of Light is a masterfully crafted mish-mash of real time and turn-based elements that combine to form a battle system as robust as ever I’ve seen. Timing and forethought are the bread-winners here.  Each character awaits their turn as their icons move along a timeline. Once a character’s turn arrives, there is a brief casting period before the selected action is carried out. During this period, it is possible to be interrupted, and sent further back on the timeline, delaying the chance to act. There is an engrossing sense of tension as you combine the skills and abilities available to you to outwit the AI and maintain control of the battle. This is where Igniculus shines (pun intended). Using a limited pool of reserve energy, Igniculus can glow extra bright, blinding a chosen opponent, and slowing them to a crawl. He tends to run low on juice, so strategic use of this ability is prudent.
Along the way, Aurora is encountered by many a down-trodden individual in need of assistance, for which Aurora is more than willing to provide. In return, many of these upstanding citizens join in her struggle to rid the land of Umbra, the bringer of darkness. Each of these individuals has a distinct personality and offers up interesting bits of information that help to flesh out the world of Lemuria — albeit through rhyming wordplay that sometimes feels stilted and forced. In combat, these party members can be swapped out as frequently as the player chooses, and battles often call for such maneuvering. You will frequently make use of every single character in your gallery over the course of a given battle. From healing abilities to skills that manipulate the pace of the fight, each character feels useful, and functions with purpose.
That is really the common thread that runs through the entire battle system. Every skill and ability is impactful at the right moment. No skill feels superfluous, no ability feels like a waste of time, and every one of them will come in handy at some point. Each character progresses along a branching skill tree with a no muss, no fuss approach to picking and choosing between the assorted abilities. After just about every fight, one or more characters will gain another level, providing a sense of accomplishment with every victory. That said, it will likely take you until the end of a New Game + before you fully max out a character. This adds a fair amount of replay value, as in New Game +, the enemies are appropriately scaled to your level and you get to keep all of your items and upgrades.
Child of Light has reinvigorated a section of the industry in desperate need of shaking up. What’s more, the game has managed to raise my expectations for an entire genre. You never feel bogged down by the mechanics, and the combat system maintains its appeal from the first battle to the last. The mellow use of color and somber lighting set the mood, showcasing the power and narrative-driven experiences that the UbiArt engine can provide. The ability to fly opens the game up to a world of possibilities, and I found myself getting lost more often than not as I felt compelled to explore every nook and cranny. Between the complex cast of characters you meet along the way, the varied and immersive environments, and the intricately crafted combat system, Child of Light has raised the bar, and I look forward to diving back in.

Finally, a GoT game that is worthy of the brand.
The first episode starts off good, and gets even better as things go along. You have to make numerous choices that have a heavy effect on the storyline and the characters are quite interesting. House Forrester, while never in the show, certainly seem like an interesting house and I finished the first episode actually caring about them. In true GoT style, things go bad very quickly and you definitely get that vibe by the end of the first episode.
The graphics, whilst not amazing, do the job well. Voice acting is certainly good, though the actors from the show really steal the scenes they inhabit. The music is a mix of familiar GoT tracks with new ones that mix in well. Combined with a capable script and some great scenes, I was very entertained from start to finish. Ever wanted to go up against Cersie or Ramsay Bolton in an argument? This gives you that oportunity and it's great.
The first episode has a good story, some nice choices and even some surprises that suit GoT perfectly. I can't wait to see where they go with this next. As long as the episodes stick to this level of quality, this should be an awesome series to say the least.

In short, a decent but flawed game that is blatantly missing it's final act.  Where I had hoped to see what the Titan's Quest team had learned since then, and how they would evolve their game, instead nearly all of the flaws of TQ are faithfully reproduced here.
Thus, it's still a decent game, solidly executed and with (to a point) a strong plot; I'd recommend it to anyone who wants a second helping of TQ, and I'll add that to it's credit the classes each have a more dynamic and better balanced set of abilities, many of which give the player an option for them to either be spammable or larger/stronger on a reasonable cooldown, satisfying at least one issue I had with TQ.
I'd be on the fence with this rating were it not for the plot very, very clearly setting up an overarching conflict thoughout the entire game that it just doesn't conclude, and the "climax" of the game in resolving a secondary conflict itself being extremely underwhelming. There are even major faction questlines that seem to be missing their capstones, and overall I was very disappointed when the game just ran out more than it concluded.  Game design is hard, and the bespoke maps of the game can't be easy to create, yet I know that for the disappointment I felt I'd feel still more if I'd bought it on someone else's recommendation, and for this reason I just can't give it mine.

I wanted this for the co-op.  I love both RPGs and co-op, and this is a rare blend of the two.  I was expecting a pretty traditional Diablo 2-like experience, but what I've found is closer to the Dungeons and Dragons pencil and paper game.  And I mean that inin the best way.  There is more focus on story and exploration.  You are not just given a list of quests to complete.  Instead you keep track of different story lines and goings on in the world of Divinity.  Sometimes these story lines will draw you into quests or maybe tie into something you learned earlier.  There are plenty of classes and choices to make so that your chracters end up pretty unique.  Playing co-op and having a friend control the other main character is a joy.  It's fun to see the different interactions and the different outcomes from situations.  Seems like it has a lot of replay value, especially given the potential for mods.  I've played about 15  hours sp far and am loving it.  Recommended to D&D fans, RPG fans, and certainly co-op gamers who enjoy the role play genre.

The Banner Saga is probably one of the best games I've played in recent memory; the cast is made of characters who are dynamic enough to be difficult to explain in one sentence or trope, the aesthetics are a marvel for the eyes, and Austin Wintory's score for the game compliments the desolate nature of the game quite well.
It's also quite nice to see a strategy game where--for the most part--turns go back and forth, almost like a game of chess, instead of moving your entire army and dominating in one turn. Many of the choices presented to you throughout the story are legitimately hard decisions to make, and the possibility of losing party members or forsaking rewards makes you think about your options, and makes each run of this game a little more unique.
I do have my gripes with it though: some of the classes don't feel too unique from each other, special attacks aside, and for the most part, the story doesn't really branch out much. Your decisions do indeed affect immediate events, but you're still locked on the story progression the game wants you to take.
Don't let that be a turn-off, however. I've poured nearly 12 hours into this game, and I've enjoyed each one of them.
FINAL GRADE: A-
Highly recommended, but there's considerable room for improvement.

"Een Soviet Russia, girls scout YOU!" Yakov Smirnoff, 1980-something...
If you're into this kind of game, you'll probably enjoy it. I'm not a fan of this kind of stuff, but the unique setting/concept and price (FREE!) drew my interest. It's a typical anime-styled visual novel thing. Except that it's set in a Soviet Pioneer (their version of the Boy/Girl Scouts) camp.
Translation is a bit rough in spots, but you can always make out what was meant from the context. Most of it is translated correctly, sometimes it's just typos and words substituting for homonyms or words they're spelled like. Devs say they're working on the translation, I'll be that's going to take some volunteers some time. What they did really well is explain various Soviet/Russian cultural references.
Thing to know though, everything in this game is seen through the lens of one of those Japanese boarding schoool anime type shows/games. Rebellious girl gets chewed out by the camp leader for tying her her shirt up Daisy Duke-style, but every third character has her hair dyed blue, green or another unlikely-there-back-then color. Unless Hot Topic imported Manic Panic from East Germany after the wall came down...
I might have preferred a bit more feeling what it might have been like living in the Soviet Union at the time (and ya know, not have it be written by someone with an agenda). It actually does some of that a bit better than you might expect it to.

Johnny Graves - The Unchosen One is an early access title by developer Stupid Stupid Games. It’s an ARPG that's a bit light on both action and role-playing.
In Johnny Graves, I play as the titular character while he fights to fend off hell-demons from a 1979 era New York. In the early build of the game I am testing, the story starts off in a subway tunnel seconds after my train was run off the tracks by said monsters.
Trusty magic revolver by my side, I quickly memorized the controls before heading out into the level. However, the mechanics and design choices as I progressed through the game were far scarier than the any of the monsters I was encountering.
For starters, the combat in this game is not easy. That’s fine, I like a challenge. The developers even state that the game is made to be hard. What isn’t fine is that Johnny Graves’ difficulty doesn’t come from a challenging and smart a.i. with mechanics that I must slowly learn and eventually master. Instead, it comes from swarming enemies that I have no way of fending off, poorly designed top-down camera angles, and boss fights that drag on far too long without any forms of recovery to cushion them.
In order to damage enemies, I have to make sure my cursor is directly on them when firing. Johnny can’t move when firing, leaving me open to attack. This is a great mechanic that I would normally recommend the game stick with, however, it likes to take advantage of that handicap a bit too much.
Take the first boss fight for example. It starts off as a simple encounter designed to ease you into fighting tough enemies. The boss then begins to summon demonic dogs. These dogs are quick to dispose of, but the boss gets into the bottom half of the screen. Due to the unmovable top down camera, I am at a severe disadvantage. The UI blocks the bottom of the screen. By the time I can see an enemy coming at me, they are already in my face and I’m taking damage. All of the enemies move faster than me and eventually overwhelm.
This would all be balanced out with some sort of melee attack that pushes them back for a second, or even a quick dodge. Instead, the dodge I get now has a long cool down. Too long to justify how short the distance is as well as how quickly the enemies catch up to me.
Johnny Graves' boss fights are long and have no recovery items. Dying and knowing I have to endure that entire fight over again is a big blow to morale. There is also the strange omission of a mini-map or any form of letting me know where I am going. The levels are not too complex, but there are multiple paths that lead to dead-ends and such, or even ones that don’t look like the right way to go. Any form of direction would greatly benefit Johnny Graves.
There is a story to the game. It is similar to Devil May Cry in that there are two demon brothers. One uses his powers for good, and the other for bad. The dialogue is passable, yet very expository.
It’s strange to me that Johnny Graves is an ARPG. There is no stat or loot system, and the skills system is about as barebones as can be. My health bar never rises. My special attacks stay the same, and my gun hasn’t changed a bit since I started playing. I want to say a lot of these issues are just because the game is in Early Access, but according to the Steam page, this is 70% of the finished game. The full release is very soon, and I can’t imagine this game being very different in whenever that is. The issues at hand are far more than just a lack of polish.
Game length is also in question. I finished the content of the demo within 45 minutes on my first play-through. There was then an update with some new content. I played through again and it only took fifteen minutes longer than the first time due to the new level.
The experience isn’t all bad, though. Johnny Graves’ levels have a nice sheen to them, and the objects and textures are charming and fit well with the universe that Stupid Stupid Games is portraying. It’s just a shame that exploring those levels is more struggle than fun.
Johnny Graves - The Unchosen One is a great example of a game that needs another year or two in the oven. There is a decent foundation here, but none of the gameplay is particularly stand-out. Nothing in Johnny Graves is done better than other games in its genre, and I have a hard time imagining any of that will change come full release.

FTL is a game that covers every beautiful aspect of the gaming industry. The game is not too hard, but at the same time, not too easy. The random events gives different experiences on every journey, some good, and some bad. The game frustrates you at times, but at others it rewards you. The main mechanic that drives the game is the Permadeath feature. No saving the game and reloading it. There is no room for error in FTL, if you are destroyed becuase you didn't purchase better weapons, tough luck. It gives a feeling of individuality. When you are on the final sector of the game, you know this is it. One way or another, you'll never see your ship again, and it makes us feel sad for the poor crew. You have to manuever and plan out as the story progresses, or else you will be destroyed. Would I recommend it? Yes. I think it is one of the best Indie titles out there. With the new expansion, the game feels even more immersive then before. One of the best improvements was added customization, the fact that every journey would be even more different then before. I give this game a 9/10, one point deducted for the head-bashing boss, which I have only beaten once on easy.

A phenomenal RPG which is a blast to play.
If you're someone who likes to sink their teeth for hours into character development and narratives, buy this game.
The Good:
+  Well paced narrative, keeps the story from ever feeling like it's being dragged out.  SImilarly, the game has very little padding.
+ Rather than having a standard currency/treasure chest dependant system, occuli takes the place of equipment in the game.  These are essentially gems that can be equipped by any character in any gear slot which provide stat bonus' to the player.  The Occuli can also be crafted into stronger versions resulting in a very flexible system feels different, yet still succeeds in creating a thoughtful character developing process.
+ The Audio and Visual - An absolute marvel to experience.
The Bad:
- The Save Slots are primitive and near worthless.  You cannot delete, copy or even choose your save files whilst you play.  As the game can only auto-save, this means you cannot go back to an earlier point in your progress something which is almost a neccessity in a game which has irreversible character/item decisions.

After owning this game for over a year, I decided to finally speak up about my thoughts on it. Now, everyone and their newborns has sung the praises for Warband. The reason being that Warband is essentially a direct upgrade. Does that mean you should miss out on Mount & Blade? Well, yeah. Mount & Blade is obviously incredible in its own right, but every step it took forward, Warband took ten. If you already own Warband, I wouldn't imagine buying this game being a good decision moneywise. However, to people who don't own Warband- this games price tag can be a bit of an advantage. Its cheaper than its sequel, but lacks the multiplayer and mods that make it such a stellar experience. As much as it might seem, I absolutely can't hate this game. It drew me towards the series and I'm forever thankful for that. If you're given the choice, though, go for Warband. Mount & Blade is a singleplayer experience that will have strong bouts of fun in short bursts. Overall I would give it a 6/10 for how solid it is despite the far superiority its sequel has over it.
TL;DR - Good, but get warband instead if you can

I'd begin this brief review by saying that, considering the price point of this game, I would not recommend buying it unless it's on sale, or at least at half its current price, because it's really really short.
Besides that, it's a pretty entertaining title that I can compare to the likes of LIMBO and INSIDE, with the difference that "Little Nightmares" was published by Bandai, and, perhaps, that's the only reason of its current/release selling price; if you enjoyed those games, then, you'll like "Little Nightmares" as well, there's no doubt about that.
The game is a really simple platformer/scroller with no complications at all, you just have to guide your little character from one point to another, just exactly as you did in LIMBO, with only a few sections where you'll need to interact with the environment in order to proceed. Maybe due to its simplicity, they tried to compensate with a few hidden thingies that will help you get some Steam Achievements later on, but they do not affect at all your gameplay, you can ignore them completely.
I enjoyed the obscure, gloomy, dark atmosphere, but the sound effects diminished the ambience because, in my opinion, they're not on par with the rest of the game, I'd dare to say that the sound effects are even worse than those you find in an alpha, pre-release or even an early access game.

- Catchy.
- Entertaining.
- Atmospheric.
- Trippy.
CONS:
- Extremely short.
- Low audio quality.
- Soundtrack available only in MP3.
- Expensive (considering how short it is
and considering LIMBO and INSIDE release
price was less than half of what
"Little Nightmares" costs.

"Een Soviet Russia, girls scout YOU!" Yakov Smirnoff, 1980-something...
If you're into this kind of game, you'll probably enjoy it. I'm not a fan of this kind of stuff, but the unique setting/concept and price (FREE!) drew my interest. It's a typical anime-styled visual novel thing. Except that it's set in a Soviet Pioneer (their version of the Boy/Girl Scouts) camp.
Translation is a bit rough in spots, but you can always make out what was meant from the context. Most of it is translated correctly, sometimes it's just typos and words substituting for homonyms or words they're spelled like. Devs say they're working on the translation, I'll be that's going to take some volunteers some time. What they did really well is explain various Soviet/Russian cultural references.
Thing to know though, everything in this game is seen through the lens of one of those Japanese boarding schoool anime type shows/games. Rebellious girl gets chewed out by the camp leader for tying her her shirt up Daisy Duke-style, but every third character has her hair dyed blue, green or another unlikely-there-back-then color. Unless Hot Topic imported Manic Panic from East Germany after the wall came down...
I might have preferred a bit more feeling what it might have been like living in the Soviet Union at the time (and ya know, not have it be written by someone with an agenda). It actually does some of that a bit better than you might expect it to.

The Banner Saga is probably one of the best games I've played in recent memory; the cast is made of characters who are dynamic enough to be difficult to explain in one sentence or trope, the aesthetics are a marvel for the eyes, and Austin Wintory's score for the game compliments the desolate nature of the game quite well.
It's also quite nice to see a strategy game where--for the most part--turns go back and forth, almost like a game of chess, instead of moving your entire army and dominating in one turn. Many of the choices presented to you throughout the story are legitimately hard decisions to make, and the possibility of losing party members or forsaking rewards makes you think about your options, and makes each run of this game a little more unique.
I do have my gripes with it though: some of the classes don't feel too unique from each other, special attacks aside, and for the most part, the story doesn't really branch out much. Your decisions do indeed affect immediate events, but you're still locked on the story progression the game wants you to take.
Don't let that be a turn-off, however. I've poured nearly 12 hours into this game, and I've enjoyed each one of them.
FINAL GRADE: A-
Highly recommended, but there's considerable room for improvement.

UPDATE June 2017: My original review was written when the game first hit EA over an year ago, and
. It is my understanding that the game has now been completed and its price lowered significantly. I hope to update this review in the future, time permitting, but for now please regard my original review as an historical document only.
----
Johnny Graves—The Unchosen One is a horror themed 3D top down action shooter currently in Early Access. The Early Access part is quite crucial, as what is on offer so far is pretty bare bones. Content wise there is one playable level that can be completed in some few tense minutes, and there is little reason to come back to it once you're done.
At first glance, this looks like a game in the style of classic ARPGs, but there are currently no progression mechanics that are commonly associated with RPGs here - that means there are no experience points to be gained nor leveling of any kind. Combat, however, is not mindless left clicking, but somewhat tactical, albeit simplistic in nature. The character has one conventional attack (an aimed shot from his revolver) and one special attack resembling something of a magic bullet that bounces from one enemy to the other, taking down multiple foes in succession. Aiming is done with the mouse and is completely manual, and your revolver must be reloaded every six shots. In contrast with a more traditional ARPG style of combat, you cannot shoot and move at the same time which can cause some tension. It is easy to get swamped by enemies if you are not careful, as the latter tend to spawn in groups and move in on you fast. In practice you will be running away from mobs of zombies a lot while reloading and waiting for your special attack meter to recharge so that you can take them down before they reach you. In a way, the combat is closer to Resident Evil than Diablo due to this rather basic shoot-and-run-dynamic, and because you control the character's movement directly with WASD keys. Failing a more diverse skill system, some other means of crowd control or maybe a melee option would have been welcome here. Add to this that there is no incentive to kill foes at all apart from ensuring your survival and progressing through the level. As mentioned above, enemies do not give XP when killed nor drop loot, so your best course of action is to just sneak your way around them, situation permitting. (Your guy can also jump if need be). Ammunition is unlimited, however, so the game feels far from survival horror despite the squishiness of your character.
Speaking of which, your character's health bar is tiered and will regenerate by itself up to the last tier it fell down to after receiving damage. Melee attacks by zombies will whittle you down quickly, but fireballs and the few chemical zombies you encounter can have an even more adverse effect on your well-being. The fire is courtesy of giant tree dwelling spiders that will attack you off screen and remain aggravatingly out of sight until you draw in close. Chances are you will die when you encounter these spiders for the first time, meaning you will have to restart the level from the beginning. For an admittedly short level this isn't the end of the world, but I found dying and having to go back to square one pretty annoying. Maybe a checkpoint system would have alleviated this.
The environment in general and the level design, while serviceable, weren't really noteworthy and it seemed I was missing some environmental effects even on max settings (e.g., swaying grass seen in the trailer - I ran the game on an AMD R9 290). The cemetery had a lot of open graves for example, with some of them emitting a yellow glow, but there was no reason to investigate further or explore, as there were no secrets to be found or anything else of interest there. There are some nice details and touches in the scenery, but as a whole I found the level a little bland. A bright point is the writing, however, which was witty and spirited, although the extent of it was a few lines of introductory exposition and some banter between the protagonist Johnny and a second character. I hope we will get to see much more of the writing and story as development progresses.
I received this game for free in a giveaway, but I feel that for the price that is being asked here, there could and should have been a lot more in regards to content, even in full consideration of its Early Access status. It is for this reason that I cannot in good conscience recommend this game in its current state. There are demos out there for other games that easily offer much more content and replay value than this. That said, the premise of the characters is intriguing and the writing (what little of it was on show, at least) is of a high standard, so I remain cautiously optimistic. If the developers put in the hours it is possible that this game will shine, but judging from what is on display so far it will take some considerable work to get there.

I truly enjoy ACE Team's games. Their art-style and game design are artistic marvels. Their choice to make a game about a director commentating over a low budget Scifi movie for DVD release was fantastic. Enemies had strings, they clearly looked fake or were puppets, and animated in a way that resembled old stop motion animation techniques of the early days of film. Hilarity ensued and I felt the need for Hollywood to go back to these and make something similar. I actually want a modern-day, low budget(visually at least), scifi movie like this now.
Though, if you are expecting something with a little more depth like their previous game Abyss Odyssey then you will be a little disappointed. I try to stretch game length by taking my time, but I finished this in 4hrs and it was no challenge at all. Weapons were given to you seemingly out of order. I got a rocket launcher half-way through the game and it one-hit nearly everything as well as slight splash damage. But its easy natured gameplay kind of fits the setting and style. I guess  this is more of a personal pet-peeve as I was looking for something a little more in-depth.
Ultimately this was a fun and creative game, albiet short. Keep up the great work ACE Team.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Johnny Graves - The Unchosen One is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was the latest as of the date of this review.
According to the information on the Steam page for this game, Johnny Graves is an action RPG and the first game in a planned trilogy of games set in an original urban fantasy / horror setting called the Night of the Creatures.
In Johnny Graves you play Johnny, a former agent of hell with a psychic link to Ivy, a woman who offers advice and assistance in your quest. Your quest itself, it seems, is to rescue someone called Paddy, but this is unclear: in its current state, the game doesn't provide any introduction or background information at all, so it's hard to work out just what the plot of the final product will be. The Steam page offers considerably more information on the game world.
Graphics - The 3D graphics are a mixed bag. Most of the environmental graphics are very nice, if touch heavy on the browns and greys. Character and zombie graphics are rather blocky, though well animated. The dynamic lighting and shadows are excellent. Exploding zombies look terrible when they explode, and the fire from the fire-spitting spiders (WTF?) is not wonderfully convincing either, but it's passable. There's no separate torso turn animation, so Johnny's gun does not follow the crosshairs used to aim.
Given that the game is essentially an action game, it also seems to be missing some visual indicators of damage, as well. Without the sound effects it's impossible to know whether a zombie is hitting Johnny or not, and Johnny's gunshots only make a very unsatisfying temporary spray of red pixels that are presumably supposed to be blood. Killed zombies collapse like ragdolls (which is cool), without any visible effects of multiple gunshot wounds (which is not cool). The graphics give no real 'feel' of taking or dishing out damage.
The game so far features a couple of conversations between Johnny and Ivy, and these include quite good 2D character portrait overlays, which is a nice touch.
Standard Unity graphics options are provided in the launcher: resolution, full screen / window, and a graphics quality drop-down allowing a selection between Fastest and Beautiful. I played in 1920x1080 in Beautiful and the game mostly performed well, although some of the larger scrolling sections had noticeable tearing. A vsync option might be effective here.
Sound - Johnny Graves features a well-produced and suitably spooky music track in the background, but so far there's only the one. Sounds, too, are limited: a grunt when Johnny is hit and a very loud gunshot when he shoots were all that I heard, I think.
At present the lack of ambient environmental, movement, and enemy sounds makes the game feel rather empty.
Gameplay - Although the Steam page claims that Johnny Graves is an "action RPG", I currently see no evidence of the RPG part; instead it plays like a fairly standard isometric third-person shooter that I suspect may end up including some platforming elements (given the inclusion of a jump control).
You move Johnny around with WASD and independently move his pistol crosshairs and shoot with the mouse. With a controller I can see that this could be controlled like a typical twin-stick shooter, although given the speed of movement of the zombies included in the game so far, I suspect the added precision of the mouse might be required.
The game is currently VERY short and only includes one level. After finishing this level (which should take around 20 minutes), you're shown a brief message that this is only level one out of seven, and level two will be released "in the summer 2016". As mentioned previously, there's also no introduction or background story provided. You're dumped from the main menu into a graveyard, Johnny and Ivy exchange some banter that doesn't make a whole lot of sense without understanding why Johnny is there, or who Ivy is, and then you start walking through the graveyard and killing zombies. According to the Steam page, there is a fairly clear plan for the rest of the content that will be included gradually as the game goes through Early Access. In its current state, though, it's barely a taste.
The in-game text conversations between Johnny and Ivy are well written so far, with mostly good grammar. I hope the final game includes more of these (with a bit of editing), as they really add some interest to the game.
In its current state, Johnny Graves also has a number of issues that make it a bit clunky to play. The worst of these is that there's no way to rotate the view; camera control is automatic, and often not ideal. Even in this short demo level I found myself being beset by enemies from very close by off one edge of the screen, and with no way to rotate the view to move a tree out of the way of the camera, I couldn't see them until they were on top of Johnny. There's also no zoom, which is a bit sad, but nowhere near as important as the missing manual camera rotation. Finally, it's very easy to get stuck in open graves, requiring frustrating jumps to get out, or up against a lamppost or other environmental object, making positioning Johnny in the heat of battle much more frustrating than it should be.
Pros:
+ Original modern horror / fantasy setting that could be quite interesting: demons, spiders, zombies, and guns
+ Existing level has nice atmospheric graphics and excellent lighting and shadows
+ Good music
+ Clear plan for Early Access progression
Cons:
- No introduction, so although the story seems like it could be interesting, it's hard to tell
- VERY short at the moment: I died once and it still only took me 27 minutes to get through the current single level
- Some clunkiness: it's easy to get stuck on level geometry, making the game more frustrating than it should be
- Character graphics are quite blocky and small, although well animated
- Bland character and enemy textures
- Very few sounds
- No way to manually zoom (minor) or rotate (major) the view; automated camera positioning is not always ideal
Johnny Graves - The Unchosen One has the potential to be a very fun game. It's not there yet -- it needs some work on the core gameplay and the developers need to finish their planned roadmap for the game -- but it's on the way.
As it stands at the moment, it's more of a demo than a game, and most definitely doesn't pass my personal value test at its current price point. But it is an Early Access title by developers with a clear plan, and I think that's worth a chance. I'd love a "maybe" button in Steam; I'm hesitant in recommending it now, but I'd expect that recommendation to get considerably stronger over the coming months as the game matures.

This game is like every playset I ever had as a kid brought to campy, awesome life. I loved the narrator, and the idea that it was actually a movie ... that is the kind of thing that makes a game memorable to me, far more than the action and the gameplay.
The constantly panning camera, both while playing and at the cutscenes, give it a panoramic feel, and keep you constantly in the action.  I also love the way the cutscenes bounce in and out of the action - remarkably well done, and the switch between preset animations and the gameplay really highlight the incredible graphics.
I am very much an atmospheric gamer - I love to immerse myself in a world, and ideally one that puts neat imagery in my head, and this game is doing a phenomenal job.
The action and gameplay in this are also great fun, with a different mix and match of tasks to keep it interesting.  I can't wait to see what new and insane monsters I get to fight next.
Playing this game has convinced me to take a close look at all the games done by the studio.

This game is a lot of fun. It's a bunch of decent, solid gameplay that's really elevated by the concept and storytelling.
The plot device here is that you're watching a modern re-issue of a 60s/70s 'B' Sci-Fi movie, with the director's commentary turned on. (You're controlling the leads of the movie.)
It's very campy sci-fi. You can see strings on the spaceships, the monsters are designed to look like they're classic practical effects, from dudes in rubber masks to claymation monsters. There's also optional post-processing for both the Audio and Video, allowing you to make the game look, or sound like an old VHS tape.
It's not too long, so if you have some kind of silly $ to hours ratio you want to keep, you might want to get it on sale, but I think this game's worth the price as-is. That, and I want ACE Team to keep making interesting games. :)

TL:DR at the bottom.
You ever have those moments where you buy a game, play it for a couple of hours and then feel the need to call up some of your friends and tell them how amazing the new game you bought was?
This is what Child of Light was for me. At its core, the game is essentially a fairy tale with classical turn based combat. However, its so much more than just these broad descriptions.
The story is well written, every piece of dialogue is written in a rhyming format, which really adds to the feel that the story is a fairy tale. The characters are all colorful and the people you meet are usually interesting.
The art style is gorgeous. It looks like like a story from a picture book, which only compliments everything ubisoft was going for. The places you see will give you reason to pause for a moment and take in the sights. The music (which is REALLY good) helps elevate each area/event from just a picture on the screen to a feeling.
The story itself makes you feel good, and reminds me alot of a disney movie. I actually had an inner-princess (no homo) moment when the plot twist happened. The story won't be revolutionary like mass effect or other games with awesome stories, but its well above average in terms of story and it gives you a good incentive to keep playing to see how it all pans out.
So now that i’ve established that the game looks awesome, sounds awesome, and has a good story, lets get into some more details.
The combat at first is pretty standard final fantasy-esq turn based combat. However, there is a twist. Rather than wait for an ATB to fill up, you need to actively pay attention to the battle. For example, you have a little companion that doesn’t take up a party slot. He floats around each battle and you control him using the right analogue (or the mouse I think). His purpose is two fold. He can either heal you, or slow the ATB bar one monster your fighting (as long as he has the “power” to do so).
In addition to him, the ATB bar is made more interesting by the fact that every move (even standard “attack”) has a cast time. If you are hit in this cast time, or if enemies are hit in their cast time (different moves have different cast times) you will be pushed back on your ATB bar and you won’t perform the attack. This adds a fresh layer to a very old and refined combat style, and often times, depending on how many enemies you're fighting will make regular fights difficult.
If you love perfecting characters or customizing them, then Child of Light has that too. Rather than purchasing different armors or swords, you equip gemstones which you find throughout the world of Lemuria. Exploring will reward you with multiple gems, which you can then combine or mix and match with other gems to create better gems. Ie, Find 3 ruby shards, created one tumbled ruby, so on and so forth, which each iteration becoming more powerful than its predecessor. The crafting alone in this game had me search nearly every nook and cranny for materials, as if wanting to see every bit of art this game had to offer wasn’t incentive enough.
My only complain about the game (having finally completed it) is that it feels too short. I got 20 hours out of it in one playthrough with a fair bit of exploration. They do have a new game plus feature, which I have dabbled with before writing my review, but I feel like i’d rather pay 19.99 for an extra few dungeons or end game content.
So TL;DR
my advice to you, is if you love rpgs, turn based combat, engaging enviroments and feel good games (because this game will make you feel good) then buy this game, its WELL worth the 14.99 they charge, (imo itd be worth 30 or more if it had a bit more content). Buy it, enjoy the story and the tight gameplay. Then feel free to thank me later;)

South Park holds a special place in my heart (and in my DVD shelf). I have been watching it for years. There are good episodes and there are bad episodes but mostly the entire series is good. So now they decided to make a game on this series. The best part of this is that Trey Parker and Matt Stone were actually part of making the game. It wasn’t just a random fighting game with a South Park paintjob and brand.
The entire game is around 16h for the main storyline and the side missions but it can go up to 20h if you want to find all the Chinpokomon, kindergarteners and hobos.  A 30€ game (7.50€ if on sale) which delivers 16h worth of South Park episodes is pretty good if you ask me.
I don’t want to spoil the plot because it is so random and so damn good but I will say this: The plot feels like multiple South Park episodes taped together, which is good for the most part. Some parts are a little more tacked on than others but they are still good. They just don’t fit in nicely.
The combat is fun but becomes repetitive after you find the correct combinations of attacks and the most powerful weapons. Most of the bosses are just enemies with ten times the HP. Just a grindfest. Most of the weapons are just direct upgrades to the last one and I only had a few moments when I was thinking “Which one of these weapons would be the best in this situation?”.
Some sections, like the battery part in Mr. Slave’s♥♥♥♥♥was really hard to figure out. I didn’t have Stan with me and the buddies didn’t give me any sign that they could help, like most other parts like it.
The humour is spot on. The customization is good. The voice acting is great.
If  you don’t like South Park, then you should propably skip this one but if you do, then this is a must have.

If you aren't instantly captivated by the truely beautiful watercolour artwork; the wonderful, peaceful background music; or the soft motherly voice that narrates cutscenes throughout the game in just the trailer - then the carefully crafted and moving storyline behind a young princesss, Aurora, as she tries to reclaim her kingdom of Lemuria and return home to save her people from a disastrous flood certainly will.
Two dimensional platformer with stunning parallax graphics. Easy to move around at a decent rate, especially once you unlock the ability to fly (which is fairly early on). All text within this game is in some form of poem, usually a rhyme. This game involves a little problem solving, many secret areas  and a ton of fun. The game uses powerful stones called Oculi to provide aditional effects to a characters health, defense and offense which are customisable for all party members at any time except during battle and cutscenes. There are eleven different oculi with their own individual effect depending on where they are applied; nine of which have four tiers of power at varying levels. (Eren's Stone can only be accessed through the purchase of a DLC and the Princess Stone is the most powerful of all and can be crafted with a Brilliant (tier 4) Diamond, Onyx and Spinel.) There are about 52 individual crafting recipies (most are repetitive among different tiers of oculi). One can also acquire and use Stardusts for permanent effects to a character's statistics. Local co-op and controller support.
Combat is turn-based... with a twist. It involves a timeline. Depending on the character's speed, they move down the timeline at different rates (this can be effected by spells, potions or Igniculus - her first companion, controlled by mouse if you are using a keyboard; also known as 'Sir Firefly'). Upon reaching the begining of the casting region near the end, a spell, potion, defense or attack can be chosen (or you can switch party members) with a length of either instant, short, medium, long or very long casting time; which is cast if the character reaches the end of the timeline without being interrupted. Although it is fairly easy to guess based on the colour of the enemy: it doesn't actually tell you what you are fighting nor what element it is. Fire(red) magic/creatures are weak to Water(blue); Water to Lightning(green); Lightning to Fire; and Dark(Varies - usually black, occasionally white) to Light. Fairly easy to level up the same old classic RPG style with several different skill trees for each party member all leading to different  or more powerful abilities.
Although the storyline is good, it's not particulary in-depth. There are many mysterious clues that are seemingly never properly explained. It's a very straight storyline, with no user input and nothing to do after the game is completed. There are several sidequests, most very short and easy to do that lead to extra treasure. To be entirely honest though; although I like the freedom of choice, this game has been made with such precision and care that I don't even mind.
I would definitely recommend this game. It has become one of my all-time-favourites. Sadly, I have finished it now however I enjoyed it so much that I will likely return to play it again several times over in the following years. Personally, the biggest disappointment for me is that there are no Steam cards, badges, achievements, emoticons or really awesome artwork that I can use as my Steam profile background (the latter being my biggest grievance).

For many of my generation, "XCOM: UFO Defense/UFO: Enemy Unknown" is the penultimate strategy game, or at least among the best of what the '90 had to offer. So it's understandable that we were more than wary when Firaxis and 2K Games decided to reboot the franchise and update it to the 21st century. Would it live up to the grandfather of turn-based squad combat?
The answer is yes, it does. XCOM is still the same old game. Small tweaks and adjustments are made to controls and gameplay and the main focus is clearly more on the turn-based combat while the base-building, researching, building new tools and toys, equipping of teams and so forth is mainly done while "waiting for alarms". Although the game in general has been quite streamlined (to the dismay of many fans) the fact is, that it's all for the better. XCOM is, in it's current form, a game that's really easy to handle, understand and play, but damn hard to master.
Just when you think you have it all under control and it becomes average, you get thrown into a desperate survival situation that you grit your teeth at for hours and suddenly you realize you are the underdog and you have to fight to survive. And isn't that what makes the great games so great?

South Park holds a special place in my heart (and in my DVD shelf). I have been watching it for years. There are good episodes and there are bad episodes but mostly the entire series is good. So now they decided to make a game on this series. The best part of this is that Trey Parker and Matt Stone were actually part of making the game. It wasn’t just a random fighting game with a South Park paintjob and brand.
The entire game is around 16h for the main storyline and the side missions but it can go up to 20h if you want to find all the Chinpokomon, kindergarteners and hobos.  A 30€ game (7.50€ if on sale) which delivers 16h worth of South Park episodes is pretty good if you ask me.
I don’t want to spoil the plot because it is so random and so damn good but I will say this: The plot feels like multiple South Park episodes taped together, which is good for the most part. Some parts are a little more tacked on than others but they are still good. They just don’t fit in nicely.
The combat is fun but becomes repetitive after you find the correct combinations of attacks and the most powerful weapons. Most of the bosses are just enemies with ten times the HP. Just a grindfest. Most of the weapons are just direct upgrades to the last one and I only had a few moments when I was thinking “Which one of these weapons would be the best in this situation?”.
Some sections, like the battery part in Mr. Slave’s♥♥♥♥♥was really hard to figure out. I didn’t have Stan with me and the buddies didn’t give me any sign that they could help, like most other parts like it.
The humour is spot on. The customization is good. The voice acting is great.
If  you don’t like South Park, then you should propably skip this one but if you do, then this is a must have.

This is kind of a dead game once Warband came out. Honestly, just get Warband. It's the same game with improved mechanics. There were some issues with the original that were smoothed out there. Example are the horses during charges.
With that being said, if you purchase this game, you will not be disapointed. It has a historic setting with real factions, kings, Jarls, etc. The graphics are not the best. This isn't a call of duty or battlefield, don't expect it to be.
Ever want to be a soldier, a lord, or even a king/queen? Here you go. You recruit an army, raise it, level it, and choose what kind of an army it will be. Want an army full of archers or crossbowmen? Go for it. Or, do you have a passion for the pagan at heart? Than command your army of Nord Huskarls in to battle. It's a game of strategy along with you command your character in to battle with your troops.
If you've ever played Kessen, this is kind of like it except remove the feel of turn base aspect in a way. Instead of turn base, when you stop in the map, the game pauses. Once in battle though you can choose to just tell your troops what to do or get involved yourself. Choice is yours.
For beginners, it may look like dynasty warriors but don't just rush in lol. It's not how that works here, that's not how any of that works. This game is where you go when you graduate Dyanasty Warriors.
Pros:
- Character Customization
- RPG style leveling
- Troop customization (troop type, not look)
- Troop leveling based on usage
- Quests
- No real need to do the quests if you don't want
- Be a bandit
- Be a lord
- Be a ruler (harder than it may seem. All fun and games until the world declares war on you)
- Trading (you can live your life here as a merchant trader without ever joining a faction)
- Trading (you can either do the normal every day trading OR you can be a manhunterish that takes prisoner of bandits or even villagers and sells them to slave traders or ransom brokers. Slave traders don't care who you sell, ransom brokers are similar but give more money).
Cons:
- Horse mechanics a little screwy but nothing game breaking.
- Warband is out (Do yourself a favor, all this is in warband plus more for about the same price)
- Graphics. Not a con but considering Viking conquests animations, this one is a bit outdated now
As a side note that can be considered either a pro or con. It can be difficult to get started. If you like a small challenge, awesome because there will be a learning curve initially. Not a huge one but it's there. Expect to be taken prisoner a few times before you learn your lesson and expect to forget that lesson and do it all over again a few times lol.
Mount and Blade: Warband (Mount and Blade, the better version)
Mount and Blade: Viking Conquest (Latest expansion. More difficult, larger battles, more mechanics, new factions, Pagan and Christain subfaction mechanic)
There are two others as well but they are not like the previous three. Fire and Sword brings you to the polish commonweath during the days of muskets. Napoleonic is a multiplayer and custom battle only expansion during the French Revolution.

After playing through the entire game and doing most of the side content, I'm still torn. I can't recommend it in good conscience however.
Gameplay: The combat feels like a classic JRPG but with some real-time elements that allow you to control a secondary character (or let someone else use the mouse to do so). This guy can collect healing objects for you, or even slow down your enemies on the timeline which is incredibly useful and adds a new dynamic to trying to interrupt your enemies. Overall I enjoyed the classic combat. My one major gripe is that you only ever can have 2 of your party members out at a time, which seems absurd to me. Especially since your enemies routinely have 3.
Art: You can't say enough about the art style. It's got a brilliant storybook feel that is woven throughout the story as well. The color palette and style is bold and refreshing. Animation leaves a lot to be desired however, as they all look more like paper cutouts hanging from strings.
Story/Writing: This is what ruins the game for me. The story is hopelessly childish and unoriginal, which leaves me wondering what the target audience is. I do realize that this matches the visual style, but there must be ways to achieve a story that is appealing to adults while maintaining the whimsical visuals. Things like Trine 2 or Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons did this wonderfully. Overall the story was sickeningly saccharine. In contrast, Brothers started out extremely fanciful, but quick got dark and serious in it's themes. They're both coming-of-age tales, but Brothers pulled it off in a much more brilliant and emotional way (and without words, yet!). In Child of Light, you'll never care about any of the characters. Speaking of words, I must say a few about the poetry. I feel as if the poetry could have saved the hokey story. However, the poetry was dreadful. The writers made no attempt to compose with any meter or rhythm, but instead stuck stubbornly to their A-B-A-B rhyme scheme regardless of the cadence of the sentences. Shakespeare is rolling in his grave. I love great poetry when it has a solid rhythm and bounce to it (See Penny Arcade's Twisp and Catsby stuff!), but this sounded more like a junior high student writing poetry for the first time. Even the rhymes were a stretch from time to time, and left you gagging or saying "oh come on, really?!".
In conclusion, I give this a "NO" with a very heavy heart. I wanted to like it so bad. There were parts of it I really enjoyed. But I found myself rushing from battle to battle in order to enjoy the combat, while the story left me wanting. I don't mind a good kid's story. But this wasn't just a kid's story, it was downright childish and lame. If you think the beautiful art and great combat can redeem an ignorable story, then maybe give this a try. But for me, it wasn't worth the 10 hours.

Deadly Tower of monsters is classic ACE Team: unique style, different genre from their previous effort and just surprising.
The game is a top-down shooter/brawler/platformer with RPG elements (it features weapon upgrades and character levelling, albeit with meager skills to choose from) presented as a B-movie from the 70s that's being re-released as a DVD. The director is providing audio commentary throughout, often hilarious, reminding me of Cave Johnson from Portal 2.
All enemies and setpieces are true to the B-movie style: Slow moving stop-motion monsters and people clearly in costumes, sometimes with strings visible. Many different monster types keep the game fresh over its arguably short running time (5 hours, which would be quite long for a movie). However, the game does not outstay it's welcome and I personally like shorter games that don't need to pad their running time out and drag on.
To summarize: the combat is satisfying, the artstyle is vibrant and pretty, the music is awesome, the voice acting really adds to it, and the game's just fun.

The game is a
2D side scrolling brawler. You have two buttons: [L] Left-Attack and [R] Right-Attack. If enemies come from the left, you hit Left-Attack, if they come from the right you hit Right-Attack. The most common enemy will die in one hit, but other enemies require different combinations of [L] or [R] to defeat. For example the German officer requires you to hit him twice; the blonde girls in white require you to hit them three times in an alternating fashion (From left [L][R][L], from right [R][L][R]).
As for controls you have the choice of using the keyboard keys [A]/[D], or [<-][->], or mouse left-click/right-click. Controllers are also supported, with all the buttons on the left bound to left attack, and all the right buttons bound to right attack. You cannot rebind the keys as there is no options menu.
Kung Fury is a hyper-stylized 2D side-scroller with an older 1980s pixelated art-style. The viewing area of the game is presented like an old arcade cabinet with a non-flat CRT monitor. The presentation of the game is meant to match the theme of the movie, so if you didn't like the movie or the old CRT look then chances are you won't like the game itself.
Go watch the
.
The game itself does not have a story, but in order to appreciate this game I recommend watching the movie. It's FREE!
As a side note the game is based on one particular fight scene in the movie, where Kung Fury fights from right to left (side scrolling).
There is no options menu. You cannot rebind your keys (though there are a fair amount of default bindings to choose from), and you cannot change your resolution or anything else. The game defaults to fullscreen, but you can change it to window mode by pressing [ALT]+[ENTER]. This is sparse to say the least, and if you are particularly sensitive to missing features such as an options menu, then don't waste your time.

The Deadly Towers of Monsters:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Gravoria is a very mysterious planet with all sorts of inhabitants, from robots to dinosaurs. Well this is just the start, as our hero and space explorer,♥♥♥♥♥♥Starspeed, and his faithful robot co-pilot will find out upon crash landing their spacecraft on its surface.
The Deadly Towers of Monsters is an adventure / isometric action shooter which takes place on a planet called Gravoria. As you start the game, you will be playing♥♥♥♥♥♥Starspped but as go along, you will meet the gorgeous Scarlet Nova, your tin can co-pilot, and be able to swap between characters when you reach some of the checkpoints. Each of the characters has its own special abilities and they will sometimes determine your progression to the next scene of the movie.
The plot is fairly simple; Scarlet will need your help to overthrown her evil father, the Emperor of Gravoria.  You will have to climb this very odd tower and fight against fun enemies: monkeys, dinosaurs (at the bottom of the tower), invisible men (apparently these actors are very cheap to hire), squids, brain flying sauces, aliens and more. Along the way, you will pick up weapons and will be able to upgrade them too. I have to be honest with you, Ladies and Gents, this game took me by surprise and I tremendously enjoyed the commentary of Dan Smith… He made me laugh several times during the gameplay and I consequently died on every one of these occasions. I really like his style, just brilliant! I can see people saying they may not like this type of in-game commentary but for me it really make the game so much fun.
Graphically the game looks great, the game runs very well and the controls are easy to master. I really like the B movie atmosphere and the soundtrack.

Little Nightmares is a horror-platformer-puzzle game focused around Six, a little girl trying to escape a vessel known as "The Maw". It's quite a short game, I beat it in 3.2 hours in my blind first playthrough so definitely take that into consideration as you might want to wait for a price drop before picking this up.
The story is told through visuals and imagery, a la INSIDE and LIMBO, without any dialogue besides the screams and wails of those you're running away from. This creates a loose narrative that if you pay attention tells you what is happening on The Maw, but the how's and why's of this are down to your interpretation and theorizing.
The gameplay is your standard 3D platformer affair. You can move in all directions, sprint, jump, crouch and grab items to move them or grab edges to climb them. The controls are good enough. They could be a little more responsive but they never caused any problems for me during play. Similar to the likes of Outlast you can't do anything to directly fight back against the creatures you go up against, although your tiny size allows you to hide under tables and in compartments to escape these creatures. Unfortunately the puzzles are all easy and you'll never need to dedicate any more than, say, 3 minutes (if even that) to solving them.
The sound is fantastic. The soundtrack is very good even if it's not very memorable. The creaks and ambient noises of The Maw crawl under your skin in just the right way. Little Nightmares never goes for big jumpscares but for an under-the-skin kind of terror that is constantly lingering throughout the entire game with atmosphere so thick you could cut it with a knife. Nightmarish is the perfect way to describe the enemies you encounter. Everything from their appearance, to the way they move, to the sounds they make all feel like they've been pulled right out of a child's night terrors. And the artistic design of The Maw itself compliments these enemies perfectly with it's dank, murky structure. All of these combine to create an art style that fully embraces, embodies and screams 'Nightmares'.
Overall this is a fantastic atmospheric horror experience and must-own for fans of under-the-skin horror or immersive single-player experiences.

As of writing, it took me 5.2 hours to beat this game, but I have yet to 100% the game!
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. Although many compare it to Inside and Limbo, the game lacks that ultra-hardcore charm of "die to figure out the puzzle". Most of my deaths were due to failing with the controls at jumps or falling from heights, or because I couldn't figure out the puzzle in time. The story and art style is great - I find the visual horror of the enemies a bit goofy but there's definitely some unexpected spooks to be had.
The game also makes creative use of backtracking - while normally that would be a waste of time, there's always something unexpected on the second runthrough.
Controls are a mixed bag, after struggling with mouse and keyboard on a segment that required rapidly changing between 2 diagonal motions to dodge, I switched to a controller...and then probably struggled more because of relearning controls :/
Another thing are the checkpoints. The checkpoints are UNCLEAR. Some of them are near lamps the player can light, other times they are somewhere??? Some of them are right at the start of chase scenes which is convenient I guess.
Finally, bugs. I've had some wonky moments where I can't tell why the AI can see me, as well as getting stuck once or twice due to throwing physics objects the wrong way. ALSO, the player ducks under some movable/climbable objects, which blocks jumping and can ruin a critical move if you jump too late onto a ledge.

After playing through the entire game and doing most of the side content, I'm still torn. I can't recommend it in good conscience however.
Gameplay: The combat feels like a classic JRPG but with some real-time elements that allow you to control a secondary character (or let someone else use the mouse to do so). This guy can collect healing objects for you, or even slow down your enemies on the timeline which is incredibly useful and adds a new dynamic to trying to interrupt your enemies. Overall I enjoyed the classic combat. My one major gripe is that you only ever can have 2 of your party members out at a time, which seems absurd to me. Especially since your enemies routinely have 3.
Art: You can't say enough about the art style. It's got a brilliant storybook feel that is woven throughout the story as well. The color palette and style is bold and refreshing. Animation leaves a lot to be desired however, as they all look more like paper cutouts hanging from strings.
Story/Writing: This is what ruins the game for me. The story is hopelessly childish and unoriginal, which leaves me wondering what the target audience is. I do realize that this matches the visual style, but there must be ways to achieve a story that is appealing to adults while maintaining the whimsical visuals. Things like Trine 2 or Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons did this wonderfully. Overall the story was sickeningly saccharine. In contrast, Brothers started out extremely fanciful, but quick got dark and serious in it's themes. They're both coming-of-age tales, but Brothers pulled it off in a much more brilliant and emotional way (and without words, yet!). In Child of Light, you'll never care about any of the characters. Speaking of words, I must say a few about the poetry. I feel as if the poetry could have saved the hokey story. However, the poetry was dreadful. The writers made no attempt to compose with any meter or rhythm, but instead stuck stubbornly to their A-B-A-B rhyme scheme regardless of the cadence of the sentences. Shakespeare is rolling in his grave. I love great poetry when it has a solid rhythm and bounce to it (See Penny Arcade's Twisp and Catsby stuff!), but this sounded more like a junior high student writing poetry for the first time. So, right off the bat, when I tried to initially play the game it would not open or give me any information as to why it would not open, and all of the guides to fix the problem from the techland support team (the official support team for the game) failed (despite these problems occuring from as early as January, if my memory serves me correctly, according to the numerous posts that have been written. I finally find a bootleg fix from someone that wasn't even the techland support team and play the game.
The game is definitely innovative, and it should have been really fun if it wasn't for the numerous problems it has. It barely gives you any information despite that the information needed is crucial for proceeding in the game. Te game features such as grappling and jumping over enemies, etc. are extremely unreliable, thus making features in the game that should be enjoyable, and fun innovative ways to survive and kill enemies purely frustrating since attempting to try and use any of these features can easily kill you and set you back heavily.
Going back to the lack of information, a high majority of the information you have to stumble upon for yourself since there is no indication it is even there, and the information you do find seems like onloy half is given. I honestly could go on about the flaws of the combat system, but I think this is more than enough.

Mount & Blade is a brilliant open world sand-box game that allows players to experience their own unique medieval adventure. Build up your own troop to protect trade caravans, hunt bandits and siege castles. Demonstrate your personal combat skills in tournaments to earn fame and fortune. Raid villages, ambush armies and ransom the leaders of your enemies.
Overall, I recommend the game for its well polished free form gameplay, exciting soundtrack and decent graphics. The game has aged well, as reflected in the large number of fan mods available. However, new players may find it better to purchase the Mount & Blade: Warband expansion instead for the updated graphics, additional features and overall improved experience.

ACE Team's games are always top notch, but this is the creme de la creme.
Doubtless, the crew spent endless hours watching old VHS copies of even older 1950's and 1960's creature features to get the feel for this game. The dialog is very good and the humor is very topical while being self-aware. The visuals (and this is where ACE Team truly shines) are beyond amazing. I have never seen so much effort go into anything to make it look authentically cheap.
There's a tiny segment of black and white that is more or less blink and it's gone. I really liked that bit, and the dialog establishes that parts of the “film” were shot in black and white. Sadly, that was the only time it's seen.  As such, it feels less like part of a the game and more like an abandoned idea that the devs forgot to fully remove. Perhaps it can return as a video filter option much like “VHS” is?
Also, what you are expected to do at the end isn't really clear. I figured it out, but believed what I did was the wrong thing to have tried. I spent time trying to figure out a mistake that wasn't. You just have to do the thing until it works, which will not on the first couple of tries.
The worst thing I can actually say is that controls are often sloppy. For a game with tons of platforming, this can be horrifying. Yes, there is mid-air teleportation, but that doesn't stop some sequences from being white knuckle and frustrating, especially towards the end.
I hate to say, but I've totally completed this game. I reached the end somewhere around the 5 hour mark. I spent the remaining time hunting for all of the achievements and extras (and sometimes just free falling for the hell of it). I now have 100% achievements and I'm waiting for any hint of DLC.
Buy the game already.

Dying Light is a really fun game.
It fuses parkour, zombies and open-world all at once. It's practically awesome. You can choose to parkour your way everywhere, or you can choose to murder every single zombie you see in your path, or just a bit of both, because doing one or another gives experience you unlock really awesome ablities that at first look only cool, but secondly they'll actually get really useful.
It's open world, so you can choose to go everywhere you want after the tutorial, there's a lot of exploration to do, and a lot of things to see.
It's a survival, so you survive to stay alive. You can buy at merchants or randomly find blueprints to craft a lot of cool equipment and medikits to keep you alive and going.
It's one of those games that you want to play for one hour but you're having so much fun that you end up playing all evening.
There's a day-night cycle that lasts fairly enough long for both night and day times, and the difficulty is well balanced because the day part is kinda easy, but then comes the night and it gets really difficult at that time. Doing too much noise will also trigger stronger zombies, so you gotta keep cool on both parts of the day.
The graphic is really nice and runs really good. There's lots of gore so you can cut zombies in many different ways or you can break some of their bones which can stun them. Damage localization is really cool and I think that every game involving zombies should have one.
In conclusion, it's a game worth both your time and money. Even at full price.

SUMMARY: An action platformer-adventure that's also a playable B-movie.  If you're a fan of both, this is the game for you.  Otherwise, read the review.
The Deadly Tower Of Monsters core idea is this - you're playing an action platformer set in a b-movie.  The game however is presented as if you're watching a comentary track (complete with outtakes) on a DVD release of this nonexistent film.  So you don't just play out the story and the action - as you do so, the director and the recording assistant make comentary, review the history of the film, and banter.  It's a game of a movie that never was done as a DVD that doesn't exist.
It's also quite clever and fun.
So there's three parts to the game.
THE GAME: The game is a pretty standard action platformer - multiple characters to choose from with different abilities, character upgrades (that affect the whole team), and various upgradable weapons, a few of which are delightfully weird.   As you journey through the environment (a tower, of course), there's hidden items, loot, achievements, and so on.  Nothing you haven't seen before, but about 1/2 to 2/3 the way through the game, it really starts pulling out some truly crazy environments, puzzles, and designs.  The controls at times are a little "soft" and wonky, but nothing game-breaking.
THE THEME: The theme of the game, the b-movie-as-game is realized exceptionally well.  The film references come thick and fast, and even a b-movie fan such as myself may not catch them all (my favorite are the Energy Imps, clear references to the Monster of the Id from Forbidden Planet).  The banter is funny and usually well done, and it's actually interesting to "play" one story while you hear about another - the making of this film.  The director, Dan Smith, is an interesting character both human and flawed - he loves films and movies, compliments his actors, is friendly with the recording assistant, but also shows cluelessness, sexism, and a bit of ego.  He's probably a bit too close to reality.
HOW IT COMES TOGETHER: The gameplay and the theme come together very well.  From the monster designs and styles (many look like stop motion), the crazy environments, the unusual bosses, and little effects and asides, it works.  It's sort of the game equivalent of "The Lost Skeleton of Cadavra," a fun parody-and-homage.
It it perfect?  Well, there's a few flaws.  The action platforming elements have the slightly "soft" controls as mentioned, and there's not any real innovation in the gameplay - it's stuff we've seen before.  Theres' a need for a bit more tutorial elements and clarity as abilities and weapons aren't always easy to understand.  Nothing is game-breaking or indeed game-stopping, but a little more polish would have been nice.
On the other hand, there's plenty here for completists.  There's many achievements and hidden items and things to upgrade.  You can have fun watching for various film references.  You can try out different weapons or play with different abilities to find what works best.
So should you buy it?
* First if you like a solid action platformer/adventure and like b-movies, you should buy it.  This is the game for you.  Buy it.
* If you know someone who'd like this, you just found a great present at a reasonable price.  Buy it.
* If you like action platformer-adventures, it's a mixed bag.  The theming is great and it's imaginative, but it doesn't bring anything new to the table - the way it works with the theme is a strong selling point.  Consider it or get it on sale.
* If you know an action platformer-adventure fan . . . it might be a decent fit.  It's a gamble.
* If you neither like b-movies or action platformer-adventures, really this isn't for you unless you just want to see an interesting envisioning of a genre.
Personally, I consider this game a little gem and a triumph of gameplay married to theme.  It's clever, witty, heartfelt, and fun.
And c'mon Dan Smith had to have made more films, shouldn't those get, ahem, "special releases . . ."
