So, as you can probably tell, this is a tongue-in-cheek action platformer sci-fi game. You play as three different heroes, all with mildly varying powers, and you can use and upgrade a variety of melee and ranged weapons, most of which are bad.
So, the presentation is rather nice, with the audio commentary from the "director" of the game talking about how he "filmed" the "movie," and some random audio engineer that makes comments for whatever reason. The commentary, which extends throughout the game, is entertaining enough, and it makes plenty of references to old and new filmmaking. The visual style of the game adds to the presentation as well with "stop-motion" enemies that move at lower frame rates and wacky enemy designs.
So why don't I recommend this game?
Well, for one, I beat this game first try in 2 hours and 45 minutes approximately. Now, even for a 15 dollar game, that is fairly short. But length isn't all that matters, right? Well, that isn't the only problem I had with it.
The soundtrack for the game is alright, but I can only remember two main songs that got repetitive after some time. There is the main combat and adventure music, and the jarring music change that plays every single time you enter freefall. And you will hear those songs for the entirety of this short game, except when the music seemingly breaks or perhaps just randomly stops playing for whatever reason, which makes the game really uncomfortably silent.
The game also randomly crashed near the end for some reason.
Graphically, this game is not bad. It is colorful, varied, and presents itself well even though the texture quality isn't particularly impressive. The animations can leave a bit to be desired at times, but it is alright.
Now, onto the gameplay. One of the primary things this game sells itself on is the freefall mechanic. In short, it is really bad. You can jump off ledges and move around slightly and then instantly teleport back to where you just jumped off like it never even happened. It just feels so disconnected from the rest of the game. The only real advantage to it is to fall through rings for skill points and achievements. Otherwise, it serves little purpose whatsoever. Even in the boss fights, at the very end of some of the bossfights, the boss falls down and you get to shoot the boss a whole bunch, but it doesn't even seem to really do anything at all. I wouldn't be surprised if not shooting the boss had the same outcome as shooting them. I honestly can't say anything more about it because there really isn't anything else to it. Freefalling feels like a slapped on mechanic, and I would have much preferred if the game didn't pretend like it actually matters at all.
Another "mechanic" of the game, if you can even call it that, is that you can shoot down the tower. I don't mean shoot the tower down, but rather you can look over the edge and shoot at enemies that are coming up the tower. The game will alert you when enemies are climbing/flying up the sides, and you can look over the edge and click them a whole bunch. Also, you can shoot targets and if you shoot enough you get a skill point. That is literally all there is to the "mechanic." It feels so disconnected from the rest of the game that I honestly can't see why it is even in the game.
So now that the whole "looking down and clicking things a whole bunch" mechanics have turned out to be boring, repetitive, and disconnected from the rest of the game, you are left with a more basic action adventure platformer game. So, how does that fair? In short, not much better.
To start off, you have two weapon types, ranged and melee. You can carry four weapons, two of each type, and you can collect and upgrade the different weapons throughout the game.
Actually, scratch that last sentence because it is a big fat lie.
So, you can use different cogs you find throughout the game to upgrade your weapons. But some of the weapons are so ridiculously strong that I cannot possibly imagine why you would use any of the other weapons. The mace/hammer weapon allows you to annihilate everything in your path with jump attacks. It can hit enemies twice, and when you land, its shockwave hits multiple enemies at once. Pair that with the fact that it does a ridiculous amount of damage even to single enemies that I am pretty sure it is more versatile than any pair of weapons in the game. The game quickly devolved into jump attack, jump attack, jump attack, win. It even works well against bosses, so every time I picked up a weapon I would switch to my other junk weapon so I wouldn't lose my hammer when the game forcefully changes my weapons. Then I would continue jump attacking to victory for most of the game.
The ranged weapons are in a similar boat. There is one lightning gun that does so much single target damage that it instantly kills even many medium strength enemies in one shot at range, and at the very least two shots them. There is also an energy mechanic where if you shoot too fast, your energy runs out and you have to wait to use your gun again, but the lightning gun doesn't even use too much energy for the insane amount of damage it does and it upgrades to max very quickly. The worst part is that the weapon can hit multiple densely packed enemies at once so I never felt hard pressed to switch to a faster weapon to kill weaker mobs because I could kill two to three at once anyway. The ranged weapons are less terrible than the melee weapons, with the machinegun, rocket launcher, and a couple others being okay but the lightning gun is just so good I had no reason to ever use my secondaries.
Each character has powers that I can barely even comment on because I never felt the need to use them except when the game forces you to use them to open up a gate or move past an obstacle. The only one of note is at the last chapter of the game and lets you instantly kill any enemy that is being held up by strings, and it recharges very quickly.
we needed more enemy types to become completely trivialized.
"What about the enemy designs?" What about them? Thematically they are varied with apes that throw feces and robot samurai and dinosaurs and so on, but most can be summed up as: Small mob creature that dies instantly, medium strength melee guy, medium strength ranged guy, big slow guy. Oh, and the "enemy that flies up the tower and you click a whole bunch as it dies helplessly" enemy type. Again, the "shooting down the tower" mechanic is so disconnected that those enemies are hardly worth mentioning. The hammer and lightning gun make short work of all of the main enemy types anyway.
The platforming is extremely basic. You can jump, and you have a jetpack that allows you to hover for a short period of time while also preventing fall damage. Basically, its not a selling point either.
And the bosses, along with the rest of the game, are laughably easy. The last "boss," if you can even call it that, is basically one last middle finger to the player as it is the easiest of them all.
All in all, unless the presentation just seems
appealing to you and the game is on sale, I wouldn't recommend it. I even got it for 10 bucks and I
wouldn't recommend it.

Comedy is incredibly difficult to pull off in a video game. Most gags rely on precise, directed timing, and taking control away from a player in an interactive medium usually results in a bad game, frustration, and few laughs in the process. Through clever narration, smart satire, and an unflinching 100% commitment to it's jokes, The Deadly Tower of Monsters plastered a perma-grin across my face for my entire playtime. It's an entertaining, creative hack n' slash puzzle/platformer to boot.
Your ultimate goal in The Deadly Tower of Monsters is to climb the deadly tower of monsters. Standing underneath the imposing structure and looking skyward (or taking a peek at the map) gives the deflating feeling that you're in for a near impossible test of will and patience. Once you take a few steps toward that journey, however, it becomes clear that many design decisions are in place to keep player convenience at the forefront. Fall off a ledge? Press “LB” and you're right back to solid ground, no penalty incurred. Getting lost? Pull up the map and you can warp to any point in the tower you've previously visited at will. (Protip: go up.) This isn't some hardcore, griefing, reflex litmus test. That wouldn't be funny. You're encouraged to fall, explore, and generally just have a good time in the campy sandbox, and you should take the game up on that offer.
On the base level the game reminds me of console-centric action/RPGs like Marvel: Ultimate Alliance or Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance. From an overhead view you have a standard melee attack which can be charged for a heavy attack, and a ranged weapon. As you progress you gain access to about a dozen different kinds of both types of weapons, and these can be upgraded by collecting components dropped by enemies or scattered around the environments. There are also perks like max HP increases, regenerating health, improved melee/ranged damage, etc. that can be earned by completing missions (main quests or side activities). You can swap between three different characters that have some unique skills needed to access certain areas, so there's also a bit of Metroidvania going on here.  Other options include the ability to parry attacks, extend your jumps with a jetpack, and shoot downward when near a ledge (that one good feature of Dark Void). It all adds up to a surprising amount of depth in a fairly short, decidedly goofy comedy game.
Even the title screen of The Deadly Tower of Monsters is full of jokes. Upon booting the game, you're immediately greeted by a narrator who is “in studio” to record a commentary track for a truly awful Sci-Fi B-movie he made some years back, and he's going to be cringe-worthingly candid and let it be know just how much of scumbag he is. You're greeted at the start with a fairly typical though beautiful movie poster of the movie, where a 50's Hollywood space man is cradling an attractive, unconscious woman. The director remarks how proud he is of the poster. Boot the game up a second time, and the gender roles are swapped, with the woman rescuing the man. “I didn't approve of this change”, the director protests. His assistant chimes in to inform him that the studio execs shot an alternate take, foreseeing a future demographic where swapping the sexes would appeal to the masses. That's some pretty poignant and ♥♥♥♥ing funny social commentary. Not content to stop there, an alternate title screen shows a robot holding the man instead... for the future robot demographic.
I debated whether or not to spoil the above gag, but the riffs are just so nonstop throughout the game that it's a small drop in a large pond of punchlines. You're controlling the “movie”, the perfectly voiced director is giving behind-the-scenes anecdotes nearly the entire time in rapid fire fashion akin to the densest, snappiest of MST3K episodes. This is more than fitting since the movie in question would feel right at home in a crappy Mystery Science Theater show: dinosaurs are convincingly stop motion animated, bats are held aloft by visible strings, nothing is shown that couldn't be created with practical effects from that era which usually means men in rubber suits. There's even more than a few cameos from (in)famous(ly bad) real movie monsters. Every environment and creature is lovingly crafted from people who are clearly fans of the genre, and the affection for the movies we love and love to make fun of is sincere and hilarious.
I'm not usually a fan of “meta” comedy, but The Deadly Tower of Monsters is so out there it absolutely worked for me on every level. The DVD commentary presentation is excellent, and it breaks the fourth (and sometimes fifth) wall with such reckless abandon you just have to laugh. From a pure game perspective it's completely solid with enough fresh ideas to be enjoyable on it's own, but smiling and giggling like an idiot while playing elevates it to a must play game. It's one of the best surprises I've encountered in a long time.

As of writing, it took me 5.2 hours to beat this game, but I have yet to 100% the game!
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. Although many compare it to Inside and Limbo, the game lacks that ultra-hardcore charm of "die to figure out the puzzle". Most of my deaths were due to failing with the controls at jumps or falling from heights, or because I couldn't figure out the puzzle in time. The story and art style is great - I find the visual horror of the enemies a bit goofy but there's definitely some unexpected spooks to be had.
The game also makes creative use of backtracking - while normally that would be a waste of time, there's always something unexpected on the second runthrough.
Controls are a mixed bag, after struggling with mouse and keyboard on a segment that required rapidly changing between 2 diagonal motions to dodge, I switched to a controller...and then probably struggled more because of relearning controls :/
Another thing are the checkpoints. The checkpoints are UNCLEAR. Some of them are near lamps the player can light, other times they are somewhere??? Some of them are right at the start of chase scenes which is convenient I guess.
Finally, bugs. I've had some wonky moments where I can't tell why the AI can see me, as well as getting stuck once or twice due to throwing physics objects the wrong way. ALSO, the player ducks under some movable/climbable objects, which blocks jumping and can ruin a critical move if you jump too late onto a ledge.

I quite enjoyed this. There are a number of characters that I really grew to care for over the course of playing this, enough to want to go back and give them all their good endings -- and the game really rewarded that. I'd highly recommend this.

The port is fairly well done, though default keyboard controls feel a bit odd, however are all fully rebindable. The controller support feels slightly off, but it isn't a big issue since you have all the time in the world in combat. Otherwise, the port is very functional, and the ability to use the mouse in selection screens is a rather nice plus.
The actual game itself is somewhat of a unique take on a JRPG, with high customization elements, an ultra cute cast and a rather large amount of content, especially with the DLC bringing up the level cap to 999. The combat system is very simplistic, but because of the simplicity, it makes the game rather casual. That being said, the balancing of the foes in the game feel slightly strange, with a large gap between the strength of regular monsters and boss monsters.
Just about everything is customizable, from your character outfits, attack combos, monster difficulty and loot obtained and the dialogue includes lighthearted humor and much fourth wall breaking. The voice overs are available in both English and Japanese and all Music and Artwork are unlocked as the game progresses for viewing at any time in a town.
Overall, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a unique JRPG that fans of the series or JRPGs in general may enjoy.

This is my attempt to provide a comprehensive review of XCOM Enemy Unknown. As a player who just recently discovered that the franchise has been revived, I was initially ambivalent toward picking up the new additions. In short, my rationale stem from a slew of disappointments I have had with many of my childhood franchises (e.g. Command and Conquer Red Alert and Tiberium Series, Heroes of Might and Magic etc.) that seemed to lost their "magic" in the 2010-2020 decade. Clearly, by writing this review, my fears have been unfounded and they have been supplanted with pleasant suprirse.
XCOM Enemy Unknown continue to hold its mantle as a sui generis turn-based tactical strategy game. Something that cannot be said for many other classic strategy franchises that seemed to have lost touch with its predessors and roots. While other franchises went astray in innovation and devolved its award-winning formula, XCOM Enemy Unknown held firm to its roots. XCOM Enemy Unknown borrows from its successful and award-winning elements from past titles while incrementally making improvements to environment, turn-based gameplay, physics, and other important aspects that impact the game in significant ways.
GREAT:
-Core gameplay, from "ant-hill management" and tactical turn-based strategizing.
-Sui Generis Mantle: not many strategy games (that I know of) out there have a sci-fi alien theme.
-Soldier customization - skill trees, weapons, armor, classes, veterancy.
-Responsive controls - mouse controls and keyboard shortcuts are excellent and intuitive.
-Polished technical aspects - movements, animations, physics, and navigation are polished.
-Mission and environment diversity - missions feel very distinct and different from one another. Maps demand the player to adjust his/her strategy according to the terrain.
-Freedom to strategize: rain fire on the enemy from a high vantage point? Take the fight to the enemy with shotguns and grenades? Pick enemies off with snipers and rockets? Have a laser tag duel indoors? Lure the enemy into an ambush? My personal favorite: mind control an enemy and use its arsenal.
-Trivial but entertaining tasks: mind-control an alien and force it to attack its allies with explosives <3 Muton.
-Cutscenes, voiceovers, and animations are amazing.
-RNG Luck: There are numbers in percentages and numbers in terms of luck. How would feel if your sniper OHKOed a dangerous alien with only 25% chance of headshot? How would you feel if an enemies missed three shots consecutively against your wounded soldier, allowing you pull her back and save her life? On the other side, I was quite upset when my assault missed a shot pointblank with 95% chance of hitting the enemy.
My minor complaint is that auto-save is not enabled by default. Some new players may find that they need to replay the mission when they took too many casualties. Another complaint is the difficulty of some missions do not correspond to the average player's progression - I had the unsavory task of trying to take down a cyberdisk without any heavy in my team on a DLC mission.
OVERALL, if you are a fan of strategy games, this is a title you do not want to miss! It'll make you think about your decisions even after you close the game. One can easily spend an entire day playing this game.
15/10 would kidnap a Muton Elite on Earth again.

I understand that this game was released in 2008. It holds up graphically to this day, and the game looks great once you iron out the performance issues with physX. However, the combat is absolutely horrendous, even for 2008. You have to either memorize an INSANELY small window where you can melee an enemy safely and take his gun, or use the slow motion which is clunky and ruins the immersion. Once you have a gun, it handles horribly and your movement speed is reduced to a crawl (unless you have the pea-shooter of a handgun). The level design is pretty bad as well. Too many times I found myself stuck in a building or something trying to find the exit. This game would have greatly benefitted from a radar system or a map, as your "runner vision" can only work if you are already close to your destination. The actual parkour mechanics are wonderful though, and it is really fun to play once you get up to speed. It is a shame that the game's had such glaring issues because the core gameplay is really fun.

Updated for Arcade Strikes Back: Story mode, voiced by the original cast with new dialogue, and a plotline! It's no longer just going for the high score! New characters to fight with - Barbarianna, who can clear a side with the chain gun every 5 hits, which is awesome; Hackerman, whose ranged weapon knocks back as it charges for a continuous double-damage combo (which often results in wild flailing back and forth as the most effective means of combat); and Triceracop, who...um...seems broken.
You see, Triceracop uses his trademark crotch shot method of attack...with guns...that has the effective range of Kung Fury's normal attacks. I don't know, maybe he's going for a 100% shot to crotch ratio or something and relies on a close range target... However, the guns have a knockback to them, pushing Triceracop backwards. This is fine, until you encounter the wave of kung-fu women who swap sides when hit. The knockback is strong enough to where you can shoot three times in the same direction and still hit them, but not 100% reliably; and you can still alternate your shot directions to hit them... but not 100% reliably. So when the wave of 8 of these women show up (with 2 robot legs) somewhere around the 3rd wave, if your recoil pushes you to the other side of one of these women and your combo breaks, you get stunned, take a hit, and are suddenly surrounded by multiple women (normally a good problem to have) each one having the potential to break your combo if your recoil puts you in the wrong spot to hit, forcing you to take another hit. The game generously provides Triceracop with more hearts than any other character in the game, which makes it feel like the designers were aware the game mechanic caused unavoidable hits.
Original Review below:
Watch the short film, then get the game. The movie is 20 minutes of your life well spent. If you play the game 8 times it pays for itself. I mean, arcade games still cost a quarter per credit, right? A genuine arcade feel to this beat-em-up, with surprisingly in-depth technique for a game that uses only 2 buttons. It's a sort of rhythm of the battle thing - go too fast for the action and you'll end up missing the next enemy and take a hit; go too slow and you'll be surrounded quickly and take a hit. The rhythm fluctuates with the density of enemies and their health. You must be the master of the rhythm of the battle if you want the high score. Wait for the enemy to approach, then buffer your inputs so that no time is wasted preparing for the next enemy. Also digging that retrowave soundtrack.

They can't do it all the time. They just can't. They can't keep taking our beloved franchises, turn them into storytelling videogames and make those GOOD. Or can they?
Telltale's (TT) newest installment features the world of A Song of Ice and Fire, more commonly known as Game of Thrones, made popular by HBO's TV series. By now, you should be familiar by the way TT approaches gameplay, artstyle or how their games are split up into a number of Episodes being released in 1-2 month intervals. It should as no surprise that you will only have access to Episode 1 of this season, and by extension this review will focus on only that. This review will be
for the actual games, but contain some spoilers from Seasons 1 through 3 for the TV series.
Game of Thrones - A TT Games Series puts focuses on the story of House Forrester, a lesser northern house that served the Starks for centuries and in return enjoyed their protection. When the War of the Five Kings broke out, however, the lands of Westeros became ravaged and the old order was more or less destroyed. The Northmen face their own problems as the Boltons seize power, backed by the Lannisters and King Joffrey.
What makes TT's game special is that it allows you to experience all those major events from a perspective you do not usually get much insight in. You, the protagonist(s), are not a global player in the overarching storyline. You have your own problems to deal with and are very much a subject to the whims of those more powerful than you. This alone makes playing the game worth it for hardcore fans as well, who might fear just "replaying what they already know". While the game needs the main plot to establish its setting, it strays from it enough to develop its own, complex story.
Different to other TT games, you get to play as multiple characters, very much in the style of the books and the show. All of these characters, so far, are members or peers of House Forrester, though. And don't worry, you will get to make plenty difficult decisions and, as usual, there is very rarely a black-or-white-dichotomy. Will you do the honourable thing, even if it means hurting those you care for or will you lie and cheat to protect your family? The choice is yours and it remains to be seen how much of an effect they will have on the rest of the season.
A special treat for fans of the show would be the inclusion of major characters from it - designed to match their TV counterparts and voiced by the actual actors. Although it is unlikely that the player's choices will have much of an effect on the main plot, it will be exciting to see how these new characters play into it.
The only downsides are that, again much in the style of the show, there is much establishing to be done before the plot can really kick off. Because of this, the first episode comes across as a little choppy, with frequent jumps between characters, often throwing you right in the middle of things. Those who know absolutely nothing about Game of Thrones will find themselves overwhelmed by the unexplained yet important things that happen around you. This being said TT's take on Game of Thrones is worth a solid recommendation for hardcore- and casual-fans alike.

I have quite a bit of love for this game, but I'll say one negative thing about it: the combat system, while getting points in my book for being unique, ultimately rewards a gameplay style that is unintuitive.

For those who haven't played it:

The combat follows a
turn-based system.  It's always Your Team -> Their Team -> Your Team -> Their Team until one of the parties has only one surviving member, which then takes the turns into sort of a "blowout mode" where the entire opposing party gets to move for each of the single unit's moves.
A character's combat effectiveness is in large part determined by their remaining health.  A character with 0 health missing will do more damage than a character with 3 points of health missing that is otherwise identical.

These two factors work together and lead to an interesting quirk - contrary to most tactical games where grouping around a single unit and removing it quickly provides the greatest strategic benefit by removing the total number of enemies faced, in the case of the Banner Saga, it ends up being best to


If you're having trouble understanding, take this example.  You have 3 units at max health and the enemy has 3 units at max health.  There will be 6 turns in a "rotation", one for each unit.  The order will be A1-B1-A2-B2-A3-B3.  If you were to completely defeat one enemy unit, there would then be 5 turns in a "rotation", one for each unit, and the order will be A1-B1-A2-B2-A3.  Now, the next turn will be B again, but it will be B1, who is a fully powered unit.  Had you left B3 alive at one or two hit points, the turn would be given to B3 instead, and since B3 is very weak, any damage dealt by it would be greatly reduced.  If B1 and B2 do 6 damage each while B3 will only do 2 damage, A1-B1-A2-B2-A3-B3 results in 14 damage to your party across three turns, while A1-B1-A2-B2-A3-B1 results in 18 damage over three turns.

By eliminating the weakest unit as opposed to leaving them in the battle, you have reduced the time between turns for the two strongest units the enemy has.  The strongest tactical decision will be leaving multiple enemies at low health to force the enemy team into "wasting" turns on the ineffective units while reducing turns for the most powerful enemies.

I want to emphasize that I do appreciate the benefits and wrinkles of this system, one would be parties who have a dwindling number of units are granted an automatically incrementing advantage.  I also appreciate the flavor of the "rout" mechanic where the lone surviving unit must give priority to each remaining opponent - it makes battles feel decisive when you're on the good end and makes them feel hopeless when you're on the receiving end.

My complaint with this "flaw" as I view it, is that it seems to be a very "meta" strategy.  That is to say, it feels at times like you're gaming the combat system as opposed to making tactical decisions -- killing the Big Bad last after maiming the rabble to ensure you only get thumped 1 of 6 turns instead of systematically answering and removing threats.

Regardless, this is a game I highly recommend.  Mechanically, it has several other devices that are quite novel.  Both the Armor and Exertion systems lend themselves to interesting decisions and interactions.

Flavor-wise, the game is outstanding.  It really makes you feel like a survivor fighting an unstoppable enemy and the grinding attrition of daily survival.

Do be aware: this is part one of a trilogy.  I did not know that when I started the game.  Without getting too spoilery, there are quite a few
moments at the end of the game that lead into a final battle that is frankly anticlimactic.  Knowing it was only the opening chapter of a grand story would have made things much more satisfying the first time around.

If you haven't played this game yet but are considering it, you're already interested enough to buy it.  The art and music are breathtaking and though your decisions end up not being the most eventful in the long run, they always result in immediate and sometimes totally unforeseen consequences.

First of all, I'm happy to see that Visual Novels are (re)-introduced in the west. Not only the 18+ versions but also the more "decent" ones. Lets start the review of this game shall we?
You start the game playing as Semyon, a socialy akward guy who's only quality is reading on the internet.
After being invited by an old friend from collage, he falls asleep in Bus 410 and wakes op in a typical Old Soviet Pioneers camp in the eighties. How did he get here. And why does everyone avoid his questions?
The characters are, well how do I put it, strange. At first they seem to be normal people, however do not talk about their past. Not only that, they avoid al possilble question related to time and space, and even start to get anoyed if you ask further. No explanation is given on who or what they are even after getting their good endings.
After a lot of playthroughs you start to learn more and more and finaly the game reveals a bit of their purpose, though they're still shrouded in mysteries.
The drawings of the characterd are generally well done, at least in the normal conversations, in case of the action scenes the drawings seems to be a bit amateuristic or hastly drawn.
The story changes according to the character you choose to go out with. This afcourse is normal in Visual Novels.
However what intriques me, is that not only the future changes with you choices, sometimes the present or even the past changes depending on which girl you choose. This only deepens the mysteries of this pioneer camp, and keeps you wondering what's going on.
To fully understand what is happening, you have to replay the game many times, unlock all the good endings, replay it again, and after the right choices, you get the answers you seek. This can be quite difficult, but there is an guide posted on the community page of you need some help.
Though this game is not realy a creepy game, there is one route which made me shiver. I'm not gonna spoil the story but I'd like to advice people not to play this route at night.
The music on sound effect are great and really put me in the mood to play this game.
Sometime they give you a serene feeling, sometime it lightens the mood, and sometimes is make you really scared.
Anyway the music is great and never feels off.
I talked a bit about the art in my character section, but there is more to it.
The backgrounds are really well drawn and gave me the feeling of watching to a painting (something even Semyon noticed). The only thing that sometimes disapointed me was the drawing of the characters in "Action" scenes.
To be honest, I don't think I can write much about. It is a visual novel, and visual novels do have the tendency to have low replayability because it takes you a while to read it. However there is the skip text function which make it doable.
It's quite tedicous to do, but since you need all the good endings to get the true ending of this game, you have a purpose to do so.
The characters are not really that interesting and sometimes seem even fake. There are a few exceptions afcourse.
This seems to be the aim of this game and after completing to game, you start to understand why.
The story is realy well done. It realy like the mystery part of it, and enjoyed it to the end. They do not lift up all the mysteries which let you, the player, interpretate it the way you think things are.
I also liked that the main character has it's own route.
I don't have to say a lot about the music. It's almost perfect, with one exeption: The heavy metal music in the bed ending credits. I liked it, but I'm not sure if it's appropiate for a game
The backgrounds and scenes are beautifuly drawed. With exception from the characters in some points.
I'm not going to judge this. As mentioned before it's realy hard to make a VN replayable.
If you do not mind the sometimes bad character art and strange personality I'd really like to recommend this game.
If you do mind, well this game is free to play so why don't give it a try? You may like it beter than you originaly thought.
Patience is key in playing visual novels, and this VN realy wants you to show that patience. However your patience will be rewarded after seeing the true ending, most things will be explained to you.

So what is Child of Light? Child of Light is a fantasy platforming role-playing game developed by Ubisoft Montreal using the UbiArt Framework engine (the same one used for the more recent Rayman games).  Despite being developed by a branch of Ubisoft, some people consider this game "Indie" (especially due to its short playthrough times - 8-10 hours for one playthrough).
The story revolves around a young child named Aurora, born to the Austrian duke
sometime before the game.  The gameplay opens in 1895 Austria, where Aurora falls into a deep sleep (I believe she is actually considered comatose in Austria), after which she is transported to the magical world of Lemuria, wanting to return back to her home.  She is tasked with finding the stars, the moon, and the sun, in order to return home.  Through the guidance of Igniculus (who is the Firefly that a second player can control), as well as the encounters with the inhabitants of Lemuria - the Populi (Mice), Capilli (Dwarves), and Cynbel (Aquatic folk) - Aurora goes through her own coming-of-age story
.  And that ends the story section because putting any more content will involve serious spoilers.  Surprisingly enough, this is probably the only RPG (or one of few) where I've actually bothered to pay attention to the dialogue to understand the story.
As mentioned before, there is a rhyming motif that follows this game because of the way it's presented: like a fairy tale.  The rhyming does seem forced at times but I would assume that's just to keep the story going smoothly.  Luckily you'll only need to deal with rhyming during character dialogue (all of it, including NPCs)...and the objective hint...and the inventory...
Aside from the story and the way it's presented, what
redeems this game and makes it worth $15?  Well, the turn-based combat is a nice throwback to older JRPGs (while I said Chrono Trigger and FF series, the system more accurately follows the Grandia series).  CoL uses a timeline to gauge who acts when.  There is a long "Wait" period followed by a shorter "Casting" period.  Hitting an enemy while it's in the "Casting" section causes that enemy to be interrupted.  Likewise, if your party members get hit while "Casting" they will be interrupted as well.  The battle flow is kind of interrupted if you're waiting for Igniculus to heal your party members or you're struggling about what to do, but other than that the combat mechanics work smoothly.
There's also a basic elemental motif, where Fire > Earth  > Lightning (Air) > Water > Fire. (no party members learn Earth magic, but there are Earth-type monsters)  The element of Light, however, is - as TVTropes calls it - an Infinity+1 Element, which means it's basically the OP element of the game.  Aurora is
the
character in the
who can use Light magic, which is super effective against Dark-type monsters and not resisted by
element. (Even though Aurora herself is
very squishy in the beginning)
The platforming itself is easy enough to manuever, although the graphics do obscure which parts of the world are able to be traversed and which parts aren't.  Considering I'm not much of a fan for platformers, I found the platforming quite do-able.  Plus, the platforming leaves room for exploration.
Some elements of the game are basic versions of more modern RPGs, such as the equipment section (which actually isn't "equipment", just gems you can craft and socket into weapon, defensive, and support slots) and the skill trees (which reminded me of FF10's Sphere Grid or FF13's Crystarium, and is also highly reminiscent of Far Cry 3's skill trees).
CoL offers a good 8-10 hour playthrough, depending on how long it takes you to progress through the platforming and bosses.  (It took me 10 on casual... but I hear you can do it in 8 or less)  There is also NG+ (New Game+), where you can restart the story with higher-leveled enemies but keep all your oculi (gems), skills, and inventory items.
As a person who normally likes shooting up people in FPS games, this is a nice game to enjoy on the side while taking a break from all the bullets.
*this is not my area of expertise
The music is well-composed (by Béatrice Martin, aka Cœur de pirate).  It touched my heart during cutscenes/dialogue and invigorated me during battles and bosses.  The game engine (UbiArt Framework) makes for some really nice 2/2.5D aesthetics.  There's also some 3D graphics for the battle animations.  To me, the aesthetics are pretty amazing and I enjoy them (a lot).  Er...other than that though, I really don't pay attention to graphics that much... :P

(In short) If you love games with female protagonists who are adorable and kickass with a sword and spells, and a fairytale type of story, having the characters talk in rhyme, and have an aesthetic eye for watercolor rendered games, you should buy Child of Light.
(For all reasons to like and dislike the game, read on.)
If you guys think that the artwork and cute story is what attracted so many people to love this game, its not. Its mainly the soundtrack. If you look at the videos of the soundtracks on youtube, they are flooded with positive comments. Everyone loves the songs and ugh just the love for this game is amazing haha. Once you finish the game, listen to the soundtrack and just cry,
of the game was amazing. It was so beautiful, you were literally flying around in a giant painting. Games rendered in a watercolor style is so beautiful in my opinion, I couldn't help but to squeal at every new map that I encountered haha. xD One can tell that a TON of effort went into the making of this game. Just from looking at the backgrounds which at first glance, don't seem like much but to anyone interested in art. The lighting and coloring of everything blends together so well and its just so UNF.
(The biggest concern I had while I was contemplating buying this game..) I guess since Uplay is mentioned on here(in the cons section) I might as well talk about the benefits about Uplay, unlike those Uplay ragers from the reviews of the game earlier in the year mentioned, Uplay isn't bad at all. (Biased opinion because I faced no problems from it but..) Uplay actually gives you these Uplay coin token things as you play the game, and with those coins, you can buy stuff. So for all of those DLC's that you've been wanting, half of them are on Uplay. You can purchase (with Uplay coins) and download backgrounds and stuff. Of course the soundtrack to support the artist is on Steam, and that one DLC that includes a new party member is also on steam. If anything really the DLC's on steam offer you 2 outfit changes and a new party member, because sure the others offers extra occuli, but you find them randomly in the game anyways. (Sometimes, even monsters drop them), so Uplay isn't all that bad, and the DLC's that Steam offers arent bad either. Half of those DLC's that you guys are complaining and bichin' about, are on Uplay. (more stuff on Uplay is at the bottom of the review.)
(?) Some people complained about the length of the game, but I thought that the game length matched the price, if anything I think that the price is just right. (The extreme fans of CoL can of course argue with me on this) Many people complained about the length of the game not matching of the price or the worth of the game, but that shouldn't be an issue, because one can just replay the game, in a harder mode if you found the game too short or too easy. I'm going to do that. (I played on Casual, like the scared little noob gamer I am) I heard that it provides more challenges, (and many deaths haha.)
The only thing that I disliked was that Aurora was 3D. Dispite the background being in 2D with with different layers in the background moving to add a bit of deph into the otherwise flat looking background, the main characters looking 3D looked a bit out of place in my opinion. I just would have preferred for the few characters (including Aurora) to be in 2D along with the bg, but I knew that would have been hard work since Aurora doesen't sit still, she flies around so I understand that its just easier for her and the few other characters to be 3D. It just bothered my eye while playing the game.
If you don't like for all of the characters to talk in rhyme (It is slant rhyme I believe) this
If you can tolerate it and not give the game a negative review just because they talk in rhyme, or because of Ubisoft, thank you. The rhyme isn't for everyone and thats okay. Scurry along somewhere else, don't just bash the rhyme.
The story itself is also very Disney like. Its basically a fairytale. Its not hard to follow at all, I think that because of the way that the game was made that it can appeal to all ages besides the very young children because they may not understand the full story.
Some people complained about there being no background information on the game. I think that the game gave all of the information that one needed to know at the beginning. And the rest of the surprises that the game throws at the player is just y'know cut scenes that are supposed to add problems and drama into the story to make it interesting.. If you pay attention to whats going on, its not difficult at all to follow.
Oh the fights there were so many complains about it. I didn't like it. It was a first for me for this type of fighting system where it was turn based. It was not difficult in terms of strategy. With different skills/abilities/spells, and your firefly friend Sir Igniculus, you can make it so that you attack more than said turn. I didn't mind it. Sure the battles were always the same. Figure out weaknesses of the enemy and kill them. You have many friends who you can switch out in the midst of the battle, whom all have different abilities and specialties which can make it somewhat more interesting than just having Aurora slash at enemies with her sword, yes? It also kept the game balanced, I mean if you were able to have like all 5 of your allies (if even 5) out to attack like 3 enemies at max of course the game'd be too easy. It limited the game in the fighting system to make it so that the battles are worth thinking about. Like do you take out a fellow damage dealer for a support character who can heal/buff you? There were not many possibilities but did require me to think a bit as I played. BUT if its strategy that you are looking for my friend, there is not much to this game in terms of the battles. I recommend setting the game to hardcore mode or something. There are also only like 3 songs that play depending on the battle. Its the same for when just grinding mobs (to level up, and its all optional too, I mean. You should.. level up to even have a chance at defeating the boss..) the only times that I've noticed the soundtrack change was in big boss fights which you will encounter as the story progresses.
I had little to no problems with it. I've read a lot of the other reviews and heard others bichin' about how because of UPlay that they don't recommend it... But honestly I thought that Uplay wasn't a problem. If anything those problems with Uplay being down and stuff, I think that those problems are fixed now because in the few days that I've played Child of Light and finished it, I had never had Uplay exiting the game for me, or for that manner, and problems from or dealing with Uplay. My game was never disrupted. The worst that it got was the second to half of second of lag that went away immediatley while I flew around in the map. Or of how sometimes in some of the battles, Aurora had no hair. It didn't bother me that much because to be honest, it was only one battle out of how many now? And the few times that it happened, it wasn't in the major boss fights so it was fine for me. Other than that I had no techincal difficulties with the game.

This game promised something new and different, but delivers neither. The elemental system isn’t different from spell casting in any other game, point and click, except here it takes two steps to do what only takes one elsewhere, a phenomenon better known as taking two steps backward. You must repeat the same effective elemental pairings every time instead of having them combined into a single spell.
The environmental application of the elements is punctual, limited and unimpressive. This isn’t Populus or Black and White.
Elemental magic was much better done in Grandia. The art direction fails at mixing realistic (the world is too much) and cartoony styles (all humanoid characters), unlike the far prettier and smoother Fable. There’s no tactical combat because there’s no resource management or large battlefields, unlike Jagged Alliance 2. The atmosphere is bland, resisting any attempts at immersion, unlike Jade Empire. Shamelessly marketed as an “open world”, a pure lie, it doesn’t even begin to come close to the true openness of a Fallout 3 (or 2 or 1).
But this game also promises to be “retro”, and thus the reason for my comparisons with excellent RPGs of yore. You can’t excuse as or call “Divinity: Original Sin” retro when it completely fails to capture any of the things that made the great games of old great. Whatever you’re looking for, you’ll find it in the games I mentioned and not here. So go play those great games instead of this piece of crap.

Dying Light is a really fun game.
It fuses parkour, zombies and open-world all at once. It's practically awesome. You can choose to parkour your way everywhere, or you can choose to murder every single zombie you see in your path, or just a bit of both, because doing one or another gives experience you unlock really awesome ablities that at first look only cool, but secondly they'll actually get really useful.
It's open world, so you can choose to go everywhere you want after the tutorial, there's a lot of exploration to do, and a lot of things to see.
It's a survival, so you survive to stay alive. You can buy at merchants or randomly find blueprints to craft a lot of cool equipment and medikits to keep you alive and going.
It's one of those games that you want to play for one hour but you're having so much fun that you end up playing all evening.
There's a day-night cycle that lasts fairly enough long for both night and day times, and the difficulty is well balanced because the day part is kinda easy, but then comes the night and it gets really difficult at that time. Doing too much noise will also trigger stronger zombies, so you gotta keep cool on both parts of the day.
The graphic is really nice and runs really good. There's lots of gore so you can cut zombies in many different ways or you can break some of their bones which can stun them. Damage localization is really cool and I think that every game involving zombies should have one.
In conclusion, it's a game worth both your time and money. Even at full price.

Controls -
Pros: The controls are two buttons, but the nice thing is, there is controller support, and you can use WASD and the directionals as well, so you can play it how you like. The gameplay is much more about timing, anyways.
Cons: Even just a super move button where you get powers for the combo level you reach, like a screen-clearing attack or a ridiculously over-the-top animated move or two, would have been cool, and would have upped the wow factor, like the movie.
Gameplay -
Pros: Difficult, but in the way that you want to keep trying over and over to master it. Also, no button-mashing allowed, since if you miss a hit, you not only lose your multiplier, but you risk losing a life. It reminds me of the Arkham combat system in 2 dimensions; very rhythmic with the combos, and each enemy has a different rhythm to beat it, whether it's a combination of different directions or a particular amount of hits per enemy, or even how far your hits knock an enemy back into the queue.
Cons: After seeing the movie, I kinda wish there was more character variation (but I've only gotten to 90k points so maybe there is), perhaps some street thugs or laser raptors, or even different locations for fighting (like in the G*dd*amn Viking Age or the Mean Streets) where there would be different enemies. It could be like Miami Shark, where it just gets increasingly more ridiculous and the enemies fill the screen and the things you fight get crazier, like in the movie. Just sayin'.
Music -
Pros: It's rad as hell. From the movie, obviously, but they nailed it in the movie, so there you have it.
Cons: I mean, it loops, but that's what you get. Also, there's no option to shut it off which kind of sucks for someone like me who likes to supply their own soundtrack.
Graphics -
Pros: Perfect. Feels retro, but polished.
Cons: It gets a little hard to combo when you have a bunch of dudes up in your shiz, but then again, I think that's kind of the point. Also, screen flash can be a bit headache-inducing and some graphics cover up the action so you don't know how close you are to an enemy, which could mean coming up short and getting hit.
Verdict: 9/10. Could be crazier, but super fun in its current state. Also hoping for Steam Cards and achievements, though I have a feeling this is the finished product, but... a man can dream.

A mere two hours into the game and it's already miles better than I'd expected it to be. Having played Hyperdimension Neptunia from its very first installment up to Hyperdimension Neptunia Victory on the PS3, I can say that having this game on PC is definitely a better experience even if just for the 60 FPS improvement alone.
I'd never played anything from the "Re;Birth" line and I've been pleasantly surprised by how much of an improvement this remake of the first game is. It's not a simple remaster at all, it's literally a remake.
Tasteful dialogue has been added to this game alongside the battle system from the later installments in the series, which makes it a genuinely fun game to go through instead of a headache-inducing experience. Speaking of headaches, if anyone here has played the first game on the PS3 then you'd know how much of a pain some of the soundtrack was to listen to. Even the soundtrack in this game has been composed completely differently and the pieces are pretty fun to listen to. High energy with catchy melodies and the mixes themselves are great.
When it comes to choosing either the Japanese or English dub, it simply all comes down to personal preference. The only gripe I have with the English dub is that it doesn't have voice acting during quite a few scenes where the Japanese one does. If you're the type of person who doesn't care about the language or expression, and would just like to have a full audio experience with speech, then the Japanese option will give you that. Otherwise the English dub is still quite good. I myself am indecisive and keep switching between the two.
The visuals are of course much better in the PC version due to the improved framerate, and although the game doesn't have an in-built 1080p resolution option, there is a work-around posted in the forums.
If by any chance you are having issues with this game involving cutscenes being automatically skipped, you simply need to go and install CCCP or the "Combined Community Codec Pack". It'll fix a lot of issues you may have with other forms of media as well. Thankfully I've yet to come across a single bug in this game myself.
It's been said by a fair few people, but it's true that a controller is optimal for playing this game. The in-game tutorials present you with buttons for a controller setup without giving you direct guidance for a mouse and keyboard, and even when you work it all out it's pretty unpleasant in its default state. Don't let that turn you off from this game if you're interested though, because you can just reassign everything obviously. Even still, go grab that controller to make it easy.
All-in-all this is the best Hyperdimension Neptunia experience I've had yet in terms of visuals, audio and performance. If you're a fan of the anime aesthetic, light-hearted humour, cool combat and JRPGs in general, then you're going to have a blast with this game. I hope to see the support being given to the PC release cause more games like this one to come to PC.

The Banner Saga has stunning landscape art, a great soundtrack, a compelling story and indeed would make a fine visual novel (provided you don't mind 80's cartoon style character art). Actually, if it were several dollars less (or on sale) it would be worth recommending on that merit. Unfortunately, they have made the mistake of attempting to pack a game in with this work of art and underlying game is really bad.
Barring some scant and predictable events, you have no control and no agency in the traveling portion of the game. Strategy essentially amounts to buying enough food at each stop to last out a journey of predictable length. The game even makes a lame attempt to reference Oregon Trail at one point but you can't alter your pace, hunt for food or any of that. All you can do is watch the caravan move and occasionally click a pop-up. While the timing of the events can be random, the results of the choices are predictable and usually so inconsequential overall they are essentiall cosmetic.
Much of the criticsm of the battle system revolves around the choices made for its turn-based system. While the system is valid, no effort has been made for the AI to take advantage of it. The opposing force scripting is simplistic in fact, that it is outright self-destructive with some units because simple checks were not put in place for splash damage abilities. The battles take place at scripted intervals with scripted rosters and all but one of the battle maps are simple rectangular grids.
Conclusion: Wait for a sale, turn the difficulty to Easy. Bear with the game and enjoy the art and story.

This is a very hesitant thumbs up. See, what this page kinda neglects to mention is this is part one of a planned trilogy. I mean, I don't think I can verbally describe to you the look of "what?" on my face when the credits rolled just after what felt like the end of the first act. And while I don't generally mind multi-part stories, I think each game should at least have a satisfying self-contained story that ties in with the larger story. One series I like to point to on that is Harry Potter. Each book in that series has a self-contained story, but they also all tie in to the series-long story. This game... there's not much in the way of resolution by the end is what I'm saying. I guess in some ways that's a good thing, since if the game were much longer it would start to drag a bit, but... I just wish I'd known.
Other than that, it's got a unique story, an interesting world, a unique visual style, the combat is decent (albeit a bit repetitive after a while), and I do genuinely think it's a good game; it just isn't a finished story.

I'm not one for writing reviews, but as someone who has played every Neptunia game localized I can't not make one.
Neptunia Re;Birth 1 is in simple words a fantastic JRPG. It may not as 'grand' as more mainstream JRPGs like Final Fantasy or the Tales of games, but it doesn't try to be and makes great use of what it can.
It's characters are all unique and personally I can't find one that I dislike. The personalities cover a wide range of the spectrum so there is almost definitely a character for everyone.
The fighting mechanics are quite simple yet effective: so if you want to grind, you can blaze through numerous battles quickly and when it comes to bosses, you can utilise the more varied commands to take them down.
The story is great and the dialogue makes it even better. Since the main setting is a parody of the real life console wars, you can expect a lot more parodies within the dialogue and it does not disappoint.
Another great thing about the game is that it does have some really good English dubs, (although there are very few problems at rare times). My only problem with the voice acting is that there is not enough of it. Main story scenes and various dialogue scenes have full voice overs but there are quite a few middle scenes which are devoid of voice overs.
I loved this game on the Vita, and while I never really care about frame-rate, having it run at 60fps looks amazing.
All in all, I highly recommend Neptunia Re;Birth 1 to any JRPG fan or any person who likes light hearted games.

THIS REVIEW IS A WORK IN PROGRESS AND DOES NOT COVER THE FULL EXPERIENCE OF THE GAME, SO FAR JUST THE FIRST EPISODE! (NON-SPOILER REVIEW)
Another Telltale Game Series, but does it live up to the hype or does it fail to deliver?
As a fan of the Walking Dead Games, and a fan of the Game of Thrones show and books, I am pleasently surprised that Telltale has succesfully implied the decission system on the Game of Thrones franchise.
The story picks up at the End of Season 3 (Show) and starts at the Red Wedding.
Here we have the House Forrester, which by my knowledge does not appear either in the show nor in the books, who has served the Starks for very long, but  am going to talk more about later.
Not only are you able to control one character, but surprisingly three, with very different story arcs. (In episode 1)
Decissions you make with one character are easily implied on the other and overall the decissions affect them all in a different way.
You will meet a few familiar faces from the show, for example fan-favorite Tyrion Lannister and his family-loving sister Cersei, but also a couple of new characters, who so far I really like.

After replaying Saints Row IV (and playing Saints Row the Third), I've decided to overhaul and update my original review.
It's a good game, (as a matter of fact, it was my first Saints Row game). I'd recommend it for anyone that wants a fun game that's not too serious. Anyway, here's my sort-of-in-depth review:
Gameplay: 82/100
SRIV offers a solid 8-12 hours of main story gameplay (16-20 with all of the side missions), and the DLC (which I picked up in the season pass), offers an extra 3-6 hours.  The gameplay was fun, similar, but at the same time totally different from Saints Row the Third.  The super powers added a whole other level to the game, and gave a fun experience.  The side activities (like store hacking, virus upload (a.k.a. survival), assassinations, flashpoints, etc.) were fun, but I found all of them, with the exception of store hacking, too repetitive.  There are the common 3rd person hiccups, but it really didn't hurt my gameplay experience.  The superpowers, while incredibly fun, made vehicles totally obsolete.  Two other things, most of this game's level design, among other things, are recycled from SR3 and there is no replay option for story missions, but I didn't feel that it was worth knocking off a lot of points for because it didn't hurt my initial or current play-through at all.
Graphics & Performance: 86/100
For a 2013 game, the graphics and performance are great.  I rarely had framerate drops on Ultra, although that may be due to the effects in the simulation.  SR3 gave me frequent framerate drops (albeit they were small) on all settings.  One problem I had was with the ship crew uniforms and some city textures (like ads or shop windows) being very lackluster.  I also noticed that there was a lot of "object crossing" (i.e. certain things like hair or weapons will enter into the character model).  It wasn't a big deal, but it would have been nice if they could have figured out how to prevent it.
Story & Characters: 82/100
The story and characters were great, as was the voice acting (to be explored in the next paragraph), but I feel that it lacked the substance and charm of SR3.
Soundtrack, Media & Voice Acting: 86/100
The soundtrack is alright, although I'm not a big fan of dubstep and some pop songs.  It was also nice to have the option to use the radio both in and out of vehicles.  However, the some of the music effects (specifically the one that plays when you jump) can be a little annoying (especially when it's not that much of a jump).
Interface & Controls: 85/100
It was a nice change from SR3, but I found the reaction time a little too slow in the menus and the organization could have been better.  The controls were nice and responsive.  I had a problem getting used to the tank and flying mechanism (which is similar to SR3).
Overall Rating: 84/100
I really enjoyed this game, inspite of the flaws.  Like I said earlier, I'd recommend it if you want a fun game that's not too serious.  One thing I would highly suggest to people buying this would be to buy the Game of the Century Edition, mainly because you'd get all of the DLC and because you won't have to deal with Steam recommending a game you already have.
tl;dr
Gameplay: 82/100
Graphics & Performance: 86/100
Story & Characters: 82/100
Music & Voice Acting: 86/100
Interface & Controls: 85/100
Overall Rating: 84/100

Everlasting Summer, a production by Soviet games, is amongst the first games I've played on steam.
I didn't really pay any attention to the visual novel tag either, so the game play I initially expected was a bit different.
In this game, it was different in a good way.
Once I got comfortable with the format of the style,
I saw the game more for what it is, and that's a well written "Read your way" graphic novel set so that you can't just skip ahead in the book to see what sort of fate would be ahead of you.
The game provided a wonderful first-time steam experience, which provided a favored theme and achievement that may've worked against the game a little.
First off, the game's free and take little space storagewise; thereby well worth it.
Though free and easily downloadable aren't really reasons to just go get the game.
It's a question of whether or not you intend to play that game and how often, and whether the content will make the game play well worth it.
The play-by-play and story-base writting ranges within decision to a certain extent,
however each result's worth-while,
else if you're taking a second time around, previously viewed sceene can be auto-forwarded.
Now, for the english version, Semyon, the protagonist, suffers from sudden darkness spells at the sight of nudity,
which really isn't a problem to me,
yet I can understand how participants might be frustrated that they would have to prove their age for adult content, in order to have that adult content censored.
Not like there's not a way around that though.
I've mention the achievement before, and yeah they can work against you a little.
I admit, the fact that the game had unlockable achievements made the game appear more attractive to play,
yet once I had my sights on an achievement, my index fingers become best friends with the space bar for a while.
I am happy to say, that there's a way to read back on the content with the expressions in mind.
You will definitely notice a theme throughout the game - catgirls.
I do not consider this a spoiler since once you go to exit you see a cat girl asking if you're sure if you'd like to leave.
This theme is reoccuring which begs a number of question like:
I though this flash back in time took place in late Soviet Russia? Where catgirls a thing there around that time?
My attempts at googling for answers didn't do much help, but I wasn't going to argue with it, the theme made for an intriguing gameplay.
So, it's the best for first-time users granted that you focus on enjoying the content, and not button bash your way through (or hold down spacebar for good measure),
And I'm a personal fan of the catgirl theme which I feel that my profile pic would give away.

Actual review:
XCOM in a way reminds me of the Fire Emblem series in terms of gameplay, although there are no waifus for you to romance and pair up with (Fire Emblem Awakening), and your abviously fighting aliens. Although XCOM, in my opinion, does share a featured quality which I love from both series, and that's the tear jerking momment when your favourite character bids their fair adieu as they fall to their abrupt end.
It happened to me many times over the course of my first playthrough, and it's the absolute epitome of frustration, feels, and hysterical laughter. I still remember my first KIA, and I was absolutly devastated when I saw my hard earned, fully speced out, veteran get mauled to death by a pack of bloodthursty chryssalids. Only then to see her return as a zombie ready to claw her petrified cadet's face off. I cursed at my monitor and grew heavily bitter, but I realized was truly inevitable and absolutely absurd that it had to happen to my prized, overly geneticly modified vegetable of a soldier. As my greiving and weeping subsided, I bitterly continued the mission, and decided to give her a fitting end by cleansing her rotting corpse with fire and then blowing it into chucks with a timely rocket. I was miserable after the mission was over, but I was convinced that losing one is better than leaving with none.
Overall, this game is really fun and absolutely addictive, but it really makes you alarmingly attached to your soldiers. Even when your units don't offer you dialogue, an H scene (Mass Effect), or even look at you in the eye(s), they'll follow your orders to their dying breath, and subdue enemies until you crush them with your advancements in science, engineering, gundams, lunatics, and geneticly nuked vegetables until you capture their captial city. And that's how you win a domination victory as Japan in Civilazation V.
10/10

Much like the film upon which it is based, experiencing Kung Fury: Street Rage is not an intellectual pursuit. Behind its attractively retro flair, complete with simulated bulbous low resolution Cathode Ray Tube display, stylized chiptune music, and sprite graphics, is an unforgiving test of pure reflex. The more you think while playing this game, the worse you'll do! There are only three buttons you need worry about: Right, Left, and Pause. Humorously, pausing the game takes it to a simulated blue screen of death, also providing you with the means to exit the game (pressing start again), causing the screen to warp and snowcrash.
While individual mileage may vary, I find that the wide variety of animations that Kung Fury can unleash to represent your simple one-button attacks to be amusing enough to completely override any semblence of boredom in the otherwise extremely simple concept of the game's mechanics. Its simplicity borders on elegance, or perhaps even meets it, as I do not believe they could have added anything to the game that wouldn't somehow damage the experience.
It boils down to this: enemies run at you from either side and you must attack them as they get close. Most are one-hit mooks easily dispatched, but as play progresses tougher and more complicated enemies arrive--ones that require frantic combinations of right and left attacks to take down, as more and more foes flock and swarm in an attempt to overwhelm you. And overwhelm you they will.
You can take three hits and then it's game over, to start again. There are no power ups, no way to heal yourself, no way to expand your character's capabilities, no other levels; this game is just You, Your Reflexes, and the High Score. Maybe it's not the most immersive experience in the world, but without a doubt it's one of the purest executions of a game ever expressed.
The fact that it's so aesthetically polished--not MERELY poor graphics but an entire suite of stylistic touches like glitches, rendering artifacts, all meant to evoke the limited hardware capacities of ages gone by--makes the whole experience an unexpected treat. Give it a whirl; you don't have anything to lose! ...except for maybe two bucks. But I humbly submit that it's worth that much.

So, just got done with the Normal campaign, and thought I'd leave my thoughts on it.
For Those Who Might Want To Play: The game has good opening introduction, a constant dark and oppressive atmosphere that matches the tone of the game, lots of lore tidbits for those who like that, that also reward exp for exploration. The class combination that I chose, Occultist/Demolitionist, was very fun, I liked that there were obvious flexibility choices as far as the styles of combat to choose from. I would have preferred access to better firearms/crossbows throughout the game. I felt mostly pidgeon holed into using two handed weapons to get the most damage done, with the best buffs, though what the dps counter showed for the weapons might not be telling the whole story. I wish there could have been a bit more diversity to the boss fights, like hazard events that you would need to interact with or avoid to progress/prevent a wipe. The extreme majority of the bosses were pretty Spank-n'-Tank, the last boss being the only one that I felt it necessary to regularly disengage from for my own good.
To The Developers: I would stand by giving the game a 9/10 for general enjoyability. It is not "rock-star amazing" like its the best thing ever, but I never once thought in my current 33 hours in, "Why am I playing this, or wow this is boring." I love the progression and escalation of the story. My class combo was very fun, very bursty, which kept the pace up instead of difficulty dragging me to a stand still. I would say that I wish there was more content, after the conclusion of act 4. The story feels rushed to a conclusion, or rather that I don't feel satisfied with where our involvement with the story stops. I would happily comment more elaborately on this, but will avoid leaving spoilers for the game here on the Review. Feel free to contact me if you want more feedback.

So this is how it started:
I wanted to play as a civilisation I wouldn't generally play as, so, after deciding to be Poland (out of a decision of Greece, Rome and Poland), I began. I settled Warsaw in where modern-day Texas is. Then I continued to build and explore. At six cities I discovered Persia and Russia.
Jump ahead about 5000 years, and I've discovered everyone. Another 1000 years and I'm hated by everybody. Jewish Germany declares war on me - ironic, right? As the Polish do, I invade Hamberg and raze it to the ground. I then launch an invasion on the mainland of Germany, breaking through Cologne and Frankfurt. Razing these to the ground, I continue to Berlin and Munich. Seizing Berlin, I decide to give Germany a chance to surrender peacefully, by handing me Munich without me having to invade.
They decline the proposal.
By this point I had researched the Manhattan Project, and I decided to test my new weaponry. Redirecting my atomic bomb to my own aircraft carrier, I sailed to where Munich rested. Surrounding Munich were my Polish Paratroopers, and what I would consider a tank regiment. Firing my atomic bomb, I wiped out Munich (and therefore Germany); the resulting explosion annihilated my entire military. All I had left were my four battleships, and two aircraft carriers.
Nevertheless, having defeated the world superpower, I continue. Declaring war on Russia, I forced my way through two cities, razing them to the ground. Next came Persia. Launching a two-pronged attack, I forgot to deal with Siam and India, who both declared war on me. They were also in the atomic age.
I watched with fear as Gandhi's entire nuclear arsenal was launched against Polish-occupied Berlin and Warsaw, destroying my nation entirely.
10/10 would get nuked by that Indian noob again!

Great game! Not perfect, but great all the same. I'd probably give it an 8 or 9 out of 10.
My main grievance about the game is that there wasn't enough of it. The campaign took me just 10 hours to complete and left me wanting so much more. The Banner Saga 2 is in the works, but would have wanted more from this initial installation (hopefully Saga 2 lengthens campaign quite a bit).
Other than that there are some gameplay mechanics that could use some tweaking. Combat can be repitive and difficult to get the hang of (I found myself on many occasions having to restart a fight because I realized I did something stupid without realizing). It would also be nice to have more freedom in the game. I'm not talking specifically of the linear storyline (I enjoyed that much), but to things like character progression, resource management, and stuff like that. It's hard to level up your characters and I guarentee you will have characters who get left unused as a result (I had a core group of guys that I consistently used even when hurt because the others weren't able to compete with harder competition even when healthy). Food, followers, and other things like that are commodities in Saga but I rarely had any control of how they were managed, collected, etc. (I wasn't sure what the point of some of them were for even by the end of the game. For example: your followers, Clansmen, use supplies in correlation to how many there are. More clansmen, more supplies needed to upkeep them. But they are different from your fighters, I never understood what benefit, if any, there was to having clansmen). Supplies are hard to come by and I found my numbers dwindling to attrition a lot the time so it would have been nice to have a few more methods of collecting resources in-game.
I should stress, the things are critiques after the fact, but they didn't mire the game whatsoever while I played it. This is a must-have Steam game in my opinion and will remain in my favourites list for a long time to come.

I could easily see a company making this game about an empowering journey of some little girl that would have loads of exposition and flash backs to a happy childhood and about how she just wants to find her mom but that♥♥♥♥♥♥isnt here, and its a far batter game for it. You literaly just wake up in some♥♥♥♥♥♥hole prison in a raincoat and you just go. In fact, there isnt a single line of dialoge in this game. This game tells you a story by just showing you everything, which makes the world far more interesting, because its fun to explore the unkown for yourself and let your imagination run wild thinking about what is really going on. This game just wouldnt be the same if Six, the girl in the raincoat, spoke and whined and whimpered or if some narrator was giving you a college lecture on the history of the twin chiefs.
The point im trying to make is that this game is very fun to play, and the game shows a lot of restraint with itself and lets you see this wierd world for yourself. The only problem I have with this game is that there is little to no reason to replay this game, and I dont see the need for a sequel. BUT, what would be awesome is if we saw more games set in this strange universe, maybe not playing as six but as someone else, and through them we could see more of this odd world.

Hardcore roguelike that switches between text-based conversations and turn-based grid combat, for better and worse.
Firstly, very story-heavy.  Some people won't like that.  The writing is solid for those with the patience and there's definitely a pay off as the game goes on.
Secondly, RNJesus is not your friend.  Resource management is gruelling and I feel like the game is a little unforgiving.
Speaking of which:  Thirdly, not a fan of how combat order is determined.  Two isolated dudes can take three times as many swings as the six guys surrounding them, which is a bit borked in my opinion.  Interesting concept; tying dps to health.
Having said that, the art is very appealing - Feels like the older Disney publications.
The music is really meaty and - much like the story - very oppressive.  There's nothing cheerful in this soundtrack.
Overall, I'm glad I played because I'm a huge fan of good stories, and TBS lives up to the 'Saga' element very nicely.  Wouldn't recommend it to people with short attention spans or who are frustrated easily, though.
