I'll begin with this, if you expect to be able to actually walk around freely, actually fight people, or test your skills at diplomacy, you'll be disappointed.
To start off, you find yourself at the Red Wedding, as a random squire (which you have no control over his appearance) for House Forrester (which you cannot select).
Immediately you're faced with the decision, to either save your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ friend's life, or warn your liege's son. The rest of the game follows this limited path of decision making, which always seems to be one-sided. Will you cut off the fingers of the 'innocent' man who stole from you? regardless of if that's the just thing to do? Or will you let him get away with it and cause everyone else to see they can get away with whatever they want as long as they give a nice argument?
But lets say you expect the RPG element of running around, viewing interesting areas as you interact with people, the enviornment, etc? Nope, sorry, walking around is reminiscent of street fighter, you can only move left and right, and it may even take you in a circle but don't expect to be able to rotate your camera, that's locked the entire game...
And combat, oh of course they'd allow you to move around, actually fight right? Wrong, instead you find yourself constantly trying to predict where the next circle will pop up on your screen to click. Maybe there will be an arrow signalling a sudden key press to the left or right, or the letter Q and E can pop up requiring you to rapidly tap. There doesn't seem to be a setting to allow these psuedo-action scenes to play out alone, and if you're too slow or too late then you're punished with an uncontrollable death.
The characters aren't much better, they're all cowards who can't act confident and stand up for themselves? You play as three: the Squire, who can alledgedly fight and act brave (yet we have yet to really see that); Lord Ethan (who is a child that is easily freightened); or Lord Ethan's Sister (who never seems to give you the option of the right thing to say). When your peers or bannermen begin to fight, yell, talk over you, whatever the case may be your character just allows it as he stands there with a worried look on his face. You can't shut them up, explain to them how you see it, or tell them what you expect. Instead you're stuck listening to Lords and Ladies run their mouths about how pathetic you are and how you're so dumb you can't even speak half the time.
It doesn't stop there though, every single dialog is timed, if you don't pick one of the limited choices (often none of them are what you would've done) then you are penalized with your character once again either being unable to say anything, the other people ignoring what you might of had to say, or of course, dying.
For a game with little to no gameplay, of course you'd expect some nice graphics, right? Well, ♥♥♥♥ you, because all you're going to get is this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ "oh it looks like it's painted, so we don't have to put any effort into making these characters high quality", and you're left with this ugly image on your screen. Who in their right minds said "Game of Thrones, the Video Game, must look like it was painted!" I mean really does it look painted in the ♥♥♥♥ing show?
But if you're interested in clicking sporadically, never beind able to speak your mind, and acting like a ♥♥♥♥♥ while you walk in a 2D setting, this game is for you!
P.S. This was only two hours of gameplay, and I never speed-through games.

There is an extremely well-written and in-depth guide entitled
for this game in which a player named "FeelZeSchadenfreude" shows how awful 90% of the guns/perks/classes are at high levels of play. After reading that I realized how unbalanced the game is and how little content there is (because one gun/perk/loadout/etc. is vastly superior to the alternatives). They occasionally add a couple of new guns, but I'm not sure if they disrupt the meta. Aside from the holiday updates (Sumer Sideshow, Halloween, Christmas) where you can tell a lot of effort went into zed design and such, the updates are mostly loot-crate cosmetics. It would be nice if the ratio of guns to hats were reversed because then it might not matter that some weapons are worse than other choices in that tier because you would have more weapon combinations to make up for it.
The first game has a better class leveling system [The "choose one of two perks every five levels" is inferior to the way you just got improved stats for your class in KF1] but the second game is built on a much better (more modern) engine so it is more fun to play. If they were to scrap the perk system and just go back to KF1s leveling the game would be perfect.
There is a horribly balanced VS mode that I don't think anyone asked for. The "holdout against endless waves of Zeds" that people DID ask for was turned into a separate, $40 Virtual Reality game which - at the time of writing - is currently "mixed" reviews on Steam.
Oh, and there is no excuse for scrapping a class and rushing out Survivalist. It's a bad class and the aforementioned guide does a great example of explaining exactly why. Tripwire is in complete denial over this class and seem to keep doubling down rather than admitting that it was a mistake.
(A couple of personal gripes)

This is one of my favorite games of all time, and there's a reason.
1. Story is great, it can get a tad bit awkward or "cringy" dare I say. This is really only an issue in the main game, and not the episodes. I think it's because they want you to get comfortable and have a liking to Alyx, but the technical limitations at the time prevented this slightly.
2. Graphics can still hold up. I know this sounds ridiculous, and maybe it's just my opinion, but the graphics are detailed enough due to bump mapping that as long as you aren't running your face into the wall looking for muddy textures, you won't see anything that looks awful.
3. Physics engine is identical to other valve games like Portal and CS:GO. This may be a pro or a con depending on your opinion of other valve games. It's a tad bit buggy at times if you're messing with props in odd environments, but the gameplay doesn't put you in situations where it will happen that often (unless you're trying to screw around)
4. Rumors of HL3 are circulating, so you might as well get the game if you want to be caught up on the game.

Yeah, you want to get this game if you like RPG. I can't believe I went so long having never heard of it.
The biggest unique asset of this game is really caring about tactical sense. Lots of turn-based isometric RPGs seem like this matters, but its really just run-and-gun. This game, however, teaches you early on that you have to implement line of sight, laying in wait, elevation, and most importantly cover. Not to mention a host of situation and class-based benefits. Another semi-unique element is that you have a whole barracks of troops, so you can mix and match your squad based on your mood, or what the mission calls for, and the classes are distinct enough for it to matter. If somebody dies? Meh, recruit another for just 15 credits.
This game seeks to solve a lot of the inherent "problems" of RPG games. Rather than move about on a map and pick your battles, the entire game takes place in one underground "base" and you then depart for missions you have little choice in saying no to. The missions themselves take place in extraordinarily designed environements, and environmental hazzards.
By eliminating the choices a "map" would create, the issue of scaling the enemy to suit your abilities is gone. Instead, you are just having fun completing the missions. The downside to this, however, is things go from intensely challenging to ho-hum once you get over the "hump" of the mid-game gear.
By far one of the best RPG games of all time, bringing WoW/Civ graphics to the genre as well.

Another great game by Ace, my go to developer for strange concepts that they make work. This one is a great platformer, disguised as an old directors cut B-movie, with the director narrating the happenings in a similar way to bastion, but with less focus on the actual character and more on how they did this scene or made that prop.
The game itself is more or less one huge level - the tower. And it's grand. It's rare to see a game so vertically inspired as this, and the developers make good use of it. Secrets frequently require you to drop down on them, or shoot them from above, and you have the ability to teleport from the air (or the ground briefly after landing) back to where you jumped from, so if you miss what you were aiming for or just feel like skydiving, it's null sweat. The view itself is phenominal once you start jumping from high up.
The graphics themselves are neat, but the art style itself is of course very different. Often enemies are clearly just people in suits, or are stop-motion animated. I personally find this amusing and interesting, but I know people who dislike it. The music fits the game well enough, and is similar to the music used in their other games, but if I'm being honest I can't really think of any of the tunes off the top of my head, so I can't say it's too memorable, maybe that will change as I play.
Look, all you really want is a recommendation, right? I say yes, wholeheartedly and unreservedly, and follow that up by saying you should also go and buy every other game ACE team has ever made, because they are all amazing. They get a strange concept that most probably wouldn't recognize the potential of, and make it work gloriously. I think I've said this before, but at this point every ACE game that comes out is an instabuy for me.

Great game - if Diablo III wasn't your cup of tea (or even if it was) get Grim Dawn, at $25, it's a steal.
I tried to think of anything that Diablo III seemed to have over Grim Dawn and I can't come up with jack.  Grim Dawn has a terrific atmosphere, graphics, physics, etc.
The combat is extremely satisfying and the leveling system is complex and enjoyable.  It's not only just that you can mix 2 classes, but you also get devotion points (think Skyrim's constellation upgrades) and then their version of "socketed items" also gives you abilities.
There are so many ways to get loot, craft loot, and obtain spells and abilities that it is really mind boggling and makes Diablo III's system look like it was designed for the lowest common denominator.
Grim Dawn is the thinking person's ARPG and is vastly superior to the other triple A games like it out there.  So for $25, what are you waiting for?

I've played Hyperdimension Neptunia on the original PS3 release, the PS Vita Re;Birth release, and now the PC version.  Each transition has improved the game experience for me, and I'm thoroughly enjoying this PC port.
Pros:
- Neptunia on your PC!  While the graphics don't appear to be much different than Vita, it's great moving it from a handheld screen to a computer monitor (or in my case, a large screen TV).
- Re;Birth vastly improves the mechanics of the original release on PS3
- 60 FPS!  Animations are fluid and quick.
Cons:
- It's not true 1080p.  In windowed mode you're capped at 1600x900, while fullscreen will upscale to your monitor resolution but all assets are still rendered at 900p.
- No graphics customization for lower end computers.
- Nothing unique/special added to the PC release over the original Vita release.
Overall, this is an excellent JRPG port in my experience.  While some users have been reporting crashes, visual glitches, and performance problems, I have not had any of these issues thus far.  The game has not crashed once, and the graphics are crisp.

+Parkour (hard at first, but gets easier once you get the hang of it)
+Pretty good story (not mindblowing, but not mediocre)
+Beautiful map and nice visuals
Cons:
-COMBAT (nice concept, poorly executed)
The long version:
Where this game really shines is in parkour. The controls are fustrating at first and will certainly♥♥♥♥♥♥you off and you'll be literally screaming at the game, but after the tutorial, you'll get the hang of it. The design of the map had a nice flow to it and I loved soaring through the rooftops without being stopped (unless the controls screwed me over). There are some parts of the map where I got completetly lost and did not know what to do, but all you got to do is be creative and try either a wall run or something.
The story was okay. I really did not get attached to the characters and the plot was not very compelling, but not bad. For me, the story got better near the end, but if you're looking for a story driven game, this is not for you.
The combat in this game is fun when it works and bat♥♥♥♥♥♥awful when it doesn't (which is probably every other combat situation you encounter). I thought the concept was good but the developers executed it poorly. Sometimes I would hit an enemy to temporarily stun them so I can get across a jump, but then my character would just run at the guy and get shot point blank in the face. Often times, disarming enemies worked... never. Maybe once if I activated slow motion, but I found it easier just to beat someone to death, which was a shame because I thought the concept of disarming your enemies was pretty cool until I tried it. I'm not trying to imply that everything that happens is the game's fault and not mine, because at certain points, it was my fault, but just look through the other reviews and you'll find it's just not me complaining about the combat.
The map is beautiful! Everywhere you go in the map, it has a sleek modern tone to it and the bright colors contrasting with the white buildings will make you feel like you're in a modern art musuem. I didn't have any problems running this game on max settings. If I didn't know this game was made in 2009, I would have thought it was made recently in the last year or so. And I was also suprised that I was enjoying an EA game. Never thought that would happen in my life time.
Overall, Mirror's Edge is a fun parkour game in a beautiful setting. It has a pretty good story, not mindblowing, but not crap. Combat is fun when it works and god awful when it doesn't. This game is fun, fast paced, and flows smoothly. It would be a mistake to miss this game.

Grim Dawn is an action role-playing game (rpg) developed by the company Crate Entertainment with emphasis on hack & slash.
+ Convincing presentation of a bleak world after a post-apocalyptic event.
+ Fitting background music enriches the melancholic atmosphere.
+ Creative level and monster design with much love for detail.
+ Diversified side quests with challenging boss encounters.
+ Exploration of the locations and its secrets is awarded with good loot and interesting lore.
o General layout and art direction of the game show parallels to its spiritual predecessor Titan Quest.
+ Fast-paced gameplay with a very good balance between combat and exploration.
+ Elaborate dual skill tree system, known from Titan Quest, allows various class combinations, each of them supporting offensive and defensive playstyles.
+ Alternative devotion system, basically a skill tree, adds further depth into character development.
+ Well done crafting system gives the player a multitude of customization options, providing useful items and trinkets.
+ Faction based bonus item system creates long-term motivation and additional customization possibilities.
+ Broad spectrum of enemies with different strengths, weaknesses and unique abilities.
+ For the masochistic gamers among us, the legendary
mode is available.
o The game follows the traditional concept of increased difficulty levels (normal, epic, ultimate), featuring tougher enemies and better loot.
+ Interesting side characters provide the player with entertaining information about the current and past events of the game world.
o Solid, slow-paced storytelling.
o Limited identification of the player with the protagonist.
Overall, Grim Dawn offers high-quality hack & slash gameplay with solid action rpg mechanics. It's a challange to reach the end and you can definitely end up putting a lot of hours into this. Addicitve and awesome all around.
In an earlier version of the game you were able to provoke the avatar of a god. In doing so, he would strike you with a lightning bolt, instantly killing your character in one attack with over 35.000 damage.

Singleplayer achievements: 124
Multiplayer achievements: none

-Clunky combat that relies more on the use of running away than fighting because enemies spot you behind walls and ambush you

The level design and the concept of the game is really good with only a few ares that have issues to do with the game not registering controls properly. I would definitely get this game on sale because it is good for a few hours but definitely not as long or in-depth as it could have been.

I'm usually not a big fan of arcade isometric(ish) shooters, but the theme of this one caught my eye, and I thought I'd give it a go.  In short, it's a lot of fun - though I'd recommend cranking up the default difficulty a bit, as it's extremely easy.
You play either a male or a female 'actor' who is travelling up a tower as part of a B-grade science-fiction movie. The director is giving the DVD commentary while you're doing it, and the creatures are a combination of people in rubber-suits, or clearly stop-motion models.  It's corny, and of course it's supposed to be.  You can even see the strings on the spaceships.
I really quite like it.
I was playing it on an Xbox controller, but found it a little frustrating. I switched to WASD/Mouse, and to be honest (apart from still needing to get used to some of the keys) it's much nicer. I guess it all comes down to what you prefer.
The sound is good. The music is typically B-grade scifi. The plot is non-existant, but the game itself is engaging enough.
Nothing's been particularly difficult so far.
If you're not a fan of the B-grade movie thing, then the attention to detail on this one is probably going to be lost on you Without this theme, it's really nothing amazing to write home about. With it, however, it's a lot of fun.
Whether it'll hold attention for subsequent play-throughs, I don't know.
Currently on around 35% special. Certainly worth the money so far.
EDIT - Took me five hours to complete on 'regular' mode, and probably will need to sit idle for a while before I can be bothered replaying it, but it was fun while it lasted. Nice twist at the end, though the final boss fight was a bit of a let-down, given some of the more fun boss fights earlier on.
If I was to give any advice, I'd say crank this up to HARD before playing. You'll get more mileage out of it, I suspect.

D:OS is definitely one of the best games I have played in a long long time, single player or co-op. Fans of games like Neverwinter Nights, Baldur's Gate, and similar RPGs will love this. The game itself is great, but the Divinity Engine toolset is disappointing. More on that later.
If you don't want to think and have to figure stuff out, you are not going to like this game. Unlike other games of the genre, D:OS does not hold your hand and tell you exactly where to go and what to do. There is a quest journal, but it is written from the perspective of "This is what we have learned about this situation so far..." and not "Go to X Town, give item to X NPC".
The turn based combat system is fantastic. The environment around you can be manipulated to help you win that tough battle. Ignite a barrel of oil, electrify a pool of water, build a barricade with anything and everything you can find in your surroundings to hold the enemy back while your ranged characters pummel them... do whatever you can think of to win. Spells and abilities can be used in succession to create devastating results. A poison cloud from one character can then be ignited with explosive results by another's fire-based ability.
Quests can be completed different ways. Say a guy wants you to bring him a special type of item. You know that you can get this by defeating a certain monster or taking the time to search other areas for it or even go to a nearby building where you know someone has a similar item and steal it from them. How you get from A to B is up to you.
Your dialog choices and actions in game change how those present view you. Get caught stealing and the shopkeeper might just summon the guards. Insult a guy enough and he might just not speak to you again. Fail to convince a goblin you only want to trade with his village and he might just call the whole village over to kill you. Choose whether you aid a certain being or side with its demonic captor. Just do whatever you can to reach your goal.
I highly recommend getting this game for the game itself. I have thoroughly enjoyed it and I still am even after nearly 80 hours of playing. However, if you're getting the game for the toolset thinking it's going to be simple and easy (like the NWN Aurora toolset), then hold off on that. In it's current state, the toolset is complex, not very intuitive, buggy, and has absolutely no official documentation (though they did make a couple of video tutorials that were just not helpful). I've used a lot of different editors in my years of gaming and I can easily say that Divinity Engine has the steepest learning curve of any of them. The video shown on the Steam Store page makes it look deceptively easy, and it just isn't. The scripting language is anything but easy (especially without any documentation as to functions). There's no word from Larian on whether or not they're going to doing something more intuitive with the toolset or even just fix the damn bugs, but if anything does change I will update this part of my review.

Anyone remember Escape From the Planet of Robot Monsters? These developers do. This game is so charming, and so much fun, and so packed full of variety, that for once it just seems churlish to pick apart the bad points. So here we go... Slightly annoying camera, got stuck in a few bits of scenery, film scratches, but no filmic technicolour look or film softening added to the image to nail the era. It's a little rough, basically. And YET, every time you're feeling a little bored, a new fun power-up appears, a new monster makes you laugh, you discover a mini-pilotwings challenge. A new kitsch-y homage, a new idea lies around every corner. The music is FANTASTIC, nailing the old sci-fi sound. This is a game packed with attention to detail, love and craft.
My one major niggle - the grating Director's commentary. The VO script is a great compliment to the main action, adding backstory, staving off repetition... but the actor? He's somewhere between Troy McClure and Bruce Campbell, but somehow, sadly, simply too self-aware in his delivery, it's too broad. The script is good, he doesn't play it dryly enough. He's just not funny. So it becomes annoying. I guess nothing can be done about that now.
Otherwise, superb all round. More imagination and heart than most other games on the steam store. Here's to some original thinking.

After the awesomeness that was the movie, I really wanted this game to (at least) be decent; however, I can't in good conscience recommend it because there's another game out there that's almost exactly the same except better in every way.
It's essentially a janky version of One Finger Death Punch, in that there's only two buttons: attack the guy on your left, and attack the guy on your right. Much like OFDP, you start out fighting some basic enemies who only take one hit, and then mix in other enemies who take multiple hits and occasionally dodge to the other side.
The problem is, I'm not entirely sure the developers ever played OFDP - or if they did, they didn't take the time to understand what made OFDP nearly perfect.
See, the key insight that OFDP had is that there's a rhythm to kung-fu fights; there's an ebb and flow, a flurry of action followed by a moment of quiet. This game doesn't have any of that; it goes at the exact same rhythm forever.
And that's completely aside from the fact that One Finger Death Punch took the concept significantly further than this game has, with unlockable skills, weapons, boss fights, and special attacks that send you leaping across the battlefield.
If you already own One Finger Death Punch and want to know how this game is different, go play Blind Survival mode with no skills enabled, then:
And you'll have an idea of what this game is like.
I'm not saying this due to some misguided idea that this game is "ripping off" OFDP - I'm actually very happy that another game's picked up on the ingenious mechanic. I'm just disappointed that this game is strictly worse than One Finger Death Punch.

I used to not recommend this game, but I have decided to change my review to positive. I don't mind that some people disliked my old review because they are overly defensive of the game, but rather I believe the game has become a bit more stable. Please keep reading to learn about the game's issue with crashing.
The game still crashes frequently but with it's most recent patch the game has become more stable. More importantly, the game renders itself at higher priority than other programs on your computer, so when the game crashes (and it will), some people may not be able to even CTRL ALT DELETE and bring up the task manager, instead just getting a black screen where the only solution is a hard reset.
The solution here is to make sure the game is running in borderless windowed mode, so it appears full screen, but is actually running in a window. This way the game will not be able to stop the task manager menu from appearing.

The gods are dead, the sun stood still and the world, inhabited by humans and giants, is on the brink of destruction - these are the first words of the Banner Saga introduction. The game was created by Stoic Studio, was founded by people from the famous BioWare Studio, gave the world such great role-playing games like Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect and Dragon Age.
World of Banner Saga is gloomy, harsh and designed to the last detail. Inspired by Scandinavian mythology and stories about the vikings. Before the player unfolds a fascinating story, will be given the opportunity to observe developments from the point of view of several different main characters. Hunter Rook with his daughter Alette are saved from their village, which was attacked by dredges, dark warriors, whose armies are threatening to destroy all life in this world. Giant Hakon leads an army together with the human prince Ludin to help Grofheim, besieged the capital of the Kingdom.
Banner Saga is role-playing game (RPG) with turn-based battles. During the 8-9 hours of the game player will have to make the hard decisions and none of the proposed options will be not definitely good, you always have to face the consequences of your decisions. The player will lead to the final goal not only the main characters, the number of which is constantly changing - someone will come, someone will leave, and someone will die. Also player will be responsible for the people, who walking in the caravan with him: refugees fleeing from dredges, who destroyed their home.
Especially I want to tell about plot and dialogues. All dialogues in the game are presented in the form of large amounts of text. The text is extremely high quality, it is like you situate in an interactive book where you decide what and how will happen next.
Music plays a huge role in creating the atmosphere of the approaching end of the world. Scandinavian themes  plays on the background of colorful snowy scenery and it is just incredible. Under calm music caravan covers the distance from one village to another, under the anxious music soldiers and giants go to the last battle against horrible dredges to protect their families. Under such musical compositions I would like to sincerely empathize with the characters.
For this game I would waste my free day, wrapped in a blanket with a cup of warm cocoa. The music and visual style of  Banner Saga make the game like complete artwork, which I will replay several times, to get new impressions.
10 brave vikings out of 10. Excellent.

TL:DR Good Game with much needed improvements over the original but with some noticable but avoidable bugs - chapter 1 boss crash after scripted death (Save before and repeat often and hope), SET COMPATIBILITY MODE TO XP to avoid post battle crash
Long version
While I have not played the original Vita version of the game, I did play the original neptunia 1 and nep mk2 on the PS3 so thats what i'll compare this too
The battle system from the PS3 original is completely done away with (thank god) and replaced with the now standard system which both mk2 and victory use.  Movement and aiming with a keyboard with default mappings is difficult but a controller is recommended. I have noticed that in my opinion the difficulty has been increased overall with a much steeper curve but after buying the plutia and peashy dlc to replace Iffy I have noticed it has got easier with a 2nd CPU
The remake system is a much needed addition which allows you to change dungeon items, enemy difficulty and other stats. Also welcome is the inclusion of many previous DLC characters like brocolli and MAGES as permenant characters ingame.
I'm not going to comment on fanservice since that speaks for itself but the humor from the 1st version has been improved upon to the point that its even parodying itself as a remake
but as all games there is some glaring flaws, grind syndrome is still existant, especially if you purchase the 3 additional content packs (300 lvls per pack allowing for lvl 999 characters) which are optional
the biggest problems is the constant crashes if you don't know why they occur with one potential gamebreaking bug that i've found
If you decide to skip audio cues after a battle (the fanfare and the level up audio) then the game has a high chance to freak out and crashes to desktop - this is the main downside to the remake/port but can be avoided if you are patient and wait for the speech to stop or change the compatibility mode to XP for the game
the gamebreaking bug is technically a spoiler but is a necessary spoiler to avoid it - at the end of the 2nd dungeon there is the first major boss in the game the 1st battle is a scripted death but the game often freezes before the following cutscene (from what i've seen online this is a common crash if you get a game over) and to date I cannot find a way to bypass or avoid it.
I have since gotten past it by sheer luck and repetition. my advice is to save at the station before the bridge and just keep repeating until it gets past it (I hope this is the only bug like this.
Overall I give the game a 7 out of 10 which would be an 8 if the bugs were fixed.

To start this review I will discuss the quality of the port for neptunia.
After scrolling through the negative reviews the most noticeable things i saw were crashes, bad optimisation and no graphics options.
As far as i have experienced, the game runs on a solid 60 FPS with sometimes (really low chances) a framedrop.
The only crash i've experienced is when
.
This was easely fixed by changing the compatibility mode to windows XP.
The lack of graphics options is not necessarily bad, I don't miss it at the moment. Though it would be nice if there were more options.
Window mode as a max of a resolution of 1600x900. Fullscreen is basicly borderless fullscreen. Fullscreen uses native resolution (in my case 1080p).
Outside of that I have not come across any other issues regarding the port performance.
I can't really say much about keyboard mouse support since I use a controller.
That said the lack of a button overlay when in events was quite confusing at the start (skip button, backlog and stop) and was a bit of a try buttons out with what their function is.
In my honest opinion IF did a far better job porting their game than Square Enix did with FF13.
FF13 may not have had crashing issues but FF13-2 did after selecting a timeline in the historia crux.
Side note to that: At least the ingame menu doesn't lag on neptunia.
Rounding this up: IF is in the right direction with their port of neptunia rebirth 1 and i am looking forward to rebirth 2.
Now onward to the game itself.
Story (generally summorised)
The game takes place in the world of Gamindustry where 4 goddesses each with their own respective country fight over rulership of Gamindustry. Our main female protagonist Neptune is one of those 4 goddesses and basicly got chosen to be the scape goat of the four by a mysterious figure in the background which made the other 3 goddesses gang up on neptune. Neptune falls down from the sky and lands right on Planeptune (basicly the country she represents) and loses her memories.
Currently as i am writing this review, i am in chapter 2 of the game and the story so far is basicly to my liking.
Combat
Not sure if the whole combat mechanics are original the closest thing i can compare it to is probably valkyrie profile (not confused with chronicles). But basicly its to my liking and it doesn't really get boring fast.
Exploration
The game is for the most part lineair regarding exploring. The dungeons are short at the start (which isn't bad because it gives the story a nice pace) but they do get longer as the game progresses further.
There isn't really an open world that u explore, you basicly get dungeons handed to you by the story and select that through the overworld (the overworld is pretty much Gamindustry as a whole).
Gameplay
The game is for the most part a mix of a visual novel and JRPG/strategy game.
Graphics
2D design of the characters are nice and unique in my opinion and thanks to live2D they become even more alive onscreen during the visual novel story parts. In dungeons the characters are all in 3D and look great.
The only less detailed part of the game is the textures of the dungeons, they aren't bad but can't say its amazing.
Beyond that characters and enemies alike both look great.
DLC
Are the DLC worth it? Well the only DLC i bought were the extra characters because... why the hell not.
I'm not sure what the additional content really entails since all of them have the same description.
Do note that the extra characters are kind of powerfull.... It's better to use them as a backup rather than main party members.
Diffeculty
In my opinion the diffeculty is set right. Not too diffeculty but also not too easy and with the planning system you can decide if to add tougher monsters in dungeons or even buff the monsters that u previously already defeated.
This game does entails some grinding but there probably will be an experience booster plan in later chapters?
Music
I like it, don't mind the repetition in certain area's. Battle music is nice and i believe there are 4 different tracks for that? Not sure.
Voice Acting
Done nicely (using Japanese dub myself). nuff said.
tl;dr
The game is great and optimisation is done properly.
It's a like it or don't like it game which can be very risky.
The game has dirty jokes and a lot of references and 4th wall comments.
IF did a great job porting this and i really hope it only gets better.
Looking forward to Re;birth 2.

This was a terrific game. It reminds me heavily of Inside. The music was terrific, the graphics looked beautiful, the controls felt odd at times but overall they were good. The story was intriguing and captivating. It took me maybe just over two hours to complete, but for $20. Despite the lack of campaign, I think $20 is a fair price.
There are a few issues with the game though. There's times where the AI enemies would get stuck on a bed/counter/doorway and I wouldn't be able to pass them without having to run up to them so they could kill me, allowing me to start at a previous checkpoint. There were times when I would hold down the 'A' or 'D' key to move, but in the middle of my character's stride, he would just stand still, I imagine he was getting caught on the invisible wall between the game-field and my computer screen, allowing him to not fall off the map, still irritating when I'm trying to run from an enemy.
Crouching in the entrance of the small corridors/airvents was a bit finicky at times too, having to line your character just perfect with the path to continue.
A huge flaw I had with the game; I finished every achievement in the game, including the one achievement that wasn't awarded to me (Hard to the Core - Finish the game in under one hour with 0 deaths). I spent so much time restarting the game trying to finish with 0 deaths, only to finish in 48 minutes with 0 deaths, and not be awarded the achievement.
I spent a lot of time writing about the flaws of the game, but I assure you, the game has much more positive aspects to it than negative. I'm impressed with the story most of all, especially the ending. It was unexpected and very much enjoyed.

As of Episode 1:
Great story so far as to be expected, however there are a few flaws. The interface is still a bit clunky, the field of view isn't optimal, and some little frustrating cliches such as two soldiers pausing to smile each other IN THE MIDDLE OF A FIGHT...you can guess what happens next. The different POV's are a nice touch but as an avid fan of ASOIAF it feels a little too convenient that House Forrester is in so many vital locations throughout the story. I would have preferred a story that didn't necessarily have to involve many main characters from the series, since it can verge on feeling forced.
On the plus side the voice acting is much better than previous Game of Thrones video games, the artwork is decent, and the world is consistent with the show so far. The choices so far haven't really been heartwrenching yet, but you can tell theres going to some major stuff going down later. Most of the choices so far have been the superficial type we saw a lot in other Telltale games, but I'm fine with having a good plot and being able to affect some details here and there. All in all Episode 1 is an 8/10, it's done a good job setting the scene and introudcing some likeable (and hateable!) characters. Hopefully future episodes can capitalize on the build-up.
All in all an intriguing setup for an immersive if a touch heavyhanded story. I would definitely recommend a buy if you have any interest in the ASOIAF story. If you've never watched or read Game of Thrones I can see the game being very confusing.

It's honestly hard to even lsit out all the things I love about this game, but in short: ACE Team has done it again, and I honestly can't decide if I like this or Abyss Odyssey more. Despite being a more story-driven game, DTM still bosts some replayability for all of its little secrets. Just reading the achievment list left me scratching my head: at no point was I ever aware that there was a even Ghost Pirate Ship with some kind of boss on it to fight. The combat is solid and enjoyable, the parrying is competent and functional for sure, and the ever changing environments and enemies keep the experience fresh.
This has to be the most honest B-Movie parody I've seen though. The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a really fun game. It's a 3rd person brawler with a 50's sci-fi aesthetic that is out of this world. This is the best looking game I've ever played. All of the environments are richly detailed and interesting to look at. The retro future look is done so well here. It's even better than in the Fallout series. The only problem I had with the look was some of the enemies are supposed to look like choppy stop-motion animation monsters, but they just come across looking poorly animated instead of that classic stop-motion animation look. The soundtrack has some really good songs that further sell the feel of the game world.  The combat is standard, but the sci-fi themed weapons are a lot of fun to use. The goal of the game is essentially to get to the top of a tower to defeat the big baddie.  This game is really more about the journey than the destination, though. The setup of the game is that a director is giving commentary on one of his old films so he's constantly explaining what's going on in the action and supposed back stories for actors that worked on the 'film'. This commentary adds yet another layer to the campy of fun of the game that is a constant blast to play through. The campaign itself took less than 5 hours to finish, but this is such a fun game world to explore that I bothered to get all the achievements. I was completely dazzled and blown away by this game. I highly recommend The Deadly Tower of Monsters!

From the start Child of Light reveals itself to be more than your average platformer. A cutscene opens up the game, like most other games use to converse, but the difference is tantalizing, delightful, rhyming in verse. It flowed like a lullaby, written as a bedtime story.

Over the time I played it I grew to love it for its beauty and mastery, its charm, and its whimsy.
I cannot express how much joy I found in playing this game. This is video gaming at its finest, where all forms of art are mastered beautifully. The soundtrack, melancholic yet hopeful, weaves with the water colored imagery and story, and even the turn based combat was invigorating. If you are a connoisseur of art, this is a game you would not want to miss.
The entire piece is rich; each singular medium flavorful in its execution. Some may call the story childish, however I believe its simplicity is one of its most emotionally impactful factors. You don’t need to second guess your mind, for your eyes, your ears, and your heart will write the story for you.

I am coming to Grim Dawn as a long time Diablo 3 player. I am not going to compare/contrast but I am sure my past experience affects my opinion of this game.
Grim Dawn is great. The sheer level of diversity is staggering and, at times, overwhelming. There are six "classes" to choose from and at level 10 you can choose a secondary "class". I am very pleased with how early on you are able to unlock the second class because I never feel gated or like I have to wait to start using the playstyle I want to use. Also playing a ranged character feels amazing, the responsiveness of the controls make kiting satisfying and rewarding. I LOVE being able to bind force move to left click and not being forced to equip a skill to that button.
At the time of this review I have 60 hours in the game and my highest level character is 45ish. With a cap of 85, I have barely experinced half of the leveling process. Grim Dawn is huge and if this is the type of game you like you will get more than you paid in hours of fun.
My favorite thing is that the loot feels powerful and satisfying. Many peices of gear, even at lower levels, give a new ability or passive buff. For the most part, the animations and buff bar are clear enough for me to know what is proccing and when. Oh, proccing! I know I said I wouldn't compare to D3 but can I just say that when an item says "15% chance on hit to proc" it really does proc on 15% of hits. Its freakin glorious.
Grim Dawn isn't perfect though. For one, I feel like I never really know what an ability does until I use it. It would help players know what to expect if skills were classified such as "targeted spell" "targeted ground effect" "area around the caster" "area around the target" and so forth. For some skills this is obvious, but for others its not and I have trouble theorycrafting if I don't understand how a spell works.
This probably comes from my D3 background, but I really have a problem with harder enemies that don't look like harder enemies. Bosses have large models and heros are marked with a star, but sometimes there are purple-named monsters in the middle of a mob and they look no different/bigger. I have died to these many times thinking I was just fighting an average mob and not realizing what happened until I was dead and able to hover over each enemy until I could see that one had a purple name.
Overall the game is well worth it. The build diversity is immense and the loot hunt is very satisfying.

I played the original on PS3, and as much as I wanted to enjoy it, the slow pacing of the game in general caused me to lose interest quite quickly. But, now that I can enjoy a remastered version on the master race's platform, let's see what we've got here.....
PROS
*Welp, the game certainly feels alot faster, and alot smoother. You'd probably think this isn't such a big deal being a turn based RPG. Trust me: It is. Anyone who played the orginial on PS3 will know what I speak of. All in all, the improvements and tweaks made here actually make the fighting feel fun rather than tedious.
*At first I wasn't sure about the revamped hub map. I kinda liked the idea of the revolving planes in the original, and only being able to jump to one another when they're in close proximity. But given the game's emphasis on 'exploration', or lack thereof, I came to see how restrictive the old hub really was. Admittedly, the map styled hub made things alot more convenient for me. Sometimes functionality is better than innovation.
CONS
*Graphics options. You have full screen, and resolution. That's it. And even then, you can only push the resolution up to 1600 by 1800. This isn't such a big deal, as the game isn't that graphically demanding. But still, a lack of graphical settings in a PC game is bad-especially for lower end rigs where being unable to scale things down will really hurt them.
*Dialogue. This is probably my biggest gripe. And it's not even about whether the original japanese audio is better than the english dub(I think both are as hammy as each other, arrest me for heresy). Rather, my issue is the completedness of each audio. In the english dub, more often than not will you encounter story segments that are left unvoiced compared to the original audio which covers the entirety of the game. I find this to be inexcusable. I mean, they brought the cast back to voice over the changes made to the story, so why not finish the dub? I don't think I'm the only one who wouldn't have minded paying an extra 10 bucks on the price if it meant having a complete dub.
*There was one more feature they removed from this remake. In the original, you were able to upload images and sprites to use in actual in-game attacks. While it turned out to be mostly useless compared to other unlocked abilities, I'm just gonna say this: I WANT MUH TROLLFACE FIRE ATTACK!!!!!
... But despite this, it's a game I'd recommend picking up while the 50% mark is on it. The gameplay feels more solid this time around, accompanied by a fun, if somewhat nonsensical story.

There is so much I want to say about this game, but in the interest of your attention span I'll do my best to only play the highlight reel of the thoughts rushing through my head.
This game is a mixture of both the old and the new. There is a large part of it that reminds me of the RPG's I grew up with; they didn't hold your hand, they were tough without being unfair, they were whimsical high fantasy with hosts of interesting interactable characters. Divinity is all of that with modern day graphics/tech; it's a beautiful game, a young body with an old soul.
I'll say this, if you're a new school RPG hound coming off of games like Skyrim that hold your hand like an overbearing parent...well, then you may not enjoy Divinity. This is more Morrowind than Skyrim. It tosses your♥♥♥♥♥into the world and says, "have fun". You won't know how to craft. You won't know how to barter. How certain spells interact with the environment. But, you will learn, over time. I was 20 hours in and still discovering new and wonderful things about this game. However, I never felt frustrated. That's the key thing to point out, it makes discovering all of these little mechanics a joy.
There's so much content here that I can't really get into it all. So many secrets to discover. Incredible loot. Interesting quests...from nurturing a blooming romance between two cats (yes, you read that right), to deciding the fate of a love sick ogre and her human companion. You'll raid dungeons and haunted caverns, you'll fight witches and fire demons, you'll argue with your party members about your decisions; who lives, who dies?
Most of all, if you're committed to learning the game, you'll have fun. Don't be put off by the learning curve, there are plenty  of guides online, plenty of people willing to lend a helping hand. If you love RPG's, you'll love Divinity. If you've never played an old school isometric RPG, well, I can't think of a better place to start.
Best wishes

Want to give a little love to Banner Saga (available on Steam, Android, and iOS). I've had this game sitting in my library for a year, but I decided to play it a few days ago. I didn't stop playing and neglected to do homework until they very last minute.
Banner Saga is a RPG-TBS similar to Final Fantasy Tactics, Disgaea, and X-Com Enemy Unknown. While not as in depth, you do need to consider how your characters develop and carefully navigate battles. When not in the fight, your cast of characters are traversing the icy plains and dangerous mountains while avoiding the hordes of an evil army known as the Dredge. Along the way, you make tough choices that can result in rewards, death or departure of characters, and some that leave you completely oblivious to the results.
With a beautiful setting and graphic style, a lovely and fitting soundtrack, my only problem was that this game was too short. For $20, about 7 hours of gameplay before I beat the game was disappointing. There was so much lore and so much more of the map that I was hoping would be explored, but the game abruptly and unexpectedly ends. If $20 is too much, then you can get it on mobile devices for $10. Of course, you can just look out for a Steam sale.

Oh the hype train for this game. I put off buying the Banner Saga for a while due to some sceptical comments i read about the game. I had heard it was fairly lengthy and the story was relatively good so in the end that was enough for me.
The positives really are in the way this game looks its very much like playing an old disney fantasy esc film. Its stricking in its colour scheme, that much is sure however during "cutscenes"  if you can call the coversations of text, cutscenes the still characters portraits dont respond physically to anything going on around them and this can create a disconnect between their expressions and whats actually happening.
The game is broken up into three parts the camping which is where the covos/levelling take place, the trekking, which is basically just you watching your little ant party move left or right.  And the combat which is about deciding whether to damage health or armour. Attacking armour first means more damage can be inflicted to the health while attacking health first will mean the enemy wont do as much damage with less health. Simple.
Turn based strategy how i love it! most of the time. This game quickly becomes dull, the enemies are the mostly the same and the action doesn’t leave much to the strategic eye compared with say, X-com or Civ. You will quickly find the best strategy and the many unused characters in your party will soon become useless because why would you use anyone thats woefully underleveled and under powered.
While there’s something relaxing about the trek across the frozen tundra there is also a tedium to it. Sure random events pop up but they do little to effect the course of the game. Alot of big decisions are actually arbitrary and change little in the narrative. This game feels less like an RPG and more like a adventure game with RPG elements tacked on.
Final thoughts, I don’t get the hype I really don’t this is an average game it really is, to me at least. The lore in the background of the story seems awesome , the map is huge! But neither are utilised to there potential, you just get carried through the story down a linear path and don’t really influence it in any great way. The art is lovely but beyond that what is there here to become engrossed in? By the end I really couldn’t be bothered It took me 7 hours and it was a slog for the last 3 the combat just didn’t go anywhere beyond its simple mechanics. The story was interesting to begin with but soon became flat at the half way point, no questions I had were answered, and at times it became rather predictable ( think game of thrones). When I have to force myself to finish something I cant recommend it, its as simple as that.

Ever wanted to be in a "B" movie that could be featured in an episode of Mystery Science Theater 3000? This game is probably about the closest that any of us can reasonably expect to come to such an experience...
The game is a basic isometric hack and slash adventure game. Action-wise it is not trying to reinvent the genre. However it is cast in a very inventive way: You are acting out the actions of the protagonists of a classic "B" movie being re-released on DVD while the director of the movie gives commentary about the film's production.
The presentation of the game is outstanding. It looks very much like an old sci-fi/horror flick from the 50's or 60's, complete with cheesy special effects such as visible strings holding flying creatures aloft.
"The effects guys promised me the strings wouldn't be visible..."
In addition to the awesome graphical presentation the director of the film is constantly talking about the production whilst throwing off many off-color stories of his egomaniacal excesses and abuses of power. This commentary is absolutely hilarious at times. Best of all, the narrator reacts to the things that you do, especially when you do things that are off-script or if you take your time in an area.
To sum it up, the game is a hilarious sendup of the best of the worst of Hollywood and a fun action game at the same time. Highly recommended, especially to anyone old enough to have at least seen these types of movies on late night tv.

An excelent game. It is a comedy, but the comedy does not get in the way of the gameplay and actually improves on the experience. Secrets and collectables can improve the gameplay thourgh upgrades, but I found that I did not need to collect them all to finish the game.
This game encourages exploration but it has a streamlined sense of continual progression. This is what I would say is it's greatest strength. You can fall down the Deadly Tower to get bonuses or reach secret areas without losing any progress.
In fact... there are two mechanics which I say make this game flow perfectly, without which would have made The Deadly Tower of Monsters a frustrating mess otherwise:
1) Checkpoints that, once you reach them for the first time, you can teleport to at any moment. This makes exploration breezy and also allows the player to have a sense of progression and sucess.
2) An ability that allows you to teleport back to a platform you just fell from. This inclusion was pure genious. First, you can fall great hieghts to get items like rings and not have to backtrack. If you miss a landing (which you will do A LOT) you can try again immediately. If an enemy knocks you off a platform... it is no loss, simply teleport back into the fight!
These two gameplay elements, in my opinion, make this game wonderful.
There are some other points of note:
Pros:
-Loading times are great. You can seemlessly fall down to a lower level without a loading screen. Teleporting up to a higher level happens in moments.
-It runs very well. If you don't like the esthetic (choppy, like an old movie would be)... you can change that.
-A large variety of enemies.
-The hilarity of dying (the load *thump* and subsequent ragdolling, combined with the comentary, always gets me).
-I would call the sound design great. The soundtrack in particular really captures the feel of an old 30's sci-fi b-movie like Flash Gordon.
Cons:
-The upgrade system is a bit... janky... (gold is so abundant it does not factor into anything, for example. I forgot I had it).
-The camera can be a bit wonky sometimes.
-Some weapons are utterly useless (bye bye shiv). Others are very OP. (lasergun FTW!)
-Movement in general can be frustrating at certain moments. Three of note are: Trying to land on a small platform using the jetpack, using sprint on conveyor belts, one or two sections where the camrea angle makes platforming a nightmare.
Overall I enjoyed The Deadly Tower of Monsters very, very much! Probably one of ACE Team's best games yet, if not their best game yet.

I've been playing Divinity: Original Sin for some time now and what a joy its been. Anyone familiar with the other Divinity titles truly must purchase this little gem (and yes, it's worth the full price). If you're more familar with games like Baldur's Gate then likewise, you'll feel right at home here. If I were to compare the two then I have to say D:OS wins hands down. The turn based combat is fun and challenging, particularly in boss fights, and the game has lots of humour strewn throughout (Weresheep anyone?). The quests are completely non-linear, which can be as rewarding as they are annoying at times. Being so non-linear you're often left with very little information and if not completed in the right order then you can end up botching a mission without even realizing it. Some of the puzzles are ridiculously complex, so if a challenge is what you want then look no further. I've literally spent hours looking for hidden passages and switches!
Overall a very solid RPG and with the modding community involved and the games level designer, I can see this game living on for many years to come. Add to this the fact that Multi-Player is so much fun, and all in all this game is a winner.
Highly recommended for traditional RPG players and Strategy fans out there. I must leave you now. I have to go and hook up my Cat friend Unsinkable Sam with some P-U-S-S-Y. ;)

Overall, the game is pretty fun, looks nice, sounds nice, and has a good story. However, there are some major flaws that do take away from the whole experience that tempted me to give the game a thumbs down. This is mainly due to controls and design. I'd be lying if I said the whole game was a smooth experience without any problems that weren't my own mistakes. I honestly found myself fighting with the controls several times, causing me to die in a stupid way and forcing me to do that part of the level again. I don't know if this is because it's an older, imperfect game, or if I simply couldn't get used to them throughout the entire game. There's one other major problem for me, that being the way the game treats combat and enemies. One of the first things the game teaches you is to try your best to avoid enemies and only fight if you really have to. After a couple of levels, I am taught the exact opposite. I find myself knowing exactly what path to take to avoid enemies and get out as fast as possible, but it just so happens to lead to a ladder or door you can't open like any other that only lets you go at a turtle's pace compared to the trek over there, meaning the enemies (all of which have guns) can easily shoot you down while you're trying to escape. After a couple of tries, I decide to try to take on the enemies face to face, and only after I take the time to clear everyone out can I actually get out alive. This gets especially irratating because you go from segments of running around buildings and rooftops to slowly fighting your way out, plus the fact that you're not supposed to really be fighting, as you would be able to tell from your vulnerability and inability to do real damage to enemies with what you have. The game seems to punish you for rushing through but encourages you to do so anyway through dialogue and mechanics. The parts of the game in which you are just running from rooftop to rooftop or chasing after some other guy are legitimately fun, however, which I would argue balances out the problems I listed above. If anything, I would want to give the game something between a thumbs up and a thumbs down, but I'm putting a thumbs down for those major flaws.
TL;DR- Game's pretty good, but controls are weird and combat is terrible but encouraged for some reason.

, an ARPG by Crate Entertainment, strives to satisfy as many diverse player types as possible, offering a huge amount of choice to have fun your own way. From its deeply customizable dual class system to its abundance of exciting loot, there’s a lot to sink your teeth into — no matter what kind of ARPG gamer you are.
, like any ARPG, has multiple classes to choose from when you first create your character. These are: Soldier, Demolitionist, Occultist, Nightblade, Arcanist, and Shaman. While you can probably guess what some of these classes are like to play, the options of how to build them go beyond simple archetypes of just “melee tank” or “glass cannon mage”. Each class has various skills that offer different ways to utilize its intended role most effectively, and the choices only become greater after selecting a second mastery for hybrid builds. It’s possible (and encouraged) to mix skills from two classes, creating lots of variety like close combat casters, dual wielding brutes, and life-draining pet masters.
To top off the already excellent customization,
has something very unique called the Devotion system. It’s based on constellations that you can apply Devotion points to, which are obtained from restoring shrines throughout the world. Each constellation offers various bonuses and even special Celestial Powers that augment your class skills. The tricky part is navigating the unintuitive UI and deciphering the dependencies and optimal path to unlock what you want. It’s quite complex and can be overwhelming at first, but Devotions are a really deep and rewarding way of offering further build variety that I’ve never seen before in an ARPG — hats off to the dev team for this great feature.
Another thing that
gets right is its crafting system. You’ll find materials and components as you kill enemies, with different ones dropping more frequently from certain enemy types. This gives you more control over targeting what your specific character needs, and feels more like a loot hunt than a slot machine. These items can be combined using recipes — some even of Legendary quality — to create top tier gear or modifications to boost your damage or mitigation. With this crafting system, you can target new gear upgrades, or cover a gear piece’s weakness. In fact, crafting is actually useful all the way until the endgame.

The gameplay itself can be thought of as a double-dragon RPG Binding-of-Isaac mashup with lasting replayability. The 1-UP experience is lovely, but you'll need a friend (or three) to fully appreciate this visionary work of genius.

I put a lot of time into this game.
Graphics: This game looks pretty good for an indie title. There's a lot of gore which is nice and the way zeds fall apart when killing them is satisfying. It's not perfectly optimized but there have been a lot of improvements since release.
Story: Who really cares about the story? There's no single player campaign. The different maps have cool bits of lore here and there, but you're not missing much if you don't notice it.
Gameplay: The number of classes, weapons, and different types of zeds offer very versatile gameplay. There are some obviously underpowered weapons and classes, but for the most part, Tripwire did a good job at balancing the game. The perk leveling system is pretty fair, but requires a lot of time. Once you reach max level on perks, it feels less rewarding when you continue to play the game, but it's still fun for me after hundreds of hours. The game can get challenging at some higher difficulties but after some time of patching, it's actually fair. You just need a really good team. Speaking of team, the community is pretty chill. Finally, I would just say thatthe gamepla is very addictive. Mowing down waves of zeds is just so indescribably satisfying. It can get clunky sometimes. You might get caught on a corner and then it's game over in 5 seconds. The other thing is that boss fights can get stupidly long if allies get picked off early on. You can exploit the kite method to win just about any boss fight.
Overall 8/10

I liked the way that I had to balance my renown between upgrading my party and keeping the entire caravan alive. The combat was a little tough to wrap my head around at first, but it definitely made me play in a unique fashion from other tactical RPGs. Because attack power is limited by a unit's current health, and a unit from each team alternates in the turn order no matter how many characters are on each side, I found myself trying to damage enemies but leave them injured for a while instead of taking them out completely. The ability to damage armor made for some interesting decisions. (Should I hit the enemy's armor so that my archers can do more damage on their next turns, or aim for the body so they can't do as much damage to my units?) The giant Varl (and certain Dredge) take up much more space than humans, so I found positioning during battles to be incredibly important.
The little events that pop up while traveling could be nail-biters at times. It was tough to figure out what might happen for each decision, and I wasn't always happy with the results, but I stuck with them anyway.
I actually thought I was going to lose the final battle, but I got lucky and finished off
with an attack that only had a 20% chance of connecting. To my surprise, it was a hit! If I missed, my party would have been wiped out.
I played mostly during lunch breaks at work, so I played without any sound for almost the entire game. I've heard that the soundtrack is pretty great, so maybe I did myself a disservice there.
I found the world of
intriguing, but it left many open questions so I greatly look forward to the next game in the series.

Forgetting for a second that the game is in dire need of a proofreader, the UI and mechanics are a mess. The HUD that appears for each character can hide important visual information in a battle. You can "lose" a medium-sized character behind a large creature or inadvertantly click an action button while trying to click something else. Playing the game for the first time requires a lot of trial and error, which would be okay if the game allowed you to save. As it is, it appears to save automatically every 30 or 45 minutes with no option to skip dialogue or the long sequences of Oregon Trail-like movement.
The game begins with a notification that your choices affect the outcome of the game, but I was on rails for the seven hours that I played.
I continued playing despite the issues I encountered because the world that was being built appeared to have promise. After multiple ominously vague and poorly written scenes, I wasn't interested anymore.

First off, this game is beautiful. Breathtaking, even. The art style reminds me of the old Lord of the Rings animated movie, but only a bit. The characters and their designs are all very interesting to look at, but the backgrounds, especially when traveling, are incredible. I can't stress enough how wonderful this game is to look at.
Luckily, the game itself is very good as well. The story seems like the same old "unstoppable monsters invade and can only be stopped by wizards" at first, but after a while, you realize there is a lot more going on. On top of that, the characters themselves are well-written and entertaining, and the background history and the map alone are full of tons of information to immerse yourself into.
I have a few gripes about the game, though they aren't big. The first pertains to the lack of a tutorial that makes sense. I played through the game about halfway and then restarted because it took me that long to figure out what all the stats meant for my characters. Maybe it was just me, but I found that to be confusing. Second, while it made me feel good to save as many of my clansmen as possible, I eventually learned that there is really no downside to letting your people starve, except morale, which is hard to keep up anyway. The developer should make it more worthwhile to keep your clansmen alive (not to be confused with your fighting party.  Play the game, you'll understand the difference.)
The biggest complaint I have about the game is the save system. What happened to the days when you could save whenever you want? The save system in this game is difficult, and routinely sent me back a ways if I was killed in battle. Repeating the same parts of the story over and over was not my favorite part of playing this game. It wasn't a dealbreaker, but it lessened the fun at times.
All that said, this game was great. It was a bit short, but what it lacked in length it made up for in substance. I can't wait for the next chapter in the saga.

The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a isometric brawler with great presntation and a sense of humour. The levels are laid out like old time movie sets, and the effects are made to look like old time special effects: You can see the string on the ship while flying, The jungle trees are made of plastic and the Dinosaurs are stop motion animated. Its all set up like your watching a director's commentary on the DVD release of a schlocky Sci-fi film from the Drive In days. The narrator is a great touch, breaking the fourth wall and basically talking jive the entire game.  The action is basic but the presentation makes up for it kind of like the deadpool game. Grim Dawn is an ARPG that does very well overall but lacking in some areas
- Exceptional character progression system - Original and thought provoking. Choices carry weight but are not irreversible. So many layers of customization that it almost feels impossible to end up with the same character as somebody else.
- Great loot system - Items have a lot of variation and you can really specialize your gear to fit your character very well. There are item upgrade, blacksmith, merchant, and item salvage systems to add more flexibility. However I would often find gear that was 10+ levels too high or too low for me when fighting monsters close to my level.
- Good combat. Not as responsive or flashy as something like Diablo 3 but still very well done. Abilities often seem pretty boring until they are upgraded and other effects added to them. The difficulty didn't become a factor until level 20 or so for me. Level 20+ is starting to feel challenging and keeps me awake - which some ARPGs can fail to do
- The "mood" of the game is fairly boring you'll find the same enemies here as other RPGS and even in the same standard sequence (zombies, humanoids, demons). Although the graphics are as good as it gets for ARPGs right now, I was never impressed by what I was fighting or where I was fighting it.
- Multiplayer feels like it still needs a bit of work. Would like to be able to drop in/out of games using the Steam friends list. There is no option to teleport to other party members. Party member's icons will disappear from the mini-map when players are only a short distance apart. Staying with other players is harder than it should be.
For me, its a solid buy. Pros outweigh the cons by FAR. Definitely worth the price - 8/10

Grim Dawn has a lot in common with the first game in the Diablo series and its somewhat similar to the Torchlight games. It has a raw edge that was lost in the latter Diablo reiterations and shares some of the quirky mystic technology steam punk elements found in Torchlight.
Is it as good as Diablo or Torchlight? I'm not sure its entirely fair to compare theses games too directly as they do have some differences but certainly its enjoyable for a lot of the same reasons. You get to gain skills and unlock quests which in turn builds on the overriding storyline . Plus as per most games of this kind you can add armour and weapons.
Is there a downside? I personally do find some of the maps a little overly "big". It can be quite hard at times finding locations and its not always clear what it is you are supposed to do when you get there. Some people I know like non-linear games but I'm a casual, on/off game player so for me its not so much of a benefit. The other challenge with this game is the respawn fucnction. If  you only play for a limited time you can find you have to  face down tough opponets again and again which can get repetitive. It would be nice to be able to turn respawn off if desired.
That said theres a lot more to like here than not. I believe this is an indie title too? For a first effort this game really is remarkable. If you like games like Diablo and Torchlight you will most likely enjoy Grim Dawn.

If you want an immersive, rewarding and friendly experience - this game is a must. It is quite possibly the best RPG that I've played all year - and it manages that because the team prioritizes engine and game aspects above graphics, (And that's not to say it looks even remotely bad.) The enemies are varied, the loot system is impeccable and the item based skill sets are fun, open ended and infinitely interchangeable.  I think I'll be stuck in the Grim Dawn for a very long time - and I couldn't be happier with it!

Almost definitely the pinnacle of the series based on what I've played (III - VI). It allows for small, rich nations to exist and opens up many options for peaceful, cultural play, something nigh impossible in most of the other games in the franchise. The AI still tends to be quite nonsensical and warhappy, unfortunately, and the vanilla game is very inadequate compared to the Complete Edition. One of my favorite games of all time, with the only downsides being 1) still more could be done to allow more strategic and diplomatic play, and 2) it lacks many significant mods, which is what made Civ 4 last so long for me.
If you have to choose between this or the newly released (at this time) Civilization VI, get this one (the Complete Edition) on sale and wait until Civ 6 gets more patches and expansions.

Can't recomend the game enough. The game is updated every few months providing plenty of time to test out the new additions and get used to the tweaks. The devs are active in the steam forums and are VERY open to discussion and reccomendations.
gameplay:
one player (chosen at random) controls the hero at the start, the other players are ghosts that control the monsters and traps.
dungeons are randomly generated and each room has a minimum pentagram(monster spawn point) equal to the number of players controlling ghosts.
each player has 3 monsters based on the god you choose to worship.
god can also provide a bonus to your hero character.
evolve monsters by damaging or effecting the hero.
branching monster evolution tree. While they are fairly limited there is still a large selection and every combination is possible.
definitely more fun with people but single player against AI is fun as well.
really the only negative is that when playing with 4 people it is possible for one player to be underleveled in one form or the other.
if the other 3 players are the only ones getting a chance at being the hero then the 4th player has higher level monsters but the lowest level hero fighting the higher level monsters. granted they will gain xp for killing the hero (which is usually enough for a 1-4 level up). the player would at this point have a massive stockpile of gold (also gained from harming the hero) and can purchase a large amount of upgrades provided they can find the store on that floor.
finding the store isnt dificult because the doors are marked with a red stairs (end of floor) blue portal (boss aka how to win the game) an anvil (shop) or a ? if an area is unexplored.
ranged weapons have been fixed from earlier versions where they were clunky but are now much smoother to use.
bosses: there are 2 bosses
a 3 headed hydra where each player controls a head
and a squid monster where one player controls the eye and the other 2 control tentacles.
great party game
