Having played only ten minutes of Ricochet I can assure, without a microgram of uncertainty,  to anyone of any background, that the interactive experience known as "Ricochet" is the cornerstone of Human achievement in the arts--nay--the peak of man's consummation itself! I see myself to be perpetually indebted to whatever deity unfurled the momentary lapse and position in which not only is this masterwork accessible, but also that I dwell in the juncture of living among the virtuosos who gave birth to the interactive marvel. How might a single mind solicit to inspect such a transcendent monument? Be forewarned, dear reader, that I, nor any man, could possibly hope to dissect a work of this calibur by his lonesome. Hell, I refuse to consider that an array of one thousand strong could decipher it! However, similar the prodigies that created it, I can only hope to muster the copious amounts of genius pouring from this work and cram it into the confines of the english language.
Upon initiating "Ricochet", you are greeted with so much symbolism to consume that most average citizens of our realm would choose to exit such a dense and meaningful screen. It is too much to the man with an anemic consciousness. I hardly know where to start when considering bringing this knowledge to the common people. I shall begin with how the work addresses the aboriginal of life and nature itself--birth. The anterior screen showcases many images, one of which tends to dominate the human's attention, as it is the most leviathan icon currently viewable. The gargantuan circle adorned by futuristic glows and structures is a symbol for the birth of the individual, as well as the birth of man into the technological age. Allow me to elaborate. The neo-digital ring depicted is an obvious allusion to the birth canal that nature devised each human to pass through. "Ricochet" proves this by how close up to the circular (or rather, somewhat polygonal) shape the art goer is. The moment is almost demonstrated as if your head is about to pass through, yet you are not quite out yet. You, dear reader, may be asking "Well, if it were the birth canal depicted, why isn't there a light on the other end? Isn't that usually how the birthing process is shown?" Well dear reader, you are absolutely right! Keen observation of yours, if I do say so myself! However, this is clearly intentional coinciding the entirety of "Ricochet"'s premise. You see, "Ricochet" proposes that in a rapidly advancing digital age, you are born into as much shadow as you were conceived in originally, hence the futuristic design of the configuration. Whether or not the craftsmen of this piece intended to imply that we are merely headed in that direction or we have already lived this concept is entirely disputable. There is much, much more to discuss about this object, but for now the picture requires more context, so I shall leave it at that. Moving on to the next point of interest, another image stands out. Yes, the icon associated with the game's title (to be discussed later)--the feature's logo. On first observation, one may assume the logo is but a relapse of something straight out of a 1980's film--font and all. Be that as it may, the visual holds a profound connotation. When the logo is rotated 180 degrees, the image appears to imitate the lower section of a triangle! Of course! Now, as you would assume from such a work, this holds a variety of nuance. However, I will discuss my interpretation of the logo's meaning. You see, the bottom of a triangle can be associated with the masses. The largest in number, yet trampled upon by its aristocratic counterparts. A classic case of the proletariats versus the bourgeoisie. The logo attaches itself with the work--"Ricochet". Clearly, the masterpiece's author's intended to represent the common man. Not only that, but the logo suggests something more, as it is rotated so the bottom of the triangle is at the top, The rotation confronts the idea that this piece will give the proletariats the power to overthrow the few that control them and restore power back to mankind itself. While this has not happened, I presume that the craftsmen who administered "Ricochet" assumed that would happen. That is one of the major reasons for the game's futuristic settings, after all. "Ricochet" shall not bring light to the people until technology and the people have collided with one another, allowing the work's true power to disseminate. Such tenacity bequeaths my soul optimism for our posterity. What beauty to behold, the day "Ricochet" provides its rightful nectar to the dry third eyes of the public! Excuse me, I got a tad passionate there. Yet, the principal still stands. I digress, there is more to discuss, and so little allotment for one lifetime! The next immensely abstract element of "Ricochet"'s title card are its four options. Of course, an important element to any interactive piece: choice. "Ricochet" insinuates that any choice you make can be boiled down into four simple decisions: "Find, Create, Options, and Quit". Allow me to elaborate on each of those phrases. Find--discovery, you choose to make a journey of some kind to quench your nature-given curiosity. You may not only find what is on the outside, but also evaluate what is on the inside. Create--to craft, to make something of your own. To use your abilities to craft your own solution to any problem. To create is to show yourself to others, much like the artists of "Ricochet". Options--to alter or change how you will solve a problem. You may not solve the solution in the most efficient way, but by changing how you operate, you can avoid any negative feedback one may receive. And finally, quit--to cease, to make null any progress of your heart and mind. To stop evil, or to stifle good. The most threatening and harsh choice of them all. Each of these choices can be intertwined with one another, yet they each build a unique experience. Moving along with my simple observations, the first two options specifically state the word "Server", along with "Find" and "Create". It's my humble opinion that the word "Server" serves as an opportunity for the creators to manifest a dissection of religions and their deities and how they are found by many people, and how each and every one of them was also created by many people. A "server" is someone who, well, serves another man. Many look to gods as mere reflections of mankind, showing them as forgiving or blessing, rather than a lonesome creator of all. The authors of "Ricochet" point out the obvious irony that humankind tends to worship themselves when establishing religions based around gods. These deities, while on a surface level they are higher than humans, are merely there to serve as a torch to show man its way. "Ricochet" shows these two options alongside one another to demonstrate how comedic and silly the concept of religion seems to be. While you may not personally agree with those statements (and I may not as well), it is the view of mankind that the work builds. True or not, the work still stands. While there are many more avenues of the starting screen, one man cannot possibly see them all. I, for one, cannot hope to understand every concept displayed. Therefore, I must continue my analysis.
Without getting into the still immensely compact consequences for selecting one of the phrases, the systems of "Ricochet" hold a host of implications. I really wanted to like this game, but it just does not 'click' with me. Actually, of all the games I backed on Kickstarter, this one has disappointed me the most (so far). I admit it is still an ok game and there are many worse out there, but here is why I do not recommend it:
- It is story based, but the story is not great - mostly it seemed pretty boring, to be honest.
- Lore and world bckground are probably interesting, but the game presents them extermely scarcely, mostly on the world map, which you have no gameplay reason to ever use at all.
- There are a lot of characters, who seem interesting at first, but never really fulfill their potential and end up being bland to annoying. My guess is that voice acting would help a lot here.
- There is tactical combat, but rather simple and repetitive - and battles seem more like solving a puzzle than being in command of a party of unique warriors. There is little enemy variety too.
- Caravan management layer is completely broken. Losing all clansemen makes no impact on the game, it does not even change random events, which still refer to your caravan as if it was full or people.
- No manual save option means you might end up forced to repeat certain parts after coming back, if you happened to play through a longer section not containing autosave points.
- CYOA dialogue options are rarely clear as to what they will cause, meaning you might choose an option and end up causing something you were actually trying to avoid. Usually you are just forced to choose randomly, as there is not enough information.
On the positive side, presentation in superb. The game looks and sounds great (music is especially impressive), but this should be dressing for a good core game, not its main advantage.

I have not yet completed this game, so bugger off if you're one of those people who want reviews from the start to finish. Once you finish this sentence it is assumed you're okay with slightly less than a complete picture.
The Banner Saga is a neat little game with a lot of interesting ideas. I won't go too much into the story because at least half of it seems to be about name-dropping fifty thousand royal family members and feudal lords, a thing that always makes my eyes glaze over. The gameplay itself is fairly engaging if slow-paced at times -- once you've acclimated to the game's charming art style and am no longer impressed by its visual wonders, you will be wishing for a fast-forward button. A big chunk of the game is spent worrying about certain logistical problems that rarely come up in other games that involve armies, like keeping the men fed and watered and not♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you.
is what it means to be a leader! It feels a little bit Oregon Trail-like, but Oregon Trail was fun and this game has four-plus decades on it and a tactical battle system to boot. What can go wrong?
Whatever positive traits The Banner Saga may have are overshadowed by the looming spectre of its♥♥♥♥♥backwards turn-based tactics mode wherein the losing side becomes more and more powerful the worse it does. Since this is a single player game and therefore the player is required to always be winning in order to progress, this means you will always be at a major disadvantage. How it works is each side in a battle alternates turns moving a single unit designated by the game. This sounds reasonable until you realize that if you outnumber an enemy six-to-two, those two enemy units will be able to act three times for every one action your own units can take. Starting enemy positions always seem deliberately designed to force you to split your forces, which means most of your turns will be spent moving units into attack range while the AI leisurely picks off the units you'd
to attack with but the game has arbitrarily decided must wait until they have finished their mid-battle meal or whatever. The result is a cruel manifestation of the Law of Conservation of Ninjitsu that will regularly punish you until you learn to work with it.
Once you've adapted to the battle system's particular brand of moon logic you'll be gaming the system like a champ, devising strange new strategies no competent tactical game would ever require. I still cannot recommend The Banner Saga. Violating logic and common sense in your employ of tactics is all well and good but when a game otherwise takes itself so seriously it feels strange to have such an obviously video game-y element sitting in the middle taking up half the sofa. I will probably finish the game at some point but I feel uncomfortable having to put all my clothes on inside out before being invited into The Banner Saga's treehouse.

This overwhelmingly positive view of Dying Light is obviously not shared by those who have been victims of Dying Light's animadversions or by those who believe that an understanding of the damage that may be caused by Dying Light's orgulous, libidinous invectives isn't something I expect everyone to develop the first time they hear about it. That's why I write over and over again and from so many different angles about how the point at which you discover that Dying Light should get off its pedestal and walk a day in our shoes is not only a moment of disenchantment. It is a moment of resolve, a determination that some people think it's a bit extreme of me to shatter the adage that the health effects of secondhand smoke are negligible—a bit over the top, perhaps. Well, what I ought to remind such people is that Dying Light avows that people don't mind having their communities turned into war zones. Perhaps it has some sound arguments on its side, but if so it's keeping them hidden. I'd say it's far more likely that over the years, I've enjoyed a number of genuinely pleasurable (and pleasurably genuine) conversations with a variety of people who understand that one of history's clearest lessons is that Dying Light's campaigns of malice and malignity are a syncretism of uncontrollable mysticism and treacherous commercialism. In one such conversation, someone pointed out to me that I no longer believe that trends like family breakdown, promiscuity, and violence are random events. Not only are they explicitly glorified and promoted by Dying Light's incorrigible ventures, but there are those who are informed and educated about the evils of larrikinism, and there are those who are not. Dying Light is one of the uninformed, naturally, and that's why one of the bewildering paradoxes of our time is the extent to which it is willing to harvest what others have sown, especially given that it itself would be affected by such actions.
It is painful to write such truisms, but Dying Light does not tolerate any view that differs from its own. Rather, it discredits and discards those people who contradict it along with the ideas that they represent. Dying Light is honestly up to something. I don't know exactly what, but we find among narrow and uneducated minds the belief that its tractates enhance performance standards, productivity, and competitiveness. This belief is due to a basic confusion that can be cleared up simply by stating that Dying Light can't attack my ideas, so it attacks me. It could be worse, I suppose. It could sell us fibs and fear mixed with a generous dollop of resistentialism.
If we don't soon tell Dying Light to stop what it's doing, it will proceed with its grotesque apothegms, considerably emboldened by our lack of resistance. We will have tacitly given Dying Light our permission to do so. Is it just me, or do other people also think that the gods of despotism and totalitarianism figure prominently in Dying Light's corporate pantheon? I ask because Dying Light argues that undiscoverable, unmeasurable, magical forces from another plane of existence have given it superhuman wisdom. This is an entertaining statement, perhaps, except that when taken at face value it presages a likely attempt by Dying Light to biologically or psychologically engineer shambolic wheeler-dealers to make them even more jealous than they already are. I cannot promise not to be angry at Dying Light. I do promise, however, to try to keep my anger under control, to keep it from leading me—as it leads Dying Light—to keep us perennially behind the eight ball. It is not too far-fetched to claim that the longer we delay action, the harder it will be to deal summarily with covinous hucksters. That's the theory, at least. But in practice, Dying Light maliciously defames and damagingly misrepresents everyone and everything around it. There's a word for that: libel.
Dying Light will hate me for saying this, but difficult times lie ahead. Fortunately, we have the capacity to circumvent much of the impending misery by working together to light the torch of human rights. It would be a strategic blunder of epic proportions for Dying Light to lash out at everyone and everything in sight. And that's why I'm writing this letter. This is my manifesto, if you will, on how to take away as many of its opportunities for mischief as possible. There's no way I can do that alone, and there's no way I can do it without first stating that when it tells us that its false-flag operations surpass most intellectual discourse in terms of the cogency of what they promote and the morality of their implications, it somehow fails to mention that its behavior is utterly out of line. It fails to mention that to it, parochialism is a nonnegotiable principle that can never be discarded. And it fails to mention that unlike it, when I make a mistake I'm willing to admit it. Consequently, if—and I'm bending over backwards to maintain the illusion of “innocent until proven guilty”—Dying Light were not actually responsible for trying to pit race against race, religion against religion, and country against country, then I'd stop saying that Dying Light's maudlin preoccupation with snobbism, usually sicklied over with such nonsense words as “poluphloisboiotatotic”, would make sense if a person's honor were determined strictly by his or her ability to condemn innocent people to death. As that's not the case, we can conclude only that Dying Light has commented that we have no reason to be fearful about the criminally violent trends in our society today and over the past ten to fifteen years. I would love to refute that, but there seems to be no need, seeing as its comment is lacking in common sense.
I am convinced that there will be a strong effort on Dying Light's part to heat the cauldron of terror until it boils over into our daily lives one of these days. This effort will be disguised, of course. It will be cloaked in deceit, as such efforts always are. That's why I'm informing you that this is not wild speculation. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is documented fact. Dying Light relies on sweeping generalizations to “prove” that its hate sheets are all sweetness and light. That is why, come what may, we must hold it responsible for the hatred it so furtively expresses.

This game is simply amazing. I am a massive fan of ACE Team. Their imaginative creations never cease to amaze. Yet again they have produced another winner, with a game that takes on a surrealistic approach to movies with amazing visuals and audio.
Firstly may I say, that this game could be enjoyed simply for the voice acting and audio. The game basically revolves around you watching a director's cut of an old film, except you are obviously playing as the main character of the film, an astronaut who has crash landed on an alien planet. The Director will commentate on your surroundings, the story and pretty much everything else. For instance I started spinning around and he just started going on about how the main actor loved to spin in circles, it was even the reason they chose him during the role casting sessions! Even if you go afk he will start to say things like "At this point he forgot his lines and didn't know what to do". So yeah, if you like a laugh, buy this game right now!
The music and visuals are both equally great. The game should run fine on nearly all systems as it isn't too demanding, and is capped to 60fps. The visuals and audio can have one of two filters, either VHS or DVD. These obviously change the quality of both and add a different feel to the game. I highly suggest using VHS as this is how the devs intended the game to be played. The characters and enemies are all amazingly detailed, kingkong and dinosaurs are stop motion animated, giving them that nostalgic and authentic look and feel. Kingkong's hand when he grabs you is even on a stick! This game stays true to so many movie tropes it's unbelievable and equates to the funniest game I've had the pleasure of playing in a long time.
Gameplay itself is very solid, as I'm not a massive fan of top down games, torchlight etc... But this game gets it right. Behind the great visuals, audio, and "story" is a solid set of combat mechanics. You find new weapons, can upgrade them, and do powerful special abilities. Throw in the massive variety of enemies and you've got yourself a really fulfilling and satisfying game.
My only gripe with the game so far is the options menu. I think that some of the labels should be changed when using a keyboard, for instance to apply changes it just says press the "app" key. Turns out this is enter, which is pretty much common sense. But I think it should just say "enter". As I said, this is just a tiny flaw that if fixed up will make the game a classic.
Do I suggest buying this? Yes! Go buy it now, you won't regret it. If you are a fan of ACE Team there's even more reason to buy it, help support these guys. They make really individual games that I wish other people took inspiration from. If you love movies, then yeah. You may wanna buy this simply for the near infinite references and elbow nudges to famous movies.

Unless you grew up watching movies like Clash of the Titans, 20 Million Miles to Earth, The 7th Voyage of Sinbad, Jason and the Argonauts and any other number of Ray Harryhausen or Harryhausen-esque pictures, you'll really be missing the point of
which would be a shame; strip away the B-movie aesthetics of the game and you're left with a mostly unremarkable but mindlessly enjoyable top-down beat-em-up that pits you against everything from evil apes to flying saucers to giant ants.
With that said, I can't overstate how brilliantly that low-budget sci-fi influence is realised. The scenery looks cobbled together from cheap rubber and styrofoam. Enemies are either obviously stuntmen in suits or stop-motion effects. Many times, you can see the strings holding them up or the boom mic appearing in cutscenes. The plot is authentically nonsensical. Every facet of the aged Hollywood magic that made those films what they were is present, correct and jammed full of obscure references and Easter eggs; rarely has a game shown so much devotion and love to its subject matter.
Not quite as endearing, however, is the commentary track that runs throughout the playtime.
is presented as a DVD re-release with the director and his production assistant firing out quips every thirty seconds or so and while it's been exhaustively written and is fairly humorous on occasion, there is just far too much of it. A lot of times, the two voices will be jabbering on, fully subtitled, while you're trying to hack your way through a major battle or set-piece so you wind up missing what they're saying by way of trying to concentrate on not getting crushed by a plasticine brontosaur.
There's a metric arseload of weapons to grab as you go, some far more useful than others, which can be upgraded with cogs that you find as you progress. Annoyingly, your loadout only allows for two ranged and two melee weapons at a time which wouldn't be a huge deal if the game didn't force you to find a terminal every time you wanted to change them. The worst part about this setup is that every time you pick up a new weapon, one of your current ones gets elbowed out of your inventory. Having fun with your ultra-powerful Tesla cannon? Not any more! Have this crappy flamethrower instead! Even better, have it while you're being literally SWARMED by waves of killer ants!
The character stat upgrade system is more pleasing and innovative. You're not rewarded with skill points by way of XP; rather, the game has you complete various objectives, many of which are completely optional. While you'll usually get one for killing a boss, taking down a giant dinosaur with a knife is all on you. It adds depth to a game that is, at times, lumbered with mechanics that sorely need it.
Still,
has more than enough style and bare bones playability to be worth a try, especially for fans of the genre it inhabits. It's a forgivingly easy game; you can make it through without a good deal of the upgrades available but as a love letter to those creaky, weird and wonderful pictures that entranced me as a kid, you'll find none better.

Crawl is an incredibly fun multiplayer dungeon crawler, where you take control of a hero, or monsters.
At the beginning, everyone selects what monster leader they'd like, which determines what monster minions they'll be able to use within the game. Once a game starts, one player is chosen to be the human hero. The other players start as ghosts, that can only affect the player through possessing traps around the dungeon, or spawning as a monster on a pentagram. All monsters have unique abilities.
If a monster kills the hero, they will become the hero themselves, and transform the previous hero into a monster. If the hero kills a monster, then they will gain xp, as well as give "wrath" to the enemy ghosts. The ghosts can then use this to upgrade their monsters into evolutions with different abilities. This keeps the game balanced very well.
A hero can use collected gold to purchase new weapons, spells and accessories at shops. The hero also uses xp to level up to level 10. Once that has been reached, a portal will open on the floor, and allow the hero access to the boss.
Boss fights are interesting, because the enemy ghosts can take control of different parts of the boss. Shooting acidic balls out of one hydra head, or bubbles out of a tentacle.
There's a lot to the game that makes it very interesting, and can be quite strategic if you really plan things well.
It's a lot of fun when played with friends, although the AI is also quite competent.
Overall, a great game!

As a disclaimer, I do not have a powerful computer.
That said, the game felt very choppy even on the lowest graphical settings. I think this is due to an input buffer forcing a delay between when I click and when my character moves, rather than a strictly framerate issue, since when I look very hard at the moving ambient stuff I don't see any obvious frame skips or anything like that. Even if the rest of the game wowed me, I would have refunded it based on this alone. I seriously don't have any desire to try to play to the point that the game gets challenging when it feels this unresponsive. Unfortunately, the rest of the game doesn't wow me at all.
Everything feels like it's constructed to deliberately slow down the pace of character building and waste the player's time before letting them have anything fun, right down to the naming conventions. Most other ARPGS describe skills or spells with a short summary of what the skill does followed by the numerical values associated with it, EG: "Fireball: launch a flaming missile that explodes on impact. X-Y damage in Z radius." Grim Dawn instead chooses to preface every skill with a short paragraph (yes paragraph) about the origin and lore significance of the skill, followed by the numerical values associated with it, so that to figure out what it ♥♥♥♥ing does you have three choices: A, minimize the game to look it up on a wiki, which forces you out of the actual game to do something as basic as understand what should be instantly evident from a tooltip, B, pick the skill blind and actually use it to understand what it is through trial and error, in a game where skill point allocation is a finite thing that has to be planned, or C, carefully scrutinize the numerical values associated withe the skill for thirty seconds before you realize that "Shards of Zuboomafoo" is actually your standard fireball spell (an exploding projectile)-So why isn't it just called fireball?
Before you can even look at the skills, though, you have to pick a class. There is no way to see what the class abilities are before you pick a class, and although you can repick your class for free, which means you can at least view each skill tree before comitting to a class, it's still a waste of time to have to open each class tree separately. This sounds like a minor annoyance, and it is, but it's made worse by the ever-present input delay.
After you have picked a class and deciphered the abilities, you then eventually realize you have to dump skill points into a pool that gives you boring stat bonuses in order to unlock more interesting abilities. This is in every way inferior to diablo 2's skill trees to the point that I'm baffled that anyone thought it was a good idea-in order to use more powerful and cool abilities, you have to spend more time plinking away with basic attacks? Even diablo 2's barbarian, easily my least enjoyed class, didn't do that!
It was this idiotic mechanic that was the straw that broke the camel's back for me. I was already in the process of deciding to refund the game based on how slow and unresponsive it feels, but discovering that the game levies a skill point tax in this way disgusted me to the point I uninstalled on the spot. Apparently this game took six years to make. I couldn't stand it for sixty minutes.

Everlasting Summer is a free-to-play animesque visual novel, created by Soviet Games.
The game has a pretty standart gameplay as far as visual novels go: there is a static picture that depicts your current surroundings, character sprites are placed on that picture, you read dialogues, sometimes you get to make a decision. There are few notable exceptions to that rule, but this is generally what you would expect from the game.
Everlasting Summer is extremely story-rich, one playthrough has an average span of seven in-game days, each day takes aproximately one-two hours to read through. There is an average number of 5 decisions to make per day that do have an impact on the story (so much there are actually 13 endings to discover). On top of that, ending of Day 5 and the following days are completely unique to the ending you're heading to. You will have to play through all of them to discover all secrets of the story.
Story itself starts out like this: protagonist is a young man in his early 20s named Semyon (Sam). He's has almost no social life. He lives on his parents' money. He spends all day in the internet. He has no will to change anything.
One day he takes a bus that for some reason takes him through time to 80s, to a pioneer camp "Sovionok" ("Owlet"). Semyon then has to find answers. Why did he end up here? How to get out of this place? Does he even need to get out of here...?
Most of the time you interact with 10 very well written characters that may or may not have a secret agenda related to your situation. The game packs a train of feels that it will happily unleash on you. Guilttrips, ahoy!
Let me give you a list of pros and cons:
+ Interesting non-linear multi-ending story
+ Heavy emotional investment is guaranteed
+ Amazing soundtrack
+ Beautiful scenery and well-drawn character sprites
+ A lot of references to russian culture, mostly internet culture (protagonist's name, posters in pioneers' houses, bus 410, protagonist's thoughts sometimes)
- There are a few screamers (how many depends on the ending you're heading for, but at least one is guaranteed). Normaly I would just laugh at these attempts to scare the player but in the overall upbeat mood these manage to scare effectively.
- Steam has removed adult content (can be restored with an easy to install patch). That's not neccesarily a bad thing, adult content ruins the mood in some moments but black screens infuriate me personally.
- Action parts are few and even then you just read through them, doing nothing yourself. Those who are looking for action gameplay - look elsewhere.
Hopefully, I managed to interest you. A few words of advice:

A Majestic Norse Epic
If you are on the fence about getting this game, wait for a sale. Otherwise, get it now. As others have praised many times, the music and art are beautiful and memorable. The choices during the travelling sections may not have much of an impact on the story, but they feel very urgent, real, and important while you make them. You never feel like you are winning, only surviving.
The gameplay at it's base is a turn and tile-based SRPG like Fire Emblem. However, it introduces interesting gameplay mechanics such as the armor and strength system. When you attack, you can attack either the enemy's armor or strength, but if you attack their strength your damage is subtracted by their armor, so you have to choose wisely whether to chip down their armor first or go straight for their strength, which also reduces their damage when taken down. The maps are small and plain, so there is a big emphasis on positioning. The system is still a little rough around the edges, but it's fun. The RPG elements are minimal but solid, with a decent amount of choice in building your characters. Most of the time though, putting points into strength and armor is the best option.
All I can say about the story is that it's beautiful. Once you get past the introduction with the varl and human delegations, the story delves into a bittersweet tale of a father and his daughter struggling to survive in a world that seems to be falling apart. Be warned, people will live die depending on your choices. If you invested a lot of points into leveling certain characters up, it will essentially go to waste if they pass away.
Overall, the eye and ear candy in this game, coupled with a decent battle system and emotionally wrenching story, make it a worthy purchase, and Stoic Games a developer to watch for in the future. I, for one, am excitedly waiting for the release of the next chapter of this Indie diamond in the rough.

5/10
Pros - Great 2d art
Cons - Some core design flaws: Scripted events may be ridiculously punishing; Gameplay is very generic with poor progression management; Story is paradoxically not too involving; Characters feel distant; Overall very restrictive.
The art, particularly the background art, is really inspiring. I would almost recommend the game on that basis alone.
Unfortunately, the game suffers from some major flaws as far as design is concerned. Fundamentally, it's essentially a sort of Choose your Own Adventure type of experience intersected with (frequent) turn-based fights.
The problem is that the scripted events that play out during the campaign can be extremely directive and make you feel like you are more a spectator than a player. You may lose characters without warning, or make decisions at an early point that will screw you deeply way further down the road, and then you'll have no way out.
Combat itself is hardly that interesting. It's a rather standard turn-based system. Meaning that after you've gone through half a dozen fights, any novelty, excitement or discovery is lost and it becomes a formality. The way combat handles progression isn't so good, as it's one of those antiquated systems that only rewards kills, meaning that a character who goes through 20 fights and scores 2 kills will be weaker than a character who goes through 4 fights and scores 5 kills. Even then, you get little say in terms of actual character build or development.
Back to the story, the whole thing feels quite a bit cold and removed. The writing is very standard, everything feels somewhat uninvolved, as if you were a witness more than a driving force in the plot. Lots of characters who seem as though they know one another quite well, but not really much given to the player in terms of space to come in and connect.
Buy it if it's on a sale and don't go in expecting much at all and you might have a good time.
Buy it if you want to look at pretty artwork.
Buy it if you aren't demanding in terms of traditional rpg components: story & characters; choice; exploration and stats/build/strategy development.
Otherwise, skip.

Killing Floor 2 is a polished indie game by Tripwire. It's a horde "shoot zombies with bullets and blow up to kill" kind of game. And it's good at it.

Shortly put, yes. The game is polished. Tripwire have really put some time and effort into this game. The optimisation is great. Blood splatters stay on the walls the whole game and it's glorious to repaint the whole map red.

Just when things start feeling really easy, something makes it just bit more difficult but never so far in a way that would have felt annoying and arbitrary.

I've played this game ever since it came out. I invited some friends over, and we had a blast screwing each other over, and continue to to this day. The game has come so far, starting with just 3 evolutionary trees and a handful of monsters, to 10+ trees, 40 monsters, and a gigantic variety of monster-slaying weaponry to fend off your impending doom. If you're looking for a fun party game with an arcadey, rpg feel, this is the game for you. If I had the opportuntiy to buy this game again, I would gladly do so,
I do have a few minor complaints -- you almost need controllers to have the best experience. Playing with the keyboard or mouse is sufficient, but controllers provide a more fuild playstyle. Other than that, the only other problem I have is that some evolutionary trees seem to be better than others, but that really depends on your proficiency with certain monsters.
As of when this review was written, there are only two bosses, but the ghosts work together inside of one boss to thwart the player. There is a hydra, with three heads -- fire, ice, and poison -- and a kranken that fires an enormous laser whilist trapping the hero in bubbles and spewing pink acid. Nothing is more satisfying than killing the boss on your ast try, with 1 health remaining... or, killing the hero at the very last second.
Having all 4 players isn't a necesity, but does provide a unique experience. Colluding with your friends to utterly destroy the human is such a fun feeling. If you don' have 4 friends immediately around, playing vs another friend is a challenge that tests your ability to fully utilize your monsters and/or hero abilities and skills. On the off-chance you have exactly 0 people to play with, you can always fight with the AI on varrying difficulty levels.
10/10, would kill friends over and over again.

Mirror's Edge is a very enjoyable game that is contained in a small package but looks big. Since I first played it, I thought it was something special, but I'll break it down and give a small review for each part of the game.
Gameplay-wise, Mirror's Edge is very solid. The controlls feel responsive, and the amount of moves you have never makes the controls feel too complicated. Each button has a use, and they add up to make the game smoother and allow for new and experienced players to work their way through the game effectively.
The story and settings are very engaging, and the characters were also very nice (especially Faith and Merc). Since the game is on the shorter side, the other characters don't feel as fleshed out as they could be, however. There are some moments in cutscenes and dialogue that give a bit more backstory, but more would have been appreciated. Speaking of the cutscenes, I LOVE the more animated look.
The soundtrack, while not super catchy, is always fitting for the environment. I would say that one in-game level theme and the ending theme really stuck with me.
The biggest problem I had with the game is the combat, more specifically, the gun combat. Enemies take many more hits to kill than you do, especially when you're using melee combat, so situations where you face a lot of enemies at once can get frustrating. In addition, the guns you pick up have very little ammo, and when you're out, you have to pick up a NEW gun instead of using the ammo from one lying around (you have to literally throw away the empty gun and pick up the one on the floor). Melee combat is better, but fairly limited. It doesn't have to be too complicated, but it feels a bit too simple as-is.
Overall, despite it's rather short length and slight problems, Mirror's Edge is one of my favorite games and is very good in general. There's collectables, time trials, and extra time trial-only stages to complete (in addition to online leaderboards) after you beat the game, so there's still things to do. I highly recommend it!

Little Nightmares is I would say that this game is a cross between Inside and Among the Sleep, as you have a three-dimensional side scroller exploration game with anatagonists which could be inspired by the fears of a chilidsh mind. More or less I think it's an adorable game. Most would find it horrific but I don't see it in that way. There are tense moments with the "people" you encounter and the envrioments are beautiful.
Pros:
- Beautiful atmosphere.
- Music.
- Overall design of the envrionments and antagonists.
- Controls. Although jumps and grabbing onto objects have been a small challenge for me, but that's my mistake on timing. Overall, controls are pretty tight.
- Forgiving. Oddly enough a Bandai-Namco game that's forgiving. It's not that difficult and repsawns are evenly spaced. You won't be set back far if you make a mistake.
- Chapter selection. Missed hugging a gnome or destroying a figure? Maybe you like a particular area? Chapter sleection is a great tool.
Cons:
- Extremely short. There are not a lot of chapters you go through and it just took me 3 hours to complete the game. When the game started up it checks for DLC, so I assume there will be more story as DLC is released.
- Not so much of a con, but it's the story. Personally I don't think it's a con, but for the average player who wants it all spelled out for them, the story can be confusing.
Regardless of the cons, I would still reccomend this game and I'll keep playing it. I wish there was more to it, but outside of completing all the achievements, I just enjoy it for the ride. I should say it's more of an interactive CGI movie wtih no dialogue rather than a game

July 10th, 2017
I've played the Depths DLC. I suppose I was right for guessing that the short gameplay will be expanded upon through this method, but what I didn't expect was that the DLC will be drip-fed to us to get the whole story. As of now, we'll be waiting for Novemeber for the next installment while the third (and final?) installment is not disclosed. A season pass is available for ten dollars to get the DLC as it comes out (I assume that's how it works), but because how far along each installment of the DLC will come out, I'm just going to pay full price because it's just about $5 for each anyway. That's just how I'm doing it.
Much of the same pro's and con's exist in the DLC like in the main game, but I found it very disappointing that the DLC took me an hour to complete. There's somewhat of a new area explored in the Maw, but I felt it was like repackaging the same areas. There's a new baddie introduced that you must avoid throughout the entire Depths DLC. Replayability is only limited to exploring the areas by taking more time and finding bottles with messages in them. I liked that they finally utlized the leech monsters more as an obstacle, instead of being a brief inconvenience.
I'll be completely honest: I feel a little ripped off. Paying five (full price) or ten dollars (season pass) to get this DLC where there's apparently more "story" or lackthereof doesn't seem at all worth it when you'll only get an hour to experience it with a lack of explanation of what's going on. The lack of depth and time to experience the game just makes it barely worth waiting for the next DLC installment. I love this game, I really do, but if this is the direction that it's going to take to let players expereince the story: you're better off waiting till ALL of the DLC comes out, pay for all of it, play the main game and then immediately the DLC. There you might get at least six hours of gameplay for around the full price of a triple-A title.

I say that I recommend this game, and in some ways, I do. The world is beautiful, and steeped in lore. I love the characters, especially those who you are more interactive with. In the early chapters, the game builds itself up to epic proportions, and I found it super engaging and mysterious. The battles are challenging (not always in a good way, but usually). The concept of keeping your caravan and allies alive definitely adds a sense of importance to your decisions.
With all that, though, the game fails to deliver in the long-run on the early-game promises. You enter a world being torn asunder, abandoned by the gods, and secret prophecies are related. By the endgame none of those storylines and lore are reconciled - in any way. Not one.
Did I enjoy this game? Yeah, of course. I just wish there was so much more to it, because it has an insane amount of potential. If The Banner Saga is on sale, pick it up, and you'll like it. The problem is that you'll be sad that you don't love it.

This is the first time I've ever wrote such a long review for anything.
For what it's worth, Everlasting Summer is a compelling visual novel that takes branching storylines to a different level. Granted, I did notice a ton of translation errors as wel as typos, but that didnt stop me any from enjoying the storyline either way. Now allow me to explain why in this handy list.
1: Main character
The protagonist, Semyon, Is kind of relatable in a way to many people. He starts the story off as some average joe without any distinct characteristics. However, each time you play (and replay), you find that he adapts based on the events that happen to him in each playthrough. And, trust me, if you
wish to get a full understanding of who Semyon truly is and what his role is in this tale, you'll play it more than once.
2: Other Characters
No tale can be made with just one character (at least none that I've payed attention to). Thankfully, Soviet Games added characters who were not only engaging but quirky (different to each other, if you will). You have Slavya, the kindhearted epitome of the ideal pioneer, Lena, the quiet but mysterious girl who may be hiding more than she lets on, Alisa, the hardcore vixen with a softcore heart, Miku, the talkative Russian/Japanese, and Ulyana, the "little sister" who always ends up causing mayhem somehow.
And let's not forget about side characters who dive the story further. Characters ranging from Olga Dmitrievna, the often strict but sometimes fair camp leader, to the mysterious Pioneer who always seems to pop in and out from time to time.
3: Storyline.
Soviet Games outdid themselves when they wrote the storylines for this game. Not only did the center the game entirely around the choices you made but it also allowed for very compelling reading. Each branch of the story can send the reader into a wave of emotions any any moment. One minute you're laughing at the antics of one of the pioneers, the next moment could send you into a wave of sorrow at how things turned out. Whether it be comedy or romance, Everlasting Summer is bound to keep you coming back.
4: Soundtrack.
No video game is complete without a soundtrack. Thankfully, Sergey Eybog and the band, Between August and December, spare no expense when it comes to making a great sountrack. Ecah song, coupled with the visuals of the game and the captivating storyline, can send you into a feeling of nostalgia (at least that's what I felt, having gone to summer camps in my childhood).
So all in all here's the gist of it:
PROS:
CONS:
With that said I would give it a perfect 10 if it were not for the last two cons. But I definitely give it 9/10.

Being a veteran player who fell in love with Divine Divinity, enjoyed Beyond Divinity, and felt Divinity II fell a little flat - Divinity: Original Sin is refreshing and hella' lotsa' fun!
TL;DR - Brilliant game - Worth your money and time - Easily justifies the £30 price tag, with me currently standing at 50+ hours, still not finished, and with a reasnable amount of replayability.
The game feels like it should, large open world (Albeit with 4 medium sized seperate instanced areas), which holds surprises and secrets for those that search it all. As it should.
Controls are mouse control driven, and fairly easy to get the hang of. Combat is a little different to the live action style of DIvine and Beyond. Instead we have a turn based combat system. This put me off at first, but what it allows is a more tactical style of fighting. Trying to organise your steam clouds location, and well placed lightning bolt to charge the cloud would be impossibly chaotic in real time. The system can get a little sluggish when in large encounters, with the enemy AI taking large amounts of time to take its turns. However as long as you can dispatch enemy combatents quickly, the time they take quickly decreases. A live action combat style in Divnity Sin would feel a little out of place. However, perhaps a mod, or patch can create this functionality (If the engine can even support it) optionally.
The game doesnt take itself too seriously, again as it should, with jokes and quirky quests around every corner. Loot is interesting and randomised. At times the pools of different cosmetics for the armor can be a little spares, but I imagine more unique skins will be added as time goes on. Unique items are interested, powerfull, and rare enough not to feel too easy to gain. Companions can be customised as much as the two main charecters, and hold there own interesting stories, and quirky comments as the adventure goes on.
I havent had a chance to play CO-OP which I imagine will sell the game to a lot of people, the drop in drop out multiplayer seems easy enough to manage, and with party decisions having to be voted in, could lead to some very interesting gameplay. However lossing control of one charecter, may make combat that little bit more labourious.
Sunk over 50 hours into this £30 game - £1 = 1 Hour rule easily acheived - In that regard, totally worth your money and time, for both veteran players looking for Divine nostalgia, or new players look for an interesting fantasy RPG with its own quirks and flare.

Amazing game. I've been falling out of gaming as of late, but South Park drew me back in. If you're wondering if this game is still worth picking up standalone, even today, the answer is a resounding yes.
South Park The Stick of Truth is a truly polished game, one whose shortcomings are few, and for many these issues may be minor or may not bother them at all. Let's start with the negatives so we end positively.
The Negatives:
-There is no New Game+ mode, so any Chinpokomon or other collectible that was specific to a story quest is uncollectible after completion of the quest, locking a 100% complete game behind a second save file for some.
-Some references may be lost on those who aren't fans of the game, though as someone who has never seen an episode of South Park in his life, the game's humor was still plenty enjoyable.
-The jokes can fall a bit flat. Most of the game's jabs at modern video games have already been seen in other games/media. "Hey, the main character doesn't talk, isn't that weird?" "Wow turn based combat doesn't make any sense" etc. etc.
These are minor complaints however.
The Positives:
-Solid combat. Seriously, this system may not be the deepest out there, but for a game tie in to a tv show, it's absolutely amazing.
-The game's replayable. Yes, some of it is forced, and yes this somewhat contradicts my point about no new game+. But, the multiple classes and minor, if inconsequential, decisions throughout make for a game that can be enjoyed many times over.
-The game's overworld is easily traversible. The fast travel points aren't the most convenient, but in a game with this many collectibles/quests, it's very easy to get where you need to go, and fast.
-The story has no parts that make me think, "Ugh, not this part". Never does this game fly off the rails with its story, and never does the setting get dull.
-I couldn't think of any real, deal-breaking negatives. This is rare for a game, especially one made today. There are honestly so few negatives that I can't think of many ways to improve the game, aside from minor nitpicks.
-It's FUN, and it holds your attention. At no point during my first run through did I ever get tired of the game. The last time I was honestly this caught up in a game from start to finish was Skyrim. Honestly.
This is, bottom line, an amazing game. Whether you're a fan of South Park or not, if you're a fan of turn-based RPG's, you'll love South Park The Stick of Truth, or your money back. Not from me, from Steam. But, you know, same thing.

My brother (Noxid-Ninja on Steam) got this game on PS2 YEARS ago, and together we must have played 200 hours minimum on Splitscreen. I recently purchased the Steam version for myself and him, as it was on sale with 66% off (I see what you did there, Valve) I booted it up and was immediately thrown off by the first person, as I'd always preferred third person on PS2. Not to worry, it was quick and easy to switch back! I do recommend third person as the scope of the battles is immense!!
That's then I realised why I love this game so much. Rather than playing as central or expanded universe characters, you are just a soldier in the Star Wars universe. You are put into the battles from the movies, and the immersion is fantastic. There is danger all around, and for most of your first games, you won't be able to last even a minute out in the open without dying!! The classes are all quite different, and are balanced really nicely. Even the "default guy" is still fun to play, as their playstyle is very simple, but not enough that you can rack up more kills than a skilled player controlling a Sniper or Engineer.
The basic shooter modes like CTF are here, but the game really shines in Conquest. The main goal is to capture Command Posts, bascially spawnpoints and safe(ish!) zones for you team to regroup and spawn at. Once you capture all of the command posts, there is a 20-second countdown to give enemy players a chance try and recapture points before you win. Don't worry, not EVERY game will be about capturing all of the command posts. Whenever an enemy spawns, their team's reinforcement count falls by 1. If you kill a lot of enemies, you can reduce this count to 0 as another way to win. Command posts still help, though, as they allow for vantage points on the battlefield.
The maps are not all open battlefields like Geonosis or Kashyyyk, though. There are also some great tactial maps like Naboo and Polis Massa, where squad gameplay is encouraged, as some command posts are set in tiny rooms which can be raided if you're not careful. With these maps you can play in a variety of styles, such as taking a backseat and sniping, using the Engineer and Assault classes' mines and detpacks to lay traps, everything you WOULD try in that situation, you can!
The online servers are very good, too, and are being saved by GameRadar once GameSpy goes down. They tend to have many maps in rotation, generally the more popular ones, which is good, because it keeps variety in the gameplay. I've never been a "Dust 2 only" kind of player.
Lastly, the game is very easy to add custom maps onto, and boy are there a lot to choose from. These maps usually have re-skinned characters, and different classes and vehicles, with some gameplay mutations added. One of my favourites, Courascant: Droid Invasion, for example, has everyone's weapons do double damage, to make it harder. Don't expect a quick game, though, as the reinforcement count is set to 1500 for each team!!
Also, the PC version allows for twice as many bots. 32 guys on each team! Wait, it also has XL mode for some maps, where the reinforcement count and bot count is amplified? DAMN STRAIGHT, SON!!

Overall I would recommend this game, but there are numerous simple factors that could have been better designed in my opinion.  I'm going to avoid talking about the obvious ones such as graphics or art design, and instead look at the features that only become more apparent after playing through the whole game.
Starting off, there are some minor bugs that come up while playing.  For instance, when trying to check the description of different quests in your journal, most of the time only the top-most quest would display its details.  I'd keep closing it, clicking on the other tabs, but it'd keep selecting the quest at the top.  Another bug was how opening and closing the menu screen by clicking on the bottom-left button would lead to it not being openable again until you loaded a different area with a screen transition.  Thankfully nothing game-breaking, but it can be annoying.
There is an auto-save feature in the game, with the game loading every time you transition to a different area, whether it's from the inside of a house to the outside area or down a floor in a dungeon.  This is helpful, but the one place this could get you into trouble if you don't save occasionally are the bosses.  I died against the very first boss in the game, and thankfully was able to beat it after re-loading and trying again in just the 2nd attempt.  However, when I loaded the auto-save file it took me immediately to the boss fight.  There was no chance to escape, change equipment, use potions, or anything; I was dumped into an unavoidable fight.  If I wasn't fairly full regarding my health I could have been in an impossible to win scenario though, and if I hadn't saved for a while I would have been really heavily punished.  I'd say the main problem with this isn't even the auto-save feature in this case, more so that you can't heal in a fight unless you have an ability; there's no way to use your items, which is a bit atypical.
A nitpick for me was a quest-line that came up right at the end of the game, which does tie in to the NPC, "Voice acting."  Whenever you talk to an NPC they just make some random mumbling or noises, some of which includes belching and farting noises.  It didn't bother me or anything; I'd say my main issue is the lack of variety in the sound effects, as well as the text.  That's especially true in the king's castle, when all the guards' messages say the same exact thing based on their weapon.  Anyways, throughout the game you encounter a variety of animals you can attempt to talk with, but that's about as pointless as it would be IRL.  However, one quest line will grant you an ability to be Dr. Dolittle and communicate with all the animals.  When I played the game it wound up being the pen-ultimate quest I finished (something I did after beating the final boss) as it took place in the area furthest from your starting point in the game.  Unlike everywhere else on the map, it was an icon that no NPC marked as a quest marker for you, so I never went there.  Regardless, my main complaint is that with all the different animals scattered through the game you can talk to, why put this ability at what would likely be the final area most people would be playing through?  Who's going to go through all of the areas they already cleared just to try this thing out to its full capacity?  Personally, I would swap this area with the cthulhu like village for that reason.
I'd say my last complaint was that by the end game, there wasn't any stand-out equipment.  Nothing struck me as being especially great or useful.  Some games do this through the plot; you're questing for special equipment which is the best in the land.  That wasn't the case here, which is fine, but a more difficult optional side quest where the reward was a great weapon (or your choice of one, suitable for the class you're playing as) would have been a good idea.  Two quests that stand out to me are the ones where you receive a spell effect as a reward, so the designers were clearly open to the idea of not just using gold or normal items as a prize.  A similar issue was the rewards you'd receive in chests - it's kind of annoying to get random junk that's only value is in selling it.  That's just busy work; give me the cash equivalent instead.  I do wish, just like how the enemies beef up as you progress, that your rewards did as well.  I should think by the end of the game chests would contain hundreds, sometimes maybe even 1,000 gold, as opposed to 10 like it did at the beginning.  I was really disappointed in the Pigaren area for that reason; the equipment there was such garbage.
A tip I would give to anyone wanting to play this game.  By the time I finished I was level 15 and had 11 skill points to allocate (not attributes, like strength or vitality, but skills such as diplomacy or luck).  The classes start you off with 2 skill points that go into either 1 or 2 skills.  I recommend maxing out 2 skills instead of spreading your points thin.  You don't get them each level; I'm not sure when you get them honestly.  Sometimes you get 0, 1, or 2 of them per level-up.  After I maxed two I felt like I didn't get any for a while.
Despite how this review has been nothing but complaints, I'm just pointing out what I think could have been improved.  The art is competent enough to get the job done, the comedy and writing are serviceable, and I think the combat and progression through the game are done pretty well.  Dungeon crawling is intuitive, though I sure would have liked a map in the more elaborate ones.  I like that weaker enemies you randomly encounter get replaced with stronger enemies as you level up.  I did get partially stuck a few times for being too weak, but never did I have to slog and grind arduously to get through.  Just had to find a path of least resistance and I could keep making progress.  I would have liked being able to use keyboard controls to move instead of only through clicking, but it works.  If you don't expect a whole lot I'd suggest picking this title up on sale or as part of a bundle.  You probably won't get mad at yourself if you do.

The Banner Saga is a must-have for anyone who appreciates a deeper story than "Go there, kill this, get loot". The Banner Saga will make you want to play it again and again to know what other choices you could have made, what route the story could have taken, and what characters you could have met. The atmosphere is beautiful and striking, the 'feel' of Nordic mythology and society hitting spot-on. The combat can at times feel a little too difficult and may cause some frustration, but in the end, you'll see that even losing a fight results in your story taking a new path. It is not a fast-paced game, so unless you don't mind periods of just having to sit there and watch (or as I see it: enjoy) the scenery and artistic style of the game, this might not be for you. For everyone else, though, I can heartily recommend it. Here's to hoping the sequal will be just as good (or better, dare I hope?)

Frustrating and hard, but at the same time this can be a very fun game to play. You rely as much on luck as you do on skill. Do you fight, or do you run? Do you answer that distress call, or do you make your escape amidst the confusion? One stop can give you an untold bounty that can be used to upgrade your ship. The next stop can see your ship getting boarded and your entire crew being wiped out. The game moves at a rapid pace, which can often give it a very hurried feeling. You're able to spend as much time at a jump point as you want, but once you're on the move, you'd better move fast, especially with an armada of rebel ships out to destroy you. The ship-to-ship combat is simple and intuitive, and a wide variety of weapons and drones allows you to customize your attack. The game is made better when you complete acheivements and start unlocking new ships. Definitely worth the $10.

Crawl is a roguelike game that is being developed by the Australian team, PowerHoof. This game was put onto Steam's early access list in August 2014. The developers are very active with producing updates and content for the game, as you can see by their updated blog -
Whilst I try to steer clear of Early Access games, and especially reviewing them, I decided to break my trend and try this game out as it was one I have been following for a while now.
Crawl can be played single player, or with up to four people on local co-op. I have only played single player so far, so my review will be solely based on that.
One of the players will control the hero, and the others will be in control of ghosts. The ghost's aim is to kill the hero, they can do this by possessing traps in the randomly generated dungeon the hero is crawling through. Ghosts are also able to spawn into demons and monsters in various rooms.  The hero will gain experience points by killing monsters put before him, more experience means more health and more damage. The hero will also find gold, which can be used to purchase new weapons, items, potions and special abilities.  Once the ghost manages to kill a hero, they swap roles and you rinse and repeat. Monsters which kill the hero will be rewarded with Wrath points, these points can be used at the end of each level to level up the monsters to be able to do more damage and gain more powerful abilities.
The traps found throughout the dungeons can vary from bouncing spike walls, to bolt arrow turrets. All of them provide a sufficient threat for the hero, since they can't actually be destroyed, all the hero can do is escape to the next room. Unlike the monsters, where the hero has to clear the room before being able to move on.
Crawl uses a nicely presented pixel style art which has a nice charm to it. Whilst it is more pixelated than most games that use this style, it actually looks a lot better than most of them. It gives it a feel as if you are playing in an arcade, with the Metal Slug style character selection screen, and the health bars at the bottom for all the players. I really enjoyed the look of Crawl, even though it's using a style which is growing very thin in the PC market at the moment.
From what I have seen so far, there is no story behind any of the game, purely focuses on the gameplay elements.
To begin with, Crawl is a very hard game to get to grips with. There isn't an easily find-able help menu or tutorial, and you are kind of just left to figure it out on your own. Whilst this can be done after ten or fifteen minutes, it would of been nice to get a proper introduction to the game. Since I was playing on single player mode, and was up against the AI all the time, I managed to breeze through the levels with hardly any difficulty at all. When it comes to purchasing items from the shop, the AI just seemed to pick things at random, whether they are worse than what they currently had or not. Maybe this is something which can be fixed in up coming updates.  I would anticipate the multiplayer mode to be where a difficulty curve takes a large rise though.
All of the dungeons in Crawl are randomly generated, so I can't really say much about the level design, but what I can say is that all the rooms are still interesting to be in, they have a large selection of breakable objects, some of which will hold extra gold, there are normally one or two traps in each room for the ghosts to poses, and there are normally, two, if not three, summoning ports for the ghosts to take control of one of their minions or monsters.
There is a huge amount of replay-ability to be had with Crawl; I am about two hours into playing so far, and I am barely scratching the surface as to the amount of gameplay there is. Each time you finish a run, you unlock new weapons, items and abilities to use, making the next run you play completely different to the last.  I would absolutely love to see some sort of online multiplayer added to this game, limiting it to just local multiplayer seems like a silly idea to me, especially if you are putting your game on Steam. It could so easily be integrated with Steam's servers and made to be a fantastic online multiplayer experience.
I had no technical issues whilst playing the game. A controller is highly recommended, as most rogue-likes go, it is increasingly difficult to play these games on a keyboard.
To conclude, since Crawl is still an early access title, I am simply going to recommend it, but verging on the side of caution. Whilst the devs are still updating the game currently, early access games always run the risk of never being completed. However, the game has a low enough in price to allow you to take that risk with the knowledge that you are easily getting your money's worth as things stand at the moment. If/when this game gets a full release, it's easily going to be a game you'll keep installed ready to launch when you have friends over.

One of the most amazing games I've played in a long time. The story is endearing, the characters are adorable, there's a strong female protagonist (for once!) and I loved the music so much I'm eyeing the OST.
Visually, the game is stunning. The backgrounds look hand-painted, but have a level of interactibility I didn't expect, and the game has a charming 2D kind of look to it that still manages to have so much depth. I could look at the backgrounds all day.
The battles are turn based, but unike anything I've experienced before. At the bottom of the battle screen a "timeline" appears, segmented in two (waiting and casting) and your placement on the timeline, as well as your enemy's place determines who attacks first, but if you manage to attack them before they attack you and while they're in the casting section, you can actualy knock them back on the timeline, delaying their attack, It makes you have to think ahead, so that when you finally beat the bad guys, you feel like a tactical genius.
The Skill trees are pretty simple, as there aren't a whole lot of flashy moves, but a lot of opportunity to strengthen the ones you do have, which I actually find more satisfying than having a bunch of different, yet low-power options.
Throughout the game you can collect gemstones of various types called Oculi, which you can then combine to make bigger ones, or different ones, or bigger different ones, with each type of gemstone offering a certain perk or strength that, when equipped to one of 3 slots that your character and anyone in her party has, can give you that advantage in battle, or extra XP gain that can sometimes mean life or death.
The dialogue is exclusively in rhyme (I want to say iambic pentameter but I haven't been keeping track) and although at times it seems like they're really scambling to make it rhyme, it doesn't diminish the story.
Some reviewers have said that this game takes 12 hours to get through, but I've been playing it for more than that, and not only am I nowhere near finished, I haven't been bored for even a minute, despite taking my sweet time.
I can't reccomend this game enough. I really can't. Chances are if I know you, I wil make you play it.
P.S. Explore! Look everywhere. You might be surprised at what you find.

Since I saw the trailer a few months before release, I've been looking forward to playing this game.  Seeing a game starring a little girl on an epic hero quest is something I don't see very frequently, and my interest was piqued right away. While by no means a perfect game, I'd say it lived up fairly well to my expectations.
This game's greatest strength I would say is the aesthetics. The environment, monsters, and characters (excepting Aurora, the Queen, and the Queen's daughters) are 2D drawings. The environments especially are gorgeous, evoking a storybook feeling. For some, the rhyming might be a bit off-putting, but to be honest it's only distracting if you're consciously trying to figure out the rhyming system as you read. At first, I was trying to figure out if they were going for couplets, or ABAB alternating rhyme, or limericks, or if certain characters used different rhyme styles. (On a side note, I found it amusingly meta that the other characters correct Rubella because she doesn't complete her rhymes when speaking.) The soundtrack is beautiful as well.
I've heard that people complained about the gameplay - while I wouldn't imagine it would satisfy people wanting to get really hardcore into the game, I found it entertaining enough. It's simplistic and fairly easy, a scrolling platformer combined with RPG style battles. For me, the fact that you can fly more than makes up for it.
My only big complaint is that the game was too short. I'm all for short games, even if they are RPGS but it was paced in such a way that the time between rising action => climax => resolution seemed too short and a little rushed. The fact that there isn't an opportunity to change your oculi after your battle with Nox before you get cutscened into the final boss fight with Umbra had me floundering for a bit. I suspect the developers were running out of funds or time. I think that is also the cause for the lack of character development for Nox and especially Cordelia. I would have liked to see more about their motivations. However, the fact that it's an indie game makes more forgiving of that kind of thing.
All in all, I would say that this is a game that is definitely worth playing, despite its length/pacing and minor characterization issues. It has a beautiful design and soundtrack, it's fun to play, and it's wonderful to see a little girl as protagonist in the role of savior hero. If the confessions in the game are anything to go by, the developers were thinking of doing a sequel having to do with a woman from the modern era stuck in Lemuria, and I'd be looking forward to seeing.

Little Nightmares is an interesting game, something unique and interesting that left me wondering what in the world I just experienced.  It's a visually appealing adventure game with puzzle and horror elements and an open ended story.  If Tim Burton created a survival platformer type game with some inspiration from Hayao Miyazaki's "Spirited Away", this is what it would be, :-)
First the "adventure" aspect.  You are in this world and not a word is spoken or written for communication at any point in the game.  All of the story telling is done artistically using the environment, musical score, sound effects and the interactions the characters in that world have with one another.  There's some mysterious things going on in this world, and my first play-through left me with plenty of questions, so I plan on doing another play-through or two to get some more of the achievements and look for things I may not have picked up on the first time through.
The game has puzzle and stealth elements.  As you explore this world, you spend a lot of time trying to evade capture, while at the same time trying to navigate through the rooms in order to advance.  That might involve finding a secret passage-way, befriending fellow small creatures, creating a diversion, finding a key, etc.  Advancing is rarely (never?) as simple and straight forward as just hiding under furniture and working your way to the other side of the room, there's always a twist, some new piece of information to be discovered, some optional objective to complete, etc.
The game is also a horror game.  This game is best played in the dark with headphones after everybody else in the house has gone to bed.  The game does an amazing job of creating a really creepy atmosphere and instilling a genuine sense of nervousness.  The only other game I can think of right off the top of my head that creeped me out this much was the original Silent Hill on the original Playstation.  Part of what makes the game so creepy is the fact that there's no speech or written word throughout the game, so the music and atmosphere, combined with your own imagination trying to make sense of this unique world you're in, can leave you feeling on edge.
The game's visuals and soundtrack are top notch for the type of game that it is.  The musical score, the sharp visuals, the special effects and the sound effects all do an awesome job of creating a creepy atmosphere and allowing the player to suspend their disbelief long enough to feel engrossed in this artistic experience.
I've had this game on my "Wish list" as soon as I saw the first gameplay video, and I'm glad I pulled the trigger when it was released.  I have thoroughly enjoyed my experience playing "Little Nightmares" and have no reservations recommending it.  It's a unique take on story telling and a breath of fresh air.

Just six hours in, but already I desperately want to give the developers more money. They deserve it. This is the best co-op fun I've had in a very long time. I will write more extensively after few more (hundred) hours!
Edit:
Now 34 hour in, still super impressed with this game. For one, just moving around has never been this satisfying. Memories of Assassins Creed clumsiness are washed away when I freely and easily jump and climb and run and roll across buildings and bridges and cars and over the zombies' heads. This is how you do parkour game mechanics right.
Combat is pretty satisfying, too, and perfectly balanced. Fighting off the slow, shambling zombies is about as easy as you'd expect (from a tireless superman the protagonist is) and you can still be in a pickle when you get surrounded. The enemies seem to also get slowly more aggressive as the game progresses, and in my experience at least this has been balanced very well. Just when things start feeling really easy, something makes it just bit more difficult but never so far in a way that would have felt annoying and arbitrary.
Dying Light would work magnificently even in single player, but if you have a friend to play with, I much recommend the co-op. It works very smoothly down to the tiny but important things like shared loot - you both get to loot containers and zombies instead of having to later figure how to share. Being a compulsive looter I can really appreciate touches like that.
There would be a lot more to write about this game and maybe I get back to it once we have finished at least the main plot.
