After six years of waiting, four of those since a successful Kickstarter, I find myself asking; was it worth it? Yes. Yes it was. I thoroughly enjoyed my 80hrs romp through the grim gritty post apocalyptic hell that was Grim Dawn :D This was pretty much everything I ever wanted from an aRPG .. Loot. Loot. More Loot. Made by some of the same developers of the legendary Titan Quest, it's not hard to understand why they managed to get the formula down so well, making the experience a true joy to play through and not just an arduous, dull, slog. The visuals were nice, not exactly CryEngine levels of pretty but the art design and overall atmosphere was delicious, and the audio was really good too - though the VA was a bit hit and miss at times. Tons of quests, near infinite replayability due to the Bounty system, and with six classes that can be multiclasses to create more combinations, there's always something to play for. Everything that made Titan Quest great has been improved, in my opinion, most especially the overall feel and weight of combat.
My only serious laments would be the frankly appalling performance mid/late game, sadly caused by the aeons old engine being hamstrung with its legendarily bad multicore performance (100% on core0, 0-15% on cores 1-3) and a small dev team without the ability or resources to really pump into optimisation. My system is no slouch, being a 4Ghz i5 2500k and a GTX780, but the framerate dropped down to mid 20s during heavy combat and that is simply unacceptable. Sadly the Steam build also plays host to some nasty anti-piracy "triggers" that the devs put in, despite the fact that they're also releasing DRM-free builds on competing services.
Lastly, the ending, or lackthere of, as once you beat the final boss.. that's it. Nothing. You barely even get a single paragraph from a quest giver and... that's it. Such a huge letdown after an otherwise fantastic experience. It feels like the entirety of Act 4 was just slapped together too quickly, and finished even quicker.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who loves loot-focused aRPGs, such as Diablo, Torchlight or the predecessor; Titan Quest. Just don't go in expecting a world-class story or any real "ending", the obvious goal is the character building.

This was a beautifully rendered tactical turn based RNG RPG with an engaging story and for the most part, stellar gameplay. The backdrop was visually stunning, and this was easily the games strongest feature. It really did a great job of not only creating a game setting, but also adding an air of mystery and intrigue and foreboding to the game.
The combat itself was fairly simplistic as far as hex based battle systems go. The RNG aspect can create some frustrating moments, but can also conversely make you so stoked that you took a low percentage chance and succeeded.
The RPG upgrading system likewise was fairly simple.
As far as the writing goes, the story itself well complemented the artistic design of the game, or vice versa, lol, and the characters were pretty interesting in my opinion, overall. They weren't fully fleshed out, but I didnt feel they needed to be, and for what the game was presenting, I thought the whole thing worked quite well.
So, based on all that, with the excellent story writing, the cool characters, the amazing set piece, and the decent combat, this game should really be one of the best. However, it had some very real issues that knock it down some.
For one, as good as the writing was, realistically, none of your choices leading up to the finale really mattered, EXCEPT who you leveled up. Speaking of which, party members only level up through use, which I feel, based on the type of game it is, is something of a failure. I feel party members should level together in games like this, or at least, the unused ones should get some sort of experience. Otherwise, you end up woefully unprepared later when you are FORCED to use certain characters, arguably the ones that held the least appeal through the rest of the story as far as using them in battle went.
So, like I say, your choices didnt really matter. You have to fight starvation and loss through battle based on your actions, which for the bulk of your group (the common soldiers, scouts, and peasants), basically affected the amount of survivors left when you get to the final city WHERE they all die anyway, lol. However, your party decisions definitely matter, and because you are forced to use certain characters later in the game, and one specifically for the final battle sequence (the daughter), you would be encouraged to use them EXCEPT, the game really doesn't hint at that. They are mostly the characters you will find least useful overall, and that coupled with a distinct lack of anything suggesting they might be important later, virtually guarantees that most players will face the same complications later in the game.
So, this matters because the final battle is two stages and relies solely on the daughters archery skills to win. However, there was no real reason to level her up through the game, and I know that most players enter that final battle with an under leveled primary use character, which generally spells defeat.
Now, it is my understanding that the developers listened to these same complaints from a large percentage of the people who played this just after release and made some adjustments, but I haven't played it since those patches were released, so I cant speak to whether they really helped out with these issues or not. My understanding was the patch release focused on the final battle, so that aspect might be better now.
Anyway, I think overall, I want to give this game an 8 out of 10, but all the issues with it make me drop my rating down to about a 6.5 out of 10.
I do intend to revisit this game and see how the patches impacted things, so I will revise this review if necessary after I do so. Regardless, it is a game worth experiencing, so I do in fact recommend it.

To start of... I could care less about whether or not decisions I make in this game have any profound effect. I've seen some negative reviews and most state that the illusion of decisions as a factor.
This often surprises me, including when I see similar reviews for the likes of Telltale games, pointing out the same issue. Some people just can't enjoy a good story without having to get bogged down in such issues.
Choices you make in a game like this have limited effect. If your expecting the developer to create a thousand different story threads for each decision, then this isn't that sort of game.
For example; in one part of the story, there is a moment when a cart is about to veer over a cliff. On the cart contains a vast amount of treasure. You have several options available to you. In my game, the cart went over. Could I save it? Maybe. I'm not going to replay it to find out. Maybe somebody already did. Maybe they found out that whatever option you chose, the cart can't be saved. Who knows. Either way, that is the illusion of choice, assuming that it can't be saved, it probably can. Either way, Is illusion of choice really that bad of a thing?
People really go on a war path when it comes to these things. I'm a more relaxed chilled gamer, I enjoy a good story, and I have to say the story in The Banner Saga is certainly captivating enough that issues like these just don't warrant my attention.
It's very easy to recommend Banner Saga to anyone who enjoys a good story, a story that will be carried onto two other sequals. It's an investment that is certainly worthy of your attention.
I've often said this time and time again about games... Music can make or break a game. Thankfully the music is absoloutely amazing in this game, fantastic stuff. It really adds to the atmosphere, and without it, well, it just wouldn't be as good. Same goes for voice acting. There is none in Banner Saga, and that is a good thing. For a game like this, I would expect high quality voice acting. I would much rather none than low-quality poor voice acting, so I'm glad the developers stuck to their guns and went without.
Now, the game isn't perfect. It has flaws. Most of these are, surprisngly, in relation to combat.
I find combat to be convoluted at times much to its own detriment. On the one hand, I enjoy the complexity of it. On the other, I find it adds too much to combat. I could see it being a bit more simplified while retaining its complexity, a hard thing to balance, but Banner Saga unfortuntely doesn't balance it well.
Often times I find myself frustrated with the mechanics. Abilities like Tempest don't blatantly show you who you'll hit, so you could easily end up hitting allies, and left wondering, 'huh?' Archers are the biggest offence here... I move an archer thinking I'd be in range, and find myself out of range. Argh!
On the other hand, combat can be tense. It is difficult at times, but just the right sort of difficulty. I never feel that the game is unfair, or that its too difficult. But it could definitely use a cleanup in terms of mechanics and interface.
Regardless, if you enjoy a good story, and feel that you won't mind if your choices will have limited effects, then go ahead and get it.

Richochet is a retro multiplayer game from Valve that runs on the Half-Life engine; I'm not sure what to call it so I'll just be calling it a first-person shooter game. From the few games I have played online this game takes place in space, and you have to bounce around the map using these floating pads, yeah, it's quite weird... But still fun! It's chaotic but I just love it so much, I like how different this game is; compared to other first-person shooter games that were out at the time. You had games like Half-Life, Doom, Counter-Strike, etc. And they all used weapons like guns were you had to shoot monsters, demons or other people but Richochet is so much more different compared to those other games.
I suggest you buy this game if you want to play an entirely weird yet fun first-person shooter game from the early 2000's. There are always active players and servers, and the community of this game is very welcoming and friendly. I'd say that Richochet is worth your money!

Grim Dawn is an absolutely great ARPG set in a Victorian Post-Apocalyptic era where numerous creatures from the netherworld (Aetherials, Chthonians) invaded the lands and there are only a handful of survivors remaining.

There is not much customization on how your character should look, but there are 6 classes (Masteries) that you can choose from, and after level 10 you can choose another one from the six and Dual Class. This gives a lot of flexibility and plenty of skills to play with. Skills are unique and effective, and boosting them with Devotion effects will give additional devastation over the enemies.
The game is the spiritual successor of Titan Quest (using the same engine) however I can say that it is much better in a lot of aspects. The graphics is quite good, very “grim” looking (changing weather conditions, night-day system) although definitely lacking from AAA titles and feels outdated, however for me it works, and does not really matter. The landscape is looking absolutely great and keeps changing as you progress.
The gameplay is really good, combat is fun and simple as well as spectacular (animations, ragdoll effects are well done). There are a
of items you can collect ranging from common magical to legendary and set items (I freakin’ love set items) so be prepared for a full inventory stash and storage chest with loads of items. Thankfully you can easily transfer items between your characters. You can also craft items, or based on your faction standing, buy unique items from faction vendors.
Of course the game is best played in Multiplayer with your buddies or anyone over the internet. However this is where the game lacks a bit as Multiplayer is not quite worked out completely as it should and there are couple of things missing that could enhance this experience (auction house, party stash, quest sharing and party progression tracking, dueling etc.)
Also there are

I've played XCOM on both Windows and Linux (thanks Feral for the Linux port!).
If you're going to play the game, check the comments for a list of useful resources (websites and mods).
Gameplay is divided in two sections: the base management component and the actual turn-based tactical combat.
The base management part is very straightforward. You build labs, workshops, satellite arrays, order new equipment, choose your research projects, hire new soldiers, and so on. Basically, you'll be stressing over budget and deadlines ("How many sectoids corpses and UFO parts do I need to sell to build that satellite to save Egypt? What... It's gonna take a whole month to research a half-decent armor? Maybe I should get more scientists...").
But of course, the core of the game are the field missions. Every in-game month you get roughly 4 or 5 of them. Most of the time your goal is simply to eradicate all hostiles targets. Every now and then you'll receive special council missions where you have to extract/escort a VIP or deactivate some bomb. In addition to all that, the
adds three story-driven council missions and the expansion pack
includes another set of linked council missions (
).
The combat requires some thinking. You'll be controlling a small squad (usually 4 to 6 units). If you move your soldiers around like they're a bunch of kids high on sugar, you're going to get your butt handed to you on an alien platter before you can say
. So, don't spread your team out! Instead, keep them tightly together if you haven't engaged the enemy yet. This is especially true if you're playing on Classic or Impossible difficulty. The first time I played, I thought the game was stupid and obscenely unfair, but upon reflection I realized I was playing too aggressively and with complete disregard to the true nature of the cover system. With that in mind, learn the strengths and weaknesses of each soldier's class (assault, heavy, sniper, support) and how the cover system really works. Always go for full cover. Most of the time half cover is a big fat NOPE! If a soldier is in half cover and you can't take the alien down in your turn, hunker down or move to full cover! When attacking, your chance to hit is based on a lot of factors as the aim skill of the soldier, type of cover of your target, range, weapon used... The RNG can be a real pain: you're going to miss some 90% shots so always have a plan A, B, C, and D before pulling the trigger.
There is a decent variety of enemies. During most of the early-mid game you're going to be completely outmatched by the aliens. But in the late game, you'll have access to some sweet, sweet gear and, with the Enemy Within expansion, gene mods. At first they may look OP, but in reality the aliens scale with you (damn you, mind-controlling Ethereals and nightmarish Sectopods that somehow take only half damage from all hits).
Greg Foertsch, the art director who also worked on Civilization IV and Alpha Centauri, did a stellar job designing the visuals of XCOM. The levels feel dark and creepy, yet the colors and effects are incredibly vibrant. XCOM really breaks the old stereotype of the awesome-but-terribly-ugly strategy game, as you can see it for yourself in the screenshots:

. My only complaint is about the textures, even on PC they are basically console-level quality. Usually you're going to look to the battlefield from a considerable distance, so at least it's not that big of a problem.
What about the soundtrack? Epic, just epic.
. Kudos for Michael McCann. The guy also did the soundtrack for Deus Ex: Human Revolution, so his work speaks for itself.
XCOM is not a narrative-driven game. The story is simple: aliens are invanding and your job as commander of XCOM is to lead Earth's finest soldiers against the bloody barbarians. So how can this game elicit such a wide spectrum of emotions, throwing the player in a mix of grief, anger, and joy?
Every soldier you get is assigned a gender, nationality and, when he or she is promoted to Squaddie, a random class. Everything else is up to the player. You can edit name, nickname, change physical appearance, choose special abilities, and so on. Differently from other strategy games like Age of Empires or Total War, you're not controlling a vast army of faceless cannon fodder. In XCOM, you typically have a roster of 15 to 25 men. After some time it's inevitable to start forming a bond with your soldiers. The game is hard, is brutal, and it's meant to be played with Ironman enabled, that is, no save scumming, no reloading, no undo.
While some games are like a dull superhero movie, where you're never in real danger and you just steamroll your foes, XCOM is more like
: your enemy will outclass you in every way, eat your best soldiers alive and make the rest go back to the Skyranger♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in their pants and crying. The thrill of battle, not knowing whether or not your men are going to survive, and the dreadful challenge of facing an unknown enemy: that's XCOM.

Now, the must-have is

Yeah, you read it right. Freaking M-E-C-H-S! You have no idea how satisfying it is to falcon punch a Thin Man in the face.

Note: Mad Nords: Probably an Epic Quest is an Early Access title. The version reviewed was current as of the date of this review (20161116).
Mad Nords: Probably an Epic Quest is a console-style roleplaying game from indie developer, Dragon's Games. It's been on Steam in Early Access since August and based on the initial four to five month estimate, should be released sometime in the next month or two. It's currently in a very playable state.
Graphics have some charm to them. They're sort-of 'old skool' pixel graphics, but mostly very clean and well defined, with minor animations that add flavour. The interface is simple and easy to use, and there are no graphics options to speak of: windowed or full screen mode (either bordered or stretched) is all you'll see.
Mad Nords harks back to classic games with its music, too, with the mostly pleasant tunes reminding me strongly of the days of midi synth music. It's nice and, although repetitive after a while, I found it easy to listen to and didn't turn it down or off while playing.
Sound effects are fairly minimal, but suitable. It's worth mentioning the NPCs' 'voices', too, which sound a bit like slightly demented Sims -- very well done.
The game plays like any console-style RPG, with world, town, and multi-level building maps (dungeons), random encounters, attack gauges, abilities, and an inventory with a handful of different slots in which you can equip items. If you've played an early Final Fantasy or any other traditional console RPG, or any of the plethora of RPG Maker games on Steam these days, you'll be familiar with the options available to you. Where Mad Nords differs is in its sense of humour.
You begin by selecting one of nine classes for your character, three classes based on each of the three professions of warrior, rogue, and wizard. I chose to be a Cornomancer -- one of the wizard classes -- but some of the others are equally weird and silly. The game proper begins then, and I found myself in a conversation with my lovely wife, who demanded that I not only clear out the cellar of some rather dangerous worms, but that I also go and find some cucumbers so that she could make her mother a nice cucumber salad.
Although not exactly the sort of quest I'm used to in a role-playing game, off I set on my quest for cucumbers, which, it turns out, are not that easy to find in the world of Mad Nords. Now, hours of game time and a handful of equally odd side quests completed, I don't really feel any closer to finding the elusive cucumbers, but my Cornomancer has become a lot more powerful, and met some interesting characters along the way.
The game is played entirely with the mouse, although you can use the keyboard for hot keys if you really want to. Clicking the left mouse button on the ground or map moves your character there, while clicking on a person, item, or other interactive object interacts with him, her, or it. The interface works well, but unfortunately there's not a whole lot of variation to what you'll find in the various locations, so you'll quickly work out that you can ignore most of the flavour items on screen. It's worthwhile chatting to everyone at least once, though; you'll have some intelligent conversations.
Combat is timed, with you and your enemy having certain attack gauges that fill up and become available with time. You have an attack gauge and an ability gauge, the latter of which uses mana, and clicking on one of the gauge icons either launches the relevant attack if the gauge is full, or wastes some of the time in the gauge if it's not full, so it pays to wait and learn the timing well. You also have a defense gauge that fills up much more quickly, with the idea being that you can activate your defense as the enemy attacks, thereby blocking the attack. I've managed to do it sometimes, but the timing can be tight and some enemies don't have very obvious tells to indicate when they're about to attack, so it can be pretty hit and miss (haha). Combat is quite fun, though, especially once you've gone up a level or two and have some abilities, equipment, and potions in your inventory, so each encounter doesn't feel like so much of a life and death gamble.
Inventory management is made easy in spite of the relatively small inventory by the game telling you up front which items are just flavour and can be sold, and which ones can be equipped or used, or are quest related. Flavour items can be sold directly from the inventory, thanks to a handy gadget given to you by your merchant neighbour shortly after you start, so there's no carting loot back and forth between dungeons and shops. Oh, and once you start racking up some gold you can buy some lovely items from the blacksmiths in the various towns, too.
The story is the main draw for me, though. I enjoy RPGs and have played them a lot, and comedy RPGs are fairly few and far between. Based on some of the comments NPCs make in particular, Mad Noords seems to have been developed by people with a similar love for RPGs. There's a lot of text in the game, but I would guess that the developers are not native English speakers. The game can be played in Russian, Ukrainian, and English, and unfortunately the English text is rather rough and could really use the touch of an experienced editor or proof reader. There are countless grammar errors and not-quite-right uses of colloquialisms
The game information on Steam says that the Early Access version includes two episodes, while the full release will include one extra episode and more content. If the first cucumber-based episode is anything to go by, there's reasonable amount of content here already, so if you enjoy the style of the game and the humour, it should keep you busy for some time.
Pros:
+ An enjoyable console RPG in its own right
+ Good sense of humour
+ Charming graphics and sound
Cons:
- Writing quality; it could really do with a proof reader.
- Poor path following makes rooms with traps more frustrating than they should be.
- Some minor bugs: when in full screen, Steam notifications cause some graphic corruption in the bottom right, and the menu button in the bottom left stopped working for me at one point, as if it was opening and then closing the menu again straight away.
Mad Nords: Probably an Epic Quest is charming and humorous, despite the fairly rough writing. It's a good effort at a tongue-in-cheek console-style RPG with a reasonable amount of content and with a little bit more polish will be a credit to the development team on its release.
Note: I received this game for free for review purposes. This did not influence my review.

I haven't written many reviews but I feel compelled to do so for this game. The atmosphere and graphics are enjoyable, however do not expect a serious and grave RPG but a lighthearted and rather funny one. It depends on what you like in games, I didn't like that much however it surely is no negative point - it is just different. Furthermore I really liked that conflicts in the game are not only solved by combat but also by logic and perception. That is very rarely done by many games these days and should be done more.
However, the character development during the game in matters of background stories and relationship in the group is nearly nonexistant and redundant. I couldn't forge an emotional binding with any character in the game and didn't care for each and every one of them. This might be a consequence of the general lightheartedness but it just made it harder for me to immerse in the world.
The game is also really bulky. It takes a couple of minutes to heal up after combat, to equip, to identify, to forge. Everything takes a lot of time and isnt done in a simple way but in the most cumbersome way possible. While it is not bad for a game to not pop up several "how to play notives" and do half the stuff for the player, a quick and comfortable layout of the game helps me enjoy it more since I dont have to stick with the "work" part of the game.
The combat might seem intuitive but I didn't find that it played a lot differently as soon as you figured out what to use when. It was nice a couple of times and then got standard procedure rather quickly. And do not be mistaken by my former explanations: There are LOTS of combats. Lots of healing, Lots of the same stuff over and over again without the feeling of smooth and streamlined gaming. Many might call it refreshingly oldfashioned, I just find it tireing since there have been better models of this all around.
THis game is not bad per se, many people can have a lot of fun with. Expect a really old fashioned RPG in a lighthearted, comical world with little immersion. It is as oldfashioned as it gets with all the advatages and disadvantages - I didnt play it through, which rarely happens for games.

South Park™: The Stick of Truth™ is definetly one of the greatest RPGs I've ever played.  As someone who grew up with Paper Mario and likes the South Park show, this one resonates with me.  It's basically a parody of RPGs...  South Park style!  You get to join Stan's quiet little mountain town as the new kid and meet new "friends" as you participate in a Fantasy game that seems to have everyone involved!  It parodizes everything from the turn-based battle system in general, to invisible roadblocks and everything we grew up around in these games.  It's not just a parody, it's a strong RPG on it's own with minigames, an actual plot and interactions with your surroundings for hilarious results.  Obviously, this is South Park, so it's not for everyone.  Let's compare South Park to Picasso.  For most, it's random and a mess, but for those who see it for what it is, it's basically art.  I know, I just called South Park art.  Go with me on this one.  It's one hell of a game filled to the brink with offensive yet hilarious comedy and charm, only brought down by a rather complex menu system and a slightly repetitive battle system.  But it's all good, it's unbelievavly entertaining to watch.  South Park is one of the best RPGs in recent memory.  It brings back fond memories of Paper Mario as a kid and is basically a super long South Park episode.  If you like the show, this is definetly a buyer.

It’s no secret that some casual games on Steam can’t really fail, because they excel at doing one seemingly simple gameplay mechanic and never stray far from their established formula. Steel Punk Ball (SPB) is just such a title. It’s not complex in any way but it didn’t require that in order to captivate me. The game just like Steamroll before it, managed to combine two aspects that I’m very fond of. Steampunk and a true classic, BRIO’s Labyrinth (involving marbles or metal balls). The dev team behind Steel Punk Ball is ExclexGame and I’m pleased by their Steam debut and so far only project on the platform.
There isn’t a story to this title and it couldn’t fit one when considering its gameplay anyway. It’s all fairly straightforward. Not even a tutorial, discussing about the controls but if you have a keyboard (why wouldn’t you?), you’ll figure it out in a matter of seconds. The goal within each of Steel Punk Ball’s 30 levels, is to skillfully traverse the maze-like environments within a certain time frame. There are both obstacles and “power-ups” that spice things up, but we’ll focus on them in the gameplay section. Even without a narrative, your imagination can run wild as to why the stages and elements are obviously steampunk, yet the backgrounds feature a cybernetic look which resembles a huge circuit board. We’re in the Matrix, right? It’s just a glitch, move along now.
Unity Engine - Personal Edition, properly credited as soon as you boot up the game. Steel Punk Ball may not include any graphical settings in its main menu, but at least it ran in my monitor’s native resolution from the start and I never experienced any bugs or crashes. The lack of vertical synchronization was noticed once the Steam Overlay reported a constant frame rate of over 300, yet surprisingly, there was no screen tearing at all. I guess that without sudden movement, it really doesn’t look like an issue. Couldn’t even force V-synch from the Nvidia Control Panel so there’s really nothing you can do but hope for a patch that will allow this crucial feature. Other than that, SPB looks great, from high quality textures to extra effects such as reflections and the obligatory steam. Wouldn’t be steampunk without it!
The soundtrack takes centre stage here, since we couldn’t expect any voice acting and the miscellaneous sound effects made by the ball hitting surfaces and so on, don’t really stand out. But the OST was a nice mix of dubstep and a few other techno songs that seem to confirm our fears of cyberpunk being the underlying theme in Steel Punk Ball. Or not.
I hope you didn’t expect this to be a smooth ride from start to finish. What kind of adventure doesn’t showcase a few bumps along the road? You’ll be forgiven for thinking that SPB is gonna be a breeze, just after you’ve finished the first five levels or so. You’re in for a treat since the game doesn’t dish out its punishment all at once. By the time you’ll reach the 13th level (not a coincidence, I presume) it will become a norm to repeat stages either for a better time record or simply because the ball took too many hits. Yes, there is a hitpoint system in place. Getting from  point A to B would have been an tedious affair, if not for an adequate challenge in the form of various traps.
From hydraulic arms to circular saw blades and even rockets, Steel Punk Ball will test out both your patience and quick reflexes. Don’t give up and strive to improve your time by cutting corners and not bumping into edges all the time. Speaking of which, the earlier mentioned bonuses come in the form of additional time added to the counter. Never miss those purple time crystals when rolling around. I compared the title with a previously reviewed one, Steamroll, because they feature a distinct gameplay mechanic that makes the difference between success and failure: physics-based animation.
More precisely, that cheeky sphere which is our “protagonist” in this case. The titular steel ball has shifting speeds and relies on momentum, to get past ramps and even well-coordinated traps. Take my advice, on some levels don’t stop and think, just go for it. Other stages may require some planning ahead and delays in your movement or approach angle. You’ll need to adapt but fortunately, trial & error shall allow you to overcome any difficulties. The keyboard controls worked flawlessly, so I could never blame “lag” for failing a particular level. After each success, you’re awarded with a star rating, from 1 to 3. You’ll need 50 stars to access level 21 and 80 stars in total, just to unlock the final 30th stage.
There aren’t many things I’d like seeing either changed or enhanced in Steel Punk Ball. Some extra assets could never go wrong as well as a level editor. You can’t really argue with what it already offers but I firmly believe that such a title deserves both Cards and Achievements. It would almost be an injustice for so much Steam shovelware to posses these collector auxiliaries and a quality casual title such as SPB to skip them altogether. Please make it happen, ExclexGame.
+ Well-balanced difficulty.

Hardware: Windows 10, i5 3570, GTX 1070, no problems.
Graphics are good, as can be seen from the video. There appears to be only one music track, and it's pretty repetitive. The overall sound design could be stronger.
The ball physics feel good; the ball has a good, solid weight, though it doesn't seem to accelerate enough on downhill slopes. Going uphill can feel painfully slow if you don't start with enough momentum. The ability to boost your speed with a button press (and using a finite resource to do so) would be welcome. I would like the ball to have a rolling sound; right now it is silent.
The game supports a 360 controller; left stick moves the ball. I had expected right stick to let me rotate the camera, but it didn't do anything and there's no controls menu. It doesn't make it impossible to play, but it does feel a bit unintuitive to have a good view of the ball only when moving on the Y axis.
The levels start out very easy and quick to finish, slowly introducing new concepts. Traps so far (I played through level 9) are designed to slow you down rather than "kill" you, for example, to reduce the speed of the ball, or to knock you off the proper path, causing you to lose time to get back.
You have a set number of seconds to finish a level, and either fail, or get rated one, two or three stars based on how well you did. Powerups on the levels increase your remaining time. Not all are mandatory, and there are some in out of the way places you may need to make the best time. You can repeat a level right away for a better time if you wish, though the only purpose of a better time is for your personal level-by-level records. Getting the best score for a level will require some trial and error as you learn the optimal path. I suspect later levels will require a fair bit of trial and error to finish them in time, as the size and complexity was ramping up rather quickly as I reached level 10.
I've never played any other similar games (such as Marble Drop), so I can't compare to them, but the game seems fairly priced at $2.

I got this game in a complete back for 75% off. Even though the titles after are good, this game destroys them in one way, which makes it way better and more playable for me. This way is combat. The other games have a function where your sword moves in the direction your mouse is moving in, while this particular game basically sets your attack in the direction of the nearest enemy. Although this sounds a lot more basic, I prefer it, along with a lot of other people.
The graphics are about what you'd expect from a 2008 title, especially from a game of this type. The scales of some of the fights are really quite amazing, even though sometimes if you're fighting a massive enemy army they have to send the rest in as reinforcements or something. This is because at the time of this game's release (over 8 years ago), there wasn't really good enough hardware to have LOADS of enemies on screen AND let you fight. (Some RTS games at the time had a lot of enemies, but the graphics were inferior and you couldn't actually fight since they're RTS titles lol).
I recommend this game to anyone who wants to invest a lot of time into one game, but also to people who don't have loads of times, as you can save and quit the game at any time you want. Seriously, GET. THIS. GAME.

Detailed thoughts:
This game never really stuck out that big to me when first released. I had seen gameplay but it never really drove me into wanting to get it. Maybe it's the idea that almost every game i buy these days are games that i'll play for maybe an hour then stop playing all together. Game's haven't been as appealing as they used to be. They're lacking a charm that made video games so popular years ago. Yes, there's still good games been released such as Fallout 4 which i loved, Life is Strange which i also love and a few others such as JC3 and so on. These are all fun games that have charm that a lot of video games these days are lacking.
Story line:
As of writing this, i have yet to complete the story. I cannot say for sure my thoughts on it yet as i really can't judge a game until i've finished playing it, however, as far as i have gotten into the story, it seems to be a decent story. Doing missions is fun especially with a friend as you can have the advantage of two people fighting their way through the hordes of zombies that may be attacking them. I think i could play this comfortably in single player but i'm hard to please when it comes to game and grabbing my attention with a good story is hard so playing this with a friend definitely boost the experience.
Mechanics:
The Mechanics in this game of the fighting and movement system and many other things is almost perfect. Killing zombies could not get anymore fun than it already is. The moment your boot touches the face of a zombie while you're in the middle of a drop kick attack is just music to my eyes and ears. I stare visciously at the pOols of BlooD aNd WiPe AwAY THe TEArS OF HAPPINESS AND THEN I TAKE OUT A KATANA AND SLICE THAT ♥♥♥♥♥ INTO A THOUSAND DIFFERENT BODY PARTS UNTIL IT LOOKS LIKE SOMEONE IS ON A REAL GORY PERIOD. Seriously though, the fighting and movement systems is just perfection. If you're ever having a real bad day or just angry of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of, you know exactly what to do buddy.
Map:
The map design isn't bad! There is tonnes of detail around the city which many games require to make for a good experience but some games lack. Although full of detail, Harran isn't entirely huge and borders are pretty awful. It lacks any countryside whatsoever although from what i understand, the new DLC released in Feburary contains a new map that's based in the countryside. Harran however just doesn't have great borders. Some areas are block off that really don't need to be blocked off and it feels like and open world game that isn't fully open. Almost like a WIP game but the mechanics and map detail makes up for this for me at least.
Visuals/Asthetics and Optimization:
This game just straight up looks good. Very pleasing to the eye and i honestly wouldn't ask for a game to look better. It may not surpass the new tomb raider game released this year but it's still beautiful. This game runs beautfiully well for the amount of detail it contains and how well it looks. It seems to me that you may need a somewhat decent CPU to run this with 60+ fps as it seems to be CPU intensive but on my medium end AMD system, i can run the game on medium graphic settings and still achieve a minimum of 30fps and a max of 60fps. Comparing to games out there like Just Cause 3, this is impressive.
Overall quick summary:
Definitely worth a buy if you have a friend to play it with. Many hours of fun will be had with this. From gore to weapons and mechanics, this game has everything a hardcore gore and zombie fan wants.
And as a side note, i want to thank my friendeio (friend) who very kindly bought me this game even though he should have kept it for himself and gotten himself a bunch of other games but i appreciate it mate.

If you're against shady and rude indie developers, don't buy this game.
If you want to hear more about why I say that follow this link:
-- Original Review---
Alright; I got this game for free to make videos on for YouTube.  Video’s a work in progress, this review isn’t 100% completed yet.  Also as a side note, I feel bad being the only one to not reccomend the game
Mad Nords (As I'll call the game from here on) is a RPG game whose writing tries to be humorous by poking fun at tropes of the genre.  To be perfectly honest I'm not sure if it’s just poor writing and oddly placed or if it’s just me not in the mentality but I didn't enjoy the attempt at humor.  It's definitely not because it just not being my humor style because I adore the humor of The Stanley Parable.  Also you have dialogue choices but they're either A. Insignificant or B. Requires non-combat skills that you're probably not going to invest in Overall; dialogue when it tries to be humor seems unfunny and obvious, otherwise it's alright, don't expect anything super special.
Also as a side note, a good example of humor that seems off, without pointing out specific dialog, is that random NPCs cycle through a few different voice sounds to play whenever they speak (It plays once when the text starts) one of these ends with a fart, which I know it sounds like humor police when I say this, I just don’t feel like it was utilized properly as a good joke.  Fart humor in general is Elementary School material, but it can be used in unique ways, and ways that can get a laugh out of you.
Mad Nord's combat is definitely it's weak point; especially as a basic warrior.  Why?  You're always waiting for cooldowns.  And you wait and wait.  That's not it though, enemies' animations and sounds both feel off, the things that are supposed to indicate attacks so you can defend feel in my experience, off que, and makes it difficult to block; there's also enemies that have really weird pauses before attacking, and attacks without any good ques.  That added to some odd difficulty spikes, that either requires you to grind it out or to have extreme luck, makes me want to not touch the game ever again.  Stale combat in a RPG ruins the game.  Maybe a sorcerer would be better, they seem to have more to do in combat from what the trailer shows, but that’d be a major time investment just to see if I can have fun fighting monsters.  If I return to this game I might have to try that.
Some other things that are bad in my opinion is that the cooldown timer for attacks and stuff punishes you if you hit it too early.  So if it’s about to be ready (And sometimes is literally just a pixel off of being ready) and you hit that key, you’re going to have to wait some more time before you can attack.  I’m not going to go in depth about why this is a bad choice, but rather give an example from one of the most popular games ever; League of Legends in that sometimes the enemy barely escapes alive, and you spam an ability to get that last bit of damage off, it will be a tenth of a second off, and instantly cast as soon as its up and possibly finish.  Not in this game, nope that timer will be back at square one and maybe some further back.  It’s just something to consider changing as I found it annoying at times.
Alright graphically the game is nowhere special; pixel art kinda feels standard to mediocre to alright.  My main gripe with it is how areas feel sameish; especially dungeons with their generic square tiles.  (I know it’s difficult to make unique areas everywhere; but that’s a strong point of doing a parody, you can go into weird places, you can change the formula up.  Have a character say “I painted this area pink cause the green made me sad”, and what do you know the area is painted pink!)  There are things added to spruce them up but it doesn't feel effective, because even those loop a ton before it’s over.  It's also notable that you're either in windowed without any ability to change resolution, full screen 1 which is actually a borderless window, and full screen 2 which is a borderless window with a giant ♥♥♥♥ing black border.  Also notable is that the game is in permanent 4:3, causing a really dated effect that I dislike; I don’t care if you're going for a retro style we aren't in an age where 4:3 is standard, you can upgrade your game, it’s called retro styled because it looks retro but is modern, so update a little and move to 16:9; have options for resolution even in windowed mode, and if you feel fancy an option to change aspect ratio, refresh rate/vsync, etc.
Now the sound design is horrible, the music I lowered extremely so I'm not going to comment about it.  But a great example of why the sounds in this game are horrible is the sound that plays when an enemy goes underground to attack; it sounds more like leaves ruffling then dirt shuffling.  And this game made it all sound like it’s coming through a horrible sound card of the 80’s.
** SOME OTHER NOTES FROM MY EXPERIENCE **
I feel like 95% of my loot were made to be sold, which in a dungeon multiple floors away from the surface doesn’t really help you.  I’m just going to ask for some armor and stuff being more common over things to sell in the dungeons, and in over worlds, towns, and stuff is where you get money loot.  Especially when I have to risk going through multiple deadly traps for 30 gold.
I find the UI's use of grey just kinda boring, not anything horrible, but at the same time with a fantasy game trying to be comedic, it should be way more flamboyant.
Also I got a game crash within less than 2 hours of gameplay, so there's probably many more glitches but otherwise it's okay I guess when it comes to stability.  Definately passable for Early Access.
SUMMARY:
I don't recommend this game.  At least not to everyone.  If you're willing to grind a bit, and be patient in combat, and willing to accept it for what it is, or at least what it tries to be, or if you're just itching for a new rpg which I admit isn't my forte either, for 10$ it's worth the money.  Personally im just a bit too much of a perfectionist to let some things slide, to be honest I'm probably overly critical on this game  It's not hate, it's more a mix of my own boredom and comedy that didn't connect with me,   If you want some quick numbers here, they are:
Overall 5/10 - I was bored playing this game, it wasn't offensively bad, I was just bored playing it.  If a game can't keep my interest, and if it gives me nothing to look forward to, why should I play it? I only give it 5 because it's a cheaper title
Graphics 5/10 - Overall they're alright, just nothing special.  Repetetive at worst.
Sound 2/10 - If you want to defend it by saying blah blah retro styled blah blah, I'll tell you this: Older games worked around their limitations and some of them had some great music (Some I'd call timeless), but this game didn't even have those limitations, they imposed these on themselves and they failed to be creative, or give me anything as a player I could say sounded good. Before giving a score (for those that need or care for one) I will list all the good and bad parts of the game, from my perspective, so lets begin.
The good:
1. The graphics are unique that I haven't seen on any other game (I haven't that doesn't mean that there aren't) that suits the environment of the game great, however during conversations of the game between characters you can see that they just repeat the same animation (it's nothing big but needs to bee mentioned).
2. The music is weary atmospheric, but for me it missed that memorable feel. It has that nordic feel that the game is going for.
3. The story is well paced and you can fell for the main character, but I got dragged out of it a bit when the switch between characters happened (game switches between more than 1 character). The world is interesting and it has a lot of mythos behind it with a lot of small additions like history of some locations. The story it self is well written but with a bit abrupt ending (I felt like it will be the ending but hoped that it would continue, shame), but the ending isn't bad.
Now we get to the games difficult part the gameplay.
The gameplay is  a mix bag for me.
It's a turn base strategy when in combat but its lacking (it's not bad).
In combat the main problem I found was that it was really hard to prevent someone from dying, but the biggest problem there was that where wasn't any balance on numbers (the less units u have the more advantage u have (not always) unless u have only 1 or the all are wounded because u could do more actions with the units than the enemy could giving u a chance to weaken the enemy units before they can move).
Then there's the leveling system for your heroes. The fact that only the one who gets the last hit gets to get stronger is a bad thing in my opinion because that forces u to play on that and that would be ok if there had been a way to switch heroes or a better way to protect other heroes but it does not. Additionally if u focus on the wrong heroes you can get ♥♥♥♥ed at he end which is really bad when u play for the first time (additionally u can lose some heroes after making decisions, this really can screw with u because u are given limited chance for leveling heroes), tho u can change the game difficulty at any time during the campaign which is good.
Last the decisions that u make impact the game weary lithe (as u probably can guess), but to it's credit there is some impact on the game experience.
The final thing that I didn't like was the caravans moral system, which is badly explained (not what it does but how it diminished one time it goes down after a way other times in 2 but the worst part is that u don't know when it is going to go down, there is no warning on scale or anything that u can look at to get the information on it).
The game takes around 14 h for one play through to finish which I believe is adequate for a game of this price.
My final score is 7.5/10 (a very good game and almost great game)

This game is far more clever than I expected it to be. The humor is sometimes hit or miss, but often a hit, despite the fact that most of my otaku cultural knowledge is second-hand. The basic premise, if you don't know, is that the console war is fought not with business meetings and product sales but with anime girls who draw power from their market share.
Combat is turn-based, but it's the fastest turn-based game I've ever played. Transitions from one turn to the next are completely seamless, the AI takes no time at all to line out moves, your movement is resrtricted to a radius around you rather than distance so there's no cancelling moves over and over to reposition yourself and once locked in combat, your character will attack four or more times with an assortment of thirteen pre-equipped moves you can swap from on the fly, yet you'll soon develop combinations for specific situations that means selecting the given moves is as simple as the press of a button. Fighting something with a full armor bar you want to whittle down? Try AAAA. if its guard is at half so you want to mix up guard breaks and damage? Go for AAYY. Shields down? AXXX. Enemy is too evasive or you need to try for a crit? AYYY. There's no scrolling through long menus to find whatever it is you need. A little slower with a mouse if you want to click things, but not by much.
You can also dress up your gamindustri (the actual name of the world in Hyperdimension Neptunia) lolis with a wide array of costumes, weapon designs and, of course, hats. This is steam. I hear people like hats.
If you like Diablo 3, you'll like this.

Digital Illusions CE also known as DICE also known as People That Know What They Are Doing?
I won't lie, I didn't play Motorhead that they did in 1998, but it was racing game, and it was pretty good as I heard plenty of times. And so Rallisport from 2002.
I won't lie about this one either, I didn't play Benefactor, but it was puzzle platform and it was pretty great too. And it was 1994.
Now, why am I talking about these old games, and DICE but not Mirror's Edge? Well, I'm mentioning them, just so people could realise that DICE is more than just Battlefield, Need For Speed and Star Wars. They've been killing it since day one and not just since the 2002 alias Battlefield 1942. But yeah, they did unbelievable games throughout the time and so they did Frostbite too and we love it right?
And then, in 2008, somebody had an idea, why don't we make action adventure game, why not some running, jumping, escaping, shooting and fighting game that won't be war related like Battlefield. And so the Mirror's Edge was born, and came out as the hell of a great game.
Story is not that deep as you may think, and it's not even long, or medium, for me it was kinda short. I wish it was a little bit longer but it is what it is. Also, I believe that if the game was released like in 2014, EA would already managed to release 2 extra story related DLCs and 4 visual DLCs. But let "what ifs" be what ifs.

You should either escape, run over, or defeat them one by one because you cannot win if you go open on more than 2 enemies. Shooting is garbage, I recommend you throwing away weapon once you get it except few levels when sniper is needed.
To sum it up, this game is unique, and yes, the Catalyst has been released few months ago, but it does not change the fact that this is the Father, and this is truly awesome game.
If you enjoy jumping between skyscrapers and running over everything like Usain Bolt with no fear of heights, there is no way that Mirror's Edge will be repetetive for you anytime soon.

Best gameplay focused on player mobility in any game I've seen. Beautifully designed parkour action, highly flexible with lots of freedom to choose your route and adapt how you move.
Very satisfying combat. Hand to hand is nicely done, guns are there if you want to play with them (and I do) but you can also beat most enemies with careful maneouvring and hand to hand.
Overall a great demonstration of designing flow into a game. You're always moving, acting, going from problem to problem, very rarely getting stuck. Visual cues make your choices clear, not forcing you to make blind guesses. When you fail at something it's your skills that are the problem 99% of the time not the game being misleading. Most games don't come even close to that level of skill-orientation.
Will be getting the sequel.
Cons:
(and they're very minor, compared to how good the game is)
I suppose the main flaw is there are times when you slow down (like when moving in vents), which not only were low points in the flow but also seemed like the character should be able to move faster given how well she moves the rest of the time.
The parkour was mostly seamless, there were glitches but few and far between.
The ending was a little unsatisfying, not quite enough to it compared to the rest of the game, but certainly not a bad ending.
I suspect the disarm action timing is a little off in places with the visual cues. Might have been just my mistake though.

For those who enjoy a vapid, soulless experience, this game is perfect. Not only is the story paper thin, but as a visual novel it fails to add anything to the story either. Although some of the art is nice, its sparse with only minor changes to the characters and backgrounds throughout the game. Incongruities are rife amongst the writing, characters, and backgrounds.
Yes, you do learn about Japanese culture whilst playing the game, but you do so to the story's detriment. Large chunks of the character’s dialogue is simply cultural regurgitation, so much so that they might as well be their own segments. Any aspect of either of the two girls is solely attributed to them because the target demograph of this game finds them appealing. A more solemn, shy girl who does her best to appease those around her, and a lively, wild girl who is sporadic in behaviour.
These aren’t characters; they are fantasies.
Not only are the two main girls terribly created, but the main character (Brian) is also insufferable. Like other main characters of a similar ilk, he’s only an empty vessel for the reader to live vicariously through, with the occasional character trait that relates to the game’s target demograph – like being an otaku, or being extremely socially awkward around girls.
If you are an otaku, are socially awkward around girls, enjoy Japanese school girls and love visual novels, them by all means you’ll love this game to its core. But for the rest of the Earth, stay away from this rancid filth.
.....oh, and don't expect a good ending or meaningful choices. They don't exist in the game.

Before giving a score (for those that need or care for one) I will list all the good and bad parts of the game, from my perspective, so lets begin.
The good:
1. The graphics are unique that I haven't seen on any other game (I haven't that doesn't mean that there aren't) that suits the environment of the game great, however during conversations of the game between characters you can see that they just repeat the same animation (it's nothing big but needs to bee mentioned).
2. The music is weary atmospheric, but for me it missed that memorable feel. It has that nordic feel that the game is going for.
3. The story is well paced and you can fell for the main character, but I got dragged out of it a bit when the switch between characters happened (game switches between more than 1 character). The world is interesting and it has a lot of mythos behind it with a lot of small additions like history of some locations. The story it self is well written but with a bit abrupt ending (I felt like it will be the ending but hoped that it would continue, shame), but the ending isn't bad.
Now we get to the games difficult part the gameplay.
The gameplay is  a mix bag for me.
It's a turn base strategy when in combat but its lacking (it's not bad).
In combat the main problem I found was that it was really hard to prevent someone from dying, but the biggest problem there was that where wasn't any balance on numbers (the less units u have the more advantage u have (not always) unless u have only 1 or the all are wounded because u could do more actions with the units than the enemy could giving u a chance to weaken the enemy units before they can move).
Then there's the leveling system for your heroes. The fact that only the one who gets the last hit gets to get stronger is a bad thing in my opinion because that forces u to play on that and that would be ok if there had been a way to switch heroes or a better way to protect other heroes but it does not. Additionally if u focus on the wrong heroes you can get ♥♥♥♥ed at he end which is really bad when u play for the first time (additionally u can lose some heroes after making decisions, this really can screw with u because u are given limited chance for leveling heroes), tho u can change the game difficulty at any time during the campaign which is good.
Last the decisions that u make impact the game weary lithe (as u probably can guess), but to it's credit there is some impact on the game experience.
The final thing that I didn't like was the caravans moral system, which is badly explained (not what it does but how it diminished one time it goes down after a way other times in 2 but the worst part is that u don't know when it is going to go down, there is no warning on scale or anything that u can look at to get the information on it).
The game takes around 14 h for one play through to finish which I believe is adequate for a game of this price.
My final score is 7.5/10 (a very good game and almost great game)

If Douglas Adams and Terry Pratchett had teamed up to make Skyrim for the Super Nintendo waaay back in the 1990s, the end result would have been... well, probably terrible, as neither of them were game developers.  Luckily they never tried, so the developers of Mad Nords were free to unleash their own silly version of this nifty mashup on the world.
Mad Nords:  Probably an Epic Quest is a retro-styled RPG that features weird, quirky humor along with the open world and quest-branching system of an Elder Scrolls or Fallout game.  The player starts out as a level 1 cannibal/bureaucrat/(insert unusual class of choice) looking for a cucumber for his wife in the next town over. Of course, this simple fetch quest won't be as easy as it should be, and so begins the main questline.
As you are continually redirected to new locations to continue with your main, cucumber-seeking quest, the overwhelming temptation to fall into the usual RPG standard of speaking to every person and breaking into every house will eventually get the better of you.  A few hours later, you'll realize that you've explored several towns and dungeons, completed a dozen sidequests, and geared yourself up with a stupendous bladed fork of +3 strength and 15% critical chance - but never really got any closer to finding that cucumber.  Which is just as it should be, as any player who has spent hundreds of hours on an Elder Scrolls game without actually beating the main quest can tell you.
Mad Nords' retro graphics and strange sense of humor are pleasantly enjoyable, making this game a fun way to while away a Saturday morning.  The game offers an abundance of fairly amusing quests, plenty of magical loot, and quite a few useful skills to invest in as you level to offer some RPG-progression.  Each starting class also features a few unique skills, which adds variety and even replayability if you want to try a different character.  I do not know how much content the end product will have (this is an Early Access title), but I do know that I came nowhere close to finding my cucumber after several hours of playtime.

Mad Nords is an entertaining parody of open-world questing with a very reasonable pricetag.  I would definitely recommend trying out this quirky game if you get a chance.

I did not expect much from this visual novel. It just looked like a generic slice-of-life read with two cute anime girls thrown in for eye candy. However, while the story was pretty short, I certainly enjoyed it. It had it's charm and actually taught me quite a bit about Japanese culture and traditions. The in-game glossary is very useful and provides good explanations and definitions for certain Japanese foods, holidays, items, etc.
The game has two endings depending on certain choices you get to make throughout the story, but they're both near identical, with only a few changes in dialogue. This is my only real complaint, and I do wish they would have put in a bit more effort into differentiating the two endings better.

I was able to get this from a Humble Bundle, but if you ever see this game on sale, it's certainly worth a try if you are interested in Japanese culture and/or are into visual novels and are looking for a cute read. Plus, it has 6 easy achievements for completionists.*
For what it is, I give it an 8/10. I do wish it could have been a bit longer, but the likeable characters, great voice acting, cute narrative, and nice art direction greatly make up for it.
*As of the time of me posting this review, all of the achievements seem to be glitched for the majority of people. There's a guide in the community hub on how to fix the issue if you want to get them legit.

I recommend this game to anyone looking for a great single-player strategy, and for many others interested in simply an interesting world. In some ways, I think this game represents a revival of some classic games, of the 1980's varieties, but it troubles me that it also represents a regression in some ways. While I recommend it, I also want to qualify my recommendation regarding the two aspects of the game, which I will loosely define as "environmental" and "tactical." While I feel very gratified with the environmental aspect, I think the tactical mode was sometimes hackneyed at and never hit the "sweet spot" of difficulty matching experience. For an old-school reference, I'm thinking of Fantasy General (SSI game, available and optimized for DOSBox (apologies if I'm not allowed to say that)) as reference. While FG was a much larger game, admittedly, and it is one of my all time favorites, I think the comparison is valid, which I mean not to so much to demean this game but rather to cast this game (Banner Saga) in a good light. Being compared to an SSI game in the strategy genre is an accolade.
In short, I'd like to address the two significant features of The Banner Saga, as I see them and define them. These are the
and the
. I feel the team overachieved in the former aspect, and barely underachieved in the latter.
, I think it is as engrossing an experience you'd find in such a game. It far surpasses that of Fantasy General in many ways. First and foremost, the graphical experience of your carivan struggling through the beautiful landscape is one of the most pleasing portions of this game, and paired with the award-winning soundtrack, almost too good to miss even if you just play on Easy mode to avoid the tactical difficulties. People with wide imaginations, remembering the game Oregon Trail, will see portions of these travel scenes in their minds, and hear the music, when imagining such a carivan off the desperate and  disparate struggling towards safety.
It's so good I want to play through again just to feel like I'm involved in such a struggle. The studio should pay the composer's fine gratis, it is so well matched. All the artist involved, should we ever meet, will get a free cup of mead (or whatever) on me if we ever cross paths. And I hope we do.
[h2]Regarding the tactical component,[/h2] I sincerely feel it could have been managed better. It just never hits the sweet spot of difficulty and experience. On my first playthrough, on medium difficulty, I had just two fails in combat, one due to simply not clicking on the correct square and the other, in the final boss fight, due to a somewhat common bug. It simply isn't difficult to win this game on the tactical field, even given numersous opponents.
The system of initiative, or the order of who moves when, the game uses is that turns alternate, which is perfectly acceptable if teams are matched. However, most times the enemy team has more fighters than the 6 (max) the player is allowed, so elements of the opposing force are only allowed to move every 1.5 or 2 turns. This was clear from the first fight, when your two heroes face off against 4 opponents. The advatage is obvious, and has been discussed widely. Due to tactical considerations, wounding an opponent to the point that he can no longer cause real damage is often better than just killing them outright. This is a critical flaw, in my opinion.
The flaw leads to a couple of unusual circumstances. It forced the devs to adapt to the system, and (as I can identify) adopt two mechanics which seriously flaw the game: attacks which have no defense (area of attack grenades, and other special activities), and just increase the number of opponents and opponent statistics beyond measure.
I can picture them sitting around the drawing board, or conference table, talking about these issues. I can see the obvious difficulty presented by the issue raised by alternation of turns. I still believe the response was hackneyed, and seriously mars this aspect of the game. I feel like this decision was made early on, and a lot of effort was given to masking it, but the effort would have been better applied to making the game work in a realistic (funny word for a fantasy game) fashion.
For instance, if you have eight fighters, and I have four, why on earth would each of my fighters act 1.5 times to your one? Having a numerical advantage can be turned to a disadvantage in this game by simply focusing on injuring (but not killing) opponents and letting your team move around more quickly than the opponent, and that's just a shame.
I also hope that, in future versions, the developer would go to the hexagonal grid system instead of squares (ala FG) and include zones of control.
[h3] In conclusion [/h3] this is a great game, one I will play through again. I rarely play through games of this type more than once, but it is intriguing and the environmental aspect is compelling. The tactical aspect is a bitter pill to swallow, because of the unbalanced nature of the initiative system and the balancing act required. Environmetally, the only suggestion I would make would be to somehow quantify distance between destinations, so that the player might know how many supplies to pack before leaving. I'd also add a mechanic to re-equip a unit before a battle.

Beautiful, tragic, surprising.
If you like turn-based tactical combat, this game shines like a thousand suns, but that is not what stuck with me. What stuck with me is the art, the world, and the characters. The artwork, while simplistic, is very beautiful and gives the game a perfect essence without getting too distracting.
Exploring the world of the Banner Saga is like tasting a new favorite cake, the general shape is comfortingly familiar, but there are new flavours. It is a fantasy adventure, but there are no elves, orcs, or dwarfs. There are giants, but they are not like you think.
The characters are very well-written, most of them lovable in one way or another, and some are enjoyably hateful. You will inevitably come to love a few of them, while you'll barely get to meet others. Any one of them may die.
I highly recommend this game.

There are some nice improvements here over the original X-COM, but there are also many things that ruin it. Fellow X-COM veterans can probably relate to what I'm saying.
Shooting and reloading ends your soldier's turn. The original X-COM games gave you a number of TUs (time units) which you were free to use as you please. This was great because it gave players more tactical freedom. I appreciate this new simplified system is to appeal to more casual gamers, but the problem is it's too simple to the point where it hinders the player artificially. Why not allow players to use their two actions freely?
No line of sight means you can't shoot unless it's a grenade or rocket. The game has destroyable terrain and cars - why can't I shoot them to flush the enemy out? In an FPS game, you'd shoot an explosive barrel if it killed an enemy in cover. (I know this isn't an FPS, I'm just thinking about this logically.)
Cover is no longer a barrier. In the original X-COM, every shot was a calculated projectile (like
). It was entirely possible for stray shots to hit your squad-mates or another enemy. In this game, it's purely a dice roll. It's entirely possible for enemies to snipe you across the map while you're in heavy cover, yet your team will miss an alien about 3 tiles away, all because you got a bad dice roll. Unlucky!
Why are squads randomly assigned their classes upon promotion? It just means you have to keep hiring/firing rookies until you get the classes you need, assuming they survive their first missions without dying and/or you have the officer upgrade that automatically promotes rookies.
Chryssalids can move great distances, insta-kill rookies and civilians which re-spawn as bullet-sponge zombies - which can also inflict a lot of damage and hatch into another Chryssalid after 3 turns. This makes terror missions painfully hard because Chryssalids run around and kill the civilians before you get a chance to save them. Chryssalids can also leap onto higher surfaces, have a 60% defence against critical hits and cannot be stunned either.
My biggest gripe with the game is the fact that aliens get a free move when
spot them in
turn. Every time you spot a group of enemies, they get a free turn of movement to get into cover or flank you. This is because (aside from terror missions) aliens do not spawn on the map until you "trigger" them - just like stepping on a land mine.
Incidentally, this is another reason Chryssalids are OP - imagine a Chryssalid runs towards your squad, they spot it, so it gets another movement to close the gap even further.
At the end of the day this is just plain cheating. They should have made this an optional setting for masochist players.
Final Thoughts:

, or you found them too complicated, then this may appeal to you. Alternatively, check out
(it's open-source/free!)

Short version:
Get it if you have 1 to 3 friends, (so, a total of 4 peeps,) that love playing new types of games on a couch.
Longer version:
Couch Conflict games are great but tend to fall into a very small selection of catagories.
A large number are 1 screen platformers.
Another swathe are 1 screen "asteroids" based twin stick shooters.
Within these 2 large pools there are some stellar gems, a lot of winners, a few minor tweaks and innovations and a lot of "others" that don't really distinguish them selves well.
For the most part, if you have a handful of entries from these groups in your library, you'll have the basics covered and dipping back in too the pools probably won't net you anything wonderfully different.
So it's always exciting when clever people come up with something that feel radically different with out over complicating what you seek out from these experiances.
Nighogg is a great example of this idea, and if you're looking at Crawl as a multiplayer couch gamer, you probably already know about the joys of that.
What Crawl offers is different again... and does take a minute more to absorb, but after that you will be drinking in a game that takes the head to head nature of this genre and mixes in a brilliant and ever changing landscape of all vs 1 and and great "begining-middle-end" arc in each session.
If you have your basic couch conflict games covered, Get Nidhogg and get this and you'll have a great little menu to pick from.
Nighog for instantly accessable gaming at snack like speed.
Twin stick arenas and 1 screen platformers for experiances with a hair more length and variable substance.
Crawl for a solid hunk of entertainment that still leaves room for multiple sessions.
(Oh and Mount your friends for dessert... because it's fruity and lite) :D

This game transfered me to my childhood. It brought back a lot of my memories. Summer camps, first love, heart dilemmas, hard decisions (in young person opinion).
Everlasting Summer gives such feelings in a great way, especially that i was teenager in 80s :)
Stories told in the game are very interesting. There are plenty endings depending on our choices during the game. Some of them are really surprising.

Japanese School Life (JSL) is a slice-of-life about a US exchange student named Brian studying in Japan for a year.  While there, he meets 2 similar-yet-different girls in his class.  Hilarity ensues.  Okay, not so much hilarity, but rather . . . . education.  Information.  Learning.  Man, I'm making this sound boring.  Hang on a sec here . . . let me try this again.
Are you interested in Japanese culture?  Do you want to know minute details about Japanese foods, festivals, holidays and such?  Then JSL is for YOOOOOUUUUUUUUUUUUU!!!!!
This VN is definitely slice-of-life. I guess. Mostly.  Well, maybe it's more educational.  But life happens in it.  A whole school year, actually.  You arrive in Japan and are immediately befriended by 2 adorable girls (Chiyoko and Arisa) who take you under their wings.  Throughout the course of the year, you'll learn minor details about each and be treated to glimpses of their personalities.  Unfortunately, that's about as deep as they get.  You see, that's pretty much the "story" here in JSL.  You meet these 2 girls, pick one to romance (sort of) and stay stuck in the friend-zone for an entire year anyways.  A very large chunk of the game is actually informational miniature "lectures" from the girls about various aspects of Japanese (and specifically otaku) culture.  I'll be honest, I learned a LOT in this VN.  But was it entertaining? Eh . . .
Graphically, the sprites and CGs are beautiful.  The game utilizes the Emote system (which anyone who's read my other reviews knows I enjoy) to make the characters more lively through animation.  The voice overs (in Japanese) are much more professional than in many games, and the characters themselves have many and varied reactions, inflections and tones in their words.  The music is decent and catchy, and had me humming a couple of the "happier" tunes after I'd close the game.
In the negative, the story is bland and forgettable.  The game feels mostly like a delivery tool for a culture lesson.  This is all well and good, but I would have rather had more actual story content (The entire game took me less than 6 horus for 2 routes) to better balance out the exposition you recieve about things like "mochi".
Also, Brian.  Ugh.  Why so many exclamation points, Brian?! How are you possibly this excited about almost everything that happens to you on a daily basis?! He uses them in every. Single. Screen. Let's be honest, Brian is a dork. He may be a lovable dork, but he's a dork none-the-less.  I mean, it took him an entire year of having these cute girls covertly throwing themselves at him to even realize he LIKES one of them, and
Despite the negatives, I believe the positives outweight them and I definitely lean more to recommending the game than not.  It's silly, it's funny (sometimes), it's long-winded (like me) and cute simultaneously.  As with many of these more modestly-priced VNs, I'd say wait and get it on a sale.  50% feels like you're getting your money's worth for sure.  I bought it at 25% off, and that seems almost a bit high to me.

) and skills to items (how about

) and monsters (just check out the snapshot with the giant's leg). Lots of good laugh is guaranteed! Also "voiceovers" are hilarious on their own.
Mechanics-wise it is an RPG (leaning more to JRPGs) where you control a single character. You travel around the big world map visiting towns and locations of interest in pursuit of what starts with a quest for a
few cucumbers.
Dialogues are pretty straightforward, but they are funny and there are plenty of unobtrusive moral choices, if you are into those. Quite often you need a certain level of particular attribute or skill to bring the talks to a successful conclusion.
Fights are reaction-based (e.g. you might want to use the block skill at the right moment), and not very difficult, but give you some food for thought regarding how to develop your hero.
Then there are dungeons filled with traps, occasionally requiring some fast reaction as well (think darts and blades and disappearing floors), but thankfully never to the point of frustration.
Overall, the game is very solid and definitely entertaining. Just don't forget to bring your sense of humour.

In my honest opinion, FTL is amazing.
When it was the standard edition I thought it was pretty good, and I still put quite a few hours into it, but to me it felt like it was just a little lacking.  After playing through a few times, I had decided upon my normal strategy, and varied little through different play throughs.  That may not be a problem for some more adventurous gamers, but after finding something that worked I just wanted to stick with it.  For me, the advanced edition solved that problem.  I thoroughly enjoy the new race, the Lanius, although my favorite part is probably the expansion of the available weapons.  Missiles, lasers, ions and beams was a good start, but often I just wished there was a little more variety in those classes themselves.  I found myself always trying to find as many 'burst laser IIs' as I could, maybe with an occasional beam weapon.  Now, I really enjoy trying to decide between the chain lasers, normal lasers, scrap throwers and ion stunners, all of which I think add a great deal of new tactics and depth to the gameplay.  Overall, I think this game is very well done, totally worth the money, and the day they come out with an FTL 2, or let you battle your ships with other players I'm sure I'll be lost in deep space for a very long time.
