There are some nice improvements here over the original X-COM, but there are also many things that ruin it. Fellow X-COM veterans can probably relate to what I'm saying.
Shooting and reloading ends your soldier's turn. The original X-COM games gave you a number of TUs (time units) which you were free to use as you please. This was great because it gave players more tactical freedom. I appreciate this new simplified system is to appeal to more casual gamers, but the problem is it's too simple to the point where it hinders the player artificially. Why not allow players to use their two actions freely?
No line of sight means you can't shoot unless it's a grenade or rocket. The game has destroyable terrain and cars - why can't I shoot them to flush the enemy out? In an FPS game, you'd shoot an explosive barrel if it killed an enemy in cover. (I know this isn't an FPS, I'm just thinking about this logically.)
Cover is no longer a barrier. In the original X-COM, every shot was a calculated projectile (like
). It was entirely possible for stray shots to hit your squad-mates or another enemy. In this game, it's purely a dice roll. It's entirely possible for enemies to snipe you across the map while you're in heavy cover, yet your team will miss an alien about 3 tiles away, all because you got a bad dice roll. Unlucky!
Why are squads randomly assigned their classes upon promotion? It just means you have to keep hiring/firing rookies until you get the classes you need, assuming they survive their first missions without dying and/or you have the officer upgrade that automatically promotes rookies.
Chryssalids can move great distances, insta-kill rookies and civilians which re-spawn as bullet-sponge zombies - which can also inflict a lot of damage and hatch into another Chryssalid after 3 turns. This makes terror missions painfully hard because Chryssalids run around and kill the civilians before you get a chance to save them. Chryssalids can also leap onto higher surfaces, have a 60% defence against critical hits and cannot be stunned either.
My biggest gripe with the game is the fact that aliens get a free move when
spot them in
turn. Every time you spot a group of enemies, they get a free turn of movement to get into cover or flank you. This is because (aside from terror missions) aliens do not spawn on the map until you "trigger" them - just like stepping on a land mine.
Incidentally, this is another reason Chryssalids are OP - imagine a Chryssalid runs towards your squad, they spot it, so it gets another movement to close the gap even further.
At the end of the day this is just plain cheating. They should have made this an optional setting for masochist players.

That was a great game. Arguably one of the greatest ARPG's ever. The graphics were super cool, the story was interesting and at times intense, the action itself was seamless, the upgrade system was super deep and yet accessible. You could play this game countless different ways and have a great time. I put right around 40 hours into the campaign playing solo before finishing it, and after I was done, there was still another area at the top of the map to unlock, and probably 3 or 4 that I missed besides that. There is also an area called The steps of Torment which will challenge any hardened players, and that area features roguelike qualities. This game carries a lot of obvious influences as well, from Diablo 2 to Torchlight to even Dark Souls, and wears them well, while still managing to create it's own distinct personality.
I'm thinking that I can still easily put in another 15 or so hours solo before I'm just grinding loot or decide to change difficulties. The game also leaves definite room for a sequel and/or expansion, and really, this is a game world that could persist for a long time. There were things said via notes in the game that absolutely open up other potential story arcs. The Aetherial Betrayer, Ulgrim, and quite a few others.
So, some cool features of the game: you can dual class, and it changes your actual class if you do so. For example, I played an Occultist/Arcanist, which made me a Warlock. The upgrade system for the actual classes is broad enough to give you a lot of variety, but condensed enough that you wont feel overwhelmed. However, there is a second upgrade system that you get points for simply by cleansing shrines, and that my friends is as expansive an upgrade system as I have seen in a game. You could spend a while reading through all of them, and then you still have to decide what will best suit your play style. They are set up as constellations, and there are a lot of them! It can seem daunting, but actually, I dont think there are really any wrong choices, although some will obviously suit your preferred playstyle better than others, and a lot of them only unlock after unlocking constellations closer to the center, where you basically choose your upgrade arc. That was quite impressive and again, lends itself to a lot of experimentation. There is a respec NPC in the game, but I never actually made use of it, so I cant say how that works.
Also, some merchants will only sell you stuff after you have gotten your town or faction disposition maxed out, and they of course have the best items, lol. You can sell to them, but I personally didnt max out any factions yet, so I havent been able to purchase those super cool items. You can also craft items via another type of NPC, and that system is also pretty deep. You can craft all the basic stuff, but you have to find blueprints to craft anything truly spectacular. Items also have one slot for gem/material upgrades, and the gems/materials can be made stronger by fusing as many as 4 of the same type together. This will often unlock a special ability like casting fireballs or gaining Aetherial defense, slams, and so on.
There is actually a ton more to this game, but I think I will leave off for now and maybe revise this once I finish the map, play through higher difficulties, and/or play through this in co-op mode.

The Banner Saga is a good game. The art is absolutely FANTASTIC, and really makes a huge difference in how much I enjoyed this game. The tactics gameplay is great, very strategic and challenging. Your health and damage share the same stat, and then you have armor which mitigates damage at a 1:1 ratio (1 armor = -1 damage). When attacking you choose to either attack their health/damage, or their armor (which uses your armor break stat). It's a great system imo, not to mention all the different classes special abilities and items you can equip and some other gameplay elements. Anything you're doing outside of combat is Oregon Trail, or cutscene/conversation. The Oregon Trail aspect is really fun, but I found it to be more stressful than fun by the end of the game. Things just start getting so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you feel like bad things are happening every 30 seconds and there is little you can do to help yourself. Of course, maybe I just made some terrible choices.
The game took me 18 hours to complete, with a few of these hours going into battle contemplation and decision making only. Even so, the game felt somehow short, and endly abruptly, as others have said. My biggest complaint is that I felt like a lot went to waste in this game. I don't plan on playing it again; I have many other games to try. And I ended the game with pretty much only one full line-up at lvl 3-5, never had enough renown (exp and money currency) to buy ANY items that were for sale, and never had enough to work on leveling my other party characters. I pretty much was only able to spend the renown to buy BARELY enough supplies for the road (often still not enough), and level up my main characters. There is plenty of replay value here, but I am not interested in another playthrough.
Overall: good game, great art, great gameplay, pretty cool story/setting/dialogue/characters, but gets a little old near the end, ends abruptly, and I didnt get to try out a lot of characters, classes, items etc. because of the scarcity of renown. They really shoulda made the xp and money 2 different currencies. But regardless, much respect for this game, it was a fun new experience.

UPDATE: So after I received a refund due to not being able to play the game after installing (meaning, not having to go into .exe files and repairing something or spending extra time researching how to fix the encountered issues), I spent a bit of time reading reviews of the game and watching soem videos of the game play. I decided that I'd give it another go, especially since I was a big fan of Titan Quest I and II. This time however, I was prepared for the likelihood that I'd have the same issue so fully expected to spend some time having to find a resolution. And I was right. I emailed the developers after 8pm to ask for assistance and much to my suprise, I got a response around an hour or 2 later (WHATTT??? Color me very impressed and kinda bummed, PLEASE have a good work/life balance! Don't burn out, we need you to keep making good games!). It was suggested that I run a repair on the .exe (as I assumed) and also some other suggestions. Here is what worked for me:
-I read in one of the forums (can't remember which one) to check the resoltion in the options menu within the game file folder (?). Discovered that it was set to something daffy like 1080 1440, so I corrected it to my monitor's native resolution (2560 1440), saved. Restarted the game, totally worked. BUT the START button was greyed out (another issue some players have encountered). TBH, I had no idea what could cause that and had NO idea of how to fix that (listen, if that's not a coding issue I don't know WHAT is!). So what did I do? Breathe and ask myself what would most likely have NO issue as an application. Think about it. It's not going to be "options", it's not goping to be "difficulty level"...It's probably going to be the "credits menu". And I promise you as I'm sitting here, after running the credits for about 20 seconds, I returned to  the main menu and miracoulously the START menu was no longer greyed out and my character was displayed (previously not). FINALLY good to go!
I've only had about an hour or so game time but I can say with certainty it is DEFINITELY worth the extra time to figure out the issues I had. Bare in mind not everyone had these issues, but if you're on the fence, it is an awesome game with great visuals , an extensive in game loot etc, HUGE map and great story line. There are many great reviews (all well deserved) so I didn't want to repeat what's already been said but rather wanted to ammend my initial insights and bring my recommendation from a "No" to an absolute "Yes".

I played the multiplayer, pre-release of this game, The Banner Sage: Factions. This is to say, I had a perceived notion of how this game was to play. Keep that in mind.
Art 10/10- The art for this game is amazing. I have seen good graphics but this game was like playing a game in a Dutch painting. Amazing artwork, I would say some of the best I have ever seen, in a game.
World Design 9/10- This game not only had good art, but the art it had was interwoven into the world they created. The factions, races and mythology of this world were all spectacular.
Combat 9/10- The combat in this game was new, interesting, and fairly rewording. Standard Strategy Role-Playing Games (SRPG). You have guys and squares on a map and you move them around to kill things. Original stats, although they had caps for each (stat/when you leveled up) and that felt constricting.
Story 1/10- This is where the game fell apart and I mean, really fell apart. The combat style of the game in no way was congruent with the storyline, they had made. The game, and I have never thought I would say this, was too story based. What makes SRPG so amazing is the openness of the story. There is one but how you go about doing it is all up to you. You can build a team of guys and they can all be the same class or all different classes, the choice is yours. You have a main storyline mission, but you can hang around in an area to get some exp., new guys, or farm some items. The story kind of goes at the pace you want it to. This game had none of that. You get what units they decide. Out of combat decisions get some of your, really hard to get, units killed. Nothing felt fair, I felt like I had to cheat the system to get somewhere. I restarted the game because I did something earlier in the storyline, which got one of my favorite characters killed, and there was no way to reverse it. This game had amazing classes but I only got access to them in some battles. The story line was also very disappointing, especially at the end.
Overall 1.5/10- The story and the really terrible, out of combat, game play made this one of the most disappointing games I have ever played.
Suggestions to the developers- Play Final Fantasy Tactics Advanced, notice what makes that game amazing and remake or make a sequel to this game. Where you keep all the good stuff, the story, art, and combat. While adding a story/gameplay mechanic which works with a SRPG.
I say this all, not because I don't want the developers of this game to get paid for their work, but because I want them to understand why the game was bad and it was a bad game.

If you're thinking about it, do it. It's a very simple JRPG
- linear story/path
- 8 Characters + DLC with 3 Skill trees each and set "classes"/niches
- turned based battle, 2 party vs. 3 monster with time bar thing for turns
- very simple, still very customizable augmenting
- minimal inventory management (just pots)
but it's very "open" in the sense that there's no waypoints, minimaps, or directions. Usually there's only one way to go, but you stay in very big maps that are kinda easy to get lost in. Hidden treasures are plenty.
Most of the difficulty is in battles. You get a little sprite/Navi like thing for your mouse (kinda like Super Mario Galaxy) that opens chests, does puzzles, and "stuns" enemies so touching them won't trigger a battle on the map. In battle, you use it to slow (a single) enemy, and heal yourself. He has his own energy bar. This, along with being able to rotate party members instantly during battle + gem customization + timing your actions to cause interrupts (attacking an enemy during the red part of the bar) means if you're good enough you can do fights without every getting attacked.
Higher skillcap than an average JRPG fight, much more active.
Art and music are beautiful and probably worth the game alone. The script is very childish. Everything rhymes (it's kinda cute), very poetic. Sometimes a little cheesy, in a funny way.
Story reminds me a little of Bastion - where you're curious as to what happened and the characters all have backgrounds that make you want to learn more, but this game's not the most story driven.
Just good combat, very engaging but not stressful play, and a relaxing artstyle.
Do it.
The only downside really is that you need UPlay. Glhf awful game.
Actual annoying parts though - while there's saveslots, there's also no save button and it's all autosave. I'm a save every 30 seconds kinda guy so it bugs me a little. But it autosaves really often (there's a spinning circle in the bottom right). Also, it's hard to gauge a sense of progress. There's a worldmap, but it only shows places you've been to and you don't really know where they are). The game is subdivided into Chapters but I don't know how many there are.
DLC is okay - I don't really like the skins. Haven't done the character one yet though.

Mirror's Edge was dissapointing. I enjoyed the game more before I played it than when I actually finished it. When I got this game I was excited for the pretty art style and the flowing parkour. I had heard great things about this game and got it on sale for $4. It seemed like a steal. Looking back, that should be the actual price for the game without being on sale. When I first launched into the game I was dumbfounded by how pretty the game looked for coming out in 2007 and was immediatly intrigued in the gameplay. The controls worked, it felt good, and I was completly in control. But as I got further  into the game I was less and less impressed. I found myself asking "Why didn't I grab that?", "How did that fall hurt me?" and "How was I supposed to know that?" For a game about keeping momentum it stops you. Like.. A LOT. I started to feel like the game was constantly messing with me. "Climb this ladder which takes to long to climb and you get shot on!" "Go here and let us all of a sudden introduce a concept that we should have done A LONG time ago!" "Heres this huge thing to climb up that is not only tedious, but extremely difficult as you start loose control and forget why you're playing this!" This game was suprisingly a rage game. You spend more time wondering where to go than spending time getting there. The art style worked for and against the game. Making it look unique and fun with red prompts showing you where to go worked if you havn't played the game. The prompts are fine but the rest is bland and you can't tell where you are because everything looks the same. A big problem was that sometimes when I pressed shift to roll from a big jump Faith (the character) just didn't. Or when I right clicked to grab someones gun from them and keep them from hitting me nothing happened. I got frustrated easier and easier knowing things were probably only going to get worse. The story was bland and predictable. The music wasn't great and was repetitive. My favorite scene was at the very end where (spoilers from here on out) Faith and Kate looked over the city and the music actually fit for once. Other than that moment I felt almost no emotional connection to any other characters. When Merc was shot (predictable) I didn't care. When you found out that celest was a bad guy (predictable) I didn't care. When Jackknife turned out to be the big baddie (predictable) I didn't care. This game was a mess and deserves a low 6/10. I do reccomend this game but only when it's on sale. Otherwise don't waste your cash or time on this game.

Since Steam has been adding more visual novels and dating sim games, i looked for some and decided to try out this one because it was free and i was in a dating sim kind of mood.
Pros:
-Free to Play, emphasis on FREE
-Gorgeous Scenery and backgrounds
-Interesting story (at the time of this review and only on Day 5)
-Hatsune Miku (or at least a character who really resembles her, which is probably why this game is free to play due to copyright)
-The following characters are interesting and/or easy to get along with. Somewhat typical and expected of a dating sim game, but the better charcaters of this game (at the time of the review): Alisa, Slavya, Lena, Miku
-Nice looking female characters (as expected of a dating sim, but especially nice since everyone's wearing identical costumes). the character designs are a good in between; not too extreme but not too generic.
*** - The creators of the game proofread the English version, so most of the typos and lose English is fixed, though you may still occasionally see Alisa's name listed as Alice in some dialouge boxes. For those who've already played the game or have old save files however, you may not be able to fast-forward as much as you want because the new English Proofread dialouge counts as 'unseen' text that you may not be able to skip past.
- Semyon is a very interesting character. You play the game from his point of view but he's very different from other dating sim male leads i've played as thus far. He actively questions what's going on around him and i've often found myself relating to him in the various situations he gets himself in and feeling the same way toward the girls he intereacts with (for better of for worse). He's very smart for a player-avatar character and i wish more of these types of characters come to future dating sims (especially when the lead is a female).
-
Cons:
***
-No gay routes, only hetero routes (though because this game is originally Russian, I can't exactly blame them for that)
-All of the characters with the exceptions of the ones i mentioned above... ARE ANNOYING AND/OR DATING SIM STEREOTYPES. Ulyana is an extremely annoying child (why can no one ever write a child character that isn't the devil, annoying or both?), Olga is extremely bossy (if i read the phrase 'line-up' one more time i might stab my computer screen and i think Seymon feels the same way), Electronik and Shurik are typical male characters in dating sims in that they either encourage hooking-up, force the player into doing something they normally wouldn't do or just being in the background compared to the main female characters of the game. And of the two other male characters, i find that only Electronik is helpful and at least somewhat interesting.
-All of the female character's I've mentioned in the con's part of the review also seem to suffer from the rapidest of mood swings. Olga is nice one second, the next second she's like a dictator; Ulyana is still extremely annoying and Zhenya seems to go from a nuetral mood to♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off for no reason within seconds. You may argue that the tsundere of the game, Alisa, also has these rapid mood swings but at least hers are enjoyable to watch and read and she isn't as bossy as Olga and
. In addition Alisa has her sweet/adorable moments unlike any of the female characters i've mentioned in the cons.
- After a while you feel like you're dragging Semyon through one event after the other. You are given some choices which will help you in getting the different endings but after a few playthroughs you already know you'll have to do certain tasks without any yes or no and you'll be forced to do them over and over again. It'll feel like a pain after a while, but this is remedied somewhat because Semyon is very nice and relatable (at least to me).

Just finished this game's story mode. Got it on sale for £2. All things considered, it felt like a bargain.
I loved the aesthetics and when you knew where you were going whilst freerunning it felt really energetic and exciting. Sometimes though, when you tried to jump to a ledge that you could easily make, you'd just plummet to your death (those situations are a mix of it being your fault even if you don't want to admit it and the parkour mechanics falling short). Sometimes it was hard to find where you're supposed to go next as well. This isn't so bad if you're in an area with no enemies and can actually be kind of fun, but you'll end up in really fast-paced situations not knowing where to go, so you have to slow right down which kind of kills the adrenaline rush you get from lightning fast parkour.
I found the story to be a bit lackluster as well. It sounds good on paper, where it's implied that the city the game takes place in is basically NSAland, but the story within the world of Mirror's Edge that focuses on Faith and those she encounters wasn't very engaging. I didn't feel any real connection to any of the characters. I won't describe what happens because nobody likes spoilers, but there are twists and events that happen that you can call very early on.
Also you'll end up in situations where you have to do the exact opposite of what the game tells you to do, which is to avoid combat with large groups of enemies. Occasionally you'll have absolutely no choice but to use the horrible gun mechanics to kill literally everyone before you can move on.
Still, I don't want to sound like I'm too harsh on it. It was an experimental IP that came out almost 8 years ago which succeeded in some areas and less so in others. Overall it's a fun game when the mechanics work properly with attractive level design and an addictive soundtrack (the main menu music is beautifully done) but I would've been disappointed if I paid the full retail price for it.

Very much the same game as "Go! Go! Nippon!" You're living in Japan for a while, and you make friends with two female high school students - one more impulsive and outgoing, the other more reserved and studious - who teach you a lot about the country. The biggest difference from that game is that Go Go Nippon focuses on the different areas of Japan, whereas Japanese School Life focuses on the culture and customs, with in-depth explanations of various festivals, traditions, and etiquette. As such, it's a good complement to that game if you're interested in a light but informative introduction to the culture.
One of the characters publishes dōjinshi and sells them at a booth at Comiket, so a large part of the story involves that.
Unlike Go Go Nippon (in which you accidentally walk in on one of the girls when she's half-naked), there is absolutely nothing suggestive in this game. Romance is limited to the main character accidentally saying the word "cute' and lots of blushing happening.
Both girls are fully voiced and well-acted. And one feature I didn't notice until late in the game is that mousing up to the top makes a menu appear with some items that aren't in the "Options" screen, such as the ability to scroll back to see previous lines of dialogue, and also the ability to display text in both English and Japanese at the same time.
There are a few decision points in the story, but I don't suspect they change the events or outcome very much. Also, the main character is named "Brian" and the girls call him by name. There is no way to change the main character's name. If your name is Brian, like mine is, then this is wonderful and I encourage more games to name their protagonists "Brian".

Short review:
Japanese School Life is a cute, fun distraction and surprisingly informative. Buy it if you're interested in learning about detailed aspects of Japanese culture and daily life that you won't find in many other games.
Long review:
Japanese School Life is — shockingly! — a visual novel focusing on the Japanese school life of an exchange student arriving from a foreign country. Using this central conceipt, the game explains various aspects of daily life as seen from the perspective of a student in Japan, in a style that is half entertainment, half cultural guidebook.
As a concept, the game is executed well. It includes detailed descriptions about Japanese culture and lifestyle that are not necessarily apparent even to people who have played many Japanese VNs or experienced other forms of Japanese media like anime and manga. The art is good, the characters are fun and well-voiced, and the music is non-intrusive. The quality of the English writing is exceptionally high for a VN voiced in Japanese.
Japanese School Life is very similar to Tokyo School Life and Go! Go! Nippon! and as such it's hard not to compare the three. All are high quality and enjoyable. Japanese School Life lacks a bit in length and depth when compared to Tokyo School Life, and is a bit less organized as a guidebook than Go! Go! Nippon! However, Japanese School Life combines some of both worlds and is clearly intended to be a simple, relaxing experience, something at which it succeeds. If you're searching for maximum value, pick it up on sale, but I didn't feel cheated at full price.
In all, Japanese School Life is an enjoyable distraction that will inform about Japanese student life even as it entertains. If you're looking for deep story and characterizations, however, it's best to look elsewhere.

Killing Floor 2 is a class-based, co-op survival-horror FPS game where players fight off waves of abominations of varied strength, weapons and tactics; buying weapons in between. Alongside that, the player character gains levels and new passive skills; growing stronger and more capable as an individual class that works together with other players. The game is a massive step-up from the first game; running on UE4 which means better visuals and effects on top of running well on most PCs. The game's classes range from fast-moving, aggressive commandos, durable berserkers and medics alongside other classes such as SWAT and flamers which invite the player to use their imagination; each class has their own unique weapons and unlockable skills.
The game has impactful gunplay where every gun feels powerful thanks to the synergy of animations, sound effects and visual feedback; enemy's heads exploding from a .50 cal headshot as they fly back. The animations are well done where it can get scary seeing the larger enemies run towards you waving their weapons; genuinely building tension. The guns are loud and need to be controlled as they recoil and take some skill to find your next target. Some weapons such as revolvers even fire as fast as the player clicks the mouse.
The player's arsenal ranges from real-world guns such as Beretta M9 and SA-80 rifle to something more crazy like a railgun, flamethrower or a microwave gun that inflates enemies; causing them to explode into gibs. The player also has to contend with boss creatures at the end of the wave where strategy is necessary to succeed since the AI plays aggressively and is surprisingly smart. Finally, the game keeps things fresh with events and updates which spices up the gameplay by either changing how enemies behave or adding things that the player must handle. (Unlimited slo-mo, exploding enemies for example)
Overall, Killing Floor 2 is an enjoyable experience with lots of satisfying combat that is playable either solo or co-op with more weapons and classes being added with time. A must-play for fans of arcade shooters and horror.

From some of the core team of Titan Quest comes... another Titan Quest. It feels a lot like Titan Quest until you realize that the controls are way more responsive, it's more fast paced, and the balance of mixing your classes is even better. If you didn't play Titan Quest, you missed out big time, so play this game. My only gripe is that multiplayer only supports up to 4 people and I have more than that many friends.

Despite the recommendation, I feel the need to explain some serious reservations I have about this game. The tone, atmosphere, aesthetic, and fascinating implied narrative are all brilliantly executed, and simultaneously a joy and a terror to experience. In these respects, the devs really achieved something truly worth experiencing. However, the gameplay, for me, left a lot to be desired. Precise navigation of a 3d environment with an effectively static, or 2d style, camera, is certainly possible, and is indeed necessary to progress through the game, but leads to some frustrating trial and error. The game is also exceedingly short, which on the surface is not something I inherently have a problem with. This game is a puzzle platformer, and only two or three puzzles throughout the entire experience really stuck out as interesting, challenging, or unique, the rest are really just a combination of observing the environment followed by precise navigation, which, again, I found to be occasionally tedious/frustrating. Personally, I find myself comparing this game heavily to Playdead's 2016 game Inside, one of my personal favorites of that year. While Inside is able to pack it's similarly short runtime with meaningful new mechanics and environmental interactions, Little Nightmares relies heavily on repetitive use of a single set of mechanics, only occasionally feeling truly clever or engaging on each new use. If you've played and enjoyed this game, but haven't checked out Inside, I highly, highly recommend doing so. If you've played Inside and are thinking about checking this out, I still recommend doing so, however this game didn't have nearly the same effect, for me personally, on the gameplay side. Regardless, this game certainly isn't perfect, but the things it manages to get right make it more than worth your time.

That was a great game. Arguably one of the greatest ARPG's ever. The graphics were super cool, the story was interesting and at times intense, the action itself was seamless, the upgrade system was super deep and yet accessible. You could play this game countless different ways and have a great time. I put right around 40 hours into the campaign playing solo before finishing it, and after I was done, there was still another area at the top of the map to unlock, and probably 3 or 4 that I missed besides that. There is also an area called The steps of Torment which will challenge any hardened players, and that area features roguelike qualities. This game carries a lot of obvious influences as well, from Diablo 2 to Torchlight to even Dark Souls, and wears them well, while still managing to create it's own distinct personality.
I'm thinking that I can still easily put in another 15 or so hours solo before I'm just grinding loot or decide to change difficulties. The game also leaves definite room for a sequel and/or expansion, and really, this is a game world that could persist for a long time. There were things said via notes in the game that absolutely open up other potential story arcs. The Aetherial Betrayer, Ulgrim, and quite a few others.
So, some cool features of the game: you can dual class, and it changes your actual class if you do so. For example, I played an Occultist/Arcanist, which made me a Warlock. The upgrade system for the actual classes is broad enough to give you a lot of variety, but condensed enough that you wont feel overwhelmed. However, there is a second upgrade system that you get points for simply by cleansing shrines, and that my friends is as expansive an upgrade system as I have seen in a game. You could spend a while reading through all of them, and then you still have to decide what will best suit your play style. They are set up as constellations, and there are a lot of them! It can seem daunting, but actually, I dont think there are really any wrong choices, although some will obviously suit your preferred playstyle better than others, and a lot of them only unlock after unlocking constellations closer to the center, where you basically choose your upgrade arc. That was quite impressive and again, lends itself to a lot of experimentation. There is a respec NPC in the game, but I never actually made use of it, so I cant say how that works.
Also, some merchants will only sell you stuff after you have gotten your town or faction disposition maxed out, and they of course have the best items, lol. You can sell to them, but I personally didnt max out any factions yet, so I havent been able to purchase those super cool items. You can also craft items via another type of NPC, and that system is also pretty deep. You can craft all the basic stuff, but you have to find blueprints to craft anything truly spectacular. Items also have one slot for gem/material upgrades, and the gems/materials can be made stronger by fusing as many as 4 of the same type together. This will often unlock a special ability like casting fireballs or gaining Aetherial defense, slams, and so on.
There is actually a ton more to this game, but I think I will leave off for now and maybe revise this once I finish the map, play through higher difficulties, and/or play through this in co-op mode.

Shadows: Heretic Kingdoms (we'll call it S:HK) was that game in the steam store that I was curious about, but wasn't certain if it was worth the $20 price. After finally giving in and buying it, I found it to be a pretty fun spin on the arpg formula.
S:HK takes place in a fantasy world with a pretty neat concept. There's magic, but no religion (from what I gathered, people were abusing religion for power so others rose against them and wiped it out), so no clerics or paladins here. As the description tells you (or maybe you ignored the description and came down to the reviews immediately you little rebel), this game has you take on the role of a demon known as the Devourer. Honestly, that is what made me want to buy this game. As the Devourer, you consume the souls of the dead and turn them into puppets. These puppets are pretty much copies of whoever or whatever was consumed, but now under the Devourer's control.
The concept of the Devourer plays into the mechanic that makes this game unique. The puppets make their way through the regular world while the Devourer explores the shadow version. You end up switching between puppets and the Devourer to bypass obstacles, find secrets,escape from one world to another to avoid a bad situation, or to kill extra enemies for those delicious experience points. You will start with one puppet and the Devourer, and you'll find others throughout the game as things go on. This is where I have to commend the developers for making such unique playable characters for and arpg. I won't spoil what they are, but, believe me, you won't be expecting some of these. This creates a cool dynaimc where the player won't run through the game with only one character, but rather switch between them to fit the situation. Maybe you'll use a mage to take out a group of smaller enemies before switching to the Devourer to take out a shaman without the others interfering, then proceeding to switch to an archerto kite and kill some of the stronger enemies, and finishing with your warrior to plow through what's left. It's a fun and engaging mechanic that makes me want to keep coming back to find new and useful combinations, and it definitely hold this game up. Levels are shared between characters, so don't worry about one getting ahead of others.
The game can be pretty short if you ignore some sidequests and know what to do, but I feel that this works to its advantage. The game has plenty of points where decisions affect the story and playing through with different puppets and different decisions adds a ton of replay value. I see people complaining about the cliffhanger ending, but I honestly feel that it's warranted. There's plenty here, and the developers likely wanted to send this out to see how it goes before investing more into a project that might fail.
The game is not perfect though. It has a few bugs, and sometimes it isn't clear what the player is supposed to do at some points. The save system can hurt at some points, but that's only if you forget to quciksave every now and then (although i understand why trapping the player with frequent autosaves could lead to issues as well). The main issue is the amount of walking you end up doing. There are points scattered around the world that you can fast-travel between, but, after you use one, you have to walk across an entire map to go into a dungeon and beat it to do your quest, then retrace all of your steps without enemies to occupy you on the way back. Also, there are quests that you either won't want to complete (I will not put myself through that Call To Arms quests, and nothing can make me) or quests that you can't complete until the next part comes out.
I feel I should address a common complaint I've seen in reviews and say that the attacking system works fine for me. Left-click on an enemy to attack, hold it down to keep attacking, and hold shift to attack while stationary. I had very problems, and even those were just trying to target the right person in a group of enemies.
All in all, S:HK isn't a perfect game, but it has a good amount of content, interesting concept, as well as a unique and dynamic mechanic that make it well worth that $20 price tag( that's like one meal at Olive Garden for at least 22 hours of entertainment). If you're a fan of arpgs or just curious about the concept in general, I'd definitely recommend it.

A great sequel in the SWB series. Battlefront II is a game that's almost completely equal to any Battlefield game with the only difference being its setting and some additional exclusive features. I played a lot in the first Battlefront, which is a great game too, and played a lot in this sequel - it took the gameplay to a totally new incredible height of quality.
SWB II has awesome space battles, enormous land action, decent FPS mechanics and a system of points which allows you to progress and open up new characters to play with, including Jedi and Sith and other well-known SW personalities. And yeah - no microtransactions and paid features! The system is based purely on your combat skills and rating. Even the graphics are rather pretty (for a game of that year).
Yes, there are some cons and lackluster moments regarding certain bugs and a poor variety of weapons, for instance, but no one's perfect, you know... However, this game really compensates for all of that with various free available mods and tons of hours of fun you can have playing on a dashing amount of 24(!) maps: 12 ground combat maps, 6+6 maps for space battles. Mods like "Star Wars Battlefront Conversion Pack", for example, and "2017 HD Graphics Mod +" will revitalite the game for you.
This game, in my opinion, deserves much more attention, and if you're a Star Wars fan you should totally check this one out.

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to be an exchange student in Japan? When I was a teen, I was obsessed with Japanese culture and this would have been a dream come true! Now there’s a new game out there that can help you live out that fantasy while learning about Japanese culture called Japanese School Life!
Japanese School Life is a visual novel that follows a foreign exchange student named Brian. Brian is in love with the Otaku culture and wanted to be immersed in it. Thus, he took an adventure and became a foreign exchange student. However, he didn’t realize how much he would learn from this experience.
Plus, Brian didn’t expect to make friends right away. Luckily two of the girls in his class, Chiyoko and Arisa decided to make friends with him. From there, they take Brian to all the places he wants to explore and teaches him about Japanese lifestyle and culture.
I admit, back in the day I was totally a weeaboo. I watched any anime that I could get my hands on and read any manga I had access to. Even though I got older and fell more into comic books, I still have always had a curiosity for Japanese culture. I still really want to go to Japan, especially since I’ve never been there.
Playing Japanese School Life really re-lit that fire in me to start saving up enough money to go to Japan. It’s fun learning about the different festivals and foods they enjoy. The fact that they can get so many different things at a convenience store blows my mind. When I think of convenience store, I think of a gas station where the hot dogs have been on the rollers for 10+ hours. Yet that’s all I know.
However, I didn’t realize that the Japanese also eat Zongzi, aka sticky rice dumplings in America. Which are some of my most favorite Chinese traditional foods, and are made for celebrating the Dragon Boat Festival. So, when Chiyoko and Arisa were explaining where Zongzi came from, I had already heard the story from my other half. I thought it was pretty cool they threw that in there.
So, if you’re wanting to learn more about Japan in the form of a Anime-like visual novel, Japanese School Life would be fun for you! Check it out!

Take one of the older Black Isle Studio games, mix in modern tabletop gaming wisdom, the tiniest dash of JRPG charm, a little bit of Ultima's morality (and furniture moving), and stick a co-op cherry on top. Divinity is an absolute blast of an RPG that gets just about everything perfectly right.
You are able to tailor each one of your characters into a specific role, and the possibilities are highly varied. Templates are offered to help get you started if you like. Anything from front-line tank, to mobile assassin, to a wizard that manipulates and shuts down the environment and uses his pets for the wetwork, to a support character that crafts the party wicked new equipment, or who enhances the treasures they already own, but there's no reason you can't treat it as a buffet and pick up a little bit of everything. Customization goes beyond the normal STR/DEX/INT stats into independent skills you can level up, abilities you can learn, and (most fun of all) fallout-style perks. Character customization doesn't stop there. There are multiple opportunities to engage in dialog with other NPCs, or even your friend/party if you are playing co-op. Your answers here define your personality traits. Reflect carefully upon them, for you are called upon in certain situations to roleplay your character consistently with previous choices!
Combat is highly tactical and turn based. I started out as an air wizard, but later found that pincushioning baddies in the back was a lot more fun for me. Those magic points weren't wasted, as they translated into excellent crowd control abilities. Charm one monster, teleport another away, then stab a third in the back. Wonderful. The power player is amply rewarded, while still allowing you the freedom to make some happy mistakes in customizing your character. Especially in the first quarter of the game, there were a few fights that we bullheadedly jumped into despite being far out of our EXP league, but we would boobytrap the entire environment, move tables and chairs around to create killing zones, and set up devastating openers and were able to squeak by. In the last quarter of the game, our min/maxed characters were so overwhelming that if we were able to get enough of an opening and get all our buffs & debuffs in line, there were very few monsters (boss or otherwise) that we couldn't take out in a single volley. This was our reward for playing so aggressively. That is not to say that combat ever became trivial or tedious, despite being a combat oriented RPG, it is amazing how memorable each and every fight was. There was always some situation that was slightly new, that required us to think a little bit differently. I don't know how they pulled it off, but the results are amazing.
I had hesitations playing an RPG game as CO-OP, but those reservations were muted almost immediately. Our very first encounter in the game resulted in us having a disagreement about how to proceed. We resolved that dispute using a mini-game, but each of our characters choices was still reflected in our personality matrix that was being built, so no one feels like they're being bulldozed or wasting their time. “Your objection has been noted in the logs”. Having a friend who specializes and is familiar with their specific character during combat is also a relief - everyone knows their job and how to perform it best.
The perfection of Divinity is what leads its rough patches to stand out in even starker detail. Keeping the storyline straight in single player might be hard enough, but in co-op at points it became very difficult.  There is a chat log that records all conversations, yours or otherwise, so this is more of a user interface issue. The writing is good, but not as good as, well, Planescape (That is perhaps unfair). Also some of the "puzzle dungeons" are more obnoxious than they needed to be. Characters don’t really seem to respond differently based on your personality matrix or reputation. Finally, in a single player game, if one of your characters maximizes a skill, say loremaster, then it's something that easily applies to your 3 companions. But in co-op, you have to keep asking your buddy to identify some equipment for you, or remind you what a monster's HP or immunities/weaknesses are. Stuff like that should probably just apply to the entire party with the value being the max of whomever is the highest. There are also a few quest glitches.  Larian seems to be releasing patches often and regularly, so maybe these issues will be buffed out by the time you play. And if you like RPGs, then let's assume that whether you will play this or not is a foregone answer.
Final rating: 4.5/5 stars

Playing Divinity honestly felt like playing Dungeons and Dragons with a fairly creative DM who managed to ♥♥♥♥ up some times.
The game is a turned based magic and sorcery RPG, with a lot of bizarre magic interactions. Let's say that there's a fire in your way. Casting rain will put out the fire, leaving behind a steam cloud that blocks line of sight and a bunch of puddles. Casting lightning on the puddles will then cause them to be electrified, stunning anyone who walks over them. There are all sorts of elemental interactions like this can make for fairly deep and nuanced combat.
The story is fairly compelling, with a well realized world and interesting intrigue between different players. I played through this game 100% coop and think that it deserves to be lauded for making a deep RPG with an interesting story that actively encourages people to work together. I feel that that's the next step for gaming. We've had plenty of Left 4 Dead-ish action co op games, but now I feel that story-oriented coop can become a real thing.
But unfortunately, the game needs some simple UI adjustments to become a bit more coop friendly. If you have two different people doing two different things in a game, then you need to clearly deliver all plot essential dialogue to both players. Often I'd be off crafting something and my partner would go and have an important conversation and I'd be left wondering what the heck was going on. Considering that the game gives you a teleport pyramid thing early on, it really wouldn't have hurt to pull the other player to important dialogues the moment they started (and to pop a dialogue window for both players the moment said dialogue began).
Another problem is that the game's puzzles are completely awful. Any puzzle where you have to run around a room looking for a button to press (which usually is impossible to see with the default camera angle) is not really a puzzle at all. Portal 2 taught us that group puzzle solving can be incredibly fun and there are moments when I got that same high of being able to figure out a solution and brag about it, but those moments were heavily outweighed by the pixel hunt puzzles.
With a little more polish in these departments, this would have been a superb game. As it stands right now, I'd call it a pretty good game (maybe even a REALLY good game) that is certainly moving in the right direction.
If they make an expansion pack, I'll certainly get it.

As a fan of turn based strategy games I can't say that The Banner Saga is a great game. The strategic part is very basic and isn't more complex than a game of checkers. Also the user interface is really abysmal, the worst I've ever seen in a strategic game. For example you can't inspect your team members attributes and abilities when choosing who to bring in battle. While in battle the interface isn't better and choosing the action to perform feels very cheap. Abilities are described "with text" like a game from 20 years ago, no icons and no visual aids. Very very basic.
Despite all this I still recommend the game; why? Because the story is tragic and mature like it rarely happens in games lately. It is really up to Norse Myths standards... The music is a masterpiece that is alone worth the price of the game and the experience, as whole, feels like a work of love from its developers. So even if I can't fully recommend it as a game I still recommend it without hesitation as a work of "art".

Banner Saga is a study in videogames as a storytelling medium. The score, the sounds, the visual style, and the writing all work together beautifully to tell the story of a merciless world falling apart. It's tense and you're always on the verge of annihilation, and the music alone could tell you so. It's gritty, and the crunches of axes breaking armor and the grunts and moans of the injured make you feel it. People are fragile and the perpetual march is exhausting, and the heavy shambling motions of bodies shows you so.  As the leader, you constantly have to arbitrate the problems of your followers, keep them optimistic, keep them fed, and keep them alive while a continent of panicking and desperate people is being overrun.  Everything harmoniously comes together to weave an atmosphere where feelings of dread and anxiety are constant. Your choice isn't whether or not people die, it's who dies now so that fewer will die later.  In every artistic regard this game is an achievement.
Unfortunately it's not for everyone, though. Its roots are in the artistry, not the gameplay--people have some valid complaints about that. Only some. I didn't dislike the gameplay at all, but I was very wrapped up in every other part of the game.
Play it for the experience.

In fact that's the best way to describe this game: 'Even more janky than the first game.'
While there's a bit more content such as the space battles, jedi and the maps, I didn't care much for it as the terrible lag has not been fixed from the first game, AGAIN IT'S EVEN WORSE than the first game. Combine that with the even more janky movement, and the blurry graphics and it's hell.

Another annoying thing is that the special classes like the jedi and the jet troopers are only usable in the game when you get a certain amount of points. I get that this is for balance reasons but not being able to even choose a limited number of jet troopers to start make it a bit more boring.
Also, the map design is appalling. Yes it was bad in the first game, but it's so much worse here it's laughable. I never even notice the map layouts on most games but here it's so bad it sticks out like a sore thumb and I have to mention it. 2 examples of what little I have played:

Mygeeto: Literally 2-3 landing platforms connected linearly by 1 bridge each.
It's just... why couldn't they do SOMETHING with the maps, quite a few are lifted from Battlefront 1 anyway. The maps are a joke, an absolute joke.

Excellent ARPG. I'm one of the half dozen or so people who purchased the classic ARPG Heretic Kingdoms at release and enjoyed it quite a bit, so I was excited for this somewhat belated semi-sequel (same world, different characters). It really delivers.
It has all the appeal of the original and its bizarre, dark anti-theistic world of the Heretic Kingdoms setting as well as great art design and graphics, rock solid controls and an interesting combat mechanic whereby you can change to a different character/form on the fly. Each form has different strengths and weaknesses and multiple ones are frequently viable in a given area. Bosses are fun, enemies are challenging without being overly difficult and all-in-all this is just a great game.
Just an FYI, this game series is single-player and campaign oriented and plays more like the Dungeon Siege or Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance than the more loot-driven, frequently multi-player oriented games like the Diablo series or Titan Quest.
Additionally, Book 2 has not been released. Even if it never is, it's still a great game and the ending doesn't feel abrupt.
If you like ARPG's, buy it.

(or Dota 2). As a huge hack'n'slash RPG fan since the first Diablo, this felt really bad to me, seeing even small details, as the health regeneration counter in the health bar, made my impression pretty much worse.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Everlasting Summer is one of the more unusual romantic visual novels I've play, with a surprisingly deep and immersive plot and enjoyable characters. There are a number of flaws, but most of them are superficial and don't diminish the enjoyability of the game to any significant extreme.
The Plot:
The plot is fantastic. For a casual romantic-visual novel player, the surface layer of the game should more than be enjoyable, with four major romantic routes and definitive happy endings. However, as you delve farther into the story of Sovionok and Everlasting Summer, the plot starts twisting and reveals rather bizarre undertones. There are three additional paths beyond the four basic love interests, one of which is only reachable having traversed the other six and getting fully immersed into the story. This final path ties the story together and really draws the game to a satisfying conclusion.
The Main Character:
Semyon, the protagonist, is honestly one of the worst elements of this game. For introverts and shut-ins, he is first portrayed as a very relatable character, and is subject to getting drawn into this bizarre world by chance. However, it doesn't take long before you're likely pulling out your hair at how idiotic he regularly is. He regularly gets lost on strange mental tangents and runs circles repeatedly over subjects that should easily be dropped. While he fortunately realizes the emotions of his female counterparts faster than your average anime protagonist, he tends to get infuriatingly confused with his own emotions. However, this is probably the only major gripe I have with this game.
The Rest of the Cast:
Each character is their own unique and special snowflake, resulting in a small but colorful cast. Some of the characters come off as rather two dimensional, but this is typically subverted as the story progresses. All of your favorite romance tropes are in full effect here - the tsundere, the vanilla sweetheart, the wallflower - fortunately, again, they aren't typically confined to their roles. Probably one of the stronger points of the game would be character development and interactions; admittedly it would be a poor visual novel otherwise.
The Art:
The art can be... peculiar. A lot of it is recycled and reused, to mixed effect. In addition, the artist's seemed to be incapable of agreeing on certain details, most notably Olga's color scheme. However for the most part the art is of acceptable quality and is at it's best at the most important times, namely the endings and emotional high points.
The Music:
Not much to note here. I don't see myself downloading an OST or coming back to listen to it specifically, but the music is of good enough quality and certainly most excellently used.
The Replay:
This game has a high, almost mandatory replay value. There are up to seven individual paths you can go down, with all but one having two endings. As previously mentioned, the final path can only be unlocked after you have completed all other paths. As far as replaying through the game goes, you will be appreciative of the fast-forward button. Many events are fully or heavily independant of which route you're going down, and being given a tour of the camp thirteen seperate times is not something I want to sit through in full.
The Notes:
Three final points come to mind. Firstmost: yes, this game was originally written in Russian. While the translation is commendable, the spelling isn't perfect and the grammar sometimes bears tinges of a speaker who knows English as a second language. Unless you are an insufferable grammar Nazi, this should be mildly distracting at it's worst. Secondly: If you are looking for a specific ending (which is likely), I would advise looking up a guide. Many, if not most, endings are near-impossible to get without knowing exactly which decisions to make. For example, the four main character's good or bad endings are decided on a points-based system: at least six points will put you on that character's path, and at least nine points will net you the good end. Alisa has exactly nine points total. In addition, Miku's path is only acchievable after certain conditions are met and you must make the exact right decisions to trigger it. Not a huge detriment, just a warning. Finally, this game was originally advertised as an adult-rated game, but as of a patch a few days ago as-of me writing this, the adult content has been removed. This doesn't really harm the story much, but it's also not particularly difficult to mod the adult content back in. Take it as you will.
In conclusion, this game has it's faults, but it is definitely one of the better visual novels available, and I highly recommend playing it. It's free, what do you have to lose? Time? If you've gotten this far through my review, you obviously have free time. Go play it.

A good old fashioned Lucasarts classic that sadly still suffers a few flaws.
I remember the good old days of Lucasarts, and Fate of Atlantis was, and still is, a great entry for anyone who enjoys point and click games. Decent voice acting, good dialog, decent graphics and an intriguing plot still hold up well today.
There are a few flaws though that keep this from being a top notch game. The music and sound effects are mainly old blips and bleeps, very little atmosphere in the music, especially in the jungle scenes. The voice recordings do come off as fuzzy sounding at times, thankfully there is captioning to help keep track of what's being said.
And there is one game breaking glitch. Upon climbing the ladder in Indy's office, it stuck in a loop of climb up, climb down, meaning I had to back up to my last save, erasing an hour's worth of play. So be sure to save before entering new rooms and trying things, especially after long dialog scenes.
Glitch and assorted cons aside, it's still a pleasure to play, with a few mind bending puzzles and several laugh out loud moments. Worth a look if you want good old fun.

One of the biggest suprises of 2014 and imo one of the best (indie)game titles of the year. This one is definitely going on my personal favorites list. Gameplay-wise it's good, nothing too bad but also nothing too spectecular. Story-wise however that's a whole another thing. Each of the 13 stories start off slow but develop into an incredible and emotional story. I would even dare to say that story-wise this game is up there a long with the bioshock-series and telltale games like TWD en TWAU.
Slightly spoiler but:
1st - the Miku-route/ending is absolutely mind blowing. It's a legit 2 hour horror movie (horror movie junkies will understand what I mean)
2nd - you should definitely try to get the Yulia-route/ending, it will explain the whole story and will leave you with a satisfied feeling (this route is also a 2 hour special, just as the Miku-route/ending)
(best played as very last storyline after you've done all the other storylines)
3rd - make sure that you save before making the choice of going further or going back in the Yulia-route/ending, because you gonna want to play the harem-ending right after the Yulia-ending for further explanation of the game and this story
4th - if you're a completionist like me and want to get the whole photoalbum completed, make sure to save before you make a decision with who you want to wake up with during the Yulia-route/ending
I would conclude with saying that I would like to thank the creators of this game for giving me and the fellow gamers who downloaded this game such an incredible experience. The fact that it's free to play suprises me because I would be happily paying 10-20 bucks for this game, considering the amount of gameplay and story we get.
Verdict 10/10

A game full of new flavor and modern twists to a timeless classic, XCOM: Enemy Unknown takes you back to those difficult days of making decisions like risking your top Liutenant to save a upcoming rookie who's in a tough pinch and finding yourself in a small room with a deadly pack of chyrssalids.
While the game fails to capture the true Fog of war terror of not knowing what is lurking behind every corner, it does strike a chord that rings the old memory bells to return a sense of the original game.
I highly reccomend the mod community for this game, as it can give it a deeper level of management and interaction from the vanilla.  However, standalone, it is still full of difficult choices and action. I enjoy roguelikes, but I didn't have fun with this one.
I won't fight the hundreds of avid fans, I don't begrudge them their tastes.
The sound track is good, the art is good, the developers are well above average in my book. I just didn't have much fun with the actual gameplay. What I wanted was a challenging spaceship management game. That it is, but it's a roguelike through and through. This game hates you, really despises you down to your core. If it could, this game would kill your whole family, and feed them to you. Afterwards it would drug you and medically amputate all your limbs while using another combination of drugs to keep you conscious during the procedure. Don't let the simple interface fool you. Don't be distracted by the fancy spaceships. This game is a short, full-force punch to the genitals every single time you boot it up. Don't bother naming your crew. Don't bother getting attached to your ship. Don't worry about missiles, you're unlikely to live long enough to run out. I believe that some people have seen the end of the game. I can't imagine spending that kind of time subjecting myself to this game.
For every instance of clever play prevailing, such as when I vented the entire ship except for the med bay in order to choke out the intruders outside, I had at least three incidents wherein I was pitted against ships that vastly outclassed mine with no chance to escape or fight back. Technically, there's infinite replay value. However, what that really means is that you're going to be replaying the beginning level over and over again until you find some way to outright cheat your way to victory.

Revolutionary back in the day and still pleasant to play. The main gameplay revolves around freerunning a futuristic and superb looking city, getting from Point A to Point B as efficient as possible, with a little martial arts and gunfights thrown in here and there. The game is set in a city, where the police is in control of everything and sharing free information has become almost impossible. The runners are the ones transporting them illegally for their customers high above the city. You play such a runner and it doesn't take long until you get in trouble with the law and may discover something bigger along the way.
The gameplay is fast and is only slowed down by some combat sequences. You can either solve them with your fists or overwhelm an officer and use his gun, but most of the time you will be evading the cops with your freerunning skills. It is not an open world game, your path is linear with a few possible variations. Combat is the weakest part of the game, followed by the story, which basically only exists to give you a reason to run to a certain point and is fairly short. Afterwards you can play the levels in time trial mode or try and find all hidden collectibles throughout the levels.
Sometimes you need to find the correct path and the game feels like a puzzler. If you are not surrounded by police and can take your time to figure things out, those parts are really enjoyable. If you're under heavy fire and have to act quickly and constantly chose dead ends or wrong jumps, because you don't have the time to study your surroundings, it can get a bit frustrating. If you are having trouble, you can enable the runner vision in the options menu (you can disable it too, of course). It highlights possible paths for you.
All in all a game I would recommend, despite its flaws. Defenitly pick it up at a discount, at full price you might be a bit dissapointed. I bought it anyway for nostalgic reasons.

I can say without a doubt Child of Light has been one of the biggest suprisies of the year for me. Being a fan of old-school JRPG's, I picked this game up the day it was released. I fell in love with the music and water-color art-style. I would even go so far as to recommend purchasing the OST, as this game contains some of the best pieces I've had the pleasure of listening to.
The characters feel hand-crafted to the world. CoL manages to maintain a certain amount of cuteness without going over-board. Everyone in the world of Lemuria speaks in the a/b/a/b rhyming scheme, (common in children's books) which I adore. There isn't any voice acting aside from the narrator, but I don't feel that it detracts any from the game.
My one complaint would be with the story at the beginning, as it was a bit hard to follow. The map is also a bit odd to use, but most of the time you won't even see it.
You
have to install Uplay in order to play CoL, which at first I was wary of. However, there are rewards obtainable from Uplay by completing achievements such as in-game items and background art which make it worthwhile.
If you are looking for an RPG with an inspiring soundtrack, beautiful graphics, and a compelling story fit for all ages, be sure to give Child of Light a try.

I want to start out by saying if you enjoy any of the Diablo games, POE,  Torchlight, or played Titan Quest then this game at its $25 price point should be a must buy. It takes all the great things about some of the most popular ARPG's puts them together into one, puts it into a dark and gritty/gothic setting, and lets you loose to enjoy its massive amount of content. Some of the major selling points for me are listed below....
1. It has 6 different selectible classes which can be mixed and matched into pairs of two for 15 different combinations of class selections or there is also the option of just sticking with one class to super level.
2. The main story/playthrough takes roughly 25-35 hours depending on play style and with 3 different difficulties to chose from its highly reccommended to run through the game 3 times (on each difficulty) to hit the end game for just 1 character. They also have the option of "Veteran Mode" which can be enabled and disabled at your leisure on every difficulty to make the game harder and more rewarding.
3. The game has a system called the "Devotion" system which is similar but greater then the Passive Grid in POE. It requires you to make little offerings to Shrines that are hidden throughout the game that award Devotion points that you can use to boost your character and even define builds with unique skills that are only obtainable through Devotion. Like for example one such constellation allows you to summon 3 skeletons just passively as enemies die around you and another has a 20% that every time you get hit Divine light gets called down in an AOE around you dealing damage to enemies.
4.  It also adds in a Faction system which is a total of 11 different factions that all have their own Reputation, bonuses, and disadvantages. All allied factions offer their own unique gear to your character, while all enemy factions learn to hate and despise you the more you kill them. The more they hate you the more spawns they have/Hero spawns they have and then also if you become so disliked by a certain faction they will start to spawn Nemesises which are basicly super bosses for you to fight.
The game has Multiplayer with Instanced Loot (or the option of Free-for-All), Secrets, Item sets, Build diversity, Hardcore mode (for the masochists), crafting, lots of content, replayability,  and everything else an avid ARPG fan could easily get lost in for hundreds of hours. If you're one of the people who love the quest for loot then you need to pick up this game.

My gripes with it are mainly cosmetic, I think the UI could be tidied up a little. A better way to look through books for instance or spellbooks. by the end of the game I had so many books in my inventory, I was sorting them into my bags, but I didnt want to get rid of any of them. this could be solved with a community mod for sure though. Would be nice to have a scrolling list of books and what not, but there are points where u know you have a book that either is used on a quest or has helpful information for a quest and you're stuck mousing over each book to read the titles. Possible my computer is slow, but I have like a 2 second delay for titles to pop up and this becomes tedious for me.
Have similar delays on a lot of other inventory things and stuff. Graphics set on lowest for me also makes it hard to do the quests that have hidden levers and what not. My computer isnt horrible, and the graphics on this game don't seem like leaps and bounds better than neverwinter or anything, so not sure why it was so laggy for me when I tried to up the graphics.
I know I wrote a lot about these few things, as frustrating as they were, i still quite enjoyed the game. I dont mind all the trial and error stuff. The game doesnt hold your hand much so be prepared to take every book or significant object you find for later use. and keep note of each group of npcs and stuff they might be talking about, typically you'll have side quests for an npc sending you to the other side of the zone for stuff.
If you like the old rpgs, you'll probably like this one a lot. Nice to see some kickstarter games having some success.

The Banner Saga is masterful cross between Oregon Trail and XCOM, with emphasis on the former.  It was developed by former BioWare developers that were funded via Kickstarter, and both these features show.
Right away, the level and quality of the animation is top-notch.  Combined with the music and sound design, I half-wish that the developers had just opted to make a long movie or multi-part series instead of a game.  I feel comfortable saying this because while the world is one I want to explore, there's no exposition.  Most characters give their entire story upon meeting them, and only one or two really reveal anything new by the end.  The dialogue they have and the friction between some heroes causes a story, but it's all leudo-narrative that eventually amounts to nothing.
There are three ways in which gameplay exists.  The trail, via decisions, dialogue at places you visit, and in battle.  The first two occupy the same vein perhaps, or one is the vein and the other the artery - both serving the same funciton in different way - but they require different mindsets.  The battles are fine, but the system they have is flimsy.  I fully expect a rework of the battle mechanics in their sequel which has been announced.  All units have health and armor.  Taking a hit to your health reduces your damage, and damage is calculated by first considering armor, then the difference in health.  Units have special abilities that you never fully utilize.  The game is over before you can take advantage of everyone, and you might end up leveling across the board instead of specific characters.  However, each battle was exhilerating from the onset, and I did get better at predicting things over time.  There's just no way to anticipate each battle before hand, as there are too many random factors.  You have to decide which troops you're using before you see the placement of the battlefield or even what you're facing.  That's fine for a game like XCOM where this is negated by varying battlefields and cover, but The Banner Saga doesn't have this.
I'm very interested in playing the sequel to this game.  I feel it'll be done much, much better than the first.  All things considered, if you're a fan of strategy games akin to XCOM and enjoy a game where you decisions have a direct impact on the gameplay, but not the story, this is right up your alley.
