I'm all for minimalist games that can just take one idea and run with it.  In Circa Infinity you venture through layers of circles each offering incremental challenges.  Simply run, jump, and dodge your way through each new challenge as you quickly progress deeper and deeper.  This is very much an arcade style game focusing mostly on high-scores and survival.  As the difficulty ramps up it becomes quite a thrilling experience forcing you to make split second decisions.  Speaking honestly Circa Infinity isn't setting out to reinvent the wheel but it is does manage to spin a new yarn.  Alright, gibberish idioms aside I'll try to make sense of this game.
The gameplay sits at the very core of this experience.  You sometimes play as a man, women, or both running around these large circles.  Starting outside the circles you have to get in through a gate at which point you then proceed to run around the inside.  Inside is a floating ball that will take you to the outside of the next circle pushing the last circle out to towards the corners of your screen.  Its makes a lot more sense once you see it but for now just imagine Alice falling down the rabbit hole.  Of course this wouldn't be much of a game without obstacles in your path, at which point monsters come into the picture.
There are a number of beasts trying to block you from completing your objective.  Actually many of them aren't trying to hard as they just sit around crying or hover without moving.  It will be up to you to jump or roll as necessary to progress.  Eventually you'll encounter more menacing threats such as creatures that chase you around or block our path entirely.  Although colliding with a monster only bumps you back one zone this game is so fast-paced that it is easy chain one mistake after another and end up a handful of zones back.  However, once you feel comfortable with a level and can be fun to go back to either improve your time or try to pass the stage with less deaths.
The minimalist visuals make it much easier to keep track of everything happening on screen at any one time.  You'll only have three or so colors on screen making it easy to distinguish where everything is at any given moment.  This is all super important because it can be very disorienting to keep track of what is your left and right when running around on a round plane.  Thankfully the music is very soothing and will help calm your nerves in what can be quite an intense game.  The sound-effects also fit very nicely and really have a pleasant pop to them.
How much you'll like this game will really depend on the type of gamer you are.  If you want a challenge and you enjoy pushing yourself to perfection then I believe this will be right up your alley.  Even if thats not really your thing there is a lot to admire about this unique concept and its clever art design.  However, this is a really tough game and after about a hour and half I was feeling like I was ready to move on.  I enjoyed the time I spent playing Circa Infinity but I was starting to hit that ceiling of difficulty where the challenge was becoming less fun and more of a chore.  That all being said this is a rather inexpensive game it does need a big host of hours to get your worth out of it.

Circa Infinity's gameplay happens within a bunch of circles. Within each circle, you are faced with a bunch of enemies/obstacles to overcome in order to advance to the next circle. Simple, right? NOPE.
This game gets absolutely challenging as you go (especially if you're gunning for the no deaths achievement). It will constantly introduce increasingly difficult enemies that you have to avoid as you progress, as well as throw sections with different types of enemies. Conquering each section will feel deeply satisfying once you figure it out.
The bosses are rather creative in how you defeat them, and are even more challenging than the rest of the game.
There's also a fun arcade mode where you try to survive an endless gauntlet of enemies, which will give you something to do once you finish the main game.
The game is not without flaws, however. The controls certainly have a learning curve to them, and will make playing more difficult than it already is if you don't get used to it. And sometimes, your jumps won't be enough to get you into the next section of the stage, which can lead to potentially infuriating deaths.
All in all, I think pros outweigh cons here. If you're looking for a real challenge, this game is for you.

Excellent and unpretentious top down roguelike dungeon crawler that's over the top when it comes to fast paced extremely satisfying and gory gameplay. This game is especially good for when you want to sit down and have a quick instant fix of fast action, because matches mostly range between 20-45 minutes, and can even last longer depending on how much you want to level up before facing the boss.
The atmosphere is on point in terms of making you feel as if you're exploring a dank dark dungeon that's haunted by an ancient evil presence, the spirits that haunt you, follow you and possess traps and summon monsters only add to this feeling... there are some references to Lovecraft's work in the level names which is always a nice touch, the rooms and map layouts are randomly generated and every playthrough is different, but unlike many other games with randomly generated rooms you don't start noticing the same variation of a room being repeated until maybe 5 or so hours, there isn't an arbituary set pattern in which you experience rooms either, the only thing that's consistent is that each floor has one store (with each floor having randomly selected different items, making way for different character builds which further ensures each playthrough is unique), one portal that leads to the final boss and one exit that leads to the floor below.... anyway regardless, even if the room layouts aren't always unique... the map layouts are always unique, the repetition of rooms isn't something you're bothered by because you're too busy trying to get the final shot on the hero or you're the hero desperately trying to cling to every last inch of your humanity and you really become absorbed in the addictive gameplay... it's also worth mentioning that the developers are awesome dudes who are very responsive to the community, always respond positively to ideas, negative criticism, and are still constantly showcasing screenshots of different environments / room layouts that are in progress so you can expect to see much more variation in that department in the future, at the rate I see them posting screenshots of new room types, my point on rooms repeating themselves once or twice per match will probably be completely and utterly void by the time this game gets a release... it's also really fun to play single player even if it's designed for co op!

A good game with excellent art and style but a basic combat system. Nice to hear the authentic accents in the few spoken lines and the music is outstanding. The gameplay consists of dialogue choices and a basic turn-based, grid combat system. As with all the best choice based dialogue games, some of the choices are the sort that cause you to sit and think for 30 minutes before selecting something you immediately regret.
The combat is repetitive and once I had a go-to team I found it difficult to break from a routine (giants at the front to smash some up the baddies, archers at the back to pick off the smashed). The combat almost feels like it was added to make the game a game instead of what could have been an excellent interactive story. It beats quick time events I guess but the lack of enemy types makes everything too easy. When got bored of the combat I bumped the Difficulty setting down to Easy only to find out it was the final battle in the game. So, it was good enough for my 10 hour play time.
Everything about the game feels very much like a touch screen was always in the back of the developers minds. This is not a complaint, the play style is perfected suited for dropping in and out to extend what can be a pretty bleak story. The odds are certainly against all of the characters and a string of badly handled choices can result in some miserable  setbacks.
I picked the game up in the Summer sale 2014, excellent value for money. I'm on board for the planned sequels. More spoken dialogue and improved combat would build on the excellent foundation set up with The Banner Saga.

When it's on sale, it's really a no brainer. For less than a buck and a couple of cents you have a lot of quality gamplay!
The Steam version is not the best. The MIDI table they use in the emulator (haven't really looked into what it runs on), is God-awful. But you can just run it through SCUMMVM, and this works so well and easy. Anyway, what are you still doing reading this!? Grab your whip and hat and travel all over the world to unravel the fate of Atlantis! Godspeed!

Updated Review (07/2016):
This game is worth buying if you like dark-themed, turn-based, and linear RPGs, but keep in mind some possible CONS:

-The game is fairly short for an RPG (taking my time, I beat the game in 13 hours on normal difficulty for my first playthrough).
-It has an abrupt and unresolved ending as it is episodic (The Banner Saga 2 continues the story but doesn’t finish it yet).
-It is not an open world if that is what you are looking for—it is linear with auto saves (you cannot choose where and when to save, although each auto save has its own save to access if you want to try something different or screw up).
-The game has a lot of reading involved (you rarely hear a person speak). In fact, this plays out similar to a point-and-click choices count story, but the turn-based fights in-between reading provide excellent strategic game play that typical point-and-click games do not.
With that said, many PROS to the game include:
-The story is dark but creative and refreshing with a unique feel and well-developed characters (be prepared to laugh, curse, and possibly cry).
-The dialogue and choices are often entertaining and feel realistic for the setting (the little bit of voice acting in the game is excellent).
-The art and score are beautiful.
-The game play/turn-based fights are addictive, and the fights even get a little challenging on the normal setting (I cursed at my monitor A LOT on hard mode, but I also like the challenge).
The game is worth multiple plays not only for achievements, but to also try out different choices as they can have a fairly large impact on the story that can transfer to the second game (The Banner Saga 2 gives you the option to continue your saves from the first game). Even though I have completed all of the achievements and played the game many times, I will probably play the game again. :]

I first played this game as a child, at the start of the adventure game craze.  I bought it on Steam because of the fond memories I have of playing it back then, and it's always been my favorite Lucas Arts title.  Being an adventure game, the pace is usually whatever you happen to play it as.  In addition, it was one of the earlier popular titles that featured a choice of play styles- one can choose fairly early on to play the puzzle, teamwork, or action pathways.
There are some things to poke holes in it.  The graphics are clearly from the early 90s and haven't held up as well as I'd hoped, although they are still servicable.  Some of the backgrounds are actually quite well done and it's only in detailed images that the quality is lacking.  In addition, the voice acting is not that good.  Since the subtitles are defaulted to on, though, one can simply put on some music and mute the actual game.
The biggest problem is that the controls on the Steam version don't work as well as those in the original version.  Since most of the time, you're simply going to be pointing and clicking, it doesn't make much difference.  However, fight sequences (which are much more common on the action pathway) may be difficult until you get the hang of the odd control scheme.
Those issues aside, the story is comparable to the movies (and better than Crystal Skull).  Most players will likely be able to complete a playthrough in several hours, but there is a save game feature should you need multiple sittings.  This is a fun game that all adventure game fans should at least try out.

Alright, so about 60-70 hours after starting my cooperative adventure with a friend, and completing the game, I think it is appropriate that I write my review of Divinity: Original Sin. Some quick context, we played the game with double lone wolf characters(A fighter and a wizard) on medium difficulty. Your experience with combat balance may vary.
First, let me start off by saying that this game is fun... Like REALLY fun. However, this is less of a game, and more of an experience. Let me explain what I mean by that. First of all, the combat is incredibly enjoyable. Every encounter feels hand crafted to give players a new strategic scenario almost every time. This was a real draw of the game for the friend I was playing with. As he put it, "it was one of the few games that actually makes a wizard feel like a wizard."
The draw for me however, was the world itself. I was in awe at this game's sense of wonder, while still remaining light hearted and humorous at times. It brought me back to childhood memories such as reading "The Hobbit" for the very first time. As the game went on, things got dark... Like really dark. It was probably my own fault for being so caught up in the game world, but I felt physically sick at times. This gave me a real drive to find the evil, and destroy it (trying not to be too spoilery).
I've seen a lot of people complain about the endless dialogue in this game, and I can understand that, but I think it depends on what you are looking for coming into this game. I adored all of the dialogue, and being able to interact with this fantasy world that truly felt alive. Luckily, for my friend that didn't enjoy that all that much was able to find entertainment out of the combat encounters, and since we were playing on coop, I could do all of the dialogue work for him.
Now, lets talk problems with the game. First of all, the game still feels like it needs to be worked on (IE missing content, and bugs). The good news about that is... It's still being worked on. Bugs and imbalances that I've found one day, I found were patched the next.
A couple of the puzzles in the game straight up feel unfair. I feel no guilt in having to have looked up a couple answers online, as some of them were simply frusterating for reasons that could have been otherwise avoided.
There are a few problems with clarity. I know this is suppose to be a hard-core game, not for those with a casual approach, but some things are just tedious, not challenging, nor do they help engage you with the world. The biggest example of this is inventory management. A simple fix would be to have a separate tab, similar to the keys tab, for ALL quest items. That way you aren't having to manage important quest items with loot, and you don't accidently sell any of those quest items. Even the sidequest items.
Something else I should touch on is the editor. This thing brings a ton of extra value to Divinity. Whether you're a modder yourself, or you just want to play someone elses adventure. There are still some problems with it, but the development team has been supporting it quite strongly from what I've seen so far.
Conclusion/tl;dr:
This is all from my own experience and perspective.

Ok, so I have a few hours into this game now. I want to impress upon you exactly how this game made me feel. I was a bit undecided at first; an ARPG style, turn-based combat, story-driven game with so much dialogue. At first I thought about how terrible this could go but then I thought about how epic it could be as well.
Upon buying, and trying, Divinity I wasn't all that impressed. It is as if my initial preceptions of the game carried on "into" the game. The game felt a bit slow at first but picked up pace dramatically as I gained the power to start exploring the first area. By the end of the first section I was completely in love with this game and how the combat works. The story is drizzled on thick like syrup on pancakes.
TL:DR Skip here
The combat in the game is slow at first but picks up pace. What I mean to say is, at early level you are extremely limited on choices for your characters. Being unable to make a lot of combos makes combat seem... unexciting. But, as you gain levels, gear, and skills/abilities, your strategic choices explode exponentially. The difference between 1-5 is like the difference between checkers and chess.
The quests can be completed in multiple ways. You can chose to do step 3 before step 2, or even step 1, and start the quest there. The outcomes can be different, which changes the story a lot. There is tons of secret stuff to find in this game if you are interested in that sort of thing. The way they hide tiny little keys and npcs is extrodinary.
In light of everything it is not a perfect game. As I have said before, combat is slow. Strategic combat can be both frustrating and boring. If you don't catch onto how spells work together early on you won't leave the starting area. The story dialogue is great in some areas and, in other areas, written like a low budget vampire flick. And, the dialogue can drag on.. and on... and on.
For 40 dollars though and the ability to close dialogue boxes, you would be worse off not having tried this game. If you are a fan of old school rpgs, and wish you had one designed for a modern audience. Then you have struck gold with Divinity. I don't know that I would give it a 9/10 but it scores at least a 7/10. This game is worth it for the money.

Child of Light is a great story with BEAUTIFUL graphics and artwork!
There ..... i just summed it up in one sentence ..... but if that wasn't enough to convince you, I'll go ahead and go into a little more detail.
Story: As i said it's an awesome story.  You play as a "princess" who has been poisoned and wakes up in another world.  You're main gold is to return to YOUR world to save your father who has become deathly ill with grief over your "death".  One thing that is very different but i thought was nice was that all the dialogue between the characters and the narrator were done in poem/balad type format.  So yes, it all rhymed lol.  I suppose you could say it added to the "Immersion" factor in the sense that people don't really TALK like that anymore.
Graphics: Lovely hand-drawn backgrounds and characters.
Gameplay: Child of Light is built upon the framework of a classic turn-based RPG, but also uses the often seen "Move bar", making combat slightly more dynamic and interactive than just "pick move, use move".  Using your little firefly elemental you can slow down enemies to make your moves go first or fall in just the right place on the move bar to be most effective.
The skill trees for all the characters are EXPANSIVE but simplistic at the same time.  You can look ahead and see where you are going so you can plan out exactly what you want the character to do for your group, whether more damage focused or control or healing.  Each character (and there are several you will unlock during your journey) has primarily 3 skill trees that expand after you recover the moon in the game.  Most skills cost only one skill point which you get each time you gain a level and once you get the expansion some of the advance skills cost 2 points.  You gain levels fairly quickly and even if you don't use a character in battle it still levels up with the whole party.  I finished with most of my characters being low to high 40s.
After the initial "tutorial" area, and you unlock your flight ability, navigating the world becomes a breeze.  The controls to fly and control that flight are simple and intuitive.  You really get the sense of freedom as you explore every nook and cranny for hidden secrets and chests.
I think I've said enough.  If i haven't convinced you to give this game a play by now then nothing more i say is going to make a difference.
This game is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!!!

In comparison to the original Killing Floor the sequel is a huge leap forward.
The visuals and overall presentation of the game is vastly improved when compared to the first.
But more importantly, the gameplay is like the original while still taking a step past its predecessor. The feel of the game is honestly quite unlike any other games I've seen before it.
Killing Floor 2 does this so well it should be used as an example to teach game dev students on how to make every animation from a first person view feel real. This applies to everything between when a character gets hit by a Zed to how the recoil of the weapons cause the character and camera to move.
KF2 also happens to fix one of the biggest hardships from the original, the leveling system. In KF1 the max level was 6, with the key way of leveling being to kill specific enemies with specific weapons for whatever perk you were playing as. This resulted in leveling being incredibly slow and tedious, while also being incredibly necessary for harder difficulties.
On the other hand, KF2 fixes the issue by increasing the level cap to 25, allowing for specific enemies and perk weapons to simply boost the amount of EXP while playing, and giving the player a choice between two different skills for every 5 levels they gain in a perk (which can be changed freely between rounds).
This fix makes the game far more fun to play as leveling doesn't feel like a chore, progression isn't nearly as slow, and each level up feels rewarding as every 5th level allows the player to further customize their play style.
Finally, there is a loot drop and loot box system in the game. So far as I've played, it has never once felt like it was a requirement to pay to unlock a box as everything inside is simply cosmetic. As an added bonus unwanted crates (cosmetic boxes) or USBs (weapon skin boxes) can be broken down to crafting material and then recrafted into a higher tier item at every 10 material. And for those of us on a tight budget the recently included Vault and daily/weekly goals are a way of unlocking both free loot boxes and cosmetics, which not only gives incentive to play but also feels rewarding to complete enough goals to unlock a new item.
The only downside of this system, is that the usual in game drops (excluding daily and weekly) can feel a little sparse, with only a drop or two a day (outside of seasonal events).
Overall I'd give Killing Floor 2 a very high recommendation, especially if you have friends to play it with.

We may only be ten days into the new year, but I’m convinced that The Banner Saga (developed by Stoic) will be one of the best games that I play this year. I powered through the campaign in just about 8 hours, but there is much room for revisiting and deep immersion. Without further ado, let’s have at it.
I – Story [10/10]
I don’t want to say too much here for fear of ruining the story for those who haven’t played and/or finished the game. A very basic synopsis of the story may be the best course of action. It is, effectively, the end of the world and you (the player) are left to explore it through two separate (but equally bleak) story-lines. The story-telling is great and the characters are incredibly well done. This is a harrowing journey from start to finish and I enjoyed every second of it.
II – UI [9/10]
The user interface was well implemented and easy to use. I never found myself struggling to figure out where something was that I needed to access or something I needed to check on. Sometimes, in combat, the UI can be a bit in the way, but not enough to cause any real annoyance. Even the menus (both in-game and main) were setup equally well.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
The story of The Banner Saga was incredible and the gameplay is the vehicle through which the player gets to experience it. As desperately as I wished for TBS to be non-linear, it was linear. That being said, it was executed very well and without hiccups. There isn’t much control-wise that the player will need to master as the mouse is your only form of interaction.
As far as strategy goes in-game, you may learn it easily, but it will take a long time to master. There are several different classes of characters you will pick up along the way and each one has it’s strengths and weaknesses. Knowing what those are can mean everything in combat. Combat is unforgiving, even on the lowest difficulty, and any mistake on the player’s part can have disastrous consequences. If you’re not thinking ahead in this one, it’s going to cost you.
IV –  Content [6/10]
While The Banner Saga is absolutely teeming with story content, the physical, in-game content was a bit lacking. The lack of character customization was completely fine, there was a story to tell and the characters needed to be just who they were. But, as I mentioned above, the game is very linear, leaving only your in-game choices to ripple out and affect the progression and end of the story.
To my disappointment though, while there were items you could equip to your characters to provide buffs for combat, that was the extent of equipping your party members. I wish there could have been more in-depth customization of character equipment, but that is only a small gripe.
There was also a lack of class development. While each class had their own set ability(ies), ranking up allowed you to only upgrade character stats and increase the existing abilities. There wasn’t much room to explore class-wise.
V – Visual [10/10]
The graphics in TBS were very unique and deeply pleasing on an aesthetic level. Everything visual in the game was done by hand; hand-painted landscapes, hand-animated battle sequences, etc. It gave it that homey feel of a novel come to life right before your eyes.
VI – Audio [10/10]
All of the auditory components were great. While there wasn’t much by way of voice-acting (the vast majority of the game’s story is told through written dialogue) it does nothing the interfere with the feel of the game. The music was fantastic and sound effects, both in and out of combat, were just great.
VII – Overall [9.2/10]

More and more I'm realizing just how much I love tactical rpgs.  The ability to take your time and plan out your moves is very relaxing despite some of the incredibly tense situations you're put in.  This is especially true in The Banner Saga.  In this game the odds are almost always against you.  There are many very tough battles and a lot of very tough decisions to make.  That said, this game does feature a very clever combat system that is quite enjoyable once you get the hang out it.  And although the story is quite bleak the characters and decisions you make will really get you drawn into this wonderful experience.
The story has things looking more and more like the end of days.  You have three species of characters; humans, varl and dredge.  The varl are gigantic, about four times bigger than the humans.  A long time a go the two species had been at war but the appearance dredge force them to unite.  The dredge appear to be a robotic species and little is known about them.  The humans and varl have defeated them twice before but this time their numbers seem relentless.  What makes the story much more personal is the characters you meet and the choices you are faced with.  Choices such as who to let join your caravans, how to handle tension between clansman, and what tactics to take when dredge appear.
The tactical combat system featured in The Banner Sage is fairly easy to learn but provides for incredibly challenging and rewarding gameplay.  Battles take place on standard flat square grids with a little variety forced by the limited starting positions.  Once the battle has started the player and enemy will always rotate turns unless someone is down to just on character.  This is really interesting as its a valuable strategy to keep enemies weaken but not kill them.   The strength stat determines how much damage you can deal and it doubles as your health.  This makes The Banner Saga on of the most realistic RPGs because as characters lose health they become weaker.  Armor reduces the amount of damage that can be done to a characters strength.  Go after armor to make it easier to hit characters but risk them doing more damage.  You also have willpower to either activate special abilities, enhance standard attacks, or gain extra movement.
As you defeat enemies and make smart decisions you're rewarded renown points.  Renown is extremely valuable as you need it to buy food, items, and promote your allies.  If you ever don't have enough food to feed your caravan at the end of each day you'll lose clansman and fighters from starvation.  Also you won't want to rest and recover morale when you know you'll going to lose people.  You can equip one item per character and the higher their level the better the equipment you can give them.  Some items give you extra strength or willpower after every turn, while resting, or after a kill.  Promoting your allies not only lets them equip better items but is essential for raising their stats and making them more useful in combat.  You'll first need to get a set number of kills before you'll be able to promote them.
This is just a wonderfully unique videogame bursting with personality.  The visuals have a very stylized look and fit the world perfectly.  The story and the choices you have to make really draw you in and make you vested in the well being of your caravans.  The combat system is super polished and really rewards clever tacticians.  I only wish it kept going but thankfully this is just the first chapter of a trilogy.  Also this kind of game highly promotes being replayed to try and make better decisions and have more prosperous run-throughs.  I really can't think of anything I don't love about this game.  After playing it on both PS4 and PC I highly recommend sticking to PC over consoles as this was clearly designed to be played with a mouse and keyboard.  Either way don't let this masterpiece slip by.

With FTL: Faster Than Light being very cheap to pick up here on Steam I would say you're getting a bargain, along with a free "Advanced Edition" [AE] for everyone with the game, with no catches; requisites or bugs.
The [AE] includes a new ship which features a new race called the "Lanius" (a force to definitely not to be reckoned with). The Lanius are able to survive without the aid of oxygen (how neat!) meaning that engaging in melee combat with these fiercesome foes may prove to be a bit tougher than you assumed.
The [AE] also come with three new upgrades for your ship, a Battery, which supplies you with reactor power for a limited time, a Mind Control system which allows you you take control and a hostile for a period of time (pretty self explanatory, eh?) and a Hacking device, allowing you to drain the power output of a system on your enemy's ship!
The [AE] also supplies you with some aethestetic touchs too, such as new soundtracks and background during your pillaging. Along with that it also adds a third variation of all the ships! (Excluding the Lanius cruiser and Crystal Cruiser) Allowing you to have a much more challenging plight across the galaxy, as their loadouts and crew members change once again. If that wasn't enough there is now also a "Hard" mode! (Like "Normal" wasn't hard enough!) Letting you take that one extra step to see you really can best the Rebels.
If you think the "Advanced Edition" is not your thing, then it is very easy to disable it and play as you would in the past. This just eliminates everything that comes with the [AE].
If I have not won you over entirely however you're slightly interested I would recommened going over to YouTube and watching some Let's Plays of FTL: Faster Than Light, so you are able to see what this is all about in front of you.

-Negatives

=Conclusion

is a fairly unique asymmetric strategy game in which the player(s) are looking to destroy the two AI command stations somewhere in the  10-120 planet map. Scouting, defense and working out the best routes to the target along with the stops on the way to pick up new technologies and ship types all becomes important as the AI grows stronger the more trouble you're causing.
When adding on the many variables of map generation, especially the many ai personalities, options and plots as well as the many ship types you can start with. It makes for a lot of replayability, as figuring out a good strategy by comparing the challenges and available bonuses will be a bit different each time. The increasing difficulty as the game goes on also helps alleviate the common trends of mopping up in many strategy games.
The game also features an excellent soundtrack which works very well setting the tone for the game.
The Low price for the game along with the high replayability makes it very easy to recommend for anyone who enjoys strategy games, especially if you can get someone to play with as the game supports up to 8 players Co-op.

Little Nightmares is a puzzle-platformer horror adventure game.The aim of the game is to guild a small Yellow raincoated character through a Ocean facility with a slowly revealed purpose.The gameplay is intense and you are always hiding from the creatures roaming the rooms whilst trying to solve small puzzles to get to the next area.The Game is around 5 to 6 hours long but contains puzzles that keep you scratching your head for awhile.

Certainly one of the better Hyperdimension games this series has great potential it still hasn't quite lived up to... still as is - a great JRPG Experience. This first installment feels... shorter than the game its remaking but that may have less to do with the game and my own experence with Victory knowing exactly what to do...
As a remake it takes the entire combat system from the first game and chucks it in a bin, replacing it with the more enjoyable combat system seen in later installements.
For those not familiar the combat system usually involves a party of three(Four in later games) being placed inside a circular area - characters are able to move freely and you're encouraged to keep them spaced apart as enemies can and will hit multiple targets cluster together - and you're free to do the same. A usual array of special attacks, skills and ultimates are there to fill the standard kit - however your normal attacks are broken up into "Combos" which can be fiddled with and swapped around to your liking.
Neptunia also keeps its notable game references and forth wall breaking humor. I personally enjoy the campness of the story and chracters, its what kept me with the franchise so far. Its lighthearded tone and utter refusal to take itself - or indeed anything else seriously is closer to a breath of freash air than most of the dower affairs I've seen on the release list lately.
Take it as a bit of unchallening junk food - like the JRPG equivelent of Dynasty Warriors.

I can't help but imagine how amazing it would be for Faith to be able to just step outside a safe house, plant 2 feet on the ground, put in some headphones and just... run. Since the release of Civ VI is right around the corner might as well review this game because if i'm hopeful i'll never have to play it again because this game's successor is a great game. Civ V can generally guarentee a unique experience every playthrough if you let it, and this is coming from a guy with 800+ hours in the game. I've seen tiles that were square, i've seen nuclear wars between the Iraquoise and Romans, yet i can promise i didn't even see everything this game can offer. The game's singleplayer is great in that the vast combinations of other ai you play with (or against) is quite high, you can even select which civs you want in your playthrough so you can spice it up. With the two expansions the singleplayer experience is safe to say at it's maximum potential, the only glaring issue is that as time progresses with any game metas are discovered, and you may fall into a pattern of how you play the game, but that pattern is always up to you anyways. The multiplayer of this game is chaos, and it's some damn fun chaos. I've played this game multiplayer with multiple different groups of friends, but primarily one select group, and the total MP games i've played can probably go up to 100. The total games i've seen finished? Like 6. The multiplayer in this game is great because it offers a tool you really can't use in singleplayer, which is communication. The last multiplayer game my friends and i will ever do of this game was about 2 weeks ago, and right from the get-go a certain warmongerer city-state ♥♥♥♥er (who we can just call Rome) was already way ahead. All our science per turn were at least 100 below his, and our armies were no where near as advanced as his. I had pikeman, he had rifleman. This game was played with 4 people, and it eventually panned out to be a two v two. My partner and i quickly realized without our combined efforts we would lose the game handidly and planned out Rome's demise. Towards the conclusion of the game (though it never finished whatasurprise) we took out his only ally, ruined his happiness, dominated world congress, caught up in tech, and together far outnumbered his military. Due to just one added method of gameplay the game already was enhanced an amazing amount, i have many more examples where i was able to manipulate the chat with other specific people, and add another layer to espionage with just simple text. All in all the game is an amazing experience, and it served me well for the 4+ years i played it. The expansions are a must and you'll be super happy with them. I hope to see Civ VI have the ability to engage me, my friends, and so many others that fell in love with this franchise with endless hours of fun and joy.

i haven't finished this yet, but hour after hour of intense enjoyment has convinced me that this game is great!
art/style:
the world is a watercolor painting that moves fluidly and beautifully.  each different part of the world has new flora and fauna, and its own color scheme.  the many layers make the world look deep and rich, despite movement being strictly 2D.  the lighting brings everything up to an incredible level of beauty.  the allies, enemies, and various populants are unique and designed with great care.  detailed in aethetics and given creative abilities, all the characters contribute something to the feel of the game.  i could easily spend half the game just looking around and exploring the world.  in fact, i did...
10/10
combat:
i have not actually played a Final Fantasy game (a problem i hope to remedy), but the combat is similar in many ways.  it's turn-based battling with various abilities frequently based on elements.  the turns are determined by a timeline-ish mechanic that is also influenced by abilities, which added a very interesting twist to an already solid system.  the mix of all the characters' unique styles of play blend VERY well together even though only two allies can play at a time.  i was a bit disappointed by this initially, but you can pretty easily switch allies during battles, so i ended up feeling okay about it.  there are potions for those that enjoy such things, but i try to do without them if i can help it.
9/10
non-combat gameplay:
there are a few "puzzles" in the game, but they are so simple that it they hardly qualify as such.  fortunately, i never felt like this was why i was supposed to play the game.  there are quests to go on that are basically "go find a few things scattered in places you've been in".  not too crazy, but i enjoyed the opportunity to explore and actually be rewarded for it beyond the fun of checking out all the nooks and crannies.  some could get impatient and bored by visiting old locations, but the quests are decidedly optional, so i wouldn't be too concerned by that.  the map isn't very fancy, but the locations are designed very well and feel very different from one another.  the upgrade tree is interesting, but mostly linear: you pretty much always have three upgrade paths to continually advance without any more options than that.  again, i like the abilites they unlock, you just don't have quite as many options as i prefer.
7/10
story/plot:
the plot isn't necessarily anything crazy or too original (yet), but it isn't really lacking either.  all words are in verse, so that's pretty fantastic!  the characters have bits of dialog often and the narrator will occasionally chime in.  the characters aren't amazingly rich and deep, but they are developed enough to care about them.  it made me enjoy helping them out whenever i could.  basically, the story does advance, and there's been a couple of fun twists, but nothing that really blew my mind.  so it's a entertaining plot with solid characters, but it's maybe not the main reason you should play this game.
8/10
music:
pretty music that really compliments the game, just not sure if it'd be good standing alone.  adds greatly to the feel of wonder and fantasy as you play, though...
8/10
overall:
i have loved every minute of this game.  i've found it to be very well balanced, beautifully made, follows a dandy tale, and is filled with plenty of likable characters.  i haven't yet seen the ending, but so far, i look forward to playing it again on its "hard" setting after finishing the "normal" one...
in my opinion, MORE THAN WORTH THE $15 I PAID FOR IT!!  i'll definitely be buying the Golem's Plight pack when i'm finished with the main game...

Legimately one of the best games I have played in a long time.
Gameplay:
- There is a fairly steep learning curve because the tutorial doesn't cover many of the game aspects, but that seems to be a part of the game's charm.  Either figure it out yourself or give in and look up a Youtube video.
- The strategy for each battle needs to be taken seriously.  Additionally, most battles are essentially decided within the first couple rounds given positioning and whether or not your first couple crowd control spells knocked down/charmed/muted the enemy.
Pros
- A lot of customization to your character.
- Great looking gear that improves over time.
- Strategic interaction between different elements and traps/items on the battlefield.  Fire igntes poison, electricity stuns everyone in a body of water, fire burns, dousing an enemy in water exposes an enemy to freezing or eletricifcation, etc.  Often losing a battle only requires a detailed analysis of the battlefield to see a couple oil barrels.  Wait a turn for the enemy to advance, douse this area with poison boulders and launch a fireball.  It can be really satisfying to lose a battle and then subsequently win without even being hit.
- The plot is pretty interesting.  The side characters are developed well.
- Teleporting mages to your front line and having Madora carve them up.  That sounds specific, but if you play Divinity you will know what I mean.  It doesn't get old.  Trust me.
Cons
- Certain spells are absolutely essential (especially on Hard difficulty) and this generally means that many other spells or abilities will never be used.  There does appear to be a strong need for cost balancing on the under utilized spells.  For example, the spell Teleport kicks serious fing buttocks.  However, spells like Earth Shield are terrible and for their cost will likely not be used.  This could be remedied by a large cost reduction and an upgrade to the underutilized abilities.
- Some of the puzzles are solved in a manner that doesn't stay true to the puzzle (and seem very arbitrary).
- There are some bugs with pathing where your characters will refuse to move, move into bizarre battle positioning immediately before the battle, or simply get stuck.  Fortunately this game encourages constant game saving/loading so when that happens you just reload.
Overall Great Game.

It had a rocky development period, but the end result is an excellent co-op (or solo, if you choose) FPS around killing zeds that could arguably surpass the original Killing Floor. My favorite parts about this game are the weapons and gore. The guns are extremely satisfying to shoot and very well animated; you'll find yourself spamming reload between waves to watch their idle and twirl animations. The gore is also excellent: shooting up or slashing zeds up and watching their brains explode or bodies get sawed in half has never been more satisfying in any other zombie game. These two elements are the game's strongest, but that's not to say that the gameplay itself is lacking. Sure, it might be repetitive, with it being a wave-based game, but thankfully we have the community to make new maps, and TripWire making new content to keep the game fresh and alive.
Overall, Killing Floor 2 is probably my favorite co-op FPS game, which is a rather niche and specific genre, but a genre that I ardour nonetheless.

I believe this is one of the most solid asymmetric PvP games I've played. At the current moment there isn't a huge amount of content, but the devs do add fairly meaty updates every few weeks. That being said, the mechanics of the game are solid, the way gaining and losing possession of the hero works is an example of good balance mechanisms. It's like a negative feedback loop where the longer you stay as either ghost or hero, the easier it is to kill the hero and be killed respectively.
And man does it have style. The music, the ever-present (aesthetic only) glitchiness, it actually makes me feel nostalgic. You can tell what the devs were going for and I think they nailed it. Some people see pixelated art as an excuse for spending less time animating, but the pixel art in this game is made by someone who obviously takes the style seriously, because it actually has a very distinct character and the animations are deceptively smooth for the resolution.
I think this one was very well worked, but looking for a balance yet.
It's a surprisingly fun game when played with friends.

If you are looking for a good narrative with plenty of lore and some solid tactical gameplay that doesn't choose to destroy you because a random number generator said so (I'm looking at you XCOM) then this is the game for you. The Banner Saga  enthralled me with its art style and music and the combat, which seemed likely to grow stale, was engaging throughout. The benefits gained from engaging the enemy are balanced between wanting them and needing them. I never chose to take the easy way out and run from a battle because fighting and winning would mean leveling up my heroes and feeding the caravan.
The most common complaint I've heard about this game is that your choices ultimately do not matter. I'll just say this, I've never played a game where your choices "really matter". The choices made here determine who is with you in the end game and also add flavor to the journey overall. However, I can say that making a lot of bad choices in the game will most likely cause you to hit the final boss battle like a stone wall. This leads to my only real gripe with the game.
The final boss battle. The last half hour of the game for me, which would have likely been longer if my characters were not prepared, lost any real feeling of tactics and became reloading until I figured out how best to exploit the battle. But 30 minutes of slight frustration really cannot be viewed as game-breaking since the other 12-15 hours of gameplay were completely enjoyable.
The Banner Saga gets a big recommendation from me. It's worth it's full retail price and becomes a must own at sale price.

If you have never played Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis, but you do enjoy the point-and-click adventure games of old, you owe it to yourself to play this one.
In typical Lucasarts Adventure game fashion, there is humor spread throughout this great journey where twists and turns are abound. Even better, the entire game is voice acted, and the environments and locales you will travel to are varied and colourful. The puzzles and solutions are generally smart and not too arbitrary, and it really feels like an Indiana Jones adventure. There is also replayability added in the mix, as there are three "paths" you can play through that completely changes the puzzles and interactions you will face throughout the course of the game.
However, this is a port of the old DOS game. This means, that the resolution is very tiny, and if you can't accept the pixellation that comes with trying to stretch the image, then that is unfortunate. However, don't let the old visuals, which still looks decent due to it's stylized form, detract you from going on an incredible adventure across the world!

the Banner Saga does a good job capturing a nordic spirit: it's beautiful but harsh, and really soul-crushing at times.
besides having to manage your caravan so everybody doesn't die, the game puts a somewhat different spin on the usual turn-based combat mechanics: armor has to be worn down before decent hp damage can be done, and hitpoints double as the attack strength characteristic. additionally, willpower lets characters push themselves further and execute special attacks depending on their class. it works well but can be a litte unforgiving of mistakes, tactics are important.
the decisions you have to make outside of combat are harsh as well - things that look like they worked out fine at first can turn around to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥later, and that includes character progression. the return of those points you spent on your hero isn't that great if they're dead or gone... you might start second-guessing a lot, but you won't really be safer for it. which makes for a rather captivating if depressing story.
I really liked the art, and the soundtrack adds nicely to the atmosphere, becoming more prominent when it is fitting.
the overarching story is interesting and makes numerous references to a rich lore - too bad that answers aren't something you'll get. this is part of what makes the rather abrupt ending somewhat unsatisfying, sadly one of the Banner Saga's weaker points. still...
it's not a perfect game, but I'd definitely recommend it!

Odds are, if you're looking at this game, you already know it's a classic, or you played it way back in the day when it first came out.
Honestly, as far as adventure games go, this one still stands out as one of the early giants of the genre. The way it allows the player to actively choose different routes based on play style is something I'm not sure I've seen since, and I think other games in the modern era could stand to take a page from that.
Graphically, the game may look behind the times, but wrapped up in it all is a classic Indiana Jones video game experience that changes itself up each time in order to not be too predictable. If you're a fan of the genre, give it a try.
